stories.title: University of Toronto launching $100-million scholarship fund to attract PhD students
stories.summary: New program aims to help school compete for bright minds at a time when elite U.S. universities are under attack by the Trump administration
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
The University of Toronto is launching a $100-million scholarship fund for PhD students that will double the pay of recipients and help the school compete for bright minds at a time when elite U.S. universities are under attack by the Trump administration.

The new U of T program, unveiled Monday, will see the university recruit 12 or 13 new PhD candidates a year to conduct cross-disciplinary research on a predetermined theme, such as sovereignty and the Arctic, or health and artificial intelligence.

Winners will be paid $80,000 a year for four years, twice the current minimum base funding for PhD candidates at U of T. Half of the $100-million endowment comes from an anonymous donation, the rest from the university.

“We’ve got an unprecedented opportunity right now to bring back Canada’s best and keep Canada’s best here,” U of T president Melanie Woodin said in an interview. “The Prime Minister has spoken about the prioritization of talent as it relates to Canada’s economic resiliency and sovereignty, and as Canada’s flagship university, we’re fully aligned because we’re in the talent business.”

The new U of T awards are called the Presidents’ Impact Scholarships. If the name sounds familiar, it could be because Mark Carney’s Liberal government last year promised $1.7-billion over 12 years for an academic recruiting blitz with a similar moniker – The Canada Global Impact+ Research Talent Initiative.

That federal campaign is part of a wider push by Canada’s top-flight universities and hospitals to capitalize on uncertainty at postsecondary institutions south of the border. Donald Trump’s government has cut funding for scientific and scholarly research, sued top universities and expressed a general disdain for science.

The infusion of public funding and attention for science and scholarship in Canada is also something of a departure from the past.

In 2023, an advisory panel’s report on the federal research support system found the funding dispersed by Canada’s three main granting councils – the Canadian Institutes of Health Research; the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada; and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada – had “not kept pace with evolving needs” or with Canada’s international competitors.

One of the shortfalls the report singled out was pay to graduate students, which they often receive via their professors’ grants.

The panel, led by Frédéric Bouchard, dean of the faculty of arts and sciences at the University of Montreal, concluded that financial support for graduate students in Canada was “at a breaking point.” The value of Ottawa’s awards for university research trainees had been stagnant for two decades, the panel’s report noted.

The new U of T scholarship program is an acknowledgment that paltry pay for graduate students can be a barrier to doctoral research, especially for those who have racked up debt as undergraduates or who are considering leaving the private sector to pursue a PhD, Dr. Woodin said.

She added that the Presidents’ Impact Scholarships will be, to U of T’s knowledge, the most lucrative PhD funding package in Canada. “Globally, it puts us pretty close to the top – so above Princeton, Harvard, Cambridge and Oxford,” Dr. Woodin said.

All that said, pay packages are just one of many factors that promising PhD candidates weigh when choosing a university.

U of T is hoping candidates for the new scholarship will be enticed by the interdisciplinary nature of the awards, which require doctoral students to work with two faculty supervisors from different disciplines.

For stem cell scientist Derrick Rossi, a Canadian co-founder of the pharmaceutical company Moderna Inc., money didn’t matter as much as living somewhere interesting and finding a PhD program that was the best fit for him.

He studied at U of T before moving to Paris and ultimately getting his PhD at the University of Helsinki.

More important, Dr. Rossi said in an interview, is the message that U of T is sending with a large scholarship for doctoral students.

“The U.S. government right now is very anti-science,” he said. “The signal that [U of T] is sending to the globe is that Canada is not anti-science and we’re serious about science.”

stories.title: London Knights blown out in first loss of season
stories.summary: The Flint Firebirds have put an end to the London Knights (4-1) perfect start to the Ontario Hockey League season.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The Flint Firebirds have put an end to the London Knights (4-1) perfect start to the Ontario Hockey League season.

The Firebirds came into Canada Life Place Sunday and pounded London 7-2.

Outshooting the Knights 35-24, the visitors chased starting goaltender Aleksei Medvedev from the net after five goals in early in the third period.Jimmy Lombardi had a goal and four assists for the Firebirds to earn first star honours.

London’s Thomas Zocco had his fourth goal of the year, while rookie defenceman Juho Piiparinen scored his first career goal.

stories.title: Missing for 22 years: Frank Davis found in Kootenay River
stories.summary: For 22 years, the disappearance of Frank Davis remained an unanswered mystery for his family. Frank was 40 when he went missing from Creston, B.C.
stories.author: Cohan Sassaman
stories.content:
For 22 years, the disappearance of Frank Davis remained an unanswered mystery for his family.

Davis was 40 when he went missing from Creston , B.C., leaving behind loved ones who would spend years wondering what happened to him.

Now, a team of divers called Adventures with Purpose uncovered a discovery beneath the waters of the Kootenay River near Creston: Frank’s car, flipped upside down at the bottom of the river, with his remains inside.

The divers start by identifying a person’s last known location and using available information to map out potential areas where their vehicle May have entered the water. The team then uses sonar to scan beneath the surface, methodically ruling out locations until they find a lead.

For Davis, the search stretched into its eighth hour before the team located his car on the opposite side of the river.

“The 11th search was where his car was on the other side of the river. We can work very fast,” said Bryon Leisek, a diver with Adventures With Purpose.

Adventures with Purpose is an American dive team known for its YouTube channel, where it documents searches for missing people and vehicles believed to be underwater.

The team works with families and law enforcement to help bring answers to long-unsolved cases and doesn’t charge the families or police departments for its recovery searches.

For families who have spent years wondering what happened to a loved one, the team’s work can help provide answers and a sense of closure.

For Davis’ brother, Reid Davis, the discovery brought back a ton of emotions. After 22 years without answers, Reid says he had almost stopped believing he would ever know what happened.

“It was numbing at first; after so long, you kind of think that you’re not going to have this moment ever, and then just a flood of memories again, all these things that you kind of put away over the years,” Reid said.

Now, Reid hopes the family can move forward by sharing stories about Frank, especially with his youngest son, who was just two years old when his father disappeared.

Frank’s niece, Lenelle Davis, remembers being young when he disappeared. But she has not forgotten the uncertainty that followed, especially for her grandmother, Frank’s mother, who died without knowing what happened to her son.

“How could you ever have any peace not knowing what has happened to your child?” Lenelle said. “I always felt heartbroken for her.”

While the discovery has finally answered where Davis was found, it has not explained exactly how he ended up in the river.

Kade Pigg, a producer with Adventures With Purpose, said the team believes the car went into the water near the abandoned ferry crossing.

“We just determined the where, not the why,” Pigg said.

Police say Davis’ death is not considered suspicious and foul play is not suspected.

For his family, the discovery means they no longer have to wonder where Frank was. As Lenelle put it, there is relief in knowing “he’s home and he’s resting and we’re just not wondering.”

stories.title: Alberta separatists’ talks with GOP spark call for change from Calgary Liberal MP
stories.summary: Corey Hogan says Canada needs to consider overhauling its laws to address the kind of freelance negotiating trips that separatist leaders have made to D.C.
stories.author: Carrie Tait, Grant Robertson, Nathan VanderKlippe
stories.content:
Revelations about talks in Washington where Alberta separatists suggested exchanging water and oil for U.S. support, and in Calgary where separatists met secretly with Republican strategists, have sparked an outcry from federalists – and a call for legislative change.

Corey Hogan, Calgary’s lone Liberal member of Parliament, said on Sunday that Canada needs to consider overhauling its laws to address the kind of freelance negotiating trips that separatist leaders have made to D.C. in advance of the Oct. 19 provincial referendum.

Mr. Hogan does not think the discussions between the separatists and the U.S. State Department meet the bar for treason, but that does not make the cross-border talks innocent.

“They’re wrong,” he said in an interview Sunday. “If we don’t have a law that covers them, I think we should at least be thinking about whether we need one.”

A Globe and Mail investigation on Saturday reported that Republican political operatives were on the ground in Alberta this year to assist the separatist campaign in its bid to leave Canada, while harbouring their own aspirations for the province to secede.

The investigation also found that when Alberta separatist leaders went to Washington to meet with the State Department, they offered up key assets from the province’s resource portfolio, including access to fresh water and royalties on crude oil, in exchange for help transitioning to independence.

Mr. Hogan, a former campaign strategist, noted that Canada and the United States have a long history of political consultants doing business on both sides of the border. But, he said, Alberta’s experience illustrates how the rules governing those activities need to be re-examined.

“A principle seems to have been violated here, even if a rule hasn’t,” he said.

As detailed in The Globe’s investigation, Dennis Modry, a former Alberta heart surgeon who is co-founder of the Alberta Prosperity Project, said in an interview that the separatists proposed a number of ideas in a document that was put on the table for discussion during meetings at the State Department last year.

They included access to valuable resources such as fresh water, agriculture, forestry, mining and precious metals. Land for a railway to Alaska was one potential idea, as was a new oil pipeline to the Pacific that would run through Washington State, with royalties from crude oil offered up as compensation, Dr. Modry told The Globe.

Such an arrangement would upend the traditional structure of petroleum extraction, in which royalties flow to the owner of the resource.

The document put into writing “the potential benefits of Alberta sovereignty to the United States of America – and to Alberta,” Dr. Modry said.

“We just brought up water as a possible issue. Does the U.S. need more water? Can Alberta provide some more water to them?” Dr. Modry said.

His comments have drawn the ire of fellow separatist leader Jeffrey Rath , who arranged the State Department meetings and disputes Mr. Modry’s characterization of the talks.

Mr. Rath told The Globe that the talks were general in nature, “about the aspirations of Albertans and Alberta for independence. And that was it.”

In response to the article, Mr. Rath wrote on social media Saturday, “We were private citizens. We had no government mandate to offer anything. We only went to Washington to express the aspirations of hundreds of thousands of Albertans for a free and independent Alberta and to gauge U.S. support for such a project.”

“We were gratified by the expressions of enthusiasm by U.S. officials and the fact that Citizens of Alberta receive a far warmer welcome in Washington than we would ever receive in Ottawa.”

Mr. Rath told The Globe previously that he believes the Albertans’ overtures to Washington garnered attention at the highest levels of the U.S. administration. In January, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described a “wealth of natural resources” in Alberta, which he said had been trapped by domestic opposition to a Pacific pipeline.

The investigation also revealed that separatist advocate David Parker brokered an invitation-only meeting near the Calgary airport in January, where Republican strategists from Michigan discussed software that could be used to boost the sovereignty campaign and help sway the referendum outcome.

The meeting involved representatives from 10X Votes, a U.S. company co-founded by Drew Born, who is part of an influential and wealthy family of Republican donors and has publicly advocated for Alberta separation and annexation by the U.S. On July 1, Mr. Born wrote on social media: “On this Canada Day, I hope this is the last year Alberta is part of Canada.”

Mr. Parker did not acknowledge multiple attempts to reach him for comment regarding The Globe’s investigation that detailed the meeting in Calgary, which had not been publicly revealed. He wrote on social media Saturday that the Republicans from Michigan were “friends who agree with me politically.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith ’s spokesman said on Sunday that she “is not affiliated with these individuals and has no knowledge of these alleged meetings.”

“She also opposes separation or becoming a U.S. state,” Sam Blackett said in an e-mail. “In fact, many of these individuals in question have been relentlessly attacking the Premier for her support for remaining in Canada.”

Jason Kenney, the former Alberta premier who has spent months sparring with independence advocates online and at town halls, said The Globe’s investigation highlighted “incoherence and chaos” within the separatist movement.

The separatist cause has never made a sustained push past 30-per-cent support in polling. Separatist leaders have called on Albertans to send a message to Ottawa by voting in favour of pursuing sovereignty. But Mr. Kenney said the discord should give Albertans frustrated with Ottawa pause.

“I just hope that severely normal, frustrated federalists who think this is a clever way of sending a message start paying attention to the movement,” he said in an interview Sunday. “They will be empowering this shambolic movement of people, including those who are colluding with a foreign power and offering to give away aspects of Alberta sovereignty.”

Mr. Kenney wants Albertans to curtail their influence.

“There’s lots of ways to send a message about the need for reform in the federation, without turning these Maga bootlickers into a major part of Alberta politics.”

Mr. Kenney has a history with some of Alberta’s most prominent separatist advocates. They railed against the public-health measures his government imposed during the COVID-19 pandemic, such as vaccine passports, and campaigned against his leadership of the United Conservative Party.

The former politician does not believe the trips to Washington meet the legal threshold to be considered treasonous or seditious.

“But it’s certainly disloyal and unpatriotic,” he said.

He stops short of calling on Canadian lawmakers to revise the rules in light of Alberta’s experience.

“You can’t prevent Canadian citizens from talking to representatives of a foreign government, as long as it doesn’t constitute a violation of actual treason, sharing national secrets.”

Alberta NDP opposition leader Naheed Nenshi said he sees nothing normal about the U.S. interest and involvement in the separatists’ campaign.

“It’s intensely bizarre, and the question is who is really pulling the strings here,” Mr. Nenshi said in an interview Sunday.

“Mr. Rath, whom I’ve never met, is perfectly happy to brag about his connections to the Trump administration,” Mr. Nenshi said. “Until it’s pointed out to him that these could be seen as potentially dangerous and seditious acts, then suddenly he backs away and says, ‘we just had a meeting with no mandate.’ ”

Mr. Nenshi said no other Canadian representative would likely get a meeting at the State Department if they just “strolled up with no mandate.”

“There’s a lot going on here.”

stories.title: Ex-defendant apologizes to Steven Galloway as defamation trial set to begin
stories.summary: Former UBC professor is suing several people who spread sexual-assault accusations about him, as well as a former student who accused him of rape
stories.author: Chris Hannay
stories.content:
A high-profile defamation trial of several people novelist Steven Galloway says perpetuated false sexual-assault allegations against him is set to begin Monday.

The case will be heard against four defendants, down from the original two dozen listed when the case was first filed eight years ago.

Ahead of the trial, one former defendant, Chelsea Rooney, who was a student of Mr. Galloway’s when he taught at the University of British Columbia, released a public apology for what she characterized as her “harmful” conduct in spreading accusations against Mr. Galloway.

“Everyone deserves fairness, including Mr. Galloway, who was the subject of very serious allegations,” Ms. Rooney said in a statement, posted online alongside the apologies of eight others. She said she regrets playing a role in collecting and soliciting complaints about Mr. Galloway, and building a case against him.

The trial is set to begin Monday in Vancouver against four defendants, according to Mr. Galloway’s long-time lawyer, Daniel Burnett: Mandi Gray, Dana Kagis, Glynnis Kirchmeier and the woman who originally accused him of sexual assault, A.B., whose identity is covered by a publication ban.

Mr. Burnett said Ms. Rooney is one of six defendants who recently settled. Two of the others settled in the summer and three settled previously. Of the other originally named defendants, some could not be identified or pursued, and one had the claim against them dismissed.

The case concerns allegations that rocked the literary community and that have tested courts on questions of whether an accused person’s attempts to defend themself contribute to the stigma of reporting sexual assaults.

The years-long legal battle traces back to an accusation made against Mr. Galloway in 2015 by a former student when he was a UBC professor.

The two had sexual relations between 2011 and 2013 that Mr. Galloway has described as consensual and his student has characterized as abusive. The student is referred to as A.B. in legal filings.

UBC fired Mr. Galloway but a retired judge hired by the university to investigate A.B.’s complaint found that, ON a balance of probabilities, it could not be established he committed sexual assault or assault. He was not charged by police.

In 2018, Mr. Galloway sued A.B. and nearly two dozen other people for making comments that he sexually and physically assaulted A.B. He says the allegations are false and have destroyed his life and career.

The case has wound through various courts over the years as judges have had to weigh whether those accused of sexual assault have a right to sue their accusers for defamation. In 2024, the B.C. Court of Appeal upheld a lower-court decision that said someone accused of being a rapist must be allowed to defend their reputations in court.

When the accusations against Mr. Galloway first surfaced, sexual misconduct by powerful men was rising in the public consciousness. Once-admired celebrities were facing allegations that would eventually lead to the #MeToo movement.

Margaret Atwood, the popular Canadian author who has written publicly about what she says was a lack of due process afforded to Mr. Galloway, told The Globe and Mail she hopes the trial finally reveals the truth of what happened a decade ago.

“It was a time of mobbing on Twitter, and this was a Twitter mob, but it was also a time of moral panic,” Ms. Atwood said.

Ms. Kirchmeier, one of the defendants, is a U.S. citizen who attended UBC from 2011 to 2013 to study and earn a master’s degree in history. She said she is being sued for comments she made on Twitter (now called X) in 2018.

She said in a legal response to the suit that the tweet at issue was taken out of context and argues her remarks represent fair comment on a matter of public interest.

She said she is representing herself because she does not currently have money for a lawyer. “I’m prepared,” she said by phone on Sunday evening.

Lawyers for Ms. Rooney, A.B. and Ms. Gray did not respond to a request for comment Sunday. Ms. Kagis could not be reached.

A.B. is not expected to testify at trial because of mental-health challenges, according to a decision released in June by Justice Neena Sharma.

When the accusations against Mr. Galloway first surfaced, sexual misconduct by powerful men was rising in the public consciousness. Once-admired celebrities were facing allegations that would eventually lead to the #MeToo movement.

Margaret Atwood, the popular Canadian author who has written publicly about what she says was a lack of due process afforded to Mr. Galloway, told The Globe and Mail she hopes the trial finally reveals the truth of what happened a decade ago.
“It was a time of mobbing on Twitter, and this was a Twitter mob, but it was also a time of moral panic,” Ms. Atwood said.

Ms. Kirchmeier, one of the defendants, is a U.S. citizen who attended UBC from 2011 to 2013 to study and earn a master’s degree in history. She said she is being sued for comments she made on Twitter (now called X) in 2018.
She said in a legal response to the suit that the tweet at issue was taken out of context and argues her remarks represent fair comment on a matter of public interest.
She said she is representing herself because she does not currently have money for a lawyer. “I’m prepared,” she said by phone on Sunday evening.
Lawyers for Ms. Rooney, A.B. and Ms. Gray did not respond to a request for comment Sunday. Ms. Kagis could not be reached.
A.B. is not expected to testify at trial because of mental-health challenges, according to a decision released in June by Justice Neena Sharma.

stories.title: Search ends for 4 Canadians, 2 Bermudians on air ambulance that disappeared off Boston coast
stories.summary: Rescue mission now becomes recovery operation to collect debris floating near Nantucket, Mass., and sweep the ocean floor for wreckage
stories.author: Erin Anderssen, Jason Kirby, Colin Freeze
stories.content:
For 66 hours, a fleet of helicopters, planes and ships scoured more than 7,100 kilometres of ocean, searching for the six people on an Ontario-based air ambulance that went missing over the dark water near Nantucket Island early Saturday morning.

Finally, ON Sunday night, the United States Coast Guard made the difficult call to end the search: The four Canadian crew members and two Bermudian passengers were not going to be found alive.

“Suspending a search is not an easy decision,” Rear Admiral Matthew Lake, Commander of the Northeast District, said in a statement. “We express our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones affected by the tragedy and our gratitude for our partner agencies who helped support search efforts.”

The rescue mission now becomes a recovery operation to collect the debris floating 32 kilometres from Nantucket, Mass., and sweep the ocean floor for wreckage, trying to explain how a seemingly routine patient transport flight ended with a plane shattered in the sea.

The Gulfstream G100, owned by Hamilton-based Latitude Air Ambulance, left Bermuda after midnight on Saturday, destined for Boston – a route this particular jet had travelled six times since early July.

A search remains ongoing off the Massachusetts coast for an air ambulance carrying six people that disappeared during a flight from Bermuda to Boston. A “debris field” was found later Saturday off the coast of Nantucket, the Coast Guard said.

The Associated Press

The plane was carrying two pilots and two medical crew members, along with a patient and their family member, for the one hour and 44-minute flight.

Clarence Togeretz, Latitude’s operations manager, said the company had been tracking the plane and lost contact around 1:30 a.m. Saturday as the jet neared Boston.

The Coast Guard launched its search half an hour later, eventually co-ordinating a fleet of fast-response ships and long-range helicopters and planes, with help from the New York Air National Guard. By late Saturday, they’d found a debris field and identified parts of the plane.

Staff at Latitude, Mr. Togeretz said, were coping with “as much positivity and optimism as we can,” and praying for a safe outcome.

As of Sunday morning, Captain John McTamney, who led the Coast Guard’s rescue operation, was still vowing to “search and saturate” the area until “we are confident that, if there were any survivors on the surface of the water, we would’ve found them.”

But hope was dwindling.

As of Sunday evening, the names of the crew and passengers have not been released by authorities.

This is the first time that Latitude had lost a plane in its 17-year history, Mr. Togeretz said on Saturday. On its website, the company claims “thousands of successful missions with a flawless safety record.”

Latitude is a privately held medical evacuation company based at John C. Munro Hamilton International Airport that offers emergency medical transportation worldwide to and from more than 130 countries, according to the company’s website.

Launched in 2009, with a single Bombardier Learjet 35 reconfigured as an airborne intensive care unit, the company has since expanded its fleet to include 10 aircraft according to Transport Canada.

From early July through to Oct. 3, the aircraft that crashed on Saturday was used for more than 90 flights in total, according to the aircraft tracking website FlightAware. Other long-distance routes included stops in Germany, Iceland, Corsica, the Azores, Mexico and the Caribbean, a flight to West Africa, and destinations across the U.S., including Florida and California.

Peter Byl, the company’s co-founder and chief executive officer, is a pilot with more than 24,000 flight hours, according to Latitude’s website.

Mr. Byl, along with his father, uncle, brother and cousin, have done medevacs in Canada and worldwide since 1958, he wrote in a LinkedIn comment posted three days ago.

Mr. Byl did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Sunday.

The company works with global insurers, governments and other organizations to fly patients between countries. In addition to the flight crew, the aircraft typically carry two medical crew and one to two patient escorts.

In 2023, Latitude broke ground on a new 44,000-square-foot facility at the airport, which was completed in 2024 and replaced space it had previously leased at the airport.

At the time, the company said it expected its work force, then 118 people, to grow by 50 per cent within two years of the facility opening.

In Canada, air ambulances are an essential part of the health care system, transporting critically ill patients to trauma teams and connecting rural and northern Canadians to clinical specialists in urban centres.

In 2025, for example, nearly 12,000 patients were transported on fixed-wing planes by Ornge, an Ontario non-profit group funded by the province.

But accidents involving Canadian medical transport airplanes are rare. In 2024, a Keewatin Air turboprop overran a runway in Goose Bay, Labrador. Nobody on board was injured and the plane sustained only minor damage, according to the Transportation Safety Board’s final report. In 2019, another Keewatin plane suffered significant damages when it landed short of the runway, but everyone on board survived.

In an interview Sunday, Gilbert Darrell, chief executive officer of Bermuda Air Ambulances, a medical transport company based on the island, spoke highly of Latitude’s professional reputation, and declared the company’s pilots and medical staff “the epitome of heroes,” for the risks they take.

He said about 200 patients leave Bermuda every year for medical emergencies that the country’s limited hospital resources cannot handle. “We can’t be thankful enough,” he said, for their contribution “to help some of our citizens.”

With reports from The Canadian Press

stories.title: B.C. NDP one candidate short of full slate for snap provincial election
stories.summary: Party’s campaign director Cheryl Oates attributed the absence from the Peace River North ballot to incomplete paperwork
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
The B.C. NDP has fallen one candidate short of fielding a provincewide slate in this month’s snap election, one of a handful of surprises revealed after nominations closed Saturday.

The final list, published Sunday by Elections BC, consists of 355 candidates vying for seats in the Oct. 24 vote, with 340 representing 10 political parties and 15 candidates running as independents or unaffiliated.

The Conservative Party of B.C. is running 93 candidates, covering every provincial riding; the NDP, 92; and the B.C. Green Party, 73. CentreBC and OneBC, both formed in 2025, have nominated 35 and 33 candidates, respectively.

The weekend deadline caps a hurried nomination period triggered by NDP Leader David Eby’s snap election call on Sept. 22 and marked by considerable political tumult, including defections, infighting and party-switching on the right, and frustration over the early vote. Candidate vetting remained a flashpoint Sunday as Mr. Eby questioned the Conservatives’ choices while unveiling a plan to raise taxes on B.C.’s highest earners.

This is the first election since 1991 in which one of B.C.’s top two competing parties has not fielded a full slate. It is also the first election since B.C.’s Election Act was enacted in 1995 that a major political party is running under an interim leader, after Lorne Doerkson replaced Kerry-Lynne Findlay to head the Conservatives following her resignation on Sept. 20.

B.C. NDP campaign director Cheryl Oates attributed the party’s absence from the Peace River North ballot to incomplete paperwork. Incumbent Jordan Kealy, who was elected under the Conservative banner in 2024 and quit to sit as an independent last year, will face Conservative Curtis Whitford. Mr. Kealy, who was charged with sexual assault in June for offences alleged to have occurred in 2024, has maintained his innocence and is awaiting trial by jury.

Asked about the Ndp’s absence from the Peace River North ballot at a campaign stop in Comox, Mr. Eby said it was disappointing that paperwork problems prevented a great candidate from going forward before contrasting the Ndp’s approach to recruitment with that of the Conservatives.

“We certainly would never run people with hateful views, conspiracy theorists, anti-vaxxers, Maga apologists, in order to fill out our slate like the Conservatives are doing,” Mr. Eby said.

He referenced a CTV Question Period interview with Mr. Doerkson that aired that morning, in which the interim Conservative leader is questioned about Chilliwack North candidate Heather Maahs, who appeared to conflate homosexuality and pedophilia in past comments. Ms. Maahs, who is seeking re-election, also invited to a 2025 reception at the B.C. Legislature a Christian lobby group that believes homosexuality is immoral, abortion should be banned and Canada’s ban on conversion therapy should be repealed.

Mr. Doerkson said he did not share Ms. Maah’s views but that she would remain in caucus.

In response to Mr. Eby’s comments, the Conservative Party said it is proud of its 93 candidates and that the party, under Mr. Doerkson, will treat every British Columbian with respect and dignity.

“The NDP called a cynical snap election that only they knew was coming and they still couldn’t run a full slate,” said Alex Shiff, the party’s director of media relations, in a statement to The Globe and Mail.

The final candidate list also reveals some last-minute twists, with some final plans differing from what parties had signalled just days earlier.

Brent Chapman, who on Sept. 22 quit the Conservative caucus to join OneBC, citing the attacks on his wife, Ms. Findlay, is now missing from the list.

Asked by The Globe about Mr. Chapman’s absence from the ballot, OneBC said Sunday that a statement was forthcoming, but none arrived by deadline.

As well, OneBC Leader Dallas Brodie had initially pledged not to challenge eight “principled conservatives” in tight races before reversing course days later in two of those contests: North Island, held by Anna Kindy, and Kelowna Centre, held by Kristina Loewen. However, the final list shows no OneBC Candidate in the North Island riding.

OneBC did not directly answer a question from The Globe about the reversal in that riding and instead pointed broadly to its strained relationship with the Conservatives.

“When it comes to dealing with the Conservatives, the instability inside the party, combined with their inability to remain consistent on any of their principles, has made it impossible to have a productive engagement with them,” the party’s campaign team said in an e-mail.

On the campaign trail Sunday, Mr. Eby announced a plan to raise income taxes on B.C.’s highest earners to fund health care improvements and measures aimed at lowering costs for British Columbians. The plan, which would start in the 2027 tax year, would increase rates on the top two tax brackets by 2 percentage points and introduce a new 24.5-per-cent bracket for income of more than $1-million, generating up to $1-billion in 2028-29, Mr. Eby said.

The changes would affect the top 4 per cent of earners in B.C. and apply only to income earned over each tax bracket threshold. Those earning $190,000 or less would see no change.

Candidate vetting remained a flashpoint Sunday as Mr. Eby questioned the Conservatives’ choices while unveiling a plan to raise taxes on B.C.’s highest earners.

This is the first election since 1991 in which one of B.C.’s top two competing parties has not fielded a full slate. It is also the first election since B.C.’s Election Act was enacted in 1995 that a major political party is running under an interim leader, after Lorne Doerkson replaced Kerry-Lynne Findlay to head the Conservatives following her resignation on Sept. 20.

B.C. NDP campaign director Cheryl Oates attributed the party’s absence from the Peace River North ballot to incomplete paperwork. Incumbent Jordan Kealy, who was elected under the Conservative banner in 2024 and quit to sit as an independent last year, will face Conservative Curtis Whitford. Mr. Kealy, who was charged with sexual assault in June for offences alleged to have occurred in 2024, has maintained his innocence and is awaiting trial by jury.

Asked about the Ndp’s absence from the Peace River North ballot at a campaign stop in Comox, Mr. Eby said it was disappointing that paperwork problems prevented a great candidate from going forward before contrasting the Ndp’s approach to recruitment with that of the Conservatives.
“We certainly would never run people with hateful views, conspiracy theorists, anti-vaxxers, Maga apologists, in order to fill out our slate like the Conservatives are doing,” Mr. Eby said.

He referenced a CTV Question Period interview with Mr. Doerkson that aired that morning, in which the interim Conservative leader is questioned about Chilliwack North candidate Heather Maahs, who appeared to conflate homosexuality and pedophilia in past comments. Ms. Maahs, who is seeking re-election, also invited to a 2025 reception at the B.C. Legislature a Christian lobby group that believes homosexuality is immoral, abortion should be banned and Canada’s ban on conversion therapy should be repealed.
Mr. Doerkson said he did not share Ms. Maah’s views but that she would remain in caucus.
In response to Mr. Eby’s comments, the Conservative Party said it is proud of its 93 candidates and that the party, under Mr. Doerkson, will treat every British Columbian with respect and dignity.

“The NDP called a cynical snap election that only they knew was coming and they still couldn’t run a full slate,” said Alex Shiff, the party’s director of media relations, in a statement to The Globe and Mail.
The final candidate list also reveals some last-minute twists, with some final plans differing from what parties had signalled just days earlier.
Brent Chapman, who on Sept. 22 quit the Conservative caucus to join OneBC, citing the attacks on his wife, Ms. Findlay, is now missing from the list.
Asked by The Globe about Mr. Chapman’s absence from the ballot, OneBC said Sunday that a statement was forthcoming, but none arrived by deadline.

As well, OneBC Leader Dallas Brodie had initially pledged not to challenge eight “principled conservatives” in tight races before reversing course days later in two of those contests: North Island, held by Anna Kindy, and Kelowna Centre, held by Kristina Loewen. However, the final list shows no OneBC Candidate in the North Island riding.
OneBC did not directly answer a question from The Globe about the reversal in that riding and instead pointed broadly to its strained relationship with the Conservatives.

“When it comes to dealing with the Conservatives, the instability inside the party, combined with their inability to remain consistent on any of their principles, has made it impossible to have a productive engagement with them,” the party’s campaign team said in an e-mail.

On the campaign trail Sunday, Mr. Eby announced a plan to raise income taxes on B.C.’s highest earners to fund health care improvements and measures aimed at lowering costs for British Columbians. The plan, which would start in the 2027 tax year, would increase rates on the top two tax brackets by 2 percentage points and introduce a new 24.5-per-cent bracket for income of more than $1-million, generating up to $1-billion in 2028-29, Mr. Eby said.
The changes would affect the top 4 per cent of earners in B.C. and apply only to income earned over each tax bracket threshold. Those earning $190,000 or less would see no change.

stories.title: Toronto art installation shines light on growing Canada-EU ties
stories.summary: Abandoned grain silos May not seem like an obvious place for a diplomatic mission. But for the Delegation of the European Union to Canada, it served as a perfect blank canvas on which to showcase shared priorities between this country and the economic bloc.
stories.author: Michael Serapio
stories.content:
Toronto - Abandoned grain silos May not seem like an obvious place for a diplomatic mission. But for the Delegation of the European Union to Canada, it served as a perfect blank canvas on which to showcase shared priorities between this country and the economic bloc.

“We want to reinforce the connection between the Canadian and European,” said Geneviève Tuts, the EU’s Ambassador to Canada. “In my view, culture and art should be part of this conversation.”

The Canada Malting Silos are former malting towers that sit unused at the base of Toronto’s Bathurst Street along Lake Ontario.

But on Saturday, those two towers came to life, as two art installations were projected onto the structures for Toronto’s Nuit Blanche Festival , an annual art celebration that transforms the nighttime city into a giant exhibition space.

Presented by the Ontario College of Art and Design (Ocad) University and the EU Delegation, the two works featured images that explore nature and the impacts of climate change.

They are works that explore a shared human experience, as well as an opportunity for the EU to help bring that art to a Canadian public.

“I was in Strasbourg two weeks ago, and I had the chance to listen carefully to our two leaders, and they were determined and committed to build, as we say, a new partnership. And this new partnership will cover a wide range of topics,” said Tuts. “This is not just about economic issues or trade issues or digital. This is also about people-to-people ties.”

It’s the kind of language that’s getting more attention these days.

Just last month, the European Commission president invited Canada to explore becoming the first associate member of the EU.

It’s not clear what associate membership would look like, since it is not an established status within the political and economic bloc.

But Prime Minister Mark Carney accepted the invitation, open to deepening economic and security ties with the European Union but also stating he’s not seeking membership.

Rather, Carney says he’s looking for a unique alliance.

However, the relationship is defined, Canada and the European Union are already working more closely together, drawn together by the defence of Ukraine and decisions made by the United States since the re-election of Donald Trump.

A shifting alliance

“The United States, which pushed that multilateral system after the Second (World) War has pulled out of it,” said Jeremy Kinsman, Canada’s former ambassador to the EU from 2002 to 2006. “They’re not supporters of it. In fact, they’re resentful of the European Union’s multilateralism.”

It was that past commitment to multilateralism and the liberal democratic order that led Europe and Canada to rely on the United States as a security backstop.

But that relationship has changed, and the shift extends beyond defence.

The Trump administration has also upended U.S. trade policy, imposing tariffs on products from both friends and foes.

“The events of the last two years — and call them Trump — have focused everybody on the value of this relationship,” Kinsman said.

Deepening economic ties

Over the past year, Canada and European partners have taken steps to deepen their economic ties.

Canada has signed a memorandum of understanding to purchase submarines from German defence company ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems .

European buyers have also expressed interest in purchasing more water bombers from Canadian aircraft manufacturer De Havilland, while German energy company Uniper has finalized a deal to buy liquefied natural gas from the future Ksi Lisims LNG project in British Columbia. First deliveries are expected in 2032.

Those developments underscore a point Kinsman says should guide the debate over the future of Canada-EU relations, regardless of whether Canada becomes an associate member.

“What is going to determine this relationship is not what it’s called, and it’s not all the words to describe why we need the relationship,” he said.

“It’s going to be concrete evidence of real capital projects, you know, between the two countries. And we’re doing them.”

The evolving relationship will come into sharper focus later this month.

Global Affairs Canada says Carney will welcome von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa to Montreal on Oct. 29 for a two-day summit.

There is already speculation that the leaders could announce agreements aimed at strengthening co-operation on critical minerals, supply chains and low-carbon energy.

“We have a lot to do together. We are sharing the same values. We are two democratic countries. We are respecting fundamental laws, the rule of law,” Tuts said. “We are fighting for multilateralism.”

Those shared ideals are helping Canada and Europe find common ground on a growing number of fronts — including an art project that lit up Toronto’s waterfront.

stories.title: Decades after her diagnosis, Adrienne Clarkson calls for better endometriosis care
stories.summary: The former governor-general says it’s ‘appalling’ patients feel they have to leave the country and pay out of pocket to access surgery
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
More than six decades after being diagnosed with endometriosis, former governor-general Adrienne Clarkson considers herself “one of the very lucky ones.”

At 21, after learning she had the painful inflammatory disease, Ms. Clarkson soon had surgery at Toronto General Hospital. She credits her gynecologist at the time, Douglas Cannell, for preserving part of an ovary.

At the time, a nurse told her any other surgeon would have done a hysterectomy because her situation was “a mess.” Dr. Cannell spent two hours in the operating room with her.

Ms. Clarkson is grateful to have had access to his expertise so she was later able to bear children – something that isn’t always possible because endometriosis is associated with infertility in about 30 to 60 per cent of cases. Many patients require fertility treatments to conceive.

Endometriosis is an inflammatory condition that sees cells similar to those on the inside of the uterus grow outside of it. It is commonly associated with severe pelvic pain, which adversely affects patients’ well-being, productivity and relationships.

It also carries a high cost burden for the health care system. A population study published in 2020 looked at hospital admissions in Canada over a five-year period for every province except Quebec. It recorded that there were 47,000 admissions, totalling $152.2-million in health care costs, which amounts to $30-million a year.

Ms. Clarkson, who worked as a CBC broadcaster before she served as governor-general from 1999 to 2005, is speaking out now after hearing stories about poor access to endometriosis diagnostics and the state of care for Canadian patients.

Many patients have to wait more than half a decade to be diagnosed and some, in the face of their persistent pain, travel out of Canada, including to Europe and the United States for surgery.

Ms. Clarkson, now 87, said it is “appalling” Canadian patients feel they have to leave the country and pay out of pocket to access surgery.

“I look at it on the large scale of things, and not my own fortunate circumstance, which depended upon a wonderful doctor in a city of a million people at a wonderful university hospital,” Ms. Clarkson said in a recent interview. “I think of the woman who is in Maple Creek, British Columbia, who does not have access to any of this and wonders what’s going to happen.”

She added: “It really, really bugs me that we have not made progress on endometriosis.”

Ms. Clarkson’s concerns are echoed by members of the medical community. A growing number of patients and surgeons are pushing for improved access to care.

Sukhbir Singh, who heads the Department of Obstetrics, Gynecology and Newborn Care at The Ottawa Hospital, says its minimally invasive gynecology research group documented how the current state of endometriosis surgical care amounts to a national problem.

Dr. Singh said the problem is underscored by the fact that Canadians are seeking care outside of the country because of factors including long wait times for referral and surgery.

And while the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada’s guideline is clear on the need for access to complex care for endometriosis, Dr. Singh describes this as virtually non-existent; many health care providers have limited access to resources, including lacking time in operating rooms.

Surgery May be required for some patients to remove scar tissue and lesions. There is no cure for endometriosis, but some patients use medication, such as progesterone, as part of treatment.

But despite the prevalence of endometriosis, the Sogc says it remains an underdiagnosed and misunderstood disease, leaving many to suffer for years before they receive proper medical care.

This May, physicians Olga Bougie and Catherine Varner co-authored an editorial in the Canadian Medical Association Journal that described how endometriosis care is often delayed and fractured and needs an overhaul.

They said consequences associated with it can be profound and range from “adverse reproductive outcomes to severe, multisystem disease.”

“Addressing these challenges requires a fundamental shift toward co-ordinated, evidence-based, and patient-centred care,” they wrote. “Strengthening interdisciplinary collaboration, expanding training and resources, and prioritizing equitable access to care are essential steps to improving outcomes and restoring trust for those living with endometriosis.”

Earlier this year, Elize Nocente, a Grade 11 student who lives in Vancouver, started a House of Commons petition , sponsored by B.C. NDP MP Jenny Kwan, to raise awareness of endometriosis in schools. She does not have the condition herself but knows others who do, and she aspires to be an obstetrician/gynecologist one day.

The petition calls for the federal government to establish a national advisory board on endometriosis education and to work with provincial and territorial governments to support the mandatory inclusion of endometriosis education in curricula.

Ms. Clarkson reached out to The Globe and Mail after reading about the high-school student’s push for more awareness. She looks at the situation of lacking diagnostics and treatment through a feminist lens.

“If it was something that was in men’s testicles, it would have been handled ages ago,” she said.

All patients should be able to choose what they do with their own bodies, Ms. Clarkson added.

“Women want choice of whether they have children or don’t have children,” she said. “They don’t want to be held up by something as vicious as endometriosis.”

And while the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada’s guideline is clear on the need for access to complex care for endometriosis, Dr. Singh describes this as virtually non-existent; many health care providers have limited access to resources, including lacking time in operating rooms.
Surgery May be required for some patients to remove scar tissue and lesions. There is no cure for endometriosis, but some patients use medication, such as progesterone, as part of treatment.
But despite the prevalence of endometriosis, the Sogc says it remains an underdiagnosed and misunderstood disease, leaving many to suffer for years before they receive proper medical care.

This May, physicians Olga Bougie and Catherine Varner co-authored an editorial in the Canadian Medical Association Journal that described how endometriosis care is often delayed and fractured and needs an overhaul.
They said consequences associated with it can be profound and range from “adverse reproductive outcomes to severe, multisystem disease.”

“Addressing these challenges requires a fundamental shift toward co-ordinated, evidence-based, and patient-centred care,” they wrote. “Strengthening interdisciplinary collaboration, expanding training and resources, and prioritizing equitable access to care are essential steps to improving outcomes and restoring trust for those living with endometriosis.”

Earlier this year, Elize Nocente, a Grade 11 student who lives in Vancouver, started a House of Commons petition , sponsored by B.C. NDP MP Jenny Kwan, to raise awareness of endometriosis in schools. She does not have the condition herself but knows others who do, and she aspires to be an obstetrician/gynecologist one day.

The petition calls for the federal government to establish a national advisory board on endometriosis education and to work with provincial and territorial governments to support the mandatory inclusion of endometriosis education in curricula.

“If it was something that was in men’s testicles, it would have been handled ages ago,” she said.
All patients should be able to choose what they do with their own bodies, Ms. Clarkson added.
“Women want choice of whether they have children or don’t have children,” she said. “They don’t want to be held up by something as vicious as endometriosis.”

stories.title: Toronto-based VPN provider plans to quit Canada over lawful-access bill
stories.summary: Psiphon, which helps people living in oppressive regimes evade online censorship, says Bill C-22 would compel it to help build a surveillance system in this country
stories.author: Marie Woolf
stories.content:
A Canadian company that has created software to help people living under oppressive regimes evade censorship and retain access to the internet says it plans to leave Canada if the federal government’s lawful-access bill passes in its current form.

The lawful-access bill, known as Bill C-22, would require telecoms, internet companies and other electronic service providers to make changes to their systems to give surveillance and monitoring capabilities to police services and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service.

Csis and law enforcement have long argued that Canada is lagging behind its Five Eyes intelligence partners in not having such a lawful-access regime to aid investigations.

But the bill has provoked a backlash among tech companies with some saying they would quit the country if it becomes law.

Toronto-based Psiphon, which has millions of users worldwide including in Iran, Russia and China, told The Globe and Mail on Friday it has started drawing up plans to move its operations out of Canada. It said the bill would force it to compromise crucial safety features put in place to protect the privacy of its users in authoritarian countries.

Psiphon, whose origins were at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, said it has about 20 million monthly users worldwide, and said the use of its software tends to surge when there is a spike in repression. In February, during a crackdown by Tehran against protestors, it had 21 million users in Iran.

The Canadian tech company has about 3.5 million users per month in Myanmar, formally Burma, where the military junta has used internet blackouts to cut off communication channels and banned the use of virtual private networks, or VPNs, that encrypt a user’s internet traffic and can disguise the location where they are connecting to the internet from.

Psiphon has devised technologies, including a VPN, to evade censorship, as well as complex routing protocols, using servers located around the world, and other security mechanisms to allow people to access the internet without being tracked. The way the system is designed and the scale of its use makes it difficult for censors to untangle, so it can keep operating if a VPN is blocked by a regime, the company says.

Kenzie Elsworthy, vice-president of Psiphon, said: “We spend our days protecting people from authoritarian surveillance. This bill would compel Psiphon to help build an arbitrary surveillance system in Canada.”

The federal government amended Bill C-22 in the House of Commons before its summer recess to address concerns, including from tech giants Apple Inc. and Meta Platforms Inc., that the bill could compromise cybersecurity and privacy. One such amendment protects end-to-end encryption. The bill is now due to be scrutinized in the Senate.

In an interview with the Toronto Star last month, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said he expects the bill to pass in its existing form. He described the current bill as “the right balance,” in which cracking encryption is “off limits” except in rare “extenuating circumstances.”

Last month, tech companies that deliver digital services to Canadians wrote to Mr. Anandasangaree urging further changes to the bill, saying it would force companies to weaken encryption or “build intercept capabilities.”

Among the signatories were companies operating VPNs including Windscribe, a Toronto-based company that has more than 100 million registered users worldwide and has warned it May leave Canada if Bill C-22 becomes law.

Psiphon is different from many software companies providing VPNs and cybersecurity in that its code is public, an “open-source” policy designed to build trust among its users. The lawful-access bill could require tech companies to make changes to their software or systems to allow surveillance, but would have to keep such changes secret.

Ms. Elsworthy said the reason Psiphon’s software is trusted is that anyone can inspect its code, but “the moment we are forced to add a secret capability, that trust is gone, and so is the product.”

“You cannot build a secret backdoor into open-source code. Every line we ship is public. Any access capability this bill forces us to build would be visible to the whole world, including the authoritarian governments our users are trying to escape. That is not lawful access. It is a published vulnerability,” she added in an e-mail.

She said there is great uncertainty over which companies would be required to introduce surveillance capabilities, as this would not be defined until after the bill is passed. Psiphon would have to work on the assumption, for business planning, that it would be covered.

“We do not want to leave Canada. We were built here, originally out of the University of Toronto, and we have been here for nearly 20 years. But if this bill passes as written, relocating is the only way the work continues. That is not a choice we would weigh. It is the only option left,” she said.

Psiphon this year received about $600,000 in federal government funding from the National Research Council to help improve its network.

Simon Lafortune, a spokesperson for Mr. Anandasangaree, said “the existence of a lawful-access framework does not, ON its own, make it impossible to operate a secure, privacy-protective service in Canada.”

“It is also important to note that the fact a company falls under the definition of electronic service provider (ESPs) does not mean that it would be the subject of lawful access obligations under the Act. Most ESPs will not be core providers, nor will they be subject to a Ministerial order,” he said.

He said the government would consider a range of factors, including the nature of the service being provided, the extent to which the service is used in Canada, when considering a company’s lawful-access obligations.

Psiphon was created as a Citizen Lab project in 2006, and spun out as a private company soon afterward. It now operates independently.

U of T professor Ron Deibert, founder and director of the Citizen Lab, said Bill C-22, as now written, “will make it impossible for a large number of invaluable privacy-preserving tools and applications from operating in Canada.”

stories.title: What Florida’s property tax vote means for Canadian snowbirds
stories.summary: A Florida ballot measure would sharply increase property tax exemptions for many permanent residents while keeping non-homesteaded properties in the tax base. Gov. Ron DeSantis has explicitly said snowbirds, including Canadians, could continue paying property taxes as Florida homeowners receive relief.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Florida voters will decide Nov. 3 whether to approve Amendment 3 , a constitutional measure that would substantially increase the homestead property-tax exemption for qualifying homeowners.

For Canadian snowbirds, who own property in Florida, the proposed tax overhaul comes with a twist: the biggest break would go to permanent Florida residents, while seasonal homeowners, including Canadians, could remain part of the tax base.

The proposal in May grew out of Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ campaign to reduce, and eventually eliminate, property taxes on homesteaded homes. He said that Florida could afford the change because “Property tax revenue collected by local governments has nearly doubled in the past seven years.”

He also made clear who would remain outside the main relief.

“We are focusing on homestead. Obviously they tax property that are non-homestead: Residential, Airbnb, Canadian snowbirds, commercial,” DeSantis said in an interview with Fox News in June.

In 2025 , while arguing against a sales-tax cut, he said he wanted “Canadian tourists and Brazilian tourists” to help subsidize Florida while residents received tax relief.

That is significant for Canadians, who make up a large share of Florida’s seasonal property owners.

The amendment , approved by Florida lawmakers, would increase the non-school homestead exemption from the current US$50,000 to US$150,000 in 2027 and US$250,000 in 2028. It would also reduce the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homesteaded properties from 10 per cent to five per cent.

In other words, the measure does not create a tax specifically targeting Canadians. Rather, Canadians who own properties that do not qualify for the permanent-resident homestead exemption would not receive the main tax break.

If approved by at least 60 per cent of Florida voters, Amendment 3 would take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Property taxes are local, not state. So we’d need to do a constitutional amendment (requires 60% of voters to approve) to eliminate them (which I would support) or even to reform/lower them… We should put the boldest amendment on the ballot that has a chance of getting that… https://t.co/WpOQmjNl0X — Ron DeSantis (@GovRonDeSantis) February 13, 2025

For Canadians, who own a winter home in Florida, the issue is therefore less about a new Canadian-specific tax than about who qualifies for the largest property tax relief and who remains responsible for local property taxes as Florida reshapes its tax base.

“We are focusing on homestead. Obviously they tax property that are non-homestead: Residential, Airbnb, Canadian snowbirds, commercial,” DeSantis said in an interview with Fox News in June.
In 2025 , while arguing against a sales-tax cut, he said he wanted “Canadian tourists and Brazilian tourists” to help subsidize Florida while residents received tax relief.
That is significant for Canadians, who make up a large share of Florida’s seasonal property owners.

The amendment , approved by Florida lawmakers, would increase the non-school homestead exemption from the current US$50,000 to US$150,000 in 2027 and US$250,000 in 2028. It would also reduce the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homesteaded properties from 10 per cent to five per cent.

In other words, the measure does not create a tax specifically targeting Canadians. Rather, Canadians who own properties that do not qualify for the permanent-resident homestead exemption would not receive the main tax break.
If approved by at least 60 per cent of Florida voters, Amendment 3 would take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Property taxes are local, not state. So we’d need to do a constitutional amendment (requires 60% of voters to approve) to eliminate them (which I would support) or even to reform/lower them… We should put the boldest amendment on the ballot that has a chance of getting that… https://t.co/WpOQmjNl0X — Ron DeSantis (@GovRonDeSantis) February 13, 2025

For Canadians, who own a winter home in Florida, the issue is therefore less about a new Canadian-specific tax than about who qualifies for the largest property tax relief and who remains responsible for local property taxes as Florida reshapes its tax base.

stories.title: Screen time limits not enough to tackle problematic social media use: experts
stories.summary: Toronto - Experts from around the world, including Canada, say the scale of digital technology use by children and youth is a public health issue that needs immediate action to prevent further harm.

By Nicole Ireland The Canadian Press

A series of papers published by the Lancet on Sunday say the responsibility for keeping young people safe from problematic use of social media and other digital technology must shift from young people and their families to big tech companies and governments.

“It’s easy to think about how technology impacts our health as being about our individual choices. And one of the things that we really want to get across in this series is that that’s not the right way to think about it,” said co-author Jay Shaw, the Canada Research Chair in responsible health innovation at the University of Toronto, in an interview.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Image 14Image 15Image 16

Efforts by parents, such as screen-time limits, as well as individual willpower by young people, aren’t enough to address the “digital determinants of health” that are now part of their everyday environment, the papers say.

“We need to think about the design choices and business models of big technology companies that have built these platforms that are designed for engagement and (to) keep us on (them),” Shaw said.

“That’s partly what drives the health-related consequences of the digitization of our lives.”

Digital technology itself isn’t good or bad, Shaw said, but the way social media companies make money is to keep people on their platforms for as long as possible and to collect data about their likes, what they share and what posts they come back to — information that can be used for advertising opportunities.

“A perfect example is the bottomless scroll or infinite scroll. If the page you’re looking at has no end, it makes it much more difficult to close off that sort of session or that activity,” he said.

Targeted algorithms through social media and AI chatbots are designed to promote and recommend tailored content, which keep young people interacting with the platform. For many, those properties make it addictive and lead to problematic use, Shaw said — including not being able to stop scrolling even if it doesn’t feel good anymore.

Depression, anxiety, sleep disruption and limited physical activity were documented harms to young people associated with problematic digital media use in an “umbrella review” of 2,790 studies, the Lancet papers say.

The review also found some health benefits, including a feeling of well-being, associated with “moderate” digital media use and active video gaming.

That shows the importance of considering “the patterns of our engagement with the technology and the kind of content that we’re looking at” when assessing benefits and harms of digital media use, Shaw said.

Big tech companies have often countered claims of mental health harm by citing insufficient causal evidence, the authors say.

While the authors acknowledge it is difficult to establish cause, they say the sheer scale of digital media’s presence and the fact some people are more vulnerable to harms than others justifies taking “precautionary public health action.”

That action includes government regulation and reforming digital platforms’ business models to prioritize the well-being of young people, they say.

Australia has already imposed regulations limiting social media access to people 16 years of age and over — and dozens of other countries, including Canada, are considering similar measures, Shaw said.

Canada’s proposed policies — Bill C-34, the Safe Social Media Act and Bill C-36, the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act — have “got (it) pretty much exactly right” if they pass into law, he said.

The legislation would create a Digital Safety Commission to oversee tech companies. It would also restrict young people under the age of 16 from using social media platforms.

But the legislation would also allow exemptions for companies that show “adequate safeguards in the regulated social media service for the protection of children,” according to the Parliament of Canada website.

“It’s that logic of incentivizing digital media companies to demonstrate safety that is the key, I think, to all of this,” Shaw said.

There are many positive uses of social media and other digital platforms, including education and recreation, he said, so a total ban for younger teens isn’t ideal.

“At the same time, I don’t see another effective way to encourage digital media companies to enhance the safety of their platforms for young people.”

Instagram’s age restriction is 13 and owner Meta says users under 16 have default account settings that allow parents to set screen time limits and see who their kids are messaging.

The default settings also block younger teens from messages from people they aren’t connected with and minimizes exposure to sensitive content, such as violence or promotion of cosmetic procedures.

The Lancet series drew on the lived experiences of six young adults between 23 and 30 who formed a youth advisory group.

Yifan Zhou, a 30-year-old Canadian in that group, said she agrees that social media can do a lot of good, including connecting with friends and peers over long distances and easier access to educational information.

But she has also talked with other young people about the darker side of digital platforms, including loneliness from reduced in-person connection and anxiety stemming from frequent comparison of what others are posting online to your own life.

Zhou said she also has a family member who was in their teens and exposed to online predators.

“It persisted for years before almost any of us really found out because they also felt that it wasn’t something that they wanted to discuss. They felt ashamed,” Zhou said.

“They also didn’t know that it wasn’t the way it’s supposed to be, but the kind of regulations and also the education and a lot of things weren’t in place.”

Dr. Michael Cheng, a psychiatrist at the Children’s Hospital of Eastern Ontario and the CHEO Research Institute, said he frequently sees the addictive nature and mental health harms of social media.

Years ago, when he was caring for children and youth at CHEO, “their question if they were being admitted was ‘can my parents visit? When are visiting hours or when can I call my mom or dad?’”

Now, the first question is often, “do I get to keep my cellphone?” he said.

Cheng, who was not involved in the Lancet series, said it’s important to see “a convergence that we are all around the globe becoming increasingly concerned about the same issue.”

“I remember 10, 15 years ago, those that were concerned, it felt like we were yelling and crying into the wind,” he said.

“Maybe the pendulum will swing back towards a safer side when we can design safer technologies.”

Zhou said even though digital technology has developed faster than government regulations, she believes change is possible.

“The release of this paper is something that gives me hope, and I am also quite active in the youth scene and I see that young people are more and more taking agency in terms of co-creating our own futures.

“So that part also gives me a lot of hope.”

stories.title: Lancet research calls for big tech regulation to reduce addictive design features
stories.summary: ‘Big technology companies are mobilizing a corporate defense playbook that was popularized by big tobacco,’ U of T researcher and study co-author said
stories.author: Zosia Bielski
stories.content:
The authors of a new, three-paper series published in The Lancet say it’s time for a major perspective shift that moves beyond fixating on youth screen time, to regulating big tech’s business models and addicting design features, which monetize ever more of people’s data, time and attention at the cost of their well-being.

“Time on screen, social comparison through social media, online bullying – these things are having a major impact on experiences of depression and anxiety, particularly for young people,” said study co-author Jay Shaw, an associate professor and Canada Research Chair at the University of Toronto’s Temerty Faculty of Medicine and Dalla Lana School of Public Health.

The series looked at 121 published reviews involving nine million people under-25 and found associations between addiction-like patterns of digital media use and various harms, including sleep disruption through key phases of neurobiological development, as well as decreased physical activity.

Even as social-media platforms are deliberately designed to be addictive, to make people put off sleep and get them riled up, anxious and angry so they keep scrolling, screen time is often still portrayed as a personal lack of self-control, or as parental failure. It’s a position that lets big tech off the hook, Dr. Shaw said.

“In some ways, we’re battling our own assumptions when it comes to thinking critically about how we engage with digital technology. We think to ourselves, ‘I shouldn’t have stayed up that extra hour last night doomscrolling.’ But the digital environment is set up to make that impossible,” Dr. Shaw said.

“Big technology companies are mobilizing a corporate defence playbook that was popularized by big tobacco, but has been used by other health harming industries facing regulation over the past few decades, where keeping attention on individual willpower prevents stronger regulation.”

Working across numerous disciplines at universities in 10 countries, the 13 co-authors are pushing for robust, international regulation of big tech business models and the design features built to pull people in, from infinite scroll and autoplay to personalized recommendation feeds.

The experts said one-off measures such as age limits aren’t enough. They’re calling for safety standards for platform design, control over how personal data are collected and used, and independent oversight and accountability.

They want to see governments force tech giants to first, assess products for risk before launching them, and second, to release internal data on how features affect users’ health – with that intel then scrutinized by independent experts. The authors are also pushing for a dedicated international body to monitor AI harms to youth.

Dr. Shaw sees promise in Bill C-34, Canada’s Safe Social Media Act, a proposed federal law focused on making online platforms safer for youth and holding tech companies accountable. In particular, Dr. Shaw appreciates the push to establish a regulator capable of preventing youth from accessing a platform until a tech firm can show it’s safe.

“This logic of incentivizing platforms to demonstrate their safety has been absent from past efforts to ban young people from social media,” Dr. Shaw said.

The Lancet papers reflect a broader shift to thinking about safety by design, said Kaitlynn Mendes, a sociology professor at Western University and project lead at DIY: Digital Safety , who was not involved in the current research.

“It’s crazy that we let tech companies release products that haven’t been proven to be safe by design. We don’t accept that with any other products on the market. You think about food, automobiles, other tech and gadgets where we’ve set standards and regulations.”

Beyond Canada, Dr. Mendes pointed to laws already enacted in the U.K. and European Union, as well as Australia’s eSafety Commissioner, an independent government regulator dedicated to online safety.

“We’re crazy if we expect tech companies to voluntarily make changes that will impact their bottom line,” Dr. Mendes said.

“There need to be third-party mediators, a place for the public to bring complaints that also sets standards and imposes fines. In the U.K., Ofcom forces tech companies to produce transparency reports every year. They make companies publish how many cases of child sexual abuse material, luring and underage accounts there are on the platform. That can be an incredibly effective mechanism for forcing companies to make changes.”

The Lancet papers also illustrate an evolving approach to age restrictions, according to Candice Odgers, co-director of the Child and Brain Development Program at the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research. She was not involved in the Lancet papers.

“Adults really have broken the internet in some pretty brutal ways, and their solution has been to kick kids off to ‘fix it.’ That is not going to fix the broken internet, broken design choices and broken business models. It’s going to do absolutely nothing to help our young people because the bans don’t work, and the blame certainly doesn’t work,” said Dr. Odgers, a chancellor’s professor of psychology and informatics at the University of California, Irvine.

Even as she acknowledges online harassment and exploitation, Dr. Odgers believes the science remains unsettled on screen time causing mental health problems and rewiring people’s brains. Even so, she stands behind regulating tech companies, not only to protect children and teens, but also vulnerable adults.

“There should be safety by design principles in place for all users, as well as the protection of data and privacy, and control over preferences for scrolling and advertising exposure,” Dr. Odgers said.

The Lancet papers acknowledge that digital media can boost young people’s quality of life, pointing to social connection, access to information, telemedicine and job opportunities.

Like the Lancet authors, Dr. Odgers wants to see a healthier online world that amplifies the good on these platforms.

“Adults often view this as something that can be switched on or off, and it’s not like that. It’s more like a circulatory system,” she said.

“Digital technology runs all through our society, our relationships, for better or for worse. We need a healthy system for society to thrive and for all people to benefit and not get sick. We’re not going to be able to extract this with a scalpel, or just kick a subgroup off. We need to fix the underlying parts of it that are broken.”
