The experts said one-off measures such as age limits aren’t enough. They’re calling for safety standards for platform design, control over how personal data are collected and used, and independent oversight and accountability.

They want to see governments force tech giants to first, assess products for risk before launching them, and second, to release internal data on how features affect users’ health – with that intel then scrutinized by independent experts. The authors are also pushing for a dedicated international body to monitor AI harms to youth.

Dr. Shaw sees promise in Bill C-34, Canada’s Safe Social Media Act, a proposed federal law focused on making online platforms safer for youth and holding tech companies accountable. In particular, Dr. Shaw appreciates the push to establish a regulator capable of preventing youth from accessing a platform until a tech firm can show it’s safe.
“This logic of incentivizing platforms to demonstrate their safety has been absent from past efforts to ban young people from social media,” Dr. Shaw said.

The Lancet papers reflect a broader shift to thinking about safety by design, said Kaitlynn Mendes, a sociology professor at Western University and project lead at DIY: Digital Safety , who was not involved in the current research.

“It’s crazy that we let tech companies release products that haven’t been proven to be safe by design. We don’t accept that with any other products on the market. You think about food, automobiles, other tech and gadgets where we’ve set standards and regulations.”
Beyond Canada, Dr. Mendes pointed to laws already enacted in the U.K. and European Union, as well as Australia’s eSafety Commissioner, an independent government regulator dedicated to online safety.
“We’re crazy if we expect tech companies to voluntarily make changes that will impact their bottom line,” Dr. Mendes said.

“There need to be third-party mediators, a place for the public to bring complaints that also sets standards and imposes fines. In the U.K., Ofcom forces tech companies to produce transparency reports every year. They make companies publish how many cases of child sexual abuse material, luring and underage accounts there are on the platform. That can be an incredibly effective mechanism for forcing companies to make changes.”

The Lancet papers also illustrate an evolving approach to age restrictions, according to Candice Odgers, co-director of the Child and Brain Development Program at the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research. She was not involved in the Lancet papers.

“Adults really have broken the internet in some pretty brutal ways, and their solution has been to kick kids off to ‘fix it.’ That is not going to fix the broken internet, broken design choices and broken business models. It’s going to do absolutely nothing to help our young people because the bans don’t work, and the blame certainly doesn’t work,” said Dr. Odgers, a chancellor’s professor of psychology and informatics at the University of California, Irvine.

The Lancet papers acknowledge that digital media can boost young people’s quality of life, pointing to social connection, access to information, telemedicine and job opportunities.
Like the Lancet authors, Dr. Odgers wants to see a healthier online world that amplifies the good on these platforms.
“Adults often view this as something that can be switched on or off, and it’s not like that. It’s more like a circulatory system,” she said.

“Digital technology runs all through our society, our relationships, for better or for worse. We need a healthy system for society to thrive and for all people to benefit and not get sick. stories.title: ‘Degrading’ sign hung during homecoming prompts response from N.S. university president
stories.summary: The sign, painted on a white sheet and hung on an off-campus house read “Drop-off zone: Acadia girlfriends.”
stories.author: Rachel Morgan, Ella Macdonald
stories.content:
The President of St. Francis Xavier University has said rape culture will not be tolerated at the school after the displaying of what he said was a “degrading and deeply concerning” sign during homecoming.

The sign, painted on a white sheet and hung on an off-campus house read “Drop-off zone: Acadia girlfriends.”

“Language that objectifies women or makes light of sexualized violence has no place at StFX or in any community,” Andy Hakin wrote in a statement to the community and on social media. “We understand the concern and anger this has caused, both within our own community and beyond it.”

The incident comes less than three weeks after a rape case at Cornell University in New York made global headlines.

Liz Leclair, an anti-gender-based violence advocate, told Global News there is a recent escalation in attitudes towards sexualized violence.

“This is part of and parcel of the culture that is being created and perpetuated here in Nova Scotia, about women and girls being property, that you can do whatever you want with us,” she said.

The university said it had to intervene twice this weekend to have the sign removed and the matter has now been referred through the university’s disciplinary process.

Leclair said she wants to see accountability be taken by the students involved.

“I think there needs to be a public statement made by the young men involved, acknowledging the harm that they’ve caused, acknowledging the impact this has on women and girls in the community,” she said.

The president of Acadia University, Jeff Hennessy, also issued a statement condemning the act.

Both schools say support is available for those who have experienced sexual violence.

stories.title: ‘Know your own body’: Breast cancer survivor gives advice during Cibc Run for the Cure
stories.summary: This year’s Participant of Hope spoke to the hundreds of people in attendance prior to the Cibc Run for the Cure.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Breast cancer survivor Isabelle Simler wants everyone to be body aware.

This year’s Participant of Hope spoke to the hundreds of people in attendance prior to the Cibc Run for the Cure.

“You have to know that when there’s a lump, you’ve got to get it checked out,” said Simler who was diagnosed back in 2008.

“There’s no waiting because stage one is a big difference between stage four. It’s just a more aggressive situation for them to deal with and for you to deal with, so it’s important for you to get at it early.”

Simler had a long history of breast cancer. She had aunts and her sister both passed away. That made her aware something was wrong in 2008 and she ended up in a high-risk program which May have saved her life.

“I had young children, so my first thought was, ‘I can’t go anywhere because they need to have their mom present like they I need to be here.’”

The run had more than 1,300 participants and raised over $340,000 this year.

Prior to the run, 37 breast cancer survivors came to the front of the stage for a photo.

“I think it’s very important that we keep having this every year to raise money so that the money can find the research and also create more awareness for the people,” said Emmanuel Ademola, director of the London run.

“The researchers and research is getting better and better every day and we are part of the people who are funding the research in Canada. Hopefully the money that we fund and raise from the run actually goes into getting more information about the cure, about the awareness and hopefully getting our research more advanced.”

Participants braved some steady rain for about an hour prior to the run, but it cleared up and the sun came out just as the walkers and runners were about to start pounding the pavement.

Simler advocates for getting a mammogram and MRI and also follow through with further investigation if something feels wrong.

stories.title: Give bees a chance: Molagri’s plan to solve global food insecurity
stories.summary: Toronto biotech startupwants to help farmers stay ahead of mutating pests and save pollinators
stories.author: Susan Nerberg
stories.content:
What happens when you take biotech, used to create breakthrough innovations for medical therapies and treatments, and apply it to agriculture? If you ask Zaky Hassan, you May have an answer to global food insecurity.

Hassan, the co-founder and CEO of Molagri, says the primary goal of the Toronto-based biotech startup is to solve pesticide resistance. A major hurdle for agribusinesses is that the pesticides they use to combat swarms of hungry insects lose their effectiveness over time because insects mutate and become resistant to different killing agents.

So farmers, who globally spend some US$80 billion annually on pesticides, and US$18 billion specifically on insecticides, resort to using even more, with dire consequences for beneficial insects and the ecosystems they’re part of. “Chemical companies can’t make new pesticides fast enough to keep up with the mutating insects,” Hassan says, “and the risk is, we won’t be able to grow enough food for everybody.” So he and Min Jin, who is co-founder and chief scientific officer, decided to leverage their biology and biochemistry skills “to do something impactful for the world,” as Hassan puts it—namely, to develop an insecticide that can be updated to help farmers stay a step ahead of mutating pests while causing no harm to bees and other pollinators.

Molagri is short for “molecular agriculture,” as the mechanism underpinning the company’s invention takes place on a molecular level. By looking at the biological structure of proteins, it can design a hyper-specific payload that targets specific pests, Hassan says, keeping bees safe from harm. It helps that Jin holds the world record in pinpointing the most detail in the biological structure of a coronavirus protein, expertise Molagri has leveraged to solve, for instance, the protein structure of the honeybee, meaning they know how to avoid targeting the wrong insects.

Chemical companies can’t make new pesticides fast enough to keep up with the mutating insects, and the risk is, we won’t be able to grow enough food for everybody.

It’s this modularity that makes Molagri’s proposal promising: The target pest and the payload can be modified to respond to geographical and temporal variations and mutations. Using sequencing and surveillance data, Molagri can tweak the engineering of the virus-like particles to build packages capable of targeting different insects.

While Hassan and Jin are both PhD candidates in biochemistry at the University of Toronto, they developed Molagri outside of academia. And they had to turn to the United States for capital since they couldn’t find any pre-seed investors in Canada—a fact that rankles Hassan. “We need to do a better job supporting entrepreneurs in the deep sciences,” he says. “Risk-averse investors don’t want to help early companies, and it forces companies like ours to rely on Americans.”

Thanks to pre-seed funding of $500,000 from Julian Capital and another $500,000 from Y Combinator—both of which are based in San Francisco—Hassan and Jin started their lab at Toronto’s MaRS Discovery District in April of this year. “We’re super new,” says Hassan, sharing that he and Jin recently completed a seed fundraising round to help beef up its headcount (Molagri now has four staffers, Hassan and Jin included). As for commercialization, Molagri’s bioinsecticides are about four years out. In theory, they could be custom-made to meet the specific needs of any given farmer’s pest problem. In real life, though, “that would involve too much time constantly going through regulatory processes,” says Hassan, referring to safety testing and regulatory approvals for each bespoke payload.

So the two protein experts are aiming to create off-the-shelf products to be used across all types and scales of farming, everywhere. At the outset, though, the first customers will be those whose need is most pressing: growers of tree nuts and fruits, including almonds and pistachios (a feast for the navel orangeworm), apples and pears (favoured by the Washington codling moth). “Because we’re so early-phase, we’ll go where the need is more acute,” says Hassan, adding that the current focus is on tree nuts. “The need for more effective pesticides is more acute for those growers because trees grow in one spot for many years, so those farmers can’t rotate their crops,” he says. “But we want to make a product for canola—a Canadian product for Canada.”

If Molagri’s evolving insecticide turns out to be as good as promised—reducing or even removing the pests that damage food crops without harming bees and other insects or contaminating soils and waterways—it will represent, as Hassan puts it, a “win-win-win” for food security, farmers and the environment.

The company is still in its infancy, but its name might be hinting at something big: If you swap the first and second vowels in Molagri, you get milagro —“miracle” in Spanish.

If Molagri’s evolving insecticide turns out to be as good as promised—reducing or even removing the pests that damage food crops without harming bees and other insects or contaminating soils and waterways—it will represent, as Hassan puts it, a “win-win-win” for food security, farmers and the environment.
The company is still in its infancy, but its name might be hinting at something big: If you swap the first and second vowels in Molagri, you get milagro —“miracle” in Spanish.

content_blocks.text: What happens when you take biotech, used to create breakthrough innovations for medical therapies and treatments, and apply it to agriculture? If you ask Zaky Hassan, you May have an answer to global food insecurity.

Hassan, the co-founder and CEO of Molagri, says the primary goal of the Toronto-based biotech startup is to solve pesticide resistance. A major hurdle for agribusinesses is that the pesticides they use to combat swarms of hungry insects lose their effectiveness over time because insects mutate and become resistant to different killing agents.

stories.title: ‘He was larger than life’: Memorial ride honours late motorcyclist Steven Steinsland
stories.summary: Members of London’s Free Riders group gathered Saturday for a memorial ride to honor 36-year-old Stephen Steinsland, who was killed in a crash at Sarnia Road and Castlegrove Boulevard in London, Ont. on Sept. 21, 2026.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
It was kickstands up for a son, brother and friend.

Members of London’s Free Riders group gathered Saturday for a memorial ride to honor 36-year-old Stephen Steinsland, who was killed in a crash at Sarnia Road and Castlegrove Boulevard in London, Ont. on Sept. 21, 2026.

“It’s incredible to see how many people, the passion they have to see how much of an amazing person he was,” said friend Josh Bumpus.

The day began with dozens of bikers gathering at Tim Horton’s on Admiral Drive.

“It’s a bittersweet day,” said friend Tiffany Vanderlaa.

“I think it’s amazing to see all these people come out. It shows how impactful Steve was. The day that the accident happened, he was at mine and Josh’s house and we were talking about plans for Florida in the future. It’s so sad I’m going forward without him.”

After leaving East London, the riders made their way around the city, ending at the crash site for a ceremony at a makeshift monument.

They held a moment of silence; tears were shed and family and friends gathered to lay flowers and other items on the memorial.

“I don’t even know how to describe him other than he was larger than life,” said Mark Steinsland, Steven’s father.

“I never realized how many friends he hung out with and this is just this is huge.”

The fatal crash remains under investigation, but some in attendance say he was traveling on Sarnia Road at the speed limit when a car turned left and hit him.

“Myself and my fiance (Vanderlaa) are both motorcycle instructors with Fanshawe for the safety course,” said Bumpus.“We are huge safety advocates and riding appropriately. Within the city, it’s just not safe.”

Vanderlaa says cars have much more protection than riders, so drivers need to always be aware of their surroundings.

“One wrong turn in front of us can end our lives,” she said.

“Steve is a great example of that. Going the speed limit and just trying to get home at the end of the day. He lost his life and it is absolutely tragic what happened.”

It was one last sendoff for a man loved by many.

“He would have loved this,” said friend Rachel Cloud.

“He would have loved it. He’s passionate about motorcycles and you realize just what an impact he made all over the place. Work, community, gym everyone loved him.”

stories.title: Quebec party leaders make final pitches to voters ahead of Monday's vote
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec's main party leaders are delivering their final messages to voters ahead of Monday's provincial election.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Quebec’s main party leaders took a look back at their campaigns on Sunday as they worked to deliver one final message to electors on the eve of Monday’s vote.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says this election is all about bringing change to the province after eight straight years of Coalition Avenir Québec rule.

“I hope that tomorrow there will be a significant change in direction, and I think that’s what the people of Quebec are expecting,” St-Pierre Plamondon said. “I believe we are the only ones who can offer that.”

Polls suggest his party is the front-runner, but St-Pierre Plamondon urged his volunteers and supporters to make one last push to undecided voters in the campaign’s final 24 hours.

He spent the last day of his campaign in the Montreal region where the PQ has had some of its weakest support over the past decade, but hopes to flip some seats.

St-Pierre Plamondon has said his top priority in his first 100 days will be to allocate a special budget for homelessness, as well as cutting red tape, abolishing taxes on used goods, lowering the gas tax, and reinvesting in community organizations and food banks.

The PQ leader’s rivals, meanwhile, were warning voters against choosing a party that has promised to hold a sovereignty referendum before the end of its first term in government.

Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette says her party is the only one that offers an alternative to the province’s sovereigntist-federalist dichotomy, by focusing on nationalism and economic growth within Canada.

She said she was proud of her campaign, but also expressed regret over not having put more emphasis on the threat posed by a referendum.

‘It’s important for people to realize this, because it’s not just a decision that could affect Quebec in three years’’, she said. “There will be impacts because uncertainty will become part of Quebec’s political and economic calendar.’’

Fréchette, whose party has been trailing in the polls, was scheduled to spend part of the last full day of campaigning door-knocking in the riding of Trois-Rivières, where she’s running for a seat.

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard described his party as the only federalist option, and urged voters who want to avoid a PQ government to vote strategically for his candidates.

He warned that a PQ minority would be out seeking support for a referendum among the other parties.

“One party that Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon won’t be calling up is Liberal Party of Quebec, because we’re proudly federalist and not ashamed to say it,” he said.

Milliard said at a campaign stop on Sunday in St-Victor, Que., that his party had gained momentum since the start of the campaign, when he was criticized for not having a picture of him on his party’s campaign bus — an image that was added later. He said the Liberal vote was likely “underestimated” in certain regions.

Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, meanwhile, urged his supporters to cast enough votes on Monday to give his party a strong voice in the legislature. Duhaime has promised to use his leverage to act as a “guard dog” who will protect taxpayer interests and attempt to block a referendum vote.

Duhaime said he’s hoping his party wins at least 12 seats and official party status, after winning none in 2022.

“I’m very, very serene, and I have confidence,” he said. “The only thing is, we have to make sure people go out and vote.”

In Montreal, Québec solidaire spokesperson Ruba Ghazal was making a final appeal to progressive sovereigntist voters who don’t identify with the “austerity” proposed by the PQ, and other parties, including Duhaime’s Conservatives.

“Send a signal that not all of Quebec has swung to the right or turned conservative, and also send people who will be the only ones to stand up to Éric Duhaime’s influence in the next parliament,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 4, 2026.

stories.title: Quebec Liberal Leader targets PQ referendum pledge on final day of election campaign
stories.summary: Sherbrooke - Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard zeroed in on the Parti Québécois pledge to hold a sovereignty referendum as he rallied the party faithful on the last full day of the provincial election campaign.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Sherbrooke - Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard said he didn’t have many regrets on the eve of the provincial election, save the fact that he didn’t make himself the face of his party’s campaign earlier.

Milliard was not a familiar figure for Quebecers before running for Liberal leadership, which he won in February. He has never held public office, but is now seeking to form a government.

stories.title: Hyundai recalls Ioniq 9 SUVs over second-row seat issue
stories.summary: Hyundai is recalling 1,460 Ioniq 9 SUVs in Canada because second-row power seats May fail to detect an obstruction. The automaker says the seats could continue moving, increasing the risk of injury.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Hyundai is recalling more than 1,400 Ioniq 9 SUVs in Canada over a potential problem with the vehicles’ second-row power seats.

The recall affects certain 2026 and 2027 Hyundai Ioniq 9 Ultimate Calligraphy models equipped with second-row captain chairs, according to a Transport Canada notice updated Thursday. A total of 1,460 vehicles are affected.

The issue involves the seats’ power-folding function. In some vehicles, the second-row seats May fail to detect an obstruction and could continue moving even after coming into contact with something in their path.

The notice added that a seat that does not stop moving could increase the risk of injury.

As a precaution, Hyundai advises owners to make sure the second-row seats are empty before using the power-folding functions until the recall repair is completed.

Hyundai will notify affected owners in writing and provide a software update for the rear power seats. The update can be delivered wirelessly to eligible vehicles, or owners can arrange to have the work completed at a Hyundai dealership. The repair will be provided at no charge.

Owners can check whether their vehicle is affected by entering its vehicle identification number (VIN) into Hyundai Canada’s recall lookup tool ⁠.

A similar recall was issued in the United States for certain 2026 Ioniq 9 vehicles equipped with Limited, Calligraphy or Calligraphy Design trim packages. The U.S. recall affects 5,360 vehicles, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.

The U.S. notice similarly warns that the second-row power seats May fail to detect a person and continue moving during functions such as automatic power folding and stowing.

U.S. owners are advised to exercise caution around the second-row seats until the software update is completed.

stories.title: CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette expresses regret as Quebec election campaign ends
stories.summary: Montreal - Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette expressed some regret as she made her final appeal to voters in the provincial election campaign.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - With hours left in Quebec’s provincial election campaign, Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette acknowledged Sunday that there are things she would have done differently.

During a stop in Shawinigan, Fréchette said she was proud of the campaign she had run, but said she should have put a greater emphasis on the consequences of a referendum on sovereignty promised by Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s.

Fréchette argued the prospect of a referendum would create uncertainty for Quebec’s economy almost immediately after the election if the PQ forms government, even though the PQ leader has pledged to delay a referendum, if he forms a government, until after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House in 2029.

’‘It’s important for people to realize this, because it’s not just a decision that could affect Quebec in three years’’, she said, adding, “There will be impacts because uncertainty will become part of Quebec’s political and economic calendar.’’

She rejected St-Pierre Plamondon’s previous accusation that the CAQ was engaging in a fear campaign by raising the possible economic consequences of another referendum.

But the referendum was not the only thing Fréchette said she would handle differently.

She said her team May have spent too much time detailing their party’s promises and not enough time laying out the broader differences between the CAQ and its opponents.

Fréchette also said she would have emphasized the party’s economic record and experience in government earlier in the campaign and acknowledged she was sometimes too reactive when she came under attack during the leaders’ debates.

Her reflections came as the CAQ entered the final hours of a campaign that could put an end to the party’s eight years in power after winning two consecutive majority governments under former premier François Legault.

Despite her regrets, Fréchette reiterated Sunday that she intends to remain CAQ leader regardless of the outcome of Monday’s vote.

She also returned to her central message: that the CAQ represents a “third way” between federalism and sovereignty.

Fréchette said she was worried Quebec politics was going back to the long-standing divide between those who want the province to remain in Canada and those who want it to become an independent country.

“Systematically taking refuge either in the Yes or in the No is too limiting,” she said.

She argued the Caq’s alternative must continue to be offered “with strength and vigour” to Quebecers.

“I think every riding in Quebec has the possibility of becoming a cradle of the coalition to keep the third way active, and we’re working toward that,” she said.

Fréchette also used her final pitch to highlight a platform focused on reducing the cost of living, improving public services and protecting Quebec’s economy and identity.

She was scheduled to spend part of the final hours of the campaign going door-to-door in Trois-Rivières, where she is running for a seat in the legislature.

Quebecers head to the polls Monday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 4, 2026.

stories.title: Parti Québécois leader says he feeling optimistic on last day of Quebec campaign
stories.summary: Montreal - Parti Québécois leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says he expects Monday's provincial election to be tight, but he remains optimistic.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - As Quebecers prepare to head to the polls on Monday, Parti Québécois leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon remains cautiously optimistic.

Speaking to journalists in Montreal, the separatist leader said he feels at peace with his performance in the campaign.

“I hope that tomorrow there will be a significant change in direction, and I think that’s what the people of Quebec are expecting,” St-Pierre Plamondon said. “I believe we are the only ones who can offer that.”

While the PQ has maintained a lead in the polls throughout the campaign, St-Pierre Plamondon said he is not taking a victory for granted.

“The only certainty is that it’s going to be a tight race,” he said.

However, his party has been considering scenarios of forming a minority or majority government as serious possibilities.

He has said that either scenario would trigger a sovereignty referendum campaign, sometime after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House in 2029.

St-Pierre Plamondon spent the entire day campaigning in the Montreal region, an area where the PQ has had some of its weakest support in the province over the past decade.

He is seeking to be reelected in a riding on the Island of Montreal. The seat was the only one held by the PQ on the island before the campaign began.

“I’m appealing to those who are not even certain they will vote tomorrow,” he said. “Please help us deliver the change you are requesting. And we need that support.”

On Saturday, the PQ leader laid out his priorities for his first 100 days in office, if his party forms government. In a news release, he said his top priority would be to allocate a special budget for homelessness, especially with winter around the corner.

In addition, a PQ government would cut red tape, abolish taxes on used goods, lower the gas tax, reinvest in community organizations and food banks, and lower immigration thresholds.

St-Pierre Plamondon boasted that he is the only political leader to have visited every region of Quebec over the last 39 days.

The PQ leader had his work cut out for him after the 2022 election, when his party only won three seats. The sovereigntist party hasn’t been in power since former premier Pauline Marois’ minority government dissolved in 2014.

St-Pierre Plamondon won the PQ leadership in 2020 after making his promise to hold a referendum in a first mandate after forming a government.

During his campaign, he attacked Ottawa and the British monarchy, calling the latter a symbol of “domination by force,” and pledging to defund the office of the lieutenant-governor, which represents the King in Quebec.

The PQ leader also leaned on nationalist sentiment and a desire for change to drum up support from those who were disillusioned after eight years of the governing Coalition Avenir Québec.

He linked “uncontrolled immigration” to problems such as the housing crisis, the decline in the French language, the struggling education system and strain on public services.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 4, 2026.

stories.title: B.C. New Democrats one short of full slate, only Conservatives field 93 candidates
stories.summary: Victoria - The office overseeing elections in British Columbia says the provincial NDP under Leader David Eby is not running candidates in all 93 ridings.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby said his party would introduce a new tax bracket for those who earn $1 million or more and raise the existing rates of the two highest brackets to help pay for health care, if re-elected.

Eby’s party said British Columbia would become the first large province with a tax bracket on individuals who earn more than a million, while the B.C. Conservatives said the move would drive doctors out of the province.

“We are glad when people are successful, it’s fantastic,” Eby said Sunday while campaigning in Comox on Vancouver Island ahead of the Oct. 24 election.

“We cheer for them, we want them to be successful, and it’s also right to ask people, who earn a little bit more to pitch-in in a moment like this, when people across the province need those strong public services.”

Documents provided by the party say that the proposed changes would start in the 2027 tax year and are projected to raise $225 million in 2026/27, $925 million the next year, and $1 billion in the year after that.

The party said that a portion of income above $1 million would be taxed at 24.5 per cent.

The portion between $265,545 and $1 million would be taxed at 22.5 per cent, while income between $190,405 and $265,545 would be taxed at 18.8 per cent.

The documents say that the changes would apply to less than four per cent of earners and only to income earned over each tax bracket.

In response, the B.C. Conservatives said in a statement that the NDP plan would mean taxing the doctors and specialists every community is fighting to recruit, and would drive doctors out of the province.

“There is no problem the NDP don’t think can be fixed by raising your taxes,” the statement said.

The Conservatives have campaigned on a promise of never raising taxes.

The announcement comes after Eby said his government would introduce price guards for certain groceries, as well as gasoline and diesel, while temporarily lowering the provincial motor fuel tax by 10 cents per litres.

Eby said during the early phases of the campaign that his party would introduce a new tax on empty condominiums and lift the speculation and vacancy tax.

When asked whether promises of new taxes and regulations would make businesses feel unwelcome, he said his party is not fighting against them, but standing up for British Columbians.

“The business community, as much as anybody else, depends on a functioning province, where truckers are able to deliver goods, where people are able to find homes, where their employees are able to find health care, and I know they understand that.”

Elsewhere on the campaign trail, B.C. Green Party Leader Emily Lowan released her party’s promises related to the forestry sector.

The Greens said they would end raw-log exports and close loopholes that allow minimally processed or rough-sawn wood to leave British Columbia without meaningful processing.

The platform also promises to permanently protect big-treed old growth and large second-growth forests from logging and provide conservation financing to support Indigenous-led protection.

The announcements came as the field of candidates running in the election was set Sunday.

A statement from Elections BC showed the British Columbia Conservatives as the only party with candidates in all 93 ridings.

Mauro Francis, the party’s president, said in a statement that the momentum is now with the Conservatives.

“The enthusiasm we’ve seen across B.C. has been incredible,” he said. “In every region, from small towns to big cities, local members and volunteers stepped up to find great candidates and get them nominated.”

Eby’s New Democrats, meanwhile, was one short of fielding a full slate after failing to find a candidate for Peace River North, where voters will choose between Independent Jordan Kealy and Conservative Curtis Whitford.

Kealy won the riding in 2024 as a Conservative, but left the party in March 2025. He was charged with sexual assault in June of this year. He has denied the allegations.

Eby said it is disappointing that paperwork prevented his party from fielding a candidate in the last riding.

“But I will tell you that I have got 92 amazing candidates in this province that I would put against any of the Conservative candidates that they are putting forward,” he said.

Elections BC said the Greens have 73 candidates, including Lowan, who is running in Greater Victoria, former provincial chief coroner Lisa Lapointe, who is also running in Greater Victoria, and Jeremy Valeriote, who is running in Greater Vancouver.

Andrew Weaver, a former leader of the Greens, is running for CentreBC, which is fielding 35 candidates, including Leader Elenore Sturko.

The former Conservative will be running in her home riding of Surrey South, where she will face Conservative Megan Knight, along with New Democrat Parik Tahlan, Green Bill McConnell and Denis R. Hurtubise, who is not affiliated with any party.

OneBC, which like CentreBC, splintered from the Conservatives, is running in 33 ridings. But its roster of would-be legislators does not include former Conservative Brent Chapman, who held Surrey-South at dissolution.

OneBC earlier announced Chapman as the candidate for the riding, but his name does not appear at all on the official list of candidates.

Chapman is the husband of former Conservative Kerry-Lynne Findlay, who resigned last month after defections and ideological divisions, just before the snap election was called.

Also not running is former OneBC legislator Tara Armstrong, who said on social media that she doesn’t want to split the anti-NDP vote. Armstrong had previously tried but failed to repeal the B.C. Human Rights Code.

OneBC interim leader Dallas Brodie, meanwhile, is running again in Vancouver-Quilchena. It’s one of nine ridings where candidates for all four major parties will face off against each other.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 4, 2026.

stories.title: Montreal transit agency investigating death of man who fell onto subway tracks
stories.summary: The Société de transport de Montréal says the man was unable to get back onto the platform and was struck by a train at the Lionel-Groulx subway station.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Montreal’s transit agency is investigating after a man in his 40s died after falling onto the tracks at a metro station on Saturday.

The Société de transport de Montréal says the man was unable to get back onto the platform and was struck by a train at the Lionel-Groulx subway station.

Montreal police confirmed the age of the man and the fact that the death appeared accidental.

A police spokesperson says a surveillance camera video showed the man wasn’t pushed and there was no criminal element.

The transit agency says it investigating the circumstances surrounding the collision.

In the meantime, it’s reminding transit users to stay behind the yellow lines on the platform and to keep a safe distance from the trains.

stories.title: Search ongoing for six people after debris found from missing Ontario air ambulance
stories.summary: The U.S. Coast Guard says the search is ongoing for four Canadians and two Bermuda nationals who were on board an Ontario air ambulance that went missing on Saturday.
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The U.S. Coast Guard says it continues to search for survivors after finding a debris field off the coast of Nantucket that’s been confirmed as being from a missing Canadian air ambulance jet.

Rear Admiral Matt Lake told a news conference in Boston on Sunday that crews from the coast guard, the New York National Guard and Massachusetts authorities have searched about 7,350 square kilometres, over a “large and demanding search area,” for the four missing Canadians and two Bermuda nationals.

“My thoughts and those of every coast guard crew member are with the people on that aircraft, their families, their friends and their loved ones during this incredibly difficult time,” he said.

Lake said the coast guard search began around 2 a.m. on Saturday after they were notified the Federal Aviation Administration had lost contact with the plane as it was flying from Bermuda to Boston.

The debris field was found about 32 kilometres off the island of Nantucket, in waters approximately 24 to 27 metres deep, coast guard officials said.

The medical evacuation jet, belonging to Hamilton, Ont.-based Latitude Air Ambulance, was carrying a patient, their family member and four Canadian crew members when it went dark early Saturday.

Lt.-Cmdr. Kastriot Kastrati said he couldn’t provide details about the debris that was recovered, and Lake noted the coast guard is working with Massachusetts authorities to get sonar-equipped craft to search the sea floor around the debris field.

Lake said the search efforts are being aided by fixed-wing aircraft, boats and a helicopter, and that next of kin for the six missing people are being updated as the search continues.

He said a black box, a recording device found in airplanes used to investigate accidents, has yet to be recovered.

Capt. John McTamney said search efforts will continue until crews are “confident that if there were any survivors remaining on the surface of the water, we would have found them.”

According to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net , the pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast.

“Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot.

The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 24,000 feet to around 10,000 feet, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24.

Mary Schiavo, who is a former Inspector General of the U.S. Transportation Department, told the Associated Press she thinks the plane May have lost its navigational instruments just as a storm moved across its path on radar.

“Something bad happened with this big drop, and they flew into this big storm. It’s a terrible place to have a loss of your instruments and be flying blind,” said Schiavo, who is an aviation attorney. “It’s very easy to get disoriented and not know if you’re turning, climbing, descending, etc.”

Lake said at Sunday’s news conference that he didn’t want to speculate if electrical problems or weather played a factor in the incident.

“That’s up to the investigative efforts later,” he said.

Latitude Air Ambulance offers emergency medical transportation by plane worldwide, according to its website, and operations manager Clarence Togeretz told The Canadian Press on Saturday that this is the first time the company has lost contact with one of its planes.

Foreign Affairs minister Anita Anand said in a social media post that she’s “deeply concerned” by the disappearance of the air ambulance carrying Canadian crew members, and that Global Affairs consular officials are in contact with the relevant authorities.

“My thoughts are with everyone on board and their loved ones. I thank the U.S. Coast Guard and all those involved in the search and rescue efforts for their tireless work,” she wrote.

stories.title: Four Canadians aboard Ontario-based air ambulance missing off U.S. coast
stories.summary: The Canadians on board a missing air ambulance off the U.S. east coast were the two pilots and two medical staff.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
The U.S. Coast Guard continues to search a debris field south of Nantucket in hopes of finding the six occupants of an air ambulance crash early Saturday morning, four of whom are Canadian employees of the private Ontario-based medical flight company.

During a Sunday morning press conference in Boston, U.S. Coast Guard officials said their priority remains finding the occupants of the Gulfstream G100 that lost contact with air traffic controllers while it was en route from L.F. Wade International Airport in Bermuda to Boston Logan International Airport.

“At this point, we are still conducting a search for the missing personnel,” Northeast district commander Rear Admiral Matt Lake stressed when asked if this was a rescue or recovery mission.

“We’ll continue to search and saturate the area until we’re at the point where we are confident that if there were any survivors remaining on the surface of the water, we would have found them.”

The aircraft’s tail number C-Grjp is linked to Latitude Air Ambulance , a Hamilton company contracted by governments, insurance companies and other organizations “to provide safe and reliable medical evacuation and repatriation services” via its 10 aircraft.

Company spokesman Clarence Togeretz told AFP the Canadians were the two pilots and two medical staff, while the other occupants were a patient and family member from Bermuda. He told The Canadian Press that this is the first time the carrier lost contact with one of its aircraft.

Togeretz said they’re “dealing with the situation with as much positivity and optimism as we can” and “praying for a safe outcome.”

Lake said they were in touch with all occupants’ next of kin, keeping them apprised of search efforts.

“I want you to know that my thoughts and those of every coast guard crew member are with the people on that aircraft, their families, their friends and their loved ones during this incredibly difficult time.”

According to data from FlightAware, the aircraft left Bermuda at 11:41 p.m. EDT on Friday and was approaching the U.S. coast just after 1 a.m. when its altitude dropped from 24,000 to 11,000 feet (7,315 to 3,352 metres) over two minutes.

The broadcaster also reported that a spokesperson at Nantucket Memorial Airport said the jet had declared an emergency before losing contact and that an air traffic controller in New York was also in contact with the troubled aircraft.

Coast guard air and surface crews were dispatched and “located a debris field that has been confirmed to be associated with the missing aircraft” on Saturday about 20 kilometres south of Nantucket.

“It’s very difficult at this point to identify exactly what those components are,” district search and rescue coordinator Lt.-Cmdr. Kastrio Kastrati said Sunday.

“The debris that we have recovered, we’ve safeguarded and kept for future investigative efforts.”

The aircraft’s black box has not yet been located.

Lake said that, with help from the New York National Guard, crews have searched roughly 2,840 square miles (7,355 square kilometres) over 53 hours as of Sunday morning. Water depth in the area is between 80 and 90 feet, so they are coordinating with authorities in Massachusetts to “get some craft out there that are equipped with sonar to be able to do some detection on the seabed floor.”

“This is a large and demanding search area,” he noted.

Capt. John McTamney, district chief of response, said weather conditions have been “favourable” for search operations, with winds at 15 to 20 knots (27 to 37 km/h) and three-foot seas.

Steve MacKinnon, Canada’s minister of transport, expressed his concern in a post on X , thanked first responders and said federal officials “are closely monitoring the situation and are working with the relevant authorities as search and rescue efforts continue.”

“My thoughts are with the six people aboard the missing air ambulance travelling from Bermuda to Boston, and their families,” Bermuda Premier David Burt wrote on Instagram before the debris had been found.

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada told National Post via email it was “still gathering information and assessing the occurrence.”

National Post has also contacted the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board. The Ontario Ministry of Transportation deferred to Canadian federal authorities.

All of us at Ornge are hopeful the aircraft and all passengers are located safely and quickly.

By John Marchesan and Denio Lourenco

Posted October 4, 2026 11:11 am.

Last Updated October 4, 2026 7:30 pm.

The United States Coast Guard suspended a search for six missing people who were aboard an Ontario air ambulance that crashed off the eastern U.S. coast over the weekend.

In a press release shared Sunday night, Rear Adm. Matthew Lake, Commander of the Northeast District said, “suspending a search is not an easy decision.”

“We express our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones affected by the tragedy and our gratitude for our partner agencies who helped support search efforts,” he added.

Earlier in the day, officials said they were concentrating their search around a debris field that was located 20 miles off Nantucket.

Coast Guard crews along with the New York National Guard’s Air Rescue Wing and Massachusetts authorities searched an area encompassing 2,840 square miles (7,356 square kilometers) using fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, boats and cutters.

“This is a large and demanding search area,” Lake said.

The depth of the water around the debris field was 80 to 90 feet (about 24 to 27 meters). The Coast Guard was in the process of deploying sonar to search the seabed floor, he said.

The plane, which is owned by Hamilton, Ont.-based medical evacuation company Latitude Air Ambulance, was transporting a patient and their family member from Bermuda to Boston when it disappeared around 1:30 a.m.

Six people, including four Canadians and two Bermudian nationals, were aboard the aircraft.

Air traffic audio indicates that the plane May have been “coming in blind” when a storm loomed ahead shortly before it vanished.

The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast, according to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net. “Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot.

That makes Mary Schiavo, who is a former Inspector General of the Transportation Department, think the plane May have lost its navigational instruments just as a storm moved across its path on radar. The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 24,000 feet to around 10,000 feet, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24.

“Something bad happened with this big drop, and they flew into this big storm. It’s a terrible place to have a loss of your instruments and be flying blind,” said Schiavo, who is an aviation attorney. “It’s very easy to get disoriented and not know if you’re turning, climbing, descending, etc.”

Files from The Associated Press were used in this report

stories.title: U.S. mayor makes appeal to Canadian travellers: 'We like you guys, we miss you'
stories.summary: A U.S. mayor has taken to social media to ask Canadians boycotting travel to the United States to return to his city.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
A U.S. mayor has taken to social media to send a message to Canadians boycotting travel to the United States: Minneapolis misses them.

Jacob Frey, the mayor of Minneapolis, Minnesota, said in the video he shared on Instagram on Wednesday: “Hey Canadians. We like you guys, we miss you. We don’t think of you as the 51st state. We know that you’re a sovereign nation.”

His message comes amid escalating trade tensions between Canada and the U.S., which most recently saw President Donald Trump accuse Canada of “taking advantage” of his country and call Canada’s leaders “very bad.”

“I understand you’ve been dealing with some kind of unreasonable stuff, and to put it lightly, we’ve dealt with some really unreasonable stuff in Minneapolis,” Frey said. “We can talk about that when you come to visit us.”

The video comes months after two people were fatally shot in Minneapolis by federal agents. Renee Good was killed by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent on Jan. 7, and Alex Pretti was shot just weeks later, ON Jan. 24, by a U.S. Border Patrol officer.

Following Good’s death, Frey demanded that ICE “get the f— out of Minneapolis” during a news conference . “Long-term Minneapolis residents that have contributed so greatly to our city, to our culture, to our economy, are being terrorized — and now somebody is dead,” he said.

In the recent Instagram video, Frey attempted to entice Canadians to travel to the Minnesota city by saying, “It’s beautiful fall right now,” and Minneapolis has “some of the best restaurants in the world.”

“But most importantly, we can have each other’s company,” he added. “So we miss you guys, and whether it’s a short flight away, or for some of you even a drive, I can’t wait to see you when you visit our city. Love, Minneapolis.”

Amid Canadians’ souring attitudes towards the U.S. , Mayor Frey isn’t the only politician to personally urge his northern neighbours to visit. In April 2025, California Governor Gavin Newsom shared a video promoting tourism to the Golden State, in which he said: “Sure, you-know-who is trying to stir things up back in D.C., but don’t let that ruin your beach plans.”

Canadians are flying back to the U.S. after three years of declining travel

Canadians spent $3.3 billion less on travel to the U.S. last year: StatCan

The state also launched a US$5.2 million tourism campaign aimed at welcoming Canadians to California, and the city of Palm Springs displayed 40 red banners featuring the Canadian flag shaped as a heart in an effort to show the resort destination’s solidarity with Canada.

Meanwhile, both Visit Florida and Travel Nevada tourism boards held promotional events in Canada earlier in the year to promote travel to their states and showcase commitment to the Canadian market.

These efforts come after a sharp decline in the number of Canadians travelling south of the border. Recently released figures from Statistics Canada revealed Canadians spent $3.3 billion less on travel to the United States in 2025 compared to 2024, which amounted to a total of 7.4 million fewer trips south. When it came to leisure travel to the U.S., visits from Canadians dropped by 3.2 million, a reduction of 21.5 per cent.

StatCan notes that the dramatic decline in cross-border travel occurred “following the change in the U.S. administration in early 2025 and the implementation of America First policies,” adding that “Canadians’ travel plans shifted abruptly” during this time.

However, figures from July suggest that might be about to change. StatCan data showed that return trips to the U.S. by air edged up 0.6 per cent year over year that month, marking the first increase since August 2023.

Combined with 2.2 million trips by automobile (a year-over-year increase of 12.6 per cent) and 26,400 by cruise ship, total return trips to the U.S. by Canadian residents reached 2.8 million in July, up 10.1 per cent year-over-year. This marked a fourth consecutive month of year-over-year growth, following 15 consecutive months of decline.

But while the July figures suggest the U.S. travel boycott May be over, the data covers a period before the latest escalations in the Canada-U.S. trade war.

After talks between the two countries broke down in August, Trump imposed 50 per cent tariffs on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods. Canada retaliated with counter-tariffs on U.S. imports taking effect in September.

With trade tensions showing no sign of easing, it remains to be seen whether Mayor Frey’s plea will be answered.

stories.title: Showers taper off in London as temperatures reach 20 C Sunday
stories.summary: London is in for a mild Sunday, with showers expected to move out this morning before a mix of sun and cloud takes over.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
London is in for a mild Sunday, with showers expected to move out this morning before a mix of sun and cloud takes over.

There is a 40 per cent chance of showers late this afternoon. Winds will strengthen from the southwest, reaching 20 km/h and gusting to 40 this afternoon.

The high will reach 20 C, with a UV index of 5, or moderate.

Tonight will be partly cloudy with a 40 per cent chance of showers early in the evening. Southwest winds at 20 km/h, gusting to 40, will shift northwest around midnight. The overnight low is expected to be 7 C.

Monday will bring cooler conditions, with a mix of sun and cloud and northwest winds reaching 30 km/h and gusting to 50. The high will be 15 C.

Temperatures are expected to climb again through the week, reaching 20 C Wednesday and Thursday. Friday will be slightly cooler at 18 C, with a chance of showers Friday night.

stories.title: Diesel prices could fall below $2 a litre in coming months: expert
stories.summary: the coming months as oil prices ease, but ongoing tensions between the United States and Iran remain a major wildcard, an energy expert says.
stories.author: Tammy Ibrahimpoor
stories.content:
the coming months as oil prices ease, but ongoing tensions between the United States and Iran remain a major wildcard, an energy expert says.

Peter Linder, a former oil and gas analyst, said oil prices could fall to about US$85 a barrel from roughly US$90 now if tensions in the Middle East ease.

“If they start even just announcing peace discussions, oil’s going to drop $5 minimum, maybe even $10,” Linder said in an interview with CTV News Channel Saturday.

He said he expects oil prices to continue falling in the coming weeks, but the outlook could change quickly, and oil prices May go back “well over $100” if the conflict between Iran and the U.S. escalates.

He said, however, that both sides prefer to make a deal.

“My feeling is that Trump needs to make a deal,” Linder said. “Iran is definitely suffering economically. They’re not getting their exports out, or very little of it out, so they’ve got to capitulate as well.”

Diesel supply remains tight

Linder said the price of diesel has been particularly elevated because of supply and demand.

“Diesel demand is very strong and supply is very weak,” he said. “There’s just much more gasoline than diesel. Gasoline is also very expensive … but diesel is a unique product today.”

Linder said diesel prices historically tended to be lower than gasoline, but changes in refining and supply have altered the market.

“Diesel supply out of Russia has been seriously affected. Diesel supply of the Middle East has been affected,” he said.

‘It’s more downside than upside’

Linder said a number of factors could contribute to lower fuel prices in the months ahead.

The summer driving season has ended, and an announcement by European countries to release up to 100 million barrels of crude oil and diesel could put further downward pressure on prices.

Linder said lower diesel prices would have broader economic benefits because diesel is widely used to transport goods across the country.

“To me, it’s more downside than upside,” he said. “We’ve peaked, I think, ON the diesel side.”

stories.title: ‘Can we chat?’: It’s the small messages that define workplace culture
stories.summary: Workplace culture is shaped not only by policies and retreats, but by the small, everyday interactions employees have with their leaders
stories.author: Déjà Leonard
stories.content:
This is the weekly Work Life newsletter. If you are interested in more careers-related content, sign up to receive it in your inbox.

“Can we chat?”

It’s the message your manager just sent you. There’s no context and the meeting isn’t until late in the afternoon. Suddenly, you’re replaying your last few weeks of work and wondering what went wrong.

It might seem like a harmless message, but Jason Murray says small interactions like this can have an outsized impact on how employees experience workplace culture.

“It’s actually a mistake for employers and leaders to think that they can rely on strategic plans or websites or annual retreats or anything of that nature to see culture form because employees experience culture in smaller everyday moments,” says Mr. Murray, founder, president and managing partner of BES Executive Search in Toronto.

That’s increasingly important as more workplace communication happens through screens.

“We don’t pick up the phone these days to actually call people to hear tone and intention and emotion,” he says.

Without those cues, employees are left to interpret the words in front of them. Mr. Murray says leaders can make that experience better by being more intentional with their language.

One place to start is adding context.

Short messages aren’t necessarily bad. Instead of simply asking, “Do you have a moment to speak?” Mr. Murray suggests adding what you want to discuss: “Do you have a moment to speak about the project that we’re working on together?”

That small addition means people know what to expect instead of “filling in the storyboard for themselves,” he says.

Leaders should also reconsider language that creates unnecessary urgency.

Words such as “ASAP,” “now” and “priority” can immediately put employees on alert, Mr. Murray says.

“Too often we think everything is critical, everything is red alert, everything is an emergency,” he says. Before hitting send, consider whether the request actually warrants that urgency.

And if being more thoughtful about every email or Slack message sounds time-consuming, he says slowing down is okay. With practice, intentional communication becomes more efficient.

It can also become part of your professional identity.

Mr. Murray tries to bring personality to his writing, using his messages to add levity to an employee’s day. He says some employees have even told him they look forward to receiving his emails because they feel like they’ll get something from them.

Even the way he ends his emails is intentional, signing off each message with “Create a great day.”

“It’s the last way that I’m communicating, which means that it’s going to have people feeling a particular way at the end of the email,” he says.

Culture may be discussed at annual retreats, but employees experience it every day – sometimes in something as small as the words at the bottom of an email.

That’s how many Canadian knowledge workers say it feels too risky to leave their job right now, according to HP’s 2026 Work Relationship Index.

Artificial intelligence is making it increasingly important for leaders to protect and develop the distinctly human capabilities of creativity, curiosity and collaborative thinking. The challenge is that creativity can weaken when people rely too heavily on familiar perspectives or limited forms of interaction.

Marilyne Crépeau and Mike James Ross, consultants from leadership advisory firm Egon Zehnder, advise leaders to deliberately seek diverse perspectives and in-person collaboration, while creating psychological safety so people feel comfortable challenging ideas, experimenting, failing and pivoting quickly. Surrounding yourself with people who think differently and engaging with them face-to-face can generate stronger ideas by exposing you to perspectives and non-verbal cues that may be missed virtually.

“I will catch myself when I’m writing where I’m like, ‘Oh my God, I shouldn’t have even written that. I should have just let AI do it because it sounds the same,” says Will Barnett, head of recruiting for a California startup. “It’s trained me to be more like it, instead of the reverse.”

This Wall Street Journal article looks at how consuming large amounts of AI-generated content may be changing the way people communicate, with some increasingly adopting “prompt speak” and other writing and speech patterns commonly used by large language models.

Cleveland-Cliffs, the U.S. owner of Stelco, says it’s well within its rights to idle its Hamilton steel mill and cut up to 500 jobs, pointing the finger at the Canada-U.S. trade war and a domestic market flooded with imports. Ottawa isn’t buying it, with Prime Minister Mark Carney threatening legal action over the job promises Cleveland-Cliffs made when it bought Stelco in 2024.

stories.title: Debris spotted from missing Ontario air ambulance
stories.summary: Debris from a missing Ontario air ambulance that had been carrying six people, including four Canadians, has been spotted off the coast of the United States.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Debris from a missing Ontario air ambulance that had been carrying six people, including four Canadians, has been spotted off the coast of the United States.

The U.S. Coast Guard said search crews found a debris field roughly 150 kilometres southeast of Boston and confirmed it belonged to the missing aircraft.

Crews searched an area more than 2,800 square miles over the course of the last 53 hours, Rear Admiral Matthew Lake, U.S. Coast Guard Northeast district commander, said in an update to the media Sunday.

The search for the missing passengers remains ongoing.

The frantic search began after the Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the plane early Saturday as it travelled from Bermuda to Boston.

The FAA told Global News in a statement it issued a Search and Rescue Alert for a Gulfstream G-100 around 1:20 a.m. Saturday.

The flight was scheduled to arrive in Boston around 1:30 a.m.

A spokesperson for the Massachusetts Port Authority, which operates Boston Logan International Airport, confirmed to Global News in an email that the aircraft did not arrive as scheduled.

According to data from Flight Aware, the plane took off around 11:40 p.m. Friday. Data shows the aircraft slowing down as it dropped from 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet around 1:05 a.m. before losing contact.

Air traffic control audio obtained by Global News shows operators having difficulty connecting with the aircraft prior to its disappearance.

“If you can hear me, at your discretion, please send me anything … please call now …I understand that you have declared an emergency,” a controller asked the pilot.

There was no audible response.

A few minutes later the controller asked the pilot of a commercial flight in the area if they could see the flight on their radar.

“No sir, I don’t see anything,” the pilot responded.

Lake said Sunday he would not speculate at this time what led to the operational failure.

The aircraft, a Gulfstream G100 jet, belongs to Latitude Air Ambulance, a Hamilton-based medical evacuation company.

Clarence Togeretz, operations manager for Latitude Air Ambulance, told The Canadian Press that the missing aircraft was transporting a patient and their family member, with two pilots and two medical staff on board.

The four crew members are Canadian, he said, while the two passengers are Bermuda nationals.

Capt. John McTammy from the Coast Guard said the search for the missing passengers continues.

“We’ll continue to search and saturate the area until we’re at the point where we are confident that if there were any survivors remaining on the surface of the water, we would have found them,” he said.

Togeretz said Saturday the company is “dealing with the situation with as much positivity and optimism as we can.”

“We’re praying for a safe outcome,” he said.

Global News reached out to Togeretz again after the debris was located but he declined to comment.

“At this time we are just not making any comments and once we are we will let you know,” he said.

The operations manager previously said this is the first time Latitude Air Ambulance has lost contact with one of its planes.

The company offers emergency medical transportation by plane worldwide, according to its website.

John Gradek, an aviation expert at McGill University, said Latitude Air Ambulance “fly high quality, good maintenance airplanes, and are very reliable,”

Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon wrote on social media that the government is closely monitoring the situation and working with authorities as the search continues.

“My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time,” he wrote.

Bermuda Premier David Burt wrote in a statement that the government is in contact with the families of those on board and U.S. searchers.

Ontario’s air ambulance service provider Ornge reacted to the news of the missing plane on Saturday, writing in a social media post that it hopes “the aircraft and all passengers are located safely and quickly.”

Togeretz said Latitude Air Ambulance is in contact with Transport Canada. Global News reached out to the federal agency for comment but was directed back to the Minister’s statement.

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada told Global News in an email it is “gathering information and assessing the occurrence.”

– With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Massacre of an ordinary life: Film captures friends' post-October 7 struggles
stories.summary: After an unthinkable day of horror, a group of women at the devastated Kibbutz Kfar Aza realized there was no alternative but to go forward
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
When Hamas attacked Kibbutz Kfar Aza on Oct. 7, 2023, a WhatsApp chat connected women living through the assault in real time. In the months and years since, the chat group has remained a communication link for survivors who lost relatives, homes and the ordinary lives they once shared.

That group is at the centre of Where Do We Belong?, a new documentary produced and edited by Canadian-Israeli filmmaker Igal Hecht and directed by Israeli filmmaker Dotan Nave. Rather than retelling Oct. 7 through the attack itself, the film follows its longer trajectory of two and a half years: grief, displacement, medical recovery, parenthood, group meetings and the difficult prospect of beginning again.

The film premieres on Israel’s Channel 8 on Oct. 5. It will then screen Oct. 7 at Toronto’s Zionist Centre and Oct. 8 at Vancouver’s Norman Rothstein Theatre, as part of the Vancouver Jewish Film Festival.

Hecht, born in Israel and raised in Toronto, will attend both Canadian screenings for post-film Q&As.

Over a career spanning nearly three decades, Hecht has produced more than 70 documentary films and 25 television series.

Dave Gordon interviewed Hecht for the National Post.

What did following these women for more than two years allow you to show that an immediate account of Oct. 7 could not?

You see the mourning process unfold and, especially with Jessica, the realization that there is no alternative but to move forward. These women endured the tragedy together in real time through their WhatsApp group. They lost loved ones and are deeply interconnected, as happens in a close-knit kibbutz. Their friendship became a support system: they mourned together, moved together, and have chosen to remain neighbours through three relocations. The film shows how essential that kind of support is — not only after October 7, but in life generally.

You and Dotan began filming three weeks after Oct. 7. Why make the women’s group the narrative spine?

'Israel is safe': The Druze Israeli telling Canadians to come visit

Hamas hostage Mia Schem on how she survived captivity — and freedom — after October 7

Dotan deserves the credit. He was volunteering at Kibbutz Kfar Aza and met Amit; after a few weeks of getting to know the women, the project began. We understood that their WhatsApp group was an extraordinary way to tell the story: it connected them as they experienced the attack in real time.

Originally, we expected to film for six months. But rather than stopping at the attack and immediate aftermath, we decided to follow what came next: the daily work of surviving — raising children, going back to work, managing social obligations, and finding a way forward after losing a husband or a home. We gradually stripped away some of the Oct. 7 material to focus on a story that had not been told before.

That longer timeline made stories possible that we could not have anticipated. Ellie, who was severely burned along with her husband and two-year-old daughter, rebuilt her life, completed her studies, became a doctor and later gave birth to another child. That is a story of recovery and renewal, and it would have been impossible to tell had we stopped after six months or a year.

What does the title, Where Do We Belong?, mean to the women?

It is less a question of where they belong geographically, than where they belong in life now. Jessica must ask whether she can find a new partner and how she moves forward. The larger question is whether they return to Kfar Aza, go elsewhere, or remain together. The film does not resolve that question, because many of the women have not resolved it themselves.

One survivor says her views on coexistence have changed. Did you find that more broadly?

Not everyone spoke openly about it, but I think many have experienced a profound reassessment — not only about coexistence, but about the reality across the border. Many Gaza-envelope communities were left-leaning and committed to peace; some residents helped Gazans reach Israeli hospitals. For people who embraced coexistence, Oct. 7 was profoundly shattering. Noa had taught her students to believe in it, but she now feels that belief was not reciprocated.

What did the women teach you about how people endure long-term trauma?

It demonstrates the strength and resilience of these women: their sacrifices for friends and children, their ability to remain standing, pursue their dreams and care for one another. We focus on three women but portray the larger group. I do not know if resilience is unique to women, but this group embodies it powerfully. To me, they also embody the resilience of Israelis in the face of enormous horror. Their strength, and determination, deserve to be celebrated.

What were the ground rules around consent and access during such a long project?

There were no forbidden subjects, but Dotan built a thoughtful, trusting relationship with the women. We did not push people. We had to judge the day: if someone was having a difficult time, we would not force a painful conversation. The first year especially, we were conscious of trauma and determined not to be exploitative. Some shoots were cancelled when participants did not feel up to them.

What do you hope Canadian audiences take from the film?

I want them to understand that the trauma did not end on Oct. 7. These women had to go on raising children, working, moving from place to place and trying to imagine a future after what happened to their families and community. This is not chiefly a political film. It is a human story about people connected by trauma who are trying, day by day, to heal and move forward.

stories.title: Moderate new Muslim group aims to broaden dialogue beyond certain 'politically charged issues'
stories.summary: The group wants to learn "what shapes Muslim Canadian life and identity, from youth and professionals to women in leadership and elders."
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
There are roughly two million Muslims in Canada. But they don’t see themselves in conversations being held in their name in Ottawa, says a leader of the new Muslim Policy Institute (MPI).

“The questions MPI cares about most, like belonging, opportunity, the pressures families are facing, and what Muslim Canadians actually prioritize, are often overlooked. Meanwhile, the national conversation keeps circling one or two politically charged issues,” said Nika Jabiyeva, the institute’s managing director of operations and partnerships, told National Post.

Jabiyeva said research last year revealed that although Islamophobia was a concern for the community, bigger concerns for Muslim Canadians, like most Canadians in general, were the cost of living and housing.

MPI “doesn’t claim to represent two million people,” she said. The group’s purpose is to learn “what shapes Muslim Canadian life and identity, from youth and professionals to women in leadership and elders, and bringing that to the public and into policy.”

There are many Muslim advocacy groups already that have “predetermined points of view and opinions,” she said. What MPI aims to do is provide research and evidence about what the community wants to prioritize.

In a recent move, nearly 1,000 prayer rooms, or “quiet” rooms, were added to federal buildings, the Toronto Sun and Blacklock’s Reporter reported, despite only two per cent of employees self-identifying as Muslim.

While Jabiyeva said that representation matters, the way the government responds to a community’s needs can “often come off as performative, and that’s what ends up dominating the conversation.”

“What actually changes the well-being of our communities are things like economic opportunity, housing, education, and real investment in cohesion between communities,” she said.

Man arrested in Ontario for promoting anti-Muslim violence online: police

Canadians view Islam most negatively, but opinion of Judaism fell furthest: poll

“None of these are quick wins, so it’s easier to invest in something that makes a quick news story. That’s where Mpi’s work comes in: finding out what Muslim Canadians need most, and bringing that evidence to policymakers.”

The institute undertakes studies on a wide variety of topics — health, safety and how foreign influence can impact Muslims — and other projects, including one committed to protecting Muslims from radicalization.

“Either all Muslims get painted with the same brush, or some of the loudest voices dismiss all discussion of it as Islamophobia. Neither is true, and that’s how we end up with the public discourse we have today,” said Jabiyeva.

In a description of the project online , it says that Muslim communities are disproportionately affected by radicalization as targets of extremist recruitment and as victims of social and political fallout when radicalization leads to violence. The project develops tools, resources and early intervention frameworks, it says.

“Few look inside the community and ask why. What makes a young person go looking in the darkest corners of the internet? Where are they not finding belonging?” said Jabiyeva.

“We also can’t be naive about the systems that fuel radicalization. It doesn’t spread by accident. It’s organized, it’s funded, and in some cases it’s backed by foreign states and movements that benefit when young people feel they don’t belong here.”

There has also been religion-based hatred towards the Muslim community in Canada, ON display prominently in recent weeks.

A Whitby man was arrested on Sept. 23 for promoting anti-Muslim violence, according to Durham Regional Police. Also last week, a mosque and Islamic schools across Canada were threatened with violence over email, the Muslim Association of Canada said .

“Of course, (Islamophobia) will be part of the research and part of the issues that we will address. But we first want to understand before coming forward with either solutions or predetermined opinions,” Jabiyeva said.
