stories.title: London Knights win against the North Bay Battalion
stories.summary: The London Knights hit the ice against the North Bay Battalion at Canada Life Place Friday night.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The London Knights remain perfect to start the Ontario Hockey League (OHL) season after a 4-1 win over the North Bay Battalion at Canada Life Place Friday.

Making his first start of the season after returning from Vancouver Canucks camp, Aleksei Medvedev stopped 38 of the 39 shots fired his way to earn first star honours.

Rookie Marcus Nordmark opened the scoring with his first OHL goal early in the second period before the Battalion answered back to tie it at one going to the third period.

Less than a minute into the final frame, Thomas Zocco took advantage of a defensive mistake and buried what would turn out to be the game winner.

Jaxon Cover scored in his first game back from Ottawa Senators camp by taking a rebound off the end boards and slipping it home. Cohen Bidgood would add an an insurance marker to round out the scoring.

London sits 4-0 to start the year to lead the Western Conference standings and will look to remain undefeated Sunday when they host the Flint Firebirds.

London will be without defenceman Maksim Sokolovskii Sunday and for the near future.

stories.title: London Mayoral debate raises questions about open drug use
stories.summary: 980 Cfpl hosted a London Mayoral debate. David Peacock moderated the nearly 90 minute debate and asked mayoral...
stories.author: Ben Andrews
stories.content:
London mayoral candidates discussed how they would tackle open drug use Friday, debate on 980 Cfpl.

Host Devon Peacock moderated the 90-minute event, which included candidates Kirsten Krose, a businessperson, Ward 4 Coun. Susan Stevenson, and Mayor Josh Morgan.

The candidates were asked how they would deal with issues related to London’s homelessness, housing, construction and public safety.

One of the key talking points that was repeatedly mentioned in this debate was the use of open drug use in London.

“ We are currently under the harm reduction model which supports and uh tries to make illegal drug use safer in our city. It’s making the problems worse,” said Stevenson. “The province gave us an extra $8.5 million in 2023 and 5 million of that 8 and a half went to increased shelter costs with no additional beds. Money that we’re getting is not getting to the people who need it.”

Morgan pointed out London police’s open-air drug policy, Project Pathways, is approaching it’s second phase, which he expects to reduce the amount of open drug use in the city.

“ We know that there is a gap in the amount of service available to refer to and that creates a barrier,” he said. “But ultimately, all of this is meant to say we’ve got to make people safer. We’ve got to continue to not only drive the stats, but make sure that it’s a feeling for people out on the streets and in our core, in the downtown.”

Krose did not mention much of Londoner’s facing open-drug use, instead, she described how she would enact policies that would broadly help those in need, such as the homeless.

“T his is a very complex issue and I don’t think that it’s a one-size fits-all. This is something that is going to require many different solutions,” she said.

“I would like to implement a 10-year stabilization strategy. I built this strategy from consulting as many as I could. The front line organizations, so everything from Unity Project, London Cares, St.Leonard’s, Ark Aid, Paul’s Place, you name it. I want to make sure that we have a broad spectrum of services that meet everywhere, meet everyone from temporary transition all the way to long-term.”

You can watch the full London Mayoral debate here.

It’s making the problems worse,” said Stevenson. “The province gave us an extra $8.5 million in 2023 and 5 million of that 8 and a half went to increased shelter costs with no additional beds. Money that we’re getting is not getting to the people who need it.”
Morgan pointed out London police’s open-air drug policy, Project Pathways, is approaching it’s second phase, which he expects to reduce the amount of open drug use in the city.

“ We know that there is a gap in the amount of service available to refer to and that creates a barrier,” he said. “But ultimately, all of this is meant to say we’ve got to make people safer. We’ve got to continue to not only drive the stats, but make sure that it’s a feeling for people out on the streets and in our core, in the downtown.”
Krose did not mention much of Londoner’s facing open-drug use, instead, she described how she would enact policies that would broadly help those in need, such as the homeless.
“T his is a very complex issue and I don’t think that it’s a one-size fits-all. This is something that is going to require many different solutions,” she said.

“I would like to implement a 10-year stabilization strategy. I built this strategy from consulting as many as I could. The front line organizations, so everything from Unity Project, London Cares, St.Leonard’s, Ark Aid, Paul’s Place, you name it. I want to make sure that we have a broad spectrum of services that meet everywhere, meet everyone from temporary transition all the way to long-term.”

stories.title: Dedicated river valley space for homeless encampments debated in Edmonton
stories.summary: The Edmonton River Valley Conservation Coalition wants to see a few dedicated encampment sites with clean drinking water, washrooms, trash cans and a safe needle disposal site.
stories.author: Joel Gotlib
stories.content:
Alberta’s capital city is no stranger to homelessness and it’s something the Edmonton River Valley Conservation Coalition wants to address.

“People are going to camp. People are camping, so why criminalize them?” asks Kristine Kowalchuk, chair of the Ervcc.

The coalition calls Edmonton’s temporary shelter prohibition inhumane and says the city’s public spaces by-law urgently needs changing.

“Rather than criminalizing people, why not support them?” Kowalchuk questioned.

The coalition wants the City of Edmonton to establish a few dedicated encampment sites with clean drinking water, washrooms, trash cans and a safe needle disposal site.

“Piloting a few encampments where people are safe, where they’re supported, where it’s contained to a safe and serviced space,” Kowalchuk explained.

Kowalchuk suggests shipping containers could also be used at sites as a form of housing.

The coalition estimates Edmonton’s homeless population at 5,000, with indoor shelter space for only half of them.

People living on the streets often have their belongings like blankets, tents and prescription medication lost in sweeps, when when law enforcement forcibly removes homeless people and their encampments from public areas.

That was the case in the winters of 2023 and 2024, when Edmonton police and city crews dismantled around a dozen high-risk homeless encampments.

6:15 Removing encampments critical for safety of all: Edmonton city councillor

The coalition’s plan seems like a tough sell for city council, however.

“We should not be settling for figuring out the best version of keeping somebody on the street,” Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack said on Friday.

“I don’t want to have to rely on a sanctioned encampment. I want a physical space we can take people to, right? Because in both of those scenarios, in either scenario those do not produce the ideal outcomes.”

Other on council agree.

“I just don’t know if, compared to the cost of actually housing somebody, I think that’s where we should be putting the emphasis on a permanent basis,” Ward Karhiio Councillor Keren Teng said.

With winter approaching, Kowalchuk would like to see dedicated encampments sooner rather than later.

“We’ve seen, year after year, that there’s not really a sufficient plan in place. We’ve got people who are freezing outside on the streets,” she said.

The Ervcc wants at least one of the encampment sites in the river valley, where many people living on the streets already set up camps in the forest.

They’re open to working with other organizations, saying it would reflect a collective investment in community care rather than throwing money into sweeps — which they argue solves nothing.

stories.title: BC NDP and Conservative leaders campaign in the Okanagan
stories.summary: BC NDP Leader David Eby and Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson were in the Okanagan Friday, making campaign promises on grocery prices, wildfire protection and public safety.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
BC NDP Leader David Eby and BC Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson crisscrossed the Okanagan Friday, making campaign promises on grocery prices, wildfire protection and public safety.

Eby began the day in Kelowna , where he announced a plan to limit the amount large grocery chains can mark up on essential foods.

“We’re going to save you money on your groceries,” Eby said outside a Save-On-Foods.

The proposed “Price Guard” would put a ceiling on retail margins for food staples.

“We’re going to cap the profits of the big grocery companies. We’re going to make sure that for the basics, for your cheese, for your eggs, for your butter, for your milk, that you and your family are protected at the till as you check out,” Eby said.

The NDP also said it would require clearer per-unit pricing and restrict some anti-competitive practices.

As Eby made his grocery announcement in Kelowna, Doerkson was in Summerland, where he unveiled a wildfire action plan in an area hit hard by the Bald Range wildfire this past summer.

The Conservative proposal includes buying new firefighting aircraft, including water bombers and reducing dangerous fuel around communities.

Doerkson also vowed to reduce bureaucracy to make firefighting easier.

“We will immediately establish a dedicated wildfire response cabinet committee, which I will personally chair,” Doerkson said. “Its mandate will be clear, cut through bureaucratic inertia, coordinate government resources and ensure British Columbia is fully prepared next summer.”

The two leaders later crossed paths geographically as Eby headed to Summerland for his own wildfire announcement, including additional support for people affected by wildfires and those who were uninsured.

2:19 Lumby candidate running in both elections

The NDP says a re-elected government would match donations to the Canadian Red Cross up to $20 million for people affected by this summer’s fires.

Following his campaign stop in Summerland, Doerkson headed to Kelowna to meet with businesses about concerns over crime and street disorder.

He said the issue is a priority for his party but stopped short of announcing specific measures.

“I’m really committed to announcing that over the coming weeks, but we are very much obviously in favour of providing more supports, housing, and certainly wraparound services that will help with this problem,” Doerkson said.

Eby also acknowledged public safety as a serious issue in Kelowna and said his party would have more to announce soon.

“We’ll have more to say about how we’re going to be supporting communities, but one of those pieces includes involuntary care here in the region,” Eby said.

The B.C. Greens were also campaigning Friday, with leader Emily Lowan unveiling further platform commitments focused on artificial intelligence and technology regulation.

stories.title: Carney launches 13-member national council to advise on artificial intelligence
stories.summary: The PMO said the National Council on Artificial Intelligence will "provide independent, practical advice on Canada's AI transformation."
stories.author: AFP
stories.content:
The Prime Minister's Office said the National Council on Artificial Intelligence will ‘provide independent, practical advice on Canada's AI transformation’

Author of the article:

Prime Minister Mark Carney on Friday launched a new council to advise on artificial intelligence, in an effort to shape responsible policy on a technology some fear poses an existential threat to humanity.

The council’s members will include Yoshua Bengio, the Montreal-based computer scientist considered one of the founders of AI.

In an interview with AFP last month, Bengio warned that “we’re losing control” of AI and said the global community needed to impose guardrails on the technology, similar to nuclear non-proliferation.

Carney said the council’s mandate will be to help his government “manage the risks, seize the opportunities, and ensure AI is used to improve the lives of all Canadians.”

The 13-member council includes academics, people who have held leadership roles in private-sector technology firms, and a former national security adviser under Carney’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau.

stories.title: Josh Kutryk’s successful flight to the ISS shifts focus to Canada’s next moves in space
stories.summary: As the Albertan astronaut begins his mission, the country’s program is at a crucial crossroad
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
Those who followed the news of Joshua Kutryk’s successful flight to the International Space Station this week can be forgiven for wondering if the Canadian astronaut stepped into a time machine rather than a space capsule.

Col. Kutryk, who hails from Fort Saskatchewan, Alta., was one of four astronauts who lifted off on Thursday morning from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida and docked with the station later that night.

Their arrival marks the start of a busy handoff period during which the population of the station will temporarily be at 11 – four of which will depart some time next week.

With astronauts from the United States, Russia, France and Canada currently on board, the image of comity and diversity on the station is certainly what proponents had in mind when construction of the orbiting laboratory began in 1998.

Today it remains a vision of a more congenial time – challenged to varying degrees by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the growing rift between Canada and the U.S., and even Alberta’s coming decision about whether it wants to remain a province.

All of these developments highlight the fact that as the station sails the airless expanse overhead, the world down below is changing fast.

It has been a big year for Canada in space, with Col. Kutryk’s mission following on the heels of Jeremy Hansen’s voyage around the moon in Artemis II last April. What is less clear is whether Canada’s next chapter in space can be as high profile and productive.

Most ISS partners, including the U.S., Canada, Japan and European countries, have committed to supporting the station until the end of 2030. Russia’s current commitment extends only through 2028. Once the station is decommissioned, it will likely be deorbited into the Pacific Ocean.

With the station’s end approaching, it remains an open question whether any Canadians will go there after Col. Kutryk’s mission is completed.

“At this point we’re working with Nasa and the other international partners to see what we can do to fly astronauts,” said Matthieu Caron, director of astronauts, life sciences and space medicine at the Canadian Space Agency.

A SpaceX rocket safely lifted off from Florida on Thursday, launching a crew of two U.S. astronauts, a Canadian astronaut and a Russian cosmonaut toward the International Space Station for a science mission devoted to human health and performance in orbit.

He noted that Canada earns credits for continued investments in the station – credits that can be put toward a future Canadian flight. But it’s not yet clear if there will be enough such credits for another Canadian to fly by the time the station reaches the end of its lifespan.

With Col. Hansen’s retirement from the agency earlier this year, there are currently only three active astronauts in the Canadian program. Of those, only Jenni Gibbons, who served as Col. Hansen’s backup on Artemis II, has not yet logged any time in space.

Mr. Caron said that for now there are no plans to expand Canada’s contingent of astronauts while the focus remains on getting at least one more mission. It’s been more than nine years since Dr. Gibbons and Col. Kutryk were selected to be astronauts. The gap since then indicates the uncertainty in what opportunities there will be for Canadians to fly once the station is retired.

It’s long been clear that the U.S. has redirected its human space program toward the moon. In 2018, Canada agreed to partner in this effort.

Canada’s main contribution was to be an updated version of the space station’s robotic arm made for Gateway, a future station to be placed in orbit around the moon. But earlier this year, Nasa sidelined Gateway to prioritize the construction of a moon base on the lunar surface. Canada is still working out how it will accommodate the pivot and provide hardware that is relevant to the revised scenario.

This contribution will help determine when a Canadian could next be heading to the moon. But much depends on whether Nasa can sustain its moon program at the accelerated pace outlined this year by administrator Jared Isaacman. That plan would see U.S. astronauts returning to the moon’s surface in 2028.

Hammering out Canada’s role on the moon is likely to be a high priority for the next president of the Canadian Space Agency , a key position that has been vacant since July.

Meanwhile, the federal government has determined that it needs to do more at home to build a viable space sector that is not overly dependent on the U.S. or other countries for access to orbit.

Ottawa has already said it wants to build a domestic launch capability in Canada as a matter of sovereignty.

Federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said this priority won’t fade any time soon “because I think that geopolitics won’t calm down.”

To that end, she said she is working toward a new space strategy for Canada and hopes to enlist Col. Hansen, among others, to participate in its development. The strategy would cover three domains of the Canadian sector, including science, defence and commercialization.

Brian Gallant, chief executive of Space Canada, an industry association, said he welcomes the effort as long as it can be accomplished swiftly to match the sector’s need for momentum.

“Space over the last few decades has changed,” Mr. Gallant said. “The role of industry has completely changed. So we need to keep pace with other governments that are rolling out programs and investments to help build the space industrial base of their respective countries.”

If taken at face value, the statements suggest that Canadian policy makers need to be as busy as Col. Kutryk will be on the space station in the coming months. By the time he returns to Earth early next year, Canada’s future in space will need a clear direction or risk becoming trapped in time.

stories.title: Downtown Wingham evacuation order lifted after grenade found at thrift store
stories.summary: A large part of Wingham’s downtown was evacuated after a grenade was found at the Salvation Army Thrift Store on Friday.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A large part of Wingham’s downtown was evacuated after a grenade was found at the Salvation Army Thrift Store on Friday.

Huron County OPP say the Grey Bruce OPP Explosive Disposal Unit (EDU) attended the scene at 5:31 p.m. and safely removed the item of concern. Following their assessment and removal of the item, all emergency resources have cleared the scene.

Josephine Street has been reopened to both vehicle and pedestrian traffic, and all previously established road closures have been lifted.

“We were just going about our normal day in the store, taking donations at the back. And, we received one particular donation that came in. Our staff were sorting through it as they normally would. And it appeared that there was something a little different in a certain box of military memorabilia. And it turned out that it was a hand grenade from kind of the First or Second World War period is what we believe, and that was quite a surprise,” said Wingham’s Salvation Army Pastor/Director Brian Dueck.

Dueck actually held the grenade in his hand before calling in police around 2 p.m.

“I was just kind of checking it out, and trying to find the wording and numbers on it to see what exactly it was. And as I was looking it up, that’s when I realized that this was probably a legitimate hand grenade. And, it had the pin in it and everything. So the next question is, well, is it actually active or is it being deactivated? So I called the police non-emergency line, and they sent the police out to come and have a look,” said Dueck.

Once police arrived, they decided it was best to evacuate not only the Salvation Army, but a large part of Wingham’s downtown stretch.

Huron County OPP says the temporary shelter that had been established at the Westcast Community Centre has now been closed.

“We were given the order as soon as the police got there to clear the building. And, then the block started clearing out, and nobody’s allowed kind of anywhere near the building for now,” said Dueck.

Dueck says he was told that a specialized bomb disposal unit is coming from London, Ont. to deal with the grenade.

“I mean, I didn’t really think much of it at first, but I guess you take every precaution, right? So, yeah, thankfully the police are really quick to, to come down and they just kind of took control of the situation and let us know what we had to do,” he said.

Dueck hopes it all turns out OK, and the grenade isn’t live, regardless it’s a scary situation that probably could have been avoided.

“Check what you’re donating, try to keep it safe, and put any paperwork with it if it’s something like that, so that we know what’s going on,” said Dueck.

Dueck says he was told that a specialized bomb disposal unit is coming from London, Ont. to deal with the grenade.

“I mean, I didn’t really think much of it at first, but I guess you take every precaution, right? So, yeah, thankfully the police are really quick to, to come down and they just kind of took control of the situation and let us know what we had to do,” he said.

stories.title: Most Quebeckers lose flu shot coverage as viral season gets early start
stories.summary: Quebec and Alberta stopped covering the COVID-19 vaccine for most people last year, but experts say there are still risks
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha, Alanna Smith
stories.content:
Quebeckers who are not considered high-risk will have to pay nearly $200 to get vaccinated against influenza and COVID-19 this season, charting a path opposite to other provinces in Canada as the viral season picks up speed.

Quebec is the only province scrapping universal flu coverage , owing its decision to guidance from the province’s immunization committee. Only some categories will be eligible for a free flu shot, such as Quebeckers 65 and older; people with certain chronic conditions – such as immunocompromised people – and those living with them; pregnant women; residents of seniors’ homes and long-term care facilities.

Those who do not qualify can expect to be charged around $150 for the COVID-19 vaccine, which came into effect in the province last year. Now, they will also need to pay between $30 and $40 for the flu shot, said Marilie Beaulieu-Gravel, a spokesperson for the association representing pharmacy owners in Quebec.

New data from the Public Health Agency of Canada, reported on Friday, show Canada’s positivity rate for flu has risen to 3.7 per cent. The flu season officially starts when the positivity rate crosses the seasonal 5-per-cent threshold, but some parts of the country are reporting that the respiratory virus season is already under way.

Nathalie Grandvaux, a University of Montreal medical school professor who is an expert on virus-host interactions, said the Quebec government is making a mistake.

“I fail to understand the logic here, which seems to be purely an economic logic, and I still don’t get it,” she said.

Flu shots are necessary because the virus mutates and new strains appear, she added.

“You don’t keep the immunity from the previous year’s vaccine,” she said. “You’re going to end up with a lot of people with flu symptoms in emergency wards, clogging up hospitals when there are other priorities.”

While COVID-19 indicators such as hospitalizations and deaths are down, people can still get infected and develop symptoms, affecting schools and workplaces. She also mentioned the risks of drawn-out debilitation linked to long COVID.

Quebec and Alberta were the only two provinces that started charging for a COVID-19 shot last season, with the exception of certain higher-risk populations. Albertans had to pay $100 per jab if they were ineligible for a provincially covered shot. The charge is the same this year.

Isaac Bogoch, an infectious disease specialist at Toronto General Hospital, who also works in the University of Toronto’s Department of Medicine, said policy makers should be reducing rather than adding barriers to vaccination.

“We really need to work harder to build back public trust in public health and health care and adding barriers does not align with that goal,” he said.

Dr. Bogoch said flu and COVID-19 gaining speed across Canada signals another early season.

“I don’t know that this should come as a surprise to anyone in that it’s fall,” he said in an interview on Thursday. “We tend to see more flu a bit later on. But there have been seasons where we’ve had earlier flu seasons, there’s been seasons where we’ve had later flu seasons, and thankfully flu shots are starting to roll out.”

Last fall, the flu season hit hard and fast, driven by low vaccine uptake and the circulation of a problematic strain that was a mismatch for the seasonal vaccine . Cases peaked at the end of December with a positivity rate of 33.3 per cent – the highest rate recorded over the past three viral seasons.

Both Prince Edward Island and the Southwestern Public Health unit in Ontario, in separate statements earlier this week, warned that the flu virus is already making its rounds. The PEI government said cases were increasing and some required hospital care.

Dr. Ninh Tran, the medical officer of health for Southwestern Public Health, said in an interview that the area’s first flu case was confirmed on Monday, roughly a month earlier than last year.

He stressed that people who are currently eligible to get their vaccine, which includes high-risk and priority groups, such as seniors, should do so now. The general public can get their shots starting Oct. 26. In all provinces except Quebec, it is free.

“There are a number of things people can do in the meantime before getting their vaccine,” said Dr. Tran. “That’s staying home when you’re sick, washing your hands frequently, covering your coughs and sneezes, cleaning high-touch services.”

stories.title: Phoebe Bridgers concert review: The indie folk star dazzled with melancholy in Toronto
stories.summary: The folk-pop It Girl’s phone-free show delivered craft mellowness and sincerity to an arena-sized crowd
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
When Phoebe Bridgers’s concert at Scotiabank Arena began on Thursday evening, an orb pulsing with lights hovered over the satellite stage at one end of the arena while a dome dominated the mainstage across the floor.

The dome lifted, revealing Bridgers and her nine-piece band on a circular stage as if they were a room service dinner. The 32-year-old Californian and the others were dressed all in black. The lighting was diffuse; the hazy aesthetic was black and white.

“I have emotional motion sickness,” the folk-pop It Girl sang on the galloping opening number, her soprano voice breathy and sincere. “Somebody roll the windows down.” The line figuratively describes her songwriting process.

The young woman to my left whipped out a pad of paper to sketch what she saw. There are no phones allowed on Bridgers’s Lost Tour. Only memories (or a pencil) record the events. Two hours later, the mostly female audience would look back on the concert as a simpler and more intimate time.

The tour is in support of Bridgers’s third solo album, Lost Weekend . Early in the first of two Toronto concerts, she addressed her big crowd with a “long time no see” greeting. She performed in 2023 as one third of the indie-rock supergroup Boygenius (with Julien Baker and Lucy Dacus) at what is now known as the RBC Amphitheatre. A year prior she played the now-defunct RBC Echo Beach venue on her own.

Bridgers typically writes and sings about love and loss. The death of her father is one of the themes to the new album. Her earnest lyrics are at turns conversational and diaristic; the chords and tempos that carry them are built to sweep the listener away emotionally. The ability to craft mellowness and relatable melancholy into arena-sized singalongs is a gift.

Bridgers has a way with imagery: “Hiding in the bathroom like Shelley Duvall” and “Dancing ourselves clean late New Year’s Eve” on The Governor’s Waltz , a dream in 3/4 time.

On Lost Boys , Bridgers rhymed “This machine is killing me” with “I pretended it was make-believe.” Perhaps a comment on the disillusion of fame.

Before she sang it, a fan had yelled out that this was their first concert. “Wow,” the four-time Grammy winner replied. “That’s a lot of responsibility for me.”

Heavy is the pop star’s head that wears the crown, but Bridgers is faring well. The new album received universally rave reviews upon release this summer. (Note: The record’s electronica and ambient touches were stripped away on stage.) Her reputation is solid; she says and does the right things. Not only did she charge a pittance for tickets to a surprise show at New York’s Madison Square Garden in June, but proceeds went to a charity that pays immigration bonds for people detained by ICE.

On the other hand, the celebrity-stocked wedding of Taylor Swift and football player Travis Kelce one month later at the same venue likely cost tens of millions of dollars. Ostentatious and thirsty is not a good look. More recently, Swift released four new tracks on The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore , an expanded version of the pop queen’s weak album from 2025. Critics suggested the move was a money grab or done for pre-Grammy exposure.

Swift is taking hits, as is Ed Sheeran, who was criticized for his apolitical stance when his promoter removed rapper Macklemore as the tour’s opening act for expressing pro-Palestine beliefs on stage. Boston -singing country-pop star Stella Lefty was lampooned on Saturday Night Live over allegations of songwriting plagiarism.

So, a rough few weeks for the charting class. Indie music sensation Bridgers, however, cruises unassailed. On the satellite stage, where she appeared alone or with her string section, she endeared herself to the audience by saying most of her favourite American songwriters were Canadian-born. She mentioned her late father was a fan of Neil Young and Joni Mitchell.

Before performing the solo acoustic Still Standing , Bridgers said while she had a “weird” relationship with her father, his death flooded her with an empathy for him that in turn made her closer to her fans. “I love you,” she said.

Captured in a cone of light from above, Bridgers sang about her dad: “You left your suitcase by the bed, like you needed to know you could go whenever you wanted.”

The night before Bridgers’s concert, I caught a set by the Toronto singer-songwriter Hayden Desser. He performed a song he rarely performed because he thought it was too earnest. Too earnest . There’s no such thing any more.

Phoebe Bridgers performs Vancouver’s Rogers Arena on Oct. 24.

stories.title: Toronto soldiers arrested on kidnapping, weapons theft and organized crime charges
stories.summary: “Following their arrests, both individuals were removed from military duties,” said a DND spokesperson.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
Two Toronto soldiers have been removed from their military duties and blocked from using their base or army equipment since they were arrested this past August on charges related to organized crime, kidnapping and theft of guns and weapons, the Department of National Defence confirmed late Friday.

Sachintha Fernando and James Moreau are members of the 7th Toronto Regiment, a reserve artillery unit based at Moss Park Armoury in Toronto.

“We are aware that both individuals were arrested by the Toronto Police Service on August 11, 2026, ON charges related to organized crime, kidnapping, and the theft of firearms and weapons,” National Defence spokesperson Andrée-Anne Poulin wrote in an email sent late Friday in response to questions the Post posed last Monday about the two soldiers.

Both men are bombardiers, a rank in the artillery branch that’s equivalent to corporal.

“Bombardier Fernando enrolled in the Canadian Army as a Reservist in January 2020. He has not deployed on a Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) operation,” Poulin said.

“Bombardier Moreau enrolled in the Canadian Army as a Reservist in March 2018 and deployed on Operation Laser in 2020.”

That operation was the Canadian military’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

“Following their arrests, both individuals were removed from military duties and their access to CAF equipment, facilities, and bases was restricted,” Poulin said.

“They remain members of the CAF pending the outcome of an administrative review. An administrative review is a formal process used to assess matters that May affect a member’s continued service while providing procedural fairness.”

The Army is supporting “the Toronto Police Service’s ongoing investigation,” Poulin said.

Canadian soldiers charged in alleged anti-government terror plot

One of four Quebec terror suspects granted bail while others remain in custody

The Toronto police was not able to immediately provide more details on the case late Friday.

One source said both soldiers have taught new recruits at Ontario’s CFB Borden.

stories.title: Multiple rental-property companies founded by former talk-radio host file for insolvency
stories.summary: At least 14 companies associated with Todd Slater’s Simple Investor Real Estate Group have filed for bankruptcy, records show
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
Multiple rental-property companies founded by Todd Slater, a former talk-radio host and real estate investor, have filed for insolvency, according to documents viewed by The Globe and Mail.

Over the past decade, the Simple Investor Real Estate Group, or SIREG, has purchased existing multifamily rental buildings across Ontario and converted them into condominiums. The company also provided property-management services, including collecting and remitting rent payments to owners.

Mr. Slater marketed these purchases online and in seminars as a simple way to become a real estate investor, and in many cases, buyers simply purchased a converted condo unit and collected rent. However, others were also sold a riskier option to contribute capital – and collect high interest along the way – to a joint venture that would purchase a new rental building and begin the conversion process.

The Globe obtained an e-mail sent Sept. 18 to SIREG stakeholders warning that future rent or dividend payments were being suspended amid “liquidity challenges.”

SIREG has appointed AlixPartners Restructuring Inc. as its insolvency trustee, and Adam Zalev of Reflect Advisors is acting as Chief Restructuring Officer, according to a Sept. 23 e-mail to investors obtained by The Globe.

That e-mail also said Mr. Slater had “stepped away” from management for “health reasons.”

Mr. Zalev declined to comment for this story.

At least 14 companies associated with SIREG have filed for bankruptcy , most of the corporations own individual buildings, according to Office of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy records.

Marcin Migdal is a SIREG investor who owns a condo in North Bay and has shares in two joint-venture agreements. One $250,000 investment should have been returned to him three years ago, but because SIREG’s property-management payments were still arriving, he didn’t question the health of the company.

“They were making payments on my condo,” he said. “We all thought it’s going to continue. I met an individual who had 14 properties: no missed payments.”

Mr. Migdal created a website to help organize SIREG investors into legal action against the group. By his estimate, there are 20 condo or rental buildings and more than $100-million in cash borrowed from hundreds of small investors at risk.

Multiple calls and e-mails to Mr. Slater and to SIREG’s head office over the past week were not answered.

Insolvency notices sent to condo owners warn that under the terms of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, they cannot break their property-management agreement with SIREG and begin collecting their rent on their own, though they can apply to a court to be let out of the contracts.

Court records related to a 2025 civil claim give some indication of potential issues with the joint-venture business model.

Janvier Kenmoe, who works for the construction union LiUNA (Laborers’ International Union of North America), and Joan Ngasa, his wife, alleged in their statement of claim that they borrowed $500,000 in 2021 using a home-equity line of credit to invest in a joint venture known as SIREG 1-4 Balmoral Inc. (The property is a 158-apartment rental building in Brockville, Ont., that was eventually converted to condos in October of 2025).

The agreement promised a two-year duration of the contract and a 60-per-cent return over those two years.

By August, 2025, Mr. Kenmoe’s agreement was three-years’ overdue and he was asking for his money back. His claim quotes an e-mail from Mr. Slater that said there had been delays in getting the building converted and registered as condos and asked for a few days to “figure out something.” After a few more exchanges, Mr. Slater stopped responding to e-mails in October.

The civil case claimed that Mr. Slater’s company had not done the “know your client” due diligence that would have shown that Mr. Kenmoe was not an accredited investor; a legal definition under securities law. Individuals or companies that sell exempt market securities – such as joint-venture shares – can face sanctions from securities regulators if investors are not accredited to buy them.

The Ontario Securities Commission declined to comment on whether it had received any complaints or had opened an investigation against Mr. Slater or SIREG.

No statement of defence was filed. The case was settled and is now subject to a confidentiality agreement.

Simply selling their condos to escape the situation may not be an option, according to Ron Butler, president of Butler Mortgage.

Mr. Butler has advised several SIREG condo owners that research by his company into some of the buildings revealed serious concerns with the governance and financial health of the condo corporations set up by SIREG. The problems included empty reserve funds, unfinished engineering reports, and in some cases, loans registered to the corporation.

“They are completely unfinanceable,” he said.

No mortgage provider would lend money to purchase an apartment in one of these buildings, Mr. Butler said. That would lead to a cash-only sale and potential losses for sellers.

“In our experience, it’s roughly a 66-per-cent price discount when they are not financeable.”

stories.title: Grenade found at Wingham thrift store prompts downtown evacuation
stories.summary: A large part of Wingham’s downtown has been evacuated after a grenade was found at the Salvation Army Thrift Store on Friday.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A large part of Wingham’s downtown was evacuated after a grenade was found at the Salvation Army Thrift Store on Friday.

Huron County OPP say the Grey Bruce OPP Explosive Disposal Unit (EDU) attended the scene at 5:31 p.m. and safely removed the item of concern. Following their assessment and removal of the item, all emergency resources have cleared the scene.

Josephine Street has been reopened to both vehicle and pedestrian traffic, and all previously established road closures have been lifted.

“We were just going about our normal day in the store, taking donations at the back. And, we received one particular donation that came in. Our staff were sorting through it as they normally would. And it appeared that there was something a little different in a certain box of military memorabilia. And it turned out that it was a hand grenade from kind of the First or Second World War period is what we believe, and that was quite a surprise,” said Wingham’s Salvation Army Pastor/Director Brian Dueck.

Dueck actually held the grenade in his hand before calling in police around 2 p.m.

“I was just kind of checking it out, and trying to find the wording and numbers on it to see what exactly it was. And as I was looking it up, that’s when I realized that this was probably a legitimate hand grenade. And, it had the pin in it and everything. So the next question is, well, is it actually active or is it being deactivated? So I called the police non-emergency line, and they sent the police out to come and have a look,” said Dueck.

Once police arrived, they decided it was best to evacuate not only the Salvation Army, but a large part of Wingham’s downtown stretch.

Huron County OPP says the temporary shelter that had been established at the Westcast Community Centre has now been closed.

“We were given the order as soon as the police got there to clear the building. And, then the block started clearing out, and nobody’s allowed kind of anywhere near the building for now,” said Dueck.

Dueck says he was told that a specialized bomb disposal unit is coming from London, Ont. to deal with the grenade.

“I mean, I didn’t really think much of it at first, but I guess you take every precaution, right? So, yeah, thankfully the police are really quick to, to come down and they just kind of took control of the situation and let us know what we had to do,” he said.

Dueck hopes it all turns out OK, and the grenade isn’t live, regardless it’s a scary situation that probably could have been avoided.

“Check what you’re donating, try to keep it safe, and put any paperwork with it if it’s something like that, so that we know what’s going on,” said Dueck.

stories.title: Niagara Region thanks Buffalo in open letter
stories.summary: Tourism board highlights recent examples of camaraderie
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Neighbourly affection between Ontario’s Niagara Region and the city of Buffalo, N.Y., is once again on display amid the ongoing Canada-U.S. trade war.

And once again, sports are a playing a big role.

Niagara Falls Tourism has placed an open letter in today’s edition of the Buffalo News, inviting Americans across the border to visit on Saturday as a fireworks display will light up the sky over Niagara Falls red, white and blue — the colours of the Buffalo Bills football team.

The letter thanks Buffalo for “being a neighbour,” saying the two regions have shared the river for a long time and highlighting recent moments of camaraderie.

It says many in Buffalo stood up and sang O Canada during the Bills’ home opener on Sept. 17, and Canadians sang along, “from the stadium, in sports bars, and on couches across the country.”

Later, the letter reads, Buffalo took out billboards across southern Ontario, referencing O Canada with the note, “We’re still singing it.”

“Well, we want to return the feeling,” the letter says.

A similar dynamic played out this spring during the NHL playoffs, with many hockey fans in the Niagara Region cheering for the Buffalo Sabres.

At the time, St. Catharines city Coun. Kevin Townsend said there is a “lifelong friendship” between Upstate New Yorkers and Niagara Region residents, even amid escalating trade tensions between the two countries.

stories.title: Nova Scotia’s new EV fee raises bigger questions for drivers across Canada
stories.summary: Electric vehicle owners will now have to pay $500 every two years in addition to their vehicle registration fee. Plug-in hybrid vehicles will have an additional $250 fee.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Nova Scotia has become the latest province to start charging an extra fee for battery-powered cars and trucks.

As of Thursday, electric vehicle (EV) owners will pay $500 every two years in addition to their vehicle registration fee. Plug-in hybrid vehicles will have an additional $250 fee.

Some drivers call it an unfair cash grab, but the provincial government argues it’s a way to pay for road repairs since EV drivers don’t pay the provincial gas tax.

Halifax resident and Tesla owner, Karina Baxter, says it doesn’t add up.

“I do save a significant amount of money on this EV: no gas, no oil changes and things like that. But I still don’t think the math is mathing,” she said.

In February, when the changes were tabled as part of the budget, Premier Tim Houston told reporters the levy was necessary.

“EVs have a wear and tear element on our roads and highways … they’re generally a lot heavier, so they sometimes have quite a bit more wear and tear, and the owners of those vehicles should pay something towards that,” he said.

Baxter says she agrees to a certain extent.

“Yes, we do affect the roads maybe a little more because a lot of people will bring up the weight of these EVs. So I’m happy to pay for these taxes and these fees, I just think there’s a better way to do it.”

She points out drivers who pay for gas are essentially fueling up what they need and therefore paying for how much they drive.

“With this, it’s a flat rate, which I don’t think is fair. They should track our kilometres or something like that, which makes it a little more fair, especially for those who don’t drive as much,” she said.

Local EV advocate, Kurt Sampson, says the number of EVs on the road is only increasing, so a solution needs further discussion.

“It would be nice to see a system that is standard and fair, equitable across all of Canada, really,” said Sampson, who is the EV expert with CAA Atlantic.

5:07 EV sales soar amid high gas prices

Saskatchewan was the first province to make the move, and doubled its fee last year to $300 annually . Alberta charges $200 a year , and the Quebec government has said it will start charging $125 as of next year.

At the same time, the federal government has been incentivizing electric vehicle purchases by launching consumer rebates .

“This year showed about 34 per cent of Canadians said that they would consider an EV for their next purchase, and that’s up from about 28 per cent in 2025,” said J.D. Ney, the director and automotive practice lead for J.D. Power Canada, a data analytics company.

2:03 Canadians buying nearly 20% more electric vehicles, StatCan data finds

Down the road, more EVs will mean less gas in tanks and less money in government coffers.

“I think there’s a wide acknowledgement in the auto industry and beyond that … almost everyone eventually will be driving an electric vehicle of some type and gas tax is going to dry up,” said David Kennedy, Toronto bureau chief with Automotive News Canada.

“If you don’t have a gas tax that keeps your roads from completely deteriorating, you need some sort of alternative in the long term. And you know I think, at least as a short term stopgap solution, maybe (EV levies) is where we’ll go.”

But Baxter worries these types of levies and fees might discourage people from making the switch to an EV, which would knock the government off its zero-emission vehicle targets.

“There’s already some people that are apprehensive about EVs because they don’t really know that much about them, so this on top of that I think is just going to have a negative impact,” she said.

— with files from David Murdock and Heidi Petracek

stories.title: Quebec Conservative Party Leader Éric Duhaime admits to using AI to write book
stories.summary: Duhaime has supported the use of AI throughout his campaign, saying it could be useful to cut bureaucracy
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Quebec Conservative Party Leader Éric Duhaime admitted to using artificial intelligence to write his latest book.

Duhaime told reporters Friday morning that he used AI as “a tool among others” to write the book, titled Destination Autonomie, which was published in April.

Duhaime, who previously worked as a columnist and radio host, said he used AI to structure his thoughts and that the ideas in the book are all his.

“AI is important to us. It’s part of reality. That said, it has to be done under human supervision. And that’s exactly what happened,” Duhaime said.

Using the AI-detection software Pangram, Quebecor media outlets reported on Thursday that 62 per cent of the book was machine-generated.

The introduction, written by Conservative candidate Maïté Blanchette-Vézina, was reported to have been completely AI-generated. Blanchette-Vézina had previously crossed the floor to join Duhaime’s party after being shuffled out of former premier François Legault’s Coalition Avenir Québec cabinet.

Duhaime’s rivals on the campaign trail made light of the revelation about his book. Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and Liberal Leader Charles Milliard both joked about whether Duhaime used AI to generate his party’s platform.

Coalition Avenir Québec leader Christine Fréchette also took a political jab at Duhaime, saying she now understands how he found time to write a book as a politician. Meanwhile, Québec solidaire posted a joke about Duhaime on social media featuring co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal looking through a telescope, saying she was searching for sections of his book that were written by humans.

Duhaime has supported the use of AI throughout his campaign, saying it could be useful to cut bureaucracy.

He also admitted on Friday to using AI in his campaign materials, including to generate charts, a table of contents and the layout of the party’s financial framework.

“Social progress has been achieved thanks to technology, not in spite of it. So, for us, it was a step forward for society, not a step backward,” he said, questioned on the ethics of his use of AI.

In his book, Duhaime reflects on how Quebec can gain more autonomy within the Canadian Confederation.

Duhaime has published four other books. He came out as gay in his 2017 book, titled La fin de l’homosexualité et le dernier gay (“The end of homosexuality and the last gay man” in French).

He has also written books critical of labour unions, baby boomers and the monopoly of Quebec’s government-owned liquor corporation.

stories.title: Michael J. Fox laments Canada-U.S. trade war, says people-to-people ties still strong
stories.summary: Ottawa - Michael J. Fox says the state of the Canada-U.S. relationship is "sad" and "pointless" but he believes ties between Americans and Canadians on the "human level" remain strong.
stories.author: Nick Murray The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Michael J. Fox says the state of the Canada-U.S. relationship is “sad” and “pointless” but he believes ties between Americans and Canadians on the “human level” remain strong.

“It’s really sad. It’s so pointless. And I have to tell you, it doesn’t reflect the opinions or the attitudes of virtually any Americans I meet outside of this little cabal of political reactionaries,” Fox told The Canadian Press.

“Americans and Canadians still have the same relationship they’ve always had, no matter how much you try to ratchet it up with the trade war and stuff. It’s not filtering down to the human level.”

The actor and activist joined 50 other people in Ottawa on Friday for an Order of Canada ceremony. Fox, who was invested as an officer of the Order of Canada in 2010, was promoted to the companion level.

Spectators stood and applauded Michael J. Fox at Rideau Hall Friday morning as Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour officially inducted the celebrated actor and Parkinson’s disease activist to the companion level of the Order of Canada. Rideau Hall says Fox was elevated to the companion level to honour his “powerful global advocacy and unflinching honesty about Parkinson’s.” (Oct. 2, 2026)

In an interview with The Canadian Press following the ceremony, Fox was asked for his thoughts on Canada-U.S. relations.

Fox, who maintains dual citizenship, was born and raised in Canada but moved to Los Angeles in 1979 to pursue his acting career. He received U.S. citizenship in 2000 and continues to live in the United States.

Canada and the United States have been locked in a bitter trade war since shortly after U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House almost two years ago and began imposing new tariffs which Canada says violate the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement.

Trump has repeatedly mused about making Canada a U.S. state and has threatened to use “economic force” to make it happen. He has mocked Prime Minister Mark Carney and his predecessor Justin Trudeau with the title “governor.”

The tensions escalated in August when attempts to solve some outstanding trade irritants broke down before a Trump-imposed deadline to impose a new round of tariffs targeting $28 billion in Canadian goods.

Canada retaliated with tariffs of its own, and the Trump administration further responded with outright import bans on some Canadian goods.

The president also signed an executive order to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, and said this week he was teaching Canada a “little lesson.”

Fox said people need to distinguish between the Trump administration’s actions and the attitudes of ordinary Americans.

“It’s really important that we realize where it’s generated from. And it’s not the guy who you used to buy bourbon from across the line,” he said.

“It hasn’t risen to the level of animus, or contention. It’s purely this guy throwing mud at the wall and seeing if it slides or sticks. And it’s sliding mostly, now.”

Fox said he hasn’t paid close attention to Ottawa’s actions in the trade war but appreciates the “reaction, fighting back and standing firm,” Fox said.

Actor and Parkinson's disease advocate Michael J. Fox says he is saddened by the cross-border battles between his home country and his adopted country, but believes it will not last forever. Fox was in Ottawa to receive a promotion within the Order of Canada, and says he is pleased Canada is standing firm and thinks there will be some "selective backtracking" from the United States in the next few years. (Oct. 2, 2026)

“Like I said, from a distance … it’s frustrating. It’s saddening. But I think a lot of change will come in the next couple of years. I think there will be some selective backtracking.”

Asked whether the Canada-U.S. relationship comes up in his social circles, Fox said, “People are aware of it.”

“People just come up and they say, ‘You believe this guy?’ That’s all it is. It’s just bashing of the president, which doesn’t do any good either,” he said.

“People that know me and know my attitude about being Canadian and my attitude about being American — they both mean a lot to me. So they’ll bring it up to me, but they don’t take you to a certain level. At a certain level you don’t take it that seriously. I don’t want to pick a fight, but I mean, come on.

“To the extent that it doesn’t take anything out of my plate, I might go along with it for a while. But people get tired of it after a while.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 2, 2026.

stories.title: Fanshawe College announces $34M training partnership with Royal Canadian Air Force
stories.summary: A new partnership between London, Ont. based Fanshawe College and the Royal Canadian Air Force has just earned its wings.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
A new partnership between London, Ont. based Fanshawe College and the Royal Canadian Air Force (Rcaf) has just earned its wings.

“And the noise behind me is absolutely amazing. It’s great to be at an airport,” exclaimed Fanshawe President Peter Devlin, as he addressed students, military personnel and civilians at Fanshawe’s Norton Wolf School of Aviation and Aerospace Technology Friday.

“I’m proud to announce that Fanshawe has been awarded a contract to deliver air maintenance engineer training to members of the Canadian Armed Forces, and specifically the Royal Canadian Air Force at Canadian Forces Base Borden,” he said.

The four-year contract is worth $34.4 million. Fanshawe will train Rcaf personnel as aviation, avionics and aircraft structures technicians at the Canadian Forces School of Aerospace Technology at CFB Borden.

“It’s critical to have air maintenance skills to be able to keep our military aircraft airworthy, combat capable,” said Devlin.

“The Rcaf stands ready to support the government’s approach on what needs to be addressed internationally, and the air force can’t function without a solid technical base,” said Col. Wes Cunningham, Commander 16 Wing, Borden.

The partnership comes at a time of heightened attention to Canadian sovereignty. Something not lost on those taking part in the event.

“The military. Of course, we include the Rcaf as part of that by definition, is tied fundamentally to Canadian sovereignty. And Canadian sovereignty has come, quite rightly, into very sharp focus,” said Peter Fragiskatos, Liberal MP for London Centre.

“Canada is investing in new aircraft, new systems, new air space capabilities,” said London West MP, Arielle Kayabaga.

Fanshawe will continue to offer the same Transport Canada approved academic curriculum to both civilian and military connected students at its Norton Wolf School of Aviation at London International Airport.

Fanshawe says the diploma programs will be delivered on an accelerated timeline, allowing students to complete four semesters in 16 month period, with fall and winter intake.

It’s expected that up to 300 Rcaf students will be enrolled each year, with the first classes getting off the ground in January 2027.

stories.title: B.C. Conservative interim leader Doerkson promises to buy firefighting water bombers
stories.summary: Victoria - British Columbia's Conservatives are promising to spend half a billion dollars on a fleet of Crown-owned water bombers and cutting-edge technology, including artificial intelligence, to fight the growing threat of wildfires, if the party is elected on Oct. 24.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - British Columbia’s major party leaders took their election campaigns to the Okanagan Friday to talk about fire safety and the high cost of groceries.

Interim Conservative party leader Lorne Doerkson is promising to spend half a billion dollars on a fleet of Crown-owned water bombers and cutting-edge technology, including artificial intelligence, to fight the growing threat of wildfires, if the party is elected on Oct. 24.

Doerkson said the proposed plane purchase and the innovation fund are part of a larger plan to improve the response to wildfire through more on-the-ground prevention and less bureaucracy.

NDP Leader David Eby stood outside a Kelowna grocery store on Friday to announce additional plans to improve affordability by putting price caps on certain groceries items, such as eggs, butter and milk.

He said that his party, if re-elected, would cap unfair increases on staples through price guards on corporate retailers, setting hard ceilings on retail margins for everyday essentials.

“We have seen prices on the basics climb beyond inflation,” he said.

“So, what we are going to do is put the same protections in place we have for farmers,” he said, referring to marketing boards that regulate their products.

Doerkson made his announcement in front of a rural property wiped out last month during the Bald Range wildfire, which destroyed more than 80 homes in Faulder, B.C., and forced thousands of people to flee from nearby Summerland.

“We are here today because British Columbians deserve a government that will act before the smoke appears on the horizon,” he said.

“We owe it to our kids. We owe to our forestry workers and we owe it to communities like Summerland, like Lytton, like Clinton to take back control of our forests.”

Doerkson, who spoke next to property owner Joel Patan and local Conservative candidate Tracy St. Claire, said having a provincial water-bombing fleet will ultimately save money, given the escalating costs of fighting fires.

“We will protect our communities, we will safeguard our health care and education budgets by avoiding billions in emergency suppression costs and economic loss,” he said.

“Most importantly, we will do everything we can to ensure families like Joel’s never again have to flee their homes in the dark with two hour’s notice.”

When asked about the costs of buying the planes, Doerkson said the province could help pay for them by renting them out to other jurisdictions when they aren’t needed.

Eby also made a fire-related announcement, saying that government would match donations to the Canadian Red Cross up to $20 million for people affected by this summer’s wildfires.

After his Kelowna announcement, he visited a coffee shop in Summerland and toured vinAmite Cellars winery, where he tasted and purchased a bottle of wine.

The Ndp’s promise on Friday of a cap on some groceries would be linked to six staples: milk, eggs, butter, cheese, chicken, and turkey, the party said in a statement.

These products are already regulated through marketing boards and the proposed measures would extend that protection to consumers, Eby said.

Just as farmers get their costs, government will put in measures that will cap the profit margins that large grocery chains can make off staples, Eby said.

He said his government would also introduce measures to prohibit predatory pricing and support smaller, independent grocery retailers.

The Retail Council of Canada issued a statement Friday saying B.C. families deserve a debate grounded in facts, not political talking points.

Kim Furlong, chief executive officer of the council, said the promise misses the mark on what actually drives grocery prices, including transportation, energy, labour and regulation.

“Retailers share the goal of affordable food,” she said. “Let’s focus on solutions that actually lower grocery bills: reducing supply chain costs, improving efficiency and strengthening competition — not promises that sound good but leave the real cost drivers untouched.”

Conservative candidate Gavin Dew, who is running in a Kelowna-area riding, noted that Eby didn’t follow through with his promise to B.C. residents of $1,000 in grocery relief after the 2024 election.

B.C. New Democrat candidate Ravi Parmar, meanwhile, questioned Doerkson’s promises.

“How is Lorne Doerkson going to pay for this?” said Parmar, who’s the forest minister under Eby’s government.

He noted that Coulson Aviation, based in British Columbia, is converting 10 federal government Hercules aircraft into water bombers. The company contracts with various agencies around the world, including BC Wildfire Service.

British Columbia is already leading the way when it comes to active forest management through commercial thinning and selected logging, he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 2, 2026.

stories.title: 12 Jewish teachers bring human rights claims against four Ontario school boards and two unions
stories.summary: The teachers allege that in many instances they were penalized for reporting discrimination.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Human rights applications have been filed in Ontario by 12 Jewish teachers who allege they were discriminated against amid ongoing antisemitism.

The applications include claims against the Toronto District School Board, York Region District School Board, Simcoe County District School Board, Ottawa-Carleton District School Board, the Elementary Teachers’ Federation of Ontario and the Ontario Secondary School Teachers’ Federation, with the applicants alleging the institutions responsible for their workplaces failed to act. The teachers allege that in many instances they were penalized for reporting discrimination.

The applicants are seeking general damages of $150,000 each for discrimination, along with compensation for psychological counselling.

Each applicant has filed individually; however, the applicants are asking the Ontario Human Rights Tribunal to hear the applications together.

They are also requesting that the Tribunal order the respondents to develop transparent, enforceable processes aimed at combatting discrimination, with input from the Jewish community. That includes adopting the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance working definition of antisemitism endorsed by the Government of Ontario, and to cease spreading antisemitic misinformation.

“For too long, Jewish teachers in Ontario have gone to work facing antisemitism,” says Kathryn Marshall, the lawyer representing the applicants. “A swastika drawn on a classroom desk is not a grey area. Neither is a teacher being publicly shut down at a union meeting for raising antisemitism. These are the kinds of experiences Jewish teachers across Ontario have been living with, and when they did exactly what they’re supposed to do and reported it — they were ignored, doubted, and in some cases disciplined.”

Marshall says that school boards and unions talk a lot about equity and inclusion, but adds that “those commitments mean nothing if they don’t apply to Jewish educators. These institutions had every opportunity to fix this internally, and they chose not to. Teachers are still in classrooms today facing this, so we can’t afford to wait years for answers. We’re asking the Tribunal to hear these cases quickly and to hold these boards and unions accountable.”

Jewish students say they have come across 'Heil Hitler' salutes, antisemitic graffiti on Canadian university campuses

Belleville shooting a wake-up call for Canadians, survivor says in new statement

The claims raise a variety of allegations of antisemitism. Marshall’s firm provided a list, which included the following.

One teacher says a student drew a swastika on a chart in the classroom and another played the Nazi anthem in class but neither faced any consequences from the school’s administration.

One teacher experienced repeated instances of Israeli flags being defaced in books and on hallway maps.

Another teacher faced an online petition falsely accusing him of racism and seeking his dismissal. The teacher alleges students chanted “Free Palestine” as they passed him, and pressured others in his class to sign the petition. None of the students were held responsible. Instead, alleges the claim, the school board’s response was to remove the teacher from the classroom.

During a union meeting, asserts another claim, the teacher attempted to raise concerns about antisemitism affecting Jewish educators and she was met with hostility and allegedly publicly reprimanded by Nigel Barriffe, the vice president of the Elementary Teachers of Toronto (ETT).

During the 2024 Trans March Social, says one teacher, ETT executive officers wore keffiyehs and pro-Palestinian symbols and distributed “divest from Israel” pamphlets. When the teacher raised concerns that this was politicization of a union event, he was accused of “anti-Palestinian racism.”

During Islamic Heritage Month a principal permitted a keffiyeh to remain in the display case despite a teacher submitting a formal complaint advising that the keffiyeh was experienced by Jewish individuals as a symbol associated with terrorism, intimidation and hostility toward Jews. Yet, during Jewish Heritage Month the school removed the Israeli flag from the display and replaced it with the Star of David, despite the Israeli flag being the flag of a recognized state and a symbol connected to the Jewish homeland and identity.

According to Statistics Canada , 70 per cent of police-reported hate crimes targeting a religion in 2024 were aimed at Jewish people. Meanwhile, Jewish university students have openly expressed concerns about facing “Heil Hitler” salutes and antisemitic graffiti on Canadian campuses.

stories.title: Catholic, Anglican bishops call for Alberta referendum voters to think consequences
stories.summary: But, late this week, both Alberta's Anglican bishops and the Catholic bishops of Alberta wrote open letters urging Albertans to have compassion and to think of the greater good when voting in the Oct. 19 referendum.
stories.author: Steven Sandor
stories.content:
The debate about whether or not religion and politics should mix is as old as, well, religion and politics.

But, late this week, both Alberta’s Anglican bishops and the Catholic bishops of Alberta wrote open letters urging Albertans to have compassion and to think of the greater good when voting in the Oct. 19 referendum.

Neither letter went as far as endorsing yes or no votes on Alberta separation or if the province should look to take more control of immigration. But it’s clear that both letters are asking followers to think hard about the immigration questions. Polls indicated that Albertans are leaning yes to the five immigration measures on the ballot, which would give the Alberta government the moral authority to ask Ottawa for more control over immigration numbers.

Last week, Alberta Jobs, Economy, Trade and Immigration Minister Joseph Schow said ballot measures that could limit immigration and charge health-care and education user fees are targeted towards temporary foreign workers and students, not those with permanent residency in Canada.

In their letter, the three Anglican bishops — The Most Rev. Greg Kerr-Wilson, Bishop of Calgary; the Rt. Rev. David Greenwood, Bishop of Athabasca; and the Rt. Rev. Stephen London, Bishop of Edmonton — reminded followers that, in the Bible, readers are “consistently reminded that they have a divinely given call to welcome and care for strangers and sojourners in their midst.”

The bishops go on to write that in the New Testament story of the Good Samaritan, Jesus does not ask his disciples to pick and choose who would be a good neighbour.

“Jesus is clear that our neighbour is not just those who we think truly belong. Rather, we have a responsibility to support and protect the lives, dignity, and worth of everyone we meet, regardless of their identity or status in our eyes,” write the Anglican bishops.

And they ask Albertans not to think selfishly when they vote.

Alberta referendum questions don't target permanent residents, new Canadians: Schow

Premier Danielle Smith caught by tears during forum on Alberta referendum, grievances with Ottawa

“When we reflect on these referendum questions as disciples of Christ, we are encouraged to do so not only in terms of what is best for ourselves as individuals, or best for Alberta alone, but rather with a concern for the common good. In other words, with an eye for how our decisions will impact all our neighbours — especially those who are most vulnerable.”

The Catholic bishops’ letter was signed by Rev. Stephen A. Hero, Archbishop of Edmonton; Most Rev. William McGrattan, Bishop of Calgary; Most Rev. David Motiuk, Bishop of the Ukrainian Eparchy of Edmonton; Most Rev. Charles Duval, Archbishop of Grouard-McLennan; and Most Rev. Gary Franken, Bishop of St. Paul.

The Catholic letter states that those who live prosperously have a duty to look after those who don’t.

“The church teaches that more prosperous nations are obliged, to the extent they are able, to welcome those seeking safety and the means of livelihood,” states the Catholic letter. “Public authorities also have a responsibility to regulate immigration for the common good. Newcomers, in turn, have duties towards the society that receives them.

“Legitimate concerns about resources and access to public services merit careful consideration. They must be addressed in ways that respect human dignity and avoid making any segment of our population the object of resentment or blame. Within our parishes, those who feel uncertain about their place in society should find welcome and pastoral care.”

stories.title: Bridal shop owner who hung boy on hook gets absolute discharge
stories.summary: A Newfoundland bridal shop owner found guilty of assaulting a seven-year-old boy has received an absolute discharge. A judge cited the man’s lack of a criminal record and the circumstances of the incident in deciding against entering a conviction.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
A Newfoundland bridal shop co-owner found guilty of assaulting a seven-year-old boy will not receive a criminal conviction after a judge determined that an absolute discharge was appropriate in the unusual circumstances of the case.

Rodney Philpott, 54, was found guilty in July of assaulting the boy, identified in the court decision as P., at the bridal shop in Grand Falls-Windsor, N.L.

The incident happened in March 2025, when Philpott was serving the boy’s mother, who was shopping for a wedding dress.

According to Provincial Court Judge Lloyd Strickland’s sentencing decision, the child was “hyper and probably a distraction” while in the store.

Philpott lifted the boy and hung him by the hood of his coat on a hanger in a dressing room.

“The boy struggled to breathe; presumably the collar of his coat was pressed firmly against his throat,” Strickland wrote in his judgement.

A bruise was later found on the boy’s neck.

Child suffered lasting effects

The boy’s father submitted a victim impact statement to the court, saying his son experienced neck pain and missed several days of school while recovering.

The child also continued to experience anxiety related to the incident.

The dad also said the boy ”had issues sleeping and has expressed a fear of returning to the mall where the bridal shop is located.”

The judge identified the child’s age as a crucial factor in determining an appropriate sentence.

“The most evident aggravating factor in this case is the age of the victim,” Strickland wrote, adding that children are among those most in need of protection.

No criminal record

Philpott had never previously been convicted or found guilty of a criminal offence and had been a businessman in both Canada and abroad for many years.

Strickland said Philpott had “very positive” antecedents and described him as a contributing member of the community and a respected businessman.

The judge also concluded that the assault was not an act of anger or an attempt to deliberately hurt the child.

“There May have been a degree of frustration with P.’s behaviour,” Strickland wrote, but the evidence indicated the incident was a “continuation of horseplay” between Philpott and the boy.

“I have no reason to believe Mr. Philpott meant to cause P. any harm,” the judge wrote.

Philpott maintained his innocence following the finding of guilt.

Why no criminal conviction?

The Crown had asked the court to enter a conviction, suspend the passing of sentence and impose probation.

It also sought supervision by a probation officer, counselling and a prohibition on Philpott contacting the boy or his family.

Philpott’s lawyer instead argued for an absolute discharge, pointing to his background and the potential consequences of a criminal conviction.

The court heard that a conviction could interfere with Philpott’s ability to travel internationally, including to the United States, where he attends bridal fashion trade shows.

Under the Criminal Code, a court can grant a discharge if it is satisfied that doing so is in the offender’s best interests and is not contrary to the public interest.

Strickland concluded both requirements were met.

“A conviction and probation are not necessary to deter him from committing a similar offence in the future,” the judge wrote.

The judge said the incident was out of character and that a criminal record could interfere with the business Philpott had spent years building.

Strickland also acknowledged that child assault cases raise concerns about general deterrence.

Nevertheless, he concluded that the finding of guilt and the assault charge were sufficient to reinforce the importance of treating children with care.

“I am satisfied that the assault charge filed against the offender and the finding of guilt sufficiently address general deterrence and remind the community that children are always to be treated with care,” Strickland wrote.

The judge ultimately ordered an absolute discharge and imposed a $100 victim fine surcharge.

“I appreciate it is rare to impose a discharge in a case involving the assault of a child,” Strickland wrote. “But the unique circumstances of this offence and this offender satisfy the Court that a discharge would not be contrary to the public interest.

stories.title: B.C. man sentenced for 'hateful' messages written on Victoria historic synagogue
stories.summary: Victoria - A British Columbia man who defaced a historic synagogue in Victoria with "unquestionably hateful" statements has been sentenced to eight months in jail.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - A British Columbia man who defaced a historic synagogue in Victoria with “unquestionably hateful” statements has been sentenced to eight months in jail.

B.C. provincial court Judge Micah Rankin’s ruling released this week says Arthur Roberts pleaded guilty to mischief and uttering threats, after he admitted to defacing the Congregation Emanu-El synagogue in downtown Victoria in the summer of 2025.
