stories.summary: London, ON (October 2, 2026) – A London Police Service (LPS) officer has been charged following an investigation by the LPS Major Crime Section into an incident that occurred during an arrest earlier this year.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (October 2, 2026) – A London Police Service (LPS) officer has been charged following an investigation by the LPS Major Crime Section into an incident that occurred during an arrest earlier this year.

On April 29, 2026, shortly before 2 a.m., a 33-year-old woman was placed under arrest by LPS officers.

Following her arrest, Oleoresin Capsicum (OC) spray was deployed. The use of OC spray in Ontario is subject to mandatory use-of-force reporting requirements and a subsequent review process.

During that review, concerns were identified regarding the circumstances surrounding the use of force. As a result, the matter was referred to members of the LPS Major Crime Section to investigate possible criminal conduct arising from the use of the OC spray.

Following the investigation, Constable Brandon Mihalides, 29, of London, has been charged with one count of assault with a weapon and has been reassigned to non-operational administrative duties.

Policing depends on public trust and confidence. Maintaining that trust requires police services to have effective systems of oversight and accountability, and to ensure that when concerns regarding police conduct are identified, they are addressed appropriately, transparently and thoroughly.

Accountability is a fundamental principle of policing and public service. Our community rightly expects police officers to exercise their authorities professionally and lawfully. It also expects its police service to identify concerns when they arise, examine the evidence objectively and take appropriate action where warranted.

As this matter is now before the courts, no further information will be provided at this time.

The accused is scheduled to attend court on December 30, 2026, in relation to the charge.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Two charged in north-end shooting
stories.summary: London, ON (October 2, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Major Crime Section have charged two London men following an extensive investigation into a shooting in the city’s north end this summer.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 2, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Major Crime Section have charged two London men following an extensive investigation into a shooting in the city’s north end this summer.

On August 9, 2026, at approximately 12:30 a.m., police responded to multiple reports of gunfire in the area of Kipps Lane and Arbour Glen Crescent. Two suspects were reported fleeing the area on foot before police arrived.

Investigators determined that two individuals had discharged firearms. While no one was injured, a vehicle leaving the area was struck by gunfire and multiple cartridge casings were recovered at the scene.

Following an extensive investigation, members of the LPS Major Crime Section identified two suspects. Both were arrested in late September.

Dante Guerrero, 19, and Kaleb Forden, 20, both of London, have been jointly charged with:

Discharge a firearm in a reckless manner; and

Possess restricted or prohibited firearm knowingly not holding a licence.

Forden has additionally been charged with one count of possession of a Schedule I substance for the purpose of trafficking.

“Gunfire in our neighbourhoods is unacceptable. Every time a firearm is discharged in our community, there is the potential for devastating consequences for innocent people,” said Detective Sergeant Micah Bourdeau of the LPS Major Crime Section. “Those who choose to use firearms in our city should expect our investigators to pursue every available avenue to identify those responsible and bring them before the courts. These arrests are the result of a determined and thorough investigation by our Major Crime investigators.”

The investigation remains ongoing. Investigators continue to ask anyone who was in the area between 12 a.m. and 12:45 a.m. on August 9, 2026, and who May have dash-cam, residential or business surveillance footage, to contact the London Police Service.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Man facing charges following investigation into data breach
stories.summary: London, ON (October 2, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Cyber Crime Unit have charged a London man following an investigation into the unauthorized access of London Hydro customer information.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 2, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Cyber Crime Unit have charged a London man following an investigation into the unauthorized access of London Hydro customer information.

On June 19, 2026, police received a report from London Hydro regarding a suspected compromise of its customer information.

Investigators learned that between June 5 and June 17, 2026, an individual accessed customer accounts and obtained customer information without authorization.

As part of the investigation, police executed a search warrant at a London residence on August 13, 2026. Several electronic devices were seized and subsequently examined.

Through a forensic examination of the seized electronic devices, investigators located evidence that linked the suspect male to the unauthorized access of London Hydro customer information.

As a result of the investigation, Rony Hotimsky, 40, of London, has been charged with:

Fraudulently obtain any computer service; and

Mischief over $5000.

The accused was arrested this morning and is expected to re-appear in London court on December 29, 2026, in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information related to this investigation is asked to contact the London Police Service Cyber Crime Unit at 519-661-5670 or CyberCrime@londonpolice.CA . Anonymous information can also be provided through Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477) or online through London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Stephen Harper warns Albertans against supporting separatists
stories.summary: "I love my country, and I love my province," the former prime minister wrote. "I do not wish to pit one against the other. I believe that is how most
stories.author: Stephanie Taylor
stories.content:
Ottawa — Stephen Harper is warning Albertans against setting the province on a path toward secession by using their votes in an upcoming referendum in an attempt to send Ottawa a message.

In an essay published Friday in the Calgary Herald , Harper also expressed optimism over how he sees the Liberals under Prime Minister Mark Carney turning a page from the “anti-Alberta” policies of Carney’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau.

“As a former prime minister of Canada, staying silent on the upcoming referendum on Alberta secession is not an option. But I wish it were,” he wrote.

“I love my country, and I love my province. I do not wish to pit one against the other. I believe that is how most Albertans feel.”

It is one of the fullest arguments the former Conservative leader has made in support of the federation and against the push for separation ahead of the referendum on Oct. 19.

Alberta Conservative MPs are defending their efforts in the province’s sovereignty referendum, arguing they’re doing all they can to keep the

But it came as some separatist leaders seek to sway Albertans by painting a vote for “Option 2” on the ballot as not a vote to actually separate, but as a way to express how they feel about their province’s treatment by Ottawa.

A towering figure within the Conservative movement, Harper served as prime minister from 2006 to 2015 as a member of Parliament from Calgary. He was first elected as a member of the populist Reform Party, which was birthed out of backlash to Ottawa’s actions in Western Canada, before he helped create the modern Conservative party and became its leader.

His call for national unity follows those of former members of his government, including Jason Kenney, a Conservative cabinet minister who later led Alberta as premier. Former Conservative MP Monte Solberg has joined Kenney in backing a third-party advertising group urging Albertans to vote to remain in Canada.

This week, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre appeared at a fundraiser in Edmonton to drum up support for another third-party group, led by one of his Alberta MPs, which is focused on getting Conservative voters in the deep blue province out to vote to secure a victory to stay .

While Albertans, Harper wrote, “are naturally inclined to love Canada and have made disproportionate contributions to every facet of national life,” they have been left to wonder “why Canada periodically seems to not love them.”

Carney has said he has looked to the former prime minister for advice since coming to power. Last month, Harper was one of the headline speakers at a summit for foreign investors Carney held in Toronto, where he declared the gathering was such a good idea that “I wish I had thought of it.”

In that speech, Harper also threw his support behind Carney’s decision to suspend trade talks with the United States, and praised his plans for regulatory overhauls to get more major projects off the ground.

He offered a similar message to Albertans after placing the blame for the bubbling up of separatist sentiments at the feet of Trudeau and his environmental policies.

“Fortunately, I believe things are already changing. While I remain a committed Conservative, the reality is that the Liberal party has not always been as an anti-Alberta as the two Trudeaus,” Harper wrote, referring also to Trudeau’s father, former prime minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau.

“At other times, it has openly enabled the growth of our energy sector. Like (Alberta) Premier Danielle Smith, I see strong evidence that this Liberal government is returning to those roots.”

When it comes to the upcoming referendum vote, Harper said he stands against separation, adding that beyond the risk that path carries “there is nothing resembling the credible leadership necessary to establish a new country.”

“However, the truth is that the referendum is not really about separation,” he wrote.

“It is a ‘referendum to have a referendum.’ Most voting for it will do so just to ‘send a message,’ in other words, to keep the threat alive in the hope of retaining the benevolent attention that the province has recently been receiving from Ottawa. I believe that approach is mistaken.”

Pointing to past battles over Quebec independence, Harper warned of the consequences of similar debates playing out in Alberta for years to come, saying he believes those “downsides” are not “fully understood” in the province.

“Did Quebec gain some favours as a consequence of the separation threat? Yes, at first,” Harper wrote.

paragraphs: Ottawa — Stephen Harper is warning Albertans against setting the province on a path toward secession by using their votes in an upcoming referendum in an attempt to send Ottawa a message.

In an essay published Friday in the Calgary Herald , Harper also expressed optimism over how he sees the Liberals under Prime Minister Mark Carney turning a page from the “anti-Alberta” policies of Carney’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau.
“As a former prime minister of Canada, staying silent on the upcoming referendum on Alberta secession is not an option. But I wish it were,” he wrote.
“I love my country, and I love my province. I do not wish to pit one against the other. I believe that is how most Albertans feel.”
It is one of the fullest arguments the former Conservative leader has made in support of the federation and against the push for separation ahead of the referendum on Oct. 19.

But it came as some separatist leaders seek to sway Albertans by painting a vote for “Option 2” on the ballot as not a vote to actually separate, but as a way to express how they feel about their province’s treatment by Ottawa.

A towering figure within the Conservative movement, Harper served as prime minister from 2006 to 2015 as a member of Parliament from Calgary. He was first elected as a member of the populist Reform Party, which was birthed out of backlash to Ottawa’s actions in Western Canada, before he helped create the modern Conservative party and became its leader.

His call for national unity follows those of former members of his government, including Jason Kenney, a Conservative cabinet minister who later led Alberta as premier. Former Conservative MP Monte Solberg has joined Kenney in backing a third-party advertising group urging Albertans to vote to remain in Canada.

This week, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre appeared at a fundraiser in Edmonton to drum up support for another third-party group, led by one of his Alberta MPs, which is focused on getting Conservative voters in the deep blue province out to vote to secure a victory to stay .

While Albertans, Harper wrote, “are naturally inclined to love Canada and have made disproportionate contributions to every facet of national life,” they have been left to wonder “why Canada periodically seems to not love them.”

Carney has said he has looked to the former prime minister for advice since coming to power. Last month, Harper was one of the headline speakers at a summit for foreign investors Carney held in Toronto, where he declared the gathering was such a good idea that “I wish I had thought of it.”

In that speech, Harper also threw his support behind Carney’s decision to suspend trade talks with the United States, and praised his plans for regulatory overhauls to get more major projects off the ground.
He offered a similar message to Albertans after placing the blame for the bubbling up of separatist sentiments at the feet of Trudeau and his environmental policies.

“Fortunately, I believe things are already changing. While I remain a committed Conservative, the reality is that the Liberal party has not always been as an anti-Alberta as the two Trudeaus,” Harper wrote, referring also to Trudeau’s father, former prime minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau.
“At other times, it has openly enabled the growth of our energy sector. Like (Alberta) Premier Danielle Smith, I see strong evidence that this Liberal government is returning to those roots.”

When it comes to the upcoming referendum vote, Harper said he stands against separation, adding that beyond the risk that path carries “there is nothing resembling the credible leadership necessary to establish a new country.”
“However, the truth is that the referendum is not really about separation,” he wrote.

“It is a ‘referendum to have a referendum.’ Most voting for it will do so just to ‘send a message,’ in other words, to keep the threat alive in the hope of retaining the benevolent attention that the province has recently been receiving from Ottawa. I believe that approach is mistaken.”

Pointing to past battles over Quebec independence, Harper warned of the consequences of similar debates playing out in Alberta for years to come, saying he believes those “downsides” are not “fully understood” in the province.
“Did Quebec gain some favours as a consequence of the separation threat? Yes, at first,” Harper wrote.

“But that dissipated badly over time as Quebec’s image was increasingly damaged in the rest of Canada. It vanished altogether when the separatists were actually in power, leading to major constitutional amendments without Quebec’s consent.”

stories.title: Software problem caused widespread 911 outage last month, Bell says
stories.summary: The outage in the early hours of Sept. 17 lasted for 87 minutes, according to the telecom giant’s report.
stories.author: Joshua Smith
stories.content:
A software problem sparked the outage that shut down 911 emergency lines for nearly an hour and half last month, Bell says.

The Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (Crtc) required the telecom giant to submit a post-outage report within two weeks of the incident, and Bell submitted it Thursday .

Here’s what Bell disclosed in an abridged version of the report:

On Sept. 17, “a software failure in Bell’s Next-Generation Core Services (Ngcs) platform — the call-routing platform of Bell’s NG9-1-1 network — caused the platform to stop accepting new 9-1-1 calls or new call transfers to public safety answering points (PSAPs) through the NG9-1-1 network,” Bell said Thursday.

In the immediate aftermath of the incident, the company attributed the outage to a “network problem,” saying at the time that it was still investigating the root cause.

The outage lasted from 3:13 a.m. to 4:40 a.m., a period of 87 minutes, Bell said.

The incident affected 911 calls transiting through the NG9-1-1 network to 79 PSAPs and 63 originating network providers in Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, according to Bell.

On Sept. 17, the Nova Scotia government said intermittent 911 outages could affect some cellphone and VoIP (voice over internet protocol) users.

At the time of the outage, Bell spokesperson Elise von Scheel said it was not caused by a cyberattack.

The company reiterated that in its report Thursday, adding that the outage wasn’t caused “by any change activity, planned or unplanned.”

“The root cause was identified on the day of the outage and has been fixed,” Bell wrote.

“Bell has since developed and deployed new independent monitoring mechanisms as a further failsafe,” the company said in the report. “Bell takes its responsibility as a 9-1-1 Service Provider with the utmost seriousness and is committed to the reliability, resilience, and continuous improvement of emergency calling services.”

The company also pledged to implement more automated alarm systems to allow for earlier call-outs to experts, among the “next steps” it listed in the report.

Bell added that it plans to hold a post-incident debrief session for PSAPs and for third-party call operators to share what it learned from the incident, and that it already had a call with other NG9-1-1 providers to do so.

The Star reached out Friday night to all five police departments in the GTA — Toronto as well as Durham, Halton, Peel and York regions — and asked whether they have changed any protocols in the wake of the outage.

“As part of our standard practice, we continually review significant incidents to identify any lessons learned and opportunities to strengthen our response,” Toronto police spokesperson Nadine Ramadan said in an email Saturday night.

Toronto police have been in contact with Bell about the outage, Ramadan added, while noting that the outage originated with the 911 service provider and “was not related to Toronto Police Service technology.” She referred any questions about changes to Bell’s systems or processes to the telecom giant.

Peel police spokesperson Tyler Bell-Morena said in an email Friday night that his department couldn’t comment until Monday at the earliest, while the other three police forces have not replied.

stories.title: PQ leader’s vow to break with monarchy raises prospect of constitutional showdown
stories.summary: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says a PQ government would introduce legislation to abolish the office of lieutenant-governor
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
The leader of the Parti Québécois says he will break with the monarchy in Quebec if he becomes premier, invoking the spectre of a constitutional battle that critics say could help him drum up support for an unpopular referendum on independence.

Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said this week that it’s “unacceptable” for a representative of the British Crown to have a role in Quebec’s Parliament. If the PQ wins the provincial election on Oct. 5, he said his government will pass a law eliminating the role of lieutenant-governor.

Quebec has for decades taken steps to reduce the visibility of the monarchy in its legislature, including when the Coalition Avenir Québec government scrapped a mandatory oath of allegiance to the Crown four years ago – a change that was also driven by the PQ Leader.

But experts say a move to unilaterally abolish the function of lieutenant- governor is transparently unconstitutional and would inevitably wind up in court.

“It’s almost being done intentionally just to cause a constitutional crisis that then bolsters the impetus for a referendum,” said Lawrence David, who teaches constitutional law at the University of Ottawa.

The PQ is widely expected to win Monday’s election and could claim a majority of the seats in the province’s National Assembly. Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to hold the province’s third sovereignty referendum by 2030, even though support for independence in Quebec is currently below 30 per cent.

On Tuesday, the PQ Leader said that it’s “not normal” for a representative of King Charles III to “tell us what to do.” Lieutenant-governors swear in premiers and cabinet ministers, open legislative sessions and grant royal assent to bills passed by provincial legislatures.

“There is nothing preventing the National Assembly from acting as a sovereign legislature and passing a law that abolishes the lieutenant-governor’s duties and stops allocating funds to this charade, which wastes money that could be put to better use,” he told reporters.

He said he would redirect the provincial government’s contribution to the lieutenant-governor’s office – about $1.3-million in the 2026-27 fiscal year – to fighting homelessness. The lieutenant-governor’s salary and pension are paid by the federal government, while the province covers a portion of office expenses.

But Mr. David said any such constitutional amendment would require the unanimous consent of the federal Parliament and every provincial legislature, and cannot be carried out unilaterally.

“Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon knows that there is no way to argue that it’s not manifestly unconstitutional,” he said. If a court struck down the Quebec law, he added, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon could argue that the only way to rid Quebec of the monarchy is through separation.

Speaking to reporters Thursday, the PQ Leader denied that he’s spoiling for a fight with Ottawa ahead of a referendum, which he has said would not take place until U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House in 2029.

“I am preparing Quebeckers for three years of true democracy, with my sole loyalty being to the interests of Quebeckers,” he said.

Patrick Taillon, a professor of constitutional law at Laval University, said Quebec has a long history of taking steps to make the monarchy “invisible” in the province without abolishing it outright.

In Ottawa, the governor-general typically delivers the Speech from the Throne to open sessions of Parliament. After Mark Carney became Prime Minister last year, the King delivered the speech himself during a visit to Canada.

But experts say a move to unilaterally abolish the function of lieutenant- governor is transparently unconstitutional and would inevitably wind up in court.

“It’s almost being done intentionally just to cause a constitutional crisis that then bolsters the impetus for a referendum,” said Lawrence David, who teaches constitutional law at the University of Ottawa.

The PQ is widely expected to win Monday’s election and could claim a majority of the seats in the province’s National Assembly. Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to hold the province’s third sovereignty referendum by 2030, even though support for independence in Quebec is currently below 30 per cent.

stories.title: Liberals struggle to gain traction in Quebec election even in historically red Eastern Townships
stories.summary: Province finds itself in a conservative era, with fears about the future of French, as the PQ looks poised to win
stories.author: Eric Andrew-Gee
stories.content:
Even the leaves were turning Liberal red in Knowlton, Que., ON the final week of the provincial election campaign, as Frédéric Beauchemin went door-knocking in his riding.

Good omens seemed to be stacking up for the Quebec Liberal Party candidate in Brome–Missisquoi. This corner of the Eastern Townships is prosperous, fairly anglophone, and historically rouge. Voter after voter told Mr. Beauchemin they were tired of the incumbent Coalition Avenir Québec and totally opposed to the independence referendum promised by the Parti Québécois. He should have been winning by default.

The Quebec Liberals (PLQ) represent change in a change election, federalism in a federalist climate, and economic credentials in an economic crisis.

Yet, despite all their advantages on paper, the PLQ are locked in a close three-way race in Brome–Missisquoi. The venerable old party looks poised to form Opposition again after being stuck in neutral during the campaign for the Oct. 5 election. This week, Mr. Beauchemin was frantically trying to get out the vote with reinforcements from Montreal; another Liberal candidate in the safe seat of D’Arcy-McGee, Elisabeth Prass, drove down to help on Tuesday because “she feels bad for me,” Mr. Beauchemin half-joked. On Thursday, party Leader Charles Milliard came to lend a hand.

What ails Quebec’s natural governing party has become the subject of a thousand op-eds in the province, but with the separatist PQ likely to form government, the woes of the provincial Liberals have become Canada’s problem, too. The province’s voice for federalism is struggling to be heard.

The pitfalls are commonly dated to the government of Philippe Couillard, a courtly white-haired neurosurgeon who came to power in 2014. He left the province with a budget surplus, but was seen by nationalist voters as too pro-Canadian and multiculturalist, without an aggressive agenda for strengthening the French language.

He was defeated in 2018 by François Legault and the CAQ, who presented themselves as defenders of Quebec identity, passing laws restricting the use of English and banning religious symbols for some public sector workers.

The PLQ opposed both. The party has historically been a defender of minority rights, and its most solid base is among anglophone and immigrant voters in the Montreal region.

But the laws were popular, and the party’s opposition hurt it badly among the French-speaking majority. The most recent Léger poll had the party supported by just 14 per cent of francophones, who naturally decide elections in Quebec.

“The francophone vote doesn’t recognize itself in the Liberal Party of Quebec, notably because of the question of identity,” said Louis Aucoin, a communications strategist and former Bloc Québécois staffer.

When former federal cabinet minister Pablo Rodriguez became the PLQ leader last year, he had name recognition and experience in his favour. But within six months of assuming the post, he resigned amidst a financing scandal surrounding his leadership campaign. Mr. Rodriguez maintains he did nothing wrong, and the results of multiple provincial investigations are outstanding, but the damage was done. For a party that struggled with allegations of corrupt campaign financing as recently as the premiership of Jean Charest in the 2010s, the optics were especially bad.

“The integrity of the party was put in question,” Mr. Aucoin said.

When Mr. Milliard, a boyish-looking pharmacist and former Uniprix executive, won a hastily assembled leadership race this past February, he was uncontested. The PLQ brand was tarnished, and the new chief would have little time to introduce himself to voters ahead of a fall campaign.

Those circumstances set the Liberals back, but a deeper obstacle was at play as well: what Mr. Aucoin called Quebec’s “deep blue streak,” has lately risen to the surface. The province finds itself in a conservative era, with fears about the future of French – amidst a massive increase in immigration and the overweening presence of English online – leaving many francophones in a defensive mood.

In this atmosphere, the party of minority rights, public sector reform, business, and federalism has had trouble gaining traction. Although only the PQ and Québec solidaire are arguing for independence, the CAQ and even the once-libertarian Conservative Party of Quebec are making strong nationalist pitches – a veritable sea of ideological blue.

It’s harder to make the federalist case because nationalism is largely based on emotion, André Pratte, president of the Plq’s National Political Commission, which acts as an internal think tank, said in an interview earlier this year.

“For many Quebeckers, being part of Canada is a rational decision, not so much an emotional decision,” he said.

Adding to this baggage, the Milliard campaign got off to a bumpy start with gaffes that were heavily scrutinized in Quebec’s intense media climate, dominated by the sovereigntist-leaning Quebecor empire. The party’s decision not to put the leader’s face on the side of its campaign bus was dissected for days, until Mr. Milliard’s visage finally appeared on the vehicle.

Since then, the party has fared better. Mr. Milliard was thought to have performed well in the debates. The polling collapse of the CAQ in recent days has seemingly directed some anti-referendum voters into the Liberal camp, with the party now sitting at 26 per cent in Léger’s latest survey, behind only the PQ at 30 per cent.

But because of the PLQ vote’s heavy concentration in Montreal, the party is projected to win about 30 fewer seats than the péquistes. Mr. Beauchemin’s move to run in the Townships, rather than in his blood-red former seat in the metropole, was an attempt by the party to strengthen its position in the regions.

It was a risky bet for the fluently bilingual former banker, who comes across as a walking embodiment of his party. With a sheaf of flyers in his hand, he marched up and down the pretty rural roads of Knowlton expounding liberal principles.

“History judges nations harshly that only treat their majorities well … The anglophones don’t have the impression of being treated equally … The role of the government is not to pick winners, it’s to create the winning conditions for everyone to succeed.”

At the doorstep, Mr. Beauchemin got a warm reception; some voters had already cast their ballots for him in advanced polling.

“There’s no question – I don’t want a referendum,” said Josianne Côté, a lifelong Liberal voter.

But the riding-wide polls were still not as kind as the townsfolk of Knowlton, and there was something tense in the candidate’s manner as he hustled down the campaign’s home stretch, trying, like his party, to stave off a PQ victory.

At times, he seemed to see the colours of his adversaries everywhere. Stopped at a peaceful stream on the side of one rural road, Mr. Beauchemin gazed into the water and sighed, “It’s got a bit of blue algae in it.”

stories.title: Advance polling station at Fanshawe College offers an important chance to be heard for voters
stories.summary: https://youtu.be/CmP4vYuMcgs In the Alumni Lounge at Fanshawe College, a polling station was set up on Thursda...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
In the Alumni Lounge at Fanshawe College, a polling station was set up on Thursday as part of the leadup to London’s municipal elections for people to vote in advance, something that is important to many of the people who arrived.

The station was one of several that will open for advance voting between Oct. 1 and Saturday, Oct. 10, according to the city of London website . Another station was also open at a conference room in Western University on the same day, both offering a chance for Londoners to vote ahead of the election day on Oct. 26.

“A lot of people can’t make it on the day of the actual vote,” said professor emeritus of political science at the University of Toronto Nelson Wiseman. “Some people are out of town, some people are working. There are all kinds of reasons, and so advanced polling is made available as a convenience.”

Despite the convenience, turnout in the Alumni Lounge polling station’s early hours was slow but steady, with lengthy intervals between people coming to vote.

When asked, Wiseman said that advanced polls can help with turnout numbers in elections, which other experts have said is a recurring problem in municipal politics and that some voters have seen for themselves.

“Last year in my ward, it was a very low turnout, and I think across the city [as well],” said Ruth Kivilahti.

Even candidates in the elections said they believe advance voting is important for voter turnout.

“It’s a shame that the voter percentage is very low,” said Thames Valley District School Board (TVDSB) Wards 1, 11, 12 and 14 candidate Smita Tajne. “As a city, we should all make a conscious effort to come in together.”

Several voters offered what they felt were good options for increasing voter turnout at advance polling stations. Kivilahti, as well as TVDSB Wards 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 candidate Pat Mehta, said they want to see polling stations made more accessible with ride sharing programs and incentives.

“Many people doesn’t know that advance voting is already on,” said Mehta. “So the city has to do some publicity.”

A sticker handed out at the Alumni Lounge polling station to advance voters. Many who showed up believed it is important for people to vote early. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

Fanshawe marketing student Zoe Chen believed candidates could advertise when advance polling stations are open.

“It’s always important to … market yourself and put yourself out there,” she said. “Not only as a candidate, but London should always get out there and get to know the people.”

For many voters who showed up to the station, voting in advance was also something they felt was important to do for a variety of reasons.

“Since I’m living in Canada, I was not aware of the power of the vote, and now I have understood,” said Romana Rustamani. “I don’t want to waste my vote, so that’s why I came early.”

For her part, Kivilahti said she showed up early because she believes the election will be very close and is worried about a split vote. Meanwhile, Addison Snook said voting early mattered to her because she wants to get out the youth vote .

“I feel like London needs a change,” said Snook emphatically. “And it’s always good to make sure all of us young people are getting our votes out there, because it’s always important and your voice matters.”

stories.title: Exclusive: Owner claims building with 13 fire code violations since early 2025 was safe prior to fatal fire
stories.summary: Fire inspection documents obtained by CTV News identify a total of 13 Ontario Fire Code violations at 745 Dundas St. since the beginning of 2025, but Toronto-based owner Radium-1 Development Ltd. claims all of the deficiencies at the residential building were resolved prior to the fire that killed a woman this summer.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Fire inspection documents obtained by CTV News identify a total of 13 Ontario Fire Code violations at 745 Dundas St. since the beginning of 2025, but Toronto-based owner Radium-1 Development Ltd. claims all of the deficiencies at the residential building were resolved prior to the fire that killed a woman this summer.

“I did everything!” asserts CEO Yaso Somalingam. “I did work with the city. I work with the fire department.”

A 29-year-old woman died, and two other people were critically injured when fire broke out in the 13-unit building on July 17.

At the time, the London Fire Department (LFD) confirmed that it had worked with the building’s owner regarding Ontario Fire Code violations, but could not provide details because a matter was before the courts.

According to documents recently obtained through the Municipal Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, there were two Inspection Orders issued since the beginning of 2025.

A fire inspection conducted on February 5, 2025 discovered 10 deficiencies:

Fire alarm is not functioning in operating condition

Emergency lighting units did not function when tested

Carbon monoxide alarm not located in the service room

Multiple holes in fire separations were noted during the inspection

Self-closing devices (on doors) were missing or broken

Portable fire extinguishers were missing (x2)

Extinguishers not inspected monthly or serviced by a qualified technician since 2022 (x2)

Smoke alarms in unit 1 and 6 required a battery (supplied by LFD)

A year later, ON Feb. 26, 2026 an inspection identified three deficiencies:

Fire watch not being conducted during period when fire alarm not functioning

Fire safety plan not located in fire safety plan lockbox

The Inspection Order from early 2026 contains additional details about the non-functioning fire alarm, “A trouble indicator is lit on the panel, and the fire alarm system has been silenced. Further to that, there are missing heat detectors throughout the building, and a report provided by your contractor indicates that the alarm is not fully functional.”

Somalingam says all of the identified issues in the two reports had been resolved and, in his opinion, the building was safe before the fire in July, “The fire alarm system was working and the alarm panel was working.”

He adds that the outstanding issue before the courts dates from prior to 2023, when he failed to meet a deadline to address other fire code deficiencies.

“If this was not safe place, those 13 people wouldn’t be living there,” Somalingam tells CTV News. “And some of them had been living over ten years in that building.”

He argues that city hall must do more to address homelessness, because the crisis is at the root of repeated break-ins, thefts, and damage to the fire safety equipment.

“The municipality is not solving the homeless issue, so all these homeless people are flooding into these private owners properties,” Somalingam said.

The London Fire Department declined to be interviewed about the Inspection Orders from 2025 and 2026, at this time, citing the ongoing legal matter.

Extinguishers not inspected monthly or serviced by a qualified technician since 2022 (x2)
Smoke alarms in unit 1 and 6 required a battery (supplied by LFD)
A year later, ON Feb. 26, 2026 an inspection identified three deficiencies:
Fire watch not being conducted during period when fire alarm not functioning
Fire safety plan not located in fire safety plan lockbox

The Inspection Order from early 2026 contains additional details about the non-functioning fire alarm, “A trouble indicator is lit on the panel, and the fire alarm system has been silenced. Further to that, there are missing heat detectors throughout the building, and a report provided by your contractor indicates that the alarm is not fully functional.”

Somalingam says all of the identified issues in the two reports had been resolved and, in his opinion, the building was safe before the fire in July, “The fire alarm system was working and the alarm panel was working.”
He adds that the outstanding issue before the courts dates from prior to 2023, when he failed to meet a deadline to address other fire code deficiencies.
“If this was not safe place, those 13 people wouldn’t be living there,” Somalingam tells CTV News. “And some of them had been living over ten years in that building.”
He argues that city hall must do more to address homelessness, because the crisis is at the root of repeated break-ins, thefts, and damage to the fire safety equipment.
“The municipality is not solving the homeless issue, so all these homeless people are flooding into these private owners properties,” Somalingam said.
The London Fire Department declined to be interviewed about the Inspection Orders from 2025 and 2026, at this time, citing the ongoing legal matter.

stories.title: This was the week Canada stopped shooting its oil patch in the foot
stories.summary: We’re finally witnessing our country act with some sense of its own self-interest
stories.author: Tony Keller
stories.content:
Back in 2015, the United States was not even a minor producer of liquefied natural gas. The amount of LNG it exported was within a rounding error of zero. The infrastructure to move gas to tidewater, cool it into a liquid and ship it overseas simply didn’t exist.

But just seven years later, the U.S. had grown into the world’s largest exporter of LNG. It continues to hold that crown. Last year, exports were valued at US$43.6-billion – up more than 30,000 per cent from a decade earlier.

In contrast, Canadian exports of LNG over the same period went from zero to nil – until, ON June 30, 2025, this country’s first-ever overseas shipment was loaded at the new LNG Canada facility in Kitimat, B.C.

This week, LNG Canada, owned by a private consortium of global energy companies, announced that it is going forward with Phase 2 of the project . Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government last year referred it to the Major Projects Office, designed to speed approvals. Private investment of $33-billion will double export capacity, which would make it one of the world’s largest facilities of its kind.

To supply the gas, TC Energy, owner of the Coastal GasLink pipeline between Dawson Creek, B.C., and Kitimat, will also invest in doubling that line’s capacity.

And on Thursday, Mr. Carney was in Fort McMurray, heart of the oil sands, to announce that a proposed, one million barrel a day oil pipeline, to be called Pacific Link , has been designated as a project of national interest under the Building Canada Act. It is expected to largely follow the route of the existing Trans Mountain Pipeline, reaching the Pacific at the Roberts Bank container terminal – a site that Ottawa has also fast-tracked for expansion.

Over the next 11 months, Pacific Link will go through consultation and condition-setting with stakeholders and Indigenous rightsholders. And then, as the federal press release succinctly puts it, the Major Projects Office “will work to finalise those conditions by September 1, 2027, clearing the way to get shovels in the ground.”

Pacific Link should be ready to move crude by 2033. And the certainty of an additional million barrels of pipeline capacity to the West Coast is expected to encourage more new investment in the oil patch, to produce more oil to fill the pipes. If all goes according to plan, Canada could be looking at a decade’s worth of supercharged investment and construction, like what we experienced before 2014.

Opinion: Is it really a good idea for the government to subsidize a pipeline?

So take a moment to celebrate. It turns out that Canada is capable of getting off the couch and getting stuff done. Maybe we don’t have to petition Parliament to designate the flightless Bureaucraticus paralysisus as our national bird.

But let’s not overdo the back patting.

This is not Canada doing the impossible at the speed of the inconceivable. It only seems so in comparison to the preceding years of slow-motion self-sabotage and learned helplessness.

What we are witnessing is our country finally acting with some sense of its own self-interest, and an interest in its own self-preservation. That, and showing a basic ability to count.

Like, you know, a normal country.

We fertilized a legal, political and regulatory environment that prioritized indecision, raised costs, sowed uncertainty and discouraged building. We dreamed that we could sideline a core national industry without undermining national unity or sapping our ability to fund social programs.

We can thank Donald Trump for the rude awakening. Nap time is over.

Oil and gas is one place where Canada has an enormous comparative advantage, because we’re sitting on so much of it. Japan and South Korea, to name just two countries, don’t produce oil and gas because they don’t have any. That’s why they import so much of the stuff.

These resources are going to be in demand for a long time to come, even as the world shifts to electric vehicles, and solar and wind power become cheaper. Try making cars, appliances, textiles or homes without plastics.

There is no reason Canada should not claim a growing share of the global oil and gas market. One of our models should be Norway – now there’s a country doing exceptional things. It has world-leading environmental standards, world-beating social programs and a multitrillion-dollar national piggy bank, funded by revenues from an oil and gas industry that progressive politicians there see no logic in undermining.

Canada doesn’t have to be smarter than the rest of the world to deliver head-of-the-class results. Our national endowments – vast natural resources, an educated population, a history of peace, order and (mostly) good government – put our starting line far ahead of most countries.

We simply have to stop shooting ourselves in the foot. This was a good week for that.

stories.title: AI hack on Canadian archive is ‘the world we live in now,’ expert warns
stories.summary: Artificial intelligence agents apparently searching for century-old divorce records tried to hack a federal government website this spring, according to an AI research firm. Canada’s cybersecurity agency says there is no indication any government systems were compromised.
stories.author: John Vennavally-Rao
stories.content:
Toronto — Artificial intelligence agents apparently searching for century-old divorce records tried to hack a federal government website this spring, according to an AI research firm. Canada’s cybersecurity agency says there is no indication any government systems were compromised.

San Francisco-based non-profit Transluce says AI agents, which can carry out tasks on their own, targeted the Library and Archives Canada website on May 28 and June 9. They appear to have been trying to dig up divorce records between 1905 and 1911.

Of the nearly 900 requests captured by a Portuguese web archive, Transluce says 13 “carried attack payloads rather than ordinary queries.”

Those included SQL injection probes, a basic hacking technique that involves entering database commands into a search box in the hope the system will carry them out.

It’s not entirely clear which AI was used, or what exactly it was asked to accomplish. But Transluce says the tactics resemble those of agents it previously linked to OpenAI during the same period, though it stopped short of blaming the company.

In a statement, OpenAI said, “We’re reviewing these findings and have provided an initial briefing to Canadian officials conducting the government’s review.”

Mark Daley, chief AI officer at Western University in London, Ont., said the agent likely was not trying to cause harm.

“The agent is just like, ‘I have a job. I’m going to try to do the job,’” Daley told CTV News.

“It went beyond just a public search and tried to hack the website so it could get the information it wanted, but it wasn’t successful.”

Daley said that is what sets the agent’s behaviour apart from that of a normal person.

“A human would stop at the point where they couldn’t get that information. They wouldn’t try to hack the website,” he said. “The agent decided that the next most obvious thing to do is to hack the website.”

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security said it is assessing the information. “There is no indication that government systems have been compromised at this time.”

It noted that public-facing government websites routinely receive automated and potentially malicious requests, which on their own do not indicate a successful cyber incident.

Canada’s AI minister, Evan Solomon, said Ottawa is still assessing what happened and promised to keep Canadians informed.

AI companies largely left to police themselves

The findings follow reports of AI agents unexpectedly breaching government and corporate systems. Australia recently said an OpenAI agent hacked into a government health data portal in June and accessed files. OpenAI apologized on Tuesday.

It also comes as AI companies are largely left to police themselves. Leaders of the biggest firms met with U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House this week and signed a voluntary accord on AI safety. Trump has refused to impose strict rules on the industry, saying they could help China win the AI race.

Daley believes rogue AI incidents now number in the hundreds “and probably that’s the tip of a very large iceberg.”

He said this was the first attempt on a Canadian government website he had heard of, but added: “I certainly anticipate we’ll be hearing a lot more of this in the future.”

“This is the world we live in now,” Daley said, “and there’s no going back.”

San Francisco-based non-profit Transluce says AI agents, which can carry out tasks on their own, targeted the Library and Archives Canada website on May 28 and June 9. They appear to have been trying to dig up divorce records between 1905 and 1911.

content_blocks.alt: The Library and Archives Canada
content_blocks.caption: The Library and Archives Canada website, which AI agents tried to hack in May and June, according to research firm Transluce. (CTV News)

content_blocks.text: Of the nearly 900 requests captured by a Portuguese web archive, Transluce says 13 “carried attack payloads rather than ordinary queries.”
Those included SQL injection probes, a basic hacking technique that involves entering database commands into a search box in the hope the system will carry them out.

It’s not entirely clear which AI was used, or what exactly it was asked to accomplish. But Transluce says the tactics resemble those of agents it previously linked to OpenAI during the same period, though it stopped short of blaming the company.
In a statement, OpenAI said, “We’re reviewing these findings and have provided an initial briefing to Canadian officials conducting the government’s review.”
Mark Daley, chief AI officer at Western University in London, Ont., said the agent likely was not trying to cause harm.
“The agent is just like, ‘I have a job. I’m going to try to do the job,’” Daley told CTV News.
“It went beyond just a public search and tried to hack the website so it could get the information it wanted, but it wasn’t successful.”
Daley said that is what sets the agent’s behaviour apart from that of a normal person.

“A human would stop at the point where they couldn’t get that information. They wouldn’t try to hack the website,” he said. “The agent decided that the next most obvious thing to do is to hack the website.”

content_blocks.alt: Mark Daley
content_blocks.caption: Mark Daley, chief AI officer at Western University. (CTV News)

content_blocks.text: The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security said it is assessing the information. “There is no indication that government systems have been compromised at this time.”
It noted that public-facing government websites routinely receive automated and potentially malicious requests, which on their own do not indicate a successful cyber incident.
Canada’s AI minister, Evan Solomon, said Ottawa is still assessing what happened and promised to keep Canadians informed.
AI companies largely left to police themselves

The findings follow reports of AI agents unexpectedly breaching government and corporate systems. Australia recently said an OpenAI agent hacked into a government health data portal in June and accessed files. OpenAI apologized on Tuesday.

It also comes as AI companies are largely left to police themselves. Leaders of the biggest firms met with U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House this week and signed a voluntary accord on AI safety. Trump has refused to impose strict rules on the industry, saying they could help China win the AI race.
Daley believes rogue AI incidents now number in the hundreds “and probably that’s the tip of a very large iceberg.”
He said this was the first attempt on a Canadian government website he had heard of, but added: “I certainly anticipate we’ll be hearing a lot more of this in the future.”
“This is the world we live in now,” Daley said, “and there’s no going back.”

stories.title: Cleveland-Cliffs CEO questions logic of Ottawa potentially suing over Stelco layoffs
stories.summary: Lourenco Goncalves says legal action against the U.S. steelmaker makes no business sense, promises laid-off workers will be called back if the trade war ends soon
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CEO Lourenco Goncalves says Ottawa’s potential lawsuit against the American steelmaker for allegedly violating employment commitments in Canada makes no business sense, promising that laid-off workers will be called back if the trade war ends soon.

On Monday, the Cleveland-based steelmaker said it plans to lay off a total of up to 500 workers at Stelco’s Hamilton plant and its Lake Erie Works operation in Nanticoke, Ont. The company said the layoffs were necessary to ensure its survival during the conflict.

When the federal government approved Cliffs’ $3.4-billion acquisition of Stelco Holdings Inc. in 2024, it imposed a series of legally binding conditions, including maintaining for five years at least the same number of unionized employees in Canada, and the vast majority of non-unionized workers.

At the time, Stelco employed approximately 2,400 people in Hamilton and Nanticoke, according to data from Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, and that number remains roughly the same.

Now with hundreds of layoffs imminent, Prime Minister Mark Carney said that the government is considering legal action against Cliffs for not living up to its employment guarantees.

“The company made representations, and has legal obligations for employment,” Mr. Carney said in a news conference on Wednesday . “We intend to use all powers that we have, and pursue them to the fullest extent of the law.”

There is legal precedent that the government can look to as it weighs suing Cliffs. After U.S. Steel acquired Stelco in 2007, it made promises under the Investment Canada Act around jobs and production levels. The federal government later sued the company for allegedly reneging on its legally binding commitments.

A settlement was reached in 2011 , with the American steelmaker agreeing to new terms.

In an interview with The Globe and Mail on Thursday, Mr. Goncalves said that he takes the Prime Minister seriously. “He said that he will sue us. But is this a good business decision for Canada? I don’t think so.”

Two years ago, Mr. Goncalves said the Canadian government “rolled out the red carpet” for the company when it announced its intentions to buy Stelco.

“I believed in Stelco. I believed in Canada. I believed in the Usmca,” said Mr. Goncalves, referring to the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, which saw Canada and the U.S. trade tariff-free in steel.

But since then, the market has changed dramatically. Owing to the 50-per-cent tariffs imposed last year by U.S. President Donald Trump, Stelco can’t sell galvanized steel into the U.S. any more because the business is uneconomic.

“The underlying condition of the market changed a lot, and it was beyond my control,” he said.

Meanwhile, if a trade pact on steel between Canada and the U.S. is reached soon, Cliffs intends to recall all the laid-off workers, Mr. Goncalves said.

The federal government, however, has been critical of Cliffs’ decision not to accept financial aid that was on the table for the company’s Canadian operations.

Gabrielle Landry, deputy director, media relations with the Office of Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, told The Globe earlier this week that Cliffs’ decision was “extremely disappointing .”

Mr. Goncalves said he declined the government’s offer because it wouldn’t have addressed the root problem, comparing the situation to a doctor offering a sick patient cash instead of prescribing a drug to cure their illness.

Accepting money from Ottawa would have not made sense, he said, because the company had no need for it for operating or capital expenditures.

The medicine the company needs most, he said, is for Canada to reach an agreement with the U.S. that will see the steel tariffs reduced to 25 per cent, or lower, a level that would allow Stelco to once again compete in the U.S.

“I’m not asking for anything other than allow me to have a market to sell my galvanized steel,” he said. “That will resolve the problem.”

Mr. Carney made it clear on Wednesday that Mr. Goncalves’s public backing of Mr. Trump’s tariffs irked him, pointing out that he “applauded President Trump for putting those tariffs on.”

Indeed, the Brazilian-born Mr. Goncalves in a conference call last year thanked the Trump administration for having “the courage to implement these tariffs.”

But Mr. Goncalves said those comments shouldn’t be perceived as an attack on Canada, but rather as support for Mr. Trump’s policies to bolster the steel industry in the U.S., in part by cracking down on imports of cheap foreign steel.

Mr. Goncalves said he was in favour of a “Fortress North America” approach that would see the U.S., Canada and Mexico band together to keep out cheap imports and bring more jobs and investment back to North America.

The federal and provincial governments have rolled out multiple initiatives to help the domestic steel industry, including providing hundreds of millions of dollars in funding, most notably a $500-million loan to Algoma Steel Group Inc .

Ottawa has also aggressively cracked down on the dumping of foreign steel into Canada through the imposition of tariff-rate quotas and mandated that publicly funded projects use Canadian steel wherever possible.

Mr. Goncalves said the Canadian government’s various moves have helped Stelco compete far better in the hot rolled steel segment, but more needs to be done in the galvanized segment.

“In galvanized steel, we don’t have a business,” he said.

stories.title: London Food Bank marks 40 year anniversary with fall food drive amid unprecedented need
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: October 1, 2026 11:05 PM | Last Updated: October 1
stories.author: Matthew Trevithick
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: October 1, 2026 11:05 PM | Last Updated: October 1
Number of families visiting food bank monthly has doubled in five years, figures show
When the London Food Bank opened in October 1986, the thought was that it would only be temporary, and wound down within a handful of years.

That the food bank is still here 40 years later makes this month’s anniversary bittersweet, the agency’s executive directors say — a cause to celebrate the generosity of the community and its volunteers, but also reason to lament that its services are still needed.

“We didn’t think the need would grow like this,” said co-executive director Jane Roy. “When we first started it was 360 families a month, now we're up at 5,700 families a month. It's average Londoners. It's seniors. Kids. It’s all sorts of different folks.”
To help feed them, the food bank’s 38th annual
Thanksgiving Food Drive begins on Friday and ends on Oct. 12. Last year’s campaign secured over 56,000 kilograms of food for the food bank and the 34 other local agencies it supports.

Food can be dropped off at major grocery stores or the food bank, and donated money is used to buy food. Donations are vital for the food bank’s operations, which have helped more than 34,300 people this year, including a growing number working people and seniors.
“A volunteer talked to me about how a senior came recently and didn’t want their family knowing,” Roy said. “She was in tears … but she was concerned it would get out that she was coming for help.”

Demand for the food bank’s services shot up during the COVID-19 pandemic and has remained high amid a cost-of-living crisis driven by the high cost of housing, food and fuel, and a trade war with the U.S.
The agency had been helping around 3,400 families per month in the five years before the pandemic, and now routinely serves around 5,700 familes, or 17,000 individuals, figures show.

One in three local children is now considered food insecure, compared to one in six in 2022, which co-executive director Glen Pearson said was a level of need he never expected to see when the food bank launched.

“It's getting worse for reasons, and we as a food bank want to help lead and speak to those reasons,” Pearson said. “Everywhere we go to speak, they always say, ‘It's too bad we have to have a food bank.’ We have a food bank because people are making mistakes, especially at policy levels.
“We’re richer than we’ve ever been as a country ... And yet we have more homelessness than ever, more hunger than ever."
Roy says the food bank recorded a slight decrease in visits following the federal GST rebate top-up in June, and the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit in July.
“We see what government intervention does,” she said. “That little bit of extra money in the pocket, people use it. They don’t come here if they don’t absolutely need to.”
The London Food Bank isn’t alone, according to Carolyn Stewart, CEO of Feed Ontario, who says more than one million Ontarians accessed food banks nearly eight million times in the past year.
“We’re just continuously riding an increasing wave because we’re not dealing with the core issues that’s driving people there in the first place,” she said.
While food banks are filling a gap, Stewart said this can give the community and governments a false impression about the severity of the situation.
"Because this is unsustainable,” she said.
Food banks were meant to help people who fell on hard times get back on their feet in a matter of months, but many people now rely on the service from 18 months to two years, Stewart said.
Government benefit programs designed to help “are so archaic that they don’t really respond to the realities of today’s workers or unemployed,” she said.
Feed Ontario has called on the Ford government to increase the amount of money someone receiving Ontario Works can earn before that money is clawed back, from $200 to $600.
The Thanksgiving food drive comes during the city’s municipal election campaign, with voters heading to the polls Oct. 26.
Advance voting got underway Thursday.
Pearson expressed disappointment about a lack of attention to hunger in the race, noting that while most candidate platforms mentioned homelessness, none he saw mentioned food.

At the federal level, he says Ottawa has expressed interest in London having a commercial food hub or food terminal as part of a larger national food security strategy . The federal minister of agriculture and agri-food, Heath MacDonald, visited the food bank last month.
“Why doesn't London set that table? They don't have to put money to it, but they could draw together the players … What they do instead is blame the other level of government,” Pearson said.
“There's room for that, but really, if the politicians decided they wanted to build a hub here, they could do it, and then we could start digging out of our own problems.”
Information on how to donate to the food drive can be found on the
London Food Bank website .

stories.content:
| CBC News | Posted: October 1, 2026 11:05 PM | Last Updated: October 1

Number of families visiting food bank monthly has doubled in five years, figures show

When the London Food Bank opened in October 1986, the thought was that it would only be temporary, and wound down within a handful of years.

That the food bank is still here 40 years later makes this month’s anniversary bittersweet, the agency’s executive directors say — a cause to celebrate the generosity of the community and its volunteers, but also reason to lament that its services are still needed.

“We didn’t think the need would grow like this,” said co-executive director Jane Roy. “When we first started it was 360 families a month, now we're up at 5,700 families a month. It's average Londoners. It's seniors. Kids. It’s all sorts of different folks.”

To help feed them, the food bank’s 38th annual

Thanksgiving Food Drive begins on Friday and ends on Oct. 12. Last year’s campaign secured over 56,000 kilograms of food for the food bank and the 34 other local agencies it supports.

Food can be dropped off at major grocery stores or the food bank, and donated money is used to buy food. Donations are vital for the food bank’s operations, which have helped more than 34,300 people this year, including a growing number working people and seniors.

“A volunteer talked to me about how a senior came recently and didn’t want their family knowing,” Roy said. “She was in tears … but she was concerned it would get out that she was coming for help.”

Demand for the food bank’s services shot up during the COVID-19 pandemic and has remained high amid a cost-of-living crisis driven by the high cost of housing, food and fuel, and a trade war with the U.S.

The agency had been helping around 3,400 families per month in the five years before the pandemic, and now routinely serves around 5,700 familes, or 17,000 individuals, figures show.

One in three local children is now considered food insecure, compared to one in six in 2022, which co-executive director Glen Pearson said was a level of need he never expected to see when the food bank launched.

“It's getting worse for reasons, and we as a food bank want to help lead and speak to those reasons,” Pearson said. “Everywhere we go to speak, they always say, ‘It's too bad we have to have a food bank.’ We have a food bank because people are making mistakes, especially at policy levels.

“We’re richer than we’ve ever been as a country ... And yet we have more homelessness than ever, more hunger than ever."

Roy says the food bank recorded a slight decrease in visits following the federal GST rebate top-up in June, and the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit in July.

“We see what government intervention does,” she said. “That little bit of extra money in the pocket, people use it. They don’t come here if they don’t absolutely need to.”

The London Food Bank isn’t alone, according to Carolyn Stewart, CEO of Feed Ontario, who says more than one million Ontarians accessed food banks nearly eight million times in the past year.

“We’re just continuously riding an increasing wave because we’re not dealing with the core issues that’s driving people there in the first place,” she said.

While food banks are filling a gap, Stewart said this can give the community and governments a false impression about the severity of the situation.

"Because this is unsustainable,” she said.

Food banks were meant to help people who fell on hard times get back on their feet in a matter of months, but many people now rely on the service from 18 months to two years, Stewart said.

Government benefit programs designed to help “are so archaic that they don’t really respond to the realities of today’s workers or unemployed,” she said.

Feed Ontario has called on the Ford government to increase the amount of money someone receiving Ontario Works can earn before that money is clawed back, from $200 to $600.

The Thanksgiving food drive comes during the city’s municipal election campaign, with voters heading to the polls Oct. 26.

Advance voting got underway Thursday.

Pearson expressed disappointment about a lack of attention to hunger in the race, noting that while most candidate platforms mentioned homelessness, none he saw mentioned food.

At the federal level, he says Ottawa has expressed interest in London having a commercial food hub or food terminal as part of a larger national food security strategy . The federal minister of agriculture and agri-food, Heath MacDonald, visited the food bank last month.

“Why doesn't London set that table? They don't have to put money to it, but they could draw together the players … What they do instead is blame the other level of government,” Pearson said.

“There's room for that, but really, if the politicians decided they wanted to build a hub here, they could do it, and then we could start digging out of our own problems.”

Information on how to donate to the food drive can be found on the

London Food Bank website .

stories.title: Murder trial hears eyewitness and officer give graphic details of east end shooting
stories.summary: The jury at the second degree murder trial of Zachary McDermott heard from it’s first civilian witness on Thursday morning.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
The jury at the second degree murder trial of Zachary McDermott heard from it’s first civilian witness on Thursday morning.

Robert Dawson, 67, a retired trucker, testified that he was sitting in his car outside the Tim Hortons at 2094 Dundas St. E. on the afternoon of Sept. 12, 2018.

He said he saw the victim Christopher Clements-Card walking with his brother and then seconds later a car pulled into the parking lot saying, “He goes around the building and starts to shoot at the young lads.”

“I could see everything, there was nothing between me and the shooter,” Dawson said. “The shooter got into the car and left and then the one lad dragged his friend into the Tim Hortons.”

Later in the day the first officer to arrive at the scene took the stand and he testified about the chaotic and mess he came upon.

London Police Det.-Const. Evan Bertin told the court that when he walked into the coffee shop, “I saw the victim in a large pool of blood screaming that he had been shot….He kept saying he couldn’t breathe and that he was going to die.”

The officer said he started doing chest compressions until the ambulance arrived minutes later, “At that point he had lost vital signs.”

At the hospital the officer said family and friends of Clements-Card started arriving and he saw that, “They were yelling they wanted to see him...obviously they were very frantic.”

The victim was rushed into the operating room but would later be pronounced dead after suffering two gunshot wounds to the back.

Days later the accused, Zachary McDermott, 26, would be arrested and charged. He has plead not guilty to second degree murder.

The trial is expected to hear more testimony on Monday morning.

stories.title: Indigenous groups given just 2 months to consult on Pacific Link pipeline designation
stories.summary: The government said it will work over the next year to complete consultations on the project itself, and to secure environmental safeguards, financing and Indigenous partnerships.
stories.author: Alessia Passafiume
stories.content:
Indigenous communities along the route for the newly announced West Coast oil pipeline were given just two months for consultations on whether the pipeline should be designated a project of national interest — and that was still more than the government had planned.

At first, the consultations were to take place over one month. They were extended to two months after Indigenous leaders raised concerns about the tight timeline for the newly-named Pacific Link pipeline in Albryas.

A summary of those consultations posted online by the federal government says Indigenous groups decried a lack of information about the project, which they said prevented them from fully assessing its impact.

Prime Minister Mark Carney promised his major projects agenda would not interfere with Canada’s obligations under the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

Indigenous leaders have warned his government risks violating their rights with “national interest” designations through the Major Projects Office and the controversial Building Canada Act.

Carney said Thursday the pipeline has received the first national interest designation under that bill, which will streamline oversight and approvals.

The government said it will work over the coming year to complete consultations on the project itself, and to secure environmental safeguards, financing and Indigenous partnerships. It wants construction to begin in September 2027.

9:20 West Coast pipeline named Pacific Link as Carney, Smith outline path to construction

The Assembly of First Nations told The Canadian Press it has identified “many red flags” in the pipeline’s national interest designation and says the federal government appears to be predetermining outcomes and approving projects in advance of meaningful consultations.

“The government’s decision today is coming only 12 days after the consultation deadline. As we have said on many occasions, First Nations support economic development and prosperity for all, but not at the expense of our rights, the planet, and the government’s legal obligations to our people,” the statement says.

The United Nations declaration — which Canada adopted — outlines the need for free, prior and informed consent before decisions are made that could adversely affect the rights and lands of Indigenous communities and people. Indigenous communities also have recognized rights under Section 35 of the Constitution.

Get expert insights, Q&A on markets, housing, inflation, and personal finance information delivered to you every Saturday.

The UN declaration is cited in the pipeline consultation document, which says Ottawa’s engagement efforts were designed with those principles in mind.

The consultation document says more than 130 Indigenous communities could be affected by the pipeline route and the Major Projects Office sent a letter in July to those communities to begin consultations.

3:17 Carney vows B.C. and First Nations consultations on carbon pricing, pipeline

Indigenous communities warned during those consultations that their participation would be held back by summer harvesting, ceremonial gatherings and wildfires, which threatened many communities and forced evacuations.

The office then extended the consultation deadline from Aug. 28 to Sept. 18.

A senior government official, speaking with reporters ahead of Thursday’s announcement on the condition they not be named, said it’s likely the national interest designation will be challenged in court.

The document says the office held over 140 meetings with representatives from more than 110 Indigenous organizations and communities.

During those meetings, many community leaders said they lacked information they needed to make informed decisions — things like routing, engineering and design, environmental effects, marine shipping, emergency responses and impacts on Aboriginal and treaty rights.

Those concerns were cited both by communities that backed the project and those that didn’t.

1:51 First Nations blast engagement on pipeline

Despite the compressed timeline, the federal document says the Major Projects Office is satisfied that it has provided a meaningful opportunity for consultations, and that further questions can be addressed as they arise.

“The GIC is satisfied that these processes provide an appropriate framework through which potential adverse impacts on Aboriginal and treaty rights, including specific concerns already raised in consultation, can be further addressed before any final federal authorizations are issued,” the document says.

Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak has said staff in the Major Projects Office do not understand how to work with First Nations communities and that “junior staffers” aren’t helping to build relationships.

“They have a lot of work to do,” she told a news conference in Ottawa last week.

She also said CEO Dawn Farrell has been unavailable to meet with leadership, including at Assembly of First Nations gatherings.

Cold Lake First Nations Chief Kelsey Jacko said while Carney has talked about building a new relationship with First Nations and partnering on major projects development, the pipeline announcement Thursday does not reflect those intentions.

Jacko said that even though his territory is situated in the oilsands, it has been left out of discussions that could affect lands and treaty rights.

“Yesterday the Treaty 6 chiefs shared grand entry with the prime minister, and I spoke to him briefly and invited him again to our nation,” said Jacko, referring to Carney’s participation in an event to mark the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Wednesday.

“Today, the leaders of the Nations and communities that will be heavily impacted should have been in the room. This runs right through our territory.”

2:50 Majority of Canadians support Alberta pipeline to West Coast: internal government poll

Fort McKay First Nation Chief Raymond Powder said he was feeling both excited and concerned about the pipeline’s designation.

“We’re excited that we get the opportunity to be a participant on the equity stakeholders and also really, really seeing the area for Fort McKay First Nation to continue to sustain the growth in our nation,” he said after the announcement.

“The areas of concern, of course, is always the challenge of the ecosystems and really being harmonious with the environment and balancing with the economy.”

He said he has been working with the federal and provincial governments on the consultation process and described it as meaningful.

“We’ve had some respectful conversations,” he said.

“Of course there’s some complexities and some challenges and we’re really addressing those with the federal and provincial governments and my brothers and sisters in the five First Nations within this region.”

— With files from Nick Murray in Ottawa and Fakiha Baig in Fort McMurray, The Canadian Press
