stories.title: Pop visionary David Marsden created Canada’s first alternative music station
stories.summary: His format-free approach to programming at Cfny inspired the Rush song The Spirit of Radio, which the band’s lyricist Neil Peart said he wrote to ‘represent all that radio should be’
stories.author: Nicholas Jennings
stories.content:
Some of the world’s best radio disc jockeys are cultural tastemakers, influencing music and helping to break new genres. Others are colourful personalities who attract ardent listeners with distinctive wit and dazzling delivery.

David Marsden, a Canadian broadcasting legend who died on Sept. 25 at the age of 85, had all that and more.

Over the course of an illustrious 63-year career that took him from AM and FM outlets across Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia to Canada’s first online radio hub, with occasional forays into television, Mr. Marsden stood out as a brave pop visionary and professional shapeshifter, revered by colleagues and admired by everyone from rock heroes Rush to egghead Marshall McLuhan.

His first on-air persona was Dave Mickie, a motor-mouth DJ at Toronto’s Ckey in the early 1960s with an extraordinary 700-words-a-minute delivery that led Mr. McLuhan to devote a full chapter to him in his celebrated book Understanding Media: The Extensions of Man .

The esteemed philosopher transcribed some of Mickie’s frenetic patter (“That’s Patty Baby and that’s the girl with the dancing feet … in the night time ooohbah scubadoo how are you booboo”) and observed that he “alternately soars, groans, swings, sings, solos, intones and scampers, always reacting to his own actions.” Mr. McLuhan concluded that while Mickie’s chatter appeared nonsensical in print, it still functioned as a cohesive, engaging performance on radio.

“The medium was the message and, for a moment, the message was Dave Mickie,” noted broadcaster, musician and impresario Jaymz Bee, in one of many online tributes.

In the 1960s, he transformed from the babbling Dave Mickie to the slow-talking, intimate hipster David Marsden, his most famous persona. The long-haired, openly gay man loved pink Cadillacs and wild promotional schemes attracting new followers with his freeform, eclectic style at several prominent FM outlets. He found perhaps his greatest success at Cfny, in Brampton, Ont., where he served as DJ and program director and created Canada’s first alternative music station.

After hearing what Mr. Marsden imprinted on Cfny, Rush recorded one of its biggest hits, 1980s fan favourite The Spirit of Radio , a gumbo of reggae, pop and metal that drummer and lyricist Neil Peart said he wrote to “represent all that radio should be.” The song’s title was taken from Mr. Marsden’s slogan for the station.

After Mr. Marsden’s death, following complications from a fall, there was an outpouring of accolades on radio and social media. Many came from people who worked with him, praising his love of format-free radio and passion for new music.

Liz Janik, the “friendly voice” cited in the opening of Rush’s song, credits Mr. Marsden with creating more than just a team of DJs at Cfny but a “community of tastemakers, creators, dreamers, free-thinkers and real people who he encouraged to be themselves on air and connect with listeners.”

Ivar Hamilton, now executive producer of Cfny: The Spirit of Radio , one of two recent documentaries in which Mr. Marsden is featured, agrees. “He was a one-of-a-kind, magical personality who inspired creative expression right across the radio landscape,” Mr. Hamilton said. “With David, we weren’t following charts or formats – we were playing music we wanted to play, something he did his whole career.”

Under Mr. Marsden’s leadership, Cfny was among the first commercial stations to introduce U2, Talking Heads, Depeche Mode and the Stranglers, giving the station greater influence than others with similar ratings. And he was unwavering in his support for a wide range of Canadian acts, including Teenage Head, the Payola$, Jane Siberry and Messenjah.

According to music journalist and historian Michael Barclay, author of Have Not Been the Same: The CanRock Renaissance 1985-1995 , the man sometimes known as Marsbar changed the way people listen. “Marsden believed in the freedom of music,” said Mr. Barclay. “What he created and curated spread far beyond the streets of Toronto. I know stories of people from all corners of North America who would trade cassettes of Cfny shows as a lifeline to underground music at the time.”

“David was there when our first independent vinyl release was played and he never stopped bringing us forward to his listeners,” remembers Mark Gane, partner with Martha Johnson in art-pop pioneers Martha and the Muffins. “His influence cannot be overestimated.”

“He was the one who broke us,” states Carole Pope, of trailblazers Rough Trade. “If it wasn’t for him, there wouldn’t have been much punk or new wave on commercial airwaves. David was an innovator and everyone else a follower.”

Born on March 2, 1941 in Toronto, he was adopted at the age of 5 by a Scottish-Canadian family and raised in Stratford, Ont., as David Michie. Bitten by the music bug after seeing Elvis Presley on television at 14, he upset his strict, conservative parents when they discovered he had rented the local Ymca to DJ dances. Before long he was managing the Revols, a group of Stratford teenagers, including singer-keyboardist Richard Manuel, later a founding member of the Band.

Dreaming of a life in radio, he changed his surname to Mickie and applied to over 30 stations, eventually finding work at Cfco in Chatham, Ont. By 1963, he had landed at Ckey, where his hyperactive style got him dubbed “the most controversial thing on Toronto radio.” Ken Stowar, now program director at Toronto’s Ciut-FM, remembers seeing Dave Mickie at Scarborough’s Cedarbrae Plaza. “There he was in a gold lamé jacket and speaking in his fast, outrageous manner,” Mr. Stowar recalled. “I was hooked.”

Two years later, Mr. Marsden was hosting both CBC-TV’s Music Hop , succeeding Alex Trebek, and his own Mickie a Go Go show on Hamilton’s Chch-TV. When the Rolling Stones first performed in Toronto, Mr. Marsden was the concert’s emcee and did a TV interview with the band because, as he later explained, “no one else wanted to do it because they said the Stones were dirty and didn’t bathe.” After the show, some of the Stones and opening act the McCoys partied at his home, which Mr. Marsden admitted “got a little out of hand.”

He moved to Montreal in 1967, working at Ckgm and later its progressive rock FM sister station Chom. There, he broadcast for the first time as David Marsden, a variation on Marston, his birth mother Mildred Levie’s married name and the spelling of front man Gerry Marsden, of Merseybeat group Gerry & the Pacemakers. At Chom, he began experimenting with programming, spinning a mix of blues, rock, folk and jazz recordings that baffled his colleagues. But he found his audience and was soon on air six nights a week, at the very moment stereo FM became the music frequency of choice.

By 1973, Mr. Marsden had returned to Toronto and joined Chum-FM, where he expanded his mind-bending approach to music programming. There, he was the first DJ to play Rush’s self-titled debut. He persuaded concert promoters to book Pink Floyd at Maple Leaf Gardens and leaked an advance copy of the English band’s Dark Side of the Moon , cheekily playing the album in its entirety in advance of a planned promotional premiere. Mr. Marsden was also the first DJ in North America to play the Genesis album The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway . “David played the whole record,” Mr. Hamilton said, “and liked it so much that he played the album all the way through a second time.”

During his time at Chum-FM, Mr. Marsden delighted listeners with engagingly fanciful storytelling – what he called his “theatre of the imagination” – as much as his daring music choices. And he invented contests, with unnamed prizes he offered to winning callers in a brown paper bag. Although no one knew what would be in the bag – albums, concert tickets, drugs or a head of lettuce – the mystery worked and another form of Marsden magic became the talk of the town.

The Globe and Mail’s Robert Martin described Mr. Marsden’s on-air personality as that of the “weird but hip music freak who talked in an intimate hush as though whispering in the listener’s ear.” Added Mr. Martin: “The music he played matched that personality, usually on the avant-garde fringes of rock.”

Mr. Marsden quit Chum-FM the day his boss handed him a playlist. “For four years, I had total freedom to play the music I loved, whatever I wanted,” he recalled. “Total freedom, until it wasn’t.” As part of the team launching Cfny in 1977, Mr. Marsden brought his trippy humour and fully baked freeform programming ideas to the station. After becoming program director, he oversaw a rogue’s gallery of popular DJs including Ms. Janik, Mr. Hamilton, Allnite André, Live Earl Jive, Pete and Geets, James Scott, Brad McNally and Deadly Hedley Jones.

Always thinking big, Mr. Marsden introduced new contests and promotional ventures. With Cfny’s promise never to play the same song twice within 48 hours, he launched “Catch Us If You Can,” where the station would send $102 (Cfny’s broadcast frequency number) to any listener who caught them breaking the rule. More ambitiously, in 1981, Mr. Marsden unveiled the U-Knows, an irreverent alternative to the Junos. By 1985, the show had grown into the Casby (“Canadian Artists Selected By You”) Awards and for the next three years, was televised on CBC, giving Cfny a profile far beyond its broadcast reach.

One of Canada’s first openly gay media personalities, Mr. Marsden came out on air after the station spoke out against the 1981 Toronto Bathhouse Raids. And he regularly stepped out of the studio to spin music, running his signature “The Mars Bar” at local gay nightclubs.

In 1987, Mr. Marsden took his Spirit of Radio dreams to Vancouver. He created Pilot One , a CBC-TV series that mixed music, comedy and interviews, hiring writers like Chris Houston, of punk rockers the Forgotten Rebels, and sex educator Sue Johanson. He then joined Vancouver’s AM station Ckst and oversaw its switch as Coast 800 to a modern rock format. But, ultimately, it failed to match Cfny’s success.

Never resting, Mr. Marsden became a pioneer in streaming radio. He returned to Toronto in 1999 to launch Iceberg Media, a platform with over 100 channels of various genres which Standard Broadcasting later bought and transitioned to satellite radio. He started his final adventure in radio at 73, with the subscription-based internet station NYTheSpirit.com which, following Mr. Marsden’s death, promises to keep its founder’s unique programming style alive.

“There was really no one quite like David,” Ms. Pope concluded, “an outrageous character with a warm, kind and slightly insane personality who just loved music and supporting artists. And in the music business, that is a very rare quality.”

You can find more obituaries from The Globe and Mail here .

To submit a memory about someone we have recently profiled on the Obituaries page, e-mail us at obit@globeandmail.com .

Although no one knew what would be in the bag – albums, concert tickets, drugs or a head of lettuce – the mystery worked and another form of Marsden magic became the talk of the town.

The Globe and Mail’s Robert Martin described Mr. Marsden’s on-air personality as that of the “weird but hip music freak who talked in an intimate hush as though whispering in the listener’s ear.” Added Mr. Martin: “The music he played matched that personality, usually on the avant-garde fringes of rock.”

Mr. Marsden quit Chum-FM the day his boss handed him a playlist. “For four years, I had total freedom to play the music I loved, whatever I wanted,” he recalled. “Total freedom, until it wasn’t.” As part of the team launching Cfny in 1977, Mr. Marsden brought his trippy humour and fully baked freeform programming ideas to the station. After becoming program director, he oversaw a rogue’s gallery of popular DJs including Ms. Janik, Mr. Hamilton, Allnite André, Live Earl Jive, Pete and Geets, James Scott, Brad McNally and Deadly Hedley Jones.

Always thinking big, Mr. Marsden introduced new contests and promotional ventures. With Cfny’s promise never to play the same song twice within 48 hours, he launched “Catch Us If You Can,” where the station would send $102 (Cfny’s broadcast frequency number) to any listener who caught them breaking the rule. More ambitiously, in 1981, Mr. Marsden unveiled the U-Knows, an irreverent alternative to the Junos. By 1985, the show had grown into the Casby (“Canadian Artists Selected By You”) Awards and for the next three years, was televised on CBC, giving Cfny a profile far beyond its broadcast reach.

One of Canada’s first openly gay media personalities, Mr. Marsden came out on air after the station spoke out against the 1981 Toronto Bathhouse Raids. And he regularly stepped out of the studio to spin music, running his signature “The Mars Bar” at local gay nightclubs.

In 1987, Mr. Marsden took his Spirit of Radio dreams to Vancouver. He created Pilot One , a CBC-TV series that mixed music, comedy and interviews, hiring writers like Chris Houston, of punk rockers the Forgotten Rebels, and sex educator Sue Johanson. He then joined Vancouver’s AM station Ckst and oversaw its switch as Coast 800 to a modern rock format. But, ultimately, it failed to match Cfny’s success.

Never resting, Mr. Marsden became a pioneer in streaming radio. He returned to Toronto in 1999 to launch Iceberg Media, a platform with over 100 channels of various genres which Standard Broadcasting later bought and transitioned to satellite radio. He started his final adventure in radio at 73, with the subscription-based internet station NYTheSpirit.com which, following Mr. Marsden’s death, promises to keep its founder’s unique programming style alive.

“There was really no one quite like David,” Ms. Pope concluded, “an outrageous character with a warm, kind and slightly insane personality who just loved music and supporting artists. And in the music business, that is a very rare quality.”

content_blocks.text: David Marsden, a Canadian broadcasting legend who died on Sept. 25 at the age of 85, had all that and more.

content_blocks.text: Over the course of an illustrious 63-year career that took him from AM and FM outlets across Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia to Canada’s first online radio hub, with occasional forays into television, Mr. Marsden stood out as a brave pop visionary and professional shapeshifter, revered by colleagues and admired by everyone from rock heroes Rush to egghead Marshall McLuhan.

content_blocks.text: His first on-air persona was Dave Mickie, a motor-mouth DJ at Toronto’s Ckey in the early 1960s with an extraordinary 700-words-a-minute delivery that led Mr. McLuhan to devote a full chapter to him in his celebrated book Understanding Media: The Extensions of Man .

content_blocks.text: The esteemed philosopher transcribed some of Mickie’s frenetic patter (“That’s Patty Baby and that’s the girl with the dancing feet … in the night time ooohbah scubadoo how are you booboo”) and observed that he “alternately soars, groans, swings, sings, solos, intones and scampers, always reacting to his own actions.” Mr. McLuhan concluded that while Mickie’s chatter appeared nonsensical in print, it still functioned as a cohesive, engaging performance on radio.

content_blocks.text: “The medium was the message and, for a moment, the message was Dave Mickie,” noted broadcaster, musician and impresario Jaymz Bee, in one of many online tributes.

content_blocks.text: In the 1960s, he transformed from the babbling Dave Mickie to the slow-talking, intimate hipster David Marsden, his most famous persona. The long-haired, openly gay man loved pink Cadillacs and wild promotional schemes attracting new followers with his freeform, eclectic style at several prominent FM outlets. He found perhaps his greatest success at Cfny, in Brampton, Ont., where he served as DJ and program director and created Canada’s first alternative music station.

He found perhaps his greatest success at CFNY, in Brampton, Ont., where he served as DJ and program director and created Canada’s first alternative music station.

content_blocks.text: After hearing what Mr. Marsden imprinted on Cfny, Rush recorded one of its biggest hits, 1980s fan favourite The Spirit of Radio , a gumbo of reggae, pop and metal that drummer and lyricist Neil Peart said he wrote to “represent all that radio should be.” The song’s title was taken from Mr. Marsden’s slogan for the station.

content_blocks.text: Liz Janik, the “friendly voice” cited in the opening of Rush’s song, credits Mr. Marsden with creating more than just a team of DJs at Cfny but a “community of tastemakers, creators, dreamers, free-thinkers and real people who he encouraged to be themselves on air and connect with listeners.”

stories.title: Former chief coroner Lisa Lapointe to run for B.C. Greens
stories.summary: Lapointe and the party will ‘put an end to the failures’ behind the overdose crisis, Green leader Emily Lowan says
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The British Columbia Green Party has named former chief coroner Lisa Lapointe as the party’s candidate in the riding of Saanich South on Vancouver Island.

Leader Emily Lowan announced Lapointe’s candidacy as the party unveiled its toxic drugs policy on Thursday.

Lowan says the overdose crisis kills many British Columbians each day, and front-line workers bear the brunt of a “politicized” system that has failed to solve the problem.

She says Lapointe and the party will “put an end to the failures” behind the crisis that has killed thousands of people since the province declared a public health emergency in April 2016.

Lapointe says the crisis can only be solved when politicians are willing to show leadership, when voluntary treatment and regulated alternative drugs are available, and when those who use drugs have the same access to resources as anyone else.

She will go up against the Ndp’s Richard Zussman, a former TV journalist turned lobbyist, and the Conservatives’ Cathie Ounsted, who served on the Central Saanich Police Board and the board of directors of the Victoria Airport Authority.

stories.title: Indigenous art installation stolen on Truth and Reconciliation Day
stories.summary: Four indigenous pieces of outdoor art, representing the four elements are missing Thursday night, after a local artist’s truck was stolen overnight in Brampton.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Four indigenous pieces of outdoor art, representing the four elements are missing Thursday night, after a local artist’s truck was stolen overnight in Brampton.

“We had all the art panels in the bed of the truck. We went to the hotel at 9 p.m., and the truck was still there. 7 a.m. we woke up and the truck was gone, and the art panels that were in the truck were gone, as well,” said Saugeen First Nation based artist Jeannette Ladd.

Ladd and her father were in Brampton preparing the landscaping, and layout at a Brampton park for the installation of her art project, the four large wood panels that took six months to create.

“I was in shock. My father and I have put a lot of time and energy into these panels. All the steel to connect them, to make sure that they stay in the ground, was all in the truck already, all ready to go. So, it’s a little bit frustrating, and I’m a little bit saddened and heartbroken about the whole thing,” said Ladd, who lives near Oliphant.

Making the theft sting even more, it happened on Truth and Reconciliation Day.

“Yesterday was Truth and Reconciliation. And, I know that they probably didn’t know that those panels were in the back of the truck, but, you know, they mean a lot to me. So I’m just hoping that someone finds them, and returns them, and they will go up in their spot, within one of the parks in Brampton,” said Ladd.

Ladd, who just unveiled seven paintings at Western’s Thames Hall last week, is on her way home on the Saugeen First Nation tonight, without her family’s 2023 brown Toyota Tundra, and without her art that would take months to try and recreate.

stories.title: Canada Rocket Company breaks ground at $30M test facility in London, Ont.
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: October 1, 2026 9:20 PM | Last Updated: 20 hours ago
stories.author: Jack Sutton
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: October 1, 2026 9:20 PM | Last Updated: October 1
Canada Rocket Company is building its new Jeremy Hansen Test Facility near the London airport
London, Ont., will be home to Canada's first large-scale rocket engine test facility as the country looks towards establishing Canadian launch capabilities.

On Thursday, Canada Rocket Company (CRC), founded in 2025, officially broke ground at the project site east of London International Airport, where the $30 million Jeremy Hansen Test Facility — named after the Canadian astronaut from London — is expected to be fully operational by 2028.

As part of Canada's 2026 Defence Industrial Strategy, space, including domestic launch capabilities, was identified as a high-value sector, and Crc's co-founder Hugh Kolias said that was the "trigger point" to start the company.
"Without that signaling from the federal government, none of this would have been possible," he said. "It's a key reason why we're standing here today"

With the help of $8.3 million in funding from the Department of National Defence, CRC will be using its new London facility to help develop and test a reusable, medium lift rocket that can carry up to 12,500 kilograms into orbit powered by its own methalox engine, the E-1.

The London facility, built on land leased from the Greater London Airport Authority on Nissouri Road, will not be used to launch rockets. The engine testing will be static, with up to three vertical and horizontal test stands capable of holding engines with more than one meganewton in thrust — a level of force similar to the Merlin 1D engines used on SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets.
The site will include a 12,000 square-foot office and shop building, housing a fabrication area for engineering, assembly and test preparation.

In total, CRC is expected to create about 40 full-time jobs in London, including engineers, technicians and co-ops, according to Kolias, and will help support Crc's broader rocket program, which the company projects will create
1,000 jobs across the country and more than $1 billion in new investment over the next decade.
The rocket testing facility is a "catalyst" according to London Mayor Josh Morgan, that builds on the vision of London as a bold and innovative partner in the future of the country.

"We are here to be a part of this," he said. "We're here to create jobs in our city, we're here to create innovation, and we're here to be part of Canada's future, especially as we move toward our own space independence and independent launch capacity"
"This is a very exciting day for London, Ontario and Canada."

Speaking to Crc's decision to make London the home of its new facility, Kolias pointed to the city's manufacturing history, talent and ambition, with more than 40 defence and aerospace companies already operating in the area.
A rocket test site is something that has never existed in Canada, he said, and many communities would turn down the opportunity because it "just seems a little too difficult."
Kolias said it was clear the London community was on board from Crc's first interaction with the city.

"Everyone was so excited at the opportunity and everyone really understood how important it was, not just for the community from an economic development perspective, but also for the country," he said.

stories.title: Narrowed rebate eligibility leaves some Nova Scotians worried about heating costs
stories.summary: As colder temperatures approach, some in Nova Scotia are raising concerns over heating costs and questioning the adequacy of the province's assistance rebate program.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Mitchell Bailey
stories.content:
As colder temperatures approach, some in Nova Scotia are raising concerns over heating costs and questioning the adequacy of the province’s assistance rebate program.

Halifax resident Miriam Williams has previously qualified for the Heating Assistance Rebate Program (Harp), but no longer does because of changing criteria.

“In a word, it’s unacceptable,” said Williams, who is also a leader with the tenant advocacy group, Acorn.

“This is not a handout by any means. This is just something that helps people get by.”

The program, which opened for applications Thursday for this season, offers eligible households up to $400.

Eligibility this year requires one of the following criteria:

have a 2025 net income of $30,000 or less and live alone with no kids or dependents

have a combined 2025 net household income of $45,000 or less and live with kids, dependents or other adults (to qualify as a single parent, you need to receive the Canada Child Benefit)

receive Income Assistance from the Department of Opportunities and Social Development

receive the Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS) or the Allowance from Service Canada

In past years, the province had expanded eligibility and raised the rebate value.

But the government made cuts last year, lowering the net income threshold for a family to qualify from $70,000 to $45,000, and lowering an individual’s threshold from $55,000 to $30,000.

A government news release at the time said 118,287 applicants received the rebate in the previous fiscal year at a cost of $71 million, while as many as 72,000 households were expected to be helped in 2025-26 at a cost of $32 million.

In a statement Thursday, the Ndp’s critic for Service Nova Scotia, Susan Leblanc, called on the Houston government to reverse changes to Harp.

“Last year, 64,000 Nova Scotians struggling to afford their heating costs were denied Harp because the Houston government changed the rules to make them ineligible,” she said.

“Those who could still qualify got $200 less. The department then left a third of its Harp budget unspent – money that could have made a real difference to the thousands of Nova Scotians who depend on this help.”

The NDP points out that the cost of heating oil has risen by 47 per cent since last year.

For Williams, she’s anticipating a tough winter ahead for herself and her neighbours.

“Most people that I know who live even just in this neighbourhood are about one bad paycheque away from losing everything. That’s a scary and stressful way to live,” she said.

The Parker Street Food and Furniture Bank’s director, Shelley Rose, says there’s now higher demand for her organization’s emergency assistance program.

That program has seen a 25 per cent annual increase in heating cost supports.

“What we hear all the time is just everything is so expensive,” said Rose.

“We are seeing an uptick in the amount of people that we are trying to help because people who would have had that rebate before don’t have it and need that extra help.”

And experts say Nova Scotia has one of the highest energy poverty rates in the country, which worsens an already difficult situation.

“Renters are struggling the most because they are paying for the heat and electricity, but they can’t choose how to upgrade or have little or no control (over) their heating system,” said Juli Bishwokarma, the Ecology Action Centre’s energy coordinator.

In a statement, Minister of Service Nova Scotia Jill Balser said she appreciates the financial pressures Nova Scotians face and that the $400 rebate will help with home heating costs alongside other government measures.

“Each year we look to deliver a program that can help as many people as we can with the resources we have. Our budget this year is just over $33 million at a time when the province is managing a $1.4 billion deficit,” she said.

“We will do more when we have more which is why it’s so important that we continue to work to create good jobs, grow the economy so we can maintain and strengthen programs like Harp.”

But Williams believes more should be done.

“ Every penny counts in this economy. And the threshold being lowered even more is simply excluding families that still dearly need this,” she said.

“A household with two income earners will blow past that cap (of $400) in a matter of weeks … They really require this benefit to make it through the winter.”

stories.title: Ground broken on $30 million rocket test facility at London Airport
stories.summary: It’s a big step for science, but a giant leap for London’s entry into the rocket building business. The Canada Rocket Company (CRC) on Thursday announced plans for a $30 million rocket engine test facility at the London International Airport.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
It’s a big step for science, but a giant leap for London’s entry into the rocket building business. The Canada Rocket Company (CRC) on Thursday announced plans for a $30 million rocket engine test facility at the London International Airport.

It means Canada May no longer have to rely on other countries’ rockets to get satellites into space.

Vic Fidelli, Ontario’s Minister of Economic Development remarked, “We’re in the middle of a trade war.” Fideli was on hand as ground was broken on Canada’s first such facility.

“Companies opening. Companies expanding. Companies digging in the middle of the field of dreams here. All at a time when our sovereignty continues to be challenged,” Fideli continued.

Named after London born astronaut Jeremy Hansen, the $30 million facility will allow the company to conduct static testing of rocket engines for its reusable, medium-lift rocket, explained CRC co-founder and CEO, Hugh Kolias.

“We’re building what we’re calling the R2. It can take up to 12,500 kilograms to low-earth orbit. Similar in size to SpaceX Falcon9. So, there’ll be nine engines on the first stage, one engine on the second stage, so 10 engines in total. And we’re looking to launch up to once a week, once we get the full cadence,” he said.

According to CRC, almost every satellite in the world gets to space on a rocket. And currently, most of them are transported by SpaceX’s Falcon9.

And those satellites run everything, from GPS to weather forecasts, from communications to emergency response. And right now, Canada is entirely dependent on other countries’ rockets.

CRC says it expects to create about 40 skilled jobs at the London facility in the next 18 months, with a broader rocket development program projected to create 1,000 jobs, and more than $1 billion in new investment over the next decade.

CRC is also developing training partnerships with Western University and Fanshawe College.

“We already have some amazing space scientists. So, we have engineers, astrophysicists, planetary scientists. So, we already have a really great space community. And adding in the rocket science, definitely very exciting,” exclaimed Sarah Gallagher, Director of the Institute of Earth and Space Exploration.

The CRC facility is funded in part by $8.3 million from the Department of National Defence’s IDEaS Program.

There are currently more than 40 defence and aerospace companies already operating in the London region.

“This is certainly a sector that is poised for significant growth going forward,” said Kapil Lakhotia, President and CEO of the London Economic Development Corporation. “Especially when we take our cues from the federal government, that’s investing more in defence and aviation projects as well,” he said.

The facility is expected to be fully operational in 2028.

stories.title: Parole board revokes statutory release for convicted killer Shawn Lamb
stories.summary: Convicted killer Shawn Lamb has had his statutory release revoked by the Parole Board of Canada for breaching his conditions.
stories.author: Marney Blunt
stories.content:
Convicted killer Shawn Lamb has had his statutory release revoked for breaching his conditions.

Lamb, 66, was charged in June 2012 with second degree murder in the deaths of three indigenous women; Lorna Blacksmith, Carolyn Sinclair, and Tanya Nepinak.

In 2013, Lamb pleaded guilty to two counts of manslaughter in the deaths of Blacksmith and Sinclair, while the charge in the death of Nepinak was stayed. Nepinak’s remains have never been found and are believed to be in the Brady Road landfill.

Lamb was sentenced in November 2013 to 20 years in prison, with credit for two years of time served in remand custody. In November 2025, he was granted statutory release, which allows federal offenders who have served two-thirds of their sentence to be released from prison under supervision. In Canada, statutory release is required by law for most federal offenders, with the exception of those serving life sentences. Lamb is now back in custody until either a new release is ordered or he reaches his next statutory release date, according to the parole board.

A written decision by the Parole Board of Canada indicated that Lamb was exhibiting positive behaviour when he first entered a community-based residential facility, or halfway house. But his behaviour started to deteriorate in March 2026, the document read.

The document stated Lamb expressed interest in volunteering with homeless encampments, but was unable to find an agency to support the work. He also tried to volunteer at a local hospital but was ineligible.

“You began “volunteering” on your own, pushing people around the hospital in their wheelchairs,” the document read. “You were directed to cease “volunteering” immediately and to report any relationships you had made within the hospital.”

The document says Lamb eventually found volunteer work at a local church.

The board says in May 2026, Lamb made numerous breaches of his conditions. It says Lamb signed out of the halfway house to go to Walmart and a pharmacy, but police observed him walking around downtown, going into an apartment, and handing unknown people small plastic bags with a white substance in it and the people giving him cash in return. Staff at the halfway house had reported that multiple people, including women, had come to the halfway house asking for Lamb.

As a result, a warrant was issued for Lamb’s arrest.

“Upon your arrest, you were in possession of $500 cash,” it read. “Although police had strong evidence of you trafficking (including images of hand-to-hand transactions), additional charges are not being pursued at this time as you were not arrested with drugs on your person.”

The parole board document says Lamb’s room was searched and officers found an additional cell phone, loose Tylenol 3 pills, a bag containing receipts from a motel for about $350, condoms in multiple locations throughout the room, multiple receipts for a storage unit totalling $4,000, and an envelope with photos of nude women.

Lamb denied selling drugs to his parole officer, telling the officer he might have been walking around handing out cigarettes, money, and gift cards to the homeless population downtown, and that some of the homeless community members had been giving him Apple gift cards in return.

“In speaking with the Board, you denied drug trafficking, rationalizing that if you were in the possession of drugs, you would have had no control and used them yourself,” it read. “Your sublocade regimen however would have an impact on that claim.”

The board also said Lamb made cryptic comments that suggest he met a woman at a hotel for sex.

“You have a report relationships condition, and this would be a notable breach, and exceptionally aggravating, as it reflects the vulnerability of your choice of victims. Your criminal conviction history reflects sexual assault and extreme violence. The nude photos of females in your possession, and second phone, indicate that your sexual preoccupation continues and this is also risk elevating to the community,” the document stated.

“The (prior) offences caused death, and it is apparent that you have returned to your offence cycle. The fact that these actions are post sex offender programming and do not align with your healing path, are very concerning.”

“Your actions are not beyond your control, yet you continue to willfully make poor decisions that place the public at risk.”

Family reaction

Sue Caribou, Tanya Nepinak’s aunt, says she was pleased to hear his release was revoked, but feels Lamb should have never been released in the first place.

“How can you trust somebody that took lives and put him back on the street?” Caribou said.

“He was back to his old self, and then denying all of these things.”

Cairbou says hearing his name brings her family a great deal of pain.

“Shawn Lamb is a monster that should be left to rot in jail,” Caribou said. “He took so many beautiful women and so many of us are still carrying that hurt.”

stories.title: Montreal jewellery designer Roger Lucas was known as Lord of the Rings
stories.summary: The son of a master jeweller, he rebelled against the conventions of the craft and set out to realize his own bold, new vision
stories.author: Fred Langan
stories.content:
Roger Lucas was a Montreal jeweller who made dazzling golden rings that ended up on famous fingers and in exhibits at museums in Europe and the United States.

The singer Aretha Franklin was often photographed wearing a ring Mr. Lucas made. “It was a huge rectangle of gold with a series of diamonds and she used to say it was her favourite piece of jewellery,” said Philippe Lucas, the jeweller’s nephew, who is an academic living in Victoria, and a keen family historian.

At the peak of his career, he was known as Lord of the Rings.

Roger Lucas, who has died at the age of 89, was from a family of jewellers. His father, Gabriel Lucas, was born in France in 1904 and came to Canada in the late 1920s as a master jeweller. In Montreal, he opened Gabriel Lucas Joailliers, ON Sherbrooke Street in the 1930s; he also met and married Mercedes Dorion.

Their first son, Roger, was born in Montreal on Oct. 3, 1936, and he grew up in the inner-Montreal suburb of Outremont, the francophone equivalent of anglo Westmount on the other side of Mount Royal. The couple had two more children, Michel and Danielle. Roger went to a private school in Outremont but from the age of 12 he wanted to be a jeweller and was in effect apprenticed to his father. At 15 he went to Paris to study at the École des arts décoratifs.

He then started working in a Cartier workshop in Monte Carlo, in Monaco. By the time he was 21 he was its foreman. He would have a long association with the storied French jewellery house.

Roger returned to Montreal to work with his father, Gabriel, whose store was next door to Brisson and Brisson, an exclusive men’s clothing store where Pierre Trudeau shopped.

Roger Lucas was a glamorous figure with movie-star looks who raced motorcycles in Europe, though he gave that up after a spectacular crash, and owned rare cars, including a Jaguar D-type (a racing model than evolved into the classic Jaguar E-type). He sold his Jaguar after owning it for only a few years. “Selling the D-type was one of the regrets of his life. He sold it for about $5,000,” his stepson, Christian d’Auteuil, said. A similar car sold this year in Zurich for US$6.43-million ($9-million).

“He lived his life as a rebel,” Philippe Lucas said. “When he was in his early 20s, he was running a Cartier atelier in Europe and on the weekends winning motorcycle races. It was the kind of life that is so exotic that it’s really hard to imagine”

Roger and his father, Gabriel, were men of great talents and even greater egos.

“My father is a dominating person like me,” Roger told the Montreal Star in 1972. “He likes to run a one man show.” He went on to say that they clashed on design ideas because he thought his father’s work was too conventional.

“My father won top prizes but he was passé for me,” Roger told the Montreal Star for a letter article. “He was a classical designer working with gems set in platinum. His jewellery were status symbols and not designed to be worn for sheer pleasure and enjoyment. I got very restless.”

The battle between father and son ended with a takeover of the business. The other partner was Lucas’s brother, Michel, who handled the financial aspects of the operation.

“He and my uncle Roger ultimately bought out my grandfather, Gabriel, in 1968 with Charles Bronfman as a silent partner,” Philippe Lucas said.

Roger and Michel Lucas wanted to appeal to a younger audience. They even unlocked the front door to the shop to make it appear more accessible.

“Both [Roger and Michel Lucas] wanted to make this long-standing enterprise appeal to a younger audience,” wrote the curator to a Cincinnati Art Museum exhibition of his work in 2021. “Roger, the designer, artist, and more avant-garde of the two, was particularly interested in promoting a jewellery-as-art concept. Roger’s ambition was to gain an international reputation as an innovative jeweller.

“Roger Lucas created one-of-a-kind pieces with a timeless quality, and although precious stones were sometimes incorporated, he considered his jewellery artwork, not investments. Thinking of himself as a designer first, a jeweller second, he approached his rings as art objects and . . . described these pieces as sculpture for the hand.”

One of his specialties was designing a style of ring that would encompass two or even three fingers, slipping over the middle finger and the fingers on either side as well. While that concept did not catch on, Mr. Lucas demonstrated his eye for trends when he told a reporter in Boston in 1969 that men would soon be wearing earrings. He was right.

Roger Lucas designed more than 90 per cent of the jewellery sold in his store. Above the shop was an atelier , or workshop, where 50 jewellers worked to produce his designs. According to a 1969 article in the Montreal Gazette, which included a photo showing a small army of jewellers at work, he was operating the largest jewellery factory in Canada at that time.

The Lucas brothers expanded into Europe and the United States. Roger Lucas was on the road, promoting his creations from Monte Carlo to Chicago.

“The U.S. is the largest moneymaker,” he told the Montreal Star. “The biggest business is in Dallas, Houston and Chicago.”

There was also an exhibit of his work in New York in 1969.

“[It is] wearable, contemporary design, but with a background of craftsmanship, history and culture, that’s why we like the work of Roger Lucas,” said Joseph Liebman, president of Cartier at the opening of the Roger Lucas exhibition of boutique jewellery in New York, according to an article by Keitha McLean in the Montreal Star in October of 1969.

For a while Mr. Lucas operated a boutique in Tokyo.

He made most of his rings out of gold, often incorporating semi-precious stones, such as lapis lazuli. “Most people start by buying diamonds and then they begin to enjoy the colours. Of course, they are a little bit harder to wear, they must fit the ensemble,” Mr. Lucas told The Globe and Mail in 1991. “Wear your rings by day and let them watch over you from your table at night.”

One of his designs for Cartier, from his Astronaut Series, inspired by the 1969 moon landing, features a round sphere of gold, meant to be the moon, with craters filled with precious and semi-precious stones.

“I discovered Roger’s work by collecting pieces signed ‘Lucas.’ I was drawn to them for their sculptural beauty,” said Kimberly Klosterman, a collector based in Cincinnati, Ohio, and Hudson, N.Y. The Lucas pieces in her collection were part of an exhibit at the Cincinnati Art Museum.

“It was only after I made the research that I discovered Roger the man. His one-of-a-kind jewellery resonated with me. I am happy he can live on through his beautiful work.”

Along with being exhibited at the Cincinnati Art Museum exhibition Simply Brilliant, which ran from 2021 to 2022, Mr. Lucas’s work was also shown at museums in Belgium and Germany.

Mr. Lucas sold the family business in 1975 and he was then semi-retired, spending time on his sailboat in the Caribbean. He was an accomplished scuba diver and would often dive for samples of corals that he could use in jewellery.

His retirement lasted only a few years. He returned to Montreal and among other things designed jewellery for Henry Birks and Sons, the retail luxury-goods chain.

After that he continued to design jewellery at a studio in his house. In the late 1990s he designed a coin for the Royal Canadian Mint. He split his time between Montreal and Sainte-Adèle in the Laurentians, north of Montreal.

“Roger was very outgoing,” said his stepson, Christian d’Auteuil, with whom he was close. “He loved to be the centre of the party but at the same time he made you feel like you were the most important person in the room. He always loved to tell stories and we teased him because he would embellish stories a little bit.”

Roger Lucas’s nephew says part of the designer’s legacy was the fact that his designs found their way to more people than just the richest customers.

“I remember always hearing from fans of Lucas Jewellers what it was like when a wife or a mother would come down at Christmas and see the Lucas wrapping paper and the Lucas ribbons under the Christmas tree. That meant something very special was about to happen,” Philippe Lucas said.

Roger Lucas died in Montreal on Aug. 22. He leaves his wife, Valerie Welland; son, Dominic Lucas; stepchildren, Christian and Annick d’Auteuil; sister, Danielle Lucas; and extended family, including Philippe Lucas.

stories.title: Alberta anti-separatist brings hard message to central Canada: show a little gratitude
stories.summary: Thomas Lukaszuk told a Toronto business audience at the Economic Club of Canada that “the promise of a pipeline” is not enough for Alberta.
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
The most striking moment in former Alberta deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk’s speech to a Toronto business audience about the perils of Alberta separatism came when he mentioned Thursday’s breaking news that Prime Minister Mark Carney will fast-track a new Pacific Link pipeline from Alberta to the West Coast as a project of national interest.

It was striking because there was no applause, not even a murmur of assent or a rustle of emotional reaction for this pipeline that is being styled as a marquee nation-building project for a divided and imperilled nation, strategically announced 18 days before Alberta votes on whether to hold a sovereignty referendum.

If anyone was looking for a case against Alberta going it alone, this was it.

So the downtown Toronto audience’s silence was an illustration of a recurring theme, that some of Alberta’s beef with the rest of Canada, especially Central Canada, is the attitude.

This came up first in the speech to the Economic Club of Canada by Lukaszuk, a staunch anti-separatist and a former cabinet minister in the Progressive Conservative governments of Ed Stelmach and Alison Redford. And it came up again in the following roundtable discussion led by former Ontario premier Dalton McGuinty.

“It’s time to admit that some of those grievances are real,” Lukaszuk said. Alberta contributes substantially to Canada as a whole and has legitimate concerns that equalization payments to the provinces give Albertans short shrift. “A certain amount of gratitude is not too much to ask.”

He said the separatist movement is boosted by unequal representation in the Senate, and by the tendency for national elections to be decided before polls even close in the West. Lukaszuk said he has had the deflating experience of hearing CBC declare a majority while he was still waiting in line to vote in Alberta.

“To us, it feels like our votes don’t matter,” he said. It is fodder for separatism, but it also encourages Albertans who are merely frustrated with their place in Canada to vote with the separatists just to send a message.

Alberta anti-separatist brings hard message to Central Canada: show a little gratitude

Alberta's separatists have a Mark Carney problem

“It’s a message the rest of Canada needs to listen to,” he said. “Please don’t pat us on the head with the promise of a pipeline, thinking that’s enough.”

Albertan separatism is based on “unsubstantiated claims and magical thinking” and it is hampered by squabbling factions, Lukaszuk said. Polling in the last few days has shown separatist sentiment to be low and falling, and pegged the remain vote as high as 70 per cent.

But Lukaszuk is concerned this is a recipe for low voter turnout, with the remainers lacking the conviction and motivation of the leavers.

“Fervent separatists will crawl across broken glass to make their vote count,” he said. “This is a genie in a bottle that magically will not be put back in. It will take strong leadership to convince Albertans that Alberta belongs in Canada.”

In Alberta, he said this current high water point for the long-running separatist movement is dividing families, dragging away investment and causing Albertan businesses to consider relocating.

“It should be enough to make people throw up their hands in despair,” he said. “And yet something else has happened.”

He credited the trade war brought by U.S. President Donald Trump with “the rekindling of Canadian pride and healthy patriotism,” and he spoke of a “uniquely Canadian combination of pride, persistence and hope.”

Last year, Lukaszuk launched a petition called Alberta Forever Canada that got more than 400,000 signatures in 90 days in favour of Alberta remaining in Canada. This year he has campaigned across the province against separatism in a recreational vehicle styled as the Unity Bus.

After his keynote address, he took questions from McGuinty alongside Martha Hall Findlay, a former Liberal MP now with the University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy, and Andrew Leach, professor of economics and law at the University of Alberta.

Hall Findlay recently published a report for the government of Alberta on the potential costs of separation, which concluded it could cost as much as $170 billion over five years.

“Those were only the five year out numbers,” she said. Her analysis ran several models, including one that assumed separation went completely smoothly, which suggested over 20 years there was “potentially a little upside,” thanks to a more efficient civil service and other factors.

But with the assumption of a turbulent separation, for example with pushback from Ottawa, the downside is “really big,” she said, with a potential provincial debt of close to $400 billion.

She compared Albertan separatism to the British Brexit movement, in the sense that then Prime Minister David Cameron thought a failed vote would take the wind out of the Brexiteers’ sails, but the momentum got away from him, and it cost him his leadership.

It will take strong leadership to convince Albertans that Alberta belongs in Canada

She spoke of an ignorance among Central Canadians for how things work in Alberta, and how much it contributes to the country, such as the Trans Mountain Pipeline expansion project that added fully half a point to national GDP when it opened in 2024. She described an “incredibly arrogant” framing of pipeline approvals as basically gifts from Ottawa, an attitude that would never be taken with infrastructure projects in Quebec, where separatism is also a perennial threat to national unity.

“Remember, we’re only 15 years removed from the federal government putting out loans to restart an asbestos mine in Quebec,” said Leach. “That mentality was very different when it came to Alberta’s business,” he said. It looked more like Ottawa thinking its job is to save Albertans from themselves, he said.

He urged the audience to consider what he has experienced in Edmonton, when an oil boom goes bust as in 2014, and how it must feel for an oil patch worker to hear the federal government say, “Oh but there might be solar panels manufactured in Medicine Hat, you’ll be fine.”

Lukaszuk said the separatist sentiment falls with Alberta’s economic successes and rises with its failures. He thinks it is driven predominantly by younger men in the oil and gas industry, overleveraged by debt, with limited transferable skills, who are noticing the economy is pivoting on them.

“Now they fear for their future, and the fear is real,” Lukaszuk said. He described this dynamic as “infectious” and catching on in Saskatchewan and British Columbia.

“If we don’t inoculate this now in Alberta, we will be dealing with it on a wider scope, maybe with different industries,” he said.

stories.title: Mild, rainy Thursday expected in London
stories.summary: London is in for a gray and wet Thursday, with rain and scattered showers expected through the day as temperatures climb well above seasonal, according to CTV News meteorologist Gary Archibald.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
London is in for a gray and wet Thursday, with rain and scattered showers expected through the day as temperatures climb well above seasonal, according to CTV News meteorologist Gary Archibald.

The high is expected to reach 23 C, about five degrees above the seasonal average of 18 C. The overnight low was 16 C, compared with a typical low of about 7 C.

“It is gray, it is wet, but it’s certainly mild above seasonal,” Archibald said.

Humidity values are expected to remain around 80 to 85 per cent, with scattered showers and breezy conditions developing.

Archibald said a shift in the weather pattern is bringing moisture and rain into Southern Ontario, with a prolonged period of rainfall expected across the region.

Areas along the north shore of Lake Erie could receive 15 to 30 millimetres of rain, while some areas farther north could see more than 30 millimetres.

In London, showers are expected to continue into Friday morning. Temperatures will be around 12 C Friday morning, with northerly winds of 30 km/h and gusts potentially reaching 40 km/h.

Friday will be cooler, with a high near 19 C. Conditions are expected to improve through the afternoon as the winds shift and skies begin to clear.

stories.title: Canadian TV show 'Mayday' cited by passenger who thwarted Flydubai attack
stories.summary: Toronto - A passenger who helped avert a catastrophe on a FlyDubai flight after the pilot was stabbed mid-air has said he credits a Canadian-made TV show for knowing what to do.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - A passenger who helped avert a catastrophe on a FlyDubai flight after the pilot was stabbed mid-air has said he credited a Canadian-made TV show for knowing how to seize control of the aircraft.

The long-running documentary series “Mayday” examines real-life air disasters, including crashes, near-crashes, hijackings and bombings.

The show’s executive producer Alex Bystram said it was rewarding to know the series has been associated with a story that has a happy ending for the more than 170 passengers.

“Whether it gave him the knowledge to do what he did or gave him courage to try to do something, or even just ensure that he didn’t do the wrong thing. It would be easy for him to go into that cockpit and then make things worse,” Bystram said. “It’s nice to get that kind of publicity, and it’s nice to be associated with a story with a happy ending like that.”

Israeli passenger Yaniv Hayoun has been praised as a hero along with others who entered the cockpit and helped subdue the co-pilot who had allegedly stabbed the captain of a flight bound for Tel Aviv from Dubai.

According to reports in Reuters and CNN, Hayoun told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu he knew how to take control of the nosediving aircraft because he watched “Air Crash Investigation,” which is the name of the docuseries outside of North America.

Other crew members travelling on the plane helped land the aircraft safely in Saudi Arabia.

Speaking from Toronto, Bystram humbly said he’s under no illusions that the TV show, which has aired since 2003, is responsible for saving the aircraft, and he cautioned that the program is “far from a teaching tool on how to fly an airplane.”

Instead, he credited the pilot, identified as Capt. Smit Machchhar from Mumbai, India, for his quick-thinking to unlock the cockpit door despite his injuries, which allowed others to intervene and take control of the Boeing 737.

“For me, this story is about a captain who just did the most remarkable thing I’ve ever heard of in commercial aviation, which is, you know, bleeding, bloodied, stabbed, your plane descending 10,000 feet per minute,” Bystram said. “You have the wherewithal to figure out to open that door to let these people in. Amazing.”

“Mayday,” which has run for more than 20 seasons, investigates real-life aviation disasters to find out what went wrong and why.

Episodes feature dramatized re-enactments based on cockpit voice recorders, accident reports and eyewitness accounts. Computer-generated imagery is used to reconstruct events, while interviews with people involved, including passengers and pilots, as well as aviation experts and investigators, further paint the picture of the emergency, its aftermath, and the resulting investigation.

Bystram, who has been associated with the series since its fifth season, said the goal of each episode is to tell a story of how investigators determined how and why an air disaster happened and the resulting response from the aviation industry to prevent a similar accident from ever happening again.

The show, which has more than 250 episodes and attracts viewers from across the world, dispels some of the mystery around flying and “pulls back the curtain a little bit,” Bystram said. As a result, he said he’s heard from viewers who told him the show has alleviated fears of flying because it reveals that, in most cases, it takes a string of errors to bring down a plane, and people “feel relieved to know that it’s not just one thing.”

“Our show has a very, I think, reassuring message, which is these plane crashes result in very specific changes to aviation that prevent these accidents from happening again,” Bystram said. “For a lot of people, there is an element of relief and comfort to know that what happened on this particular flight isn’t going to happen on my flight that — that problem is being fixed.”

The executive producer said he’s also heard from pilots who have learned how not to react during emergencies from watching the program.

“Most pilots aren’t in accidents like this, so they watch how the pilots reacted, and they can see what the outcome was, and I think it’s a teaching tool for them,” he said.

“Mayday” is produced in Toronto by the Canadian media production company Cineflix Media. The homegrown team behind the show also includes professional pilots, who check scripts for accuracy and work with the actors hired for the re-enactments.

The series airs in about 175 countries worldwide and is known by several different names, including “Air Disasters” in the United States.

With the show’s 27th season set for release in the new year, Bystram said the recent FlyDubai incident was a reminder of the show’s wide reach.

“You sort of lose touch with the fact that people are watching the show you make,” he said. “For me to hear that not only are people watching the show, but they’re learning something from the show that caused them to take this kind of action, it’s rewarding. And it’s a good reminder that the information that we give better be accurate.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Labour board rules Manitoba Dynacare lab staff to be essential workers
stories.summary: In the event of a strike or lockout, core functions like lab testing, home visits and mobile collections must continue, the decision states
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The terrain of the ongoing collective bargaining battle involving workers who do medical tests across Manitoba shifted Thursday with a ruling from the province’s labour board.

The board, in a written decision, said the staffers who carry out and interpret medical tests for the private company Dynacare are to be classified as essential workers in the event of a future strike or lockout.

The board said it accepted the province’s argument that the testing, while routine, can have major ramifications on everything from cancer diagnoses to strokes. It noted on average 15 routine tests a day find critical issues in patients.

“An interruption or a significant backlog to those services would create a clear and foreseeable risk to health and safety,” the board stated. The board ruled that in the event of a strike or lockout, core functions like lab testing, home visits and mobile collections must continue.

Dynacare’s 23 locations in the province provide about half of blood sampling services and 40 per cent of lab testing, performing more than 24 million lab tests a year.

The decision notes that Dynacare estimates a backlog of about 34,000 per week if workers were to go on strike and that testing through Shared Health is already strained.

More than 350 workers went on strike in early September only to have the province secure an interim order from the labour board to send them back to work the next day.

The company and union still need to hash out what an essential services agreement will look like on top of existing contract talks.

Union president Jason Linklater said the labour board has given the company and government exactly what they wanted.

“These people have been trapped by government and by Dynacare, and it’s a very terrible situation that they’ve been put in, and it’s certainly a red flag to any unionized employee in this province,” Linklater said.

He said the NDP government isn’t standing up for health-care workers and needs to fix the contract it signed with the company.

“Only government has the ability to ensure that this problem is solved and that these wages are dealt with.”

The union – the Manitoba Association of Health Care Professionals – has been pushing for higher wages, saying its workers earn 20 to 50 per cent less than counterparts in the public system.

Since members were forced back to work, wait times on weekends have been growing as some locations haven’t opened due to staffing issues.

Dynacare welcomed Thursday’s decision, saying it has reached out to the union to negotiate an essential services agreement.

It said the process will determine which specific services, roles and staffing levels are necessary.

Manitoba Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara said the government is working to fully understand the ruling, but said it’s up to the company to fix the underlying problem.

“My message remains the same to Dynacare: get to the table and give those workers a fair deal.”

Premier Wab Kinew has been outspoken on the issue. It was his government that ended the strike after one day on Sept. 8 when it went to the labour board to seek an emergency decree to order staff back.

Kinew said at the time that the workers were right to be frustrated, that they deserved a pay raise and that “Dynacare sucks,” but said as leader his job is to ensure essential health services are available.

He blamed the issue on previous governments outsourcing to private providers fundamental public services like health care. He mused about de-privatizing the testing but warned that would be an extremely costly proposition.

stories.title: Canada-U.S. border agencies announce changes for Nexus applicants
stories.summary: New deadlines for Canadians applying for Nexus travel cards were announced by the Canada Border Services Agency. Here’s everything you need to know.
stories.author: Joe Van Wonderen
stories.content:
New deadlines for Canadians applying for Nexus travel cards were announced by the Canada Border Services Agency.

Here’s everything you need to know.

Starting April 1, 2027, applicants must schedule their enrolment interviews within two years of receiving conditional approval, the Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) said Thursday in a news release.

Nexus interview deadlines are changing! The temporary pandemic extension is ending, returning to the two-year rule. Check your application status and book your appointment as soon as possible so it doesn't expire! More info: https://t.co/JVapO0T2fj pic.twitter.com/vygk7v57Y7 — Canada Border Services Agency (@CanBorder) October 1, 2026

This is an update from the five-year timeframe Cbsa temporarily extended due to delays caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

“Now with more enrolment interview capacity available, the two-year deadline is returning,” the agency said.

According to Cbsa, applicants who were conditionally approved before April 1, 2027 must schedule their interview within five years of their approval date, or by April 1, 2029, depending on which day comes first.

For anyone still waiting for an interview, Cbsa said to “book your appointment as soon as possible so your application does not expire.”

After submitting an application, would-be Nexus travellers need to schedule an interview with both Cbsa and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

Cbsa says that both border agencies will conduct fingerprinting, identity verification and questioning from both Cbsa and CBP officers.

Nexus cards expedite the border clearance process for travellers between Canada and the U.S. and May grant access to priority lanes at certain points of entry. T

Travellers are also granted TSA PreCheck in the U.S. and Global Entry benefits.

Nexus memberships are valid for five years and require a US$120 application fee. Every traveller in a party needs their own card, although the fee is waived for children.

Nexus applications in Canada dropped by around 50 per cent in 2025 amid U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war against Ottawa. In 2024, 695,533 Canadians applied for membership, but in 2025, that number dropped to 344,257.

With files from CTVNewsCalgary.CA reporter Timm Bruch

stories.title: As Texas declares state of emergency over fuel shortage, what’s dyed diesel
stories.summary: As global oil supplies continue to tighten up amid ongoing geopolitical conflicts that have pushed up fuel prices, the governor of Texas has declared a state of emergency.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
As global oil supplies continue to tighten and fuel prices soar , the governor of Texas declared a state of emergency over a shortage of diesel fuel.

Declaring a state of emergency can unlock a government’s ability to temporarily modify certain policies in order to protect the general public: in the case of Texas, this includes waiving restrictions on what’s known as dyed diesel.

Governor Greg Abbott of Texas issued an emergency notice on Monday.

“The shortage of diesel fuel poses an imminent threat or occurrence of harm to the public health and safety in the State of Texas,” the notice says.

“A shortage of diesel fuel will impose harmful effects upon the agriculture and ranching industries by increasing the price per acre to achieve similar yields, reducing investment in farm and ranch machinery, and driving up supply chain expenses.”

Abbott also states that truckers and construction companies are facing higher costs that are making it difficult to maintain operations or spend on new projects.

This also comes after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to ban exports of U.S. diesel as supplies come under strain as a result of the repeated closure of the Strait of Hormuz from his war with Iran.

Opher Baron, a distinguished professor of operations management at the Rotman School of Management, says the U.S. is trying to maintain its presence as a superpower by using its leverage on energy wherever it can.

“If you look at some of the international actions of the U.S. regime over the last 12 months or so, they are very much focused on the energy market,” says Baron.

“Obviously, before the midterm elections coming up next month, there is pressure on this main goal.”

Abbott says his government is taking specific steps to suspend certain regulatory measures, including the use of dyed diesel fuel, weight limits on commercial shipping, and some standards for diesel emissions in order to provide financial relief amid a global diesel squeeze.

Baron says these measures could provide some short-term relief for American consumers and businesses, but whether or not they are sustainable affordability solutions is unclear.

Dyed diesel is, literally, reddish in colour because of an additive used to identify it as fuel used mainly for off-road purposes, such as agriculture and construction, which does not require a motor-fuels tax.

Easing restrictions on the use of dyed diesel on the road allows for businesses to tap into their off-road fuel stocks for commercial road transport purposes and bypass retail fuel tax costs, where they would otherwise face record-high diesel prices.

The proclamation also states that vehicles loaded with fuel, agricultural or timber products weighing up to 95,000 pounds will not be required to carry additional state permits for being oversized or overweight.

Finally, the governor formally requested the Environmental Protection Agency to waive certain rules for diesel fuel that apply in Texas, which he says will remove some limits on which diesel can be sold, and he requested a waiver to allow more fuel to reach pumps in the state.

“What needs to be considered is, does this have any second round impacts on other parts of the economy? Because if you’re going to put a policy in place that provides relief in one place, but provides strain in another, then it’s worth questioning the effectiveness of that policy,” says economist Marc Ercolao at TD Economics.

“In this case of Texas, it very well May have local positive impacts in the diesel space. But should that have other impacts in other fuels, you might just end up at an offsetting point where it was neither a benefit nor a detriment.”

1:48 New Middle East attacks threaten oil supply

Could similar measures work in Canada?

Canadian consumers and businesses are also grappling with higher gas and diesel prices, and the Bank of Canada has warned that the longer these oil and gas prices remain elevated, the more likely those higher prices will be reflected in other areas like food, housing, and just about everything else.

The federal government has extended a pause on the fuel excise tax until the end of January 2027 , which brought immediate relief at the pumps for both regular and diesel fuels as well as jet fuels when it was introduced earlier this year. The tax will then return at a 50 per cent rate from Feb. 1 through March 31, 2027.

But diesel prices have been climbing faster than regular gasoline.

In Canada, the national average for diesel fuel is hovering around C$2.60 per litre, according to Natural Resources Canada, up from $2.35 last month, and about $1.54 a year ago.

The Canadian national average price for regular gas is about $1.75 per litre, according to the Canadian Automobile Association, up from $1.71 last month and $1.35 a year ago.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has proposed eliminating all tax on diesel sales until at least Canada Day by extending the full fuel excise tax cut until July 1 of next year and removing the GST from the purchase of fuel.

Ercolao says niche quick-fixes, like in Texas, May not be as necessary in Canada because of the country’s refining capacity, or ability to produce more diesel for consumption, and tax relief measures May be more effective.

“Most of the relief measures that we have seen here have been through taxes and domestic consumption, like being able to meet our domestic demand through our own production and refining,” says Ercolao.

“As far as the current tax relief goes, it’s definitely providing that relief at the pump, and for diesel as well. Those are net positive for consumers and businesses.”

– with a file from The Canadian Press

stories.summary: The victim and accused were known to each other.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
The victim of a stabbing earlier this week has died in hospital.

London police identified as Charles Alexander Raymond George, 34, of London.

At about 6:15 p.m. on Monday, officers responded to the call on the north side of the Dundas Street, just east of Adelaide Street.

When they arrived, officers found a man suffering from life-threatening injuries — he was taken to hospital by paramedic services.

Police were able to identify a suspect and he was arrested Wednesday night in the downtown core.

Luis Angel Rivera-Perez, 26, of London, has been charged with second degree murder, and fail to comply with release order.

The victim and accused were known to each other.

The accused remains in custody and was scheduled to appear in London court today in relation to the charges.

stories.summary: Ranked second in the Canadian Hockey League, the London Knights have just added three NHL draft picks to their roster.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Ranked second in the Canadian Hockey League, the London Knights have just added three NHL draft picks to their roster.

“I can’t wait to get started back here. It was really fun in Ottawa for the couple of weeks I was there, but I’m happy to be back and can’t wait to get started with these guys.”

Cover didn’t play in any NHL exhibition games but turned heads – including his own – with seven points in two games during a two-game rookie prospect tournament.

“I surprised myself a little bit going into it,” said Cover.

“I wasn’t too focused on points or scoring or anything, just trying to make sure I’m playing my game and playing the right way. Then the puck, kind of kept finding my stick, so, I just kept shooting it.”

“It all comes down to like really watching the (NHL) guys and talking to them, asking the questions,” said Medvedev.

“Being in the spot of a younger guy there, you kind of come back here and you have a little have a little more sympathy for the younger guys here and kind of you try to help them all even more.”

Medvedev has been open about his play last season where he lost his starting job to Sebastian Gatto. He’s been working hard during the offseason to make sure it doesn’t happen again.

“There are so many things to prove for me,” said Medvedev who is expected to start Friday night.

He spent hours on the technical side of goalkeeping.

“The biggest body of work done was kind of building and creating new routines, kind of new habits,” added Medvedev.

“That helped me kind of manage the game, kind of just self-reflecting and working on kind of the mental side. I think those are the biggest changes.”

Brittany Howard ready for St. Thomas homecoming

The Joe Thornton Community Centre (Jtcc) in St. Thomas, Ont. will be packed with family and friends as Western Mustangs Women’s Hockey Coach Brittany Howard steps behind the bench Saturday.

Howard’s Mustangs will play a preseason game against the Guelph Gryphons as part of Panther Day which is a day dedicated to girls’ hockey in her hometown.

“My aunt was our MP (Karen Vecchio) in our area in St. Thomas for 10 years and she’s going to drop the puck,” said Howard.

“My other aunt, who was a principal in the area, she’s going to do our lineup read. I know they’re both absolutely jazzed to do and participate. I have 13 cousins on my mom’s side, and I hope they all show up.”

Howard – who grew up in St. Thomas – has a banner recognizing her Ncaa and professional career inside the Jtcc.

“It’s a huge opportunity for us to give back to the community,” said Howard.

“Last year our players went out for a skate with the organization, and it was a phenomenal event, and I think it really made an impact with our roster. So, I think going into this year, setting up the game against one of the best opponents we can in our conference was an amazing opportunity. I hear we are going to get a great crowd, and I think it will be great for our girls to play in front of that.”

Mustangs Football prepares for undefeated Queen’s

Both Western and rival Queen’s are perfect at 4-0 and share top spot in the OUA.

In front of 14,000 fans last weekend at Homecoming, the Mustangs held on for a 32-25 win over McMaster in what they admit was not their best effort.

“With our 3-0 start, it wasn’t the toughest scheduled to start and we knew it was going to get significantly tougher,” said Michael Faulds, Mustangs head football coach.

London Smash wins Canadian National Pickleball League title

The Smash established itself as one of the premier organizations in the Canadian National Pickleball League (Cnpl).

London advanced through the playoff rounds and defeated United to win the 2026 title.

It was an extraordinary season capturing the Cnpl Mid-Season Championship, finishing first at the Central Split in London, capturing first place at the Vancouver Split, securing a first-round playoff bye, and ultimately raising the championship trophy in Waterloo.

Ed Sater was named owner/manager of the year while captain Ryan Torresin received the Player’s Choice Award, voted on by his peers across the league.
