stories.title: Small caps to watch: Ag Growth shares soar on ‘encouraging’ update, plus news from Primaris Reit, AutoCanda and more
stories.summary: A look at some small-cap stocks making news - or about to.
stories.author: Brenda Bouw
stories.content:
A look at some small-cap stocks making news - or about to. This file will be updated throughout the day on Thursday.

Canada’s S&P/TSX Small Cap Index ( Txtw-I ) is up by about 30 per cent over the past 52 weeks. It hit a record 1,496.55 on June 2. The Russell 2000 in the U.S. is up about 15 per cent over the past 52 weeks and reached a high of 3,069.71 on Aug. 14.

Invesque Inc . ( IVQ-U-T ) shares shot higher on Thursday after the company announced a deal to be taken private by a controlling shareholder.

In a statement, the company said the deal is with a special purpose entity managed by Magnetar Financial LLC, which will buy the shares it doesn’t own for 10.1 US cents, or 14.3 cents Canadian.

The consideration is a 68-per-cent premium on a spot basis, and a 30-per-cent premium to the volume-weighted average trading price of the shares for the 20 trading days ended Sept. 29.

“Management and the board of directors have worked diligently over the last several years to sell assets and return capital to shareholders. This transaction allows the return of capital much sooner than would otherwise occur,” CEO Adlai Chester stated.

A shareholder meeting to vote on the deal is expected on or before Nov. 20, the company added, with closing expected before the end of the year.

Enerflex Ltd. ( EFX-T ) jumped on Thursday after the company announced it was awarded a “major” engineered systems (ES) project to design, engineer, fabricate, and assemble approximately 450 megawatts of “behind-the-metre” natural gas-fired power generation units for a North American data center developer.

“To support this award and expected growth across Enerflex’s core markets, the company is investing in expanding the capabilities of its ES business line,” the company said, adding that it has $15-million in its capital budget and $85-million of investments in its ES facilities and capabilities to help support the cost.

“These investments, combined with ongoing initiatives to enhance collaboration, leverage scale, improve operational efficiency, and solidify capabilities, are expected to significantly increase revenue capacity of Enerflex’s ES business line,” it added.

Pulse Seismic Inc. ( PSD-T ) shares rose on Thursday after the reported preliminary third-quarter results, including a 400-per-cent increase in revenue versus the same period last year.

After markets closed on Wednesday, the Calgary company that provides seismic data to the Western Canadian energy sector, said it generated approximately $17.3-million in seismic data licensing revenue, bringing expected total revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30 to about $22.8-million.

It said third quarter revenue increased more than 400 per cent compared to the third quarter of 2025, while revenue for the first nine months of 2026 decreased by 49 per cent compared to the “near-record revenue” for the first nine months of 2025. The company didn’t provide more specific data in the release.

“Consistent with previous disclosure, the timing of new seismic data licensing is impacted by a variety of factors affecting industry activity and is subject to significant fluctuations,” the company stated.

“These strong third-quarter sales results demonstrate the continued value and strategic importance of our extensive seismic data library to our clients,” said CEO Pamela Wicks in a release. “While our market experiences natural fluctuations tied to broader energy sector activity, we remain confident in our competitive position and the long-term value of our asset base.”

The company said the data is preliminary and has not been audited or reviewed by its auditors. It said final results for the period are expected to be released on Oct. 21

Primaris Reit ( PMN-UN-T ) announced a deal to buy a 100-per-cent interest in Upper Canada Mall in Newmarket, Ont. for $411-million in cash.

“The acquisition further advances Primaris’ strategy of acquiring market-leading enclosed shopping centres in growing Canadian markets, where the Reit can deploy its full-service operating platform to drive income growth and long-term per unit value creation,” it stated.

It said Upper Canada Mall will become its fourth-largest shopping centre by total commercial retail unit (CRU) sales volume.

“Upper Canada Mall is a dominant GTA shopping centre with strong demographics, an exceptional tenant mix and significant embedded growth potential,” said president Patrick Sullivan,

The company also lowered its fiscal 2026 funds from operations guidance to $1.83 to $1.88 from $1.85 to $1.90 based on an assumed transaction closing date of Oct. 31.

“Primaris Real Estate Investment Trust (Primaris) continues to aggressively consolidate the enclosed mall market in Canada, with a focus on higher-end malls that generate well-above-average sales per square foot,” Canaccord analyst Mark Rothschild said in a note. “Management is tweaking 2026 guidance lower by 1 per cent, due to a timing difference between the recent $230 million equity raise, which closed last week, and the closing of the acquisition, which is expected by the end of October. We do not expect any notable change to 2027 consensus from this acquisition.”

Added Mr. Rothschild: “We understand that the property is being acquired from a joint venture between Omers and CPP, as they look to reduce their exposure to direct real estate. We note that the Reit acquired Les Galeries de la Capitale for $325 million from this joint venture in October 2024. Though management indicated that the acquisition will be initially accretive to FFO per unit by $0.02, or 1 per cent, we believe that, over time, the return can be improved materially.”

He said “significant upside” exists from leasing up vacant space, with 263,400 square feet of former HBC, Sears, and Toys “R” Us space currently representing 27 per cent of the mall and the core of the property’s value-creation opportunity.

“Though it May take a couple of years, we estimate that, when stabilized, the NOI yield could exceed 8.0 per cent, adding $0.02 to FFO [funds from operations] per unit. Well located along key transportation infrastructure in a major population centre,” he wrote. “Consistent with the Reit’s recent acquisitions, the mall is highly productive and dominant within its trade area.”

RioCan Reit ( REI-UN-T ) announced on Wednesday that Dennis Blasutti will resume his duties as chief financial officer, effective Oct. 1, following a temporary medical leave.

Franca Smith, who served as interim CFO from March to September, will continue as senior vice-president of finance.

Ag Growth International Inc. ( AFN-T ) stock shot up on Wednesday, before paring back some of those gains on Thursday, after the company updated investors on its capital strategy, balance sheet improvement initiatives, strategic review process and outlook, which at least one analyst described as “encouraging.”

“As AGI enters 2027, the company is seeing positive market signals across many of its core businesses which support increasing confidence in its outlook,” it stated in a release before markets opened. “Farm markets have strengthened with a notable pick-up in order intake over recent months and commercial quoting activity is rising across key global regions. Overall, AGI continues to benefit from leading market positions across a range of geographies including North America, Emea, India, and Brazil.”

The company said the outlook, combined with more than $30-million of expected annualized cost savings and approximately $50-million of identified surplus real estate monetization opportunities, makes it “well positioned to improve earnings, strengthen cash flow, and accelerate balance sheet deleveraging.”

Ag Growth said it has secured covenant relief under its senior credit facilities through the second quarter of 2027, giving it extra operating and execution flexibility. It also said it has earmarked about $50-million of “excess, non-core real estate” to sell and plans to put the proceeds towards paying down debt.

“The real estate program is one component of a broader non-core asset monetization initiative and does not include potential proceeds from other non-core businesses or assets currently being evaluated by the company and the board’s strategic review committee,” it added. “Management is focused on using internally generated cash and proceeds from non-core asset monetization to reduce senior indebtedness and progressively strengthen the balance sheet.”

Ag Growth also said its targeted $30-million in annualized savings has so far included closing its Naperville office, restructuring underperforming North American business units, and an “overhaul of the senior executive team, among other actions.”

It also said its previously announced review of strategic alternatives is ongoing.

TD analyst Michael Tupholme said in a note that the update “contains some encouraging incremental items (i.e., now expects a higher level of proceeds from excess/non-core real estate monetization initiatives), while certain other items included in the update have been previously disclosed/are not new.”

Dye & Durham Ltd. ( DND-T ) reported fourth quarter results that largely beat expectations.

Before markets opened on Tuesday, the legal software company reported revenue of $104.2-million for the quarter ended June 30, down 1 per cent from the same period a year ago. Excluding the impact of the disposal of Credas Technologies Ltd. from all periods, revenue increased by 4 per cent year over year, the company stated. The result beat expectations for revenue of $94.9-million, according to S&P Capital IQ estimates.

Its net loss was $21.9-million or 32 cents per share, compared to a net loss of $29.6-million or 44 cents a year ago. The expectation was for a loss of 21 cents, according to S&P Capital IQ.

Adjusted Ebitda was $55.1 million up from $47.7-million a year ago. Excluding the impact of the disposal of Credas, adjusted Ebitda increased 18 per cent, it stated. The expectation was for adjusted Ebitda of $44-million.

BMO analyst Thanos Moschopoulos maintained his “market perform” (hold) on the stock and raised his estimates after the results he said were “well above consensus, with a return to y/y [year over year] organic revenue growth for the first time in several quarters.”

Added Mr. Moschopoulos: “Management didn’t provide much color on the key drivers of the revenue strength or of its sustainability, beyond noting that transaction volumes and customer churn have been improving. Net, while we’re encouraged by the results, we don’t view the stock’s valuation as sufficiently compelling given Dnd’s leverage and the current lack of a permanent CEO/CFO.”

AutoCanada Inc. ( ACQ-T ) said this week that it’s initiating a strategic review of its collision operations, including a potential sale.

On Tuesday, the Edmonton-based company said its board has set up a special committee of independent directors to analyze and evaluate “a range of strategic alternatives intended to maximize value for AutoCanada and its shareholders and to support the continued growth of its collision operations.”

The company said the alternatives May include, but are not limited to, separating the business from AutoCanada and potentially selling all or part of the business.

“The board believes the value and growth potential of the company’s collision operations May not be fully reflected in AutoCanada’s current public market valuation,” the release stated.

National Bank analyst Maxim Sytchev said the announcement was “somewhat of a surprise” in a note.

“Bottom line – announcement wasn’t expected; value-creation initiatives are appreciated, but macro needs to cooperate for the stock to really work; exit multiple of course can make a bigger swing,” he wrote. “From an accretion/shareholder value perspective, the impact of a potential monetization of the Collision business remains relatively value-neutral, in our view. ”

Slate Grocery Reit ( SGR-UN-T ), a Canadian-listed company that owns grocery-anchored retail centres in the United States, capped a volatile bout of trading with news of its acquisition by two American buyers.

On Monday, Slate announced its sale to Brixmor Property Group Inc., a publicly listed company, and Everview Partners, L.P., which is privately owned. Together, the buyers are paying US$13 in cash per unit, amounting to an equity value close to US$800-million. (Slate Grocery trades in U.S. dollars on the Toronto Stock Exchange.)

The sale itself wasn’t necessarily a surprise, because Slate launched a strategic review in May. However, the timing caught investors and analysts off guard.

Sangoma Technologies Corp. ( STC-T ) announced a deal to be bought by BRC Holdings, Inc. ( RLY-Q) in a deal valued at about US$204-million, or $289-million Canadian, or roughly $7.40 per share.

On Monday, the company said shareholders will receive US$4.925 in cash for each Sangoma share they own and 0.04767 of a share of common stock of BRC. “The consideration payable under the transaction represents a premium of approximately 47 per cent and 51 per cent to Sangoma’s closing price and 10-day Vwap, respectively, ON the TSX for the period ending on September 28, 2026,” the company stated.

It said officers and directors of Sangoma, collectively holding approximately 27 per cent of the issued and outstanding Sangoma shares, have agreed to vote in favour of the deal. The deal requires approval by two-thirds of votes cast by Sangoma shareholders at an upcoming special meeting, as well as regulatory approvals.

Stifel analyst Suthan Sukumar said the takeover offer follows a strategic review announced last quarter.

“A takeout was the optionality we flagged, and while the price sits at a discount to our C$9 target, the premium does capture value following Stc’s business transformation,” he wrote. “Net/net - we view this as a clean, credible outcome for a name that had run out of catalysts as a standalone public company. We see little risk of a higher bid, given a comprehensive sale process run since May 2026 that assessed other proposals, 27 per cent of shares locked up in voting support, and a 3-per-cent break fee.”

stories.title: Toronto board of trade calls for regulatory reforms to spur housing growth
stories.summary: The Toronto Region Board of Trade is urging the province to amend zoning and building code rules as it says Ontario is on pace to fall well short of its new home goal.
stories.author: Sammy Hudes
stories.content:
The Toronto Region Board of Trade is urging the province to amend zoning and building code rules as it says Ontario is on pace to fall well short of its goal of getting at least 1.5 million new homes built by 2031.

In a report published Thursday, the board said the target is unachievable by the current deadline, which was set by the provincial government in 2022, even if housing production increases over the next five years. Based on budget forecasts, Ontario is projected to fall more than 550,000 homes short of the pace needed by 2029, according to the analysis.

“We already had a massive gap. It was called the housing crisis for a reason,” said board president and CEO Giles Gherson in an interview.

“There’s been a lot of effort and a lot of work gone into, ‘How do we close this housing gap? How do we build houses faster?’ But the disappointing part of it is that the gap remains very, very large.”

The board said that even if ambitious reforms were adopted immediately, municipalities would need to update plans, amend zoning bylaws, align infrastructure investments, service land, and process applications. Those steps could take years, making the 2031 goal unrealistic.

Gherson said the key to unlocking new development at a quicker pace is through regulatory changes.

He described rules around zoning and building codes as “very fragmented” across the province, and “out of date.” In Toronto alone, builders face dozens of different requirements across the city, which makes it difficult to standardize production.

“It really adds a huge amount of cost and delay to housing development and that impacts the ability for the city to attract and retain our workforce that we need,” he said.

“But also, we know it is impacting the social fabric as the next generation sees home ownership as really a pipe dream, and that’s a really big problem.”

The report said Ontario should develop a provincial zoning code that provides every municipality the same framework and terminology.

That code could set a baseline of what housing types can move forward without special approval, starting with townhouses and multiplexes. The standard could also establish provincewide limits on the rules that most often block housing, such as parking, setbacks, lot coverage, height, density, and how far upper storeys must step back.

Meanwhile, it recommended key changes around building codes, saying there should be an assessment of every requirement for the cost it imposes to build, run and maintain over the life of the building. The report also proposed allowing single-stair buildings up to six storeys, along with smaller elevators in smaller buildings, as long as safety and accessibility are still prioritized.

Gherson said other cities in Canada are proof that a less patchy model can lead to meaningful housing growth. He pointed to Edmonton, where he said it’s more common see multiplexes in different types of neighbourhoods.

“Where we’ll have single-family dwellings on major roads, they’ll have a lot of these multiplexes and the reason is they have more flexible permissive zoning and they don’t have as many zoning codes,” he said. “There’s a city that’s been a fast-growth city for the last five decades … so we need to look to other places that have been successful.”

The call for action comes as affordability challenges persist for Toronto’s housing market, even as prices have been on the decline over the past year.

Last month, the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board said the average selling price in the Greater Toronto Area stood at $993,410 for August, down 2.7 per cent year-over-year, while the composite benchmark price, meant to represent the typical home, was down 4.5 per cent.

But the trade board’s report said housing remains out of reach for many residents, especially compared with past decades. It said that between 2006 and 2025, Toronto-area home prices, as measured by the composite price, increased by around 187 per cent. That significantly outpaced the cumulative increase for inflation over that time, which was around 51 per cent.

“Durable affordability depends on increasing the supply of homes,” the report said.

“Without continued housing construction, recent affordability gains are likely to prove temporary.”

stories.title: An AI agent tried to hack Canadian government website, researchers say
stories.summary: Transluce said it informed the Canadian government on Monday, Sept. 28, following which the Canadian Centre for Cybersecurity issued a statement on Tuesday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
A rogue artificial intelligence agent attempted to hack a Canadian government website earlier this year, an incident report by an AI research group revealed.

Two attempted hacks took place, one on May 28 and another on June 9 on a Canadian government website, the report by Transluce, an independent, nonprofit research lab dedicated to public oversight of AI, said on Wednesday evening.

The group observed 899 requests hitting the “collection-search” service of Library and Archives Canada, the group said, calling the attempted hack “rudimentary.”

The requests were associated with retrieving data on divorce records in Canada between 1905 and 1911.

Transluce said it informed the Canadian government on Monday, Sept. 28, following which the Canadian Centre for Cybersecurity issued a statement on Tuesday.

2:08 Australia to investigate if OpenAI hack broke the law

“We are aware of reports identifying suspicious activity, including suspected AI agent activity, targeting publicly accessible websites, such as the Government of Canada. There is no indication that government systems have been compromised at this time,” a statement from Canadian Centre for Cyber Security read.

The Cyber Centre said it is “working closely with government partners to assess the information referenced in the reports.”

The agents appeared to have used Arquivo.pt, a national Portugese web service that allows a user to search and access historical versions of web content collected since 1996. AI agents can often use Arquivo to retrieve information, since it can recover information from pages that are unavailable on the live web.

It is not yet clear whose AI agent attempted the hack, but the report suggested the “tactic” are similar to those that OpenAI has used in previous hacks.

0:46 Canadian archival website targetted by AI hack, AI firm says

“We do not confidently attribute these attempts to OpenAI, but they exhibit tactics consistent with prior observed agent activity that we have attributed to OpenAI in a similar timeframe, including the use of Arquivo.pt, conducting aggressive data collection focused on targeted, obscure information, and probing for cybersecurity vulnerabilities,” Transluce said.

The group added, however, that they “do not believe that these probes were successful.”

The report also detailed attempted hacks of the U.S. Department of Education website. This included more than 200,000 requests by the AI agent that attempted to look up school statistics.

1:59 OpenAI claims rogue model hacked other site

Incidents of rogue AI agents have been reported with growing frequency this year.

Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed details of the June hack, which targeted the website for Medicare, Australia’s publicly funded universal health insurance plan.

The AI agent accessed “both public and non-public files” from the Australian medicare website, Albanese said.

OpenAI said in a statement it had reviewed activity involving several Australian government departments and discovered “our models took actions we did not intend.”

“The Government of Canada is aware of the incident reported by the Government of Australia and is following developments closely. The security of Canadians and of the systems they rely on remains a top priority,” a spokesperson for Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada told Global News in a statement.

While this was the first time a government website had been reportedly hacked by a rogue AI agent, it is not the first such incident overall.

In July, OpenAI revealed that its artificial intelligence system escaped from a testing ground and used stolen credentials to break into the servers of Hugging Face, an AI development hub and marketplace, to obtain information it needed to carry out a task.

Since then, OpenAI’s rival company Anthropic said its AI models hacked into three other organizations during testing, triggering a company review into whether the models were able to access the internet from within testing environments that should have been sealed off.

Meta has said a “misconfiguration” during testing resulted in an AI model accessing the internet on its own and hacking another company. Google recently made a similar disclosure.

Generally, when AI companies are testing the capabilities of their agents, they are placed within a secure environment known as a “sandbox.”

Some experts say AI companies should answer some tough questions on the strength of their sandboxes.

“If they said these agents broke out of the sandbox, it was not a sandbox to begin with,” said Ebrahim Bagheri, professor at the University of Toronto’s Faculty of Information.

“A sandbox is something where you put an agent in and there is no internet connection. If that computer or sandbox is connected to the internet, then that is not a sandbox,” he added.

stories.title: Hydro-Québec to face off against industry actors like Google in data centre hearing
stories.summary: A Hydro-Québec proposal that could double the cost of energy for data centres is being put to the test at a public hearing.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
Analysts for Hydro-Québec made the case Thursday morning that the utility needs to act urgently to limit the impact of the growing data centre industry on energy costs for Quebecers.

In a public hearing in Montreal, the provincial utility called for a new energy rate that could double the cost of energy for data centres.

“I don’t think I will surprise anyone by saying that the context has changed deeply and that the era of energy surpluses is now behind us,” Sarah Trabelsi, chief of costs and pricing at Hydro-Québec.

This was part of the utility’s first presentation at a provincial energy regulator hearing. It is pitting Hydro-Québec against tech industry actors like Google as well as environmental advocates like Greenpeace.

Hydro-Québec is asking the Régie de l’énergie — the regulator — to consider a new electricity rate for data centres that require a capacity of over five megawatts.

The proposal would raise energy prices to an average of 13 cents per kilowatt hour. Data centres currently pay an average of 6.82 cents per kWh, according to Hydro-Québec’s calculations.

With the average cost of energy at around 12 cents per kWh and increasing, Hydro-Québec said it wants to ensure it does not keep selling energy to data centres at a discount that will leave other customers footing the bill.

“We’re proposing these rates in an effort to manage and mitigate, or control, the impact on our customer base as a whole,” said Trabelsi.

Hydro-Québec said data centres that would be subject to the new rate currently consume 190 MW at peak consumption and could reach 1,000 MW by 2035.

Energy costs for data centres in Quebec are much lower than in most other jurisdictions, said energy analyst Jean-François Blain in an interview.

“It creates an exceptional draw that benefits Quebec, as long as they can supply those companies,” he said.

The new rate would bring their rates closer to those of other areas.

The first part of the hearing is scheduled to last until Oct. 9, with a second part planned in December. The hearing will involve actors from several industries, such as the Canadian Federation of Independent Business and a coalition of environmental groups including Greenpeace and Nature Québec.

The provincial energy regulator will be reviewing whether a new rate for data centres is fair and sustainable.

stories.title: Highway 401 closure following crash
stories.summary: Police, and fire crews are on scene with no details available as of publishing time on possible injuries or the cause of the crash.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A section of Highway 401 is closed Thursday morning following a crash between a transport truck and a passenger vehicle.

OPP say traffic is at a standstill in the eastbound lanes between Union Road and Colonel Talbot Road.

An OPP spokesperson told CTV News that one person was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

A tow truck is on its way to the scene to remove the car that is blocking traffic and police hope to have a lane opened soon.

More information will be provided as it becomes available.

stories.title: Large, corner unit sells in the overcrowded Toronto market
stories.summary: The unit’s layout, with the living room separating two bedrooms, convinced the buyers to make the deal
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
300 Balliol St., No. 612, Toronto

Asking price: $789,000 (May, 2026)

Selling price: $745,000 (June, 2026)

Previous selling prices: $340,000 (August, 2006); $191,328 (December, 1999)

Taxes: $3,845 (2025)

Days on the market: 36

Listing and buyers’ agents: Robert Greenberg and Amir Kiabi, Harvey Kalles Real Estate Ltd.

Potential buyers toured this two-bedroom condo almost every day for five weeks this spring, but none returned with an offer to purchase. Many potential buyers liked its relatively large footprint and prime views from one corner of a boutique building siding onto Mount Pleasant Road.

“This unit had approximately 945 square feet [of living space], it was a corner unit, and it had southwest exposure, which is very desirable because it gets a lot of sun,” agent Amir Kiabi said. “That all adds to the scarcity factor. Looking at units 900 square feet and up, there were only six units that transacted in that building since 2022.”

By coincidence, Mr. Kiabi was showing different clients other large units nearby. The unit’s layout, with the living room separating the bedrooms, convinced them to buy it.

“They chose this one, No. 1, because of the layout,” Mr. Kiabi said.

This 27-year-old unit has windows in both bedrooms and a balcony wrapping around the living room.

There is a kitchen with an island, two full bathrooms and laundry machines.

The unit has a storage locker and one parking spot. Monthly fees of $842 cover water, heating and use of a gym and party room.

“The building has a good reputation; it’s well-managed and was recently improved,” Mr. Kiabi said.

“It’s in a very popular school district, and to get into that school district, you usually need to have a house.”

stories.title: Collapse of an affordable housing dream
stories.summary: Assembly Corp. was seen as a leader in the sprint toward factory-built housing. Now, its projects are in limbo after it filed for bankruptcy protection
stories.author: John Lorinc
stories.content:
It was, and May still be, the home-building industry’s version of the chicken-and-egg quandary.

When Leith Moore, an architect and infill developer, in 2021 decided to take a run at constructing modular housing, his firm tapped into a stream of small-scale affordable projects backed by governments or non-profits aiming to build quickly. Their “volumetric” components – rooms, effectively – could be built in a factory, then assembled on site.

Yet after Mr. Moore and his Assembly Corp. partners began scaling up in anticipation of a surge of new factory-built projects promised to flow through Ottawa’s new Build Canada Homes (BCH), as well as the massive planned redevelopment of the former Downsview Airport lands, actual orders simply didn’t come fast enough to sustain their capital investment.

“I feel we were early for what we thought would happen with the federal government and off-site fabrication,” he said in an interview. “That is going to come about a year after when we needed it. There’s a lot of good things happening, but they didn’t happen in time for us.”

A spokesperson for Build Canada Homes – which is the centrepiece of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s effort to drive affordable housing construction using factory-based automation, dubbed “modern methods of construction” (MMC) – said the agency “is focused on creating a predictable pipeline of housing opportunities that can support manufacturers, suppliers and builders.”

“Roughly 50 per cent of the units committed by BCH,” the spokesperson added, “incorporate MMC approaches, including modular, panelized, prefabricated and factory-built housing.”

Assembly Corp., founded in 2018 and formerly known as R-Hauz, sent shock waves through Toronto’s affordable housing circles this summer when it was forced to declare bankruptcy, just months after entering receivership in May. “We’d given [the creditors] a proposal because we thought we could do it more cost-effectively and help wind them up at a lesser cost and faster. But after many lawyers and many meetings, that didn’t really transpire.”

Several of its mass timber or modular projects, for partners such as WoodGreen, the Ymca and the Elizabeth Fry Society, are in limbo.

“The City of Toronto has actively engaged with the non-profit housing providers impacted by these proceedings,” Aviva Levy, housing development office director, said in a statement. “This includes working closely with the court-appointed receiver and non-profits to develop a path forward for completing the projects.”

According to filings posted by receiver GlassRatner , seven nearly finished housing projects with a total of 153 affordable and deeply affordable units and a combined value of almost $70-million have been affected by the bankruptcy. Three involve First Nations. Mr. Moore and several investors, including former Evergreen CEO Geoff Cape, had invested $4-million in equity and debt in the firm since 2001, according to court records. The firm had 26 employees when it applied for creditor protection.

Creditors include numerous general contractors and suppliers, most of whom have registered liens against Assembly’s projects, as well as PaceZero Capital Partners, which had provided Assembly with $5-million in financing.

Besides these projects, the company last year purchased automated fabrication equipment from a Swedish firm and was negotiating a lease with Canada Lands to build a 124,000-square-foot factory next to the 370-acre Downsview site, a cquired in 2018 by the real estate arm of PSP Investments, Northcrest . A spokesperson for Northcrest declined to comment.

“We had assigned a lease at Downsview to build a plant there supposedly this year,” said Mr. Leith. “There [are] plans for 63,000 housing units up at Downsview,” Mr. Cape said in an interview with The Globe last year. “If we can secure 5 per cent of that, that’s a billion and a half dollars [of] work that helps us become a viable company.”

Mr. Moore said he couldn’t comment on the state of the automated equipment, which is currently subject to the bankruptcy proceedings.

Both Mr. Cape and Mr. Moore hoped to see more progress in the policy environment, including more financing to sustain the factories where the components for this kind of housing could be mass produced. Mr. Cape last year fronted a lobbying effort by other modular builders while Mr. Moore was hoping for movement as part of a broader reform effort driven by Canada’s wood products sector, which released a 60-page report in the spring.

Among other things, the Canadian Forest Sector Transformation Task Force recommended a range of policies to kick-start the MMC industry, such as accelerating Bch’s procurement activities and promoting the use of Canadian wood in mass timber products.

Task force co-chair Ken Kalesnikoff , principal a B.C.-based producer of factory-based modular components made from wood, says that boosting this market involves a range of policy fixes – among them, making more land available for logging and streamlining the permitting process. U.S. tariffs and procurement restrictions are also cramping the industry. But, he adds, “Build Canada Homes really has to get their act together and get that building started.”

Mr. Moore added that the challenge was finding suppliers interested in selling Assembly the kind of specialized cross-laminated timber products it needed for its modular projects. “The issue has been that there are so few fabricators [so] there is not a lot of incentive for change.”

In the end, Assembly was unable to figure out how to create both a reliable supply chain and an order book with enough business to justify the cost of building the kind of factory required to churn out easy-to-assemble housing. “Just timing,” Mr. Moore said with a sigh. “Everything didn’t work, and so it all came crashing together, with a whole bunch of contractors and liens and financing guys and lack of patience. It was a real lesson.”

Special to The Globe and Mail

stories.title: AI agents tried and failed to hack a Canadian government website, research firm says
stories.summary: Agents attempted to access Library and Archives Canada on May 28 and June 9, Transluce said
stories.author: Kanishka Singh, Christian Martinez and Deepa Seetharaman
stories.content:
AI agents trying to obtain Canadian divorce records from the early 1900s queried a Library and Archives Canada database hundreds of times.

When they couldn’t get what they were after, they turned to hacking, according to a Sept. 30 report by AI research firm Transluce and cybersecurity firm Corridor, both of which are based in San Francisco.

“What we uncovered is that in the course of trying to obtain this mundane data, the agents seemingly ran into various roadblocks,” said Jack Cable, CEO and co-founder of Corridor and one of the report’s authors.

“They couldn’t access some of the data that they had been prompted to get, and then decide to go and attempt to access the data through other means, including attempting very basic hacks,” Mr. Cable said.

As far as the researchers can tell, the hacking attempts failed. But the incident is the latest example of the lengths to which semi-autonomous AI agents will go to achieve the tasks set for them by humans.

It also appears to be the first publicly reported intrusion attempt of a Canadian government website by AI agents.

Agents created by San Francisco-based OpenAI have infiltrated the systems of several organizations this year, including AI platform Hugging Face and the Australian government , and have interacted with U.S. government websites, including that of the Securities and Exchange Commission, in unexpected ways.

Independent researchers have discovered that the company’s agents have also used more than 10 websites to communicate with one another, including a tool that the University of Toronto uses to make web links easier to share .

Mr. Cable said he and his fellow researchers were scouring the web for AI agent activity and found evidence of it on arquivo.pt, an internet archive operated by the Portuguese Foundation for Science and Technology.

The archive recorded 899 requests sent to Library and Archives Canada in late May and early June, searching for data on divorce records between 1905 and 1911. Thirteen of those requests were malicious, Mr. Cable said.

Although the researchers could not definitively link the activity to OpenAI, it had many of the hallmarks of previous behaviour by the company’s agents, including the use of arquivo.pt to fetch information, the aggressive collection of data on obscure topics and the attempts to probe for cybersecurity vulnerabilities.

Mr. Cable and his colleagues alerted the Canadian government, which is reviewing their findings. He emphasized that what the researchers can see is just a “sliver” of what AI agents are doing on the web.

“We were fortunate and lucky in many ways that we were able to stumble across this data, that the agents left these public trails in the first place, but that certainly isn’t always going to be the case,” Mr. Cable said.

OpenAI said it’s reviewing reports of its models attempting to access information from Canadian government websites and has provided an initial briefing to the officials conducting the review.

The ChatGPT-maker is currently in the midst of a broader review of instances where its models behaved in misaligned ways. Misalignment is an industry term that refers to an AI system behaving contrary to human values, safety rules or intentions. Part of that process involves investigating findings in third-party reports and comparing them with its own findings, OpenAI said in a statement.

“Most of the activity we’ve reviewed involved routine research tasks, including accessing public web content. Some involved government websites, which our models often use as authoritative sources of public information,” the statement said.

OpenAI recently announced it has developed a framework for tracking, investigating and disclosing misalignment.

Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon’s office said in a statement that it’s working closely with the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security as part of Ottawa’s assessment.

“At this time, there is no indication that Government of Canada systems were compromised,” the statement said.

Communications Security Establishment Canada, the federal agency that provides the government with tech security and foreign signals intelligence, said it’s aware of reports of suspected AI agent activity targeting publicly accessible websites, including Canadian government sites, and is working closely with government and industry partners to assess the information referenced in the reports.

Mark Daley, Western University’s chief AI officer, said that although the hacking attempts were unsuccessful, it’s alarming that the agents would resort to such measures in an attempt to retrieve data. “A human employee presumably wouldn’t do that,” he said.

Although the Canadian government deserves “a pat on the back” for having properly secured the website, the attack was not particularly advanced, Mr. Daley noted.

“The broader problem is that these agents are going to get more and more sophisticated,” he said.

stories.title: Improved team and arena renovations make it ‘a great time to be a Sting fan’
stories.summary: When Sarnia Sting fans arrive for the home opener Friday against Sault Ste. Marie, they are going to see much more than a first-place hockey club.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
When Sarnia Sting fans arrive for the home opener Friday against Sault Ste. Marie, they are going to see much more than a first-place hockey club.

Massive renovations have taken place at Progressive Auto Sales Arena in Sarnia, Ont. during the Ontario Hockey League (OHL) offseason.

“We’re really excited to launch District 94,” said Jake Bourrie, vice president of business operations for the Sting.

“It lives in the heart of Progressive Auto Sales Arena. We’re thrilled to have ownership here with the Sting from Ryan Finch, David Legwand and Mark Guy who have made a significant investment into the food and beverage experience here and it starts here in the restaurant.”

“Whether we win or lose, we want our fans to leave saying, ‘I had a great time, and I’m looking forward to the next game.’”

On the ice, the Sting are off to a great start. They played all four of their games on the road as the arena renovations are ongoing and won three of four including their first victory in Ottawa in nearly two decades.

“I think you don’t want to look too far ahead,” said Sting captain Alessandro Di Iorio.

“You want to play hard and you want to play tough and fast. I think we’ve done on the first three games and if we keep playing, I think we’ll be very successful.”

The Sting have missed the playoffs for three consecutive seasons. After undergoing an ownership change last year, they brought in head coach Mathieu Turcotte in November 2025, replacing Alan Letang.

“The biggest thing is kind of gaining that respect back overall is pretty much the theme this year,” said Turcotte.

“With the past few years, we want to make sure that we shift things, we turn things around and make sure that we fight for that division every year.”

There have been a lot of roster turnover and new faces, with the new owners striving for a winning culture on and off the ice.

“They are making the investments but also the commitment and the sweat equity that they’re putting in,” said Bourrie.

“They’re here rolling up their sleeves and helping support in all aspects of our business. It’s a great time to be a Sting fan.”

“Our ownership group put a lot of time and effort and obviously money into all the renovations here so it’s a great fan experience,” said Turcotte.

stories.title: Toronto board of trade urges Ontario to amend zoning and building code rules to spur housing growth
stories.summary: Province is on pace to fall well short of its goal of getting at least 1.5 million new homes built by 2031
stories.author: Sammy Hudes
stories.content:
The Toronto Region Board of Trade is urging the province to amend zoning and building code rules as it says Ontario is on pace to fall well short of its goal of getting at least 1.5 million new homes built by 2031.

In a report published Thursday, the board said the target is unachievable by the current deadline, which was set by the provincial government in 2022, even if housing production increases over the next five years. Based on budget forecasts, Ontario is projected to fall more than 550,000 homes short of the pace needed by 2029, according to the analysis.

“We already had a massive gap. It was called the housing crisis for a reason,” said board president and CEO Giles Gherson in an interview.

“There’s been a lot of effort and a lot of work gone into, ‘How do we close this housing gap? How do we build houses faster?’ But the disappointing part of it is that the gap remains very, very large.”

The board said that even if ambitious reforms were adopted immediately, municipalities would need to update plans, amend zoning bylaws, align infrastructure investments, service land, and process applications. Those steps could take years, making the 2031 goal unrealistic.

Gherson said the key to unlocking new development at a quicker pace is through regulatory changes.

He described rules around zoning and building codes as “very fragmented” across the province, and “out of date.” In Toronto alone, builders face dozens of different requirements across the city, which makes it difficult to standardize production.

“It really adds a huge amount of cost and delay to housing development and that impacts the ability for the city to attract and retain our work force that we need,” he said.

“But also, we know it is impacting the social fabric as the next generation sees home ownership as really a pipe dream, and that’s a really big problem.”

The report said Ontario should develop a provincial zoning code that provides every municipality the same framework and terminology.

That code could set a baseline of what housing types can move forward without special approval, starting with townhouses and multiplexes. The standard could also establish provincewide limits on the rules that most often block housing, such as parking, setbacks, lot coverage, height, density, and how far upper storeys must step back.

Meanwhile, it recommended key changes around building codes, saying there should be an assessment of every requirement for the cost it imposes to build, run and maintain over the life of the building. The report also proposed allowing single-stair buildings up to six storeys, along with smaller elevators in smaller buildings, as long as safety and accessibility are still prioritized.

Gherson said other cities in Canada are proof that a less patchy model can lead to meaningful housing growth. He pointed to Edmonton, where he said it’s more common see multiplexes in different types of neighbourhoods.

The call for action comes as affordability challenges persist for Toronto’s housing market, even as prices have been on the decline over the past year.

Last month, the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board said the average selling price in the Greater Toronto Area stood at $993,410 for August, down 2.7 per cent year-over-year, while the composite benchmark price, meant to represent the typical home, was down 4.5 per cent.

It said that between 2006 and 2025, Toronto-area home prices, as measured by the composite price, increased by around 187 per cent. That significantly outpaced the cumulative increase for inflation over that time, which was around 51 per cent.

“Durable affordability depends on increasing the supply of homes,” the report said.

“Without continued housing construction, recent affordability gains are likely to prove temporary.”

stories.title: New rules for short-term rentals in London start today
stories.summary: As part of the changes through the city, hosts will be limited to one short-term rental and one short-term rental licence.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
take effect today. As part of the changes through the city, hosts will be limited to one short-term rental and one short-term rental licence. Hosts also cannot own or partly own more than one home or unit used as a short-term rental.

“These changes help protect housing in London and support responsible hosting in our neighbourhoods,” says Amanda Pfeffer, director of municipal compliance. “Hosts are responsible for making sure their rentals are licensed and follow City rules.

That includes being ready for the new limits on Oct. 1.” Short-term rentals include homes or rooms rented for stays of 28 days or less. Hosts already need a City business licence before advertising a rental or welcoming guests.

The rental must be at the address where the host lives. The licence number must be included in all ads and listings. Residents can check whether a rental is licensed on the City’s website. To report concerns about an unlicensed rental or nuisance issues, call Municipal Compliance at 519-930-3515 or email licensing@London.CA.

stories.title: Foundation proposes national policy agenda on menopause
stories.summary: Menopause Foundation of Canada is calling for more training among health providers and increased research funding
stories.author: Tavia Grant
stories.content:
A new national campaign is calling on governments to boost support for Canadian women experiencing menopause, laying out what it says is a blueprint to help Canada become a world leader for care.

The Menopause Foundation of Canada, with backing from other groups, including the Society of Obstetricians and Gynecologists of Canada, is releasing a menopause policy agenda on Thursday. It calls for more training of health providers, more funding for research and expanded access to treatment.

“Menopause isn’t just a women’s health issue. It’s a matter of public policy, workforce sustainability and economic resilience,” Janet Ko, the foundation’s president and co-founder, said in an interview.

Unmanaged symptoms of menopause cost the Canadian economy $3.5-billion a year, the foundation has estimated. Women older than 40 make up a quarter of the country’s paid workforce, and most will reach menopause between the ages of 45 and 55. Many will experience symptoms that range from difficulty sleeping to night sweats, brain fog, migraines, heart palpitations and anxiety.

Those symptoms May cause some to reduce their hours, turn down promotions, or step into lesser roles, denting incomes in their peak earning years, the foundation said.

As The Globe and Mail has previously reported, Canada doesn’t have a national strategy on menopause. It hasn’t had a national health campaign (Australia currently has one underway). And funding for dedicated research is still scarce.

In a paper to be released Thursday, the non-profit organization sets out seven priorities for provincial, territorial and federal governments. These include mandating menopause education for all physicians and nurse practitioners, adjusting fee structures so that physicians are adequately compensated for care, and ensuring menopause medications are accessible and affordable.

“Despite more conversation about menopause, systemic barriers are keeping women from getting the care they deserve,” Ms. Ko said.

“This is an urgent call to action for government to transform menopause care, support and research in Canada,” she said. The policy priorities provide a blueprint for decision-makers, and “an opportunity for Canada to lead the world in equitable menopause care and support.”

The foundation’s surveys have found that one in two women feel unprepared for menopause and perimenopause, a transition period where the body prepares to stop having periods. Two in five feel their symptoms were undertreated by their health care provider.

This is the first-ever proposed national policy agenda on menopause in Canada, and was two years in the making, the foundation says.

Access to menopause care is not equal, the report says, citing research , and many women are having difficulty finding help. The gaps are widest for Black, Indigenous, and racialized women, as well as for newcomers, those living in rural and remote communities, gender-diverse people, and those with lower incomes. A lack of access is forcing some to pay out of pocket – or go without care.

“Access to safe, evidence-based menopause care should never depend on a person’s ability to pay,” Ms. Ko said, adding that public menopause clinics and publicly funded virtual care can help fill the gap.

Other recommendations include policies that support women in the workplace, and more training for doctors. Currently, there is no standardized menopause curriculum for healthcare providers in Canada.

Nnamdi Ndubuka, president of Black Physicians of Canada, is among those supporting the initiative. “Better menopause education for healthcare providers is essential to ensuring that every patient receives the care they deserve,” he said in a release.

The foundation also named Sophie Grégoire Trudeau, an author, advocate and public speaker, as its first ambassador.

Perimenopause can last for eight years or longer and brings varying experiences. For some, symptoms are mild, while for others, they can be debilitating.

“Too many women are suffering through this transition without ever being told that menopause is at the root of their experience,” Ms. Grégoire Trudeau said in the report. “They are dismissed, misdiagnosed, or left to figure it out alone. Failing half our population comes at a cost we all share.”

Research on the health of half of the population is scant. One 2025 study found that just 7 per cent of all funded grants went to female-specific research over a 15-year period; of that small pool, little went to menopause research.

This research gap has consequences, the report said, as health care providers and policy-makers lack the data to support women through midlife transitions that have a lasting impact on heart, bone and brain health.

stories.title: Minimum wage hike is now in effect across five provinces
stories.summary: Bumps of between 25 and 40 cents come in Ontario, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Manitoba and Saskatchewan
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The minimum wage is going up in five provinces.

The bumps of between 25 and 40 cents come in Ontario, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Manitoba and Saskatchewan.

Like other government announcements, Ontario has tied the increase to the rising cost of living.

It’s moving its minimum wage up to $17.95 an hour, while P.E.I. is boosting it to $17.30 and Nova Scotia moves it to $17.

In Manitoba, the wage goes up to $16.40, and in Saskatchewan to $15.70.

The changes mean all provinces and territories will have raised their rates this year with the exception of Alberta, which hasn’t increased its minimum wage since 2019.

Alberta maintains the country’s lowest minimum wage at $15 an hour.

Nunavut lifted its minimum wage at the beginning of September and leads the country at just over $20 an hour.

The victim has been identified as a 34-year-old from Thames Centre.

Thames Centre - One person has died after a crash involving a vehicle and a cyclist in Thames Centre.

Police say it happened on Richmond Street shortly before 12:30 p.m. yesterday, between Gore Road and Marion Street.

stories.title: Saskatchewan mayor who clashed with ‘Queen of Canada’ cult to step down
stories.summary: Village of Richmound says Brad Miller’s resignation takes effect Oct. 14 and that information about a by-election will be shared once a date is set
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The mayor of a southwestern Saskatchewan village that spent two years bedevilled by the Kingdom of Canada cult is stepping down.

A brief social media post from the Village of Richmound says Brad Miller’s resignation takes effect Oct. 14 and that information about a by-election will be shared once a date is set.

The village first made headlines in 2023 when the so-called “Queen of Canada” Romana Didulo and her followers set up a compound in a former school and soon began badgering residents.

The school had its sewer and water access cut off and was later closed for health reasons, as open sewage could be seen bubbling on the grounds.

Didulo, who rose to prominence from the 2022 “Freedom Convoy” in Ottawa, was among 16 arrested in a police raid of the compound in September, 2025, though charges against her were stayed in March.

Miller said at the time that he hoped Didulo and her followers would leave Saskatchewan.

stories.title: B.C.’s major parties on track to field candidates in all ridings as deadline looms
stories.summary: Smaller parties are struggling ahead of the Oct. 3 nomination deadline
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
The major parties running in British Columbia’s election appear to be on track to fill each of the 93 ridings, but smaller parties are struggling ahead of the Oct. 3 nomination deadline.

Elections BC lists 43 official candidates for the B.C. New Democrats, while there are 32 on the list for the Conservatives as of Sept. 30.

Both parties say on their websites that those numbers are much higher, but candidate figures for those running in the smaller parties remain in the single digits.

CentreBC and OneBC have one official candidate each, while seven Greens candidates have been registered with Elections BC.

All three parties say their candidate count is higher than that, but all are under 20 each.

Neither CentreBC nor OneBC existed during the last election in 2024, but emerged as the fledgling B.C. Conservative Party splintered amid disagreements shortly after coming within a few seats of forming government.

stories.title: Canada’s role in space exploration
stories.summary: Alberta-native Joshua Kutryk will be on his way this week for a six-month visit to the International Space Station.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
stories.content:
In today’s The Big Story podcast, another Canadian is heading to space! Alberta-native Joshua Kutryk will be on his way this week for a six-month visit to the International Space Station, alongside three other crew members onboard NASA’s SpaceX Crew 13 mission. They plan on conducting research, maintenance, as well as experiments as they orbit the Earth.

Host Catherine Jetté speaks to Major Erin Edwards, NASA Deputy Branch Chief for Crew Operation and ISS CAPCOM instructor. They discuss Kutryk’s mission, and Canadian impacts on space exploration and advancement at large.

You can subscribe to The Big Story podcast on Apple Podcasts and Spotify .

stories.title: New bill should help prevent strikes in the 'centre of the economy,' think tank report says
stories.summary: The Carney government’s recent legislation designed to avoid crippling strikes was an important response, a new think tank report says.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Carney government’s recent legislation designed to avoid crippling strikes in the transportation sector was an important response to a growing trend that had the potential to cause serious economic damage, a new think tank report says.

In a report to be released Thursday, the Montreal Economic Institute (MEI) writes that Ottawa is justified in stepping in when the two sides in a labour dispute are not “remotely close to reaching common ground” and millions Canadians are paying the price.

The report cited recent lockouts at the ports of Montreal and Vancouver in 2024 and a labour strike a year later at Air Canada as examples of work stoppages that threatened major swaths of the Canadian economy and thousands of jobs. Airlines, ports and rail services are considered key parts of national infrastructure and are relied on by miners, manufacturers, farmers and many other economic sectors.

In August, 2024, for example, the simultaneous shutdowns of rail services at CN and Cpkc threatened the transport of about $1-billion of goods a day, the report says.

Gabriel Giguère, a senior policy analyst at MEI and the report’s author, said these types of transportation companies are different than most other employers and warrant unique legislation to help keep them in operation.

“It’s at the centre of the economy,” Giguère said of the transportation sector.

Christopher Monette, a spokesman with Teamsters Canada, whose members include truck drivers and dock workers, said the Canadian economy can withstand limited disruptions much more than “anti-union voices” suggest. More than 95 per cent of collective agreements are resolved without a work stoppage, he said.

“Claiming that few remaining cases are enough to cripple our economy is factually baseless and sells Canada short.”

Canada's unions considering legal action to protect right to strike

Business groups applaud Liberal government’s bill to curb work stoppages and fast-track project approvals

Ottawa’s response to the sector’s stoppage threat was Bill C-39, more commonly known as the Building Canada Strong Act, an omnibus bill that was introduced last week. The proposed legislation is designed, among many other things, to make it easier to resolve labour disputes in federally regulated transportation industries by clarifying the process for government intervention.

The bill’s measures include an increase in the conciliation period before a strike or lockout and the explicit ability for the labour minister to intervene in the event of a “significant adverse national impact.”

The MEI says the problem of work stoppages in these important sectors has been on the rise. There were 22 recorded work stoppages in the transport sector between 2024 and 2025, an annual average almost three times the four work stoppages in those sectors in 2016.

The government was able to force resolutions to some work stoppages in the industry but its legislative authority was sometimes called into question. This legislation clarifies Ottawa’s ability to take action, as well as the process for doing so.

Monette said the number of referrals have been on the rise because employers lobby the government to use the existing legislation, then point to its frequent use as proof of its importance.

Workers’ rights to strike and to collective bargaining are protected in the Canadian constitution, Monette added, and those rights can’t be ignored because of an alleged economic disruption.

stories.title: How a couple with vastly different financial attitudes managed a $1-million inheritance
stories.summary: A free spender who came into money had a what’s-mine-is-yours mentality, but her frugal spouse wasn’t convinced the funds should be communal
stories.author: Rosemary Counter
stories.content:
The beneficiaries: “Christopher” and his wife “Jacqueline” are government workers in Toronto with good (but not great) pensions in their future. They’re both on the cusp of 50, and have a university-aged daughter. Like many couples, Christopher and his wife – one money-minded saver and one a laissez-faire spender – have very different approaches to money and finances.

The inheritance: A few years ago, Jacqueline’s well-off parents died in short succession, bequeathing Jacqueline an impressive inheritance she always knew was coming her way: After taxes and red tape, it was almost a million dollars cash. “She came right to me and said, ‘What should we do with it?!’,” says Christopher. He was relieved and grateful for her generous what’s-mine-is-yours mentality, but wasn’t quite convinced the money should be communal after all.

What they learned: Firstly, some important context: “We come from two very different families,” he says. “I grew up lower-middle-class and my parents divorced when I was a kid. They worked long hours and double jobs, and I put myself through school with loans.” Christopher came into their marriage with plenty of debt he’s since worked diligently to pay off. All of it’s been paid off except the mortgage, which they got after getting married with some help from his in-laws, but still Christopher monitors their money very closely.

Jacqueline enjoyed a far more privileged upbringing in a nuclear family. “They were both professionals, very comfortable with their house being paid off completely, and they’d received family money as well,” says Christopher. His wife therefore never had to rely on loans from banks, indeed never learned much about managing or budgeting money and spends freely most of the time, be it on Uber Eats or arts-and-crafts supplies. “She’s a retail therapy kind of person,” he says. “If she sees something she wants, she buys it.”

Despite their different spending habits, newlyweds Christopher and Jacqueline pooled their money together and have been navigating life via joint account ever since (That’s the approach taken by about a quarter of Canadian couples, according to a new study by personal finance website MooseMoney, though thanks to younger demographics, that percentage is shrinking). Jacqueline agreed to discuss any purchase she makes that’s more than a couple hundred dollars in advance; Christopher agreed to relax a bit and stop asking permission from his wife for every little purchase he makes. Their strategy works well to balance the other out, he notes.

But for reasons he can’t quite articulate, Christopher didn’t and doesn’t feel comfortable casually tossing a million dollars into the joint pot. It doesn’t relate to his parents’ divorce, he says, although he agrees that the psychology of money runs deep. “Yes, we’re married, and yes, it’s a partnership, but it doesn’t feel like my money. It’s her money and if she wants to spend it freely, I wouldn’t fight her. I might try to nudge her in another direction, but no fighting.”

What they did with it: Luckily, the couple’s first big decision was almost made for them. “My father-in-law had told us that when he went, he wanted us to pay off the mortgage. He wanted us to have that sense of comfort that they had,” says Christopher. A large lump sum paid off the principal a decade earlier than anticipated.

Jacqueline’s neglected TFSAs were then topped up to the max, and for both pragmatic tax reasons and because she insisted, Christopher’s were, too. Since those accounts are filled, they next opened a spousal Rrsp and rejigged the timeline so that Jacqueline can retire early if she wants. To their daughter who’s about to enter the working world, they gifted $10,000 to ease the tough transition. “We want her to have a bit of a safety net and something to learn to build on,” Christopher says.

The couple hundred thousand that was left over is currently sitting in an investment account in his wife’s name. “It’s the only separation we have in terms of finances, but I want her to have something that’s just hers,” he says. If she spends it all on vacations and takeout, that’ll have to be fine by him, though he’ll do whatever he can to mitigate the damage from any spending he feels is frivolous.

“Her money’s under her name, but I have the account passwords to double-check dividends and reinvest wisely,” he says. Now she can spend and he can save so everyone’s happy in their element.

stories.title: Right? Left? Blue? Red? How do I choose a side when no party reflects all my values?
stories.summary: An ethicist answers a Globe reader’s question on how to balance concerns about climate change and free speech
stories.author: Shawna Cohen
stories.content:
Divisive political debates are a constant these days, with or without a federal election campaign on the horizon. For some Canadians, it can be hard to decide who to support when more than one party has policies they agree (or disagree) with.

In the first instalment of Conscience Call – a new series exploring everyday ethical, moral and philosophical dilemmas – we pose a reader’s question about voting strategies to an expert for advice.

Do you have a dilemma you’d like some guidance on? Tell us about it here .

Our reader Shane from Toronto writes:

I am someone who is deeply concerned about the climate crisis. At the same time, during the last three federal elections, I voted for the Conservative Party of Canada, even though I do not agree with its policies when it comes to protecting the environment.

Although I worry about what a Conservative government would mean for Canada’s fight against climate change, I would also never vote for the Liberal Party of Canada because, in my opinion, it has become increasingly illiberal through abandoning classically liberal values such as free speech, the rights of the individual and equality under the law.

I feel stuck between a rock and a hard place, because each of the two major political parties have ideas and policies that I strongly agree with, as well as those that I disagree with. How can I find a way to fight climate change while safeguarding classically liberal values?

From the ethicist: Arthur Schafer, professor and founding director of the Centre for Professional and Applied Ethics at the University of Manitoba

In Canada, with our electoral system, we have just a few major parties and each is a big tent. They include people with very different interests and priorities, all working together under one banner.

Each party represents policies on a broad range of issues, and if you’re looking for one that exactly represents your preferences and values on several different matters, you’re likely not going to find it. You’re never going to find a perfect match.

Most of us have several fundamental values, and we somehow weigh and balance those against the policies of a particular party. The question is: Which of your values should trump the others or be given the heaviest weight?

The weight you give those values can also change. In different circumstances, one value might deserve a higher priority. If we’re having a crisis in our health care system, a party that’s going to protect universal health care might become my priority. That May not ordinarily be at the top of my list – it might be the environment. But if universal coverage is threatened with collapse, I might vote for a party that has the best policy on protecting it, even though I disagree with them on other issues.

So ask yourself: At this time in Canadian history, and at this point in my life, what matters more to me, my family and my fellow citizens?

But how do you weigh two things that are both extremely important to you at the same time? Here’s an analogy: You’re trying to decide if you should take a job where the work is really satisfying but the pay is kind of poor, or one where the work is not fulfilling, but it pays really well.

The competing values aren’t commensurable. They’re apples and oranges. How do you weigh salary against work satisfaction? Yet, we do it all the time, such as when we’re choosing a job, a life partner or where to live. We somehow commensurate the incommensurable, but it’s mostly intuitive. There isn’t an easy way.

In your case, there is another question worth asking: Are the two values you’ve identified really as separate as they appear? The issues aren’t in silos. I would urge you to think about how your commitment to climate change is related to your commitment to freedom of expression. Look at the way the different policies you care about interact with one another. They May overlap and reinforce each other, or they May cut against each other.

Next, consider what you want your vote to accomplish. Ask yourself: Do I vote for the party whose policies and values are second-best because it’s the most likely to form government? Or do I vote on principle for the party that embodies the values I care about, even if I know it’s extremely unlikely to win the election?

You might vote for a party, even though you believe it’s not likely to win. The purpose might be to send a message that you’re someone who has this set of values. Or should you go for the second-best to minimize the harm done by another party you feel most opposed to?

There’s a cost regardless of the strategy you adopt. By voting pragmatically, you May be voting for policies that you don’t really agree with, in order to prevent even worse policies. But you’re also reinforcing the likelihood that the best policies will never be on the agenda, because the people who favour them haven’t sent a strong enough message.

I don’t think there’s any once-and-for-all best answer. It’s going to depend on the circumstances. It’s going to depend on you as a person. The question is what matters most to you under the circumstances you are facing now.

As told to Shawna Cohen. Responses have been edited and condensed.

stories.title: Cybersecurity vendor Field Effect growing fast with new tool targeting ‘shadow AI’ at companies
stories.summary: Ottawa company’s customer base has jumped 33 per cent since launching AI detection and response tool in June
stories.author: Sean Silcoff
stories.content:
Matt Holland started his career with Canada’s cybersecurity espionage agency, writing code for offensive security missions and breaking into information technology systems of the country’s enemies following the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001.

The cyberspy-turned-cybersecurity entrepreneur is still targeting threats, but he’s no longer going after al-Qaeda. His new pursuit is artificial intelligence – specifically, AI that lurks undetected within companies or is misused by employees.

In June, Mr. Holland’s company, Field Effect Software Inc., introduced an AI detection-and-response tool to help its small and medium business clientele. It prevents employees from unwittingly uploading sensitive corporate data to platforms like Claude or ChatGPT, blocking use that violates corporate policies, and will soon track prompts – the instructions users provide to generate AI content.

The program also stops so-called “shadow AI” programs operating within corporations – such as AI features added to cloud software they’ve used for years – from unknowingly accessing and transmitting their data to places they aren’t supposed to go. Mr. Holland, Field Effect’s chief executive officer, said in an interview his AI tool is “like a chaperone with a grimace and a large stick to smack the AI when it’s gone off the rails.”

That is what many companies want. In less than four months, privately-held Field Effect has seen its user base jump by about one-third, to 12,000 companies from about 9,000, largely driven by demand for its AI-targeting tool. The Ottawa-based company’s annualized revenues are approaching $50-million, up from $26-million last year.

Mr. Holland estimates Field Effect will add 3,000 more customers this year and aims to raise US$100-million in 2027 to fuel expansion. Field Effect also plans to launch the AI tool this fall as a stand-alone product for companies of all sizes.

“Once we start to put that money to use on the commercial side, I will be shocked if we don’t grow 80 per cent to 100 per cent a year for the next five years,” he said. Recent stories that AI bosses themselves worry their tools are dangerous “are creating the business case for us in real time.”

Field Effect is one of several companies offering digital nannies to help organizations ensure the proliferation of AI applications within their operations won’t cause harm.

Toronto’s Signal 1 has developed an AI management system for health-care organizations to oversee all the new tools and making sure, for example, that AI-generated draft e-mails from doctors to patients conform to hospital standards. Teramind Inc. of Aventura, Fla., polices employee activity on computers, networks and other digital “end points” to ensure they aren’t using unapproved AI tools or uploading corporate data. Nvidia Corp. Nvda-Q this week announced a security platform that will set boundaries it says could stop rogue activity by AI.

“A lot of organizations haven’t figured out how to utilize AI correctly, let alone what is it being given access to, and there’s virtually no real controls around it,” said CEO Jeff Farr of Dallas-based Sera Brynn LLC, which manages cybersecurity services for companies and deploys Field Effect products to customers. Its new AI tool, he said, “has been eye-opening for several of our customers when they actually look” at the issue. “The light bulbs are going off in a big way, because almost nobody has a clue.”

Rob Schenk, chief strategy officer with Las Vegas-based Intelligent Technical Solutions, another third-party cybersecurity services provider that deploys Field Effect to about 800 clients, said “AI is becoming a driver of additional revenue for companies like ours.” Field Effect’s AI tool, he said “complements the direction that clients need to go. It’s accelerating the conversation.”

Canada’s plan to counter the U.S. and China in AI is taking shape. Will it work?

Mr. Holland joined the federal Communications Security Establishment’s Tailored Access Operations (TAO) group in 2000 after studying computer science at University of New Brunswick, earning a reputation as one of the best in the trade at understanding operating systems, and how to defend and exploit them.

After the Sept. 11 attacks. Tao’s profile within the cyberespionage unit swelled. Mr. Holland left in 2007 to start Linchpin Labs, which built software for Canada and its “Five Eyes” intelligence-sharing allies – the U.S., Britain, Australia and New Zealand – to run cyberintelligence operations. He self-funded the company and sold it to defence giant L3 Technologies in 2018 for US$200-million.

Mr. Holland decided to focus next on helping small companies protect against threats from cyberattacks. With Field Effect he set out to create an all-encompassing, affordable and simple product for small businesses offering the kind of protection large companies get. That platform combines a range of internally built capabilities to comprehensively monitor a client’s vulnerable digital assets, including network, computing devices, connected sensors and cloud operations.

Mr. Holland believed its holistic approach and “zero trust” modus operandi (as in never trust, always verify) would serve Field Effect well as it developed its AI detection tool. Now, he said, “We have the technology that guards against AI going off the rails.”
