stories.title: West Coast pipeline deadline day: Carney, Smith to make announcement in Fort McMurray
stories.summary: Thursday marks Ottawa's deadline to decide whether to designate a proposed pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia's south coast as a project of national interest.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has designated a new West Coast pipeline project as being in the “national interest,” paving the way towards approval for a project to ship an additional one million barrels of crude oil daily to Asian markets.

Carney made the announcement over the newly dubbed Pacific Link pipeline in Fort McMurray , Alta., Thursday flanked by Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

“We have to do this, because the world is facing an energy crisis on three dimensions,” Carney said.

“There’s an immediate challenge of affordability and in some countries the very availability of hydrocarbons, there is a structural challenge of energy security and the existential challenge of climate change.

“These challenges are forcing countries to think differently about where their energy comes from and who they can rely on to supply it.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "These challenges are forcing countries to think differently about where their energy comes from and who they can rely on to supply it."

Carney said that oil demand is expected to “continue to be significant for decades to come, even under any plausible net zero scenario.”

Global oil supply, meanwhile, is becoming more volatile with the U.S. war against Iran.

“So the question is, who will emerge as the world’s trusted suppliers? It should be us. It must be Canada,” Carney said.

The decision to classify the pipeline as in the national interest means it will fall under Carney’s Major Projects Office (MPO), a government branch meant to speed federal approvals for significant economic initiatives.

The project will still need to undergo a regulatory review by the MPO as well as public hearings led by the Canada Energy Regulator. The government is expected to then issue a “conditions document,” which would outline the requirements for the project proponents.

The MPO is expected to issue those conditions by Sept. 1, 2027.

The pipeline is expected to jointly owned by Trans Mountain Corporation (TMC), the Alberta Petroleum Marketing Commission (Apmc), and the Pembina Pipeline Corporation. A minimum of 10 per cent equity in Pacific Link will be offered to Indigenous peoples.

Pacific Link would transport roughly one million barrels per day of crude from Bruderheim, Alta., to a deepwater port outside Delta, B.C., spanning approximately 1,250 kilometres.

The oil would then be loaded on large tanker ships for export to markets in Asia.

The project is a major test of Canada’s new major projects strategy and its ability to deliver regulatory certainty and predictable timelines, according to business management analyst Lance Mortlock, the managing partner of EY’s energy market segment and a University of Calgary associate professor.

“It’s signals that we want to build again,” said Mortlock, adding the announcement sends a broader message about Canada’s commitment to building infrastructure within globally competitive timelines.

“Markets will be watching less for the announcement itself, but more whether governments can now deliver that regulatory certainty, clearer timelines, and more predictable investment conditions.

“So now that process starts.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "So now that process starts."

In a briefing before the announcement, the government tied the decision directly to the trade war with U.S. President Donald Trump and the instability caused by his trade war.

“When you think about the geopolitical backdrop — tension in the Middle East, war — the world needs energy security and I think a lot of Asian markets are looking for diversification and optionality,” Mortlock said.

“Canada is coming forward, and I think it happens at a really important time.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Canada is coming forward, and I think it happens at a really important time."

Oil and gas is Alberta’s biggest industry and global energy prices have a significant impact on provincial coffers , but the landlocked Prairie province has been hampered for decades by not enough shipping capacity to get product to tidewater.

“Resource wealth is only valuable if you can actually reach markets,” Mortlock said. “We’ve got all this resource wealth across this great country, but if we can’t get it to market, it’s not worth the wealth that we talk about.”

The need to diversify export markets, the government argued, is a matter of national sovereignty.

“Today, 90 per cent of Alberta’s oil goes to the U.S.,” Carney said. “Pacific Link will materially reduce that dependence by allowing us to export an additional one million barrels a day to growing markets in Asia.”

“That means more customers, more choice, and higher prices for all Canadian energy producers.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "That means more customers, more choice, and higher prices for all Canadian energy producers."

In a statement, NDP Leader Avi Lewis blasted the Carney government for committing public money to back a pipeline in the midst of the climate crisis, and suggested the project would face legal challenges making it “not worth the risk.”

“Throwing billions in public money behind a pipeline at a time of climate breakdown – while sweeping aside environmental protections, meaningful Indigenous consultation and workers’ right to strike – is absolutely not in the national interest,” Lewis said.

“Projects that truly serve the national interest would lower costs, create good jobs, and protect the people and places we love — like renewable energy projects, 21st-century public transit systems to connect our communities, and a massive build-out of non-market housing Canadians can actually afford.”

But while Lewis criticized the government for “rushing” the pipeline’s approval, the Conservatives faulted the Liberals for taking too long.

Carole Anstey, the Conservatives’ natural resources critic, says the party wants the pipeline built but noted Thursday’s announcement was not putting “shovels in the ground.”

“I think Canadians certainly heard a promise from the prime minister to move at speeds not seen in generations … We would like to see this move forward at the speed that the prime minister promised,” Anstey said in an interview.

Oil and gas producers have, in recent years, shied away from big-ticket extraction investments — in part due to a shortage of pipeline infrastructure to bring their oil to market.

Industry has welcomed Ottawa’s moves to simplify the regulatory process, roll back Trudeau-era environmental policies and beef up tax incentives for new investments.

Smaller scale, shorter-term pipeline expansion projects are now in the works heading to the U.S. and West Coast.

“We will start to see the companies develop big capital projects again,” Mortlock predicted.

“Do I think that we’re going to see the mega mines that we saw 10 years ago? Probably not. But do I think we’re going to see 150,000, 200,000-barrel-a-day in situ expansion? Yeah, for sure,” Mortlock said, referring to steam-driven operations with a smaller footprint.

A TD Economics report released this summer said the potential pipeline would boost oil exports by 20 per cent and more than double what Canada currently sends to Asia via tankers.

“The opportunity is not just the pipeline, the opportunity is proving that Canada can once again execute large nation-building projects that attract capital, strengthen trade competitiveness and create Indigenous prosperity and improve economic sovereignty,” Mortlock noted.

“The risk is that Canada proves it can announce faster than it can deliver. So what we need to do now is back it up to say, ‘we can announce fast — but we can deliver fast too.'”

But whatever economic benefits a pipeline project brings, it carries both environmental and political risks for the Carney government.

The prime minister attempted to cushion that blow Wednesday, announcing that the federal government would commit $1.2 billion for ocean protection projects in B.C., where Carney has also backed proposed expansion to the Port of Vancouver.

With files from Lauren Krugel, The Canadian Press

Pipelines faced key challenges in the past. Can Alberta’s overcome them?

stories.title: Former deans of medicine call on Ottawa to intervene in Alberta’s dual-practice health care model
stories.summary: In a letter to Carney, deans from the University of Calgary and the University of Alberta assert public-private model violates the Canada Health Act
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
Four former deans of medicine in Alberta have joined a growing chorus of critics asking Ottawa to intervene in the province’s dual-practice health care model, which allows eligible doctors to toggle between the public and private systems.

Tom Feasby, Jon Meddings and Eldon Smith, all formerly with the University of Calgary, and Tom Marrie, who was with the University of Alberta – sent a letter on the contentious issue to Prime Minister Mark Carney on Tuesday. They expressed “deep concern” about the public-private model and assert it violates the Canada Health Act.

“It is clear that the Alberta government is not going to change course and, therefore, we strongly request that you and the federal government step in and defend the principles of the Canada Health Act,” said the letter, which was also sent to Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

Alberta’s model is unlike any other in Canada, allowing some surgical specialists to bill the public purse while also privately charging patients for their services. The legislation, which took effect Sept. 1, covers such procedures as hip and knee replacements, cataract surgery and dermatology.

There is intense debate about whether it contravenes federal law.

The model has come under widespread scrutiny, including from the Canadian Medical Association and its Alberta counterpart, which argue it could create a two-tier system where people who can afford to pay out of pocket receive faster care. In March, 23 health and labour organizations across the country called on Mr. Carney to take action.

Dr. Meddings, in an interview on Wednesday, said there are other countries where a similar model has worked, but Alberta’s health care system is not conducive for a marriage between public and private care.

“I have nothing against dual practice per se, or some sort of private practice, in the same way as I don’t have anything against somebody paying extra money to fly business class on an airplane,” he said.

“The difference in Alberta is, because we have such a restricted number of both beds and physicians, that when somebody pays for this, it’s not an extra spot that wouldn’t have been used. It is taking it away from somebody who would have needed that spot.”

The Prime Minister has been largely silent on the issue, but federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel has expressed concern about how the policy will co-exist with the Canada Health Act.

Alexandre Bergeron, press secretary to Ms. Michel, did not address the letter directly in a statement on Wednesday but said the minister is in conversation with Adriana LaGrange, Alberta’s Minister of Hospital and Surgical Health Services.

“Minister Michel is engaged in ongoing, targeted discussions with her Alberta counterpart focused on ensuring access to medically necessary care and the core principles of the public system are protected while respecting Alberta’s jurisdiction,” he said.

Maddison McKee, press secretary to Ms. LaGrange, said in a statement that Ottawa must respect Alberta’s jurisdiction to determine how health care is delivered. She also reiterated the government position that dual practice does not contravene the Canada Health Act.

“Our priority is a strong public system and ensuring Albertans never have to pay out of pocket for medically necessary care,” Ms. McKee said. “Expanding access through dual practice does not take away from that. It adds to it. This is not an either/or debate. It is about giving Albertans more choice.”

The former deans said dual practice will harm patients by allowing those who can afford private care to jump to the front of the line, rather than providing care to the sickest first. This, they stressed in the letter, is what the Canada Health Act was designed to prevent.

Alberta has defended the dual-practice model as a way to reduce strain on the public system. The signatories argue that there is no evidence that shows a parallel public-private system will have that effect. Rather, they said, it will cause patients to wait longer in the public stream.

The province has said 400 expressions of interest were received over the summer to join the dual-practice system. As of mid-September, physicians were able to formally apply. Surgeries are expected to begin later this fall when the application process is complete.

While the letter did not specify what Ottawa should do, Dr. Meddings sees two ways in which the federal government could address the Alberta practice.

He said Mr. Carney and Ms. Michel can use the power of “moral suasion” with their counterparts in Alberta to push for changes to the legislation.

There is also what Dr. Meddings described as the “nuclear option,” where the federal government withholds or deducts health transfer payments to Alberta, which is permitted if a province violates the Canada Health Act.

stories.title: A country with its elbows up faces separation threats on two fronts
stories.summary: In Alberta and Quebec, Canada’s national unity paradox hits home
stories.author: Eric Andrew-Gee
stories.content:
When Barry Cooper was six years old, he and his mother were stopped at a level crossing while a train passed.

“There goes the goddamn-CPR,” he chirped.

His mother reached into the back seat and slapped him. Stop blaspheming, she said.

Young Barry was puzzled. He thought goddamn-CPR was just what the company was called. Growing up in the Western Canada of the early 1950s, he’d only ever known the railway as a source of bitter resentment. Freight rates designed to help business in the east meant that it was cheaper for the Coopers to buy apples from Nova Scotia than the nearby Okanagan.

The goddamn-CPR, with its headquarters near Montreal’s Golden Square Mile, represented the almost colonial arrogance of the Laurentian elites, who seemed to view Alberta and Saskatchewan as provinces “in the Roman sense” – breadbaskets to be exploited and kept passive.

As a child, Barry may not have reached for that classical allusion, but it comes to his lips easily now, at the age of 83, sitting in his office at the University of Calgary department of political science.

All these years later, Prof. Cooper has emerged as the intellectual godfather of the Alberta separatist movement. His mother’s slap didn’t have the desired effect: He has continued to blaspheme against Canada’s sacred institutions, from equalization payments to official bilingualism to Confederation itself.

For the West, and especially for Alberta, the Canadian federation has been a terrible misadventure, Prof. Cooper believes.

“One hundred and twenty years of history have been 120 years of economic exploitation,” he said in his dimly lit office, decorated with taxidermied deer and pheasant, during a long interview this summer.

Few separatists have so many copies of Virgil and Thucydides in their libraries, but a significant percentage of Albertans share Prof. Cooper’s worldview. The province is about to embark on its first independence referendum, of sorts – really a vote about holding a vote on independence.

Leaving Canada is effectively on the ballot in not one but two provinces. Alberta’s referendum will come just two weeks after a provincial election in Quebec on Oct. 5, where the Parti Québécois is leading the polls with a promise to hold a third “popular consultation” on independence.

This could hardly be more alarming to many Canadians. They see national unity being attacked from within at the most dangerous time, when American threats to our sovereignty have bred existential anxiety about our closest neighbour as well. It can seem like Canada is battling for survival on three fronts, apparently out of nowhere.

But there is more to the story. The anger and alienation endangering Confederation run centuries deep. Canada has too much geography for it to be otherwise: With population and resources scattered across an expanse of 5,500 kilometres as if by some spiteful Greek god, and more languages than the Habsburg Empire, it is no wonder we have always had separatist movements. They are a case of chronic inflammation in the Canadian body politic, not a sudden infection.

The reassuring news for federalists is that the current separatist fever may be breaking. The same upsurge in elbows-up patriotism that has rallied Canadians against the American threat has the potential to undermine the drives for secession in Alberta and Quebec.

But this is not an argument for complacency: Support for independence in both provinces hovers around 30 per cent. If that sounds high, it has become the norm in Wild Rose country and is well below average in la belle province .

In the future, these movements could flare up again, more severely than before.

Blue is a popular colour at separatist gatherings in 2026, from this PQ rally in Quebec City to a pro-independence protest in Edmonton. But judging by opinion polls, most of those who live under the blue provincial flags of Quebec and Alberta support remaining in a united Canada. Jacques Boissinot and Amanda Erickson/The Canadian Press

Separatist movements are as old as Confederation and as authentically Canadian as maple syrup. From the beginning, from Victoria to St. John’s, the virtues of coming together as a country were far from obvious.

Nova Scotia was dragged into the Dominion reluctantly; separatists dominated the first provincial legislature in Halifax. Many British Columbians wanted to leave when the pace of railway construction slowed. Manitoban farmers threatened to break away partly because of, yes, CPR freight rates.

Alberta, too, was born angry – a baby with teeth. Carved out of the former North-West Territories in 1905, some of its leaders hoped to remain conjoined with Saskatchewan in a bigger province, to be called Buffalo.

The federal government rejected the idea – it had a vision of the West as an inland empire, supplying grain for the rest of the country and a captive market for Central Canadian manufacturers.

Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba were denied control of their natural resources, unlike other provinces, a power grab that was only reversed in 1930.

Newspapers such as the Calgary Herald raged against Ottawa’s treatment of the West from the beginning. “Can Albertans be forced to eat dirt and say they like it?” one editorial thundered. The first book floating the idea of Alberta independence was published as early as 1911.

Alberta was developing its own identity, influenced by American immigrants who constituted the largest group of newcomers. “The Yankee province” was recognized for its swaggering, democratic personality and its entrepreneurial spirit. It was the U.S. promoter Guy Weadick who organized the first Calgary Stampede in 1912, an enduring embodiment of that culture. A member of the Cooper ranching dynasty, Barry’s uncle, called the annual rodeo for decades.

Barry’s father bucked the family trend and became a doctor in B.C., raising his son to be a proud Canadian who revered the Red Ensign. The unifying force of the Second World War had defanged Western alienation for a generation.

So it was a shock for the young Prof. Cooper, living in Central Canada as a novice academic in the 1970s, to find all was not well with the federation. It wasn’t just meeting Quebec separatists for the first time and finding them surprisingly persuasive. It was also the sheer “parochialism” of his students from Southern Ontario, the only Canadian region that doesn’t consider itself a region. They couldn’t have known or cared less about Western Canada, he found. For the boy with Alberta in his blood, who used to sit on the chutes at the Calgary Stampede and pet the roughstock, this was hard to stomach.

Hugh MacLennan’s novel Two Solitudes was a popular metaphor for the gulf between English and French Canada at the time, but Prof. Cooper was beginning to feel that Canada contains “many more solitudes.”

Canada’s regional rifts widened further in the 1970s, the political heyday of Peter Lougheed in Alberta and René Lévesque in Quebec. Both clashed with Pierre Trudeau over his vision of Confederation. The Canadian Press; Globe and Mail archives, 1976

The angriest part of Alberta may very well be the rural corridor between Edmonton and Calgary, where billboards made from converted trucking containers wage a culture war on the side of the highways. Signs for ABforAbortion and Flat Earth Canada compete with more recent referendum ads: “Send them a message they’ll never forget – Vote Yes in October,” reads one, with Justin Trudeau’s and Mark Carney’s faces set against a dark, sinister background.

It was also here – no coincidence – that a gusher of crude burst out of the Leduc No. 1 oil well in February, 1947, and permanently changed life in Western Canada. It was the beginning of Alberta’s energy boom; from then on, the province would be not only angry, but rich, and its identity would be intimately bound up with a single industry.

Leduc has become part of the Alberta vernacular, like heavy sour, wildcat, roughneck and tidewater, the oil jargon that trips off the tongue with total fluency here. But if Leduc represents the blessings of Alberta’s natural bounty, another bit of provincial shorthand, the NEP, represents the dark side. In Alberta, the phrase NEP captures with remarkable efficiency the province’s sense of having had its good fortune exploited by undeserving outsiders.

Prof. Cooper was back in his ancestral province teaching at the University of Calgary when the National Energy Program was hitting Alberta hardest. An attempt to Canadianize the oil industry, it siphoned off billions in revenue to the federal government, capped prices for consumers and contributed to a harsh recession in the province.

That independence movement quickly fizzled, but even pro-Canadian Albertans recall the NEP with horror; Senator Paula Simons watched as her father lost his businesses in Fort McMurray and some of his friends died by suicide during the downturn.

This was also the climate in which Prof. Cooper became politically active, providing intellectual ammunition to the nascent Reform Party, Preston Manning’s vessel for channelling Western Canadian rage. In retrospect, its demands look relatively quaint. The party called for Senate reform to improve regional representation in Ottawa and a hands-off approach to resource development; its explicitly non-separatist slogan was “The West Wants In.” In a very Albertan metaphor, Mr. Manning called his movement a “relief well” designed to intercept an out-of-control oil strike.

It is easy to forget that two parties rooted in grievances with Canadian federalism took turns as the Official Opposition. The old Reform crusader Stephen Harper brought Mr. Manning’s ideas even further into the mainstream when he became prime minister in 2006.

But the old Alberta anger continued to bubble like sour crude beneath the country’s surface, waiting for a wildcatter to tap into it.

It was a natural location for the Alberta Prosperity Project, a leading independence organization, to host its Pulpit and Politics event in August.

Pickups filled the parking lot outside a sprawling event hall on a sunny Wednesday evening, including one bearing a placard that read, “Saving My Grandkids from Carney’s New World Order.”

It was the first hint of how much time the speakers inside would devote not to defending Alberta oil and autonomy but to the prevailing cultural tide of the country.

For every reference to equalization payments, there was one to the “plandemic;” for every allusion to Senate reform, a smear on “illegal immigrants.” For every complaint about pipelines, speakers added another about drag queen story hour. Extended discussions of constitutional issues and budget math seemed to bore the audience.

It was another sign of the overlooked cultural dimension of Alberta separatism. In conversations with leaders and foot soldiers of the movement, it becomes clear that the progressive drift of the country under Justin Trudeau – with its strict COVID measures, increased immigration and “wokeness” – convinced many conservative Albertans that they didn’t belong in Canada anymore. Separatists often say that Canada seceded from them, not the other way around.

When comparing the Alberta and Quebec separatist movements, it’s common to say Alberta’s isn’t about culture, but that’s wrong, said the Calgary-based pollster Janet Brown. The single most predictive factor in determining support for Alberta independence is not working in the energy industry, but the salience of religion in a person’s life, she noted. Breaking away from Canada has become as much about the prominence of right-wing evangelical Christianity in Alberta – part of its original American flavour – as about oil and gas.

“It is about culture,” Ms. Brown said. “Grievance with the federal government is only the starting point.”

The Trudeau government’s environmental policies clearly outraged many Albertans; they are often cited as a major reason for the current flare-up of separatism in the province. But it is notable that gestures toward reversing those policies have not stopped the independence movement in its tracks. When Mr. Carney reached a memorandum of understanding with Alberta in November, 2025, promising to support the construction of a new pipeline to B.C. and peel back environmental regulations, many separatists dismissed it as mere verbiage. The feeling of broken trust and cultural alienation was too deep for quick repair.

Like many in his movement, the good professor has lost faith with Canada on a more elemental level, beyond the reach of policy fixes. His alienation goes far deeper than the Trudeau government’s climate-change agenda, all the way back to CPR freight rates, the loss of the Red Ensign and the NEP – issues that are obscure to most people outside of his province but deeply ingrained in Albertan culture.

His father served proudly in the Royal Canadian Air Force during the Second World War, he said, but those ties of patriotic sentiment have been broken for him.

“That Canada was the Canada of our parents, and it’s not here anymore.”

The elbows-up nationalism sweeping the country under Mr. Carney fills him with contempt, even though – or especially because – it has made headway in Alberta. Pro-Canadian activists in the province gleefully report more Maple Leaf flags flying from rural barns than they’ve ever seen before; personal identification with Canada has increased in recent polls.

It is perhaps no wonder the current Prime Minister is such a hateful figure to Prof. Cooper and others committed to Albertan independence. Separatists often refer to Mr. Carney and his acolytes as “elbozos.”

When the subject of the PM comes up, the erudite professor drops his references to Leo Strauss and Plato and reverts to a blaspheming six-year-old in the back of his mother’s car.

“How stupid do you have to be to trust that son of a bitch?” he said.

From the Arvida aluminum plant to the farms near the river, the Saguenay region has held on to Quebec’s traditional industries. Support for the PQ runs deep here. Charles-Frederick Ouellet/The Globe and Mail

Alberta and Quebec, 3,000 kilometres apart, are in some ways very different beasts. The contrast is visible in Red Deer County’s gleaming new megachurches with names such as CrossRoads and Impact Life on the one hand, and the century-old stone churches and seminaries of Chicoutimi, Que., their copper roofs rusted green, that haven’t seen a Catholic service in years.

These are places with very different histories and worldviews, like the movements they have nurtured. Where Alberta separatism is entirely right-wing with a strong evangelical bent, Quebec’s is aggressively secularist. The first is nominally about oil money, the second nominally about language. One is a populist insurgency with little institutional support, the other backed by the province’s largest media empire, Quebecor.

Because this is a land of paradox, however, it’s also true that both movements, for all their differences, emerge from the same wellspring of regional alienation that has always troubled the country. And if there’s one thing many residents of Red Deer and Chicoutimi can agree on, it’s that they would be better off outside of Canada.

No region voted more overwhelmingly for the Yes side of the 1995 sovereignty referendum than Chicoutimi’s Saguenay—Lac-Saint-Jean, two hours north of Quebec City, with an average of about 70 per cent. It’s an area that bleeds péquiste blue.

Just as the steakhouses, oil money and rolling parkland around Red Deer incarnate certain clichés about Alberta, so too does Saguenay exude le Québec profond . It’s a land of lumber camps where the smell of pine trees wafts through closed car windows. The farmland is dominated by dairy concerns that crank out delicious cheese curds. Local factories harness the region’s ample hydro power to zap bauxite into aluminum.

The retired city councillor Jean-Marc Crevier is a classic Saguenay man. He owns a little piece of property with friends on Lac Saint-Jean where he sails a catamaran. Like Prof. Cooper, he blasphemes colourfully and often, preferring an old religious curse that is antiquated even by Quebec standards: simonaque , meaning one who is guilty of simony, or trading in sacred things.

Like his father, he worked for decades in the Alcan aluminum plant in Arvida, a company town built by an eccentric American tycoon in the 1920s. The English-speaking managers who bossed him around were commonly called têtes carrées , a pejorative term for anglophones.

Mr. Crevier rose to be a union leader, first in the aluminum industry, then with the provincewide Fédération des travailleurs et travailleuses du Quebec. As sure as night followed day, he voted for the Parti Québécois. It was an identity as much as a choice.

The dialectic of federalism and separatism is centuries old in Quebec, older in a way than Canada itself. The British victory on the Plains of Abraham in 1759 produced an enduring desire to reclaim self-government and self-esteem. Nearly every generation saw violent eruptions of national pride: the Patriotes rebellion of 1837-38; riots against conscription in the First World War; the terrorist campaign of the Front de libération du Québec.

By the time the PQ emerged as a democratic force calling for political independence from Canada in the 1970s, the separatist impulse was part of Quebec’s DNA. The insouciant confidence of René Lévesque helped convince enough of his fellow citizens that “Quebec would be stronger on its own,” as Mr. Crevier put it. There was an undeniable flush of pride in imagining a Québécois head of state meeting the Canadian Prime Minister on an equal footing and finally earning his people the respect they deserved.

Ahead of the 1976 election, Mr. Crevier bet his fellow aluminum workers $50 that the underdog PQ would win, and sure enough they did. It was a no-brainer when the party held referendums in 1980 and 1995: He proudly voted Yes both times. Premier Bernard Landry even tried to recruit the charismatic union boss to succeed Lucien Bouchard as a local PQ candidate in the early 2000s. He declined mainly because it would mean spending less time in Saguenay.

The party had been in power for almost a decade by then. Especially in the Saguenay, separatism was a default ideology, the wallpaper of political life.

“If people talked politics in the dining room, it was PQ,” Mr. Crevier recalled. “If someone was Liberal, they were hiding in the corner.”

It’s been more than 30 years since the big referendum showdown between federalists, led by prime minister Jean Chrétien, and Quebec separatists allied with premier Jacques Parizeau. Andy Clark/Reuters

When premier Jacques Parizeau took the stage at Montreal’s Palais des Congrès on the night of Oct. 30, 1995, he was expecting to give a victory speech. Instead he blamed “money and ethnic votes” for his narrow referendum defeat, and his movement was permanently changed.

In a literal sense, Mr. Parizeau was right. Sixty per cent of francophones voted to leave that day, feeling burned by successive failed attempts to reform the constitution. Even long-time Canadian patriots such as André Pratte, future editor of the federalist La Presse newspaper and later a Canadian senator, felt the impasse was serious enough to vote Yes.

When Mr. Parizeau spoke those notorious words, many Quebeckers were ashamed of his outburst. Mr. Pratte recalls feeling revulsion and immediate regret for his Yes vote.

Others, felt a deep sense of recognition in Mr. Parizeau’s assertion of a French-Canadian nous , set apart from a sea of others. Cultural survival has always been a primal goal of French Canada, surrounded as it is by hundreds of millions of English-speakers in North America. Now, as Quebec’s own population becomes more diverse thanks to declining birth rates and increased immigration, the challenge can seem to come from within.

This siege mentality has an undeniable resonance for some Quebeckers. Ninety-eight per cent of Saguenay residents have French as a mother tongue, according to the most recent census, yet it’s still common to hear that immigrants there imperil French. In Quebec, language and culture can seem precarious even in their most impenetrable fortresses.

Appealing to voters like these, who feel left behind by a changing Quebec, turned out to be a dead-end for the PQ. The party dropped to an all-time low of three National Assembly seats in 2022 as François Legault and his Coalition Avenir Québec promised to protect Quebec interests and culture without the upheaval of another independence vote.

Even then, as the PQ drifted further and further to his right, Mr. Crevier stayed true to his sovereigntist faith. This election, with his party leading in the polls and promising a third referendum, he should have been ecstatic. You might have expected to find him knocking on doors for the local PQ candidate, Jimmy Bouchard, an old friend and colleague on the Saguenay city council.

But in a country of contradictions and cross-hatched loyalties, perhaps nowhere is shaded with more subtlety than the mind of a Quebec voter. And sure enough, this hard man of the labour movement, with a granite face, salt-and-pepper hair and a navy-blue windbreaker, finds himself politically “ shaké ” this election season. He is rattled for a simple but powerful reason: “Everything that’s happening with the United States.”

Saguenay’s industrial neighbourhoods kept a careful eye on this summer’s Canada-U.S. trade talks, whose collapse was partly due to disagreements over French language laws. Charles-Frederick Ouellet/The Globe and Mail

In the current trade war with the U.S., American tariffs or demands have targeted virtually everything the Saguenay holds dear: aluminum, dairy and lumber, to say nothing of protections for the French language and culture. From where Mr. Crevier is sitting, the U.S. President looks like a far bigger threat to his nation and his region than Canadian federalism.

Like everything in Quebec, this is an old story. When Americans threaten, Quebeckers choose the ambivalent embrace of the British Crown and the Canadian federation. Benjamin Franklin came to Montreal as an emissary of the American Revolution and was firmly rebuffed. During the War of 1812, French-Canadian heroes such as the fur trader Dominique Ducharme helped fight off the Yankee invasion. The former patriote rebel George-Étienne Cartier became a Father of Confederation in part because he dreaded American annexation.

Quebeckers have always believed their distinct society was better protected within the Canadian mosaic than as a stray ingredient in the American melting pot. It is this existential belief, as much as the pain of tariffs, that has rallied the province to the Maple Leaf during this trade war.

On Aug. 31, another minor chapter of this story was written when Daniel Gobeil, the Liberal candidate in Chicoutimi–Le Fjord, won a landslide victory over the Bloc Québécois in a federal by-election. His face was still Liberal red after a night of celebration and speech-giving when he credited his victory to a hunger – even in deep-blue Saguenay – for “Canadian unity.”

This was the second by-election Mr. Carney had snatched from the Bloc in a separatist stronghold this year, after the Montreal-area riding of Terrebonne in April. The Prime Minister has become the most popular politician in Quebec thanks to his economic nationalism and defiance of Donald Trump’s trade aggression.

Meanwhile, the PQ’s popularity has flatlined. They sit atop the polls because of voter fatigue with the CAQ and disarray within the provincial Liberal party. But the party has failed to reach out beyond the slightly under 30 per cent of Quebeckers who want independence, a historically low level for the province. If the PQ forms government, it will arguably be because the other parties split the federalist vote, not because voters want to leave Canada. And yet, the PQ almost certainly will form the next Quebec government, and hold a referendum if they secure a majority.

All this weighs heavily on Mr. Crevier, someone who has always believed in the sovereigntist catechism but is having his faith tested like never before. These days he is prone to delivering the pained soliloquy of a wavering separatist, one who is considering throwing in his lot with the CAQ and even – simonaque – the federal Liberals.

It is an uncertain time for the country as a whole. A generational upsurge of Canadian nationalism is coinciding with a generational threat to national unity. The independence drives in Alberta and Quebec may be stalling, but they are showing little sign of going away; Prof. Cooper’s profane rage and Mr. Crevier’s profane ambivalence both give voice to permanent doubts about their provinces’ place in Canada.

In the coming years, our leaders will have to find creative ways of renewing the Canadian contract, especially when the American threat isn’t there to unite us. This country is vast and varied enough to contain the oil wealth and donut shops of Red Deer, along with the aluminum plants and casse-croûtes of Chicoutimi. That kind of diversity can be a source of bounty or vulnerability, depending on how it’s managed.

Over bottomless cups of coffee at a chain diner two days after the Chicoutimi by-election, the anxious words tumbled out of Mr. Crevier like they were being spoken through the brass latticework of a parish church confessional.

“People are saying, better to improve it then break it down … In a referendum, we tear our shirts in the public square, we spit in each other’s faces, then, when we have our independence, we’ll go say to Ontario, ‘Hey let’s work together against the U.S.’ They’ll say, ‘Hey, go eat crap’... It’s made me change my mentality personally, me who’s voted PQ since 1976. People feel less embarrassed to say, ‘Let’s vote for the CAQ’ … I have more confidence in the CAQ to work with Canada right now … If you look around the world, who’s standing up to Trump? I’m listening to what Carney has to say … I’ve never voted Liberal in my goddamn life. I’m shaken on every side, provincially and federally … Simonaque …”

Blue is a popular colour at separatist gatherings in 2026, from this PQ rally in Quebec City to a pro-independence protest in Edmonton. But judging by opinion polls, most of those who live under the blue provincial flags of Quebec and Alberta support remaining in a united Canada. Just as the steakhouses, oil money and rolling parkland around Red Deer incarnate certain clichés about Alberta, so too does Saguenay exude le Québec profond . It’s a land of lumber camps where the smell of pine trees wafts through closed car windows. The farmland is dominated by dairy concerns that crank out delicious cheese curds. Local factories harness the region’s ample hydro power to zap bauxite into aluminum.

The retired city councillor Jean-Marc Crevier is a classic Saguenay man. He owns a little piece of property with friends on Lac Saint-Jean where he sails a catamaran. Like Prof. Cooper, he blasphemes colourfully and often, preferring an old religious curse that is antiquated even by Quebec standards: simonaque , meaning one who is guilty of simony, or trading in sacred things.

Like his father, he worked for decades in the Alcan aluminum plant in Arvida, a company town built by an eccentric American tycoon in the 1920s. The English-speaking managers who bossed him around were commonly called têtes carrées , a pejorative term for anglophones.

Mr. Crevier rose to be a union leader, first in the aluminum industry, then with the provincewide Fédération des travailleurs et travailleuses du Quebec. As sure as night followed day, he voted for the Parti Québécois. It was an identity as much as a choice.

The dialectic of federalism and separatism is centuries old in Quebec, older in a way than Canada itself. The British victory on the Plains of Abraham in 1759 produced an enduring desire to reclaim self-government and self-esteem. Nearly every generation saw violent eruptions of national pride: the Patriotes rebellion of 1837-38; riots against conscription in the First World War; the terrorist campaign of the Front de libération du Québec.

By the time the PQ emerged as a democratic force calling for political independence from Canada in the 1970s, the separatist impulse was part of Quebec’s DNA. The insouciant confidence of René Lévesque helped convince enough of his fellow citizens that “Quebec would be stronger on its own,” as Mr. Crevier put it. There was an undeniable flush of pride in imagining a Québécois head of state meeting the Canadian Prime Minister on an equal footing and finally earning his people the respect they deserved.

Ahead of the 1976 election, Mr. Crevier bet his fellow aluminum workers $50 that the underdog PQ would win, and sure enough they did. It was a no-brainer when the party held referendums in 1980 and 1995: He proudly voted Yes both times. Premier Bernard Landry even tried to recruit the charismatic union boss to succeed Lucien Bouchard as a local PQ candidate in the early 2000s. He declined mainly because it would mean spending less time in Saguenay.
The party had been in power for almost a decade by then. Especially in the Saguenay, separatism was a default ideology, the wallpaper of political life.
“If people talked politics in the dining room, it was PQ,” Mr. Crevier recalled. “If someone was Liberal, they were hiding in the corner.”

It’s been more than 30 years since the big referendum showdown between federalists, led by prime minister Jean Chrétien, and Quebec separatists allied with premier Jacques Parizeau. Andy Clark/Reuters

When premier Jacques Parizeau took the stage at Montreal’s Palais des Congrès on the night of Oct. 30, 1995, he was expecting to give a victory speech. Instead he blamed “money and ethnic votes” for his narrow referendum defeat, and his movement was permanently changed.

In a literal sense, Mr. Parizeau was right. Sixty per cent of francophones voted to leave that day, feeling burned by successive failed attempts to reform the constitution. Even long-time Canadian patriots such as André Pratte, future editor of the federalist La Presse newspaper and later a Canadian senator, felt the impasse was serious enough to vote Yes.
When Mr. Parizeau spoke those notorious words, many Quebeckers were ashamed of his outburst. Mr. Pratte recalls feeling revulsion and immediate regret for his Yes vote.

Others, felt a deep sense of recognition in Mr. Parizeau’s assertion of a French-Canadian nous , set apart from a sea of others. Cultural survival has always been a primal goal of French Canada, surrounded as it is by hundreds of millions of English-speakers in North America. Now, as Quebec’s own population becomes more diverse thanks to declining birth rates and increased immigration, the challenge can seem to come from within.

This siege mentality has an undeniable resonance for some Quebeckers. Ninety-eight per cent of Saguenay residents have French as a mother tongue, according to the most recent census, yet it’s still common to hear that immigrants there imperil French. In Quebec, language and culture can seem precarious even in their most impenetrable fortresses.

Appealing to voters like these, who feel left behind by a changing Quebec, turned out to be a dead-end for the PQ. The party dropped to an all-time low of three National Assembly seats in 2022 as François Legault and his Coalition Avenir Québec promised to protect Quebec interests and culture without the upheaval of another independence vote.

Even then, as the PQ drifted further and further to his right, Mr. Crevier stayed true to his sovereigntist faith. This election, with his party leading in the polls and promising a third referendum, he should have been ecstatic. You might have expected to find him knocking on doors for the local PQ candidate, Jimmy Bouchard, an old friend and colleague on the Saguenay city council.

But in a country of contradictions and cross-hatched loyalties, perhaps nowhere is shaded with more subtlety than the mind of a Quebec voter. And sure enough, this hard man of the labour movement, with a granite face, salt-and-pepper hair and a navy-blue windbreaker, finds himself politically “ shaké ” this election season. He is rattled for a simple but powerful reason: “Everything that’s happening with the United States.”

Saguenay’s industrial neighbourhoods kept a careful eye on this summer’s Canada-U.S. trade talks, whose collapse was partly due to disagreements over French language laws. Charles-Frederick Ouellet/The Globe and Mail

In the current trade war with the U.S., American tariffs or demands have targeted virtually everything the Saguenay holds dear: aluminum, dairy and lumber, to say nothing of protections for the French language and culture. From where Mr. Crevier is sitting, the U.S. President looks like a far bigger threat to his nation and his region than Canadian federalism.

Like everything in Quebec, this is an old story. When Americans threaten, Quebeckers choose the ambivalent embrace of the British Crown and the Canadian federation. Benjamin Franklin came to Montreal as an emissary of the American Revolution and was firmly rebuffed. During the War of 1812, French-Canadian heroes such as the fur trader Dominique Ducharme helped fight off the Yankee invasion. The former patriote rebel George-Étienne Cartier became a Father of Confederation in part because he dreaded American annexation.

Quebeckers have always believed their distinct society was better protected within the Canadian mosaic than as a stray ingredient in the American melting pot. It is this existential belief, as much as the pain of tariffs, that has rallied the province to the Maple Leaf during this trade war.

On Aug. 31, another minor chapter of this story was written when Daniel Gobeil, the Liberal candidate in Chicoutimi–Le Fjord, won a landslide victory over the Bloc Québécois in a federal by-election. His face was still Liberal red after a night of celebration and speech-giving when he credited his victory to a hunger – even in deep-blue Saguenay – for “Canadian unity.”

This was the second by-election Mr. Carney had snatched from the Bloc in a separatist stronghold this year, after the Montreal-area riding of Terrebonne in April. The Prime Minister has become the most popular politician in Quebec thanks to his economic nationalism and defiance of Donald Trump’s trade aggression.

Meanwhile, the PQ’s popularity has flatlined. They sit atop the polls because of voter fatigue with the CAQ and disarray within the provincial Liberal party. But the party has failed to reach out beyond the slightly under 30 per cent of Quebeckers who want independence, a historically low level for the province. If the PQ forms government, it will arguably be because the other parties split the federalist vote, not because voters want to leave Canada. And yet, the PQ almost certainly will form the next Quebec government, and hold a referendum if they secure a majority.

All this weighs heavily on Mr. Crevier, someone who has always believed in the sovereigntist catechism but is having his faith tested like never before. These days he is prone to delivering the pained soliloquy of a wavering separatist, one who is considering throwing in his lot with the CAQ and even – simonaque – the federal Liberals.

It is an uncertain time for the country as a whole. A generational upsurge of Canadian nationalism is coinciding with a generational threat to national unity. The independence drives in Alberta and Quebec may be stalling, but they are showing little sign of going away; Prof. Cooper’s profane rage and Mr. Crevier’s profane ambivalence both give voice to permanent doubts about their provinces’ place in Canada.

In the coming years, our leaders will have to find creative ways of renewing the Canadian contract, especially when the American threat isn’t there to unite us. This country is vast and varied enough to contain the oil wealth and donut shops of Red Deer, along with the aluminum plants and casse-croûtes of Chicoutimi. That kind of diversity can be a source of bounty or vulnerability, depending on how it’s managed.

Over bottomless cups of coffee at a chain diner two days after the Chicoutimi by-election, the anxious words tumbled out of Mr. Crevier like they were being spoken through the brass latticework of a parish church confessional.

“People are saying, better to improve it then break it down … In a referendum, we tear our shirts in the public square, we spit in each other’s faces, then, when we have our independence, we’ll go say to Ontario, ‘Hey let’s work together against the U.S.’ They’ll say, ‘Hey, go eat crap’... It’s made me change my mentality personally, me who’s voted PQ since 1976. People feel less embarrassed to say, ‘Let’s vote for the CAQ’ … I have more confidence in the CAQ to work with Canada right now … If you look around the world, who’s standing up to Trump? I’m listening to what Carney has to say … I’ve never voted Liberal in my goddamn life. I’m shaken on every side, provincially and federally … Simonaque …”

content_blocks.text: The Trudeau government’s environmental policies clearly outraged many Albertans; they are often cited as a major reason for the current flare-up of separatism in the province. But it is notable that gestures toward reversing those policies have not stopped the independence movement in its tracks. When Mr. Carney reached a memorandum of understanding with Alberta in November, 2025, promising to support the construction of a new pipeline to B.C. and peel back environmental regulations, many separatists dismissed it as mere verbiage. The feeling of broken trust and cultural alienation was too deep for quick repair.

content_blocks.text: Alberta and Quebec, 3,000 kilometres apart, are in some ways very different beasts. The contrast is visible in Red Deer County’s gleaming new megachurches with names such as CrossRoads and Impact Life on the one hand, and the century-old stone churches and seminaries of Chicoutimi, Que., their copper roofs rusted green, that haven’t seen a Catholic service in years.

content_blocks.text: These are places with very different histories and worldviews, like the movements they have nurtured. Where Alberta separatism is entirely right-wing with a strong evangelical bent, Quebec’s is aggressively secularist. The first is nominally about oil money, the second nominally about language. One is a populist insurgency with little institutional support, the other backed by the province’s largest media empire, Quebecor.

content_blocks.text: The dialectic of federalism and separatism is centuries old in Quebec, older in a way than Canada itself. The British victory on the Plains of Abraham in 1759 produced an enduring desire to reclaim self-government and self-esteem. Nearly every generation saw violent eruptions of national pride: the Patriotes rebellion of 1837-38; riots against conscription in the First World War; the terrorist campaign of the Front de libération du Québec.

content_blocks.text: By the time the PQ emerged as a democratic force calling for political independence from Canada in the 1970s, the separatist impulse was part of Quebec’s DNA. The insouciant confidence of René Lévesque helped convince enough of his fellow citizens that “Quebec would be stronger on its own,” as Mr. Crevier put it. There was an undeniable flush of pride in imagining a Québécois head of state meeting the Canadian Prime Minister on an equal footing and finally earning his people the respect they deserved.

The former patriote rebel George-Étienne Cartier became a Father of Confederation in part because he dreaded American annexation.

content_blocks.text: Meanwhile, the PQ’s popularity has flatlined. They sit atop the polls because of voter fatigue with the CAQ and disarray within the provincial Liberal party. But the party has failed to reach out beyond the slightly under 30 per cent of Quebeckers who want independence, a historically low level for the province. If the PQ forms government, it will arguably be because the other parties split the federalist vote, not because voters want to leave Canada. And yet, the PQ almost certainly will form the next Quebec government, and hold a referendum if they secure a majority.

stories.title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk set to launch to International Space Station
stories.summary: Merritt Island - As the sun rises over Florida's iconic Kennedy Space Center on Thursday morning, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk will be making the final preparations to fulfil his lifelong dream of blasting off into space.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Merritt Island - Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk’s first thought after being told Thursday he had made it to space was one of disbelief.

“I don’t really believe it yet,” Kutryk said after being told the crew was in orbit, about 10 minutes after blasting off from Florida as part of the Nasa SpaceX Crew 13 mission to the International Space Station.

“It does feel weird, though.”

The 44-year-old is a mission specialist on the four-person crew, which also includes commander Jessica Watkins and pilot Luke Delaney — both of Nasa — and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov, another mission specialist.

Four astronauts pulled up at the International Space Station on Thursday after launching on an eight-hour express that set a United States speed record. The SpaceX Dragon spacecraft carried Nasa astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov.

Nasa says the Crew 13 mission had the fastest flight ever to the International Space Station, taking just under eight hours to reach the facility.

After another two hours or so of docking procedures, Kutryk and his crewmates emerged from a hatch and were greeted with hugs and handshakes from the seven people aboard the station.

Speaking during a brief welcome ceremony, Kutryk expressed disbelief at finally being on the space station and said it’s great to have Canada represented there again.

“Looking forward to a good mission after some sleep. That’s what I’m going to go do next,” he said on the Nasa broadcast.

The crew is to spend six months at the station conducting experiments, doing research and taking part in critical maintenance work.

Kutryk also faces a unique situation during his months-long deployment off Earth — his wife is set to give birth to their third child.

The space station is a long way from the Alberta cattle farm where Kutryk grew up. Before the launch, Kutryk said the crew members felt like “some of the luckiest people on Earth.”

The crew of Artemis II successfully splashed down in the Pacific on Friday night. It brings a rare, refreshing moment of unity to a close.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly watched the launch from the ground. It was the first she had ever attended.

“It was absolutely fantastic,” Joly said with a smile at the Kennedy Space Center. “It’s a very humbling experience as well because ultimately we’re very, very small humans in an extremely vast universe.”

Joly said the launch offered an important symbol of international co-operation during “tense geopolitical times.”

“When it comes to space, I think this is a place where we can collaborate and co-operate,” she said. “That’s what we’ve done.”

Collaboration on space innovation has continued despite U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs and continued threats of annexation.

Joly has been on the front lines of Trump’s trade war with Canada, first as foreign minister and now in her current portfolio, where she’s tasked with mitigating many of the tariffs’ effects.

She met with Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman for about 30 minutes Thursday. She said they spoke about how the Canadian Space Agency can contribute to exploration, particularly of the moon and Mars.

Joly said she always talks about the importance of ending the trade war when she meets members of the Trump administration and other American politicians.

At a post-launch news conference, Isaacman said he has fruitful discussions with Canada, particularly on a future lunar base. Pointing to the well-known Canadarm and its followup Dextre, Isaacman said Canada’s robotics expertise would play an important role in achieving America’s lofty ambitions in space.

“We are going to be counting on it as part of the architecture,” he said.

Kutryk’s mission adds to a memorable year for Canadian space exploration and research.

Canadian Jeremy Hansen was one of four astronauts aboard the Artemis II mission in April — humanity’s first trip to the moon in more than 50 years. The 10-day lunar fly-around saw Hansen and his crewmates travel farther from the surface of the Earth than anyone before them.

Mathieu Caron, director of astronauts, life sciences and space medicine at the Canadian Space Agency, told Thursday’s news conference that for the first time in his three-decade-long career, his children think he’s cool.

“Across Canada, we really see a renewed enthusiasm for human space exploration,” Caron said.

Joly said Canada was looking to push its space capabilities further by diversifying space partnerships and working more closely with the European and Japanese space industries, as well as other middle-power countries.

But Ottawa wants to do things faster and with more ambition, she added.

Joly said Canada’s defence industrial plan recognizes the importance of the space sector and new funds have been dedicated to the Canadian Space Agency. She said Canada must embrace the industrial part of space investment to create domestic jobs while also doubling down on science and civilian research.

A new president for the Canadian Space Agency is to be named in the coming weeks, Joly said. A new space strategy would also be unveiled in the coming months, which will promote Canada’s goals of creating opportunities, playing a larger role in the sector and sending more astronauts off Earth, she added.

“I think space exploration is important for our country,” she said.

“Also we benefit from the different research done … for our industry, for creating jobs but also to protect our sovereignty and also when it comes to science and the betterment of humankind.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 1, 2026.

She met with Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman for about 30 minutes Thursday. She said they spoke about how the Canadian Space Agency can contribute to exploration, particularly of the moon and Mars.

Joly said she always talks about the importance of ending the trade war when she meets members of the Trump administration and other American politicians.

At a post-launch news conference, Isaacman said he has fruitful discussions with Canada, particularly on a future lunar base. Pointing to the well-known Canadarm and its followup Dextre, Isaacman said Canada’s robotics expertise would play an important role in achieving America’s lofty ambitions in space.

“We are going to be counting on it as part of the architecture,” he said.

Kutryk’s mission adds to a memorable year for Canadian space exploration and research.

Canadian Jeremy Hansen was one of four astronauts aboard the Artemis II mission in April — humanity’s first trip to the moon in more than 50 years. The 10-day lunar fly-around saw Hansen and his crewmates travel farther from the surface of the Earth than anyone before them.

Mathieu Caron, director of astronauts, life sciences and space medicine at the Canadian Space Agency, told Thursday’s news conference that for the first time in his three-decade-long career, his children think he’s cool.

“Across Canada, we really see a renewed enthusiasm for human space exploration,” Caron said.

Joly said Canada was looking to push its space capabilities further by diversifying space partnerships and working more closely with the European and Japanese space industries, as well as other middle-power countries.

But Ottawa wants to do things faster and with more ambition, she added.

Joly said Canada’s defence industrial plan recognizes the importance of the space sector and new funds have been dedicated to the Canadian Space Agency. She said Canada must embrace the industrial part of space investment to create domestic jobs while also doubling down on science and civilian research.

A new president for the Canadian Space Agency is to be named in the coming weeks, Joly said. A new space strategy would also be unveiled in the coming months, which will promote Canada’s goals of creating opportunities, playing a larger role in the sector and sending more astronauts off Earth, she added.

“I think space exploration is important for our country,” she said.

“Also we benefit from the different research done … for our industry, for creating jobs but also to protect our sovereignty and also when it comes to science and the betterment of humankind.”

Nasa says the Crew 13 mission had the fastest flight ever to the International Space Station, taking just under eight hours to reach the facility.
After another two hours or so of docking procedures, Kutryk and his crewmates emerged from a hatch and were greeted with hugs and handshakes from the seven people aboard the station.

“Looking forward to a good mission after some sleep. That’s what I’m going to go do next,” he said on the Nasa broadcast.

stories.title: Police seek answers in crash that killed 2 elders, hurt 2 others on B.C. First Nation
stories.summary: Delta - Community members on the Tsawwassen First Nation lined the road, drummed and chanted as the bodies of two elders were loaded into coroners' vehicles outside a shopping centre near the nation's reserve south of Vancouver.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Family members of two Tsawwassen First Nation elders killed in a collision outside a shopping centre in Delta, B.C., ON Wednesday say the women were “cultural pillars” of their community.

Statements shared by the nation on social media on Thursday say that wilapiya, also known as Barb Joe, and Virginia Splockton died in the collision at the Tsawwassen Mills mall.

The women were killed and two others were seriously injured by a pickup truck whose driver was in apparent medical distress and drove into an area where nation members were to unveil four traditional carvings known as house posts.

Joe’s family said in the statement that she was a knowledge keeper and matriarch who revived the nation’s language.

The Splockton family described Virginia Splockton as a generous great-grandmother who “touched countless lives” and loved crafting, drumming and singing.

“We recognize the profound impact this tragedy has had on our community as a whole,” the nation wrote in its statement. “We also extend our sincere gratitude to the first responders, emergency personnel, and all those who assisted at the scene.”

Delta police said the driver involved has been released from hospital as investigators assessed whether their medical emergency played a role in the crash.

Police said in a news release on Thursday that there is no information to suggest the collision was intentional.

The nation was hosting a community walk in recognition of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation near the time of the crash and had invited people to meet at the mall’s entrance for the posts’ unveiling after the walk.

Police said the collision was not related to the walk and there is no evidence to suggest any connection between the collision and the house post event.

They said the driver received medical attention and was interviewed by investigators before being released from hospital.

The two injured people remain in hospital in critical condition, and while the investigation remains ongoing, no charges have been laid, police said Thursday.

Dylan Kruger, a city councillor who is running for mayor in the Oct. 17 local elections, said he was taking part in the community walk that was about halfway through when the crowd saw emergency vehicles drive by and two helicopters land in the mall’s parking lot.

“Obviously everybody at that point was getting very nervous. They knew something had gone very seriously wrong,” Kruger said in an interview Thursday.

He said he thought some in the crowd were “flashing back” to the deadly ramming attack at the Lapu Lapu Day festival in Vancouver last year.

But Kruger said organizers kept the crowd calm amid the initial confusion and panic, and people returned safely to their vehicles.

He said it was traumatic for some people in the crowd, which included many families with young children, as they had to walk past the scene that was eventually obscured with screens.

He said the tight-knit First Nation is grieving but has full support from the community of Delta.

“We’re giving them space to do that, but everyone will be there when they’re ready,” he said.

First Nations, politicians and community leaders were among those who expressed condolences over the deaths and injuries.

The Indian Residential School Survivors Society said in a post on social media that the loss of the two “beloved” elders was devastating, while the Huu-ay-aht First Nations on Vancouver Island said it felt the tragedy deeply as one of the elders who died was a grandparent of one of its citizens.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith began her news conference on Thursday about the proposed Pacific Pipeline between her province and B.C., saying her heart was with the grieving families and community.

The pipeline would carry crude oil to the Roberts Bank Terminal in Delta on the waterfront of the Tsawwassen First Nation.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and leaders on the B.C. election campaign, David Eby, Emily Lowan and Lorne Doerkson, also expressed their condolences to the families and the First Nation after the crash.

Video from the scene of the crash on Wednesday shows a pickup truck with the logo for the company Alpine Building Maintenance printed on its side.

The company released a statement on Thursday and confirmed one of its vehicles was involved in the collision.

“We are co-operating with the appropriate authorities to support their investigation. Our thoughts are with everyone affected,” it said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 1, 2026.

stories.title: B.C.'s large parties on track to field candidates in all ridings as deadline looms
stories.summary: Victoria - The major parties running in British Columbia's election appear to be on track to fill each of the 93 ridings, but smaller parties are struggling ahead of the Oct. 3 nomination deadline.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Promises to lower the cost of gasoline from B.C. New Democrat Leader David Eby and praise for a planned pipeline from Conservative interim leader Lorne Doerkson fuelled British Columbia’s snap election campaign on Thursday.

Eby’s platform for relief at the gas pumps comes in two parts: a temporary reduction of the provincial motor fuel tax by 10 cents per litre on both gasoline and diesel, and a permanent “price guard” to regulate the price at the pumps.

The leader said the measures would save the average two-car family up to $100 per month, but would also cost the provincial treasury about $250 million, with additional details forthcoming.

The fuel promise was criticized by Lorne Doerkson, the interim B.C. Conservative leader, who reminded reporters that Eby made a financial promise before the 2024 election that he didn’t keep.

“Just two years ago, there were promises made for a thousand-dollars of relief to families and to homes and to people in this province, and he failed to deliver that, and I think he needs to answer that,” Doerkson said.

Eby had promised a direct rebate of $1,000 to the average household as one of his campaign’s signature planks in the 2024 election.

In February 2025, then-finance minister Brenda Bailey said that government could not pay the so-called “grocery rebate” because of the provincial deficit.

Asked whether voters could trust his promises, Eby pointed to the elimination of the carbon tax, which he said was “probably the largest” tax cut in provincial history at $2 billion.

He acknowledged that “circumstances” changed after the 2024 election but said they’ll “make sure the tax cut actually reaches the pockets” of B.C. residents.

The Ndp’s proposed measures against price gouging mirror rules that already exist in Atlantic Canada, where they have worked, he added.

“We’re going to ensure stability for gas prices, predictability and transparency,” Eby said. “These are pieces that have been missing, and as a result, British Columbians are paying too much for gas.”

Eby said Thursday that if the NDP was re-elected in the Oct. 24 election his government would ask the B.C. Utilities Commission to set the maximum price that fuel stations can charge.

It would be updated weekly as the benchmark price for crude oil fluctuates, he said.

“Yes, government needs to step up and say, ‘we’ll reduce the tax on gas in this time to support families,’” he said. “But also, government needs it to use its force. We need to use our authority. We need to use our rules to make sure that British Columbians are not gouged.”

Big oil and gas companies have been exploiting conflicts overseas to make record profits, leaving ordinary drivers and truckers paying the price every time they fill up, Eby said.

He made the announcement at a gas station in Surrey, a riding-rich area that the NDP needs to win if it’s to form government.

Doerkson spoke at a campaign event in Vancouver, where he praised the federal government’s decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline a project of national interest.

He said his party supports a second pipeline from northern Alberta to B.C.‘s southern coast, because the world desperately needs Canadian energy.

“We welcome it because British Columbia’s economy desperately needs a boost. And the events of the last few years have shown just how important this is to be self-sufficient,” Doerkson said.

Eby said during a later media availability that the province has an important role to play in the pipeline process to protect the interests of B.C. residents, “but we also recognize that our projects, our priorities, need the same level of attention from the federal government,” he said.

That is why, Eby said, his province fought so hard for the Canada-British Columbia Co-operative Prosperity Agreement announced in July.

The accord calls for federal investments worth about $20 billion into infrastructure and resource projects across B.C.

The B.C. Green Party announced a high-profile candidate on Thursday as it released its platform on the toxic drug crisis.

Former B.C. chief coroner Lisa Lapointe will run under the Green banner in Saanich South, the same riding where former Global TV reporter Richard Zussman will run for the NDP.

Lapointe was B.C.‘s chief coroner for 13 years and made recommendations to save lives, some of which were rejected by the NDP government.

“I recognize that the toxic drug crisis will only be solved when politicians are willing to show leadership; when regulated alternatives are available, when voluntary treatment is available when people need it, and when people who use drugs have the same access to resources, medical care, housing, dignity and respect as anyone else,” Lapointe said in a statement issued Thursday.

She said in testimony to a B.C. Supreme Court last December at a constitutional challenge by founders of a compassion club that the NDP government ignored multiple recommendations from experts to create a safer drug supply that did not require a prescription.

The judge in that case tossed out criminal convictions for the founders this week and gave the government six months to rework the law because the act that prohibited them from selling safer drugs “criminalizes life-saving conduct” by the pair.

Lapointe’s name has not yet appeared among the 11 candidates officially running for the Greens.

CentreBC has five official candidates, while OneBC has two official candidates.

All three parties say their candidate count is higher than that, but all are under 20 each and the cut off to register candidates looms on Oct. 3.

Elections BC lists 55 official candidates for the B.C. New Democrats, while there are 45 people confirmed for the Conservatives as of Oct. 1.

Both parties say on their websites that those numbers are much higher and both appear on track to field candidates in all 93 ridings.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Quebec parties make final pitches with election days away
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec’s political parties are making their final pitches to voters with just days to go before the provincial election.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The leader of the Parti Québécois asked voters on Thursday to give him a majority government, as his party continues to lead in the polls with just days to go before the provincial election.

Paul St-Pierre Plamondon delivered the message in separate morning radio show interviews in both English and French.

He says he needs a majority government to get things done and to implement his program.

In an interview with English-language radio station Cjad, St-Pierre Plamondon said his party was considering the scenarios of either a minority or majority PQ government as serious possibilities.

He repeated that sentiment later in the day in an address to supporters, who he urged to not take anything for granted.

“It will be tight, there will be tight battles in every region until the end,” he said.

St-Pierre Plamondon also told Radio-Canada Thursday that his government would be “handcuffed” in a minority scenario, and called for a strong and stable government to reverse the damage from eight years of Coalition Avenir Québec leadership.

Later, St-Pierre Plamondon urged each Parti Québécois voter to try to convince one undecided person to vote for his party, and launched an appeal to voters who haven’t yet made up their minds.

“We believe that the change we want to see will come through the quality of the team, but also through the stability and strength of a government that will truly have the means to realize its promises.”

The major party leaders spent much of the day on the defensive, working to shore up support in ridings that are expected to be tight.

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard spent time in the Eastern Townships regions, where he’s battling to secure himself a legislature seat.

Québec solidaire’s Ruba Ghazal was in Montreal to pitch a plan to ban evictions during the winter, as polls suggest her party could be in trouble in some of the ridings it won in 2022.

Ghazal noted that the race isn’t over, and urged people to vote “with their hearts,” instead of strategically.

Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette, meanwhile, suggested that St-Pierre Plamondon and U.S. President Donald Trump both want to “weaken Canada,” even as she faced a new round of questions about her response to allegations of foreign interference earlier in the election.

Fréchette had made an early statement saying she was “very concerned” by a report of possible interference coming from the U.S., before later saying there was no reason to be concerned about the integrity of the election.

Fréchette admitted that she should have waited to have more information before sounding the alarm.

Quebecers go to the polls on Oct. 5.

Later, St-Pierre Plamondon urged each Parti Québécois voter to try to convince one undecided person to vote for his party, and launched an appeal to voters who haven’t yet made up their minds.

“We believe that the change we want to see will come through the quality of the team, but also through the stability and strength of a government that will truly have the means to realize its promises.”
The major party leaders spent much of the day on the defensive, working to shore up support in ridings that are expected to be tight.
Liberal Leader Charles Milliard spent time in the Eastern Townships regions, where he’s battling to secure himself a legislature seat.
Québec solidaire’s Ruba Ghazal was in Montreal to pitch a plan to ban evictions during the winter, as polls suggest her party could be in trouble in some of the ridings it won in 2022.
Ghazal noted that the race isn’t over, and urged people to vote “with their hearts,” instead of strategically.

Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette, meanwhile, suggested that St-Pierre Plamondon and U.S. President Donald Trump both want to “weaken Canada,” even as she faced a new round of questions about her response to allegations of foreign interference earlier in the election.

Fréchette had made an early statement saying she was “very concerned” by a report of possible interference coming from the U.S., before later saying there was no reason to be concerned about the integrity of the election.
Fréchette admitted that she should have waited to have more information before sounding the alarm.
Quebecers go to the polls on Oct. 5.
