Last Updated September 30, 2026 5:28 pm.
OTTAWA — The federal government has identified “anti-Zionism” as a driver of anti-Jewish hate — a major policy shift that has prompted a range of reactions.
The change took place on Sept. 24 when Public Safety Canada published a progress report on federal efforts promised in January to combat antisemitism.
The report said Ottawa sought to do a better job of recognizing and responding to “contemporary manifestations of antisemitism, including anti-Zionism.”
Here’s a closer look at the terminology, why it’s being used now and what it all means for free speech.
What is Zionism?
The Canadian Oxford Dictionary defines Zionism as “a movement originally for the re-establishment and now the development of a Jewish nation in what is now Israel.”

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, which identifies itself as a Zionist organization, says it means supporting the idea that “the Jewish people have the right to self-determination in their ancestral homeland.”
Opponents of Zionism argue the term has come to embody a colonial mentality that allows the Israeli government to subjugate Palestinians and seek to expand its borders.
The State of Israel was declared founded in May 1948, after the end of British rule over Palestine.
The founding of the state saw Zionist paramilitaries violently disperse Palestinians who were living there, while Arab states around the region responded by deporting Jews to Israel.
Carleton University political scientist Mira Sucharov surveyed American Jews on their views of Zionism and anti-Zionism in 2022.
“Self-proclaimed Zionists (Jewish or otherwise) and anti-Zionists (Jewish or otherwise) are talking about completely different things,” she wrote in a commentary in Haaretz.

She concluded that Jews embrace Zionism when it’s defined as “a belief in a Jewish and democratic state” and reject the term when it’s defined as “the belief in privileging Jewish rights over non-Jewish rights in Israel.”
What is anti-Zionism?
For decades, Jews in Canada and around the world have debated how Israel should operate and whether it amounts to a colonial project.

Independent Jewish Voices identifies as an anti-Zionist organization. It defines anti-Zionism as “the rejection of Jewish settler-colonialism in Palestine and belief that Palestinians deserve dignity and safety like all other people.”
The Association for Canadian Studies offered its own definition, which has prompted criticism from left-leaning groups.

“Anti-Zionism refers to a movement that calls for the erasure of Israel and denies the Jewish people the right to self-determination in part of their ancestral homeland,” the association wrote in a report Ottawa commissioned.

The Network of Engaged Canadian Academics, a group of mostly Jewish academics, argues “the latest incarnation of Jew hatred is anti-Zionism (which) relies on libel and distortion to claim that the Jewish collective, Israel, rather than the individual Jew, is uniquely evil.”
That ideology, the group argues, claims Jews have fabricated a claim to their ancestral land.
“Anti-Zionists dismiss Jews as nefarious settlers who have usurped the rights of the true Indigenous people, Palestinians,” the group wrote in a brief to senators.

Since the Gaza war started in October 2023, many Canadian Jews have reported that words like “Zionist” have become pejorative terms. Some have reported Jewish people being branded with Zionism-linked slurs such as “a Zio.”

The war started with a brutal Hamas attack on Israel that killed roughly 1,200 people. That prompted Israel to launch an assault on Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and has led to repression in the occupied West Bank.
Israel also has expanded its military footprint in Lebanon and Israeli cabinet ministers have talked openly of ethnic cleansing or mass killings of civilians.
What has Ottawa said?
Last week’s federal progress report said anti-Zionism is a modern manifestation of antisemitism. It cited a 2024 government report, though that report did not mention anti-Zionism.
The report also took note of a Windsor man sentenced in April for public incitement of hatred after he used the term “Zionists” as a derogatory term for Jews.
“This is particularly important because Ontario is increasingly seeing the use of this term by protesters who try to shield otherwise hateful speech from criminal liability,” the federal report said.

The Senate human rights committee avoided weighing in on the terminology in its April study of antisemitism in Canada. Committee chair Sen. Paulette Senior said the focus of the study was on how to stop the hatred.
What do proponents say?
Groups that advocate for Israel such as CIJA have generally been supportive of the government’s shift, and have argued that Jewish Canadians are the ones to describe how they experience antisemitism.
“Anti-Zionism is driving violence against Canadians,” CIJA wrote in a tweet before the release of the federal report.
“The demonization of Israel offers a green light for extremists who target the Jewish community. This includes when governments single Israel out or hold it to a double standard.”

Liberal MP Anthony Housefather welcomed the federal shift. He said last week’s report is “an important document” that “makes clear the Canadian government recognizes that anti-Zionism is a form of antisemitism.”

University of Ottawa professor Michael Geist was also supportive, writing that “Anti-Zionism is too often thinly veiled antisemitism, as if substituting the word Zionist for Jew renders the unacceptable acceptable.”
What do opponents say?
Independent Jewish Voices says Ottawa is embracing terminology that will suppress free speech.
“This definition isn’t only wrong, it’s dangerous,” the group wrote.
The group refers to Zionism as “a Jewish supremacist ideology” that is incompatible with Palestinian self-determination because it encourages occupation and suppression.
The Canadian Muslim Public Affairs Council took a similar view of Ottawa’s change last week.
“Conflating opposition to Zionism with hatred or discrimination against Jewish people risks collapsing the important distinction between political expression and antisemitism,” the council wrote.

The council is one of several organizations which have rejected a definition of antisemitism adopted by the federal and provincial governments that was written by the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance.

The IHRA definition says criticism of Israel can cross the line into antisemitism when it is persistent, when it compares Israeli policies to Nazi ones, and when it goes beyond criticism levelled at other countries.
The Ottawa Forum on Israel Palestine argued no one should conflate anti-Zionism with anti-Jewish hate.
“The Government of Canada should make it clear that supporting Zionism or opposing it are equally protected by free speech,” the group wrote in a brief to senators.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 30, 2026.
Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: St. Thomas business owner shares emotional personal story on Truth and Reconciliation Day
stories.summary: Chris Patriquin had planned to take the microphone and continue to advocate for clean drinking water on Oneida Nation of the Thames during Truth and Reconciliation Day festivities.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Chris Patriquin had planned to take the microphone and continue to advocate for clean drinking water on Oneida Nation of the Thames during Truth and Reconciliation Day festivities.

The St. Thomas, Ont. man owns a water business and makes multiple deliveries every week to serve local First Nation communities.

“Sadly, this is a yearly reminder for all of you that our closest indigenous neighbors are still without clean, safe drinking water,” said Patriquin.

“The boil water advisory in Oneida Nation of the Thames continues to this day, seven years after it was initially announced. As I’ve stated before, in my opinion, the conversation around Truth and Reconciliation cannot truly start until all indigenous communities have clean, safe drinking water.”

However, his speech quickly pivoted to a very personal story after seeing a protest against Orange Shirt Day by Second Sons Canada this week.

“These cowardly, masked protesters were holding a sign that said, ‘Got Bones?’ similar to the ‘Got Milk?’ campaign,” said Patriquin.

“They were trying to deny the trauma of residential schools and the conversation around Truth and Reconciliation unless someone or anyone could produce the remains of dead children as proof, the residential school system was designed to take the Indian out of the child. It did not need to leave a body in every field to succeed. The evidence is in the families that are still healing, three and four generations later. Every indigenous person you meet is a survivor of this system.”

Patriquin said every Indigenous person is a survivor whether or not they ever set foot in a residential school.He went into detail about how when he was 23 years old, he tried to end his life.

He is grateful to have woken up 48 hours after taking pills and alcohol.Ten years later, his cousin took his life. He said they were both abused as young boys and after being told to keep it a secret, they did.

“Anger, insecurity, substance abuse, broken relationships, that’s what intergenerational trauma looks like,” he added.

“When there are no graves to dig and no bodies to count, it lives in the living. It shows up in the suicide rates, the addiction rates, the incarceration rates, the broken trust and the silence that still sits at so many kitchen tables.”

He says this day is about remembering a six-year-old named Phyllis Webster who had her orange shirt taken from her.

“That same system took the language, culture and safety from thousands of kids, some of those kids never came home,” said Patriquin.

“Many more came home carrying wounds that they are still passing down. The damage is real. The trauma is real. You do not need a body to prove it. You only need to listen to the living.”

The microphone was then handed to grass dancer Jonas Phillips.

He spoke about years of trauma leading to a family which used alcohol and drugs. He proudly told of his ability to get clean and sober and bringing his grandchildren to be in attendance to support teachings about the past.

“I heard someone today say the world reconciliation,” said Phillips.

“It should be Truth and Action. People like me have to be strong and get away from drugs and alcohol and do what they have to do to survive.”

He added that all Indigenous people are lucky to be alive.

“We all survived,” said Phillips.

“A very small percentage of people survived a very big genocide. I would like to show other people what I’m doing better, why I’m doing better, and how I could do better. If I can do it, anyone else can do it.”

The ceremony featured performances by Black Ops singers drum group, Indigenous hip hop artist Braeden Rickwood, Jingle Dress Dancers and guest speakers.

stories.title: Young Canadians less hopeful about future of democracy: Statistics Canada
stories.summary: Prairie provinces, including Alberta, had the highest percentage of respondents who felt no hope at all about democracy while British Columbia led with those who felt very hopeful.
stories.author: Dayne Patterson
stories.content:
A study released Tuesday suggests young Canadians are more likely to feel hopeless about the future of democracy in Canada than older residents.

The Statistics Canada study found about a quarter of respondents aged 25 to 44 were “not at all hopeful” when asked to think about the future and about how democracy works in Canada.

In comparison, those 65 and older were more likely to feel very hopeful (about 18 per cent) than not at all (about 10 per cent) about democracy’s functions.

The vast majority of those 15 and older were a little or somewhat hopeful about democracy in the country.

The study used data from a survey series conducted from 2022 to 2024 with a targeted sample size of about 70,000 people about democracy, their confidence in institutions and information, as well as their voting behaviour.

The response rate of the fifth and final panel, where the question was asked about hopefulness in democracy, was about 24 per cent.

1:49 Young Canadians want less addictive AI chatbots, report finds

Respondents were asked to respond to how hopeful they were about certain topics when thinking about the future in Canada, including “the way democracy works in Canada.”

They were asked to rate their feelings in one of four categories, ranging from not at all hopeful to very hopeful.

They were also asked about their confidence in institutions and information sources, voting behaviours and political participation.

The report comes as three major votes are set to be held in Canada in October — provincial elections in Quebec and British Columbia and a referendum in Alberta with a question on separation.

The Prairie provinces, including Alberta, had the highest percentage of respondents who felt no hope at all about democracy, about 25 per cent. British Columbia led with those who felt very hopeful, about 15 per cent.

The study didn’t find a link between faith in democracy and voter turnout but says those with no hope were more likely to participate in political activity.

2:31 Democracy ‘has fallen’ in U.S.: Anti-ICE protests erupt in Texas following release of Liam Ramos

The report also details how non-immigrants reported a less hopeful view on democracy than immigrants and non-permanent residents.

And it suggested that people with better mental health were more likely to feel very hopeful than those who reported poor mental health.

Respondents who said they were not hopeful at all about democracy reported lower trust in scientific experts and civic institutions, like Canadian news media and the justice system, and instead placed their trust in local businesses and police services.

Overall, the more faith respondents had in democracy, the more trust they said they placed on civic institutions, including Parliament and the school system.

stories.title: Guelph police seek help identifying people caught on videos of rowdy homecoming party
stories.summary: Guelph - Police are asking for the public's help to identify people seen in videos of a rowdy homecoming celebration near the University of Guelph that investigators said led to vandalism and put others in danger.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Guelph - Police are asking for the public’s help to identify people seen in videos of a rowdy homecoming celebration near the University of Guelph that investigators said led to vandalism and put others in danger.

Guelph police have posted on their website images of seven people who appeared in social media videos of the chaotic scene last Saturday.

stories.title: 2 killed, 2 hurt in crash involving medical emergency at B.C. mall
stories.summary: Police in Delta, B.C., say two people have been killed in a crash at the Tsawwassen Mills mall, and two others are injured.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Delta - First Nations members sang and drummed near the bodies of two elders who were killed outside a shopping centre south of Vancouver on Wednesday.

The lament was heard from behind large white sheets that officers held up to give them privacy.

The Tsawwassen First Nation said the crash occurred during its walk to mark the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

Two others were also hurt in what police said was believed to have been set off by a medical emergency involving the driver of a pickup outside the Tsawwassen Mills shopping centre.

Later, community members, many of them dressed in orange, linked arms or held their hands to the sky as the bodies were loaded into a coroner’s vehicle.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said on social media that the Nation lost two beloved elders in an accident on a day already so heavy with grief.

“My thoughts are with the loved ones of those who died, those who were injured, and the entire community who are in grief and shock,” he said on social media.

Police said the injured were treated at the scene by ambulance teams and taken to hospital.

“Preliminary information indicates the driver of the involved vehicle May have experienced a medical emergency prior to the collision,” they said in a statement.

There was no ongoing public safety risk, and police said the crash was not related to the event being held by the community to mark the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

The Nation then cancelled events planned to mark the day.

“Tsawwassen First Nation is deeply saddened to confirm that an incident occurred during today’s Truth and Reconciliation Walk,” it said in a statement.

The call for help went out about 10:30 a.m., and the Provincial Health Services Authority said it sent 12 ground ambulances and two helicopters.

Video posted online shows a black truck against the mall’s exterior and police tape surrounding the area, along with ambulances and a helicopter in the parking lot.

By early afternoon, police tents had been set up around the crash site in front of a Boston Pizza restaurant beside one of the entrances to the shopping centre.

The pickup towing an equipment trailer could be seen bearing the word “Alpine” on its front door, though police later covered the logo.

The vehicle’s front end was damaged.

Police spent much of the day with First Nations members and others in the nearby Milestones restaurant. Many of those inside came to the window to watch as the bodies were loaded into a coroner’s vehicle.

NDP Leader David Eby told reporters at an unrelated event Wednesday marking the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation that the day is already a challenging one.

“We send all of our love to the people of Tsawwassen, Tsawwassen First Nation, and with respect and appreciation for the work that they’re doing now to support the community in the wake of this tragedy,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published on Sept. 30, 2026.

— With files from Darryl Dyck in Kamloops, B.C.

stories.title: Federal Indigenous spending quadrupled to $40.8B under Trudeau, with 'negligible' improvement to communities
stories.summary: From 2014/15 to 2024/25, federal Indigenous spending increased to $40.8 billion, growing seven times faster than overall federal spending.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
In the decade leading up to 2024/25, inflation-adjusted federal Indigenous spending jumped from $10.3 billion to $40.8 billion, growing seven times faster than overall federal spending, according to a new study published by the Fraser Institute .

The independent think tank found that inflation-adjusted federal Indigenous spending increased by an average of 4.3 per cent per year from 1969/70 to 2014/15. But from 2014/15 to 2024/25, average annual Indigenous spending increased 17.1 per cent, not including the “substantial” spending on lawsuits and court settlement payouts.

Broken down by federal spending per province, annual federal Indigenous spending ranges from a low of $73 million in P.E.I. to a high of $8.8 billion in Ontario.

In B.C. in 2024/25, the federal government spent approximately $6.3 billion on program benefits for Indigenous people in the province — an average expenditure of $20,306 per Indigenous person, according to the study.

“Ottawa’s Indigenous spending has skyrocketed in recent years, even more so than general federal spending, which itself has increased substantially,” said Tom Flanagan, co-author of the study and senior fellow at the Fraser Institute.

“Canadians need to understand the magnitude of Ottawa’s Indigenous spending in recent years if they’re ever to properly assess what that additional spending is achieving in terms of results for Indigenous people.”

And in the spring economic update in April, the Carney government announced $601 million for culturally relevant elementary and secondary education on reserve, and $700 million over six years to support Indigenous communities implementing jurisdiction for child and family services.

Indigenous involvement and Canadian materials required in restoration of 24 Sussex Drive

Alberta wins praise for stressing Indigenous support in new pipeline plan

However, Statistics Canada’s Community Well-Being index (CWB), which gauges the socio-economic health of Canadian communities, suggests the spending increases have led to little improvement for Indigenous communities.

The Fraser Institute’s analysis found that in 1981, the difference in the index between First Nations communities and other Canadian communities was 19.5 points. In 2016, the gap was 19.1 points, showing essentially no change after 35 years.

In 2021, the most recent year for which the data is available, that gap had shrunk somewhat to 16.3, but the Fraser Institute study argues that “closer analysis shows that improvement was due to an increase in the Canada Child Benefit, which is a general family support measure not included in Indigenous program spending.”

It adds that the positive impact of these spending increases on First Nations’ reserve communities “has been negligible.”

The Fraser Institute study, published on Tuesday, comes as Canada marks the sixth National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, which honours residential school survivors and their families.

It is not the first report to suggest that the government is failing to improve the lives of First Nations people. In October 2025, an Auditor General follow-up on First Nations programs found that Indigenous Services Canada had made “unsatisfactory progress” in implementing recommendations made in six audits completed from 2015 to 2022.

The report said: “Despite an 84 per cent increase in the department’s spending on programs since the 2019-20 fiscal year, significant challenges remained in improving services and program outcomes for First Nations communities.”

Elsewhere, a 2022 analysis carried out by the Office of the Parliamentary Budget Officer found that while financial resources allocated to providing Indigenous services had “increased significantly” for the 2015/2016 to 2022/2023 period, it hadn’t resulted in an improvement in the ability of the organizations to achieve their goals.

In fact, the document said, “the ability to achieve the targets specified has declined.”
paragraphs: In the decade leading up to 2024/25, inflation-adjusted federal Indigenous spending jumped from $10.3 billion to $40.8 billion, growing seven times faster than overall federal spending, according to a new study published by the Fraser Institute .

The independent think tank found that inflation-adjusted federal Indigenous spending increased by an average of 4.3 per cent per year from 1969/70 to 2014/15. But from 2014/15 to 2024/25, average annual Indigenous spending increased 17.1 per cent, not including the “substantial” spending on lawsuits and court settlement payouts.
Broken down by federal spending per province, annual federal Indigenous spending ranges from a low of $73 million in P.E.I. to a high of $8.8 billion in Ontario.

In B.C. in 2024/25, the federal government spent approximately $6.3 billion on program benefits for Indigenous people in the province — an average expenditure of $20,306 per Indigenous person, according to the study.

“Ottawa’s Indigenous spending has skyrocketed in recent years, even more so than general federal spending, which itself has increased substantially,” said Tom Flanagan, co-author of the study and senior fellow at the Fraser Institute.

“Canadians need to understand the magnitude of Ottawa’s Indigenous spending in recent years if they’re ever to properly assess what that additional spending is achieving in terms of results for Indigenous people.”

And in the spring economic update in April, the Carney government announced $601 million for culturally relevant elementary and secondary education on reserve, and $700 million over six years to support Indigenous communities implementing jurisdiction for child and family services.

However, Statistics Canada’s Community Well-Being index (CWB), which gauges the socio-economic health of Canadian communities, suggests the spending increases have led to little improvement for Indigenous communities.

The Fraser Institute’s analysis found that in 1981, the difference in the index between First Nations communities and other Canadian communities was 19.5 points. In 2016, the gap was 19.1 points, showing essentially no change after 35 years.

In 2021, the most recent year for which the data is available, that gap had shrunk somewhat to 16.3, but the Fraser Institute study argues that “closer analysis shows that improvement was due to an increase in the Canada Child Benefit, which is a general family support measure not included in Indigenous program spending.”
It adds that the positive impact of these spending increases on First Nations’ reserve communities “has been negligible.”
The Fraser Institute study, published on Tuesday, comes as Canada marks the sixth National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, which honours residential school survivors and their families.

It is not the first report to suggest that the government is failing to improve the lives of First Nations people. In October 2025, an Auditor General follow-up on First Nations programs found that Indigenous Services Canada had made “unsatisfactory progress” in implementing recommendations made in six audits completed from 2015 to 2022.

The report said: “Despite an 84 per cent increase in the department’s spending on programs since the 2019-20 fiscal year, significant challenges remained in improving services and program outcomes for First Nations communities.”

In fact, the document said, “the ability to achieve the targets specified has declined.”

stories.title: Canada urges France to back off plan for snow crab fishery off coast of Newfoundland
stories.summary: ST. John's - Canada's fisheries minister is encouraging France to abandon its plan to launch a snow crab fishery in waters near Newfoundland and the French territory of St-Pierre-Miquelon.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - Canada’s fisheries minister urged France on Wednesday to abandon a plan to launch a snow crab fishery in waters near Newfoundland and the French territory of St-Pierre-Miquelon.

Joanne Thompson said France made no mention of its plan to Canadian officials, despite Prime Minister Mark Carney visiting French President Emmanuel Macron earlier this month in St-Pierre-Miquelon, a small archipelago about 25 kilometres from Newfoundland’s Burin Peninsula.

The apparent snub comes as Canada cozies up to the European Union amid an ongoing trade dispute with the United States.

“Families in Newfoundland and Labrador and St-Pierre-Miquelon have been connected for generations,” Thompson said in a statement posted to the X platform on Wednesday.

“At a time when we need to be working more closely together, it is disappointing that France intends to take this action unilaterally.”

According to a story last week from French news outlet franceinfo, Macron promised an exploratory snow crab licence to a St-Pierre-Miquelon fishing company during his recent visit to the islands. The company would be allowed to fish 1,500 tonnes of snow crab annually for five years, the article said.

Thompson said the promised licence is in waters beyond Canada’s 200-nautical-mile economic exclusion zone, in a region Canada has claimed through the United Nations Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf.

A 1972 treaty allows the two countries to fish in each other’s waters. However, an international ruling in 1992 gave the French islands a 24-nautical-mile zone and added a narrow 10.5-mile strip, known as the French Baguette, which extends south and stops short of Canada’s 200-nautical-mile limit.

In 2014, France told the United Nations Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf that the 1992 ruling did not weigh in on French claims to the continental shelf beyond 200 nautical miles from St-Pierre-Miquelon.

France said this ambiguity could pose a problem for Canada’s claims to the region.

Thompson said Wednesday that the federal Fisheries Department is discussing its next steps with Global Affairs Canada.

In Newfoundland and Labrador, Premier Tony Wakeham said he shared Thompson’s disappointment about Macron’s pledge. He issued a statement saying France had no authority to make such a decision.

Snow crab is the province’s largest and most lucrative fishery, worth about $708 million in landed value in 2025, according to government figures. Newfoundland and Labrador fishing boats work in the area of the proposed French licence, said Dwan Street, president of the union representing inshore fishers in the province.

They’re worried about surrendering any part of the resource, even a tiny fraction as proposed by Macron, she said. But Street said she didn’t foresee Canada allowing any French snow crab licences in the area.

“Those are Canadian resources,” she said in an interview, adding: “I’m fairly confident in Global Affairs Canada, and in speaking with the minister’s office, that this is very likely going to get dealt with quickly.”

Fishers from St-Pierre-Miquelon have largely been valuable partners to those in Newfoundland and Labrador, which made Macron’s decision to promise a licence without consulting Canada all the more baffling, she added. Fishers from the archipelago often sell their catch to Canadian processors, she added.

“They rely on Canadian ports for maintenance, for supplies, and all kinds of things other than off-loading the fish and getting it processed,” she said. “It is a strange one to throw this out there and try to jeopardize that relationship.”

However, fishers in St-Pierre-Miquelon told Macron during his visit that they wanted to be able to process their catch locally and have more autonomy, according to footage captured by franceinfo.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said earlier this month that she was opening the door to negotiating terms for Canada to become the first associate member of the European Union.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 30, 2026.

stories.title: Riders host Stamps in important division showdown
stories.summary: It's another important West Division contest for Trevor Harris and the Saskatchewan Roughriders.
stories.author: Dan Ralph
stories.content:
It’s another important West Division contest for Trevor Harris and the Saskatchewan Roughriders.

Saskatchewan (8-6) hosts the Calgary Stampeders (7-8) on Friday night. The Riders can sweep the season series 2-0 with a win after earning a 40-37 overtime decision back in June.

Conversely, a win by four or more points would not only move Calgary into a tie with Saskatchewan in the standings but give it the season series — and the tiebreaker if the two teams ended the year with identical records.

The defending Grey Cup champions are coming off a 31-24 road loss to B.C. (8-6) that gave the Lions the tiebreaker in that series.

The Stampeders are coming off a home-and-home sweep of the Ottawa Redblacks. Vernon Adams Jr. threw for 422 yards and three TDs in last week’s 45-31 victory while Jalen Philpot (six catches, 127 yards), Tevin Jones (eight catches, 122 yards, TD) and Clark Barnes (three catches, 109 yards, TD) all cracked the century mark in receiving.

Saskatchewan has dropped its last two contests. Harris completed 26 of 33 passes for 297 yards and a TD last week versus B.C., and the Riders’ offence had the ball for almost 34 minutes in the contest.

But Lions’ starter Nathan Rourke finished 22 of 28 passing for 375 yards and four TDs.

Calgary comes in leading the CFL in offensive points per game (33.1) and offensive TDs (53) and stands second in passing TDs (31). But the Riders should present an interesting matchup with a defence that’s allowed a league-low 35 offensive touchdowns and is second in fewest offensive points (25.5 per game) surrendered.

The Stampeders have allowed 34 sacks this season, behind only Winnipeg (36). Saskatchewan’s defence has 32 sacks, second-most behind Toronto (37).

Pick: Saskatchewan.

Hamilton Tiger-Cats vs Ottawa Redblacks (Friday night)

At Ottawa, two teams eliminated from playoff contention look to snap long losing streaks. Hamilton (4-11) has dropped five straight, including last week’s 37-35 overtime decision in Edmonton that ended its playoff hopes. Harrison Frost completed 17 of 34 passes for 214 yards with two TDs and two interceptions. McLeod Bethel-Thompson is expected to remain the starter for the Redblacks (0-14) after passing for 418 yards and two TDs last week versus Calgary. The offence had 475 net yards, but the Stamps rolled up 520 yards. However, the Ticats are last in offensive yards (330.4) and passing (253.3) and just ahead of last-place Ottawa (23.6) in offensive points scored (23.7).

Pick: Ottawa.

B.C. Lions vs Toronto Argonauts (Saturday afternoon)

At Toronto, the Argos (9-6) chase a fifth straight win, having already clinched second in the East. Chad Kelly leads the CFL in passing yards (5,067), TDs (33) and interceptions (24) and was limited in practice Wednesday (hand) after not practising at all Tuesday. If he can’t go, veteran Nick Arbuckle will look to improve the team’s record at BMO Field to 5-0. B.C. comes off its big win over Saskatchewan and is looking for a third straight victory and eighth in nine games. Rourke is the offensive catalyst, but Zander Horvath has a CFL-best 16 rushing TDs and is within striking distance of the league records for most rushing touchdowns (19) and total touchdowns (23) in a season.

Winnipeg Blue Bombers vs Montreal Alouettes (Saturday night)

At Montreal, the Alouettes (11-3) come off a bye week with a chance to clinch first in the East with a win and a Toronto loss to B.C. The Als are 9-2 coming off a bye under head coach Jason Maas, who’s in his fourth season at the helm. They’re also 7-0 at home thus far. Dru Brown starts again for Winnipeg (7-7) with incumbent Zach Collaros (head) out. paragraphs: It’s another important West Division contest for Trevor Harris and the Saskatchewan Roughriders.
Saskatchewan (8-6) hosts the Calgary Stampeders (7-8) on Friday night. The Riders can sweep the season series 2-0 with a win after earning a 40-37 overtime decision back in June.

Conversely, a win by four or more points would not only move Calgary into a tie with Saskatchewan in the standings but give it the season series — and the tiebreaker if the two teams ended the year with identical records.
The defending Grey Cup champions are coming off a 31-24 road loss to B.C. (8-6) that gave the Lions the tiebreaker in that series.

The Stampeders are coming off a home-and-home sweep of the Ottawa Redblacks. Vernon Adams Jr. threw for 422 yards and three TDs in last week’s 45-31 victory while Jalen Philpot (six catches, 127 yards), Tevin Jones (eight catches, 122 yards, TD) and Clark Barnes (three catches, 109 yards, TD) all cracked the century mark in receiving.

Saskatchewan has dropped its last two contests. Harris completed 26 of 33 passes for 297 yards and a TD last week versus B.C., and the Riders’ offence had the ball for almost 34 minutes in the contest.
But Lions’ starter Nathan Rourke finished 22 of 28 passing for 375 yards and four TDs.

Calgary comes in leading the CFL in offensive points per game (33.1) and offensive TDs (53) and stands second in passing TDs (31). But the Riders should present an interesting matchup with a defence that’s allowed a league-low 35 offensive touchdowns and is second in fewest offensive points (25.5 per game) surrendered.
The Stampeders have allowed 34 sacks this season, behind only Winnipeg (36). Saskatchewan’s defence has 32 sacks, second-most behind Toronto (37).
Pick: Saskatchewan.
Hamilton Tiger-Cats vs Ottawa Redblacks (Friday night)

At Ottawa, two teams eliminated from playoff contention look to snap long losing streaks. Hamilton (4-11) has dropped five straight, including last week’s 37-35 overtime decision in Edmonton that ended its playoff hopes. Harrison Frost completed 17 of 34 passes for 214 yards with two TDs and two interceptions. McLeod Bethel-Thompson is expected to remain the starter for the Redblacks (0-14) after passing for 418 yards and two TDs last week versus Calgary. The offence had 475 net yards, but the Stamps rolled up 520 yards. However, the Ticats are last in offensive yards (330.4) and passing (253.3) and just ahead of last-place Ottawa (23.6) in offensive points scored (23.7).
Pick: Ottawa.
B.C. Lions vs Toronto Argonauts (Saturday afternoon)

At Toronto, the Argos (9-6) chase a fifth straight win, having already clinched second in the East. Chad Kelly leads the CFL in passing yards (5,067), TDs (33) and interceptions (24) and was limited in practice Wednesday (hand) after not practising at all Tuesday. If he can’t go, veteran Nick Arbuckle will look to improve the team’s record at BMO Field to 5-0. B.C. comes off its big win over Saskatchewan and is looking for a third straight victory and eighth in nine games. Rourke is the offensive catalyst, but Zander Horvath has a CFL-best 16 rushing TDs and is within striking distance of the league records for most rushing touchdowns (19) and total touchdowns (23) in a season.

At Montreal, the Alouettes (11-3) come off a bye week with a chance to clinch first in the East with a win and a Toronto loss to B.C. The Als are 9-2 coming off a bye under head coach Jason Maas, who’s in his fourth season at the helm. They’re also 7-0 at home thus far. Dru Brown starts again for Winnipeg (7-7) with incumbent Zach Collaros (head) out. Brown completed 16 of 28 passes for 193 yards with two TDs and two interceptions in last week’s 30-28 home loss to Toronto. The West Division team did earn a 44-28 win in the last meeting between the two squads in August, although Alexander also had four TD strikes in that contest.
Pick: Montreal.
Last week: 4-0.
Overall: 45-20.

stories.title: Breaking: Four pedestrians struck during Truth and Reconciliation Day walk near Tsawwassen Mills, B.C.
stories.summary: Delta police are asking people to stay away from Tsawwassen First Nation lands in South Delta after 4 pedestrians were struck by a vehicle.
stories.author: David Carrigg
stories.content:
Two pedestrians were killed outside an entrance to the Tsawwassen Mills mall in South Delta on Wednesday morning.

According to the Delta Police Department, the driver of the vehicle that hit the pair May have experienced a medical emergency before the collision. Two other pedestrians were injured.

“Four pedestrians were struck and, tragically, two people have died as a result of their injuries,” the police statement said.

“The remaining injured individuals were treated at the scene by B.C. Emergency Health Services and transported to hospital.”

Police said the incident was not related to the Truth and Reconciliation Walk that was taking place nearby on Tsawwassen First Nation lands at the time. The mall is also on the First Nation’s lands.

However, images from the scene show many people affected by the tragedy were wearing orange Truth and Reconciliation Day T-shirts.

The Tsawwassen First Nation confirmed that the incident had occurred at the same time as their Truth and Reconciliation Day walk was underway.

“Out of respect for Tsawwassen First Nation families and ongoing response efforts, we will not be providing additional details at this time. Further information will be shared when appropriate,” the TFN statement read.

“Tsawwassen First Nation extends its sincere gratitude to the Delta Police Department, emergency responders, and community members who assisted during the incident.”

“Tsawwassen First Nation is in our hearts today. To lose two beloved elders — in such a terrifying accident and on a day already so heavy with grief — is devastating,” he said. “My thoughts are with the loved ones of those who died, those who were injured, and the entire community who are in grief and shock.”

The black truck that appeared to have struck the pedestrians was towing a trailer and was marked Alpine Services. Alpine Services has had a cleaning contract at the mall since 2019.

In a brief statement provided Thursday, the company said it is aware of the collision.

“We are co-operating with the appropriate authorities to support their investigation. Our thoughts are with everyone affected.”

The company declined to provide further details, citing the ongoing investigation.

The incident occurred close to the No. 3 south entrance to the mall. It appears that the truck was being driven close to the entrance when it crashed through an awning in front of Boston Pizza, then struck a brick wall.

An air ambulance and several road ambulances were dispatched to the scene.

On Thursday afternoon, Delta Police said in an update that the two individuals killed were elders of Tsawwassen First Nation. Two others were flown to hospital where they remain in critical condition.

Investigators say they don’t believe the collision was intentional and that the incident was not related to the Truth and Reconciliation March taking place nearby. Police said the individuals struck had been in the area preparing for a house post unveiling that was scheduled to begin after the walk.

Online posts by the Tsawwassen First Nation ahead of Wednesday’s events noted that a house post unveiling was set to take place at 10:15 a.m. near entrance No. 3 of Tsawwassen Mills, where the collision unfolded.

“Although the unveiling had not yet begun, some individuals were present in the area preparing for the ceremony,” said police.

“At this stage of the investigation, there is no information to suggest any connection between the collision and the planned event.”

B.C. Premier David Eby said he was awaiting more information on the incident.

“On a day already set aside for solemn reflection, a tragedy during the Tsawwassen First Nation Truth and Reconciliation event has shocked and saddened us all,” he wrote on social media.

“Police say it appears the driver of the vehicle experienced a medical event before the collision. As we wait for more details, our thoughts are with the families, with those injured, and with everyone at Tsawwassen First Nation.”

stories.title: Police in Delta, B.C., say four hurt in crash involving medical emergency
stories.summary: Delta — Police in Delta, B.C., say four pedestrians have been struck and hurt by a vehicle in what appears to have been a medical incident.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
First Nations members sang and drummed near the bodies of two elders who were killed outside a shopping centre south of Vancouver on Wednesday.

The lament was heard from behind large white sheets that officers held up to give them privacy.

The Tsawwassen First Nation said the crash occurred during its walk to mark the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

Two others were also hurt in what police said was believed to have been set off by a medical emergency involving the driver of a pickup outside the Tsawwassen Mills shopping centre.

Later, community members, many of them dressed in orange, linked arms or held their hands to the sky as the bodies were loaded into a coroner’s vehicle.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said on social media that the Nation lost two beloved elders in an accident on a day already so heavy with grief.

“My thoughts are with the loved ones of those who died, those who were injured, and the entire community who are in grief and shock,” he said on social media.

Police said the injured were treated at the scene by ambulance teams and taken to hospital.

“Preliminary information indicates the driver of the involved vehicle May have experienced a medical emergency prior to the collision,” they said in a statement.

There was no ongoing public safety risk, and police said the crash was not related to the event being held by the community to mark the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

The Nation then cancelled events planned to mark the day.

“Tsawwassen First Nation is deeply saddened to confirm that an incident occurred during today’s Truth and Reconciliation Walk,” it said in a statement.

The call for help went out about 10:30 a.m., and the Provincial Health Services Authority said it sent 12 ground ambulances and two helicopters.

Video posted online shows a black truck against the mall’s exterior and police tape surrounding the area, along with ambulances and a helicopter in the parking lot.

By early afternoon, police tents had been set up around the crash site in front of a Boston Pizza restaurant beside one of the entrances to the shopping centre.

The pickup towing an equipment trailer could be seen bearing the word “Alpine” on its front door, though police later covered the logo.

The vehicle’s front end was damaged.

Police spent much of the day with First Nations members and others in the nearby Milestones restaurant. Many of those inside came to the window to watch as the bodies were loaded into a coroner’s vehicle.

NDP Leader David Eby told reporters at an unrelated event Wednesday marking the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation that the day is already a challenging one.

“We send all of our love to the people of Tsawwassen, Tsawwassen First Nation, and with respect and appreciation for the work that they’re doing now to support the community in the wake of this tragedy,” he said.

stories.title: Two dead, two injured after vehicle hits pedestrians at B.C.’s Tsawwassen Mills mall
stories.summary: The driver May have experienced a medical emergency prior to the crash, police say
stories.author: Alanna Smith, Zosia Bielski
stories.content:
Two people were killed after being struck by a vehicle on the Tsawwassen First Nation in British Columbia on Wednesday, according to police, who believe the driver suffered a medical emergency.

Delta Police, in a statement , said the collision took place at approximately 10:25 a.m. local time in the parking lot at Tsawwassen Mills mall. Four pedestrians were hit, two of whom have died as a result of their injuries. The injured victims were transported to hospital.

The First Nation was holding an event marking the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. Police said the crash was not related to the event. There was widespread speculation on social media that it May have been a targeted attack.

“Preliminary information indicates the driver of the involved vehicle May have experienced a medical emergency prior to the collision,” said the service. “Our thoughts are with the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this tragic incident.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney identified the deceased as “two beloved elders” in a social-media post offering his condolences to the affected families and Tsawwassen First Nation.

“To lose two beloved elders – in such a terrifying accident and on a day already so heavy with grief – is devastating. My thoughts are with the loved ones of those who died, those who were injured, and the entire community who are in grief and shock,” he said.

Delta Police did not respond to requests about the ages of the victims, condition of the driver or what type of vehicle was involved.

The service, earlier on Wednesday, said the “investigation remains in its early stages as officers work to determine all of the circumstances surrounding the collision.” Police said there was no continuing risk to public safety.

Tsawwassen First Nation, in a statement , said it is “deeply saddened” by the crash, which they said occurred during a Truth and Reconciliation walk. The nation said there is no indication that it was intentional.

“Out of respect for Tsawwassen First Nation families and ongoing response efforts, we will not be providing additional details at this time,” said the nation, which extended its gratitude to police, emergency responders and community members for their efforts.

Sofia McGinn, who answered questions from The Globe and Mail over Facebook Messenger, was visiting the mall with her toddler and parents when the collision occurred.

They were set to watch the unveiling of an Indigenous house post – a carved wooden pillar with cultural significance in certain Indigenous communities – as part of the First Nation’s planned events.

A crowd wearing commemorative orange shirts was gathered outside one of the mall’s entrances for the reveal before chaos ensued. Ms. McGinn did not see the collision as she was inside the doors with her family when it happened.

“I saw mall, staff and security closing off the entrance and then I just felt the energy in the air shift,” Ms. McGinn said, adding that she could see emergency and medical personnel converging on the scene, with security redirecting people away from the doors.

“I looked out and saw someone performing CPR on someone,” she said, describing an environment of commotion and confusion. “People just looked at a loss.”

Some 15 minutes before the incident, Ms. McGinn said she saw a black pickup truck with a trailer holding a red barrel-type object driving in the opposite direction. A vehicle of a similar description is seen in a social-media video of the site after the collision.

Ms. McGinn said the event has been difficult to process.

“My toddler is so unaware. [I’m] feeling very uneasy, sorrowful, and just almost a shocked feeling. I was leaving the parking lot, and I could still see people gathering, who probably had no idea what was happening on the other side of the mall,” she said.

In a statement, B.C. Premier David Eby said that his thoughts were with the community.

“On a day already set aside for solemn reflection, a tragedy during the Tsawwassen First Nation Truth and Reconciliation event has shocked and saddened us all.”

stories.title: U.S. trade court scrutinizes Trump’s forced labour tariffs
stories.summary: Four small businesses and 25 Democratic-led states argue that the tariffs, applied to imports from 60 trading partners, including Canada, far exceed the president's authority.
stories.author: Dietrich Knauth
stories.content:
The U.S. Court of International Trade on Wednesday scrutinized the legal and factual underpinnings of U.S. President Donald Trump’s latest global tariffs , which were imposed on nearly all U.S. imports over allegations trading partners aren’t doing enough to stop forced labour.

A panel of three judges appointed by Presidents Trump, Barack Obama and Joe Biden heard arguments in Manhattan over lawsuits alleging that the latest tariffs are an attempt to revive the unchecked tariff power the Supreme Court struck down in February.

Four small businesses and 25 Democratic-led states argue that the tariffs, applied to imports from 60 trading partners including Canada, the EU and China, far exceed the president’s authority.

Pratik Shah, an attorney representing small businesses that sued over the tariffs, told the court that the Trump administration has misused a law that offers only a “carefully constrained” tariff authority.

In its rush to impose new tariffs, the Trump administration skipped the legal requirements to make country-specific findings that each of the tariffs was justified, Shah said. Shah contrasted the tariffs with duties imposed under the same law during Trump’s first term, when the US Trade Representative produced country-by-country reports and imposed tariffs tailored to each economy.

“If you’re going to do it at breakneck speed and try to cover the entire globe, you still have to satisfy the statutory requirements,” Shah said.

Eric Hamilton, representing the U.S. Department of Justice, said the U.S. Trade Representative had thoroughly evaluated the prevalence of goods produced with forced labour in international commerce. The government did not need to show “with metaphysical certainty” that forced labour was a “burden” on US commerce before imposing tariffs, he said.

The panel is expected to issue a written ruling in the coming weeks.

The plaintiffs asked the court to throw out the tariffs entirely. The court could also issue a more limited ruling that asks the government to re-do its investigation to provide more detail and justifications for the tariffs, as the court did with some of Trump’s tariffs in his first term.

0:50 U.S. hits dozens of countries, including Canada, with new 10% tariff

The judges interrupted attorneys for both sides soon after they began their arguments, peppering them with questions about the level of detail required in the government’s investigation into forced labour in other countries before deciding to apply tariffs.

They asked Shah whether he was simply asking for “more paper” from the government, and they asked Hamilton whether the government was ignoring more detailed statutory requirements that dealt specifically with forced labour, rather than relying on broader authority about “unreasonable” trade practices.

Trump has made tariffs a central pillar of his foreign policy, using them as leverage to negotiate trade deals around the globe. But the Supreme Court ruled against most of Trump’s widest-ranging tariffs on February 20, finding that the president cannot use emergency economic powers to unilaterally impose tariffs on all US trading partners.

Trump responded by immediately imposing a temporary 10 per cent global tariff under a different U.S. law. When those temporary tariffs expired, he invoked another legal authority to impose in July the forced labour tariffs now being challenged, which range from 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent.

The plaintiffs’ lawsuits, consolidated before the court, argue the administration failed to satisfy the legal requirements for imposing the tariffs and is using concerns about forced labour as a pretext to revive a broad tariff authority that U.S. courts have repeatedly rejected.

The Trump administration argued in court papers that it had conducted real investigations into other nations’ failure to prevent imports of goods produced with forced labour, and concluded that tariffs were warranted for each of the 60 investigated trading partners.

The government did not need to show “with metaphysical certainty” that forced labour was a “burden” on US commerce before imposing tariffs, he said.
The panel is expected to issue a written ruling in the coming weeks.

The plaintiffs asked the court to throw out the tariffs entirely. The court could also issue a more limited ruling that asks the government to re-do its investigation to provide more detail and justifications for the tariffs, as the court did with some of Trump’s tariffs in his first term.

The judges interrupted attorneys for both sides soon after they began their arguments, peppering them with questions about the level of detail required in the government’s investigation into forced labour in other countries before deciding to apply tariffs.

They asked Shah whether he was simply asking for “more paper” from the government, and they asked Hamilton whether the government was ignoring more detailed statutory requirements that dealt specifically with forced labour, rather than relying on broader authority about “unreasonable” trade practices.

Trump has made tariffs a central pillar of his foreign policy, using them as leverage to negotiate trade deals around the globe. But the Supreme Court ruled against most of Trump’s widest-ranging tariffs on February 20, finding that the president cannot use emergency economic powers to unilaterally impose tariffs on all US trading partners.

Trump responded by immediately imposing a temporary 10 per cent global tariff under a different U.S. law. When those temporary tariffs expired, he invoked another legal authority to impose in July the forced labour tariffs now being challenged, which range from 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent.

The plaintiffs’ lawsuits, consolidated before the court, argue the administration failed to satisfy the legal requirements for imposing the tariffs and is using concerns about forced labour as a pretext to revive a broad tariff authority that U.S. courts have repeatedly rejected.

The Trump administration argued in court papers that it had conducted real investigations into other nations’ failure to prevent imports of goods produced with forced labour, and concluded that tariffs were warranted for each of the 60 investigated trading partners.

stories.title: Staying the course: why some Fanshawe students switch programs
stories.summary: For some Fanshawe students, the program they start in isn't always the program they finish. Interests, career ...
stories.author: Torey Joseph Legarrie
stories.content:
For some Fanshawe students, the program they start in isn’t always the program they finish. Interests, career goals and new experiences can all play a role in deciding whether to stay or make a change.

Human resources student Sahar Yousefi said her original program pre-health didn’t meet her long-term goals.

“I decided to switch because I kind of realized that the program didn’t really fit my long-term goals. I had kind of like a switch desire and career path. So I kind of wanted to take a different route with my career,” she said.

She said that her original program wasn’t what she expected and why she switched.

“No, it was kind of odd that I expected a lot of math, science and whatnot, just wasn’t really aligning with what I had envisioned for my future,” she said.

She said that switching has affected her, and caused a set back.

“It’s set me back in some time, that’s for sure. I don’t really pay attention to the cost, which maybe I should, but I’m kind of putting that in the back of my mind for now and kind of focusing on what I need to get done and what feels comfortable for me,” she said.

She said students can decide to switch their programs for a lot of reasons.

“This could be a lot of reasons. It varies from person to person. Sometimes people kind of like, have a change in mind or like they get a feel of their program and realize its not really what they’re looking for, and that’s totally okay and it happens. That’s what college is for,” she said.

“Its one of those kind of things where you have to kind of jump in and see what its like to really see if its a right fit for you or not,” she said.

Cited federal national center for education statistics (Nces) longitudinal estimate found about 30 per cent of U.S. undergraduates switch their programs at least once according to [Research.com].

Robyn Naylor, co-operative education consultant employment and student entrepreneurial services at Fanshawe College said that she thinks there’s a variety of reasons why students switch.

“I think a lot of times they find out that the program wasn’t the right fit for them. They might have learned a little bit about some of the career pathways and those aren’t aligning with what they want to be doing. Or they might find that the courses are either too challenging or aren’t challenging enough and don’t fit what they kind of signed up for,” she said.

“It could end up costing you more in the end because you would have maybe already paid for a program and hadn’t made the decision in time and then have to sign up again to enroll into a new one,” she said.

Fanshawe human resources student Dansea Steckly said that she wanted to stay in her program because she likes business, and she loves the environment.

“I really like business and it was the cheapest option,” she said.

“I really love all the classes I have and all the teachers are so friendly,” she said.

“Its been pretty much exactly what I’ve expected, like a mix of all the business courses, and I find it all very interesting and I love it,” she said.

“I was kind of considering switching into marketing, but I’m not sure yet because its only been a month, but we’ll see,” she said.

“I took a bunch of marketing classes in high school, so I have already like, know a bunch of boat marketing and I think its like the most interesting thing ever. And I would love to do that, but as of right now, I’m in human resources,” she said.

She said that she does not feel confident yet if she chose the right program for her future.

“Not yet, because I haven’t actually taken like an actual human resources course yet. But I’ve taken like all the other business ones and I’m confident that I want to be in business,” she said.

Naylor said that Fanshawe has many supportive resources for students who are considering the switch.

(Torey Joseph Legarrie)

“Absolutely, they can speak to program coordinators, academic advisors, pathway coordinators, career consultants, any folks in the student services area to get some support there,” she said.

“I think talk to your faculty, make sure that you’re taking the time to thoughtfully make the decision, do research in the new program that you’re looking for. Whether that would be looking at different career paths, different outcomes of employment on the Canada Job Bank, to really make sure you’re making a thoughtful decision around it,” she said.

stories.title: Sharia law 'religious divorce' fails to fly with Immigration and Refugee Board
stories.summary: "Honesty is not the prerogative of educated people," said the Immigration and Refugee Board panel in its decision.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A Canadian Muslim who tried to sponsor his Ethiopian wife for a permanent resident visa is out of luck because her “religious divorce” from her first husband under Sharia law isn’t recognized here.

Fetno Umer Kemo appealed a visa officer’s decision to deny Rahama Adem Abdi the document that allows foreign nationals to live, work and study anywhere in Canada indefinitely to the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada. But the panel concluded that Kemo failed to establish that Abdi was “free to marry” when they wed in 2021.

“Mr. Kemo has not shown that Ms. Abdi’s religious divorce in 2017 was valid under Canadian law,” the panel said in a decision published in June in French and this month in an English translation.

“As a result, the officer’s decision not to issue his wife a visa is valid in law. The couple’s marriage is not valid, and Ms. Abdi is therefore not a member of the family class. The panel does not have jurisdiction to consider humanitarian and compassionate considerations in this case. The appeal is dismissed.”

The visa officer further determined that the couple’s relationship was not genuine and that their marriage was entered into primarily for immigration purposes.

The panel said it didn’t have to consider “the issues of the genuineness of the couple’s relationship or their intent at the time of their marriage” because their marriage isn’t “valid under Canadian law.”

Canada’s Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations “state that a foreign national shall not be considered the sponsor’s spouse if the foreign national was, at the time of their marriage, the spouse of another person,” said the decision.

During her immigration interview last year, Abdi said her divorce was carried out verbally by religious authorities in Ethiopia. Her ex-husband took part remotely by telephone, she said.

What to do with the gold? Divorce cases with Islamic marriage contracts pose challenge for courts

Couple's young daughters taken from Canada to child-custody limbo in Casablanca

In the same interview, Abdi didn’t “submit any official document attesting to her divorce,” said the decision.

That led the visa officer to conclude that, “at the time of her marriage to Mr. Kemo, Ms. Abdi was still legally married to her first husband, contrary to the requirements of the regulations.”

Kemo argued that Abdi’s first marriage and divorce “took place in Ethiopia in a rural context where issuing and registering official documents is the exception, not the rule,” said the decision.

Kemo gave the panel a document attesting to Abdi’s divorce. “It is a judgment issued by Ethiopian judicial authorities recognizing Ms. Abdi’s divorce. The judgment was rendered on January 1, 2026.”

The panel sided with the visa officer, finding that Abdi’s first marriage was not legally dissolved in 2021, and she was therefore still married to her first husband when she married Kemo.

Abdi is approximately 38, but she doesn’t know her exact age. “At the hearing, she described herself as someone who could not read or write.”

Canadian immigration authorities interviewed her in April 2023 in Canada, and again in June 2025 in Ethiopia.

At her first interview, Abdi said her first marriage to Abdulasit Aman “lasted approximately one and a half years.”

They had a child, according to the decision.

“When the officer asked why her first marriage and child had not been disclosed in the immigration forms, Ms. Abdi gave contradictory answers. Ms. Abdi initially stated that she had argued with her ex-husband about whether or not to include her child in the immigration documents. Ms. Abdi then stated that she and Mr. Kemo had agreed not to include this information in the sponsorship application.”

At the end of the 2023 interview, the visa officer told Abdi “that he was refusing the sponsorship application and that she had to leave Canada, given her misrepresentations,” said the decision, noting that Adbi had the right to try again.

Kemo submitted a second application to sponsor Abdi in August 2023. “At her second interview, in 2025, Ms. Abdi stated that she had been abducted and forced into marriage. Ms. Abdi recounted how two days after her abduction, her marriage to her first husband was celebrated and validated at a Nikah ceremony attended by the elders of both families.”

Abdi went on to say “that her first marriage was not legal because she had been forced to marry her first husband.”

paragraphs: A Canadian Muslim who tried to sponsor his Ethiopian wife for a permanent resident visa is out of luck because her “religious divorce” from her first husband under Sharia law isn’t recognized here.

Fetno Umer Kemo appealed a visa officer’s decision to deny Rahama Adem Abdi the document that allows foreign nationals to live, work and study anywhere in Canada indefinitely to the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada. But the panel concluded that Kemo failed to establish that Abdi was “free to marry” when they wed in 2021.
“Mr. Kemo has not shown that Ms. Abdi’s religious divorce in 2017 was valid under Canadian law,” the panel said in a decision published in June in French and this month in an English translation.

“As a result, the officer’s decision not to issue his wife a visa is valid in law. The couple’s marriage is not valid, and Ms. Abdi is therefore not a member of the family class. The panel does not have jurisdiction to consider humanitarian and compassionate considerations in this case. The appeal is dismissed.”
The visa officer further determined that the couple’s relationship was not genuine and that their marriage was entered into primarily for immigration purposes.

The panel said it didn’t have to consider “the issues of the genuineness of the couple’s relationship or their intent at the time of their marriage” because their marriage isn’t “valid under Canadian law.”

Canada’s Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations “state that a foreign national shall not be considered the sponsor’s spouse if the foreign national was, at the time of their marriage, the spouse of another person,” said the decision.
During her immigration interview last year, Abdi said her divorce was carried out verbally by religious authorities in Ethiopia. Her ex-husband took part remotely by telephone, she said.

In the same interview, Abdi didn’t “submit any official document attesting to her divorce,” said the decision.
That led the visa officer to conclude that, “at the time of her marriage to Mr. Kemo, Ms. Abdi was still legally married to her first husband, contrary to the requirements of the regulations.”
Kemo argued that Abdi’s first marriage and divorce “took place in Ethiopia in a rural context where issuing and registering official documents is the exception, not the rule,” said the decision.
Kemo gave the panel a document attesting to Abdi’s divorce. “It is a judgment issued by Ethiopian judicial authorities recognizing Ms. Abdi’s divorce. The judgment was rendered on January 1, 2026.”
The panel sided with the visa officer, finding that Abdi’s first marriage was not legally dissolved in 2021, and she was therefore still married to her first husband when she married Kemo.
Abdi is approximately 38, but she doesn’t know her exact age. “At the hearing, she described herself as someone who could not read or write.”
Canadian immigration authorities interviewed her in April 2023 in Canada, and again in June 2025 in Ethiopia.
At her first interview, Abdi said her first marriage to Abdulasit Aman “lasted approximately one and a half years.”
They had a child, according to the decision.

“When the officer asked why her first marriage and child had not been disclosed in the immigration forms, Ms. Abdi gave contradictory answers. Ms. Abdi initially stated that she had argued with her ex-husband about whether or not to include her child in the immigration documents. Ms. Abdi then stated that she and Mr. Kemo had agreed not to include this information in the sponsorship application.”

At the end of the 2023 interview, the visa officer told Abdi “that he was refusing the sponsorship application and that she had to leave Canada, given her misrepresentations,” said the decision, noting that Adbi had the right to try again.

Kemo submitted a second application to sponsor Abdi in August 2023. “At her second interview, in 2025, Ms. Abdi stated that she had been abducted and forced into marriage. Ms. Abdi recounted how two days after her abduction, her marriage to her first husband was celebrated and validated at a Nikah ceremony attended by the elders of both families.”
Abdi went on to say “that her first marriage was not legal because she had been forced to marry her first husband.”
The panel noted Abdi “said nothing about a forced marriage” at her first hearing.

“Ms. Abdi instead explained that her mother had wanted her to marry and that she agreed to do so. That explanation directly contradicts Ms. Abdi’s statements at her second interview and at the hearing,” said the decision.
The panel gave “more weight” to her first explanation, “in accordance with the principle that ‘a person’s first story is usually the most genuine and, therefore, the one to be most believed.’”
But the officers who interviewed her in 2023 and 2025 “both concluded that Ms. Abdi had not answered their questions truthfully.”

The officer who interviewed her last year “confronted Ms. Abdi, who had stated that she spoke little Amharic and did not understand. Ms. Abdi defended herself by stating that she did not talk much at the 2023 interview. When the officer pointed out to her that the recording of the 2023 interview shows she spoke throughout it in Amharic, Ms. Abdi gave no explanation.” The panel noted the 2023 interview lasted more than three hours.
The panel “does not find” Abdi credible, said the decision.
“Throughout the sponsorship application process, Ms. Abdi had a duty of candour and truthfulness,” it said.
“Ms. Abdi cannot discharge this duty by pointing to her illiteracy. Honesty is not the prerogative of educated people.”

stories.title: Indigenous constable designs uniform patch for Western officers to signal safety, support
stories.summary: Indigenous officer Jonathan Jamieson designed a new patch for Western Special Constable Service uniforms to open dialogue and promote safety.
stories.author: Megan Stacey
stories.content:
An idea that came to Jonathan Jamieson in the middle of an overnight shift is now being implemented across the Western Special Constable Service, with a new addition to uniforms during Truth and Reconciliation Week.

Jamieson designed a patch for Wscs members to show support and open dialogue with Indigenous communities. His concept was inspired by the Medicine Wheel, a teaching framework used and adapted across many Indigenous communities. In this patch, the Medicine Wheel is represented by four quadrants of white, yellow, red and black.

“It’s surreal that this is happening. It’s so cool to know my patch is going to be worn by our team,” said Jamieson, an Indigenous special constable who joined Wscs in 2024.

“I want to promote open and honest communication that fosters the positive interaction between our service and the Indigenous community. Normalizing positive interactions with those in the uniform is one of my priorities, because I know the barriers can be big and deep. I hope this design helps to signal ‘yes, I’m wearing a vest, but I’m a human being still,’” he said.

Jonathan Jamieson with the Western Special Constable Service designed a patch to be worn on uniforms during days of recognition for Indigenous communities, including National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. (Christopher Kindratsky/Western Communications)

Jamieson said he understands the trauma and uncertainty many Indigenous people carry and feel toward law enforcement.

He hopes the new patch – which will be worn during special days and times of year, including National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, Treaty Week in November, National Day of Awareness for Missing and Murdered Women, Girls, and Two- Spirited people (Red Dress Day) on May 5 and Indigenous History Month in June – will highlight special constables as a supportive force for all on campus.

“I want to help build understanding and trust. We know there are some who won’t report concerns to us because there’s mistrust. We want you to come to us when you have troubles,” he said of Western constables.

Bill Chantler, director of Campus Safety and Emergency Services at Western, said he was pleased to see Jamieson’s vision come to fruition.

“We are very proud of Jonathan and this initiative towards building a stronger community. Jonathan is very thoughtful and genuine, and he truly makes a difference with our campus community through his service as a member of the Western Special Constable Service,” Chantler said.

‘Help someone through a tough time’

Joining Wscs showed Jamieson the possibilities that come with community-focused approaches to policing, from clothing drives to supporting those in mental health crises.

“We’re always seeking genuine engagement. Not just our patrol division, but the community resources team as well. It’s inspiring to be here and be part of that,” he said. “I want to be that person who can help someone through a tough time. I want to make their life a little bit easier, a little bit better.”

Jamieson is no stranger to facing challenges.

Raised by his grandmother, who died when he was 16, Jamieson navigated significant instability, including bouts of homelessness.

“I focused on how I could pick myself back up. I managed to get back on my feet after having nothing. I got my security licence and started building connections.”

It led him to the world of policing, starting at Fanshawe College with the police foundations program. He started to dream of a world where he could make a difference.

After working for campus and hospital security teams, Jamieson applied to work with Wscs. Two years into his role at Western, he sees himself staying long-term, now setting goals to becoming a coach officer and sergeant.

Colleagues and mentors have demonstrated the importance of prioritizing relationships and human interactions, whether that’s responding to students in crisis or addressing emergencies on campus.

“There’s always an emphasis on support first – how can we make this better, make life easier? I don’t think I would be in this position today if I hadn’t gone through what I went through. I base it on my own experience.”

It’s also what inspired the new patch.

Jamieson is excited to see his idea turned from dream to reality, and eager to see the design worn by Wscs members throughout the year.

“This wasn’t for profit or to give me an advantage; that was never my mindset. I did it for change, for hope, for building new trust within the community,” Jamieson said.

“Sometimes people see us and they don’t see the people behind the vest. I’m hopeful this patch eventually fosters this change.”

Learn more about how Western is navigating new realities.
