stories.title: Why the safer-supply program persists despite opposition
stories.summary: Authorities put the brakes on safer supply, yet in Ontario it has refused to die
stories.author: Marcus Gee
stories.content:
One hot morning this summer, a group of weary-looking men and women gathered outside the door of a Hamilton pharmacy, waiting for opening time. Just before 9, they started filing through the door to collect the medicines they take for their various addictions. The meds are designed to help them fend off the agony of withdrawal and perhaps even get on the road to recovery.

But within minutes of emerging, one of them, a bearded man in a baseball cap, was emptying his bottle of pills into the palm of another guy, who in return gave him a small handful of a yellowish powder: fentanyl, the potent opioid that causes most drug overdoses.

Transactions like this are commonplace on the streets of Hamilton, so routine that those involved hardly bother to conceal them. This one took place just around the corner from the pharmacy on James Street South, a busy avenue in the heart of the city. The two men exchanged their drugs right in front of me, after I explained who I was and what I was writing about.

The pills were a potent painkiller called hydromorphone. Sold under the commercial name Dilaudid, they are normally used to treat severe pain from cancer, bone fractures or burns.

About a decade ago, some doctors began prescribing them to people with addictions. They reasoned that, with fentanyl flooding the streets, it was safer for patients to satisfy their need with a regulated, prescription medication than a dangerous, illegal drug. Health authorities sanctioned the practice, which became known as safe supply or safer supply.

Before long, though, evidence started to mount that many patients were selling or exchanging the pills, which became popular street drugs in their own right.

In 2021, Hamilton police seized a total of just eight hydromorphone pills. Last year, they seized 1,639. The price has dropped as the supply has increased, until a pill cost less than a can of beer.

Authorities eventually woke up to the problem – known as drug “diversion” – and governments began imposing more controls. But in Ontario at least, safer supply continued to thrive.

A group of 36 alarmed physicians wrote to the Ontario government in July demanding action. One of them, Lori Regenstreif, 63, used to work at a clinic just a few steps away from the James Street pharmacy where the pills-for-powder trade happened. She told me her “blood boils” over what the mass dispensing of safer-supply drugs is doing to her patients.

Because hydromorphone pills are so easy to get, some of them are falling back into using street drugs after years of stability on the standard addiction medicines she prescribes.

“You are turning people into criminals instead of patients,” she says. “They’re trying to move forward, and you’re pulling them back in.”

With doctors like her raising a fuss and the media asking more and more questions, regulators began moving this week to further tighten the rules on safer supply. But not before the program caused what she calls “horrible” damage in cities like Hamilton.

Dr. Regenstreif took me on a tour of its downtown, pointing out the addiction pharmacies that dot the city and the struggling people who congregate outside them. Over the next few weeks, I spoke with doctors, pharmacists, addiction experts, police, community leaders and drug users on the streets.

What emerged was a picture of a well-intentioned policy gone wildly off course. Though federally funded clinics supplying safer-supply drugs closed down, and the provincial government banned new ones, individual doctors kept prescribing large quantities of hydromorphone pills.

A network of pharmacies and clinics sprang up to distribute them. Taking advantage of a billing system that rewards them for the heavy traffic they get from addiction medicine, they collect fees from the health system and send their customers out the door with bottles of highly addictive medicines, which then make their way into the street-drug market.

The spread of the pills echoes the origins of the opioids crisis, which began with the mass prescribing of addictive pain pills. Ontario neighbourhoods from North Bay to downtown Toronto are coping with the side effects, which include open drug use and dealing. Dr. Regenstreif says she is seeing more and more young people turning to the pills, some of them in their early teens. Indigenous communities are seeing more of them, too.

Safer supply sprang from the best of motives. When drug overdoses started soaring a decade ago, advocates argued that we should treat the opioids crisis as a health, not a crime, problem.

To reduce the spread of diseases such as Aids and hepatitis C, they handed out clean needles. To reduce the toll of overdoses, they offered people supervised places to take their drugs, with trained staff on hand to revive them in case they collapsed.

Harm reduction was the goal and safer supply was the next step. At the program’s peak, 5,000 people were approved for the drugs in British Columbia, ground zero of the opioid crisis. B.C. even introduced vending machines where selected users could get their pills.

From the start of Canada’s safer-supply experiment, though, many patients were selling the pills to give themselves some pocket money or to buy more powerful drugs. In London, Ont., police said the number of prescription hydromorphone pills they were discovering in drug busts had soared from 1,000 in 2019 to 30,000 in 2023.

In Prince George, B.C., police seized 10,000 prescription pills in a single raid in 2024. They said safer-supply drugs were being trafficked by organized criminals and deployed by drug users “as a form of currency to purchase more potent, illicit street drugs.”

A series of articles in the National Post shone a spotlight on the issue. The pharmacies dispensing the pills began coming under scrutiny. A Globe and Mail investigation in 2024 found that some B.C. pharmacies were paying prohibited cash incentives to patients so that they would go to those pharmacies to get their prescriptions filled.

A leaked B.C. Ministry of Health document last year confirmed the practice, saying that more than 60 pharmacies were being investigated for offering kickbacks. It also said that a “significant portion” of prescription opioids are sold – trafficked provincially, nationally and internationally.

As a result, since the end of 2025 British Columbia has been prohibiting most safer-supply patients from taking their addiction medications out of the pharmacy, insisting they take the meds on site, under observation – a system known as “witnessed dosing.” Meanwhile, the federal government quietly halted its funding for safer-supply programs last year. In 2024 the Ontario government brought in a law, the Safer Streets, Stronger Communities Act, that bars new safer-supply programs.

But Canadian doctors have wide latitude to prescribe drugs as they see fit, if they believe their patients will benefit from them. Many have continued to approve daily doses of hydromorphone pills to patients with serious addictions.

“There is no way anyone can tell me this is harm reduction,” Dr. Regenstreif said. “It is harm promotion.”

The daughter of a Winnipeg city planner, she studied genetics and molecular biology at university, then went into medicine. She moved to Hamilton in 2004, started treating the homeless and the mentally ill and gravitated to addiction treatment.

I think there is a level of patient care that is missing. It’s very transactional. — Priya Sandhu, Hamilton pharmacist

She has seen wave upon deadly wave of the drug crisis roll over Hamilton since, but nothing has left her as discouraged as the chaos wrought by safer supply. In the last few years, she says, the clinics and pharmacies offering the program have spread “like wildfire.”

The facilities can be found everywhere from Niagara Falls to the Toronto suburb of Pickering to Elliot Lake in Northern Ontario.

True North Medical has more than 100 addiction-medicine clinics, from Red Lake in the northwest of the province to Kingston in the southeast. Arrow Medical, established in 2023, offers “urgent, compassionate, evidence-based care for people living with opioid use disorder, without judgment, barriers or delay.” It has 11 locations around Southern Ontario, as well as a virtual clinic.

The James Street pharmacy in Hamilton, Wellkare, offers “fast, friendly” service and short wait times. “We are accepting new patients!” an ad on the outside wall says.

Visitors can come out of the door with their pills in minutes. Many pharmacies have doctors on site to write prescriptions. If a doctor is not there, clients can often talk to one by video.

Hamilton pharmacist Priya Sandhu says such outfits have discovered that specializing in addiction medicines can be a money maker. Many of their clients are on multiple medications. Along with hydromorphone, they might be receiving addiction meds such as methadone, Suboxone and Kadian, as well as drugs for anxiety, insomnia, infections and high blood pressure. The pharmacies can charge dispensing fees for each, plus another charge for observing the taking of the drugs, if that is required.

Ms. Sandhu figures they can make $40 a day off some customers. That means that, in theory, a pharmacy could earn nearly $15,000 a year from a single person.

“It’s a great business model,” she says. But “I think there is a level of patient care that is missing. It’s very transactional.”

Defenders of safer supply insist it is a vital service. Arrow Medical’s founder, Joshua Fletcher, says traditional addiction meds such as methadone and Suboxone May calm patients’ drug cravings but they don’t provide the high that some of them seek. Better that they should get it from fast-acting hydromorphone pills than street fentanyl laced with dangerous additives, says Dr. Fletcher, who is affiliated with North York General, a Toronto hospital.

The founder of True North, addiction doctor and University of Toronto professor Chris Cavacuiti, told me by e-mail that his clinics prescribe safer-supply pills only in combination with more standard addiction meds and that “any patient identified as diverting medication is discontinued from the program.” He said the program’s aim is “to reduce reliance on street drugs and keep patients connected to health care providers.”

David D’Souza, the founder of another chain, New Dawn Medical, acknowledges that diversion and “lax prescribing” happens. But in an Aug. 27 paper for the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, an Ottawa think tank, he wrote that safer supply “properly targeted and rigorously regulated, can be a pragmatic response to the new realities of today’s illicit-drug market.”

The pharmacies, too, defend their practices. They stress their job is to dispense addiction medications, not prescribe them. That is up to the doctors.

The pharmacies also say they have strict protocols in place to prevent diversion, such as taking urine samples from patients to make sure they have traces of the prescribed drug in their bodies and requiring them to take at least some of their meds in front of pharmacy staff.

Staff at the Wellkare pharmacy showed me the small washroom where patients go to produce a sample. It has a video camera inside to discourage them from tampering with their samples. A sign warns visitors it is there. The owner declined to speak to me on the record.

None of these measures seem to do much to prevent the buying and selling of the pills. I visited four different Hamilton pharmacies over several days this summer and often found people waiting outside to buy hydromorphone pills. They had no problem finding sellers.

A steady stream of people came out of the pharmacies, holding white plastic bags containing their meds. Some told me they would take only one or two of their pills so that the drug showed up in their urine test at the pharmacy, but trade the rest for fentanyl or sell them for cash.

Jesse Steingart, 44, said pill selling and trading is a fact of life in Hamilton. He used to sell his hydromorphone to get fentanyl “because that’s a hard drug to afford.” Now, he says he sells them just once or twice a week, “whether it’s to get laundry done or to get a pizza in my stomach.” With the pills in his pocket, “it’s just inevitable.”

Joshua Gordyn told me he sells or trades the pills he gets daily from his pharmacy. The eight-milligram pills go for about $2 on the street in Hamilton – more in communities where they are less common. Mr. Gordyn said he could get $10 a pill if he took them to a nearby Indigenous reserve, Six Nations of the Grand River.

Police there confirm that outsiders bring pills to the reserve. Detective Sergeant Rob Monteforte of the Six Nations drug squad said that, in a bust last year, they seized more than 1,000 from suspected Toronto-area traffickers.

Locals on safer supply sometimes sell their meds, too, he said. If police find a pill bottle with a name on it, they call the prescribing doctor and ask him or her to cut the patient off.

Brett Stubbs works as a security guard at a church soup kitchen across the street from a well-known Hamilton addiction pharmacy. He told me that, once, when he was reviving someone who had suffered an overdose, he had to cut open the man’s pants to give him a life-saving injection. About 70 pills tumbled out of his pockets.

“It’s so blatant, it’s frightening,” said Regan Anderson, head of Wayside House of Hamilton, a live-in addiction-treatment centre. He sees people using and dealing pills right on the steps of a nearby pharmacy.

It would be one thing, he told me, if the array of drugs that people get at such places was helping them get better. Instead, “they’re staying unwell, and to the point of being basically publicly intoxicated or paralyzed on the street, without a real strong road map to change or to recovery.”

Dr. Regenstreif has done lots of work with youth who have run afoul of the law. They told her hydromorphone pills are cheap and easy to find. For those with limited experience using opioids, and thus a low tolerance, they pose a serious threat.

The eight-milligram Dilaudid pills, or D8s, are so strong they are not often used in ordinary medicine. Yet some safer-supply patients are walking out of the pharmacy door with 10 or 20 D8s at a time.

Though the death rate from opioids has been trending downward in Canada, 165 people died in Hamilton last year of suspected overdoses, a staggering number for the Southern Ontario city of about half a million. The victims of this 21st-century plague can be seen all over downtown, passed out of the sidewalk or bent over, swaying, in the half-conscious state that comes from consuming opioid drugs.

Critics of safer supply like Dr. Regenstreif say the practice is contributing to the problem, by giving drug users a marketable commodity that produces ready cash on a daily basis – just what they need to support their habit.

Hamilton police say that although fentanyl is still the main threat, they know prescription pills are being sold on the streets. This July, they carried out a two-week investigation of suspected drug dealing around a local pharmacy. They arrested nine people and seized 284 hydromorphone pills, along with quantities of fentanyl, methamphetamine and other drugs.

Hamilton is far from the only Ontario city struggling with the fallout from safer supply. In North Bay, drug-squad officer Brad Reaume said the Northern Ontario city was blindsided by the spread of diverted safer-supply drugs, hit when “we had our backs turned.” He said some pills end up in Indigenous communities farther north, where they are less numerous and fetch a higher price.

In London, downtown business owners have complained about open drug use, vandalism and other problems around pharmacies that specialize in addiction meds. In April, city council voted unanimously to ask the provincial government to review what one councillor, David Ferreira, called the “variety-store” model of dispensing them.

In Ottawa, merchants and residents complained about similar issues around a clinic in the Chinatown district. “It’s creating a very visible, very active and I would say dangerous open-air drug market,” city councillor Ariel Troster said. “It’s just the absolute Wild West with these private clinics.”

Even at one of Toronto’s trendiest intersections, Dundas and Ossington, residents have been complaining on social media about open drug use outside an addiction pharmacy. In a scene much like that outside the Hamilton pharmacies, a collection of people gather in the morning to wait for it to open.

Province-wide, the Ontario Provincial Police say they seized 12 times as much hydromorphone in 2025 as they did in 2022, though they cannot say for certain how much came from diverted safer supply.

Regulators are aware of the diversion issue.

Lily Barnes, press secretary for Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones, said that “to be absolutely clear, our government does not and will never support the distribution of illegal drugs,” though it was up to the bodies that oversee pharmacists and doctors to make sure their members were following the rules about opioids.

The Ontario College of Pharmacists said it was looking into complaints about certain addiction pharmacies and “reviewing standards, policies, guidelines and other requirements.”

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario brought in new rules this May requiring doctors to see patients in person (rather than just online) before starting them on safer-supply drugs, to offer them other addiction medicines first and to assess patients in person every three months.

Then, this week, it went much further. It said it would direct doctors not to prescribe safer supply except in combination with other more standard addiction drugs; to limit prescribing of the drugs to eight weeks; and to require patients on safer supply to undergo “a comprehensive in-person clinical assessment” at least monthly. Most significantly, it would direct doctors to specify that patients should not take their pills out of the pharmacy or clinic.

The new directive will go to the college’s directors for approval on Oct. 13 and, provided they give the green light, take effect on Nov. 16. “These amendments would not prohibit safer supply prescribing,” said Laura Zilke, a spokeswoman for the college. “Rather, they would strengthen clinical oversight of prescribing, while minimizing the risks associated with diversion and supporting a short transition for patients from safer supply to OAT,” she said, referring to opioid agonist therapy, the blanket term for treatment with standard addiction meds.

The college of pharmacists is also considering change. Without specifying what it would do, its board voted Tuesday to make it a priority “to strengthen pharmacy practice related to opioid dispensing for safe supply.”

The change of tack comes too late for Dr. Regenstreif. In an emotional open letter in August, she said she was leaving her addiction practice after 15 years, fed up with “a business model bent on making a profit for doctors and pharmacies by keeping people on the addictive opioids that got them into trouble in the first place.”

Some of her patients cried when she told them, but she said that, as much as she cared for them, she could not keep working in a system “that has lost sight of recovery as a goal.”

A leaked B.C. Ministry of Health document last year confirmed the practice, saying that more than 60 pharmacies were being investigated for offering kickbacks. It also said that a “significant portion” of prescription opioids are sold – trafficked provincially, nationally and internationally.

As a result, since the end of 2025 British Columbia has been prohibiting most safer-supply patients from taking their addiction medications out of the pharmacy, insisting they take the meds on site, under observation – a system known as “witnessed dosing.” Meanwhile, the federal government quietly halted its funding for safer-supply programs last year. In 2024 the Ontario government brought in a law, the Safer Streets, Stronger Communities Act, that bars new safer-supply programs.

But Canadian doctors have wide latitude to prescribe drugs as they see fit, if they believe their patients will benefit from them. Many have continued to approve daily doses of hydromorphone pills to patients with serious addictions.
“There is no way anyone can tell me this is harm reduction,” Dr. Regenstreif said. “It is harm promotion.”

The daughter of a Winnipeg city planner, she studied genetics and molecular biology at university, then went into medicine. She moved to Hamilton in 2004, started treating the homeless and the mentally ill and gravitated to addiction treatment.
I think there is a level of patient care that is missing. It’s very transactional. — Priya Sandhu, Hamilton pharmacist

She has seen wave upon deadly wave of the drug crisis roll over Hamilton since, but nothing has left her as discouraged as the chaos wrought by safer supply. In the last few years, she says, the clinics and pharmacies offering the program have spread “like wildfire.”
The facilities can be found everywhere from Niagara Falls to the Toronto suburb of Pickering to Elliot Lake in Northern Ontario.

True North Medical has more than 100 addiction-medicine clinics, from Red Lake in the northwest of the province to Kingston in the southeast. Arrow Medical, established in 2023, offers “urgent, compassionate, evidence-based care for people living with opioid use disorder, without judgment, barriers or delay.” It has 11 locations around Southern Ontario, as well as a virtual clinic.
The James Street pharmacy in Hamilton, Wellkare, offers “fast, friendly” service and short wait times. “We are accepting new patients!” an ad on the outside wall says.
Visitors can come out of the door with their pills in minutes. Many pharmacies have doctors on site to write prescriptions. If a doctor is not there, clients can often talk to one by video.

Hamilton pharmacist Priya Sandhu says such outfits have discovered that specializing in addiction medicines can be a money maker. Many of their clients are on multiple medications. Along with hydromorphone, they might be receiving addiction meds such as methadone, Suboxone and Kadian, as well as drugs for anxiety, insomnia, infections and high blood pressure. The pharmacies can charge dispensing fees for each, plus another charge for observing the taking of the drugs, if that is required.
Ms. Sandhu figures they can make $40 a day off some customers. That means that, in theory, a pharmacy could earn nearly $15,000 a year from a single person.
“It’s a great business model,” she says. But “I think there is a level of patient care that is missing. It’s very transactional.”

Defenders of safer supply insist it is a vital service. Arrow Medical’s founder, Joshua Fletcher, says traditional addiction meds such as methadone and Suboxone May calm patients’ drug cravings but they don’t provide the high that some of them seek. Better that they should get it from fast-acting hydromorphone pills than street fentanyl laced with dangerous additives, says Dr. Fletcher, who is affiliated with North York General, a Toronto hospital.

The founder of True North, addiction doctor and University of Toronto professor Chris Cavacuiti, told me by e-mail that his clinics prescribe safer-supply pills only in combination with more standard addiction meds and that “any patient identified as diverting medication is discontinued from the program.” He said the program’s aim is “to reduce reliance on street drugs and keep patients connected to health care providers.”

David D’Souza, the founder of another chain, New Dawn Medical, acknowledges that diversion and “lax prescribing” happens. But in an Aug. 27 paper for the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, an Ottawa think tank, he wrote that safer supply “properly targeted and rigorously regulated, can be a pragmatic response to the new realities of today’s illicit-drug market.”
The pharmacies, too, defend their practices. They stress their job is to dispense addiction medications, not prescribe them. That is up to the doctors.

The pharmacies also say they have strict protocols in place to prevent diversion, such as taking urine samples from patients to make sure they have traces of the prescribed drug in their bodies and requiring them to take at least some of their meds in front of pharmacy staff.

Staff at the Wellkare pharmacy showed me the small washroom where patients go to produce a sample. It has a video camera inside to discourage them from tampering with their samples. A sign warns visitors it is there. The owner declined to speak to me on the record.

None of these measures seem to do much to prevent the buying and selling of the pills. I visited four different Hamilton pharmacies over several days this summer and often found people waiting outside to buy hydromorphone pills. They had no problem finding sellers.

A steady stream of people came out of the pharmacies, holding white plastic bags containing their meds. Some told me they would take only one or two of their pills so that the drug showed up in their urine test at the pharmacy, but trade the rest for fentanyl or sell them for cash.

Jesse Steingart, 44, said pill selling and trading is a fact of life in Hamilton. He used to sell his hydromorphone to get fentanyl “because that’s a hard drug to afford.” Now, he says he sells them just once or twice a week, “whether it’s to get laundry done or to get a pizza in my stomach.” With the pills in his pocket, “it’s just inevitable.”

Joshua Gordyn told me he sells or trades the pills he gets daily from his pharmacy. The eight-milligram pills go for about $2 on the street in Hamilton – more in communities where they are less common. Mr. Gordyn said he could get $10 a pill if he took them to a nearby Indigenous reserve, Six Nations of the Grand River.

Police there confirm that outsiders bring pills to the reserve. Detective Sergeant Rob Monteforte of the Six Nations drug squad said that, in a bust last year, they seized more than 1,000 from suspected Toronto-area traffickers.
Locals on safer supply sometimes sell their meds, too, he said. If police find a pill bottle with a name on it, they call the prescribing doctor and ask him or her to cut the patient off.

Brett Stubbs works as a security guard at a church soup kitchen across the street from a well-known Hamilton addiction pharmacy. He told me that, once, when he was reviving someone who had suffered an overdose, he had to cut open the man’s pants to give him a life-saving injection. About 70 pills tumbled out of his pockets.

“It’s so blatant, it’s frightening,” said Regan Anderson, head of Wayside House of Hamilton, a live-in addiction-treatment centre. He sees people using and dealing pills right on the steps of a nearby pharmacy.

It would be one thing, he told me, if the array of drugs that people get at such places was helping them get better. Instead, “they’re staying unwell, and to the point of being basically publicly intoxicated or paralyzed on the street, without a real strong road map to change or to recovery.”

Dr. Regenstreif has done lots of work with youth who have run afoul of the law. They told her hydromorphone pills are cheap and easy to find. For those with limited experience using opioids, and thus a low tolerance, they pose a serious threat.

The eight-milligram Dilaudid pills, or D8s, are so strong they are not often used in ordinary medicine. Yet some safer-supply patients are walking out of the pharmacy door with 10 or 20 D8s at a time.

Though the death rate from opioids has been trending downward in Canada, 165 people died in Hamilton last year of suspected overdoses, a staggering number for the Southern Ontario city of about half a million. The victims of this 21st-century plague can be seen all over downtown, passed out of the sidewalk or bent over, swaying, in the half-conscious state that comes from consuming opioid drugs.

Critics of safer supply like Dr. Regenstreif say the practice is contributing to the problem, by giving drug users a marketable commodity that produces ready cash on a daily basis – just what they need to support their habit.

Hamilton police say that although fentanyl is still the main threat, they know prescription pills are being sold on the streets. This July, they carried out a two-week investigation of suspected drug dealing around a local pharmacy. They arrested nine people and seized 284 hydromorphone pills, along with quantities of fentanyl, methamphetamine and other drugs.

Hamilton is far from the only Ontario city struggling with the fallout from safer supply. In North Bay, drug-squad officer Brad Reaume said the Northern Ontario city was blindsided by the spread of diverted safer-supply drugs, hit when “we had our backs turned.” He said some pills end up in Indigenous communities farther north, where they are less numerous and fetch a higher price.

In London, downtown business owners have complained about open drug use, vandalism and other problems around pharmacies that specialize in addiction meds. In April, city council voted unanimously to ask the provincial government to review what one councillor, David Ferreira, called the “variety-store” model of dispensing them.

In Ottawa, merchants and residents complained about similar issues around a clinic in the Chinatown district. “It’s creating a very visible, very active and I would say dangerous open-air drug market,” city councillor Ariel Troster said. “It’s just the absolute Wild West with these private clinics.”

Even at one of Toronto’s trendiest intersections, Dundas and Ossington, residents have been complaining on social media about open drug use outside an addiction pharmacy. In a scene much like that outside the Hamilton pharmacies, a collection of people gather in the morning to wait for it to open.
Province-wide, the Ontario Provincial Police say they seized 12 times as much hydromorphone in 2025 as they did in 2022, though they cannot say for certain how much came from diverted safer supply.
Regulators are aware of the diversion issue.

Lily Barnes, press secretary for Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones, said that “to be absolutely clear, our government does not and will never support the distribution of illegal drugs,” though it was up to the bodies that oversee pharmacists and doctors to make sure their members were following the rules about opioids.
The Ontario College of Pharmacists said it was looking into complaints about certain addiction pharmacies and “reviewing standards, policies, guidelines and other requirements.”

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario brought in new rules this May requiring doctors to see patients in person (rather than just online) before starting them on safer-supply drugs, to offer them other addiction medicines first and to assess patients in person every three months.

Then, this week, it went much further. It said it would direct doctors not to prescribe safer supply except in combination with other more standard addiction drugs; to limit prescribing of the drugs to eight weeks; and to require patients on safer supply to undergo “a comprehensive in-person clinical assessment” at least monthly. Most significantly, it would direct doctors to specify that patients should not take their pills out of the pharmacy or clinic.

The new directive will go to the college’s directors for approval on Oct. 13 and, provided they give the green light, take effect on Nov. 16. “These amendments would not prohibit safer supply prescribing,” said Laura Zilke, a spokeswoman for the college. “Rather, they would strengthen clinical oversight of prescribing, while minimizing the risks associated with diversion and supporting a short transition for patients from safer supply to OAT,” she said, referring to opioid agonist therapy, the blanket term for treatment with standard addiction meds.

The college of pharmacists is also considering change. Without specifying what it would do, its board voted Tuesday to make it a priority “to strengthen pharmacy practice related to opioid dispensing for safe supply.”

The change of tack comes too late for Dr. Regenstreif. In an emotional open letter in August, she said she was leaving her addiction practice after 15 years, fed up with “a business model bent on making a profit for doctors and pharmacies by keeping people on the addictive opioids that got them into trouble in the first place.”
Some of her patients cried when she told them, but she said that, as much as she cared for them, she could not keep working in a system “that has lost sight of recovery as a goal.”

stories.title: First Nation students celebrate Orange shirt day with artwork
stories.summary: Fanshawe's Institute of Indigenous learning has numerous activities prepared for Orange shirt day. These inclu...
stories.author: Ben Andrews
stories.content:
Fanshawe’s Institute of Indigenous learning has numerous activities prepared for Truth and Reconciliation Day (also known as Orange Shirt Day) this week. These include an Indigenous student art gallery, as well as an artisan square to support local Indigenous businesses. Natalie Fletcher, the Manager of Indigenous Student Success at Fanshawe and a member of the Caldwell First Nation, says campus initiatives are important given the way Indigenous Peoples have been historically treated by education systems in the country.

“A place like a college wouldn’t allow you to speak your own language,” Fletcher said. “We weren’t allowed to celebrate the way that we used to , w e really had to adapt to a new way of life.”

“U p until the 1920s, as part of the Indian Act, if a student or an Indigenous person sought higher education, they lost their status,” added Rochelle Smith, the Indigenous Recruiter and Community Relations Coordinator at Fanshawe from the Chippewas of the Thames First Nation. “If they would seek their higher education, they’d be considered assimilated, which means th ey lost their rights to their community and their culture.”

Orange shirt day was created to raise awareness of the horrors suffered by Indigenous children at Residential school, as enforced by the Indian act of 1876. While there are no more Residential schools open in Canada, there are still parts of the Indian act that Smith and Fletcher believe to still be discriminatory to Indigenous people.

“A lot of First Nations don’t have that ability to manage their own land,” said Smith. “ But they can’t without the interference of the government .”

“T he Indian Act gets to determine who is considered Indigenous in Canada,” said Fletcher. “ Reservations were created, which separated people, a nd then status cards also created a further division of people from their communities.”

“(My mother) lost her status and therefore was not eligible to remain in the community, or to access the services that existed there for her.” she added.

Both the art gallery and the artisan square both intend to raise awareness of the discrimination, both past and present, faced by First Nation individuals through artwork. According to Smith, art is a very important aspect of First Nation communities because it’s how the have historically told stories.

“W hen we tell stories, we depict it,” said Smith. “I t’s also a way that we can show that we’re still here, a nd there’s a different way of believing that it’s not just written fact.”

Fletcher says that artwork is a way that Indigenous people can show pride in their culture ans their heritage. “ I love supporting artisans who are doing the beading and the work that goes behind earrings, jewelry, and lots of artwork that we do,” she said. “ There’s just so many cool things that highlight pride and that feeling of greatness and being an Indigenous person.”

stories.title: RMC Construction students gifted with tools for their trades
stories.summary: Some of London’s future builders have been gifted with much needed tools to start their trades.
stories.content:
Some of London’s future builders have been gifted with much needed tools to start their trades.

Students from the Regina Mundi Construction Academy were invited to Copp’s Buildall on York Street in London Tuesday for a shopping spree.

“We’re always looking for trades. I’m just happy that you guys are getting exposed, and have an interest, and follow your passion whatever way that goes,” Allan Drewlo, President of Drewlo Holdings told the group of 13 aspiring builders.

“We’re really excited for being a part of this program because we get to provide tools to you guys who are the future generation that are going to build our city,” said Mac Copp, of Copp’s Buildall.

Part of the funding has also been set up as an account the program can draw from through the year.

The event gave students a chance to pick out tools they will train on. It also provided them an opportunity to speak with trade representatives on hand.

“Well, they gave me just a bunch of everything. They gave me a new hammer, which is pretty cool, measuring tape, a little belt. A lot of different things. Very useful,” said Natalie Lima Tobias, a student in the program.

“I love to work with my hands. I never really wanted to go to university, so this is like a good opportunity to get into the trades,” said student Liam Galem.

Students from the Regina Mundi Construction Academy were invited to Copp’s Buildall on York Street in London Tuesday for a shopping spree.

“We’re always looking for trades. I’m just happy that you guys are getting exposed, and have an interest, and follow your passion whatever way that goes,” Allan Drewlo, President of Drewlo Holdings told the group of 13 aspiring builders.
“We’re really excited for being a part of this program because we get to provide tools to you guys who are the future generation that are going to build our city,” said Mac Copp, of Copp’s Buildall.
Part of the funding has also been set up as an account the program can draw from through the year.
The event gave students a chance to pick out tools they will train on. It also provided them an opportunity to speak with trade representatives on hand.

stories.title: Fatal shooting in downtown London; suspect in custody
stories.summary: Police said officers were called to the area of Central Avenue and Richmond Street at about 5:45 p.m. Tuesday after receiving reports of a possible shooting.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley, Brent Lale
stories.content:
London police are investigating a fatal shooting of a man in the downtown core.

Officers were called an apartment building at the corner of Central Avenue and Richmond Street at about 5:45 p.m. Tuesday after receiving reports of a possible shooting.

Employees of a neighbouring barber shop said they heard a gunshot, described as a pop and then witnessed a person leaving the apartment building before running towards Victoria Park.

EMS arrived to the apartment where police said a man suffering from life-threatening injuries was located and transported to hospital, where he was later pronounced dead.

One man has been arrested and the investigation remains ongoing.

The London police K9 unit arrived on scene. Officers with the police dogs were investigating in the area near Victoria Park.

Another officer was stationed outside one of the three apartments were the shooting took place.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area between 5:30 p.m. and 6 p.m., and who May have information, dash-cam footage or residential or business surveillance video, to contact the London Police Service at 519-661-5670.

stories.title: MP Leslyn Lewis says in lawsuit that York professor worked 'behind the scenes' to torpedo her hiring
stories.summary: Ontario MP alleges York cultivated "toxic culture" of "wokeism" that let a professor blindside her with unfair and defamatory questions.
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
New details are emerging in the defamation case against York University by MP Leslyn Lewis, a former leadership candidate for the Conservative Party of Canada.

Lewis alleges the Toronto school cultivated a “toxic culture” of “wokeism” that allowed a professor to blindside her with unfair and defamatory questions in the interview process for a scholar position reserved for a Black person of African descent.

Lewis applied for this job while also campaigning in the 2021 federal election, when she won the position she still holds, representing Haldimand-Norfolk in rural southern Ontario.

In a new filing in Ontario Superior Court in reply to York’s statement of defence, Lewis accuses the school of “gatekeeping” her candidacy, and gives further detail on her claim that the school is liable for the “traumatizing” experience of not getting the job on what she claims are unfair ideological and political grounds.

She accuses one professor in particular of working behind the scenes to alert academic decision makers to his defamatory allegations that Lewis was racist, anti-gay, anti-refugee and opposed to women’s reproductive freedom.

“Faculty who disagreed with her on ideological grounds worked against her behind the scenes,” reads the reply her lawyer filed with the court.

She alleges Sean Rehaag, a professor of refugee law named as a defendant along with York, acted in a manner that was not “relevant, foreseeable, or within the proper scope of a recruitment seminar. Without notice, Professor Rehaag used excerpts of her political media appearances that he had prepared in advance and questioned her on political matters unrelated to her academic presentation.”

The fact she was allowed to answer these questions did not make the process fair, Lewis claims.

Peter MacKinnon: Political agendas have no place in university research applications

MP Leslyn Lewis sues her alma mater, and professor for 'traumatizing' job interview

More broadly, she says the ideological environment at York was not “neutral or ordinary,” and that she was forced to take an unscheduled break, and claims the chair of a committee later phoned her to apologize.

Lewis denies that the alleged defamation of her character is saved by fair comment or justification, as York and Rehaag have claimed in their defence against the lawsuit. Both York and Rahaag say there was never any campaign of “vetting out” or “lobbying” against Lewis.

“Identifying isolated political positions does not prove the far broader sting that Dr. Lewis is racist, anti-refugee, or hostile to the 2SLGBTQIA+ community, and material facts about her record were omitted or not investigated,” Lewis’s legal reply reads. It mentions her work as a refugee lawyer on behalf of sexual minorities.

Lewis claims York is “directly liable in negligence and vicarious liability for Professor Rehaag’s conduct.”

“The true issue was not whether Dr. Lewis met the advertised qualifications, which she did, but whether her conservative political, philosophical, and Christian beliefs made her acceptable for a position created for a Black scholar,” reads Lewis’s reply. “Political beliefs, religious beliefs, and ideological conformity were not among the advertised and assessed criteria.”

Rehaag’s suggestion of seeking input from groups representing racial or sexual minority students was not “a neutral consultation” but rather an effort by Rehaag to make “sweeping and damaging characterizations of Dr. Lewis’s character and beliefs.”

“I think it’s important people understand that this is a university that likes to trumpet its DEI (diversity, equity, inclusion) bona fides,” said Lewis’s lawyer Darryl Singer. “But there’s two places where it doesn’t occur.”

One is with Jewish people, Singer said, and his firm is involved in a separate class action lawsuit against York University and the York Federation of Students claiming the school failed over many years to address antisemitic incidents, in violation of its non-discrimination policies. That claim has since expanded to include other schools and student unions across Canada.

“The other place it doesn’t apply is in Leslyn’s case,” Singer said.

“It’s not just York, we’re seeing it all over now. They like to say we’re all about equity, and we’re all about diversity, and we’re all about women and Black empowerment,” Singer said. “Unless the woman happens to be part of the Conservative party.”

“When you go out there trumpeting these values, and then you act completely contrary to those values for the sole reason you don’t like her political party, that’s a story to me,” Singer said. “If she was an NDP candidate, she certainly in my view would have been treated with the dignity and respect that she deserved and certainly would have been given a fair opportunity.”

Next steps include mandatory mediation in advance of a potential trial.

stories.title: Canada doesn’t have enough Indigenous teachers. This initiative aims to close the gap
stories.summary: Rideau Hall Foundation’s Indigenous Teacher Education Initiative has supported 22 projects seeking to understand and address the barriers Indigenous teachers face
stories.author: Dave McGinn
stories.content:
Growing up in Burns Lake, a small community in B.C., Dustin Louie never had an Indigenous teacher.

This experience is familiar to many Indigenous youth, and it has detrimental effects, he said.

Indigenous students are more likely to do better at school when they have Indigenous teachers, and not having those teachers influences students’ ideas about the careers they might pursue, said Prof. Louie, now 45 and director of the Indigenous Teacher Education Program at the University of British Columbia.

“That sets the expectation for those students about what’s possible for them,” he said. Not having Indigenous teachers could discourage them from pursuing education as a career themselves, perpetuating the pattern.

Last September, the UBC program launched a field centre in Prince Rupert to deliver the university’s full bachelor of education program to more than 40 Indigenous students from the area, funded by a grant of nearly $1-million from the Rideau Hall Foundation.

“Within four years of getting those funds, there are going to be at least 25 new teachers in this school district that is 63 per cent Indigenous,” he said. “You cannot overemphasize the implications of this region having 25 new Indigenous teachers.”

When the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada issued its 94 calls to action in 2015, among them was a directive to the federal government to work with Indigenous groups to “develop a joint strategy to eliminate educational and employment gaps between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal Canadians.”

One program that takes aim at both gaps is the Indigenous Teacher Education Initiative, launched by the Rideau Hall Foundation, a non-partisan national charitable organization, in 2022.

The initiative has two overarching goals, said Annette Trimbee, co-chair of the foundation’s national advisory committee on Indigenous teacher education.

The first is to understand how teachers move through the educational system, what inspires them to become teachers and what barriers they face.

“We’re trying to understand all the things that might be behind the underrepresentation of Indigenous teachers,” she said.

The second goal is to support the recruitment and retention of 10,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis teachers across Canada.

The initiative has supported 22 projects to date, including several research projects, Dr. Trimbee said.

“I really see it as a bit of a catalyst and accelerator because there are phenomenal things happening all across the country,” she said.

“Education opens doors, and Indigenous students do better when they have the opportunity to learn from Indigenous teachers who they can share culture, history, language with. It creates a sense of pride.”

The foundation has estimated there are 6,000 to 8,000 Indigenous teachers in Canada, added Dr. Trimbee, who is also president of MacEwan University in Edmonton.

Increasing the number of Indigenous teachers is key to improving high-school graduation rates for Indigenous students, said Evelyn Steinhauer, associate dean of Indigenous teacher education at the University of Alberta and a member of the Rideau Hall Foundation’s advisory committee.

“Graduation rates don’t really go up when you keep sending our children to schools where people don’t understand us,” she said.

The high-school graduation rate for First Nations youth is 63 per cent, compared with 91 per cent of the non-Indigenous population, according to the 2016 census, the most recent data available.

For those living off reserve, the graduation rate is 73 per cent, while for those living on reserve it is just 46 per cent.

Last year, the teacher education program that Prof. Steinhauer helps oversee received a nearly $1-million grant from the Rideau Hall Foundation. She said it has been pivotal in helping build relationships with Indigenous communities.

The grant will support up to 90 students annually between 2025 and 2029 to bring traditional practices and perspectives to field experiences, while also connecting them with mentor teachers, among other things.

Training Indigenous teachers who will then take up positions in their communities is vital to the success of students who live there, Prof. Steinhauer said.

“We have to have somebody who’s from the community that understands,” she said. “If you don’t have the lived experience, how can you really relate to what the children are saying?”

Often, teachers working in remote Indigenous communities come from other parts of Canada, and frequently stay only for a couple of years, Prof. Louie said.

That can have a very negative affect on students in those communities, he said.

“Students kind of see the teacher as being transient, and there’s only so much that you open up, create trust, want to connect with somebody if the expectation is they’re just going to leave,” he said.

Prof. Louie said this shows the value of the field centre model: “We want to educate people from those communities because we know they’ll stay there.”

Having more Indigenous teachers across the country is good for all students, not just Indigenous ones, especially considering how much Indigenous material is included in curriculums, said Nicole Bell, an associate professor of education at Trent University whose research focuses on Indigenous culture-based education.

“The way we teach our Indigenous teachers how to teach in culturally appropriate ways is found to be extremely beneficial by all students,” she said. “It’s just good pedagogy for everyone.”

Indigenous teachers can help all students better understand themselves and the world, Prof. Louie said.

“We think of the massive benefit for the settler students – not just having enough certified teachers to be able to fill the schools, but the new types of learning that they’re going to be exposed to that’s going to fundamentally change their view of the world as well.”

“I really see it as a bit of a catalyst and accelerator because there are phenomenal things happening all across the country,” she said.

“Education opens doors, and Indigenous students do better when they have the opportunity to learn from Indigenous teachers who they can share culture, history, language with. It creates a sense of pride.”
The foundation has estimated there are 6,000 to 8,000 Indigenous teachers in Canada, added Dr. Trimbee, who is also president of MacEwan University in Edmonton.

Increasing the number of Indigenous teachers is key to improving high-school graduation rates for Indigenous students, said Evelyn Steinhauer, associate dean of Indigenous teacher education at the University of Alberta and a member of the Rideau Hall Foundation’s advisory committee.
“Graduation rates don’t really go up when you keep sending our children to schools where people don’t understand us,” she said.
The high-school graduation rate for First Nations youth is 63 per cent, compared with 91 per cent of the non-Indigenous population, according to the 2016 census, the most recent data available.
For those living off reserve, the graduation rate is 73 per cent, while for those living on reserve it is just 46 per cent.

Last year, the teacher education program that Prof. Steinhauer helps oversee received a nearly $1-million grant from the Rideau Hall Foundation. She said it has been pivotal in helping build relationships with Indigenous communities.

The grant will support up to 90 students annually between 2025 and 2029 to bring traditional practices and perspectives to field experiences, while also connecting them with mentor teachers, among other things.
Training Indigenous teachers who will then take up positions in their communities is vital to the success of students who live there, Prof. Steinhauer said.
“We have to have somebody who’s from the community that understands,” she said. “If you don’t have the lived experience, how can you really relate to what the children are saying?”
Often, teachers working in remote Indigenous communities come from other parts of Canada, and frequently stay only for a couple of years, Prof. Louie said.
That can have a very negative affect on students in those communities, he said.

“Students kind of see the teacher as being transient, and there’s only so much that you open up, create trust, want to connect with somebody if the expectation is they’re just going to leave,” he said.
Prof. Louie said this shows the value of the field centre model: “We want to educate people from those communities because we know they’ll stay there.”

Having more Indigenous teachers across the country is good for all students, not just Indigenous ones, especially considering how much Indigenous material is included in curriculums, said Nicole Bell, an associate professor of education at Trent University whose research focuses on Indigenous culture-based education.
“The way we teach our Indigenous teachers how to teach in culturally appropriate ways is found to be extremely beneficial by all students,” she said. “It’s just good pedagogy for everyone.”
Indigenous teachers can help all students better understand themselves and the world, Prof. Louie said.

“We think of the massive benefit for the settler students – not just having enough certified teachers to be able to fill the schools, but the new types of learning that they’re going to be exposed to that’s going to fundamentally change their view of the world as well.”

stories.title: John Cleese is not dead yet
stories.summary: The 89-year-old is travelling on a Canadian tour screening Monty Python and the Holy Grail alongside Q&A sessions
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
A few years ago in Los Angeles, the Monty Python comedian John Cleese had a precancerous growth surgically removed from his arm. It was a minor procedure that required a few stitches.

“As the guy left the room, he said, ‘Tis but a scratch,’” Cleese says, speaking on a video call.

The pop-culture reference “Tis but a scratch” comes from the 1975 British comedy classic Monty Python and the Holy Grail. Cleese, 86, is travelling with the film on a Canadian theatre tour that begins with three screenings and Q&A sessions at Toronto’s Winter Garden Theatre ( to Oct. 2), part of the Just For Laughs Toronto comedy festival. The tour then moves on to Kitchener, Ont., Hamilton, Ont., Montreal and Ottawa.

The film is a zany parody of the Arthurian legend, written collectively by Cleese and the other Python members: Eric Idle, Terry Gilliam, Michael Palin and the late Terry Jones and Graham Chapman. Idle later adapted the movie for the stage musical Spamalot, also known as Monty Python’s Spamalot: A New Musical (Lovingly) Ripped Off from the Motion Picture Monty Python and the Holy Grail .

The name of Cleese’s tour is Not Dead Yet! , inspired by a memorable scene from the movie. An old man resists being placed on the plague cart because he’s still alive. Other 51-year-old quotes Python aficionados like to throw around include “Just a flesh wound” and “I fart in your general direction.” Who knew flatulence humour would age so well?

“It’s lovely to think that people have these words in their minds,” Cleese says.

He’s speaking from his place in London’s Chelsea neighbourhood. “It’s a 10-minute walk to Harrods, which pleases my wife very much.”

For those keeping track, Cleese is on his fourth wife. He says their flat is relatively small. “It’s all I could afford after the divorce.” (Cleese went on a tour called A Ludicrous Evening with John Cleese − Or How to Finance Your Divorce in 2009 after expensively splitting with his third wife, psychotherapist Alyce Faye Eichelberger. Another series of shows, dubbed The Alimony Tour, followed.)

Jokey online memes or lines from today’s Saturday Night Live don’t quite stick around the way Monty Python ’s catch phrases used to. Comedy fans remember lines from Kids in the Hall , older SNL sketches , Sctv , even the Cleese co-written Fawlty Towers from 1975 like they heard them yesterday. Contemporary equivalents, however, are ephemeral.

“We had much, much better television in England 40 years ago, ON just four channels,” Cleese says. “The sad thing about comedy today is that when you come up with something they ask, ‘Can we make it into 12 one-hour segments, and can we put dragons in it?’”

The troupe’s second feature film, 1979’s Monty Python’s Life of Brian , is prescient, even though it was a satire set in biblical times. Cleese wrote a scene − “with a little help from Graham Chapman, who was drinking quite a lot at the time” − in which a man wants to be a woman (named Loretta) and have babies.

Stan/Loretta, played by Idle: “It’s every man’s right to have babies if he wants them.”

Reg, played by Cleese: “But you can’t have babies!”

Stan/Loretta: “Don’t you oppress me!”

It was meant as satire on political thought in the 1970s, when the left in England had become splintered. “What was funny, and is often true, is that they hated the splinter groups more than they hated the original enemies,” Cleese explains.

As for a man wishing to give birth, the idea had to do with the discussion on human rights in the 1970s. “I was trying to think what would be a ridiculous right. Well, it’s the right to have a baby if you were a fellow. So, that got sort of tacked on.”

The troupe released its final feature film, Monty Python’s The Meaning of Life , in 1983. Unlike the narrative-driven absurdity of the previous two movies, it was made up of sketches and musical numbers. Cleese thought it was a backward move and wasn’t happy with some of the sketches and began to branch out on his own.

“My thought was that I didn’t want to go on making other people’s mistakes. I wanted to make my own.”

He first collaborated with British director and editor Charles Crichton on the well-received heist comedy A Fish Called Wanda in 1988. If there were mistakes with the film starring Jamie Lee Curtis, Kevin Kline, Python’s Palin and himself, they weren’t noticed. At the 61st Academy Awards, it was nominated for Best Director and Best Original Screenplay and won a Best Supporting Actor statuette for Kline.

Monty Python last reunited in 2014, when they gave ten concerts at the O2 in London.

“Comedy relies on freshness and newness,” Cleese says. “In the beginning, it was as if we were going into a field of flowers nobody had ever been in. We would go around picking flowers, these lovely sketches, but after a time there were fewer and fewer flowers that hadn’t been picked. There’s a certain point where you just run out.”

stories.title: Want to book a reality-series mansion in B.C.? Here’s what you need to know
stories.summary: B.C’s Chateau Okanagan is the real-life location of the Netflix show Million Dollar Secret
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
On the Netflix reality series Million Dollar Secret , 12 strangers are sequestered at a palatial lakeside retreat where they vie to identify the “millionaire” amongst them.

Many of the show’s fans, meanwhile, are racing to uncover the real-life location of the opulent cliffside mansion set high above a deep blue lake.

An online search leads to Chateau Okanagan , a 17.8-hectare private estate in Kelowna, B.C.

The chateau was originally built as a family home by Kelowna real estate developer Michael Holzhey, who created a 20,000-square foot stone, timber and copper residence and filled it with a container load of antiques imported from France.

Holzhey and his family lived in the home for a time but decided to give the hospitality business a go when he and his wife became empty nesters. The estate opened up to guests in 2022.

Visitors who don’t blink at the price of booking the property – $13,200 and up a night with a minimum three-night stay – have access to six suites in the Grand Residence, a two-bedroom beach house, five slivers of pebbly beach, two swimming pools, one tennis court and three acres of vineyards.

A more affordable option is a $900-per-night suite in the new four-bedroom villa that opened in June for a bed-and-breakfast experience.

So how does the show’s backdrop translate into a real-world experience?

I joined a small group of travel writers and influencers at the chateau in late May to see what a stay would be like, and experience the gastronomy, wines and outdoor life of B.C.’s Okanagan Valley.

I settled into the Arrowleaf suite, where French doors open to a shared terrace with views of Okanagan Lake below and the forested hillside on the opposite shore.

The influencers set to work filming the parterre gardens, luxurious spa and infinity pools in cinematic slo-mo.

A chef created meals with B.C. spot prawns, oysters and other delicacies and the gracious staff smoothly respond to every request.

While the Netflix contestants engage in such challenges as outrunning snarling dogs and diving into Okanagan Lake, our group engaged in more sedate pursuits — examples of what the Chateau Okanagan concierge can organize for guests.

We started in the kitchen, where chef Scott Geiring taught us how to roll and shape the little pillows of ricotta gnocchi that would become our dinner, accompanied by a syrah from Le Vieux Pin Winery.

Sundowner cocktails around the outdoor fireplace became a nightly ritual.

One day we were ferried by helicopter to nine holes of golf on the signature course of the wildly beautiful Rise Resort in Vernon B.C., followed by lunch with views overlooking the lake.

The afternoon included a tour of the area’s wine cellars and a ride back to the chateau by chauffeur-driven Rolls-Royce.

The most serene experience was a trip across the lake to the storied Mission Hill Family Estate Winery, designed in monastic style by renowned American architect Tom Kundig.

After a tour of the starkly beautiful underground cave cellars, we settled in for an al fresco dinner overlooking the vines and sipped rare vintages of Oculus, the Bordeaux-style red Mission Hill is known for.

The next morning, I joined a sunrise yoga class at the water’s edge. After lunch, I hiked down a steep path to a secluded black-stone beach hoping to see the local spotted sandpipers but no birds were about. (The estate’s beaches are not technically private because the shoreline can be accessed by the public.)

On my clamber back up the slope, I spotted yellow-bellied marmots, deer and a bald eagle perched in a ponderosa pine.

During a poolside soiree, Holzhey acknowledged that filling the calendar with bookings for the full estate has been a challenge, but local zoning rules would not permit the property to rent out rooms individually like a boutique hotel.

Then Netflix came along.

The show streams to a global audience in more than 190 countries, but it still seems astounding that many fans have sufficiently deep pockets to follow through with a reservation.

“It has been a surprise to me, too,” quipped Brian Dower, the affable managing director of Chateau Okanagan, adding that bookings soared after the show began streaming.

He received an e-mail from a couple in Brazil just that morning.

Corporate travel is big, he explained, and families sometimes take over the grand residence for a wedding on the lakefront terrace.

The popularity of the Netflix show inspired Holzhey to expand the experience to a wider audience with the new Estate Villa on the property.

The contemporary poured-concrete and glass aesthetic May also draw a different crowd from the old-world style of the chateau.

The suites have a private bathroom and bedroom, and there’s a communal great room at the centre with lounging, dining and a kitchen. Outside, the villa has a deck and hot tub.

Next year pinot noir grapes will be planted on the slope just outside the front door because visitors to the Okanagan Valley covet the experience of a lake view and vineyard setting, Dower said.

During the summer of 2026, British Columbia declared a state of emergency as out-of-control wildfires burned in the province. Evacuation orders covered some parts of the Okanagan, including areas in the vicinity of Vernon and Summerland, but the chateau was not included.

Dower had previously blocked off a chunk of time in August for the filming of Million Dollar Secret . As it turns out, the producers weren’t ready to go until September, when they descended with the crew and contestants for the filming of season three currently underway.

Cassandra Zerebeski, chief executive of Tourism Kelowna, notes the province did not issue a travel ban, but some visitors did postpone or cancel trips to Kelowna and the surrounding area in August.

Some hotels, wineries, attractions and local entrepreneurs estimated a 30 per cent drop in business during the month, she says.

“They count on August.”

Zerebeski says Kelowna is popular year-round so some travelers will reschedule for another season.

Genuine millionaires who enjoy golf, wine-tasting and soaking in healing waters will love the chateau. Fans of Million Dollar Secret without such deep pockets can still enjoy the adventure by booking a stay at the villa.

The writer was a guest of Chateau Okanagan, which did not review or approve this article. Stories are based on merit; The Globe does not guarantee coverage.

stories.title: Maple Leafs fall to Canadiens as McKenna, Marchenko make their Toronto debuts
stories.summary: Leafs head coach Jim Hiller said it will take some time for the roster to find cohesion, with newcomers Darren Raddysh and Sergei Bobrovsky.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Joshua Clipperton, The Canadian Press

Posted September 30, 2026 5:57 am.

Gavin McKenna has known for quite some time his NHL debut would come Tuesday night. Kirill Marchenko wasn’t even a member of the Maple Leafs at the start of the week.

The pair were among 10 players to suit up with Toronto for the first time in a 3-2 loss to the Montreal Canadiens as the NHL regular season opened for both teams.

McKenna was selected first overall at June’s draft after the Maple Leafs missed the playoffs for the first time in decade before beating the lottery odds, while Marchenko was acquired from the Columbus Blue Jackets in a blockbuster trade just over 24 hours prior to puck drop that saw Matthew Knies head the other way.

“It’s pretty hard to forget a day like this,” said McKenna, an 18-year-old winger from Whitehorse. “Getting to have that rookie lap, seeing my family on the glass in warm-ups, hearing your name called in player intros — it’s all pretty special.”

Marchenko had a much shorter runway to prepare, and only learned around lunchtime he would be able to suit up after his immigration paperwork was completed.

“It’s crazy,” said the 26-year-old Russian winger, who signed a six-year contract extension worth US$75 million with Toronto. “We packed, we moved with my wife … really busy. But I’m happy it’s done and I’m happy to be here. I hate that we lost, but it’s still a great memory.”

“Dream for everybody being with the Toronto Maple Leafs,” he added. “But it’s happened quick.”

McKenna had a few nice moments, but also had some turnovers he wanted back before finishing a minus-2 with one shot on goal in 15 minutes 19 seconds of action.

“The first exhibition game, he talked to (the media) and said, ‘Ya, it was just an OK night, I’ll learn from it,'” Toronto head coach Jim Hiller said. “He came back and had a really strong game. It’s up another level again. You just keep taking the test, and he’ll be back. I thought he was all right. But he’ll probably want to be better.”

Marchenko was fired out of a cannon in his debut with eight shot attempts, including four on target, in just over 20 minutes of ice time.

He picked up an assist on William Nylander’s opener 48 seconds into the first period and had a couple of great chances on Canadiens goaltender Jakub Dobes.

“A big boy, can make plays, shoots it,” said Maple Leafs centre Auston Matthews, who centred a line with Marchenko and Jack Roslovic. “I thought for what he had to endure the last 24 hours — getting traded, flying here last night, getting here today, new everything, getting a visa, all that stuff — we had some really good opportunities.”

Hiller said it will take some time for the roster to find cohesion with so many new faces, including defenceman Darren Raddysh and goaltender Sergei Bobrovsky, following a truncated training camp and pre-season.

“We looked a little bit like a new team,” said the coach. “We just weren’t connecting with our passes. I don’t know if that has anything to do with nerves or being in the building for the first time, and the first time everybody together.

“We just weren’t clean as a team.”

McKenna, Marchenko and the rest of the Maple Leafs will get another chance Wednesday when they host the New York Islanders.

“It’s pretty special,” McKenna said of his debut. “There’s not much I’ll forget about this day.”

Maple Leafs general manager John Chayka was asked Tuesday morning about his expectations for the club after acquiring Marchenko.

“It’s unchanged … our expectations are always high,” Chayka said. “We’re the Toronto Maple Leafs and ownership’s spared no expense to try to put the best product on the on the ice and support the guys and give us every resource to be successful.

“We think Kirill could be a big part of that. But we felt like we had a good group going in.”

Toronto would have normally paid tribute to Cliff Fletcher following his death in June at age 90, but the former executive’s family was unable to attend Tuesday’s opener.

The Maple Leafs will honour Fletcher, whose first tenure included the franchise-altering trade for Doug Gilmour in 1992, ON Oct. 15 when the club hosts the Buffalo Sabres.

stories.title: Western student creates orange shirt design for National Day for Truth and Reconciliation
stories.summary: New orange shirt design created by student Kolbi Williams for National Day for Truth and Reconciliation is available at Western University
stories.author: Colleen MacDonald
stories.content:
A fourth-year English and creative writing student crafted a new orange shirt design as part of Western University’s recognition of National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, with proceeds from t-shirt sales supporting an Indigenous-led preservation initiative.

Kolbi Williams’ artwork, inspired by Haudenosaunee teachings, is featured on this year’s orange shirts sold at Western.

Kolbi Williams, a member of the Mohawk Nation from Six Nations of the Grand River, created the artwork titled Tewa:aráton and Its Creations, after a call for submissions from Western’s Office of Indigenous Initiatives. Her design illustrates a Haudenosaunee creation story about lacrosse, known in her community as Tewa:aráton, and its origins as a gift from the Creator to bring relief during a time of hardship and conflict.

According to Haudenosaunee tradition, in the first game of lacrosse played between four-legged animals and birds, the mouse and squirrel were ostracized by their own team because of their small size. They asked to join the birds, who accepted them as teammates and fashioned wings for them. With the game tied at nightfall, the mouse – transformed into a bat – ultimately scored the winning goal.

“This story teaches us not to judge another by the way they look because you don’t know what they’re capable of,” Williams said. “It’s the same in the community – you might not know what someone’s teachings and gifts are.”

Williams says this message is at the heart of reconciliation as Canadians reckon with the legacy of the Residential School System for Indigenous children. From the 19th century until 1996, more than 150,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis children were forced to attend church-run residential schools where they were stripped of their languages, cultures and traditions.

(L to R) Mike Cywink, community engagement coordinator for Indigenous Initiatives, Mikayla Antone-Gregory, Indigenous Students’ Association president and Kolbi Williams, student artist, wear orange shirts symbolizing the loss of identity, culture and family experienced by Indigenous children in residential schools, while honouring children who never returned home. (Western Housing and Ancillary Services)

“Coming together to appreciate all people’s gifts is one way to better understand and share the gifts that children in residential schools were denied access to and punished for using,” Williams said.

Survivors have described abuse, neglect, malnutrition, harsh working conditions and unsanitary living quarters. The National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation documented thousands of children who died at the schools and says the true number is likely much higher.

Orange Shirt Day began in 2013 as a grassroots movement under the rallying cry “Every Child Matters” to remember the children who never made it home and honour survivors of residential schools. It evolved into the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation in 2021 to promote awareness of the harms caused by residential schools and grow reconciliation across Canada.

Wearing an orange shirt is considered a way of standing with Indigenous communities in remembrance and healing. Orange shirts with Williams’ design will be sold year-round at the Dellelce Family Bookstore in Western’s University Community Centre. Proceeds will support the Save the Barn campaign, a project to preserve the last remaining building from Mount Elgin Industrial Institute, a residential school on what is now Chippewas of the Thames First Nation, near London, Ont.

Mount Elgin, one of the first residential schools in Canada, operated until 1946. It included a farm where children were forced into labour tending livestock and growing crops, though the harvest was rarely used to supplement their meagre diets. A barn bearing inscriptions students left on the walls is the only structure still standing. The First Nation has been fundraising to restore it as an interpretive centre to document local history and help revitalize the community’s language and culture.

“Our communities did so much work to keep our language, culture and people alive in a time when everything was against them,” Williams said. “It’s a big part of why the Save the Barn campaign is such a vital part of National Day for Truth and Reconciliation here in London. While this city was being developed, the trauma of residential schools was happening just a half hour away to local First Nations children.”

Western supports National Day for Truth and Reconciliation by designating September 30 as a non-instructional day with no regular classes, allowing the campus community to participate in educational and commemorative events. Attendees are encouraged to wear orange. Williams said she hopes her design prompts meaningful reflection on the ongoing responsibility to remember the past, learn from it and carry those lessons forward.

“When people put on an orange shirt, I hope they have reconciliation in mind and put it into action in their daily lives when thinking about and interacting with any Indigenous Peoples.”

Learn more about how Western is navigating new realities.
