stories.title: Good medicine: LHSC’s Visiting Elders program brings culture, connection, and healing to patients
stories.summary: September 30, 2026
stories.content:
September 30, 2026

At London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC), the Visiting Elders program is helping First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous patients access cultural and spiritual support as part of their care journeys. Through the program, patients, families, staff, and care teams can meet with Elders from local First Nations communities, who provide teachings, ceremony, Traditional medicines, counselling, and cultural support.

Elders are respected Knowledge Keepers, cultural advisors, and spiritual guides from local First Nations communities. Many have spent decades practicing Traditional healing and ceremonies, and carry languages, knowledge, and teachings passed down through generations. They help patients reconnect with culture, find comfort during difficult moments, and navigate challenges that extend beyond physical illness.

For Chantel Antone, LHSC’s Director of Indigenous Health, the Visiting Elders program is an essential step in ensuring Indigenous patients and families can access care that reflects their needs, traditions, and values.

“This program was initially launched in 2022 to support patients with their mental, spiritual, and physical well-being,” says Antone. “Over the years, we have seen countless stories where the wisdom, lived experience, and knowledge that our Elders offer has been invaluable to the healing process.”

The program exists alongside LHSC’s Indigenous Healing and Cultural Practices Policy , which helps ensure these services are available as part of a patient’s healing journey. Patients and families who would like to access the Visiting Elders program or Indigenous healing and cultural supports can speak with a member of their care team, who can help connect them with the service.

Elder Tracey Whiteye visits LHSC from Elunaapéwii Lahkéewiit (Delaware Nation of the Thames) and is a regular presence in LHSC’s Mental Health Indigenous Healing Space . For Whiteye, healing begins when people reconnect with themselves, their culture, and the world around them.

“Everything has spirit,” she explains. “The land has spirit, the plants have spirit, everything is alive. When we connect these spirits together, it also connects our spirit. And with that, healing happens.”

Whiteye says some Indigenous patients carry the impacts of colonization, Residential Schools, and historic trauma with them when they come to the hospital for care. For many, reconnecting with ceremony, medicines, songs, language, or teachings can awaken what she calls “blood memory” and remind people where they come from.

Her vision for health-care is one where Indigenous and Western approaches work side by side.

“Let's put our Indigenous lens and our Western lens together,” she says. “That way, we can focus on our strengths, our wisdom, and our knowledge. Ultimately, we're here for the patients.”

Elder Mike Hopkins also visits LHSC from Elunaapéwii Lahkéewiit (Delaware Nation of the Thames). He believes that healing requires caring for the whole person.

As an Elder, Hopkins has spent more than four decades learning Traditional teachings. He often reminds patients, families, and staff that every healing journey is unique.

“Everyone that comes in, they're all different,” he says. “They have to be treated differently.”

Through ceremony, prayer, Traditional medicines, and spiritual guidance, Hopkins helps patients care for the needs of the spirit as well as their physical wellness.

“When we have a patient in the Healing Space, and their body and spirit are disconnected, we do the best we can to take care of that,” he explains. “We also take care of the spirit so it can become one that will heal itself.”

His work extends beyond patients, as Hopkins routinely supports LHSC staff by teaching cultural knowledge, sharing Indigenous values, and helping people navigate personal and professional challenges.

Elder Wendy Hill visits LHSC from Six Nations of the Grand River Territory and feels the need for cultural healing is deeply connected to history.

“For too long Indigenous Peoples have been deprived of it,” she says. “The knowledge, teachings, history, ceremonies, and languages have been hidden from us.”

She recalls supporting an Indigenous woman nearing the end of her life who had become estranged from her family after experiencing the impacts of Residential Schools. Through conversations grounded in compassion, understanding, and cultural teachings, Hill helped the patient begin forgiving herself and repairing damaged relationships.

“It was just a real healing moment that I saw with her,” Hill remembers. “I don't know if she would have gotten that from anywhere else.”

For Hill, stories like these demonstrate why cultural support belongs in health-care.

“Sometimes just smelling the sage or tobacco, or hearing the prayers and the language, is what really heals their spirit.”

Elder Myeengun Henry visits LHSC from Deshkan Zibing (Chippewas of the Thames First Nation). He states that the future of health care lies in bringing together the strengths of Indigenous and Western approaches.

“For generations, many of us were discouraged from practicing Traditional ceremonies or accessing cultural supports within health-care settings,” says Henry. “There’s still a fear of coming to hospitals because of the treatment that we’ve had over the years.”

LHSC’s Visiting Elders program helps remove those barriers by creating safe spaces for Indigenous patients to access care that aligns with their identity, beliefs, and healing traditions.

“We have to build it so that everybody can feel the wealth of healing, which they're entitled to,” says Henry.

He sees hope in the growing number of young people learning their languages, ceremonies, and cultural teachings, and in health-care organizations willing to walk alongside Indigenous communities on the path toward Reconciliation.

Elder Chris George visits LHSC from Onyota’á:ka (Oneida Nation of the Thames), and brings teachings rooted in Traditional medicine, public speaking, and knowledge passed down from the Elders who came before him. He believes that being an Elder means carrying those teachings forward and sharing them in ways that support healing, understanding, and connection.

For George, meaningful Truth and Reconciliation in health-care settings requires hospitals and care providers to better understand the different histories, teachings, and worldviews that Indigenous and non-Indigenous people can bring into a shared experience.

Traditional ways of healing carry deep spiritual teachings and cultural knowledge, while Western medicine is shaped by its own philosophy and systems. To George, Reconciliation means making room for both, so Indigenous patients can receive care that respects their identity, honours their healing traditions, and helps rebuild trust.

“People need to know there are two understandings when it comes to Reconciliation,” says George, reflecting on the relationship between Indigenous spiritual teachings and Western philosophy. "Knowing this is essential for us to create a future where Indigenous patients feel that their culture, spirit, and medicines are embraced as part of their healing.”

Looking ahead, George finds hope in seeing more Indigenous communities become strong and healthy through Traditional healing and cultural practices. It is a vision where Reconciliation is actively lived through care that honours the individual and helps build a stronger future for generations to come.

The Visiting Elders program is part of a broader Indigenous Health strategy underway at LHSC, positioning the organization as a leader in advancing culturally safe, Indigenous-led care within hospital settings.

Over the past several years, the hospital has worked closely with Indigenous communities, Elders, Knowledge Keepers, patients, and leaders to build culturally safer care environments. Those partnerships have helped shape LHSC’s Indigenous Healing and Cultural Practices Policy, which affirms Indigenous patients’ right to access ceremony, traditional medicines, healing spaces, and Elder support as part of their care.

For Antone, this work is ultimately about building trust.

“This program represents another positive step in our efforts to build trust with Indigenous patients, families, and communities, and create a hospital environment where they feel seen, heard, and supported in every aspect of their healing.”

At London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC), the Visiting Elders program is helping First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous patients access cultural and spiritual support as part of their care journeys. Through the program, patients, families, staff, and care teams can meet with Elders from local First Nations communities, who provide teachings, ceremony, Traditional medicines, counselling, and cultural support.

Elders are respected Knowledge Keepers, cultural advisors, and spiritual guides from local First Nations communities. Many have spent decades practicing Traditional healing and ceremonies, and carry languages, knowledge, and teachings passed down through generations. They help patients reconnect with culture, find comfort during difficult moments, and navigate challenges that extend beyond physical illness.

For Chantel Antone, LHSC’s Director of Indigenous Health, the Visiting Elders program is an essential step in ensuring Indigenous patients and families can access care that reflects their needs, traditions, and values.

“This program was initially launched in 2022 to support patients with their mental, spiritual, and physical well-being,” says Antone. “Over the years, we have seen countless stories where the wisdom, lived experience, and knowledge that our Elders offer has been invaluable to the healing process.”

The program exists alongside LHSC’s Indigenous Healing and Cultural Practices Policy , which helps ensure these services are available as part of a patient’s healing journey. Patients and families who would like to access the Visiting Elders program or Indigenous healing and cultural supports can speak with a member of their care team, who can help connect them with the service.

Elder Tracey Whiteye visits LHSC from Elunaapéwii Lahkéewiit (Delaware Nation of the Thames) and is a regular presence in LHSC’s Mental Health Indigenous Healing Space . For Whiteye, healing begins when people reconnect with themselves, their culture, and the world around them.

“Everything has spirit,” she explains. “The land has spirit, the plants have spirit, everything is alive. When we connect these spirits together, it also connects our spirit. And with that, healing happens.”

Whiteye says some Indigenous patients carry the impacts of colonization, Residential Schools, and historic trauma with them when they come to the hospital for care. For many, reconnecting with ceremony, medicines, songs, language, or teachings can awaken what she calls “blood memory” and remind people where they come from.
Her vision for health-care is one where Indigenous and Western approaches work side by side.
“Let's put our Indigenous lens and our Western lens together,” she says. “That way, we can focus on our strengths, our wisdom, and our knowledge. Ultimately, we're here for the patients.”
Elder Mike Hopkins also visits LHSC from Elunaapéwii Lahkéewiit (Delaware Nation of the Thames). He believes that healing requires caring for the whole person.
As an Elder, Hopkins has spent more than four decades learning Traditional teachings. He often reminds patients, families, and staff that every healing journey is unique.
“Everyone that comes in, they're all different,” he says. “They have to be treated differently.”
Through ceremony, prayer, Traditional medicines, and spiritual guidance, Hopkins helps patients care for the needs of the spirit as well as their physical wellness.

“When we have a patient in the Healing Space, and their body and spirit are disconnected, we do the best we can to take care of that,” he explains. “We also take care of the spirit so it can become one that will heal itself.”
His work extends beyond patients, as Hopkins routinely supports LHSC staff by teaching cultural knowledge, sharing Indigenous values, and helping people navigate personal and professional challenges.
Elder Wendy Hill visits LHSC from Six Nations of the Grand River Territory and feels the need for cultural healing is deeply connected to history.
“For too long Indigenous Peoples have been deprived of it,” she says. “The knowledge, teachings, history, ceremonies, and languages have been hidden from us.”

She recalls supporting an Indigenous woman nearing the end of her life who had become estranged from her family after experiencing the impacts of Residential Schools. Through conversations grounded in compassion, understanding, and cultural teachings, Hill helped the patient begin forgiving herself and repairing damaged relationships.
“It was just a real healing moment that I saw with her,” Hill remembers. “I don't know if she would have gotten that from anywhere else.”
For Hill, stories like these demonstrate why cultural support belongs in health-care.
“Sometimes just smelling the sage or tobacco, or hearing the prayers and the language, is what really heals their spirit.”

stories.title: Thousands of stories of residential school survivors will soon be destroyed. This group is fighting to preserve them
stories.summary: The 38,000 testimonies are set for destruction next year for privacy reasons. Many survivors are unaware the records are being destroyed.
stories.author: Gabriel Hilty
stories.content:
A Toronto-based advocacy group is working to preserve a trove of 38,000 testimonies from residential school survivors that documents some of the worst abuses of Indigenous children.

The Indian Residential School Records Project says it wants to return agency to survivors to decide the fate of their records, which are currently slated for destruction due to a Supreme Court ruling over privacy considerations.

“The records that are set for destruction in 2027 are the most comprehensive archive that exists,” Connie Walker, co-leader of the project, told the Star ahead of a Wednesday panel at Evergreen Brickworks with other leaders of the project. The panel discussion coincided with the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

Speaking at a panel Wednesday at Evergreen Brickworks, Connie Walker, co-lead of the Indian Residential School Records Project, talked about the significance of survivor testimony from residential schools.

“Survivors had to disclose in very detailed ways the abuse that they experienced at Indian residential schools,” said Walker, an award-winning investigative journalist and member of the Okanese First Nation in Saskatchewan.

More than 150,000 Indigenous children were taken from their families to attend the schools run by churches and the Canadian government, a scheme the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada (TRC) called “a systematic, government-sponsored attempt to destroy” Indigenous culture and languages.

Operating for more than 150 years until 1997, residential schools were often underfunded, and thousands of children suffered physical and sexual abuse, according to the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation . Records show 4,200 children died at the schools but incomplete and missing files indicate the total is likely higher.

“The right to truth belongs first to the survivors, their families and their communities,” said project co-lead Kimberly Murray.

Murray is a member of the Kanehsatà:ke Mohawk Nation and is an independent special interlocutor for missing children and unmarked graves and burial sites associated with residential schools.

“Survivors themselves must determine what happens to their testimony … we’re hearing that survivors don’t even know that these records are being destroyed in less than a year,” said Murray.

In the 1980s, ‘90s and 2000s, thousands of residential school survivors came forward and sued the government and churches for the abuse they experienced, Walker said.

The process resulted in the 2007 Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement , the largest class-action settlement in Canadian history that provided a base financial compensation of $10,000 to survivors, with an additional $3,000 for every year spent in school.

The out-of-court settlement also formed the TRC, which had a mandate to document the experiences of survivors and inform Canada.

However, speaking to the Independent Assessment Process (IAP) was the only way for survivors to pursue compensation for claims for sexual and serious physical abuse.

While the TRC collected around 6,000 voices, “more than five times that many survivors participated in the IAP,” Walker explained.

The IAP outlined that all documents, where survivors often had to detail abuses they experienced in graphic detail, would be treated as “highly confidential.”

The Supreme Court of Canada determined in 2017 the promise of confidentiality meant that the documents had to be destroyed after a retention period and a notice program to survivors.

“We have concerns about the notice program to tell survivors about their options,” Murray said. “There’s an important difference between choosing destruction, and having the truth destroyed because you didn’t know you had a choice.”

Over the summer, the project began outreach efforts to raise awareness about next year’s looming deadline.

Drawing on public lawsuit records filed before the Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement, the group is also working to create a new archive of testimony, which can act as a resource to communities, Walker said.

“There are so many communities that have started doing their own research and are starting to try to get access to these records. And so we’re hoping that our research will be helpful for them,” Walker said.

Stephen Kakfwi, former premier of the Northwest Territories, shared his experience as a residential school survivor.

Stephen Kakfwi, a Dene leader and former premier of the Northwest Territories, shared some of his residential school experiences with the packed audience wearing orange shirts at Wednesday’s event.

He told of being abused at nine years old.

“It took years before I spoke of it,” Kakfwi said. “I spoke to the Commission when it was in Yellowknife, and to the adjudicator in a more graphic, ugly way of what it was like.”

For Kakfwi, it’s important to preserve the history for his children and future generations.

“To protect and keep secure the records of what happened to us, no matter how graphic or ugly it is … it’s important so that it’s not denied or belittled,” Kakfwi said.

stories.title: Expert insight: Local journalism faces growing crisis in Canada – is government support part of the solution?
stories.summary: Western journalism professor Chris Arsenault examines whether government funding impacts journalists' freedom to report.
stories.author: Jacquelyn Mitchell
stories.content:
In defending an independent press, American founding father Thomas Jefferson famously remarked that he would prefer “newspapers without a government” to a “government without newspapers.” So it’s doubtful the third president of the United States would approve of a program for the government to pay reporters’ salaries.

But desperate times for Canadian media, where newspapers are closing and journalists are losing their jobs, especially at the local level, May call for desperate measures.

At least one-third of journalism jobs in Canada have simply disappeared since 2010, according to government data, as news outlets collectively lost some $4.9 billion.

Canada has faced a net loss of at least 343 local news outlets since 2008, according to the Local News Research Project. It doesn’t require an investigative reporter to determine this is a crisis.

Against this backdrop, the federal government has spent $128.8 million since 2019 to support the hiring of more than 400 journalists under the Local Journalism Initiative(LJI) at newsrooms across the country.

The goal? Quality coverage in communities where the free market alone cannot support reporting, particularly news on local governments and civic affairs.

The money is doled out by administrator organizations – such as News Media Canada – representing different sections of the media industry and at arm’s length from the government of the day. Politicians don’t pick which reporters get funded.

News outlets apply to these organizations to hire reporters; individual journalists or content creators can’t apply on their own. All stories produced under the initiative are published under a Creative Commons licence on The Canadian Press news wire, meaning other media outlets are free to republish them, expanding the pool of local information available to everyone.

The program has been controversial. Journalists have a responsibility to hold powerful entities, including the government, to account. Critics, including some leading journalists, argue “taking money from the people we cover will place us in a permanent and inescapable conflict of interest,” producing “newspapers concerned less with appealing to readers than to grantsmen.”

Audiences don’t like how this smells either. Two polls came to similar conclusions, one commissioned by Toronto-based news outlet The Hub, which has been critical of the LJI, and the other commissioned by journalism support organizations. More than 70 per cent of Canadians believe news outlets could struggle to hold the government accountable while taking its money.

LJI critics also contend this infusion of government cash won’t do much to make the local news business sustainable over the long term.

On this last point, a majority of reporters funded under the initiative agree, according to my new research published in the journal Journalism Practice.

But the study, based on interviews with 22 LJI-funded reporters, paints a more complicated picture of conflict of interest.

Two-thirds of respondents expressed at least some concern with the appearance of a conflict of interest.

Yet no one could point to a specific story they were unable to cover assertively or that editors or grantors pressured them to change or drop as a result of the funding. Several of the same journalists, in contrast, offered clear examples of malign local advertiser influence earlier in their careers.

One now-veteran reporter was chasing tips that a grocery store in British Columbia was selling rotten meat to customers, exactly the kind of local accountability story audiences want. He recounted:

“I was told in no uncertain terms I was to stop working on the story, as the grocery store was the biggest advertiser for the paper. I had to do what I was told. The guys I worked with would have thrown me right off the bridge for the advertising money … I am sure most people who work in news could tell you a similar situation.”

No one described anything comparable involving LJI funding.

This isn’t to say the program is perfect. Many reporters complained about the sheer volume of stories they were expected to produce. Some said their LJI contracts stipulated they needed to write 12-15 stories each week. Under that kind of pressure, it’s nearly impossible to do serious investigative work holding governments, or anyone else, to account.

It’s much easier to rewrite a simple news release under those workload demands than to dig through campaign donations for local city councillors, analyze zoning board reports or engage in genuine investigative journalism.

These kinds of complaints about volume over value will be familiar to anyone who has worked in a newsroom. Still, many reporters financed by the initiative said they wouldn’t have a job without it, meaning no one would be keeping an eye on local officials, covering community events or writing the first draft of history in small-town Canada.

In years past, many viewed government control or censorship as the biggest threat to a free press. Today, that might not be the choice.

Of the options facing an industry in crisis, some targeted, arms-length government support might be the least bad option available. The audience, however, is right to be concerned. Journalists, like the people we cover, deserve scrutiny for our financial choices.

The key will be ensuring government cash isn’t the only option. In the U.S., non-profit foundations have increased their funding for journalism amid the industry’s business crisis.

Media Impact Funders, a network of grantors, estimates that the 25 largest journalism funders gave US$1.1 billion to journalism grantees globally between 2018 and 2022, based on 2024 data.

Smaller news outlets in Canada and elsewhere are trying new business models beyond selling advertising, including printing services, website hosting and even online gambling, in the case of Torstar, the company behind the Toronto Star.

Perfection shouldn’t get in the way of progress – or even risky experimentation – when it comes to saving the news industry.

The future of journalism May look like a loot bag following a kid’s birthday party – a little advertising money, subscription funds from loyal audience members, some entrepreneurial activities outside of the standard news business, and yes, perhaps some government support.

Today, the “government without newspapers” Jefferson feared is closer than ever. In some communities, it’s already here.

Ironically, some taxpayer assistance might be what the industry needs if we are to keep both our local news and some level of government accountability.Image 1: The Conversation

Chris Arsenault, Chair of the Master of Media in Journalism and Communication Program (Mmjc) and assistant professor of journalism, Western University

The money is doled out by administrator organizations – such as News Media Canada – representing different sections of the media industry and at arm’s length from the government of the day. Politicians don’t pick which reporters get funded.

News outlets apply to these organizations to hire reporters; individual journalists or content creators can’t apply on their own. All stories produced under the initiative are published under a Creative Commons licence on The Canadian Press news wire, meaning other media outlets are free to republish them, expanding the pool of local information available to everyone.

The program has been controversial. Journalists have a responsibility to hold powerful entities, including the government, to account. Critics, including some leading journalists, argue “taking money from the people we cover will place us in a permanent and inescapable conflict of interest,” producing “newspapers concerned less with appealing to readers than to grantsmen.”

Audiences don’t like how this smells either. Two polls came to similar conclusions, one commissioned by Toronto-based news outlet The Hub, which has been critical of the LJI, and the other commissioned by journalism support organizations. More than 70 per cent of Canadians believe news outlets could struggle to hold the government accountable while taking its money.
LJI critics also contend this infusion of government cash won’t do much to make the local news business sustainable over the long term.
On this last point, a majority of reporters funded under the initiative agree, according to my new research published in the journal Journalism Practice.
But the study, based on interviews with 22 LJI-funded reporters, paints a more complicated picture of conflict of interest.
Two-thirds of respondents expressed at least some concern with the appearance of a conflict of interest.

Yet no one could point to a specific story they were unable to cover assertively or that editors or grantors pressured them to change or drop as a result of the funding. Several of the same journalists, in contrast, offered clear examples of malign local advertiser influence earlier in their careers.
One now-veteran reporter was chasing tips that a grocery store in British Columbia was selling rotten meat to customers, exactly the kind of local accountability story audiences want. He recounted:

“I was told in no uncertain terms I was to stop working on the story, as the grocery store was the biggest advertiser for the paper. I had to do what I was told. The guys I worked with would have thrown me right off the bridge for the advertising money … I am sure most people who work in news could tell you a similar situation.”
No one described anything comparable involving LJI funding.

This isn’t to say the program is perfect. Many reporters complained about the sheer volume of stories they were expected to produce. Some said their LJI contracts stipulated they needed to write 12-15 stories each week. Under that kind of pressure, it’s nearly impossible to do serious investigative work holding governments, or anyone else, to account.

It’s much easier to rewrite a simple news release under those workload demands than to dig through campaign donations for local city councillors, analyze zoning board reports or engage in genuine investigative journalism.

These kinds of complaints about volume over value will be familiar to anyone who has worked in a newsroom. Still, many reporters financed by the initiative said they wouldn’t have a job without it, meaning no one would be keeping an eye on local officials, covering community events or writing the first draft of history in small-town Canada.
In years past, many viewed government control or censorship as the biggest threat to a free press. Today, that might not be the choice.

Of the options facing an industry in crisis, some targeted, arms-length government support might be the least bad option available. The audience, however, is right to be concerned. Journalists, like the people we cover, deserve scrutiny for our financial choices.
The key will be ensuring government cash isn’t the only option. In the U.S., non-profit foundations have increased their funding for journalism amid the industry’s business crisis.
Media Impact Funders, a network of grantors, estimates that the 25 largest journalism funders gave US$1.1 billion to journalism grantees globally between 2018 and 2022, based on 2024 data.

Smaller news outlets in Canada and elsewhere are trying new business models beyond selling advertising, including printing services, website hosting and even online gambling, in the case of Torstar, the company behind the Toronto Star.
Perfection shouldn’t get in the way of progress – or even risky experimentation – when it comes to saving the news industry.

The future of journalism May look like a loot bag following a kid’s birthday party – a little advertising money, subscription funds from loyal audience members, some entrepreneurial activities outside of the standard news business, and yes, perhaps some government support.
Today, the “government without newspapers” Jefferson feared is closer than ever. In some communities, it’s already here.
Ironically, some taxpayer assistance might be what the industry needs if we are to keep both our local news and some level of government accountability.Image 1: The Conversation

stories.title: Government overreach the true motivation behind Alberta separatism, not Canada itself, Poilievre says
stories.summary: In an Edmonton speech, the Conservative leader set aside Liberal attacks in favour of a more neutral takedown of Ottawa's relentless excesses
stories.author: Jesse Snyder
stories.content:
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre urged Albertans to vote to stay in Canada in the province’s upcoming referendum, arguing that Alberta’s resentments are best addressed by doubling down on the values that the Canadian Constitution was originally meant to uphold.

At a keynote speech in Edmonton, Poilievre made a classical conservative case for why the province’s deep resentments toward confederation are actually due to years of relentless government overreach rather than issues with the country itself.

“What Albertans are complaining about is not Canada,” he told a gathering of Conservative supporters. “It is the government policies that are actually inconsistent with how Canada was meant to work in the first place.”

At the root of the problem, Poilievre said, is that Ottawa has continued to expand its reach into areas of public life that it was never mandated to preside over, while trampling on the personal freedoms of citizens for political gain.

“Simply put, the last decade the federal government has done terribly at the things that are actually its job: immigration, crime, military spending, borders, while intruding into things that are not its job: regulating our resources, going after hunting rifles which are private property, just to name a few examples.”

“The problem with all of these things is not Canada,” he said. “Separation will not solve those problems.”

Poilievre’s address comes as more pro-federalist voices have started to make the case for keeping Alberta within confederation just weeks ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum. The federal Conservatives have long opposed Alberta’s separation, and earlier this month launched a “Conservatives for Canada” campaign in an effort to sway public opinion.

Support for separation on the Canadian prairies has reached new highs in the last few years, spurred on by frustration over everything from Ottawa’s over-regulation of its oil and gas sector to the federal government’s COVID-19 vaccine mandates during the pandemic.

Poilievre appoints Edmonton MP to lead party's pro-unity campaign ahead of Alberta separatism referendum

Poilievre vows to speak to 'Albertans on both sides of this referendum,' in national unity speech

Notably, Poilievre’s speech never once mentioned the federal Liberal Party or Prime Minister Mark Carney, leaving aside politically-charged attacks in favour of a more statesmanlike appeal to the problem of government excess.

The Canadian project was explicitly intended to give Alberta and other provinces control over its own affairs, Poilievre said as part of his address, with governments expected to intervene only within narrow and specified areas of public life. That means provincial governments sticking to matters like health care and education, and Ottawa focusing on matters like borders, national defence and criminal law.

Canada’s founding constitutional document, the British North America Act, gives governments direct instructions to “mind your own business,” the Conservative leader said.

Poilievre also made a more practical case for Alberta staying in Canada, saying the province ought to “lock arms” with the rest of the country under a shared border and common military.

“Simply put, Alberta has had more independence in the past, and we’ll have more independence in the future as part of a united Canada as part of that gigantic country, sharing a military and borders with millions of other Canadians than we would ever have if we were isolated and alone.”

Poilievre, who is from Calgary but spent much of his political life in Ottawa before losing his seat in the city in the 2025 federal election, also made an emotional plea on behalf of Alberta’s unique identity and the shared traits of its people.

“I love Alberta,” he said. “I love what it represents — hard work, generosity, unpretentiousness, resilience, common sense. I love the grit of the people.”

The Conservative leader also called on the rest of Canada to listen to the anger among some Albertans over its treatment within the federation, saying that efforts to appease that anger would likely benefit the broader country.

“If you listen carefully to what Albertans are asking for, they don’t want to take away anything from anyone else. In fact, their demands would not only make Alberta better off, it would make all of us better off.”

stories.title: Sentencing hearing for man who randomly stabbed elderly woman
stories.summary: Elizabeth O’Loughlin who was out for a walk with her dog along Brydges Street in Aug. 2024 when she was viciously attacked by a man who stabbed her six times.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Elizabeth O’Loughlin who was out for a walk with her dog along Brydges Street in Aug. 2024 when she was viciously attacked by a man who stabbed her six times.

The 78-year-old was rushed to hospital at the time and received dozens of stitches for her wounds.

The senior has since passed away from issues not related to the attack.

Last December, Cristefer Young-Hough, 33, plead guilty to aggravated assault in connection to the incident. He also plead guilty to assault causing bodily harm after he attacked a corrections officer while in custody at the Elgin-Middlesex Detention Centre.

The court has heard that Young-Hough has suffered a lifetime of mental health issues.

At his sentencing hearing on Tuesday, the Crown asked that he receive a total of nine years behind bars with the defence asking for time already served.

Before wrapping up Justice Michael Carnegie told the court, “This is a very difficult proceeding.”

Justice Carnegie is expected to hand down his sentencing decision on Oct. 26.

stories.title: Truth and Reconciliation includes promoting women to leadership positions: Indigenous knowledge sharer
stories.summary: With National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Wednesday, a local Indigenous Knowledge Sharer says women should be at the forefront of leadership in our communities.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
With National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Wednesday, a local Indigenous Knowledge Sharer says women should be at the forefront of leadership in our communities. “There’s 94 calls to action, but they always focus on one.

We need to focus on other aspects that really get overlooked. So, we’re focusing on the importance of women,” said Ray John Jr. of Oneida First Nation near London. John will speak at “Approachable Conversations with an Indigenous Man” Wednesday at Fanshawe College in London from 10:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. at Canada Village Square at Fanshawe.

An event co-hosted by Fanshawe and Canada Life Innovation Village. John says his message is about how promoting women into positions of leadership is one way to fulfill Truth and Reconciliation commitments. “It starts in your home.

Then it goes into your community. Then it goes into the nation. So, when they’re speaking on behalf of the nation, it’s because they came straight from here, right from the beginning. And then so, we have doctors, we have lawyers, we have people in positions of power.

But we need to hear them more,” he stated.

stories.title: Nearly dozen of Winnipeg school trustees acclaimed ahead of election
stories.summary: Eleven school trustees have been acclaimed ahead of election day, which is nearly three times more acclaimed races than last election.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
Eleven school trustees have been acclaimed ahead of election day, which is nearly three times more acclaimed races than last election.

Four candidates were acclaimed in the previous election, according to official election results in 2022. The Winnipeg School Division had the most, five, uncontested school trustee seats this election.

“It feels different. To win by acclamation is I guess a relief, but it feels a bit weird, because you’re winning a race you didn’t run,” said Tamara Kuly, an acclaimed school trustee in the Winnipeg School Division.

Kuly was contested when she ran for school trustee in 2022, according to official election results.

“There’s two reasons why trustees get acclaimed, one is they do a great job, and the other reason is democracy is tired,” said Laura Reimer, a former school trustee at the St. Boniface and Louis Riel School Division in the early 2000s.

stories.title: Edmonton condo owners accuse investment firms of ‘predatory’ takeovers
stories.summary: Some Edmonton condo owners say investment firms are making individual offers on multiple units at the same time, in order to gain enough control to turn the property into rentals.
stories.author: Erik Bay
stories.content:
Condominium owners in Edmonton are trying to stop what they’re calling a ‘hostile takeover’ of their buildings.

They say investment firms are making individual offers on multiple units at the same time, in order to gain enough control to turn private homes into rentals.

“They can start taking control of the board of directors and issuing special assessments and levies that the other owners maybe can’t afford,” explained Darlene Reid with the Realtors Association of Edmonton.

“Now these people are being forced out of their homes and forced to sell.”

Condominium owners and board members at The Berkeley near 101 Avenue and 116 Street say they are being inundated with letters from companies offering to buy their units.

The letters promote the idea of converting the condominium building into rental housing through a process known as deconversion, while promising owners above-market prices for their units.

Some owners say they are concerned companies could acquire a majority voting stake in the building, leaving remaining owners with limited options if they choose not to sell.

One of the companies identified by owners provided a statement to Global News.

Harmani Investments said its goal is to create long-term rental housing, but acknowledged that not everyone supports condominium deconversion.

The company said it respects those views, makes voluntary offers to purchase units and exercises the rights associated with any units it owns.

Darlene Reid said the takeover approach is happening at several buildings in Edmonton.

“It is totally legit and legal — I just don’t think it’s very ethical.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "It is totally legit and legal — I just don't think it's very ethical."

stories.title: One of two teens charged in sexual assault involving mini hockey stick in Nova Scotia pleads guilty
stories.summary: Sentencing and the case of the second teen, who has pleaded not guilty, are expected to be heard next year
stories.author: Lindsay Jones
stories.content:
A teenaged boy pleaded guilty to sexual assault with a weapon in a Nova Scotia youth court Tuesday after a violent hockey hazing incident last fall.

A second boy, who is facing four charges related to the assault and who has pleaded not guilty, is scheduled to go to trial next February.

In the Truro courtroom, the first teen, now aged 15, stood with his hands on the front of his slacks, rocking slightly as Judge Brian Warcop read out the charge. The boy’s father sat next to him in the front row, his head down, his elbows on his knees. Dozens of supporters of the three victims listened intently on the opposite side of the courtroom as the details of the violent sexual assault at a team sleepover party were read aloud from the agreed statement of facts.

The identities of the victims and accused cannot be named under the Youth Criminal Justice Act.

News of the assault struck a chord nationwide as hockey, and the sports bodies that regulate them, has faced a reckoning in recent years for a culture of silence and toxic masculinity. Hockey Canada, which governs amateur hockey in the country, opened an investigation into the Nova Scotia incident, but the sports body said it is confidential.

The court heard that on the evening of Oct. 3, 2025, the under-15 boys hockey team gathered at a teammate’s house for a team party and sleepover at or around Colchester County. The gathering had been organized so the more senior players could get to know the rookies.

The players’ parents gathered downstairs, while the boys socialized upstairs in two rooms. In one room, a 13-year-old rookie player was laying down on his stomach on a bed, scrolling on his phone, when two older players, who were 14 at the time, pinned him down, pulled down his pants and underwear and exposed his buttocks. The boy who has pleaded not guilty allegedly pushed a mini hockey stick between the younger boy’s buttocks. The rookie shouted for them to stop and started crying, later telling authorities that the assault lasted 15 to 20 seconds, but it “felt like forever.”

The court heard that he always planned to tell his parents but didn’t know how to raise the subject and he didn’t want to get anyone in trouble.

After the assault, the two older boys went after two other rookies and removed their pants, but were unsuccessful in taking off their underwear. The younger boys kicked themselves free of their attackers.

The victim’s father eventually heard about the incident, went to the RCMP on Jan. 30 and filed a complaint, according to the statement of facts.

In court, it was agreed that a psychological and psychiatric study on the boy who pleaded guilty would be presented to the court prior to sentencing, which is expected to take place in the new year. The defence and the Crown attorney told the court they would be recommending a joint sentencing submission for the boy’s case.

The sentence for sexual assault with a weapon for a youth can range from an absolute discharge to a period of secure custody and community supervision, senior Crown attorney Patrick Young said after the hearing.

Mr. Young told reporters he couldn’t disclose the discussions that took place ahead of the guilty plea, but he said that the agreement, sentence and statement of facts can all be negotiated by counsel. “Because they’re privileged it would be inappropriate for me to comment on that.”

The teen is also facing two other charges of sexual assault. Those charges will carry over to sentencing and be disposed of at that time, Mr. Young said.

His guilty plea also impacts the case against the second teen because he now potentially becomes a compellable witness for the Crown, Mr. Young said. The trial of the second teen is scheduled to begin Feb. 22. That boy, who is also now 15, has pleaded not guilty to charges of sexual assault with a weapon, two counts of sexual assault and one count of assault.

Hockey Canada has been embroiled in controversy over its handling of sexual assault allegations made against five members of the 2018 national junior team (they were found not guilty in a criminal court last year), and for quietly using registration fees from players across the country to settle such cases.

In response to that scandal, Hockey Canada launched an independent third party (ITP) process in 2022 for confidentially handling hockey-related maltreatment complaints and to ensure possible Criminal Code offences are reported to law enforcement and child protection services.

Hockey Nova Scotia, a branch of Hockey Canada and the organization that governs the sport in the province, initially suspended and later disbanded the team involved in last year’s hazing incident. The Globe and Mail is not naming the team to protect the identities of the victims and accused.

The incidents of sexual violence involving the team were reported to Hockey Canada’s ITP and an investigation was launched earlier this year, Hockey Canada chief of staff Jeremy Knight said, adding he couldn’t comment on the status or outcome of the process, which is confidential.

The ITP has the power to make their decision public. They did not immediately respond to The Globe’s query about what they plan to do.

stories.title: Plane pull at London airport takes flight, fundraises with a unique experience
stories.summary: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mJ67EM0lyWU On the tarmac of the London International Airport, the only specta...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
On the tarmac of the London International Airport, the only spectacle that could match the sound of jet engines idling and loudspeakers blaring Mamma Mia by Abba, was the sight of groups of people pulling a small jet airliner across the runway.

And many of those people said they couldn’t be happier to be there.

The Elgin Middlesex United Way hosted its second annual Plane Pull fundraiser Tuesday, with teams of 10 to 15 people pulling aircraft weighing 19 and 27 metric tonnes, respectively, across the airport tarmac.

“Some of our United Way friends from across the country have done this … and we said ‘nobody’s doing this in London, let’s try this’,” said Elgin Middlesex United Way director of m arketing and communications Chris McInnis when asked how the event came to be.

McInnis also explained that the money raised at the event will fund 35 United Way agencies across Elgin Middlesex so they can provide assistance such as food, toiletries, housing stability and youth mentorship.

“We’re basically just trying to build a better community any way we can,” he said.

Other organizations besides United Way were also there in hopes of making a difference. Western University’s commercial aviation program

A Girls in Aviation kiosk at the event. The Plane Pull offered opportunities for other organizations to reach out to people alongside the United Way fundraiser. Photo by: Curtis Stokman was one of several different kiosks set up along the edge of the runway, offering brochures and speaking to people about the program.

“We always like to come to events that involve the community and involve students,” said Sebastian Fredrich Yap, one of the people manning the kiosk.

Western’s kiosk sat underneath a tent emblazoned with a Girls in Aviation logo, and Yap believes what the kiosk was doing helps to promote an otherwise male-dominated industry to women.

“The more we can introduce young girls to aviation and show them that’s a legitimate career path for them, I think is beneficial long-term,” he said.

The primary showcase of the event, though, was the people hauling the aircraft through a combination of teamwork, effort, and very large ropes.

The London Community Foundation team trying to pull a 19-tonne jet aircraft. Many of the teams at the event were excited for the experience, even if it wasn’t like anything they’d done before. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

“None of us have ever done anything like this before and it’s such an amazing opportunity,” said London Community Foundation director of philanthropy Jennifer Cahill.

Many teams tried different strategies to pull their plane. Lerners Law Firm team leader Andrew Johnson admitted that his team’s preparations amounted to “sitting at our desks”, while the RBC Bank Rollers said they stretched beforehand and selected their members carefully.

“We set up the best absolute team to do a great job here today,” said Steven Mattis, the Bank Rollers’ team leader.

Some teams were even comprised of high school students. Maiyar Altawil was a part of a team from Westminster Secondary School in London, and was cheered on by her friend Teniola Olaoye. They, like many other teams, found pulling a plane to be a unique experience.

“It was actually … easier than I expected,” said Altawil. “You actually have a whole team backing you up, and that’s what I feel like is just so beautiful and meaningful about this whole thing.”

In the end, after many teams had put their backs into hauling a passenger jet and gone to adjacent kiosks for pizza and ice cream, they agreed it was all for a worthy cause. Organizers said they expect the event to return next year, so several teams also believed they will as well.

“[United Way] are really the backbone of the community,” said Cahill. “They bring all of the organizations together, whether they be for-profit or public or agencies themselves.”

stories.title: Canada seeking mediators to help rescue Ukrainian children
stories.summary: In many cases, Russian officials have changed the children’s personal information, making positive identification difficult
stories.author: Geoffrey York, Janice Dickson
stories.content:
The international campaign to rescue Ukrainian children from Russian control has been complicated by identity verification issues and the search for intermediaries to negotiate the return of the children, officials say.

Canada, Ukraine and Norway led a conference in Toronto this week to seek progress on the return of the estimated 20,650 Ukrainian children in Russian hands in occupied Ukrainian territory or in Russia itself. But the effort will need to rely on countries with closer ties to Moscow to serve as mediators, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand acknowledged.

Ms. Anand said 83 countries and international organizations attended the conference, of which 54 signed a “Toronto pledge” to help recover the children, along with detained civilians and prisoners of war. This exceeds the number who signed a similar commitment at a Montreal conference two years ago.

Under the new pledge, the countries expressed grave concern at the deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children by Russia. They called for global efforts to identify, trace and locate the children and verify information about each case.

“We have pledged to bring them back, knowing that it can be dangerous, complex, difficult, but above all necessary,” Ms. Anand told the conference.

She cited India, Germany and the United States as countries that could be mediators on the issue, since they have better relations with Moscow. The conference participants agreed on the need for “sustained and expanded diplomatic efforts” to find “additional states that could act as intermediaries,” Latvian official Dace Melbarde told the closing session.

Alexandra Chyczij, the president of the Ukrainian Canadian Congress, said “back channels” are crucial for the release of the children because Moscow won’t talk to those who openly support Ukraine. “I think we need to continue to use every possible channel we have,” she told journalists.

Another potential mediator is South Africa, a longtime friend of Moscow, which is working with Qatar on a parallel initiative to seek the return of the children. South Africa has been “engaging with the Russians,” but the process “has not been easy,” said Zane Dangor, director-general of South Africa’s Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO).

Disagreements on how to verify the identities of the children – whose personal information has often been changed by Russian officials – are among the obstacles on the issue, the South African government says.

“That has been a sticky point,” said Chrispin Phiri, a spokesperson for DIRCO. “There is a dispute about what verification process can be used to ascertain the identity of the kids amongst others.”

South Africa sees itself practising “shuttle diplomacy” between Ukraine and Russia, including on the issue of the Ukrainian children, Mr. Phiri told The Globe and Mail. But it hoped the Toronto conference would help clarify the process for verifying their identities, he said.

Ms. Anand, speaking at the opening of the Toronto conference, noted that Russia has “altered children’s identities and personal information” as part of its efforts to erase their Ukrainian identity.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky , in a visit to Pretoria last year, handed South African President Cyril Ramaphosa a list of 400 Ukrainian children and asked him to help secure their return.

Asked whether South Africa had made any progress on the list, Mr. Phiri said the effort was stalled by technical issues, including verification and safe passage mechanisms.

Mr. Ramaphosa raised the issue directly with Russian President Vladimir Putin earlier this month in New Delhi at the annual conference of BRICS countries (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa and five others).

South Africa was grateful to be invited to the Toronto conference, but “we will want to hear your views on that as well, because we would like to attend, to see how best we can continue advancing our relations,” Mr. Ramaphosa told Mr. Putin in their Sept. 11 meeting. It was unclear if the two leaders discussed the issue further.

South Africa has declined to join the 51-member International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children, which was founded in 2024 and is co-chaired by Canada and Ukraine. It reportedly made the decision because the coalition is dominated by Western countries that are perceived as enemies of Moscow.

Instead it has been working with Qatar and the Vatican – two other states that declined to join the coalition or sign the “Toronto pledge” Tuesday − in a separate initiative to seek the children’s return. Qatar told the conference that it has helped rescue and return 87 Ukrainian children since 2023.

Mr. Ramaphosa first raised the issue of the children with Mr. Putin in 2023 when he led a delegation of African leaders to Moscow to seek peace in Ukraine, but Mr. Putin brushed off the issue and insisted that Russia was merely ensuring the safety of the children.

South Africa describes itself as a “non-aligned” country and has abstained on most United Nations votes about Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. But last December it broke from this stand to vote in favour of a UN General Assembly resolution calling for the immediate return of the children.

stories.title: Judge dismisses injunction over Saskatoon homeless encampment
stories.summary: Justice Richard Danyliuk issued a written decision Tuesday, ruling the plaintiffs who brought forward the injunction request had no standing to do so.
stories.author: Chris Vandenbreekel
stories.content:
A Court of King’s Bench judge in Saskatoon has dismissed an emergency injunction request to prevent the City of Saskatoon from clearing an encampment located in the Pleasant Hill neighbourhood.

Justice Richard Danyliuk issued a written decision Tuesday, ruling the plaintiffs who brought forward the injunction request had no standing to do so.

The 46-page decision details several uses of hearsay and opinion contained in submissions from the plaintiffs, lawyer Crystal Fafard and Sheela McLean, while citing several documented warnings provided to the encampment occupants by the City of Saskatoon.

Fafard filed for an injunction last Wednesday to prevent the clearing of an encampment at 301 Avenue K South and two other nearby sites at 1112 and 1202 19th Street West until those living there can find shelter.

The Saskatoon Fire Department had plans to clear the two encampment sites on 19th Street West last Thursday, but paused its operations after being met with “aggressive protestors,” according to the city.

All efforts to remove the camps were then paused while the injunction matter was before the courts.

In response to the decision, the City of Saskatoon said in a statement that it “remains committed” to working with its community partners and plans to continue following its established encampment response processes to provide support to those who need it.

“The City’s approach to the encampment has consistently focused on connecting individuals with available supports and services while addressing significant health and safety concerns for people staying at the site, the nearby school, neighbouring residents, businesses and the broader community,” the statement said.

It is unclear whether the city will move ahead with encampment clearing in the days ahead, with the city’s lawyers telling the court Monday it will decide next steps following a court decision or an emergency situation requiring its intervention.

In the decision, Danyliuk says the city was responding to a serious issue, given the various health and safety concerns of the camp, and that the city was not seeking an “eviction” as argued by the applicants, since the land is owned by the city with there being no termination of occupation rights.

Fafard identified herself as an Indigenous advocate in a Court of King’s Bench courtroom Monday afternoon, filing the application on behalf of encampment residents seeking temporary relief until the status quo can be restored for them.

But the judge noted in his decision that this raised a procedural issue in the case, as Fafard appeared in court Monday as an applicant, lawyer, and witness simultaneously, which is prohibited in a Saskatchewan court.

Fafard told reporters outside the courthouse Monday that she had “very short time” to pull the application together and hoped the judge would look at the issue at hand rather than the rules of the court.

Danyliuk also acknowledged in his decision a worsening homelessness situation in Saskatoon, but says it is a matter that should be solved through policy rather than in a courtroom.

Both applicants are also ordered to pay the City $250 in costs for the case, with Danyliuk noting that costs that are “too high” could discourage future litigation.

Saskatchewan’s Attorney General was an intervenor in the case because it raised constitutional concerns.

The city says it started noticing the encampments around 20th Street growing in size earlier this month, noting dozens of structures stretching to nearby lots and an escalating number of complaints from nearby residents, businesses and an elementary school.

With files from Chris Vandenbreekel

stories.title: Manitoba to dedicate a memorial at burial site linked to a former residential school
stories.summary: On the eve of National Truth and Reconciliation Day across the country, the province and the City of Brandon have bought a burial site linked to a former residential school, and they have plans to dedicate a memorial at the site. The school opened in 1895, and historical records show a cemetery was used there […]
stories.author: Cole Fortner
stories.content:
By Justin Hardy

Posted September 29, 2026 6:54 pm.

On the eve of National Truth and Reconciliation Day across the country, the province and the City of Brandon have bought a burial site linked to a former residential school, and they have plans to dedicate a memorial at the site.

The school opened in 1895, and historical records show a cemetery was used there between 1895 and 1912.

The burial ground was later developed into a park, and eventually became Turtle Crossing Campground in 2001.

The province says historical records and family knowledge indicate unmarked graves are still located within parts of the campground.

“This land contains the buried remains of children who attended the Brandon Indian Residential School and their existence has been documented for more than 100 years,” said Premier Wab Kinew. “These graves have been known about since long before the invention of ground-penetrating radar.”

Future decisions about the site will be guided by survivors and affected First Nations, including Sioux Valley Dakota Nation, which has stepped up as steward of the land.

“This is important work for our nation and for Indigenous peoples across Canada,” said Chief Jennifer Bone, Sioux Valley Dakota Nation. “Sioux Valley Dakota Nation’s investigation is Indigenous-led, with specialized support for a careful, non-invasive search. Technical expertise and community knowledge will guide the work, with respect for the children, their families and this sacred site at every stage.”

Manitoba Keewatinowi Okimakinak will also be involved. The organization says the site includes 56 children from eight of its communities.

The province says acquiring the land is part of its work to protect residential school burial sites and support truth and reconciliation.

stories.title: More than 70,000 visit International Plowing Match near Walkerton
stories.summary: Thousands of people walked the dirt roads of the International Plowing Match (IPM) near Walkerton last week.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Thousands of people and 1,700 volunteers walked the dirt roads of the International Plowing Match (IPM) near Walkerton last week.

71,330 is the official attendance figure, according to the Ontario Plowmen’s Association, the highest attendance figure since 2022 when the IPM returned after COVID.

That number is on par with previous Ipm’s, but below the 100,000 visitors, Bruce County organizers were aiming for.

Attendance grew each day, from 10,238 on opening day, Sept 22, to 18,670 on closing day Sept. 26.

Bruce County has hosted the IPM four times in the past 50 years. At the first match in 1976, nearly 200,000 took in the tented city. In 2008, at the match in Teeswater, nearly 95,000 took in the event.

Organizers are still calling the five-day event a success, drawing in visitors to farmer’s fields near Walkerton, from around the world for the agricultural showcase.

stories.title: Politics Insider: Carney talks energy and oceans in B.C.
stories.summary: Prime Minister announces LNG Canada expansion project while also pledging $1.2-billion for ocean safety and protection later in the day
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Hello, welcome to Politics Insider. Let’s look at what happened today.

There will be no newsletter tomorrow as The Globe recognizes the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. However, our website will be staffed so please visit theglobeandmail.com for the latest news. We will be back in your inbox on Thursday.

It was double duty for Prime Minister Mark Carney in Vancouver today: first energy, then oceans.

First there was the announcement that LNG Canada is going ahead with the $30-billion Phase 2 expansion project at its liquefied natural gas export terminal in Kitimat, B.C.

“The speed of this project shows that now when Canadians want something built, we get it built,” Carney said.

As Jeffrey Jones reports, Shell and its partners are banking on decades of rising demand for liquefied natural gas, predicated on a longer-term transition away from more carbon-intensive fossil fuels, according to LNG Canada chief executive officer Chris Cooper.

Later in the day, the Prime Minister’s Office acknowledged that expanding strategic infrastructure along the West Coast will help diversify trade, but also “place increased pressure on our ocean ecosystem.” To that end, Carney announced $1.2-billion for ocean safety, protecting marine wildlife and strengthening front-line conservation enforcement.

“We inherited these oceans, and it’s our obligation to pass them on better than we found them,” Carney said during his remarks at his second public appearance of the day.

Environmentalists are not impressed. Reacting to the LNG news, activists said the investment in the project runs counter to what they predict will be a worldwide transition to fossil-fuel-free energy, and that the LNG Canada expansion will double greenhouse gas emissions from the facility and from increased drilling activity in northeast B.C. to supply the plant.

This is the daily Politics Insider newsletter, curated by

. It is available exclusively to our digital subscribers. You can sign up for more than 20 other newsletters on

Anand sidesteps calls for Havana Syndrome inquiry

The unexplained health ailments experienced by Canadian diplomats stationed in Cuba almost a decade ago are a human-resources concern, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said.

The promise of a referendum puts Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon on centre stage

Days ahead of the Quebec election, he seems destined to become the province’s 34th premier and could eke out a majority win that would pave the way for him to hold the third referendum on independence he has promised since taking over the party.

Economist warns Brexit was ‘cakewalk’ compared with what Alberta separation would entail

The years-long trade wrangling and uncertainty that faced Britain in the wake of the Brexit vote was a “cakewalk” compared with what Alberta’s separation from Canada would involve, according to the author of a new report.

On our radar

The House of Commons is on a break this week, but there’s plenty going on.

“Any Canadians here? Please, if you’re on K Street, get the hell out of our country.” - Donald Trump adviser Peter Navarro, at a conference in Washington today, in reference to an area of the city where lobbyists work, as he warned Canadians not to interfere in next month’s U.S. midterm election.

The new U.S. import ban hit Canada at 12:01 a.m. today - affecting Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and some dairy products. Approximately how much alcohol (in dollars) was exported to the U.S. last year?

Scroll to the bottom of this newsletter for the answer.

Perspectives

The ugly reckoning coming for Danielle Smith

Everything about this referendum on separation and the other nine questions on the ballot – among other things they attempt to scapegoat immigrants for many of the province’s problems – is contemptible. It’s a phony, illegitimate exercise Ms. Smith has lent credibility to in order to save her job. — Gary Mason

Why Trumpenomics will outlive its author

A president can do a lot of governing without Congress, especially when it comes to foreign affairs – as Mr. Trump has spent the last 20 months demonstrating. — Tony Keller

It’s probably true that Alberta and Canada, were separation to occur, would figure out a separation agreement and then life would go on on both sides of the border. But that it could happen smoothly is no guarantee that it will, and that it could be a success is even less of an argument in favour of separation than you might think. — Tyler Dawson

Got a news tip that you’d like us to look into? E-mail us at tips@globeandmail.com . Need to share documents securely? Reach out via SecureDrop .

The answer to today’s question: Canada exported about $1.4-billion in alcohol products to the U.S. last year, with more than $740-million in spirits coming from Ontario.

stories.title: Conservative MP Scott Aitchison expected to resign by the end of the year
stories.summary: Conservative MP and former leadership contender Scott Aitchison is expected to resign from the House of Commons by the end of the year.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi, Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Ottawa — Conservative MP and former leadership contender Scott Aitchison is expected to resign from the House of Commons by the end of the year, becoming the eighth party member to leave the caucus since last election.

Aitchison represents Parry Sound—Muskoka, a large rural Ontario riding a few hours north of Toronto and was first elected for the Conservatives in 2019 after serving for decades on Huntsville Town Council, where he was mayor from 2014 to 2019.

He also ran for Conservative leadership against Pierre Poilievre in 2022, where he finished fourth in a pool of four candidates.

His resignation was first reported by CTV News.

A source close to Aitchison confirmed to the National Post that the MP is planning to resign his seat before the end of 2026 to pursue “other opportunities.” Aitchison is expected to have more to say about this later this week, the source said.

Aitchison’s resignation will spark a new political test for Poilievre as poll aggregator 338Canada suggests that Parry Sound—Muskoka could flip to the Liberals if a byelection were held today. Aitchison won the riding in 2025 with a 10 point lead over the Liberals.

This summer, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberals won the Quebec riding of Chicoutimi—Le Fjord from the Tories during a by-election sparked by Conservative MP Richard Martel’s appointment to the Senate.

Poilievre will also eventually have to fight to maintain the Ontario riding of Brantford—Brant South left vacant after the recent resignation of Conservative MP Larry Brock, who returned to his previous job as Crown prosecutor.

stories.title: Police file criminal, provincial charges over University of Guelph homecoming party
stories.summary: Off-campus party results in objects thrown, people climbing buildings, shoplifting and vandalism, Guelph police say
stories.author: Maan Alhmidi
stories.content:
After an off-campus University of Guelph homecoming party descended into chaos last weekend, other Ontario universities say they are working to minimize the impacts of similar upcoming events.

The unsanctioned party in Guelph on Saturday risked the safety of students and neighbours, university president Rene Van Acker said in a statement.

Videos circulating online show massive crowds of young people filling the streets, and some of them throwing bottles and other items as police officers tried to control the situation. The videos also show police putting some people in handcuffs.

“The University of Guelph is deeply disappointed by what occurred, and we are clear that this cannot happen again,” Van Acker said, adding that the school will review the incident.

He said the people who got involved in property damage and other disruptive behaviour also included those who do not attend the university.

Guelph police said the gathering was “significantly larger” than similar events in recent years and officers were dealing with objects being thrown, people climbing buildings, as well as shoplifting and vandalism at nearby businesses.

They said officers laid several criminal and provincial charges, including causing a disturbance and numerous alcohol-related offences.

“Homecoming is an opportunity for students, residents and visitors to celebrate together. Most people enjoyed the day responsibly, but behaviour that puts others at risk cannot be accepted,” said Guelph police Chief Gord Cobey.

Guelph is not the only university town that has at times struggled to contain rowdy off-campus parties in the fall.

In Ottawa, the annual Panda Game between Carleton University and the University of Ottawa football teams is taking place this weekend and Carleton said it recognizes the event can affect nearby communities.

Post-game misbehaviour in recent years included people flipping a car and stealing street signs, and has sent several people to the hospital.

Carleton University spokesperson Steven Reid said the school is working closely with the University of Ottawa, the city, Ottawa Police and others to ensure safety for everyone this year.

“We are taking steps before, during and after the game to minimize those impacts,” he said. “We are also continuing to communicate with students about their responsibilities, the importance of being good neighbours and the consequences of unlawful or disruptive behaviour.”

Another homecoming party is scheduled in Kingston, Ont., starting on Oct. 16 for Queen’s University students and alumni.

A spokesperson for the school said preparations for the event include planning and co-ordination with the city, police, student leaders and groups across the university.

Students are reminded of local bylaws and potential fines, as well as responsible behaviour, the university said.

“Those found in violation of nuisance party regulations, noise bylaws, or open liquor laws can face fines from $50 to $2,000 and sanctions under the Queen’s University Non-Academic Misconduct system,” it said.

The institution said Kingston police will focus on community outreach on campus and in the near-campus neighbourhoods leading up to the event.

Back in Guelph, Mayor Cam Guthrie said police are working to find those responsible for putting residents, businesses, and emergency responders in danger.

“We all must agree that this type of reckless behaviour can never be allowed to happen in our city again,” he said.
