stories.title: Sean Ward's death during synagogue attack should not taint COVID-19 lawsuit he and other ex-soldiers filed, his lawyer says
stories.summary: Ward was one of 128 Canadian Forces members and ex-members who claim their careers were damaged or destroyed by COVID-19 vaccination mandate
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
The shocking death of Sean Ward in a shootout with police protecting a Belleville synagogue from his “hate-motivated” attack should not taint the public’s view of a large lawsuit he was part of against the Canadian military’s COVID-19 mandate, says his lawyer.

“There is an obvious risk that intense public attention focused on one plaintiff May obscure the experiences of the many other military members and veterans involved in these proceedings,” Catherine Christensen, the lawyer for dozens of Canadian soldiers and former soldiers named in the lawsuit, told National Post.

“The events in Belleville involving Sean Ward and police outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue were extremely serious. Our thoughts are with the injured police officer, the members of the congregation, and everyone affected,” she said.

“Sean Ward was one individual claimant among a large number of serving and former CAF members who have sought legal remedies arising from the vaccination directives, the exemption and accommodation process, administrative measures, releases, and resulting career consequences.

“The litigation did not originate with Mr. Ward, and its factual and legal foundation does not depend upon him.”

Ward, 29, was involuntarily discharged from the Canadian Armed Forces in 2022 when he was deemed “unsuitable for further service” after defying the military’s vaccine mandate during the pandemic, according to court documents. He was seeking $1.5 million in general damages and additional compensation for a financial loss of $140,000.

He was one of 128 members and former members of the Canadian Forces who claimed their military careers were damaged or destroyed by a mandatory COVID-19 vaccination mandate.

The lawsuit describes Sean Douglas Reginald Ward as holding the rank of corporal in the infantry with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, based at Canadian Forces Base Edmonton. The lawsuit claims Ward refused to be vaccinated “on religious grounds” but his exemption was denied by military officials.

Synagogue attacker Sean Ward was embroiled in lawsuit against military's COVID-19 vaccine mandate

'You are going to die for the Jews,' said Belleville shooting suspect: police

“Beyond information contained in that (court) record, we will not discuss confidential communications relating to Mr. Ward or any other client,” Christensen said.

“The circumstances surrounding Mr. Ward’s death remain the subject of investigation. Police have publicly stated their conclusions concerning the nature and apparent motive of the incident. Mr. Ward is deceased, those allegations will not be tested through a criminal trial, and it would be inappropriate to speculate about his intentions or state of mind,” she said.

Belleville’s Chief of Police, Murray Rodd, said Ward came heavily armed with a shotgun, other undisclosed firearms, a significant amount of ammunition, containers of gasoline and additional resources in a planned attack on the synagogue where about 25 people had gathered for Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

Rodd said during a firefight with two police constables outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue Ward yelled, “You are going to die for the Jews.” One officer was seriously injured when ambushed by Ward, who was shot and killed by police. “This was a targeted attack against the Jewish community. The suspect had the means, the motive and the mechanisms to cause a mass casualty and the destruction of the Jewish synagogue,” Rodd said.

“It is equally important that the public understand the much broader history of the litigation,” Christensen said of the ongoing COVID lawsuit.

“The present proceeding is not the first large civil action brought by CAF members arising from the COVID-19 vaccination directives. An earlier Federal Court mass tort proceeding was commenced on behalf of approximately 330 serving and former members and advanced constitutional and civil claims arising from the mandate and its enforcement.

“That earlier proceeding was struck at the pleadings stage on a technical issue. The underlying allegations concerning the CAF vaccination policy were therefore not determined following a trial on the evidence.

“The claims raise questions concerning the legality of those measures, the accommodation framework, the administrative and career consequences imposed on members, and the constitutional and other legal obligations of the Canadian Armed Forces and the Government of Canada,” she said.

She said those issues need to be heard and considered separately from the circumstances of Ward’s death and the attack at the synagogue.

“Hundreds of serving and former CAF members have pursued grievances or litigation arising from the vaccination policy over a period of several years. They have different service histories, different circumstances and different experiences under the policy. Their claims should be understood on their own facts.”

In a statement of defence filed in court by Department of Justice lawyers, the Canadian government and military “deny each and every allegation” in the lawsuit.

The government defended the vaccine mandates in a court filing as having a primary objective of protecting the “readiness, health, and safety of the Force, the entire Defence Team, as well as members of the public they May be called upon to serve.” The government says “a member’s failure to comply with the Directives demonstrates an unwillingness to obey and support lawful authority.”

stories.title: Stelco layoffs highlight domino effect of U.S. tariffs: industry experts
stories.summary: The job cuts are the latest in a string of tariff-linked layoffs in the province and come after plans for more than 1,000 job cuts at Algoma Steel.
stories.author: Brett Bundale
stories.content:
The latest round of layoffs in Ontario’s steel belt highlights the ripple effects of U.S. tariffs as their impact reverberates through Canada’s manufacturing supply chain, industry experts say.

Stelco Holdings Inc. on Monday said it was laying off up to 500 workers at its Hamilton and Lake Erie facilities, with the company citing the ongoing trade crisis, weak demand and continued import pressure.

The job cuts are the latest in a string of tariff-linked layoffs in the province and come after plans for more than 1,000 job cuts at Algoma Steel in Sault Ste. Marie and the closure of ArcelorMittal’s Hamilton wire-drawing mill.

Alan Arcand, chief economist at Canadian Manufacturers and Exporters, said the decline in Canadian steel demand reflects the way tariffs are working their way through highly integrated manufacturing supply chains.

Companies that use steel are losing U.S. sales and cutting production, which in turn reduces the amount of steel they buy from Canadian producers, he said.

“Supply chains have been optimized on the assumption that we would have free trade with the U.S. and you yank that away suddenly without warning and these are the consequences,” Arcand said.

“You have impacts within the firm being directly hit by the tariff and the firms within the broader supply chain.”

Stelco called the layoffs “unfortunate but necessary” to ensure its survival, noting U.S. tariffs have significantly shrunk the market for its cold-rolled and galvanized products.

The end users for those products can include automotive and parts manufacturers, machinery and fabricated metal producers, appliance makers, and construction and electrical equipment manufacturers.

Those manufacturers are facing U.S. tariffs of up to 50 per cent on steel-intensive and derivative products, while automakers face separate trade barriers, weighing on exports and production.

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, which represents workers at Stelco’s Hamilton plant, said the union is disappointed in the situation and wants the ongoing tariff issues settled.

“We’re hoping this trade situation resolves itself so our members can get back to work,” he said.

Wells said Lourenco Goncalves, the chief executive of U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs, which acquired Stelco in 2024, said on a recent earnings call that coated steel prices in Canada are significantly lower than in the United States.

“He’s blaming this on Canada not tariffing steel being imported into Canada, which drives down the price,” Wells said of Goncalves’ comments. “They’re claiming they can’t make any money selling coated products.”

Arcand said there is “significant overproduction” of steel globally.

“There’s a lot more steel being produced than consumed,” he said. “It’s mainly a China story and that’s been a long-running issue.”

Arcand said that while the government has responded with anti-dumping duties and other measures, it needs to keep monitoring steel import volumes and adjust its policies as needed.

Meanwhile, Brendan Sweeney with the Pacific Manufacturing Association of Canada said Honda and Toyota are still producing at steady levels in Canada and continue to buy significant volumes of Canadian steel, suggesting the weakness in Stelco’s domestic demand may be coming from other manufacturers or different parts of the auto sector.

“Production is not down,” said Sweeney, president and chief executive of the trade association, which was launched by the two major Japanese automakers last April. “Production is pretty stable despite the tariffs.”

He said Honda and Toyota are among the top consumers of Canadian-made steel from southern Ontario and “it’s important for us to have steel mills around.”

Sweeney added: “We don’t see an immediate impact on our operations as the result of this (Stelco) announcement … I don’t know what the lasting effects are going to be.”

Stelco called the layoffs “unfortunate but necessary” to ensure its survival, noting U.S. tariffs have significantly shrunk the market for its cold-rolled and galvanized products.
The end users for those products can include automotive and parts manufacturers, machinery and fabricated metal producers, appliance makers, and construction and electrical equipment manufacturers.
Those manufacturers are facing U.S. tariffs of up to 50 per cent on steel-intensive and derivative products, while automakers face separate trade barriers, weighing on exports and production.

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, which represents workers at Stelco’s Hamilton plant, said the union is disappointed in the situation and wants the ongoing tariff issues settled.
“We’re hoping this trade situation resolves itself so our members can get back to work,” he said.

Wells said Lourenco Goncalves, the chief executive of U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs, which acquired Stelco in 2024, said on a recent earnings call that coated steel prices in Canada are significantly lower than in the United States.

“He’s blaming this on Canada not tariffing steel being imported into Canada, which drives down the price,” Wells said of Goncalves’ comments. “They’re claiming they can’t make any money selling coated products.”
Arcand said there is “significant overproduction” of steel globally.
“There’s a lot more steel being produced than consumed,” he said. “It’s mainly a China story and that’s been a long-running issue.”
Arcand said that while the government has responded with anti-dumping duties and other measures, it needs to keep monitoring steel import volumes and adjust its policies as needed.

Meanwhile, Brendan Sweeney with the Pacific Manufacturing Association of Canada said Honda and Toyota are still producing at steady levels in Canada and continue to buy significant volumes of Canadian steel, suggesting the weakness in Stelco’s domestic demand may be coming from other manufacturers or different parts of the auto sector.

“Production is not down,” said Sweeney, president and chief executive of the trade association, which was launched by the two major Japanese automakers last April. “Production is pretty stable despite the tariffs.”
He said Honda and Toyota are among the top consumers of Canadian-made steel from southern Ontario and “it’s important for us to have steel mills around.”
Sweeney added: “We don’t see an immediate impact on our operations as the result of this (Stelco) announcement … I don’t know what the lasting effects are going to be.”

stories.title: Carney announces $1.2B for ocean conservation ahead of pipeline decision
stories.summary: Ottawa faces a Thursday deadline to decide whether to designate a proposed pipeline from Alberta to the southern B.C. coast as a project of national interest.
stories.author: Breanna Owen
stories.content:
By Breanna Owen The Canadian Press

Posted September 29, 2026 5:41 pm

Prime Minister Mark Carney says the government is making a new $1.2 billion investment in ocean conservation as the country inches toward a decision on a new West Coast pipeline.

Speaking in Vancouver today, Carney said the funds will go to several new measures, including an expansion of the Canadian Coast Guard’s capacity to monitor marine traffic and a national marine mammal oil spill response plan.

Ottawa faces a Thursday deadline to decide whether to designate a proposed pipeline from Alberta to the southern B.C. coast as a project of national interest.

Albertans will also head to the polls in a matter of weeks to vote in a referendum on separating from Canada.

Carney said that as more ships enter the Port of Vancouver, the government must bolster systems for protecting marine life.

Earlier in the day, LNG Canada said it will proceed with a Phase 2 expansion of its facility in Kitimat, B.C., a project that would double its capacity.

stories.title: Jury watches victim’s final moments before fatal shooting in east London
stories.summary: As the Crown’s case got underway at the second degree murder trial of Zachary McDermott on Tuesday two Agreed Statement of Facts were read to the jury.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
As the Crown’s case got underway at the second degree murder trial of Zachary McDermott on Tuesday two Agreed Statement of Facts were read to the jury.

In one it stated, “On Sept. 12, 2018 Zachary McDermott fatally shot Christopher Clements-Card in the parking lot of Tim Hortons at 2094 Dundas Street... it is admitted that the accused before the court shot the deceased.”

After that the Crown proceeded to show surveillance camera footage from various nearby locations.

London police Det.-Sgt. Jon Pain testified that in one you can see the accused pull up to where Clements-Card’s girlfriend lives off of Bonaventure Drive in East London.

Then minutes later the victim is seen showing up to the same location and he is seen to be visibly upset with the woman, with the officer saying, “You see Mr. Clements-Card smashing something to the ground...it did not seem positive.”

Then cameras track Clements-Card, 21, leaving the area and going to a nearby coffee shop with his brother. Moments later a car identified as the same Silver Chevy driven by McDermott, 26, pulls up and goes towards the victim. Within seconds the car is seen taking off down Dundas Street.

Emergency crew rush to the scene and Clements-Card is taken to hospital where he would be pronounced dead after suffering two gunshot wounds to the back.

McDermott who was 18 years old at the time would be arrested days later on Sept. 21, 2018 and he has plead not guilty to second degree murder.

The trial and the Crown’s case resumes on Thursday.

stories.title: Cleveland-Cliffs could face legal action for layoffs at Stelco
stories.summary: Job cuts fall afoul of pledges made when U.S. company acquired Canadian steelmaker, union says
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
U.S. steel maker Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CLF-N could face legal action from Ottawa for violating job commitments stemming from its 2024 acquisition of Stelco Holdings Inc. after announcing hundreds of layoffs in Canada on Monday, but the devil will be in the details, a legal expert told The Globe and Mail.

In 2024, the Cleveland-based company announced its intentions to buy Stelco for $3.4-billion. The federal government approved the transaction, but only after imposing a series of legally-binding conditions on Cliffs.

Those included Cliffs promising to maintain for five years at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees.

Cliffs on Monday said it was laying off a total of up to 500 workers at Stelco’s Hamilton plant and its Lake Erie Works operation in Nanticoke, Ont. The company said the layoffs were necessary to ensure the company’s survival during the trade war with the United States.

Some of the workers affected by the layoffs will be offered jobs at Lake Erie Works, but the number won’t be nearly enough to fill the void left by the cuts.

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, said that there are only 46 openings at Nanticoke and he is now pushing for Ottawa to hold Cliffs to its promise to maintain employment levels.

“We’re hopeful that the Canadian government enforces the Investment Canada Act,” he said. That act stipulates that major investments into Canada by foreign companies should benefit the domestic economy.

The Globe asked the office of Industry Minister Mélanie Joly whether the government considers Cliffs to be in violation of its commitments, and whether it is intending to sue the steel maker.

“Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs have made significant commitments to Canadian steelworkers,” Gabrielle Landry, deputy director, media relations with the office of Ms. Joly wrote in an e-mail.

“We will use every lever possible to defend Canadian industry, protect jobs, and secure our supply chain.”

Cliffs did not respond to a request for comment.

Subrata Bhattacharjee, national chair of the competition and foreign investment review group with Borden Ladner Gervais LLP, said that without knowing the details of the legal agreement between the company and Ottawa it is impossible to know with certainty whether Cliffs is offside.

“Until you actually see the agreement, you can’t really say for sure,” he said.

At the very least, however, he believes Ms. Joly will be having a conversation with the company around the promises it made in the agreement.

“Cleveland Cliffs will likely be trying to explain how the tariff situation is out of its control, and that it will need either some other deal, or have to be released from the undertaking, and then we’ll see what happens,” Mr. Bhattacharjee said.

“The process now includes the opportunity to renegotiate or mediate another solution, and I suspect that in the current environment, it’s quite likely the government May try to seek some other type of assurance.”

There is precedent for the government to act and it revolves around the same Canadian steel maker. After U.S. Steel acquired Stelco in 2007, it made commitments under the Investment Canada Act around jobs and production levels. After the financial crisis hit in 2008, U.S. Steel laid off workers in Canada. The federal government later sued the company for allegedly reneging on its legally-binding commitments. A settlement was reached in 2011 with U.S. Steel agreeing to a new set of commitments , including around production levels and investment in Canada.

Canada’s steel sector has been throttled by 50-per-cent tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump last year. The federal and provincial governments have rolled out multiple initiatives to help the industry, including providing hundreds of millions of dollars in funding, cracking down on the dumping of foreign steel into Canada and mandating that publicly funded projects use Canadian steel wherever possible.

Ms. Landry said that financial aid has been offered by Ottawa to Stelco to keep its operations going during the trade war in order to maintain employment levels, but it was turned down.

“For some time, o ur government has made clear to the company that we are ready and willing to provide financial support to sustain operations and protect jobs,” she said.

“Its decision to reject these practical proposals and continue with layoffs is extremely disappointing.”

By News Staff

Posted September 29, 2026 5:32 pm.

Winnipeggers will see some service changes and opportunities to take part in reconciliation events as the city marks the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Wednesday, Sept. 30.

Southern Chiefs Organization Healing Walk & Pow Wow

An opening ceremony will take place at Oodena Circle for the 6th annual Southern Chiefs Organization Healing Walk & Pow Wow on Wednesday.

Following the ceremony, a Healing Walk to Canada Life Centre will take place.

Several streets (which are listed below) will be closed between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m.

Westbound Forks Market Road from Israel Asper Way to the Forks

Northbound Israel Asper Way from Forks Market Road to York Avenue

Westbound York Avenue from Israel Asper Way to Main Street

Southbound Main Street between York Avenue and Portage Avenue

Eastbound Portage Avenue from Main Street to Hargrave Street

Hargrave Street from St Mary Avenue to Portage Avenue

Additionally, northbound Main Street between York Avenue and Portage Avenue will close for periods of time.

Other events

The Forks

Assiniboine Park and Zoo – Sacred Fire

Winnipeg Art Gallery-Quamajuq

Canadian Museum for Human Rights

Manitoba Museum

stories.title: Canada’s military seeking anti-drone defences for bases, facilities
stories.summary: The Department of National Defence says they need anti-drone defences to protect personnel, equipment and facilities across Canada.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
The Department of National Defence (DND) is looking to purchase anti-drone defences for military installations within Canada, federal procurement documents show.

In a short notice posted online Monday, DND said they need a system that can defend personnel, equipment and facilities from drone attacks at locations across Canada. The details of what DND is looking to buy — including what threats the system is meant to defend against — is only being made available to qualified suppliers.

DND did not respond to Global News’ request for information Monday or Tuesday.

The Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) has spent years and hundreds of millions of dollars bolstering its drone defences for personnel deployed as part of Operation Reassurance in Latvia — part of Nato’s efforts to bolster its eastern flank as Russia continues its invasion of Ukraine.

The deployment in Latvia has offered a front-row seat to Canadian and allied forces for the evolution of drone warfare tactics since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022.

Canadian military installations at home, though, are far from the threat of direct combat with advanced drone warfare technology — but that doesn’t mean there is no threat, experts say.

Stephanie Carvin, a professor at the Norman Paterson School of International Relations and former intelligence analyst, said the CAF is likely more concerned about hostile powers hiring help within Canada.

Carvin pointed to the recent spate of hired gunman in Canada, allegedly working under the direction of nation states or their proxies.

“It’s very, very hard to sneak operatives across borders. So the model really is just to find people on social media and convince them to engage in this. And it is becoming a major focus of not just the CAF, but the RCMP (which) has a counter-drone unit,” Carvin said in an interview.

“Obviously (the RCMP are) worried about drugs, but I also think they’re worried about public events and policing.”

Carvin noted that Canada already has deployed counter-drone systems to protect critical infrastructure, such as nuclear power plants.

“I would say that the use of counter-drone technology around critical infrastructure is becoming the norm,” Carvin said.

The CAF previously budgeted between $100 million and $249 million for a vehicle-mounted anti-drone system to be used by soldiers deployed in Latvia. That system includes detectors and jammers for radio frequencies and global navigation systems used in drone targeting.

Separately, the federal government launched the Defence Drone Initiative in July 2026 to scale Canada’s ability to produce low-cost uncrewed and autonomous systems at home.

“Recent conflicts have shown that drone technology evolves rapidly,” a statement announcing the initiative read.

“The DDI will help build a more responsive and scalable Canadian ecosystem and it reflects the Government of Canada’s commitment to provide the CAF and (Canadian Coast Guard) with access to Canadian-developed technologies that enhance operational readiness while supporting Canadian innovation, skilled jobs and long-term economic growth.”

The DDI program is intended to study both drone combat systems — including the ability to launch long-range precision strikes — as well as drone interceptor systems meant to defend against hostile uncrewed vehicles.

stories.title: Carney announces $1.2 billion for oceans ahead of expected pipeline decision
stories.summary: Vancouver - Prime Minister Mark Carney says the government is making a new $1.2 billion investment in ocean conservation as the country inches toward a decision on a new West Coast pipeline.
stories.author: Brenna Owen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Prime Minister Mark Carney announced $1.2 billion in federal funding for ocean protections Tuesday as the country moves toward decisions on a new pipeline to the West Coast and the expansion of a major port in Metro Vancouver.

The major projects would mean “more ships on the water and more pressure on the habitats that we are all working to protect,” Carney said.

“So we must scale up our systems to protect marine life in the event that something goes wrong,” he said.

The funds have been earmarked for several new measures, including expanding the Canadian Coast Guard’s capacity to monitor marine traffic, a national near-shore weather forecasting system and a marine mammal oil spill response plan.

Carney said the work will also involve upgrading search and rescue stations and improving seabed mapping and fisheries conservation efforts.

The announcement in North Vancouver, B.C., came ahead of a Thursday deadline for Ottawa to decide whether to designate a proposed pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia’s south coast as a project of national interest.

“This project would diversify our economy, create almost 150,000 new jobs right across Canada, and make us much less dependent on the United States,” Carney said.

“But we know it’s not just what we build, it’s how we build. And this government is taking a protect-while-we-build approach to new investments.”

Carney said the proposed pipeline would avoid “highly sensitive areas” and its route would be similar to the existing Trans Mountain pipeline, while the tanker ban along B.C.‘s north coast will remain in effect.

Albertans head to the polls in a matter of weeks to vote in a referendum on separating from Canada.

Earlier in the day, LNG Canada confirmed it will proceed with a Phase 2 expansion of its facility in Kitimat, B.C., a project that would double its capacity.

Carney has also previously backed the proposed expansion of the Port of Vancouver’s Roberts Bank terminal, telling reporters during a visit to the facility in July that his government was looking to provide about $10 billion for the project, part of Ottawa’s effort to “grow our exports away from the United States.”

As more ships call at the Port of Vancouver, he said the government must bolster measures for protecting the ocean and marine life, including the endangered southern resident killer whales that depend on waters off B.C.‘s south coast.

Carney highlighted plans to address underwater noise that affects whales, saying Ottawa is providing $100 million to build long-term capacity to monitor, assess and mitigate the noise along all three coasts, Pacific, Atlantic and Arctic.

In waters off Vancouver, he said Ottawa was setting a goal to hold underwater noise to 2023 levels, even as vessel traffic increases.

There will be “rigorous conditions” around construction, he said.

“To put it simply, if a killer whale gets too close to the site, work must stop,” Carney said of the proposed Roberts Bank expansion.

The terminal is located near the mouth of the Fraser River in Delta, B.C., and Carney said there will be funding for Indigenous-led stewardship and restoration in the Lower Fraser River Estuary.

Another $90 million will be used to boost front-line fisheries enforcement and equip fisheries officers with modernized tools, including drones, Carney said.

The new funding also includes $186 million for the Northern Shelf Bioregion Reconciliation Framework Agreement to advance what Carney’s office described as collaborative governance, conservation, waterway management, emergency preparedness and cumulative effects work in the Great Bear Sea region.

Coastal First Nations welcomed the funding, with the group’s president, Samuel Schooner, saying it marked a step toward advancing collaborative efforts to prepare for the expected surge in vessel traffic that would stem from major projects.

“This brings increased risks of accidents as well as impacts on sensitive coastal ecosystems,” Schooner said in a statement. “Our communities have consistently advocated for investments in safe and responsible shipping to keep pace with increased economic development.”

The Wilderness Committee, meanwhile, said $1.2 billion for oceans protection was “pennies” compared with Ottawa’s $10-billion contribution to the proposed Roberts Bank expansion, while the federal government’s newly proposed bill C-39, aimed at strengthening the economy, undermines protections for species at risk.

stories.title: Former Montreal synagogue lead rabbi Leigh Lerner advocated for ‘radical inclusivity’
stories.summary: He performed a groundbreaking interfaith wedding in Minnesota in the 1970s and continued that practice in Montreal, where he also presided over same-sex civil unions and later same-sex marriages
stories.author: Lisa Fitterman
stories.content:
Rabbi Leigh Lerner’s catchphrase was “Go do it,” no matter if the goal was to start a food bank, combat human trafficking, fight for Lgbtq rights or overcome opposition to interfaith marriage. As a university student in the United States in the mid-1960s, he was steeped in the tradition of social justice advocacy, with a finely honed sense of right and wrong and the quiet determination to get things done, even if others disagreed with him.

As the long-time lead rabbi of the reform Temple Emanu-El-Beth-Sholom in Westmount, Que. (upon his retirement in 2012, he became the synagogue’s “Rabbi Emeritus”), he saw the job as something that was rooted in tradition but needed to change to respond to the times. Like the Talmudic scholars of yore, he believed that issues needed to be discussed openly, not only within the confines of the Jewish community, and that faith should encompass everyone who wanted to participate, even in the most peripheral of ways.

In 1977, when Mr. Lerner was the senior rabbi at the Mount Zion Temple in St. Paul, Minn., he officiated over what the state’s historical society calls the first interfaith wedding in any Minnesota house of worship. He continued that practice in Montreal, where he also regularly presided over same-sex civil unions and then same-sex marriages when they became legal.

“If you spend 23 years leading one congregation and over 50 years in the rabbinate, like Leigh did, you don’t do it well without perseverance and a commitment to who you are and what you do,” said Rabbi Lisa Grushcow, his successor at Temple Emanu-El-Beth-Sholom. “He left a strong and healthy community in a city where we are the only Reform congregation with all the unique pressures that entails. And he did it by bringing us to the table with a radical inclusivity.”

Mr. Lerner died in Las Vegas on Sept. 5 from complications due to a stroke. He was 81 years old, a tall, lean, polyvalent man who learned French when he moved to Montreal in 1989 in order to better understand the city at large, and who was given to striding the streets in a deerstalker hat, his hands folded behind his back.

His friend, Rabbi Bob Alper, with whom he studied at Hebrew Union College in Cincinnati, said their relationship really began a few years after they had both graduated. That was when Mr. Lerner returned class notes he had borrowed from Mr. Alper in their final year.

“I had asked for the notes to be returned but Leigh insisted he had no idea what I was talking about,” Mr. Alper recalled. “Then, as he was going through old boxes in St. Paul, he found them, sent them to me with an apologetic note.

“That was a spark for me. He was a man of quality and modesty, with great strength of character.”

It demonstrated what his friend was so good at, Mr. Alper continued: creating sparks of kindness and understanding day by day, year by year, that represented the highest form of Judaism.

For 22 years, Mr. Lerner marched in Montreal pride parades, while he was a member of the advisory council of the now-defunct Across Boundaries Multifaith Institute in Montreal, a past president of the Montreal Christian Jewish Dialogue and a supporter of the Montreal Muslim Jewish Dialogue. He was wont to say that it was through such dialogues that people learned of the diversity that thrives on the other side of the table.

“Is inter-religious dialogue realistic? Is it practical? Yes, and it is very necessary,” he once said during a panel discussion in November 2003. “It is remarkable for me to see how people who have been in dialogue for some time are discovering that others are coming to them and saying, ‘Can we get in on it?’

“They realize that there is a gap, there is something missing in the quality of our understanding of one another, and that only dialogue is a viable and safe way for people of different faiths to understand each other.”

At a time when anti-Semitism is on the rise, including a firebombing of the Temple Emanu-El-Beth Sholom earlier this year, Mr. Alper said that his friend’s message is more important than ever.

“As grief-stricken we all are, as upset, angry at what the world has come to, Leigh would have been consoling and strengthening people where he could, encouraging people to be strong,” he noted.

Leigh Lerner was born in a military hospital in Fort Snelling, Minn., ON March 3, 1945, the first of David and Edith Lerner’s two children. At the time, his father was overseas with the army in the final months of the Second World War; when he came back, he worked as a car salesman. The family lived in St. Louis Park, a suburban community just west of Minneapolis before moving to Atlanta for about a decade, then to Chicago. Perhaps because of the moves, Leigh and his little sister, Trudie, were close; when they fought, as siblings will do, it was always the brother who would approach his sister later, hand outstretched and asking for them to be friends again.

Neither parent wanted their son to enter the rabbinate. Indeed, his mom pushed for him to become a doctor. Wanting to please her, he took premed classes at Duke University in Durham, N.C., but was drawn more to English and writing, eventually getting his undergraduate degree in English literature.

While he was at Duke, his mother became gravely ill. As she lay dying, she gave her son her blessing to become a rabbi. In 1972, he was ordained by the Hebrew Union College-Jewish Institute of Religion in Cincinnati and embarked on a career that would take him from St. Paul to Montreal and, upon his official retirement, to minister to congregations during stints in Italy, for which he learned Italian. As much as he loved Montreal, he was happy to leave snow and ice storms behind, so he established a new home in Las Vegas.

Among the highlights was a trip he took with Mr. Alper in 1983 to Moscow and Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg) to meet with Soviet refuseniks, the term for Jewish citizens who were denied visas to emigrate.

“It was one week of an amazing, dangerous, scary, spiritually uplifting experience, the most important week of my life as a Jew,” said Mr. Alper. “We met in the Frankfurt Airport, where we walked around and around, coding our notes, memorizing them, then throwing them out because we knew the last thing the KGB wanted was for nosy American rabbis encouraging dissidents.

“I have this memory of Leigh standing tall and straight in Moscow next to a woman we’d hired as our tour guide for a day, laughing delightedly when I told them to smile and say ‘visa’,” he continued. “His smile was just one of the innumerable sparks he lit that will continue to light our way into the future.”

Mr. Lerner was awarded the Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee Medal in 2012 for his contributions to the community and to Canada. He leaves his wife, Loren Lerner; his sister, Trudie Lerner; a half-brother, Terry Brashem; his daughters, Meredith Bloom and Sasha Lerner; his stepsons, Sam and Daniel Singer; and four grandchildren.

stories.title: Rush frontman Geddy Lee endorses Brad Bradford for Toronto mayor
stories.summary: Lee says he fears for future of city with current leadership
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
Canadian rockstar Geddy Lee has endorsed candidate Brad Bradford for Toronto mayor. The frontman for the legendary band Rush posted his approval for the centre-right municipal politician on Instagram.

“I was born in Toronto and have built a life with my family here,” Lee wrote in his post on Monday. “It was always a place I’ve been proud to call home. But it’s changing, and not for the better. I’m not one to make public statements about politicians, but I truly fear for the future of Toronto with its current leadership, and believe that Brad has energy, fresh ideas and really cares about ALL of this city’s communities.”

Holding his Norwich terrier Dottie Wasserman, the Working Man singer posed with Bradford, who lost to Olivia Chow in 2023, coming in eighth place. He is thought to be Chow’s strongest challenger in the municipal election set for Oct. 26.

Lee, the 73-year-old son of Jewish Holocaust survivors from Poland, grew up in the suburban Willowdale area of Toronto. He once had a home in the Upper Beaches neighbourhood, which Bradford has represented on Toronto City Council since 2018.

Rush is currently on a wildly successful international tour after being inactive since 2015. Lee and guitarist Alex Lifeson, along with two touring musicians, sold out four concerts at Toronto’s Scotiabank Arena in August.

Though Rush is not known to be a political band, the lyrics penned by the late drummer Neil Peart were influenced by Russian-born American author and philosopher Ayn Rand. Singer-bassist Lee wrote in his 2023 memoir My Effin’ Life that it was in Rand’s The Fountainhead that he found “moral reinforcement” in the band’s early struggles with its management and record label.

“In the novel her protagonist Howard Roark stands up defiantly for the rights of the individual, and passionately against the concept of artistic compromise,” Lee wrote in his book.

Lee has endorsed Bradford at a time when Canadian musicians are increasingly flexing their political muscles. Two days before Canada Day, B.C.-based Bryan Adams released the single 51st State , a rocking protest song directed at U.S. President Donald Trump: “So let me give you some advice, mister. You might have too much on your plate. Go and load us up with tariffs, but we’ll never be the 51st state.”

In April, 2025, Toronto-born Neil Young, who has a summer residence in Ontario, implored Prime Minister Mark Carney to fight what he described as a threat to Canada’s “very existence” from the United States.

“They want our resources, they want our land, they want our fisheries, they want our water, they want our Arctic, maybe they want our souls,” the Rockin’ in the Free World musician wrote in an open letter on his news site, NYA Times-Contrarian.

Editor’s note: This story has been updated to state that Neil Young endorsed Mark Carney in April, 2025, not 2026 as previously published.

stories.title: 'Not in the public interest': Liberals won't try to recoup $34 million paid by 'green slush fund' to ineligible projects
stories.summary: The Liberals says they will not try to recover any of the $34 million in ineligible funding paid out by the so-called "green slush fund".
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Liberal government says it will not try to recover any of the at least $34 million in ineligible funding paid out by the so-called “green slush fund,” saying such efforts would not be in the public interest.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly quietly made the revelation in a response tabled last week to questions by Conservative MP Luc Berthold on the now defunct Sustainable Development Technology Canada (Sdtc).

Sdtc was a scandal-plagued cleantech fund derogatively referred to as the “green slush fund” by Conservative MP. It was dissolved in 2024 by then industry minister François-Philippe Champagne after a scathing report by the Auditor General on the organization.

In the response, Joly said roughly $34 million was paid out by Sdtc to ineligible recipients who applied and performed “in good faith.”

“Therefore, as a matter of fairness and sound stewardship of public funds, it was determined that further pursuit of recoveries was not likely to be successful, and not in the public interest,” reads the document.

In a statement, Berthold and colleague Aaron Gunn lambasted the decision, which they said flies in the face of the will of MPs of all political stripes. In 2024, the Commons Public Accounts committee unanimously expressed “extreme concern with the blatant disregard of taxpayer funds” called on the government to recoup them.

Furthermore, she found 90 cases where an Sdtc board member participated and voted in a discussion about a contract despite being in a conflict of interest.

Government still redacting, withholding 'green slush fund' docs despite Speaker ruling it shouldn't

Former chair of Liberals' 'green slush fund' found to have 'improperly furthered' business interests

Hogan also found the organization had serious governance issues.

“It’s not always clear that funding decisions made on behalf of Canadian taxpayers were appropriate and justified,” she wrote of Sdtc.

At the time, Sdtc leadership only partially agreed with some of the key findings in Hogan’s report. It disagreed with some of her findings on funded project eligibility.

The report not only led to the dissolution of Sdtc (whose activities were folded into the National Research Council), it also sparked multiple parliamentary committee studies, a call by Conservatives for an RCMP investigation and a months-long logjam in the House of Commons over access to documents.

Joly’s response tabled last week sheds new light on what happened to Sdtc after Hogan’s report.

It reveals that Sdtc decided to conduct its own review of 158 projects it funded, including those audited by Hogan. The review included “three independent third-parties,” which are not identified.

Despite reviewing three times more projects than Hogan, the foundation concluded that only five (compared to Hogan’s 10) were ineligible for the funding they received.

Those projects received $34 million in total funding from Sdtc since 2017. The document does not identify them and a spokesperson for Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada declined to do so.

Joly’s response said the review found the five funding recipients negotiated and performed “in good faith,” suggesting blame for the error lied entirely with Sdtc.

In a statement, Ised spokesperson Alison Reilander explained that a new Sdtc board appointed after Hogan’s audit launched an “enhanced process” to re-evaluate funding recipients’ eligibility. She also noted that the auditor general’s office “did not examine the technological merits of the projects.”

“The enhanced review included a detailed reassessment of all the projects, supported by independent third-party reviewers,” said Reilander.

“As a result of the enhanced review process, five projects were determined to be ineligible for funding under the terms of Sdtc’s contribution agreement with the Crown and one project was found to have been awarded funding to support certain ineligible costs.”

In a separate statement, Hogan’s office declined to comment on the results of Sdtc’s eligibility review.

“To maintain our independence, we do not comment on the government’s policy decisions or provide opinions or assessments on matters beyond the information contained in our published audit reports,” wrote spokesperson Jayita Phulsunge.

stories.title: Goderich family paying it forward with “Fun-dation” in memory of son
stories.summary: Ken Costello will never forget how Goderich and area supported him and his family, while their son Hunter was fighting leukemia.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Ken Costello will never forget how Goderich and area supported him and his family while their son Hunter was fighting leukemia.

“The community was huge for us. The amount of support they did, the amount of fundraisers that were done for us. It was a big inspiration for why we started what we do. We wanted to pay it forward and, you know, start the charity and give back to the community that gave to us,” said Ken Costello, Hunter’s father.

Sadly, Hunter died in 2016. A year later, his family started the Hunter Costello Memorial Fun-dation, to help Huron County families with expenses around ill or special needs children.

“Whether it’s they have a hospital stay, or even if it’s just stuff at home, that we’ve helped out with. Chairlifts and, special beds and stuff like that, just to make life easier for kids with special needs,” said Ken.

Since 2017, the Hunter Costello Memorial Fun-dation has given $110,000 to more than 25 families, to help them during their darkest days.

“We’ll tell a family, all you need to do is give us your email address. That’s it. And then we’ll send you an e-transfer. And if you need more help, you have our contact information and get a hold of us. So, it’s been for me, almost therapeutic to be part of,” said Joe Hallam, family friend, and Hunter Costello Fun-dation board member.

One of those families the Fun-dation helped was Roo Fox’s. A couple of years ago, Fox’s family needed help after she went blind during pregnancy, her son was very premature and had trouble breathing, and her husband was laid off, all at the same time.

“We wouldn’t really have been able to do it, if we didn’t have that foundation supporting us, not only just financially, but, you know, as a community. Like, we’re here for you. We see you. You’re not alone. So, that that was really nice. And I’m sure other families feel the same way too,” said Fox.

“The community helped us. It feels good to help others that need it, and they appreciate it. And we appreciate the fact that they appreciate it,” said Ken.

The Fun-dation is holding a wrestling fundraiser Oct. 17 in Goderich to raise funds to help more Huron County families, as well as improve the playground bearing Hunter’s name.

“We always want to keep helping families. That’s the number one goal. But, the next goal is to improve upon this wonderful playground behind me. We’re looking at getting some rubber matting put on it. Maybe a pavilion nearby, all sorts of other stuff,” said Ken.

“For the fundraiser, if you can afford to put some money in the bin, that’d be great. We can give that to a family in need, and if you can’t, then just enjoy the show and have some fun,” said Hallam.

stories.title: All in the classroom: how artificial intelligence is changing education
stories.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI), is changing the way students approach schoolwork, with some using it regularly, ...
stories.author: Torey Joseph Legarrie
stories.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the way students approach schoolwork, with some using it regularly, while others refuse to use it.

Jada Kaasti, London Christian High student, said that AI has changed how she completes assignments, and that teachers are vague on telling the rules of AI use.

“It makes it so much easier. Now it feels like there’s less effort I have to put into it. It’s not as hard to keep my grades up,” she said.

“Sometimes, but not always. Usually it’s vague,” she said.

The growing use of AI is making professors rethink how they create and grade assignments, while raising questions about its potential impact on student learning and critical-thinking skills.

Jeff Miles, associate dean, school of arts and language at Fanshawe College said that it’s trickier now.

“So for example, a lot of our online courses used to be essay-based. So students would write their essay and then put them in a submissions folder. That’s a little bit trickier now because we can’t be certain who actually did the work,” he said.

“It’s created a lot of difficulty in students submitting essays because we’re not sure if they’ve actually done the work or not, or if it’s just the writing has been done by ChatGPT,” he said.

“There’s AI detectors out there, of course. But the AI detectors are not very reliable. So sometimes professors will use a high AI detection score,” he said.

He said the rules are clear if you are allowed or not allowed to use AI.

“Absolutely. So one of the college requirements is that we need to indicate on assignments what level of AI is acceptable,” he said.

In 2026, 57 per cent of U.S. students aged 13 to 17 reported using AI to search for information, according to [programs].

AI use is rising. For example, 19.2 per cent of Canadian businesses reported the use of AI to produce goods and deliver services in 2026 according to [Government of Canada].

Fanshawe College student Josh Dinkel said that he will never use AI because it is prone to be inaccurate, and can provide false information.

“AI is prone to many mistakes and hallucinates a bunch of random things that don’t happen, and it brings up random sources that don’t involve the thing that you May look up,” he said.

Dinkel said that students who do use AI don’t have an advantage.

“No, not really, because it could mess something up and it could bring their grades down. Or they could get something wrong and put it down,” he said.

Dr. David Bourget, associate professor of philosophy and Matcha developer at Western University said that using AI negatively affects students’ learning.

“It obviously can affect their learning negatively if they don’t learn, because they’re doing everything with AI, which you know, when measures are not taken, that can happen,” he said.

Bourget said advances in AI have begun affecting some entry-level jobs, but universities and colleges are on top of it.

“AI can do a lot of what people do in their desk jobs, and that creates a situation where effectively entry level jobs are not needed anymore. AI right now can replace entry level programmers very well. For example, that’s probably the field that’s the most affected at this time,” he said.

“Right now universities and colleges are geared towards training people for the entry level positions for those positions are disappearing, so they need to start aiming higher. They need to provide more training,” he said.

He said that he predicts that the future with AI will be not only be more strict on the rules for using it, but students will also be prepared on how they can use it.

“I think probably we’re gonna be systematically, holding back AI in some ways. But also, of course, trying to prepare students to use it in other ways,” he said.

stories.title: Canada’s peacekeeping myth ‘needs to fade away,’ retired general writes in memoir
stories.summary: Canada's former top soldier says the country's "persistent myth" about being a nation of peacekeepers hasn't kept up with a changing world and it "needs to fade away."
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

Posted September 29, 2026 4:10 pm.

Last Updated September 29, 2026 9:14 pm.

Ottawa — Canada’s former top soldier says the country’s “persistent myth” about being a nation of peacekeepers hasn’t kept up with a changing world and it “needs to fade away.”

In a new memoir, retired general Wayne Eyre says traditional, UN-style peacekeeping is not only dead, it has been a ghost for decades. He says he knows because he was there when it died — at Medak Pocket in 1993.

Eyre details his experiences in peacekeeping in Croatia, Bosnia and Cyprus — along with his later time in Afghanistan and eventual rise to the top of the Canadian Armed Forces — in his book Into the Breach: A Soldier’s Journey, which comes out on Oct. 6.

In it, he describes in great detail his experiences in the Battle of Medak Pocket in the former Yugoslavia, where he was deployed as a captain in the 2nd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry. He calls it a “turning point that saw the death of traditional UN peacekeeping.”

Canadian Forces in the former Yugoslavia faced artillery and heavy machine-gun fire in the neutral zone but ultimately drove back Croatian forces. In the book, Eyre describes his battalion pushing past a roadblock into the village of Lički Čitluk, where they found evidence of ethnic cleansing among the burning buildings.

A traditional peacekeeping operation deploys a minimally armed force to separate combatants and act as a buffer. Eyre writes that multiple sides in the former Yugoslavia made targets of the under-resourced peacekeepers and the mission failed to prevent a brutal escalation of the violence.

“The only thing that the belligerents respected was force,” Eyre said in an interview with The Canadian Press, adding the wider United Nations Protection Force mission was unable to provide enough of that force.

He said peacekeeping was “an era for the Canadian military” that lasted decades and ended in the early 1990s. Modern missions, he said, are set against a very different geopolitical backdrop.

“Take a look now at where most peacekeeping operations are — Africa, where there is an extreme local reluctance to have large Western forces on the ground there, for various historical reasons, to keep the peace,” he said. “And the utility of many of those missions are in question.”

Medak Pocket was a formative experience for Eyre and many of his colleagues. He writes about the overpowering smells of smoke and death hanging over the field and how, for many years afterward, he could not “smell a campfire without being taken back” to that moment.

His book, which runs to just over 400 pages, covers the ups and downs of his career, from the battlefield to top command.

Eyre said he felt the need to describe history as he saw it from his front-row seat.

“In the Canadian military, we don’t have a tradition of senior military officers or generals and admirals capturing history,” he said in the interview.

Eyre said as chief of the defence staff, he frequently fielded requests from politicians who didn’t always understand the potential impacts of their decisions — or how thinly spread the Canadian Armed Forces had become after decades of underfunding and the launch of the Russian deterrence mission in Latvia.

“I know I irritated some in government. I was told at one point I was being seen as obstructionist, but it’s the reality of what we had on the shelf,” he said.

Eyre said Canada’s future in a shifting international order depends on strong alliances and selectively deploying military power on very specific operations.

He called Latvia — where Canada leads a battalion on Nato’s eastern flank and has stationed 2,000 troops — the most “geopolitically significant deployment that Canada has undertaken since the end of the Cold War.”

Eyre’s own time and experiences in the military were shaped by major turning points, starting with the end of the Cold War and continuing through the 9/11 terror attacks and the start of the Afghanistan war. In Afghanistan, Eyre commanded Canada’s largest combat advisory mission up to that point.

Eyre stepped into the role of chief of the defence staff somewhat reluctantly just five years ago, when Admiral Art McDonald stepped aside in the face of a sexual misconduct allegation. The allegation did not lead to charges.

Eyre said he initially thought he would only be in the job for weeks as acting chief — and soon after considered resigning on principle.

He said he wondered whether cabinet had lost trust in him when then-deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland openly criticized his decision not to fire Navy commander Vice-Admiral Craig Baines amid a scandal.

“The lesson here is just the messiness of political-military relations,” he said, adding the book is not meant to be a political “tell-all.”

He said he felt he had the confidence of Prime Minister Justin Trudeau but it took “a while to develop” at a time when, thanks to the pandemic, meetings were all being conducted by video.

Eyre helmed the forces from 2021 to 2024, a tenure he writes was consumed by “crisis stacked upon crisis.”

On top of the series of sexual misconduct allegations against top brass that rocked the armed forces, Eyre’s time in the top job also coincided with a global pandemic, the evacuation of Canadians from Afghanistan in 2021, the start of the war Ukraine, the “Freedom Convoy” that occupied Ottawa, chaotic gang violence in Haiti and forest fires and floods at home.

He said he fielded nearly two dozen requests for international disaster response and upwards of 100 for help with managing the COVID-19 crisis, in addition to other domestic requests.

“My observation was all of these crises stacked upon each other was really limiting the bandwidth of our decision makers,” the retired general said in the interview.

“That’s where something like understanding and having clearly articulated national security interests and objectives can provide you guardrails so that when the pressure is on, when time is tight, you have something to help you make those decisions.”

He said that while he empathizes with elected officials, he struggled with the slow pace of government peacetime processes.

Eyre said in one instance, he worried he had he overstepped his authority by committing Canada to training Ukrainians in Latvia at a time when Ottawa was not giving him “decisions at the speed of war.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Little Debbie snacks make a comeback to Canada
stories.summary: Little Debbie snacks are back on Canadian shelves four years after leaving the Canadian market.
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
By Joseph Ryan

Posted September 29, 2026 3:53 pm.

Little Debbie snacks are back on Canadian shelves four years after leaving the Canadian market.

McKee Foods Corporation tells CityNews the popular sweet treats brand has returned across Canada in Loblaws banner stores.

“While McKee Foods is excited to bring our products back to Canada and plans to reintroduce additional varieties, we do not yet have specific details on which products will launch or when,” Mike Gloekler, McKee’s Corporate Communications & PR Manager wrote in an email.

The company says they reintroduced four family pack varieties including: Swiss Rolls, Honey Buns, Oatmeal Creme Piesike Gloekler and Cosmic Brownies.

Little Debbie snacks were off Canadian shelves since 2022, after their sole Canadian distributor cut ties with McKee Foods.

McKee Foods, owner of the Little Debbie brand, is an American company based in Tennessee.

stories.title: Canada not going to apologize to Trump amid trade war, LeBlanc says
stories.summary: Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc dismissed the idea that Canada would apologize to the U.S. in the coming weeks, as President Donald Trump stated.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc dismissed the idea that Canada could apologize to the U.S. in the coming weeks as the trade war stretches on, as President Donald Trump has said he expects.

Trump made the comments from the Oval Office on Monday while speaking to reporters after being asked how recent trade developments between Canada and the U.S. will end, and after multiple rounds of U.S. tariffs and Canada’s counter-tariff measures.

“They’re going to come in and they’re going to say, ‘sir we are sorry,'” Trump said in response.

“We’re not negotiating detailed text as we were five, six weeks ago, but we remain in contact with them,” said LeBlanc.

“If the prime minister concludes at some point that there’s a deal possible that protects the sovereignty of our country, that would be in the economic interests of the country, then obviously we would be in a position to have that conversation.”

“But for the moment, we’re focusing on what we can control in Canada.”

Earlier on Tuesday, Trump’s senior council for trade and manufacturing, Peter Navarro, said his message for Canadian lobbyists in the United States is: “get the h— out of our country!”

The comments were made at a conference appearance, when Navarro criticized Canada’s attempts to lobby in the Washington – an expression sometimes referred to as “K Street.”

“Canada, economically, is like a row boat. We’re an aircraft carrier, how’s that going to end? Any Canadians here? Please, if you’re on K Street, get the h— out of our country,” said Navarro.

stories.title: Halifax gets nearly $2M in federal funding to prevent gun, gang violence
stories.summary: The federal government has announced nearly $2 million in funding for the Halifax area to help prevent gun and gang violence in the community.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Mitchell Bailey
stories.content:
The federal government has announced nearly $2 million in funding for the Halifax area to help prevent gun and gang violence in the community.

“We’re giving them the tools to turn away from crime,” said Canada’s Minister of Public Safety Gary Anandasangaree in Dartmouth, N.S. Tuesday.

“This funding will support projects that address risk factors associated with gun and gang violence, specifically focusing on the underlying social conditions that lead young people to crime.”

The funds for Halifax Regional Municipality (HRM) will be delivered through the federal government’s Build Safer Communities Fund, which is part of a larger $157.5-million commitment nationwide over the next three years.

Halifax Mayor Andy Fillmore says these measures will strengthen community groups and hopefully steer vulnerable youth away from crime.

“The best public safety work often begins much earlier. It begins when a young person finds a mentor or a program that they can believe in, a place where they belong,” said Fillmore.

Since 2022, the municipality has received more than $3 million during the federal program’s first installment. The city’s public safety advisor, Amy Siciliano, says the new funding will help expand crisis de-escalation supports for youth in need.

“We’ve really been able to build our internal capacity to better support community organizations as well as our own facilities like recreation centres, library work, to work alongside community to improve the conditions that create those safer places for everyone,” said Siciliano.

As well, officials say the support will improve spaces for youth to connect with a mentor and help them receive educational and mental health resources.

Some ideas include programs specific to anti-trafficking and sexual exploitation.

“We would like to develop tools and training to educate young people around healthy relationships and things to look out for online,” said Sylvia Ofunne, a social policy strategist with the municipality.

The federal government says funding was issued based on the severity of crime in a community. HRM data shows there were nine homicides and 30 shootings in 2025.

With these additional supports, officials say they hope those figures will be reduced.

“(We) want to counter that with off-ramps that will enable young people to not fall into that trap of the criminal justice system,” said Anandasangaree.

stories.title: Museum marks Phyllis Lambert’s upcoming 100th birthday with a yearlong program
stories.summary: Montreal - Canadian architect and activist Phyllis Lambert says Montreal needs greater citizen involvement in shaping the city as she approaches her 100th birthday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - After nearly a century watching Montreal change around her, architect and activist Phyllis Lambert believes citizens need a greater voice in shaping the city’s future.

Speaking at a Canadian Centre for Architecture news conference Tuesday, unveiling plans for her centennial, the 99-year-old described Montreal as a “city of communities” and pointed to growing public participation and consultation in decisions about how the city develops.

Lambert, who founded the Montreal-based research institution and museum, became an influential figure in modern architecture through her involvement in the development of New York’s landmark Seagram Building. She later became a prominent advocate for heritage preservation and urban issues in Montreal.

Lambert’s approach to citizen involvement was shaped in part by her work in the 1970s in Milton-Parc, a central Montreal neighbourhood where residents fought plans to demolish much of the area for highrise redevelopment.

Reading excerpts from her forthcoming memoir, “My First Hundred Years,” Lambert recalled how the experience changed her approach to architecture.

“I often said Milton-Parc was my Yale and my Harvard,” Lambert said. “That’s where I learned to listen to people.”

Architect and activist Phyllis Lambert reflects on Montreal’s future and the importance of strong communities as she prepares to turn 100. (Sept. 29, 2026)

Lambert said that as a practising architect, she had been accustomed to making decisions and telling others how things should be done.

“I was still an arrogant architect,” she said, adding that working with citizen groups taught her to do things differently and work with the community.

Lambert contrasted the urban challenges she confronted decades ago with those she sees today. In the 1960s and 1970s, she said, urban renewal programs allowed older buildings to be demolished, neighbourhoods to be destroyed and thousands of residents to be displaced.

Today, she said, she is concerned about a lack of vision and know-how in urban planning and stressed the need to work with residents who experience the city’s problems every day.

One place on her mind is the historic Villa Maria estate, a 1.7-million-square-foot property in Montreal that has been owned by the Congrégation de Notre-Dame since 1854 and was put up for sale this summer.

Lambert said she is “very worried” about what will happen to the property, pointing to its history and extensive green space.

She said the site should not be transformed by highrise development that comes at the expense of that greenery.

“You need to breathe, you know,” Lambert said, broadening her comments to the importance of preserving open space in the city. “We have the mountain, thank God.”

Lambert’s reflections come as she prepares to mark a century of a life closely tied to architecture, urban planning and preservation.

Her memoir, “My First Hundred Years,” is set to be released in January. During Tuesday’s event, she read excerpts tracing her career from the Seagram Building to her urban activism and the creation of the Canadian Centre for Architecture.

The centre is also launching a yearlong program to mark Lambert’s centennial, with exhibitions, films, publications and public discussions focused on some of the urban issues she has worked on throughout her career.

Among them is a series of conversations called “Speaking of Tomorrow,” which will bring together experts and community voices to discuss issues including housing, development, heritage and the environmental challenges facing cities.

Lambert turns 100 on Jan. 24.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

stories.title: Saskatchewan to pursue two large nuclear reactors: Premier Moe
stories.summary: Saskatoon - Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe says his government is looking at building two large nuclear reactors in the province's northwest.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Saskatoon - Saskatchewan’s premier says his government is moving forward with a plan that could see the first of two large nuclear reactors up and running in 16 years.

Scott Moe announced Tuesday they’re looking at building two large reactors somewhere in the province’s northwest, and the first could be online in 2042.

SaskPower, the province’s electrical utility, will evaluate potential locations and speak with people who live in those communities.

“We are charting a path forward for one of the largest energy economic development opportunities in our province’s history,” Moe said.

The premier said it’s premature to estimate how much the reactors would cost. New builds in the United States have been pegged in the billions of dollars.

Moe also didn’t specify where the province would construct the reactors, but said that they could be somewhere along the North Saskatchewan River.

He said the province is open to accepting private sector financing and Indigenous equity partnerships for the projects.

The announcement comes as Saskatchewan looks to ensure its energy needs and others are met.

Moe said nuclear power will support new industrial projects and a growing population. Saskatchewan also hopes to export electricity to neighbouring provinces and the United States.

Should the reactors be built, Moe said, they would supply 2,600 megawatts by 2050 — enough to power 2.6 million homes.

Saskatchewan has 1.2 million people and currently doesn’t use nuclear power. The province is the world’s second-largest uranium producer.

The province is also exploring whether to build a small modular nuclear reactor near Estevan, southeast of Regina.

Moe said the government is looking at the Rafferty Dam as a possible site for the small reactor, though he didn’t rule out building a bigger one there.

Companies in the uranium and nuclear sector – including Cameco and AtkinsRéalis – said in statements they support the province’s plan.

Moe said companies will compete by bidding to build the reactors.

Nuclear development has come up before in Saskatchewan.

In 2008, Bruce Power proposed constructing a plant in west-central Saskatchewan. The project, facing public concern, did not proceed after former premier Brad Wall’s Saskatchewan Party government decided not to endorse it.

Moe said Tuesday times have changed and that countries around the world are planning to build more nuclear plants.

“When you attend nuclear global summits today, they are talking about the dry decade where we were not building nuclear power globally and we should have been,” he said.

“That is about to change.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

— By Jeremy Simes in Regina

stories.title: Csis May have misused special powers when gathering information, says spy watchdog
stories.summary: Some Csis employees May have committed offences without required designation, review agency finds
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The Canadian Security Intelligence Service May not have complied with the law when using special powers to gather information, a review by the national spy watchdog has found.

The Csis Act allows designated spy service employees to commit certain offences when collecting information – a measure intended to ensure Csis operations do not break the law.

A newly released National Security and Intelligence Review Agency report notes there are limitations and requirements tied to this authority to ensure legal curbs on Csis activities.

For instance, the authority does not permit Csis to wilfully obstruct justice, infringe on a Charter right or detain, torture or kill a person.

Employees committing offences or directing sources to do so must spell out why they believe the actions are reasonable and proportional in the circumstances.

The intelligence review agency looked at Csis’s use of the authority in operations in 2022 and 2023.

The Csis Act says all employees committing an offence, including those engaged in covert activities, must be specifically designated to do so.

The act also requires designated employees to obtain the authorization of a senior official to direct another person to commit an offence.

The review agency says Csis complied with the restrictions on the types of permissible offences under the framework.

But the watchdog found some employees May have committed offences without the required designation, and that direction May have been given to commit some acts without the authorization required by law.

The report also says Csis sometimes failed to adequately document the justification for offences.

Employees are supposed to consider multiple elements, including the nature of the threat, the negative effects of committing the offence, the rational link between the offence and the expected results and alternative courses of action.

The report says some justification statements didn’t describe the nature of the threat at all, neglected to outline the anticipated downside of carrying out the offence, or didn’t bother to document consideration of any alternatives.

In addition, the report says, some required internal reporting and notifications to the review agency were not done.

The spy watchdog says Csis has a duty to ensure all of its operations respect the law, especially when those operations require activity that would otherwise be considered illegal.

The review agency recommends that Csis improve internal guidance, oversight and quality assurance to ensure use of the justification framework complies with the Csis Act and internal policy.

Csis spokesman Eric Balsam said Tuesday that while the intelligence service May not agree with all of the review agency’s findings, “Csis holds the same strong commitment to transparency and accountability, and takes all potential non-compliance seriously.”

Csis welcomes the review agency’s recommendations and will take “appropriate steps” proposed by the assessment, he said in a statement.

The review agency’s findings are “deeply disturbing,” said Tim McSorley, national co-ordinator of the Ottawa-based International Civil Liberties Monitoring Group.

“Once again, we see a case where Csis pushes the boundaries of the law and fails to abide by the rules and regulations meant to instill confidence that they can be trusted with such sensitive powers in the first place,” McSorley said in a statement.

The public deserves clear answers on accountability for the Csis officers involved and how such lapses will be prevented in the future, he added.

stories.title: N.S. man sentenced to six years for killing ailing wife after they were evicted
stories.summary: Douglas Andrew Smith pleaded guilty in April to manslaughter in the death of his wife, Iris Dodd, in 2022.
stories.author: Global News
stories.content:
A Nova Scotia judge sentenced a man to six years in prison for killing his 72-year-old wife after promising to help her take her own life so she could avoid being hospitalized or sent to long-term care.

Iris Dodd and Douglas Andrew Smith had been married for nearly 33 years in 2022, when they found themselves facing eviction from their home in Kingsport, N.S., with nowhere else to go, according to an agreed statement of facts read aloud in provincial Supreme Court on Tuesday.

Dodd was nearly blind and could barely walk, and she asked her husband to lay out her pills and go for a drive, so he’d be free from any responsibility when she took them all and died, the court head.

Smith, then 71, agreed. But he worried the overdose would only make her sicker.

stories.title: RCMP arrest 15 people following years-long organized crime probe in Montreal area
stories.summary: Montreal - RCMP have arrested 15 alleged members of a Montreal-based organized crime group following a years-long drug- and money-laundering investigation.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - RCMP have arrested 15 alleged members of a Montreal-based organized crime group following a yearslong drug and money-laundering investigation.

The Mounties said the suspects range in age from 24 to 73-years-old and face multiple charges including trafficking cocaine, laundering proceeds of crime, possession of and trafficking in property obtained by crime, conspiracy and offences committed for the benefit of a criminal organization.
