stories.title: Ikea finally arrives in London
stories.summary: After years of anticipation, Swedish furniture retailer Ikea has opened its first store in London, Ont., welcoming hundreds of shoppers to White Oaks Mall on opening day.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
After years of anticipation, Swedish furniture retailer Ikea has opened its first store in London, Ont., welcoming hundreds of shoppers to White Oaks Mall on opening day.

The new location, a compact-store concept that is the first of its kind in Canada, opened Tuesday morning following a ribbon-cutting ceremony shortly before 10 a.m.

Customers began lining up hours before the opening. Among them was Western University student Micka Soria, who said she and her friends arrived around 2:30 a.m. to secure a spot near the front of the line.

“We had to wait for maybe more than four hours just to get in, and the weather, too, is really cold,” Soria said. “Growing up, I was always going to Ikea in Toronto. When I moved here, Ikea was nowhere.”

Ikea Canada CEO and chief sustainability officer Selwyn Crittendon said the company has long recognized demand for a location in London but noted that traditional Ikea stores require significantly more space.

“We know that it’s hard to plop down 300,000 square feet anywhere in the country, so now it’s about being more accessible,” Crittendon said.

The London store spans about 43,000 square feet and features curated room displays, more than 2,500 home furnishing and seasonal products, and a self-serve warehouse area with about 400 furniture items available for immediate purchase.

Ikea officials said the store’s product selection was tailored to local demand using purchasing data from the company’s Burlington location.

“We took a quite deep dive into what the London market has been buying and what the needs are,” said Danny Santana, deputy market manager for Ikea Burlington. “We really wanted to prioritize everyday essentials and convenience for the product assortment here.”

The opening follows a lengthy effort to bring Ikea to London. More than two decades ago, the company announced plans for a south London store but later abandoned the proposal amid changing market conditions.

Crittendon said the compact-store model is better suited to London’s market and allows the company to expand into communities where a traditional Ikea store May not be feasible.

Opening-day celebrations included giveaways, contests and special promotions, while shoppers also had access to Ikea’s food offerings, including its signature Swedish meatballs.

stories.title: Dangerous high-risk sex offender to live in Surrey, B.C. police say in a warning
stories.summary: Leonard Michael Ramstead is subject to a 10-year long-term supervision order and a host of bail conditions.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Police in Surrey, B.C., have taken the step of advising the public that a dangerous high-risk sex offender will be residing in the community.

In a press release and on posts to social media , Surrey Police Services (SPS) said it was issuing a Public Interest Disclosure after being notified that the offender, Leonard Michael Ramstead, will be residing in the city. Ramstead has previously been convicted of sexual offences involving children and is believed to continue to pose a risk for violent sexual offences against children, police said. Surrey is part of the metropolitan Vancouver region.

Police have released an image and a description, and say Ramstead is a 58-year-old white male, 5-foot-7 and approximately 235 lbs. He has brown hair, blue eyes, and normally has a beard.

Ramstead is the subject of a long-term supervision order, defined by the Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) as “a non-custodial sentencing option available to the courts to extend the length of time that the CSC will supervise and support an offender in the community.”

The order cannot exceed 10 years, and Ramstead has been given the maximum duration. He also has a long list of bail conditions, which include not consuming alcohol or drugs; avoiding all contact with past or present victims of offences for which he has been convicted, or any known members of their families; and having no contact or to be in the presence of any children under the age of 16.

This incudes a ban on being near day cares, elementary or secondary schools, parks and playgrounds, swimming pools, and recreational centres, or seeking any employment or voluntary work that involves being in a position of trust or authority towards someone under 16.

Anyone seeing Ramstead breaching his release conditions is asked to immediately call 911.

Surrey Police Services took over as the police of jurisdiction from the local RCMP detachment in 2024. However, the RCMP has also announced it will be partnering to surveil Ramstead via traditional police methods, as well as through electronic monitoring.

Ramstead was first convicted in 2019 for sexual interference with a person under age 16, and again in 2021 for the same charge with a person under 14. He is considered a high risk to young people and children.

He was given statutory release in April 2024 upon serving two-thirds of his fixed-term sentence. RCMP at the time warned the community of his release, which concluded this month with the transition to the long-term supervision order.

Ramstead’s statutory release in 2024 coincided with that of another dangerous sex offender, prompting consternation from Surrey’s mayor, Brenda Locke.

“It is beyond comprehension why several high-risk offenders are being unleashed into our city, which has the largest youth population in B.C.,” she said. “This is utterly unacceptable. The blatant disregard for the safety and security of our community, particularly our most vulnerable individuals, is a grave injustice that cannot be overlooked.”

stories.title: Alberta CEOs join ‘stay’ camp as Calgary Chamber warns of separatism economic fallout
stories.summary: A University of Calgary study estimates trade costs would rise by five to eight per cent and Alberta could see up to 175,000 jobs cut and a $62-billion annual hit to the economy.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
Alberta business leaders have signed on to an open letter from the Calgary Chamber of Commerce warning of the dire economic consequences if the province were to separate from Canada .

“We must remain at the table and prioritize relationships, opportunities and stability that have helped make this province and this country prosperous,” reads the letter released Tuesday along with an analysis into the trade, labour and fiscal implications of separation.

“Alberta can be proud of Its identity while remaining confident in its future within Canada.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Alberta can be proud of Its identity while remaining confident in its future within Canada."

Among the signatories to the letter are the heads of AltaGas, Atco, AltaLink, Capital Power, Keyera, BHE Transmission and Chirp Foods Inc., Canada’s largest McDonald’s franchise business. Tourism Calgary and Calgary Economic Development have also signed, as well as a former CEO of Trans Mountain Corp.

The chamber said more are expected to join.

In three weeks, Albertans vote on 10 referendum questions, including one on whether the province should remain in Canada or begin the process of holding another referendum on separation.

The study by University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe estimates trade costs would rise by five to eight per cent — the range the United Kingdom has seen since its withdrawal from the European Union.

It said Alberta is the most trade-exposed jurisdiction in the country, with nearly one in three workers having jobs in sectors significantly vulnerable to such disruptions.

The higher trade costs would translate into to job reductions of up to 175,000 in Alberta and an up to $62-billion annual hit to the economy, the report said.

Alberta would also find itself with a $9-billion fiscal shortfall if it were to separate, Tombe concluded. Closing the gap would require a 13 per cent sales tax, a 10 per cent corporate income tax hike or a 40 per cent cut in the transfers Alberta businesses and individuals now receive, like the Canada Child Benefit and old age security.

“When you hear something like GDP contracting, it seems like an abstract statistical notion, but this translates directly into real incomes and wages. How much goods and services can you afford to purchase with an hour of work?” Tombe told reporters.

Chamber president and CEO Deborah Yedlin said Alberta splitting from Canada would be like scoring on its own net, just to send a message.

“I grew up with this notion of the Alberta advantage — no sales tax, low taxes, good education, health care, social services. All of that would disappear and we would not be able to sustain that level of support for Albertans,” she told reporters.

“That, in turn, turns into a negative feedback loop, and you don’t get the investment, you don’t generate the tax revenue, you can’t provide the services unless you change how you operate, and that’s just not something anybody really wants to see.”

The vote also comes as “we stand on the doorstep of some significant opportunity,” Yedlin added.

The world is clamouring for stable supplies of energy as wars rage in the Middle East and Russia. And the federal government under Prime Minister Mark Carney has made a raft of policy shifts embraced by businesses while demonstrating an eagerness to build new energy infrastructure.

Some people might be looking to send a message with a pro-separation-referendum vote after 10 years of former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s less oilpatch-friendly approach, Yedlin said.

“It’s easy to look in the rear-view mirror and it’s easy to be aggrieved and to focus on that. It’s much harder to be an optimist, but we’re at a point in time where we need to have that optimism.

“This is a different set of circumstances, a different environment for Alberta, for the energy sector and we do need to look forward.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "This is a different set of circumstances, a different environment for Alberta, for the energy sector and we do need to look forward."

Yedlin said some business leaders May have been reticent to wade into the debate so far because they don’t want to alienate workers in the field sympathetic to the separatist cause.

“The reality is, though, that as an entity, you can say this is what you stand for. And at the same time, you respect the right of your employees to vote according to what they feel is important to them,” she said.

“Ultimately, where you need to be is on the right side of history.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Ultimately, where you need to be is on the right side of history."

stories.title: Poilievre set to speak on national unity in Edmonton ahead of separation referendum
stories.summary: Edmonton - Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is set to speak on national unity tonight in Edmonton, with less than three weeks to go until Albertans vote on separation.
stories.author: Fakiha Baig The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre tried Tuesday to convince Albertans to vote to stay in Canada with less than three weeks to go until a provincial vote on separation.

His speech at a downtown Edmonton hotel was among others he has given or plans to give in the province as part of his efforts to convince Conservative voters that Alberta is stronger within a united Canada.

Poilievre, who is from Alberta, said separatists have a problem with the federal Liberal government — not with Canada.

“Many Albertans are legitimately frustrated that a costly and controlling, big and bossy government has gone far beyond its jurisdictional boundaries,” he told a crowd of supporters holding Canadian flags and “Conservatives for Canada” signs.

Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservative Party government has called a 10-question referendum for Oct. 19. The 10th and final question asks Albertans whether they want to stay in Canada or have a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

Smith has said she supports Alberta staying a part of Canada and plans to vote that way in the referendum, but that hundreds of thousands have signed petitions for and against separation, and it’s time to put the issue to rest.

Critics, pointing to long-standing opinion polls indicating massive support for Alberta staying in Canada, have accused Smith of calling the vote to appease restive separatist hardliners in her party.

Poilievre said Liberal government policies have left Canadians struggling to make ends meet, everywhere from the gas pump and the grocery store to buying a house.

“Our businesses and workers are frustrated that our oil and gas is left in the ground and our opportunities are left there with it,” he said Tuesday.

The solution to those problems is not an independent Alberta, he said.

“Separation will not solve those problems. Becoming even more Canadian will,” Poilievre said.

“The solution is to double down on the way the country was always meant to work.”

He said Albertans should keep fighting by, for example, forcing Ottawa to unlock the power of Alberta’s oil and gas industry.

Earlier in the day, Poilievre attended a fundraiser for Conservatives for Canada, a group of federal politicians making the case for Alberta to stay in Confederation.

He has tapped Dane Lloyd, a member of Parliament who represents an Alberta riding, to lead that effort.

On Tuesday night, Lloyd gave a shout-out to the Conservative MPs in the room who have campaigned for the federalist side of the separation debate.

“Conservatives are patriots,” Lloyd said. “We love our country. We love our home province of Alberta.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

stories.title: ‘Separation will not solve problems’: Poilievre speaks in Alberta ahead of referendum
stories.summary: Edmonton — Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre tried Tuesday to convince Albertans to vote to stay in Canada with less than three weeks to go until a provincial vote on separation.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Fakiha Baig, The Canadian Press

Posted September 29, 2026 2:01 pm.

Last Updated September 29, 2026 11:16 pm.

EDMONTON — Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre tried Tuesday to convince Albertans to vote to stay in Canada with less than three weeks to go until a provincial vote on separation.

His speech at a downtown Edmonton hotel was among others he has given or plans to give in the province as part of his efforts to convince Conservative voters that Alberta is stronger within a united Canada.

Poilievre, who is from Alberta, said separatists have a problem with the federal Liberal government — not with Canada.

“Many Albertans are legitimately frustrated that a costly and controlling, big and bossy government has gone far beyond its jurisdictional boundaries,” he told a crowd of supporters holding Canadian flags and “Conservatives for Canada” signs.

Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservative Party government has called a 10-question referendum for Oct. 19. The 10th and final question asks Albertans whether they want to stay in Canada or have a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

Smith has said she supports Alberta staying a part of Canada and plans to vote that way in the referendum, but that hundreds of thousands have signed petitions for and against separation, and it’s time to put the issue to rest.

Critics, pointing to long-standing opinion polls indicating massive support for Alberta staying in Canada, have accused Smith of calling the vote to appease restive separatist hardliners in her party.

Poilievre said Liberal government policies have left Canadians struggling to make ends meet, everywhere from the gas pump and the grocery store to buying a house.

“Our businesses and workers are frustrated that our oil and gas is left in the ground and our opportunities are left there with it,” he said Tuesday.

The solution to those problems is not an independent Alberta, he said.

“Separation will not solve those problems. Becoming even more Canadian will,” Poilievre said.

“The solution is to double down on the way the country was always meant to work.”

He said Albertans should keep fighting by, for example, forcing Ottawa to unlock the power of Alberta’s oil and gas industry.

Earlier in the day, Poilievre attended a fundraiser for Conservatives for Canada, a group of federal politicians making the case for Alberta to stay in Confederation.

He has tapped Dane Lloyd, a member of Parliament who represents an Alberta riding, to lead that effort.

On Tuesday night, Lloyd gave a shout-out to the Conservative MPs in the room who have campaigned for the federalist side of the separation debate.

“Conservatives are patriots,” Lloyd said. “We love our country. We love our home province of Alberta.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

Fakiha Baig, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Csis can break the law. They need to document it better, watchdog warns
stories.summary: The National Security and Intelligence Review Agency (Nsira) said Csis did not properly document justifications for illegal activities as required.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Canada’s spy agency needs more oversight into operations that include illegal activities in order to gain intelligence, a new watchdog report suggests.

The Canadian Security and Intelligence Service (CSIS) is authorized in certain circumstances to take actions that would ordinarily break Canadian law in its pursuit of information about national security threats.

But while the National Security and Intelligence Review Agency (CSIRA) found that CSIS stayed within the bounds of the illegal activities they’re permitted to use, the spy agency lacked documented justifications and rationale for taking those actions.

“CSIS has a duty to ensure that all of its operations respect the rule of law, even more so when those operations require activity that would otherwise be considered illegal,” the review body wrote in a report released publicly Tuesday.

The review body examined operations from 2022 and 2023 where CSIS operations involved actions or omissions that would normally break Canadian laws. The powers were granted to the agency by the Liberals’ 2017 national security reforms, which also placed limitations on what illegal actions the spy agency can engage in.

According to CSIS 2025 report, the powers were authorized 173 times in 2022-23 and 178 times in 2023-24.

CSIS is still prohibited from certain activities, such as causing bodily harm, obstructing justice, violating someone’s sexual integrity and torture. Instead, eight “classes” of illegal activities have been approved by both the minister of public safety and the independent intelligence commissioner — although each instance requires authorization and written justification and explanation after the fact.

It’s the documentation that NSIRA found issue with.

In some cases, the review agency said, CSIS operatives failed to document the nature of the threat that led them to believe illegal activities were justified. In others, CSIS employees did not document the nature of the illegal activities or their negative consequences.

In other operations, the agency didn’t detail what alternatives were considered before engaging in illegal activity.

NSIRA noted that the team within CSIS tasked with oversight for these activities is under-resourced, and said increased internal guidance and review is needed to make sure CSIS is following the rules.

“Many of the deficiencies … noted above can be attributed to confusion or lack of understanding of the requirements and the consequences of not meeting them,” the review agency wrote.

In a statement to Global News Tuesday afternoon, CSIS welcomed the NSIRA review — but suggested the agency may disagree with some of the review body’s findings. The agency said a full response to NSIRA’s recommendations will be posted publicly in the future.

“While CSIS may not agree with all NSIRA’s findings, CSIS holds the same strong commitment to transparency and accountability, and takes all potential non-compliance seriously,” the agency said in a statement.

“As such, CSIS will take appropriate steps proposed by NSIRA’s assessment, and will continue to collaborate effectively with NSIRA, which includes notifying the review body as per its requirements in the CSIS Act.”

While CSIS may not agree with all of NSIRA’s findings, CSIS holds the same strong commitment to transparency and accountability, and takes all potential non-compliance seriously. As such, CSIS will take appropriate steps proposed by NSIRA’s assessment, and will continue to collaborate effectively with NSIRA, which includes notifying the review body as per its requirements in the CSIS Act.

stories.title: French-only Quebec election voter guides prompted 160 complaints over five days
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec’s election oversight body received an influx of complaints after it announced that it was sending unilingual French information guides to all voters ahead of the Oct. 5 elections.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - When Derek Heatherington, a retired college professor living in the Eastern Townships region of Quebec, heard that the provincial elections agency was sending out unilingual French information guides this year, he decided to act.

“This situation really spoke to me, because we’re getting to the point here where we’re talking really about voter suppression,” he said.

Élections Québec announced on its website on Sept. 1 that it was not sending out any English language guides due to legislation adopted in 2022 requiring provincial government institutions to issue public communications only in French. Instead of the usual bilingual documents, the agency suggested voters could scan a QR code on the guide to find the English information online.

Quebec’s election oversight body saw an influx of complaints after it announced that information documents would be sent in French only ahead of the Oct. 5 elections. (Sept. 29, 2026)

Heatherington responded to that announcement by filing a complaint and sharing it as a template on social media to encourage others to do the same.

Heatherington is part of the board of the Task Force on Linguistic Policy, an advocacy group that is accusing the elections authority of creating barriers to democracy and violating constitutional rights ahead of the Oct. 5 provincial election.

Documents released through access to information legislation reveal Élections Québec received 160 complaints over five days after the agency announced it was sending the unilingual guides.

Twenty-seven of those complaints were identical to Heatherington’s template.

“Those are the processes that are going to be heard, a lot more than people going online and saying ‘I think this is horrible,’” he said.

In one of the complaints, a person who identified themselves as an English-speaking Quebecer noted how they were part of a minority forced to fight hard to have their rights respected.

“I’m disappointed to learn today that my right to vote will be compromised,” wrote the complainant.

Another said the change made it more difficult for their son, who has autism and can only speak English, to participate in the elections.

“I’m (an) Italian-Canadian Quebecer, born here, I have the right to English (services). I demand the correspondence be bilingual,” the complainant wrote.

A Superior Court judge temporarily suspended provisions of the language legislation on Sept. 16, ordering the agency to send out bilingual reminder cards to voters in response to a separate legal challenge launched by a resident of Westmount, Que.

Élections Québec spokesperson Julie St-Arnaud-Drolet said the campaign period was too short to send English mailouts to anglophones who qualify for English services and Indigenous people.

“Some voters feel really angry about it. For us, it’s very difficult, because it’s not up to us to decide,” she said.

She said that, as a non-partisan organization, Élections Québec could not go against governmental legislation and run the risk of appearing to endorse or reject a party’s platform.

“Can we fault a democratic institution for respecting the laws? If an institution like ours did not respect Quebec laws, it seems to me that it would be then that, democratically, we would have a problem,” she said.

The agency’s internal documents also show that Élections Québec analyzed the risks of sending French-only guides. An evaluation dated on Jan. 1, 2025, lists lower turnout in groups that do not speak French, complaints, and loss of interest or trust towards democratic institutions as possible risks.

“We of course are concerned about the voting turnout, but (language legislation) is a political matter,” said St-Arnaud-Drolet.

Letters between Quebec’s chief electoral officer, Jean-François Blanchet, and the provincial government show that he requested an exemption from the language legislation, warning in April 2025 that the results of the election could be challenged due to French-only correspondence with voters.

Heatherington does not blame the election oversight body for the decision to send out unilingual information documents, acknowledging that they have to follow language laws.

“They don’t have a whole lot of choices aside from trying to find some middle ground. And it’s really an unfortunate position for us to be in — for citizens to be (in) and for them to be (in),” he said.

He hopes the flurry of complaints can help Élections Québec push back against the language legislation.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

stories.title: Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe to lay out nuclear development plan
stories.summary: Countries across the globe are either building or promising to construct more nuclear power plants as many look for ways to reduce emissions.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe has unveiled the province’s nuclear energy plan, including a power production goal within 24 years.

Under the plan, the province aims to produce at least 2,600 megawatts of nuclear power by 2050. By comparison, Ontario’s Pickering Nuclear Generating Station produces 2,100 MW of electricity, powering 1.5 million homes annually, according to the Government of Canada

“Our future electricity mix in this province will include, yes, natural gas; it will include hydro, wind, solar as well as some thermal,” Moe said Tuesday. “But we must also invest in a future source of power that is reliable in every season. Available around the clock, is affordable for decades to come, affordable for us to continue to attract that investment, but also, most importantly, affordable for the families that live here.”

The province says its plan contains four priorities:

The first priority is focused on nuclear energy providing a reliable source of non-emitting electricity to strengthen the reliability of the power grid and meeting growing demand.

Incorporating large reactors will see SaskPower begin planning for the potential development of such structures in northwestern Saskatchewan.

Moe said more than 2,000 of that 2,600 megawatt goal will come from large-scale nuclear reactors, the first of which is planned to come online by 2042.

“To put that into perspective, 600 megawatts can power the equivalent of Saskatchewan’s two largest cities, Regina and Saskatoon,” Moe explained. “Twenty-six hundred megawatts could power the equivalent of 2.6 million homes.”

Consultations with local communities near the proposed reactors and Indigenous peoples would be part of SaskPower’s evaluation of potential locations.

Crown Investment Corporations Minister Jeremy Harrison told reporters that 2042 for the first large reactor was a “very realistic timeline.”

He said there have been “very good” discussions regarding long-term plans with the federal government, along with the governments of Alberta and the Northwest Territories.

“I’ve said publicly often that, you know, there’s a lot in Canada that pushes us apart. Nuclear is one of those things that really can bring the country together from Ontario to Western Canada to New Brunswick,” Harrison said Tuesday.

Saskatchewan has already been looking into the idea of nuclear energy, with the government and SaskPower in a multi-year planning phase of a proposed small modular reactor (SMR) by the mid-2030s.

Those SMRs are highlighted in the province’s plan, with the Rafferty site near Estevan selected to undergo further study for development of such a reactor. The utility plans to advance planning for potential SMR deployment with a goal of delivering at least 600 megawatts.

“This plan gives SaskPower a clear path to meet growing demand and support the investment and industries that keep our province strong,” said Crown Investments Corporation Minister Jeremy Harrison in a news release.

The final goal of Saskatchewan’s plan is focused on ensuring electricity supply keeps up with demand.

The province says it plans to engage with Indigenous rights holders, municipalities, industry stakeholders and other leaders as it makes further plans for nuclear energy.

Tim Gitzel, CEO of Cameco, one of the largest uranium mining companies in the world, said the plan recognizes the “essential role” nuclear power plays in supporting growth.

“We understand the economic, environmental and energy security benefits that safe, reliable and carbon-free nuclear power can provide for our people, communities, and industries,” Gitzel said in a news release. “We look forward to competing for the province’s business as it embarks on this transformative plan to build a reliable energy grid, utilizing nuclear energy to power Saskatchewan’s future.”

Nuclear energy will also provide more than just electricity, Moe said, it will provide opportunities for tradespeople, Indigenous businesses, technological companies, fabricators and suppliers.

He told reporters the Saskatoon-based mining company is working with the federal government on regulations and opportunities to expand its workforce. When asked by reporters about costs, he said the numbers “change over time.” Harrison said there was the potential for private sector financing to be “part of the conversation.”

— with files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Star reporter Moira Welsh's 'The Astonishing Lives of Older Women' among finalists for $70K Balsillie Prize
stories.summary: The winner of the 2026 Balsillie Prize for Public Policy will be announced Nov. 24.
stories.author: Samm Mohibuddin
stories.content:
Toronto Star political reporter Moira Welsh is among the five finalists for the prestigious 2026 Balsillie Prize for Public Policy , awarded annually to a nonfiction book that advances and influences policy debates on a wide range of social, political, economic, or cultural topics relevant to Canadians.

The award comes with a $70,000 prize; runners-up receive $7,500.

Welsh was nominated for ” The Astonishing Lives of Older Women: How to Create Pleasure over Peril in Peak Longevity ,” which examines what growing old looks like for women, including issues around finances, relationships, health, housing and loneliness.

The jury said the book explores both the “promise and peril” of growing older as a woman, highlighting the financial vulnerability faced by those who depend on Old Age Security and the Canada Pension Plan.

Welsh, who works at the Star’s Queen’s Park bureau, has co-authored investigations that won three National Newspaper Awards and a Michener Award for Public Service Journalism.

The other nominations for the Balsillie Prize are:

" Under Assault: Interference and Espionage in China's Secret War Against Canada ," by Dennis Molinaro, who tackles foreign interference involving China. Molinaro is a former national security analyst and policy adviser for the federal government and an assistant professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University.

Rick Westhead's " We Breed Lions: Confronting Canada's Troubles Hockey Culture, " which examines sexual assault allegations and the hazing culture prevalent in Canadian hockey. Westhead is a journalist with TSN and two-time Canadian Sportswriter of the Year.

” Wild Fire: Dispatches from a Country Ablaze ,” by former Toronto Star reporter and photojournalist Jesse Winter. Winter’s book takes readers to the front lines of Canadian wildfires and examines their causes and growing frequency whilst addressing preventive measures.

And ” The Age of Extraction: How Tech Platforms Conquered the Economy and Threaten Our Future Prosperity ,” by Tim Wu, a professor at Columbia University, explores the rise of tech platforms and how they are a machine for collecting data, money and our attention.

The winner of the 2026 Balsillie Prize for Public Policy will be announced Nov. 24.

stories.title: $22.4M investment to unlock 165 acres at Kelowna Airport
stories.summary: The federal government is providing up to $22.4 million for infrastructure that will open up the airport land for industrial and aerospace development.
stories.author: Cohan Sassaman
stories.content:
There is a lot of room to grow at Kelowna International Airport (YLW) and a major investment announced Monday is set to start unlocking it.

The federal government is providing up to $22.4 million for infrastructure that will open up 165 acres of airport land for industrial and aerospace development.

The funding will help pay for the water, sewer, electrical, communications and stormwater infrastructure needed to service the site.

Philip Elchitz, director of operations and innovation at Kelowna International Airport, says YLW already has a significant economic footprint, supporting about 9,000 jobs and generating roughly $2 billion in annual economic output.

The airport expects that footprint to grow as the East Lands are developed.

“If you add up the current and the future, we expect to go to 3 billion dollars in annual economic output per year and approximately 12,000 jobs per year, both direct and indirect.”

But the entire site will not be built out right away.

The first phase will service roughly one-third of the available land. That leaves two-thirds open for future investment.

Three aerospace companies, De Havilland Aircraft, Wildcat Helicopters and Fire Swarm, are already in talks with the airport about opportunities on the site.

For Wildcat Helicopters, a larger footprint could mean expanding its operations and workforce.

“Oh, absolutely. We’ll be hiring more people. Yeah, there’s no doubt about it,” says Mike Michaud, President, Wildcat Helicopters

The expansion is also being matched by investments in training.

Okanagan College’s new aerospace facility is expected to open in 2027. The college currently trains about 64 aircraft maintenance engineers, a number expected to rise to 144 once the new facility opens.

Most of the new infrastructure will be built on the east side of the runway. The airport says construction is expected to begin next spring, with the work scheduled to wrap up by the end of 2028.

For now, much of that side of the airport remains open space.

The plan is to turn it into a growing aerospace hub, with new taxiways, hangars, offices, companies and, ultimately, more people working at YLW.

stories.title: Immigration increase could be on the horizon, Carney suggests in interview
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney suggested a "controlled increase" in the country's population could be on the way in a recent interview with the New York Times.
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says with Canada’s immigration system back under control, the question now is about when to begin a “controlled increase” of the country’s population.

Carney made the remark in a recent interview with the New York Times, just over a month before the government is required by law to release its immigration levels plan for the next three years.

The last three federal immigration plans focused on reducing the number of people coming to the country after a rapid post-pandemic population spike.

The government also started setting targets for annual temporary arrivals to reduce the number of short-term workers and students to five per cent of the population after they cracked seven per cent in October 2024.

The C.D. Howe Institute’s immigration targets council recommends the government continue to shrink the number of arrivals over the next three years.

That council includes several top academics who study immigration policy, a former deputy minister and former Alberta premier Jason Kenney.

stories.title: Carney set to make energy announcement in Vancouver
stories.summary: Carney's announcement comes after LNG Canada said earlier Tuesday that it will go ahead with the multibillion-dollar Phase 2 expansion of its liquefied natural gas export terminal.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney announced in Vancouver on Tuesday that LNG Canada is moving forward with the Phase 2 expansion project in Kitimat, B.C.

“Today’s $33 billion investment in LNG Canada 2 will make LNG Canada the second-largest facility of its kind in the world. It will create thousands of new jobs,” Carney said.

“It will connect low-cost, low-carbon Canadian energy to global markets, providing the secure supply our partners in Asia and Europe need.”

The expansion comes as global energy markets have been in turmoil amid the war in the Middle East and the closures of the Strait of Hormuz over recent months, sending prices soaring.

Carney added that this is a “great” day for Canada.

“The scale of this investment shows it,” he said.

“The partnership proves it. The speed confirms it. Canada is working. Canada is building big again”

Carney said that this project represents Canada coming together on a bigger scale.

“It’s above and beyond this project,” he added.

“It’s the way it’s come together. It’s the way it’s being built. It’s the teamwork that’s here that teaches a lesson for all Canadians.”

BC NDP leader David Eby called the announcement a “big deal.”

“I want to recognize a few people who are very key to getting us here today,” Eby added.

“But I also want to take a moment to reflect on what it means to have the partners that we have committing to Phase 2 of this project in British Columbia and in Canada.

“We have very high standards, unapologetically. Workers have to be treated right. Indigenous partners need to be at the table. We need to ensure that when we build a project like this, that it has world-leading environmental standards and there has to be a fair return to Canadians and to British Columbians.”

Eby said he visited Kitimat and spoke to those working in Phase 1 and they wanted to know when Phase 2 would become a reality.

“This project means 4,000 in just the Phase 2 project, 4,000 high-paid jobs,” he added.

“It doesn’t talk about all the ancillary jobs that come with that. It means $28 billion over the life of the project in revenue for governments to pay for the services that people depend on.”

Former B.C. premier Christy Clark said she was thrilled by Tuesday’s announcement.

“I am so delighted,” she said.

“We started talking about LNG in 2011. Everybody made fun of us, and me in particular. And I think John Horgan and David Eby both said that I was like some kind of crazy dreamer just making stuff up. And I’m glad they both turned out to be so wrong.

“This is so good for workers and for our economy.”

Clark added that if B.C. had embraced LNG years ago, the province would not be in the position that Carney is now trying to fix.

“He says we don’t have diversified markets, we don’t have partners in Asia, we’re not selling enough of our natural resources,” she said.

“That was the whole point of LNG. Create jobs at home and diversify our market so that we’re no longer so dependent on the United States. If we’d been allowed to just, you know, by other levels of government, federal government in particular, but then subsequently the NDP governments of Horgan and Eby, we’d been allowed to go ahead, we would be way ahead of the game right now, much better protected from the aggressive moves from the American government against us on tariffs.”

BC Green Party Leader Emily Lowan was not excited, however, about the Phase 2 announcement. “LNG Canada is an entirely foreign-owned project,” she said in a statement.

“It is owned by Shell, one of the most profitable companies in history, several foreign state-owned oil companies, and U.S. private equity. LNG Canada’s owners also own the fracking operations in the Peace (region) that feed the project.

“The profits from LNG development flow directly to shareholders and governments abroad, while the costs stay here. ”

Lowan referred to the announcement as a “nation-draining” project.

With a file from The Canadian Press.

stories.title: Deloitte slashes 2027 economic outlook by 20% as trade tensions worsen
stories.summary: A new report released Tuesday from Deloitte says the Canadian economy performed better than expected so far this year, but that momentum is losing steam amid new trade tensions.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
A new report released Tuesday from Deloitte says the Canadian economy performed better than expected so far this year, but that momentum is losing steam as worsening trade tensions between Canada and the U.S. led the firm to change its outlook for 2027.

The firm dropped its economic growth projection for next year by 20 per cent, warning that it expects recent trade flare-ups “to become more pronounced in 2027.”

Deloitte’s fall economic outlook report, titled Weathering change: Canadian businesses navigate renewed uncertainty, was released Tuesday, and on the same day a U.S. import ban on Canadian alcohol, dairy products and motorcycles took effect.

GDP is projected to rise a total of 1.6 per cent next year, according to Deloitte’s estimates, which is a downward revision by 0.4 per cent from its last report .

“Canada’s trade outlook has deteriorated following the renewed escalation in trade tensions with the United States,” said Dawn Desjardins, chief economist at Deloitte Canada, who authored the report.

“Canada’s economy will face challenges in maintaining its recent upward momentum.”

This also follows several new waves of U.S. tariffs , including 50 per cent duties on hundreds of Canadian goods, as well as Canada’s “dollar-for-dollar” reciprocal counter-tariff measures.

“Amid the persistent threat and implementation of tariffs by Canada’s largest trading partner, household and business confidence remain subdued,” said Desjardins in the report.

“For consumers, concerns about job security and the prospect of higher prices may further dampen spending.”

The report’s projections for how Canada’s economy will perform took into account the first wave of 50 per cent U.S. tariffs under Section 338 that started on Aug. 22, as well as Canada’s reciprocal tariffs that began on Sept. 8.

However, the timing of the report’s research meant the Sept. 15 changes to the Section 338 50 per cent tariffs, which added more products while removing others, and the more recent import ban on Canadian alcohol, dairy products and motorcycles, were not factored into Deloitte’s projections.

The report says these additional measures that were not included in Deloitte’s calculations “represent a downside risk to the forecast” and are expected to drag on the economy.

Here’s what Deloitte expects over the next few months and into next year.

These newly implemented tariff measures, Deloitte says, will likely have a delayed effect on Canada’s economy, and 2026 is still expected to be positive overall because of the momentum built through the first half of the year.

According to the report, the Canadian economy will grow by an estimated 0.9 per cent in 2026, which was revised upward by 0.2 percentage points from Deloitte’s summer report.

The report highlights a sharp uptick in Canadian exports this year, strong business investments in machinery and equipment, as well as gains in the job market and a decline in the unemployment rate. At the same time, Deloitte says specific sectors “continued to struggle” from the impacts of U.S. tariffs.

Manufacturing has seen some of the most consistent job losses since the trade war began last year, and most recently led steelmaker Stelco to lay off 350 workers , according to the union.

In sectors where there is weaker hiring or shrinking workforces, Deloitte says consumers will take a hit from tariffs.

“Households will not be immune to the economic ramifications of the new rounds of tariffs with job growth expected to slow. This will work to suppress household spending into next year,” said Desjardins in the report.

Although there was some economic weakness to start the year that sparked some debate about whether or not the economy was in a technical recession, those worries were eased after GDP numbers for the first quarter were revised higher and the second quarter saw a 3.3 per cent annualized gain in GDP.

But new tariff measures are expected to lead to a gradual decline in Canada’s exports over the next few months as many businesses in both the U.S. and Canada face higher costs and uncertainty.

“Many firms are stuck in a wait-and-see mode as tariff exposure and uncertainty over future U.S. market access cause some firms to postpone capacity expansions,” said Desjardins in the report.

Deloitte says business investment in 2026 will increase by 1.6 per cent, and although many businesses will likely pull back on plans to expand into 2027 amid tariff and trade uncertainty, the economy as a whole will likely still show positive business investment growth because of two factors.

One, AI data centre projects that are currently in the works are set to advance to the construction phase next year, including Meta’s in Alberta and Bell’s in Saskatchewan . Both, however, continue to face significant opposition from voters amid pushback to expanded data centre construction.

Second, 2027 is set to see some investment decisions through the federal government’s Major Projects Office become finalized.

But the economy may still be on shaky ground, as Deloitte says, “the economy remains vulnerable to renewed trade tensions.”

Higher oil prices and retaliatory tariffs are also raising the risk of pushing up inflation in Canada, but Deloitte says that likely won’t have much of an impact this year beyond what consumers pay at the pump.

This is also one of the reasons Deloitte says the Bank of Canada will likely keep its benchmark interest rate on hold at 2.25 per cent for the rest of 2026.

But, as many as four potential interest rate hikes are expected next year.

“Despite an economy under pressure from this new round of tariffs and non-existent population growth, the Bank of Canada’s next move is likely to be a hike,” said Desjardins in the report.

“The Bank will remain on the sidelines this year as it monitors how the economy responds to the latest trade tensions before beginning a gradual hiking cycle in 2027 when four rate hikes are anticipated.”

Interest rate hikes can lead to more expensive mortgages and other loans for consumers and businesses, and Deloitte says the housing market is likely going to cool off over the next few months and “remain unfavourable” into next year.

The report says economic uncertainty will weigh on consumers, who may push back big purchases like a home.

In addition, rising bond yields are expected to make some mortgages more expensive, and unsold condo inventory will mean less new construction, which could lead to fewer available homes to purchase.

“Further complicating the outlook is elevated inflation risks. The longer energy prices stay high and tariffs remain in place, the greater the risk of pass-through to other goods,” said Desjardins in the report.

stories.title: Watchdog finds problems with spy service’s use of legal authority to commit offences
stories.summary: Ottawa — The national spy watchdog says the Canadian Security Intelligence Service May not have complied with the law when using special powers to gather information.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

Posted September 29, 2026 1:14 pm.

Last Updated September 29, 2026 5:28 pm.

OTTAWA — The Canadian Security Intelligence Service may not have complied with the law when using special powers to gather information, a review by the national spy watchdog has found.

The CSIS Act allows designated spy service employees to commit certain offences when collecting information — a measure intended to ensure CSIS operations do not break the law.

A newly released National Security and Intelligence Review Agency report notes there are limitations and requirements tied to this authority to ensure legal curbs on CSIS activities.

For instance, the authority does not permit CSIS to wilfully obstruct justice, infringe on a Charter right or detain, torture or kill a person.

Employees committing offences or directing sources to do so must spell out why they believe the actions are reasonable and proportional in the circumstances.

The intelligence review agency looked at CSIS’s use of the authority in operations in 2022 and 2023.

The CSIS Act says all employees committing an offence, including those engaged in covert activities, must be specifically designated to do so.

The act also requires designated employees to obtain the authorization of a senior official to direct another person to commit an offence.

The review agency says CSIS complied with the restrictions on the types of permissible offences under the framework.

But the watchdog found some employees may have committed offences without the required designation, and that direction may have been given to commit some acts without the authorization required by law.

The report also says CSIS sometimes failed to adequately document the justification for offences.

Employees are supposed to consider multiple elements, including the nature of the threat, the negative effects of committing the offence, the rational link between the offence and the expected results and alternative courses of action.

The report says some justification statements didn’t describe the nature of the threat at all, neglected to outline the anticipated downside of carrying out the offence, or didn’t bother to document consideration of any alternatives.

In addition, the report says, some required internal reporting and notifications to the review agency were not done.

The spy watchdog says CSIS has a duty to ensure all of its operations respect the law, especially when those operations require activity that would otherwise be considered illegal.

The review agency recommends that CSIS improve internal guidance, oversight and quality assurance to ensure use of the justification framework complies with the CSIS Act and internal policy.

The review agency says CSIS complied with the restrictions on the types of permissible offences under the framework.

stories.title: Rush frontman Geddy Lee endorses Brad Bradford in Toronto mayoral race
stories.summary: Toronto — Though his mind is not for rent, you can put him down as a Brad Bradford voter.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Alex Nino Gheciu, The Canadian Press

Posted September 29, 2026 12:59 pm.

Last Updated September 29, 2026 4:03 pm.

TORONTO — Though his mind is not for rent, you can put him down as a Brad Bradford voter.

Rush frontman Geddy Lee is openly endorsing the city councillor in Toronto’s mayoral race.

The Canadian vocalist and bassist posted a series of photos of himself holding a small dog alongside Bradford, with a caption explaining his support for the councillor.

Lee said that while he’s always been proud to call Toronto home, the city is “changing, and not for the better.”

He added that he truly fears for the future of Toronto “under its current leadership,” and believes Bradford has “energy, fresh ideas and really cares” about all the city’s communities.

Bradford looks to dethrone Toronto mayor Olivia Chow in the upcoming election on Oct. 26. Among his campaign promises are to cut Torontonians’ water bills by 25 per cent and hire 1,000 new police officers.

Lee’s post was met with mixed reactions, including Toronto hardcore punk band F***ed Up, who simply replied with vomit emojis.

In a longer statement shared on the Beaches-East York councillor’s website, Lee said that while touring the world over the last 50 years, he always felt relief when returning home. But he said that has changed.

“Toronto was the city that worked. As I look around now, it’s not the same,” he wrote. “Something has gone wrong, and it isn’t the people. It’s the leadership.”

Lee added that his parents, both Holocaust survivors, came to Toronto “after surviving the worst the world could do to them, and this city gave them the one thing they wanted most: a safe place to raise their kids.”

Among other Canadian musicians getting involved in the mayoral race are Blue Rodeo frontman Jim Cuddy, who appeared on stage to throw his support behind Chow at her reelection campaign kickoff earlier this month.

He performed Blue Rodeo’s song “It Could Happen to You” — about socioeconomic inequality — before introducing Chow.

Other performers included Toronto rapper DijahSB and the Pan Fantasy Steelband, one of the city’s most recognized steel pan ensembles.

Chow’s campaign slogan is “caring, affordable and safe,” referring to the type of city the mayor says she’s built and intends to continue building.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

Alex Nino Gheciu, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney suggests immigration increase is on the horizon in New York Times interview
stories.summary: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney says with Canada's immigration system back under control, the question now is about when to begin a "controlled increase" of the country's population.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By David Baxter, The Canadian Press

Posted September 29, 2026 12:55 pm.

Last Updated October 1, 2026 11:26 am.

OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney says that with Canada’s immigration system back under control, the question now is when to begin a “controlled increase” of the country’s population.

“Now the question starts to become, when do we resume some controlled increase in the population, which is the nature of Canada?” Carney told the New York Times.

“So that will happen, and we just want to make sure that we’ve got it under control.”

Carney made the remark in a recent interview with the New York Times, just over a month before the government is required by law to release its immigration levels plan for the next three years.

Carney said in July the government had “taken back control” of the immigration system after rapid population growth under the government of Prime Minister Justin Trudeau.

A spokesperson for Immigration Minister Lena Diab’s office said the prime minister cited significant declines in the number of new student and temporary worker arrivals in his interview.

The spokesperson also pointed to an October 2025 TD Bank report that suggested reduced immigration is easing housing market pressure, and to a Statistics Canada report tracking low population growth.

When asked if the government is planning any increase this year, the spokesperson said the 2027-2029 immigration levels plan will “ensure immigration remains at sustainable levels.”

That plan must be published by law by Nov. 1, with a grace period if that date doesn’t fall on a parliamentary sitting day. The deadline falls on a Sunday this year.

Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner said now is not the time to plan for more immigration.

“Immigration levels need to go down, not up,” she said on social media.

The government had planned to increase the number of permanent residents being admitted to Canada annually to 500,000. It changed course with the 2024/25 immigration plan and started reducing the intake.

The government also began capping the number of temporary workers and students being admitted to Canada after it said major increases in those populations had contributed to strains on the housing and job markets, health care and other services.

The government has set a goal of reducing the temporary resident population to five per cent of the total population by the end of next year.

The most recent immigration levels plan set a target of admitting 380,000 permanent residents annually between 2026 and 2028.

The government did introduce two temporary measures to welcome about 148,000 more permanent residents over the next two years that are not counted in the broader plan.

The C.D. Howe Institute’s immigration targets council recommends the government continue to reduce the number of arrivals over the next three years. The council recommends admitting 380,000 permanent residents next year, 350,000 in 2028 and 340,000 in 2029.

Parisa Mahboubi, the council’s chair, said it would be better for planning if Canada admitted immigrants at a steady rate, linked to a target percentage of population, instead of changing the plan every few years. She said those periodic shifts in immigration policy led to the government admitting “more than what Canada could absorb.”

She said a sign of a balanced immigration system would be the government no longer having to reduce the intake of temporary immigrants.

The council includes several top academics who study immigration policy, a Trudeau-era deputy minister and former Alberta premier Jason Kenney.

Mikal Skuterud, an economics professor at the University of Waterloo and C.D. Howe panel member, said the panel is still recommending historically high immigration rates at around 0.9 per cent of the population.

Carney told the New York Times Canada’s GDP is shrinking due to limited population growth. Statistics Canada estimated 0.5 per cent population growth year-over year as of July 1.

Skuterud cautioned Carney against listening too closely to “the business lobby” and said his government shouldn’t address a “tight labour market” with immigration.

“Businesses have to compete for scarce labour. And how do they compete? Well, they’ve got to offer higher wages to compete, or more attractive jobs more generally,” he said.

“I worry that Mark Carney, because the business lobby is going to pressure him … that the lobbying from them is going to cause him to make the same mistakes the previous governments have done, that he’s going to see immigration as a solution for businesses. And that’s a problem.”

The council also says it “strongly recommends” the government track all permanent resident admissions through a single target number to clearly indicate how many people it plans to admit in a given year.

It also recommends the government treat the five per cent target for the temporary resident population as a ceiling. It says the goal should be to reduce the number of temporary residents to three per cent of the population.

Statistics Canada estimates non-permanent residents accounted for 6.7 per cent of the population as of July 1.

Skuterud said this suggests the government is going to have a hard time meeting its goal of shrinking that population to five per cent of the total population by the end of next year.

Mahboubi said it’s hard to accurately estimate the non-permanent resident population because of limited exit tracking and the fact that some people overstay their visas or become permanent residents.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

content_blocks.text: “Now the question starts to become, when do we resume some controlled increase in the population, which is the nature of Canada?” Carney told the New York Times.

stories.title: Mother speaks out after video shows fight at London school
stories.summary: A London mother says her two children were assaulted during recess at C.C. Carrothers Public School and is raising concerns about what she describes as ongoing bullying.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Warning: Graphic content

A London, Ont., mother says her two children were assaulted during recess at C.C. Carrothers Public School and is raising concerns about what she describes as ongoing bullying.

Sammy Riley shared a video on social media that she says shows her 11-year-old daughter and nine-year-old son being attacked by other youths at the school.

The graphic video appears to show a young girl being hit by several people before a young boy is kicked in the head.

“I was heartbroken, I was sick to my stomach,” Riley said. “That was a vicious and vile attack.”

Riley says she took her son to hospital, where she says he was diagnosed with a minor concussion.

She also alleges her children have experienced ongoing bullying at the school for the past three years.

“I’ve been dealing with this school for the past three years, with the bullying and the constant everything, it’s just getting brushed under the rug,” she said.

‘No place for violence’: school board

Riley says she previously tried to have her children transferred to another school, but that request was denied because of where they live.

She has since contacted the Thames Valley District School Board, London police and other authorities.

The school board declined a request for an interview but said it is aware of the incident and an investigation is underway.

“The school board takes incidents like these very seriously and there is no place for violence inside or outside of TVDSB classrooms,” the board said in a statement.

Police investigating

The London Police Service says it began investigating on Sept. 24 after receiving a report of an assault at a school earlier that day.

Police say the investigation is in its early stages as they gather information and determine the circumstances surrounding the incident. All those involved are youths.

Police say no charges will be laid, if all parties involved are under the age of 12.

Riley says she has removed her children from the school for the time being but remains concerned about the safety of other students.

“I feel that they’re not doing anything to make it better or a safer situation for any of the children, because I’m not just worried about my own children now,” she said. “I’m worried about all those other children there.”

The Thames Valley District School Board says students are subject to its Code of Conduct, which includes policies and procedures related to suspension, expulsion, and other disciplinary measures.

stories.title: B.C. top court judge rules in favour of operators of illicit-drug compassion club
stories.summary: Lawyers had argued the pair who tested illicit drugs for fentanyl before reselling them offered a safer alternative to toxic supply
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
A B.C. Supreme Court judge has struck down a provision in Canada’s federal drug law that prohibits possession for the purposes of trafficking, ruling that it violates the Charter rights of people who use drugs by preventing access to safer alternatives to toxic street drugs.

The Tuesday ruling was in response to a constitutional challenge by Jeremy Kalicum and Eris Nyx, who were convicted of trafficking for operating a compassion club in Vancouver that provided drug users with such unadulterated alternatives for more than a year.

B.C. Supreme Court Justice Catherine Murray declared Section 5(2) of the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act (Cdsa) to be “of no force or effect,” finding that it infringes on sections 7 and 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which guarantee the right to life, liberty and security of the person, and equal protection under the law.

While the trafficking section of the law was declared invalid, Justice Murray suspended that declaration for six months to allow for legislative amendments. She also stayed the pair’s convictions.

The federal Public Prosecution Service of Canada has 30 days to decide whether to appeal the ruling. Prosecutors are reviewing the judgment and assessing “any potential next steps,” the agency’s spokeswoman Alessia Bongiovanni said.

People in the courtroom gallery cried as the judge read her findings and addressed Mr. Kalicum and Ms. Nyx directly.

“I applaud you for what you’ve done,” Justice Murray said. “I think you should be very proud of yourselves, and it’s people like you who make a difference. And you just did.”

For more than a year, the compassion club founders Mr. Kalicum and Ms. Nyx operated as the Drug User Liberation Front (Dulf), buying illicit heroin, cocaine and methamphetamine from the dark web and testing the products at university labs for fentanyl and other impurities. They then sold the drugs at cost to their group’s 43 members.

At the heart of the ruling is what Justice Murray found to be a fundamental contradiction in Canada’s drug laws: A prohibition intended to protect public health and safety can also criminalize actions that can reduce the risk of overdose. But a critic of B.C.’s approach to drug use said the decision fails to account for broader societal harms and called the judge’s praise of the pair “insulting” to police combating the criminal organizations behind the illicit drug trade.

During a multiweek trial and constitutional challenge that unfolded over nine months, the court heard that Mr. Kalicum and Ms. Nyx regularly engaged with top health, government and police officials as they pursued legal pathways to operate the club.

Vancouver Coastal Health officials provided letters of support as they applied to Health Canada for an exemption from drug laws required to operate. Mr. Kalicum regularly e-mailed top police brass with updates.

The court also got a window into the pair’s motivations; the two have responded to more than 100 overdoses and described panic and distress from having watched friends and co-workers die from drugs.

Health Canada denied their application in April, 2022, saying that acquiring drugs from the dark web was “not a viable option.” Jennifer Saxe, director-general of the controlled substances directorate, said the department “is committed to supporting efforts to expand access to a safer supply” nonetheless, and conveyed appreciation for the pair’s “willingness to think and act creatively in search of new solutions.”

Despite the denial, Dulf began openly operating the compassion club in August, 2022, out of a Vancouver storefront provided by B.C.’s Ministry of Health. The local health authority provided Dulf with up to $200,000 in annual funding for drug-checking and overdose prevention services.

The tides turned in September, 2023, when a magazine article on the pair ignited what Justice Murray called “a maelstrom of activity.” Members of the political opposition rebuked the B.C. NDP for supporting the illegal activity, successfully putting pressure on officials to end funding and the site lease.

In October, 2023, Vancouver Police raided the site and arrested Mr. Kalicum and Ms. Nyx. They were each charged with three counts of possession for the purposes of trafficking and found guilty in November, 2025.

Lawyers Stephanie and Tim Dickson, the married co-counsel for Dulf, called 14 witnesses, including five experts, who testified to the causes of the toxic drug crisis, the inadequacy of the current response, the efficacy and limitations of existing prescribed alternatives programs, and the urgent need for expanded access.

In her ruling, Justice Murray said there are “no legally and practically available safety valves in the Cdsa to support the implementation of a non-medicalized safer supply program,” which she said is “urgently needed to save lives.” She also found that the compassion club “reduced the harms associated with the toxic drug crisis and did not negatively impact the community or public safety.”

Mr. Dickson called the judgment a vindication.

“This case is about the federal and provincial governments’ refusal to implement that life-saving measure, and it is also about how the federal legislation effectively blocks any effort to implement that measure,” he said outside the courthouse.

CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko, who as the former BC United addiction critic in 2023 called for an investigation into the public funding of Dulf, called the ruling worrisome. She argued that Justice Murray gave insufficient weight to the broader harms of the program, including its funding of criminal organizations through dark-web drug purchases.

Ms. Sturko, a former RCMP officer, supports providing pharmaceutical alternatives to illicit drugs through medically supervised programs, but rejects models that make them available outside of a health care setting.

She said governments should focus on recovery-oriented systems of care and urged Ottawa to appeal the decision.

“British Columbians have resoundingly said that they do not think that the answer to our drug crisis is more drugs,” she said.

John Conroy is a Vancouver-area lawyer who was involved in successful challenges at the Supreme Court against parts of the federal drug law, first in 2011 in the Insite case over supervised drug injection and then in 2015 in the Smith case over medical marijuana. The top court, in both cases, ruled parts of the drug legislation violated Section 7 of the Charter, similar to Tuesday’s ruling.

“This is very good news,” Mr. Conroy said of the latest judgment. “It is going to be interesting to see what the government does to rectify the unconstitutionality.”

In the Insite case, the Supreme Court ordered Ottawa to allow the facility to keep operating. In the medical marijuana case, the court said the government had to provide reasonable access for patients for possession and use of cannabis through a health care practitioner.

Editor’s note: The headline on this story has been corrected to state that the ruling was made by a B.C. Supreme Court judge. The story has also been corrected to refer to the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act, not the Canadian Drugs and Substances Act, as previously published.

stories.title: ‘Vicious and vile attack’: Mother speaks out after video shows fight at London school
stories.summary: A London mother says her two children were assaulted during recess at C.C. Carrothers Public School and is raising concerns about what she describes as ongoing bullying.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Warning: Graphic content

A London, Ont., mother says her two children were assaulted during recess at C.C. Carrothers Public School and is raising concerns about what she describes as ongoing bullying.

Sammy Riley shared a video on social media that she says shows her 11-year-old daughter and nine-year-old son being attacked by other youths at the school.

The graphic video appears to show a young girl being hit by several people before a young boy is kicked in the head.

“I was heartbroken, I was sick to my stomach,” Riley said. “That was a vicious and vile attack.”

Riley says she took her son to hospital, where she says he was diagnosed with a minor concussion.

She also alleges her children have experienced ongoing bullying at the school for the past three years.

“I’ve been dealing with this school for the past three years, with the bullying and the constant everything, it’s just getting brushed under the rug,” she said.

‘No place for violence’: school board

Riley says she previously tried to have her children transferred to another school, but that request was denied because of where they live.

She has since contacted the Thames Valley District School Board, London police and other authorities.

The school board declined a request for an interview but said it is aware of the incident and an investigation is underway.

“The school board takes incidents like these very seriously and there is no place for violence inside or outside of TVDSB classrooms,” the board said in a statement.

Police investigating

The London Police Service says it began investigating on Sept. 24 after receiving a report of an assault at a school earlier that day.

Police say the investigation is in its early stages as they gather information and determine the circumstances surrounding the incident. All those involved are youths.

Police say no charges will be laid, if all parties involved are under the age of 12.

Riley says she has removed her children from the school for the time being but remains concerned about the safety of other students.

“I feel that they’re not doing anything to make it better or a safer situation for any of the children, because I’m not just worried about my own children now,” she said. “I’m worried about all those other children there.”

The Thames Valley District School Board says students are subject to its Code of Conduct, which includes policies and procedures related to suspension, expulsion, and other disciplinary measures.

stories.title: Toronto woman says Meta won’t let her talk to a human after killing her accounts
stories.summary: Ottawa — A Toronto woman says Meta permanently shut down her Facebook and Instagram accounts without warning — and her only recourse has been to talk to AI chatbots.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

Posted September 29, 2026 12:33 pm.

Last Updated September 29, 2026 5:10 pm.

OTTAWA — A Toronto woman says Meta permanently shut down her Facebook and Instagram accounts without warning — and her only recourse has been to talk to AI chatbots.

Jasmine Ault told The Canadian Press she has not been able to reach a human being at Meta since the accounts were deactivated on Sept. 24.

She said the company shut down her 20-year-old Facebook account, an Instagram account that dates back to 2011 and another Instagram account dedicated to her dog.

“It’s actually quite scary to think about the trust that we put in the social media platforms that can all be taken away in one day,” she said in an interview.

Ault compared the experience to losing belongings in a fire.

“That’s how it feels. And it’s really upsetting because the hypothetical, the metaphorical fire that I’m referring to, is my memories.”

She said she has lost her social media contacts and is unable to let people know she hasn’t blocked them and isn’t ignoring them.

“There’s a dead end and I can’t even communicate to the people I want to communicate with,” Ault said.

She described the experience as isolating, leaving her unable to look back at memories, connect with people, or see what they are up to through their posts.

Meta didn’t give Ault a reason for shutting down her accounts and said only that her Facebook account “doesn’t follow our rules.”

Ault said she hadn’t posted on Facebook in years, though she did post frequently on Instagram.

She said she suspects someone tried to hack her account because she found a record of suspicious login attempts shortly before the account was deactivated. Meta also had her phone number associated with a person who lives in India.

Ault said she has only been able to talk to Meta’s AI chatbots, which have not been able to resolve the issue. After she requested a review, the chatbot told her it was unsuccessful and her Facebook account had been “permanently disabled.”

She said she hasn’t been able to contact a human being at the company despite signing up for and paying for a verified account, a service that Meta says includes direct help from human agents.

“If Facebook wants to be the main conglomerate for social media, they need to be accessible,” she said.

Media outlets have reported similar experiences among users of Meta’s platforms in the United States. In July, The New York Times profiled several users whose accounts were deleted by AI, and who then had to rely on AI to resolve the issue.

Meta restored some of the accounts after the newspaper flagged them to the company. Two of those accounts had been hacked before they were deactivated.

Markus Giesler, a professor of marketing at York University, said social media platforms have become very important to people’s personal lives and careers.

“We like to think of this as a customer service case when in actuality it’s a case of platform accountability,” he said.

“These platforms have been woven so much into our social fabric, into who we are as individuals and communities, that access to them is really important.”

Giesler said efforts to regulate social media platforms should also address issues like access and being able to talk to a human being at a company.

He said suspending an account can have personal financial consequences.

Ault, who is working full-time as a manager of marketing and communications, said she has used her social media in the past to find clients for her own consulting agency. Without her accounts, that’s not possible at the moment.

“They have nothing to look at. They can’t see my portfolio of work,” she said.

When contacted by The Canadian Press, a Meta spokesperson pointed to a blog post that provides information on how to access account support. It includes an update from March saying Meta was rolling out an AI support assistant.

The spokesperson did not provide any comment or respond to questions — such as how a person with a deactivated account can contact a human being at Meta.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press
