stories.title: Surveillance video expected to play key role in McDermott murder trial
stories.summary: A jury has been selected for a second-degree murder trial at the London courthouse.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
A jury has been selected for a second-degree murder trial at the London courthouse.

After jury selection concluded Monday morning, the Crown delivered its opening address late in the afternoon.

Crown attorney Bianca DiBiase told jurors the case stems from a daylight shooting on Sept. 12, 2018.

According to the Crown, 22-year-old Christopher Clements-Card went to visit his girlfriend in the Bonaventure subdivision and encountered the accused, Zachary McDermott.

“There was a confrontation and Mr. Clements-Card punched Mr. McDermott,” DiBiase told the jury.

The Crown alleges Clements-Card then left and went to a nearby coffee shop.

Jurors were told surveillance video will show McDermott driving into the parking lot moments later.

“Mr. McDermott pulls into the parking lot ... seconds later Mr. McDermott shot Mr. Clements-Card twice,” DiBiase said.

The Crown alleges both bullets entered the victim’s body through his back before McDermott returned to his vehicle and drove away.

Clements-Card was taken to hospital, where he was later pronounced dead.

McDermott, now 26, has pleaded not guilty to second-degree murder.

The court has heard more than 100 people are connected to the case. The trial is expected to last about four weeks.

stories.title: Internal Montreal police records describe ‘radicalized’ subculture among officers
stories.summary: Documents reveal details police chief never shared with the public about what May have led police management to disarm and dismantle a 16-member patrol unit
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
A “radicalized” subculture formed among the ranks of officers at a Montreal police station in a multicultural neighbourhood before it was rocked by allegations of racism and criminal misconduct, newly released internal briefing notes say.

The documents, obtained by The Canadian Press through access to information legislation, are part of a package prepared for the appearance of Fady Dagher, Montreal’s police chief, before a municipal public safety committee in August.

The newly released records reveal details Dagher never shared with the public about what May have led police management to disarm and dismantle a 16-member patrol unit at the station located in the city’s Montréal-Nord borough.

The documents include a copy of Dagher’s presentation to the municipal committee and draft speaking notes describing how police handled the incident at the Montréal-Nord station.

The speaking notes say the reaction inside the force – after some officers blew the whistle about alleged misconduct by their colleagues – reflects how the police force was seeing cracks in a “code of silence” as part of a cultural shift in the organization that left a few officers feeling isolated.

The internal records also confirm police had enough evidence to take action against members of the patrol unit a day before they dismantled the unit and informed the public late on a Friday night in mid-June.

Montreal police chief defends response to allegations of racist behaviour by officers

The draft speaking notes say a subculture was developing within this patrol unit at the station, involving “a marginalized fringe [group] of our employees who were radicalized” and resisted efforts to eliminate misconduct and change the culture of the police force.

“These people reject all the work accomplished by Montreal police in recent years,” said one passage in the internal documents. “They rejected it and, in a way, made that known. They sought to recognize each other.”

The documents do not explain what the force meant by “radicalized,” how many employees it believed the term applied to, or what it meant when it said they had sought to recognize each other.

Dagher and other police officials have not shared details about alleged incidents that led police to dismantle the patrol unit; however, he has confirmed one of the allegations under review is about officers who allegedly cut the hair of racialized civilians to keep as trophies.

Montreal police said they were working on responses to questions from The Canadian Press about the newly released documents but did not immediately provide answers.

However, in a statement published Monday, police said they had sent the evidence to Quebec prosecutors, who will determine whether criminal charges should be laid.

Experts and anti-racism advocates have expressed alarm after being told about the language used in the internal documents.

Editorial: Montreal police must confront racism on the force

The police force “is basically admitting that a process of change will create little cliques of marginalized people that become even more brutal,” said Ted Rutland, a professor of geography at Concordia University who researches policing in Canada. “And that is believable and scary, so it’s interesting that [Dagher] didn’t say that out loud.”

Martin Geoffroy, a sociology professor at Cégep Édouard-Montpetit, says it’s possible that officials were referring to far-right radicalization.

Geoffroy co-authored a federally funded study of far-right groups in Quebec and has studied far-right movements for over 20 years.

But he noted that he was speculating about what had happened within the patrol unit since the documents do not provide a detailed definition or explanation of its description of “radicalized” officers.

He said that his previous research found former police officers and military personnel were among members of far-right groups.

“What we can see in [the documents] is that there is resistance” to efforts to change the culture, he said.

The documents also reveal new details about how employees reacted to the scandal, suggesting that most of the force were upset about the alleged actions of officers at the Montréal-Nord station.

“You have no idea how many Montreal police officers wrote to me expressing shock about what they had learned,” said the speaking notes. “It was to the point where they were furious with their colleagues for dishonouring their uniform and destroying all the work they had tried to accomplish over the years.”

Sixteen Montreal police officers sanctioned over racism allegations

Dave Poitras, a sociologist at Université de Montréal who specializes in radicalization, said police forces are large organizations that can reflect the range of beliefs found in society.

But he cautioned that ideology alone cannot explain the alleged conduct at Station 39. He said the factors that lead someone to commit such acts “obviously go beyond adherence to any ideology.”

stories.title: TD executive sues after being fired for adding Christian symbol to her email signature
stories.summary: TD Insurance VP claims discrimination after losing $210,000 job; bank says she ignored warnings to bring her email signature into compliance
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
A Christian addition to her TD Insurance email signature has cost a senior manager her $210,000-per-year job.

In a statement of claim filed with the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Toronto, Sonja Denobrega seeks more than $400,000 in damages from TD, alleging she was wrongfully dismissed after tagging “I am HIS ✝️” on to the end of her email signature in a stand against a company policy that she says “only allowed for gender/sex identification and allowed no room for other identities.”

Denobrega, the company’s former associate vice-president of underwriting operations, claims that her January 2026 firing was discriminatory, alleging that her termination was based partly on her creed and age.

For its part, TD says that 52-year-old Denobrega’s dismissal had nothing to do with her creed, age or any other protected characteristic under human rights legislation. Instead, the company’s statement of defence says that it had just cause to terminate Denobrega’s employment without notice, as a result of her wilful subordination after she repeatedly ignored warnings to bring her email signature into compliance.

“The Plaintiff’s employment was terminated solely due to her failure to comply with TD’s standards regarding email signatures, which were explained to her on several occasions,” the court document reads. “As a senior employee in a leadership position, the Plaintiff was expected to model compliance with TD’s policies, not to defy them. Her misconduct undermined TD’s ability to rely on her to follow TD procedures and guidelines and resulted in a loss of trust that irreparably damaged the employment relationship.”

According to Denobrega’s claim, she told a HR representative that she wanted TD to remove pronouns from its signature lines. However, the company’s response says that its policy of permitting – but not requiring – employees to identify their pronouns was non-negotiable.

Lawyer sues firm that specializes in workplace inclusion, claiming she was bullied out of job by racism

Former CBC human resources employee sues over workplace so toxic staff were given a 'crying room'

“TD cannot reverse this policy as doing so would be a breach of its obligations under the Canadian Human Rights Act,” the company says in its statement of defence.

None of the allegations in either document have been proven in court. Denobrega did not respond to a request for comment, while a TD spokesperson said the company was unable to say anything further as the matter is before the courts.

Denobrega has more than 25 years of experience in the insurance business, but had only been at TD for a few months following a switch from a rival insurer, before the email-signature saga began in late October 2025.

According to TD’s account of events, that’s when its HR department received a complaint about one of Denobrega’s colleagues, who had modified her email signature to add “Pronouns: I am HIS ✝️,” which the complainant said could be taken as a micro-aggression against members of the Lgbtq+ community.

Denobrega’s claim says that the incident spurred her to offer support to the colleague and look into TD’s Christian-related resources, which ultimately left her unimpressed. Denobrega “felt that there were fewer resources for Christians at TD and more resources for the Lgbt community which she found unfair,” the statement of claim says.

When Denobrega found out that the colleague had been asked to remove the line from her email signature, she took her support a step further, adding the “I am HIS ✝️” line (without the reference to pronouns) to her own in solidarity.

In a meeting with her boss and two HR representatives, Denobrega called for a TD-wide review of email signature compliance, explaining that her problem with company’s policy was that she felt it “only allowed for gender/sex identification and allowed no room for other identities.”

Several more meetings followed, in which TD’s insistence that the email signature additions be removed and Denobrega’s push for a company-wide email signature check and escalation to the CEO were each rebuffed by the opposing sides. However, Denobrega did succeed in convincing TD to send an email blast reminding around 10,000 of its insurance division staff of the current email signature standards, according to her claim.

In court documents, Denobrega is seeking compensation for $235,000 in lost pay and bonuses during a 12-month notice period, as well as a further $210,000 for punitive damages and human rights violations, arguing that TD’s punishment was disproportionate to her alleged misconduct.

“Sonja had no intention of behaving in a manner that would jeopardize her employment” and was “completely unaware that her actions would result in her termination,” Denobrega’s claim reads.

TD’s defence says that the code of conduct it provides to every employee warns that any breach could result in discipline, including termination.

Meanwhile, its email signature standards prohibit personalization through “quotes, taglines, icons, images, slogans, or other personal statements.”

In addition, TD’s email signature rules permit “only limited, optional identifiers such as personal pronouns, consistent with its obligations” under the company’s code of conduct, respectful workplace policy and applicable law, the statement of defence continues.

Toronto employment lawyer Paulette Haynes, who has no involvement in the case, says each party will face its own challenge as the dispute progresses through the court system.

On the issue of alleged discrimination, Denobrega will have the burden of proving a link between her religious views and the reasons for her termination, Haynes explains.

“The bank’s defence says that she has not established that causal nexus,” she adds.

Meanwhile, the onus will shift to TD to back up its claim for “just cause” termination, which allows an employer to fire a worker without paying any severance.

“I always tell my employer clients that it’s an uphill battle when you terminate for just cause,” Haynes says.

“The misconduct has to be so egregious that it basically breaches the employment contract in a fundamental way,” she adds, explaining that proving a case depends heavily on the specific facts.

A judge who ultimately hears the matter will look closely at the context when assessing whether an employer was right to invoke just cause, including the worker’s employment history and disciplinary record, Haynes says.

“It’s a unique case and I’ll be watching closely,” she says.

stories.title: Bed Bath & Beyond Canada relaunches online, hopes to open first store next year
stories.summary: Bed Bath & Beyond Canada's new owner is hoping to use online shopping to wake up the dormant brand before it makes a brick-and-mortar comeback.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — Bed Bath & Beyond Canada’s new owner is hoping to use online shopping to wake up the dormant brand before it makes a brick-and-mortar comeback.

Sleep Country Canada relaunched the home goods retailer Tuesday through an e-commerce website expected to precede stores opening next year.

The online revival comes about a year after Sleep Country purchased the Canadian and U.K. rights to the Bed Bath & Beyond name and logos from Overstock.com.

The online marketplace had picked up the trademarks in 2023, after Bed Bath & Beyond Canada filed for creditor protection and closed its stores amid “dramatic” declines in revenue. The U.S. arm of the company followed suit a few months later.

The retailer’s new Canadian iteration aims to revive the most cherished elements of the brand’s past but also take a more curated approach befitting an evolving market with the rise of e-commerce, new competitors such as H&M Home and Simons, the loss of Hudson’s Bay and sluggish home sales.

“We feel the timing is right and we feel like the market is ready for what we are doing,” Bed Bath & Beyond Canada president Carol Deacon said.

“There are endless options online … and there’s also a lot of other physical retail where there’s some very distinct styles and designs, but we think there’s an opportunity to make sure there’s a bit more choice.”

The new business will stock about 6,000 products in classic Bed Bath & Beyond categories like kitchen, decor, bedroom and bathroom, but also mix in trendier and domestic brands consumers are demanding.

That means shoppers will find KitchenAid, Umbra and Calvin Klein products alongside merchandise from Lacoste, Smeg and Sleep Country affiliates Endy, Bloom, Simba, and Silk and Snow.

While many parts of the Bed Bath & Beyond Canada business won’t dramatically change, two areas are being revamped significantly: furniture and baby.

The company is paring back on furniture, at least initially, because there’s a lot of competitors out there and it’s a category that is difficult for shipping, Deacon said.

With baby, it wants to focus more narrowly on products consumers could use to prepare their home for an infant rather than on everything tots would need.

“For us to come up with an offering across the home that we really were proud and comfortable with, we just went a bit narrower in some areas, but we know we will be expanding over time,” Deacon said.

That expansion will also eventually bring back the brick-and-mortar stores most customers remember Bed Bath & Beyond for.

The brand is still working out its store strategy but is on track to open a first location in late 2027, she said.

When it faltered in 2023, the company had 54 Bed Bath & Beyond stores and 11 BuyBuy Baby locations.

Deacon signalled that the brand is unlikely to have the same kind of store count or hulking properties it once did.

“It will likely be a lot more focused than it was historically for Bed Bath & Beyond in terms of footprint and store size,” she said.

Lisa Hutcheson, J.C. Williams Group retail strategist, thought it made sense for Bed Bath & Beyond Canada to test its revival online before opening small stores.

“There is infrastructure and whatnot required with e-commerce, but (this way) you’re not making those commitments to physical stores and you’re starting to learn more about how the customer is shopping your product,” she said.

What Bed Bath & Beyond will likely find is the retail environment it left is not the one it is returning to. Home sales are down and Canadians are making fewer home goods purchases, Hutcheson pointed out.

Statistics Canada data from July showed furniture, home furnishings, electronics and appliances sales dropped 4.9 per cent from a year prior.

“Mortgage rates aren’t coming down. They’re going up and there’s still that wave of people that have cheap mortgages that are coming up for renewal, so they’re being very, very cautious,” Hutcheson said. “And home furnishings typically are a bit more expensive.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Vancouver transit operator expands into real estate
stories.summary: TransLink hopes to improve transit network connections and create more housing
stories.author: Howard Chai
stories.content:
Vancouver’s major public transit operator is expanding to become a residential and commercial landlord.

As part of its 2022 investment plan, TransLink, which operates Vancouver’s SkyTrain, SeaBus and other public transportation services across the region, announced it will turn its real estate assets into a new non-fare, non-taxation revenue source.

Now known as its Real Estate Development Program, the initiative aims to enhance transit network connections and create more housing to the Metro Vancouver region as it grows.

The program speaks to the value of real estate in British Columbia and is the latest example of a non-real-estate business venturing into real estate development. Other recent examples in Canada include Vancouver-based telecom Telus and local bakery chain Breka Bakery , both of which submitted applications this year to redevelop properties they own into high-rise towers.

In late July, and in partnership with local developer PCI Developments, TransLink broke ground on its first real estate project: A 31-storey tower located at the southeast corner of West Broadway and Arbutus Street in Vancouver’s Kitsilano neighbourhood. Once complete, the property will include 256 at-market rental units, 47 below-market rental units, retail space and a public plaza.

TransLink, a publicly owned agency created by the Province of British Columbia, says it’s taking a long-term approach by developing on excess land that it owns instead of selling it. That approach allows TransLink to play a role in how the projects are built and ensures smoother integration with existing transit infrastructure.

In separate interviews, TransLink CEO Kevin Quinn and PCI Developments president Tim Grant said that the 50/50 partnership emerged because the two companies owned neighbouring properties that could better serve as a single site. The two organizations have had a long-standing relationship since PCI primarily develops large mixed-use hubs that are integrated with transit stations, such as the Marine Gateway in Vancouver and the King George Hub in Surrey.

The TransLink-PCI project comes as British Columbia nears completion on an extension of the SkyTrain’s Millennium Line – connecting Burnaby, Port Moody and Coquitlam to Vancouver’s Broadway corridor, where six new stations are being added. The project will be located across the street from the line’s final terminal, Arbutus Station. A ground-floor retail unit in the new building is also being built so it can be reconfigured into a secondary entrance for Arbutus Station if needed.

Mr. Quinn says the vision for the project was a “complete community” and transportation network, which is why a public plaza will connect the future Arbutus Station to the existing Arbutus Greenway – a nine-kilometre trail for pedestrians and cyclists that runs from near Granville Island to South Vancouver.

Throughout its history, TransLink has bought and sold pieces of real estate, usually in relation to its transit facilities and operations. It also manages retail space in some SkyTrain stations and often co-ordinates with developers that have projects near transit stations.

But developing housing is a completely new endeavour for the transit operator, which has already identified about eight sites that have the potential to be redeveloped, Mr. Quinn says. A few of those projects are already in the pipeline as part of the organization’s Real Estate Development Program, which first started to take shape in 2019.

One of those projects includes a new community development in Surrey, B.C. – a partnership between TransLink and the Surrey City Development Corporation (Scdc) that will see 35 city-owned acres and five TransLink-owned acres transformed into 2,200 news homes, 150,000 square feet of retail space and a new community centre. The property, part of TransLink’s and the Scdc’s Newton Master Development Plan , will be supported by a new rapid-transit bus route and station.

Elsewhere, TransLink is also planning a two-acre project with mixed-use towers rising 14 and 12 storeys near Moodyville Park in North Vancouver, as well as a redevelopment of a nine-acre site next to Coquitlam Central Station in Coquitlam that could accommodate as many as nine towers.

Mr. Quinn says TransLink has received feedback from both North Vancouver and Coquitlam and is now refining its designs, with the aim of returning to both councils with updated proposals in 2027. He says TransLink May also partner with private developers on those projects, recognizing that the company’s expertise is in transportation and not in development.

For TransLink, diversifying its revenue is important to the organization’s long-term growth.

“Certainly, a key part of this is looking at ways to diversify and generate long-term revenue, so we can continue to invest and upgrade our transit system,” says Mr. Quinn. “It allows us to rely a little less on fares and taxation. It’s a new innovative source for us that takes pressure off of other sources.”

Mr. Quinn says TransLink’s three major revenue streams are transit fares, the fuel taxes it collects from remitted gasoline sales and the property taxes it collects from homeowners.

Revenue generated from the organization’s Real Estate Development Program – an estimated $22-million over 10 years, according to Mr. Quinn – would be considered ancillary, along with revenue from other sources such as the development charges collected on new real estate developments in the region.

Asked whether TransLink will stick to rental housing and stay away from condo development, Mr. Quinn says the company is looking at projects on a case-by-case basis, including how they May support the goals of the local municipality.

TransLink is not the first transportation operator in the world to get into the real estate development business. The organization has looked toward Hong Kong’s MTR Corporation and MTR Properties as inspiration, but Mr. Quinn says he hopes to inspire others.

“Getting into the real estate development business is something we’ve wanted to do for quite some time. I’d like to think that we’re leaders in North America in this space – this new revenue stream – and we’re really proud of that,” he says.

Editor’s note: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that TranskLink's first real estate project, in partnership with PCI developments, is located at the southwest corner of West Broadway and Arbutus Street in Vancouver’s Kitsilano neighbourhood. It is on the southeast corner.

The TransLink-PCI project comes as British Columbia nears completion on an extension of the SkyTrain’s Millennium Line – connecting Burnaby, Port Moody and Coquitlam to Vancouver’s Broadway corridor, where six new stations are being added. The project will be located across the street from the line’s final terminal, Arbutus Station. A ground-floor retail unit in the new building is also being built so it can be reconfigured into a secondary entrance for Arbutus Station if needed.

Mr. Quinn says the vision for the project was a “complete community” and transportation network, which is why a public plaza will connect the future Arbutus Station to the existing Arbutus Greenway – a nine-kilometre trail for pedestrians and cyclists that runs from near Granville Island to South Vancouver.

Throughout its history, TransLink has bought and sold pieces of real estate, usually in relation to its transit facilities and operations. It also manages retail space in some SkyTrain stations and often co-ordinates with developers that have projects near transit stations.

But developing housing is a completely new endeavour for the transit operator, which has already identified about eight sites that have the potential to be redeveloped, Mr. Quinn says. A few of those projects are already in the pipeline as part of the organization’s Real Estate Development Program, which first started to take shape in 2019.

One of those projects includes a new community development in Surrey, B.C. – a partnership between TransLink and the Surrey City Development Corporation (Scdc) that will see 35 city-owned acres and five TransLink-owned acres transformed into 2,200 news homes, 150,000 square feet of retail space and a new community centre. The property, part of TransLink’s and the Scdc’s Newton Master Development Plan , will be supported by a new rapid-transit bus route and station.

Elsewhere, TransLink is also planning a two-acre project with mixed-use towers rising 14 and 12 storeys near Moodyville Park in North Vancouver, as well as a redevelopment of a nine-acre site next to Coquitlam Central Station in Coquitlam that could accommodate as many as nine towers.

Mr. Quinn says TransLink has received feedback from both North Vancouver and Coquitlam and is now refining its designs, with the aim of returning to both councils with updated proposals in 2027. He says TransLink May also partner with private developers on those projects, recognizing that the company’s expertise is in transportation and not in development.
For TransLink, diversifying its revenue is important to the organization’s long-term growth.

“Certainly, a key part of this is looking at ways to diversify and generate long-term revenue, so we can continue to invest and upgrade our transit system,” says Mr. Quinn. “It allows us to rely a little less on fares and taxation. It’s a new innovative source for us that takes pressure off of other sources.”
Mr. Quinn says TransLink’s three major revenue streams are transit fares, the fuel taxes it collects from remitted gasoline sales and the property taxes it collects from homeowners.

Revenue generated from the organization’s Real Estate Development Program – an estimated $22-million over 10 years, according to Mr. Quinn – would be considered ancillary, along with revenue from other sources such as the development charges collected on new real estate developments in the region.

Asked whether TransLink will stick to rental housing and stay away from condo development, Mr. Quinn says the company is looking at projects on a case-by-case basis, including how they May support the goals of the local municipality.

TransLink is not the first transportation operator in the world to get into the real estate development business. The organization has looked toward Hong Kong’s MTR Corporation and MTR Properties as inspiration, but Mr. Quinn says he hopes to inspire others.

“Getting into the real estate development business is something we’ve wanted to do for quite some time. I’d like to think that we’re leaders in North America in this space – this new revenue stream – and we’re really proud of that,” he says.

Editor’s note: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that TranskLink's first real estate project, in partnership with PCI developments, is located at the southwest corner of West Broadway and Arbutus Street in Vancouver’s Kitsilano neighbourhood. It is on the southeast corner.

stories.title: London police chief orders investigation after video surfaces of officers with alcohol, firearm
stories.summary: London’s police chief has ordered an investigation after a video surfaced appearing to show officers leaving a restaurant and entering an unmarked police vehicle with alcohol visible inside and a service-issued firearm stored in a manner that raised concerns.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
London’s police chief has ordered an investigation after a video surfaced appearing to show officers leaving a restaurant and entering an unmarked police vehicle with alcohol visible inside and a service-issued firearm stored in a manner that raised concerns.

In a statement, London Police Service Chief Thai Truong said the incident took place in Toronto on June 24, 2026, following a police funeral.

Truong said he personally reviewed the video and immediately directed that the matter be referred to Toronto police for a criminal investigation into the handling and storage of the firearm.

Once the criminal investigation is complete, the conduct of the officers involved will also be reviewed under the Community Safety and Policing Act, the statement said.

One senior officer has been suspended with pay pending the outcome of the investigations.

According to Truong, the decision on suspension should not be viewed as minimizing the seriousness of the allegations, noting that the legislative framework governing police discipline has not met the threshold required for a suspension without pay at this stage.

“Police officers are entrusted with significant authority and responsibilities,” said Truong. “With that comes an expectation that we will conduct ourselves in a manner that maintains the confidence of the community we serve.”

He added that those expectations apply to all members of the service and are particularly important for officers in leadership positions.

Truong said there will be no further comment on the evidence, citing the need to protect the integrity of the investigations, but said additional information would be released when appropriate.

No criminal charges have been announced and investigators have not released the identities of the officers involved.

stories.title: Flu Season Begins in Swph Region
stories.summary: Flu season is off to an early start in Oxford, Elgin and St. Thomas.
stories.author: Marcie Culbert
stories.content:
News Home

Tuesday, 29 September 2026 06:06

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

Flu season is off to an early start in Oxford, Elgin and St. Thomas.

Swph - Southwestern Public Health is reporting its first lab confirmed case of the flu this season.

This means the virus is circulating through Oxford, Elgin, and St. Thomas, marking an early to the flu season.

Medical Officer of Health Dr. Ninh Tran is encourging everyone take steps to protect themselves.

"Stay home when you are sick, cover coughs and sneezes, wash your hands frequently, clean high-touch surfaces regularly, and consider wearing a mask if you have symptoms or are visiting people at higher risk. These actions can help protect you, your family, and the most vulnerable members of our community."

He adds the flu vaccine should arrive in the province shortly.

"When flu vaccine becomes available this season, getting vaccinated will be an important additional layer of protection against serious illness."

The flu shot will be offered to high risk groups and priority populations first. All Ontarians over the age of six months old will be able to receive the publicly funded vaccine starting October 26th.

The common flu symptoms include fever, cough, sore throat, fatigue, body aches, and chills.

Oxford MP Holds Food Drive for the County The need for items at food banks is high, and Oxford MP Arpan Khanna wants to help.

New Award Program Coming to Woodstock Volunteers in the Friendly City will have the opportunity to be honoured with a new program being launched.

Pjhl Preview - Oct 2nd and Oct 3rd The Braves, the Merchants and the Trojans will spend the weekend in Oxford County.

Navy Vets Preview - Oct 2nd to Oct 4th Woodstock will host LaSalle tonight, Listowel tomorrow night, and visit Chatham Sunday night.

Woodstock Chamber Hosts Candidate Open House It was an opportunity for Woodstock residents to chat with the candidates in the upcoming municipal election.

Norwich Business Owner Shares Development Charges Dilemma Jade Horinga's development charges estimate went from $0, to $2,800, to $29,000.

Mock Emergency Drill Hosted in Tillsonburg Woodingford Lodge in Tillsonburg held a mock emergency drill this morning.

Thefts Under Investigation in Tavistock The Oxford OPP are investigating after valuables were taken from multiple vehicles in Tavistock.

New Family Doctor Coming to Woodstock Oxfordia Medical Centre will be getting a new Family Doctor.

Oxford MP Talks New Role and Town Hall Oxford County MP Arpan Khanna stopped by the Heart FM Studio and took the time to discuss a few topics.

Fall Fest Returns to Downtown Norwich Fall Fest will takevover downtown Norwich on Saturday.

Operation Full Plate in Oxford County Members of the OPP auxiliary unit will be collecting donations for local food banks.

Cyclist Killed in Thames Centre Crash The victim has been identified as a 34-year-old from Thames Centre.

Minimum Wage Increases in Ontario Ontario's minimum has increased to $17.95 per hour.

Tip Tuesday with the Oxford OPP - September 2026 Constable Randi Crawford called the Heart FM studio for the September edition of Tip Tuesday this morning.

Suspect Wanted in Dirt Bike Hit and Run Police say an OPP officer was hit by a dirt bike during an unrelated traffic stop Friday afternoon.

Stelco to Lay Off Hundreds of Workers The steelmaker says it will indefinitely idle finishing operations at its Hamilton plant.

National Day for Truth and Reconciliation in Oxford County A sunrise ceremony will be held in Woodstock and Heart FM will air special programming throughout the day.

A Record Breaking Hike for Hospice in Woodstock Up to 415 hikers attended the event in Roth Park on September 19th.

Interview with a City Councillor - September 28th, 2026 Councillor Liz Wismer-Van Meer talked about the taxi licensing and community grant applicants during the Heart FM Morning Show.

stories.title: Parti Quebecois ready to ‘put the pedal to the metal’ in final week of election campaign
stories.summary: If Quebec party leaders stick to their promise, the final stretch of the province’s election campaign will be a busy one.
stories.author: Genevieve Beauchemin
stories.content:
Montreal - If Quebec party leaders stick to their promise, the final stretch of the province’s election campaign will be a busy one.

Parti Quebecois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has been leading in the polls for three years and is now eyeing a majority in the National Assembly.

“Put the pedal to the metal, isn’t that what they say in Nascar?” said Plamondon. “Yeah, we go all the way.”

With a majority, Plamondon would have the green light to go ahead with his promise of holding a referendum in his first mandate. He has been working to convince Quebecers not to fear the prospect of independence.

“I think they shouldn’t be afraid of that,” Plamondon told reporters at a stop in Ulverton, Que. “Hundreds of nations are governing themselves with their own government and their own institutions, and they’re doing it very well.”

But he also said that the decision before Quebecers now is not whether the province should be a country, but who should lead the province after the Oct. 5 election.

stories.title: Supreme Court takes on more cases than in recent years, reversing trend
stories.summary: The top court has been hearing fewer appeals this decade, prompting concern from some in the legal community
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada is busier than it has been since the late 2010s, an increased workload that comes after criticism that the top court was not producing enough judgments.

The court each year receives several hundred applications to have cases heard in Ottawa, but in the 2020s the judges have said yes to only 7 per cent of the requests.

This year, however, the court is saying yes much more often. It has agreed to 13 per cent of appeal applications.

Last week, the Supreme Court said yes to two more applications, bringing the number of new cases for 2026 to 41. This is the highest number of new appeals granted since 2018, when the court agreed to hear 42 new cases.

The judges do not reveal why they say yes or no to new cases, but the Supreme Court Act outlines the two main criteria: whether a top court ruling would answer questions of national importance, or settle conflicting judgments in the lower courts.

Supreme Court produces fewer rulings than in past years

Concern among lawyers about the number of cases the Supreme Court hears each year centres on worries about the development and clarity of the law across the country. Fewer rulings from the top court means more legal questions are left unresolved.

The Supreme Court aims to hear as many cases as possible, said Daniel Byma, executive legal officer and chief of staff to Chief Justice Richard Wagner.

“The court does not set targets for the number of [appeal] applications it grants in a given year,” Mr. Byma said in response to questions about the court agreeing to more cases than in recent years.

While the court’s workload has increased this year, it remains lower than in the 2010s. The Supreme Court in the 2020s has agreed to hear an annual average of 34 cases – two-thirds the average of 52 in the 2010s.

Chief Justice Wagner, at his annual press conference in June, said the court is projecting its workload to rise back to the levels seen before the COVID-19 pandemic started in 2020.

Justice Mahmud Jamal in February was asked about trends in the court’s workload after a speech about the judges’ collegial decision-making.

“We aren’t looking to take fewer cases,” Justice Jamal said. “Quite the opposite.”

One of Canada’s largest law libraries is on the move along with the court it serves

Questions about the court’s output have spiked at times over the decades. The court heard more than 100 cases a year for most of the 1990s.

That workload was seen as overly heavy, as the judges sometimes struggled to produce timely judgments, but when it dipped in the mid-2000s to around 60 cases a year, some lawyers worried the court was hearing too few cases.

The more recent decline in the 2020s sparked renewed worries that the Supreme Court wasn’t delivering enough judgments on important issues of law across the country.

Lawyer Paul-Erik Veel of Lenczner Slaght LLP in Toronto has tracked trends in the court’s workload in recent years. In a report in June, he highlighted the sudden increase in the percentage of appeal applications the court has agreed to hear.

Mr. Veel, as he has said in the past, argued that a shorter list of Supreme Court cases has real consequences: “It leaves more legal questions left unresolved.”

Mr. Veel’s analysis noted the court is taking on more cases in public law, which involve constitutional questions and other issues, and private law, which include disputes between individuals or businesses.

He said the shift to hearing more cases, and a wider range, May suggest judges on the Supreme Court are looking to take on issues outside the usual fare of criminal law.

“If that is right, that would be a welcome development,” Mr. Veel said.

Supreme Court rejects strict deadlines during criminal sentencing

Chris Sewrattan, a Toronto criminal defence lawyer who closely follows the work of the Supreme Court, said the judges May simply be seeing more cases of national importance this year than they had in recent years. He said he doubts the increased workload is a response to criticisms in the legal community and noted the Supreme Court’s varying number of judgments has not captured the attention of Canadians.

He also said the court has been busy in recent years, even with fewer cases, given the length of many of its written decisions.

“If we are entering a new era of more judgments and shorter decisions, I welcome the change,” Mr. Sewrattan said.

The court’s fall session begins in early October, and the schedule is packed with 27 hearings.

The dispute that will likely garner the most attention is set for Nov. 9 and 10, when the court will hear four appeals on the federal government’s 2020 firearms regulations. Those rules effectively prohibited more than 1,500 firearms that had previously been legal for licensed ownership and use. Ottawa has described the banned guns as assault weapons that have been used in mass shootings.

Legal challenges against the gun prohibitions have twice failed, first at the Federal Court in 2023 and then again at the Federal Court of Appeal last year.

The Supreme Court agreed to hear the four firearms appeals in March this year.

stories.title: Why Canadian menswear retailers are betting big on luxury
stories.summary: With the middle of the market getting squeezed, the menswear landscape appears to be splitting into affordable basics and expensive purchases worth seeking out
stories.author: Ben Kriz
stories.content:
Canadian retail has seen better days. After nine years in business, Nordstrom left the country in 2023, and the collapse of the 355-year-old Hudson’s Bay two years later left a giant hole in the nation’s retail landscape. But amid the headline-making closures, an unlikely market is attracting new investment: premium and luxury menswear.

Harry Rosen just opened an ambitious new 38,000-square-foot, three-storey Yorkville flagship 200 metres away from its longstanding Bloor Street location in Toronto, after renovating a handful of other stores across the country. Holt Renfrew expanded its Bloor Street menswear space, Queen Street fashion boutique Absolutely Fabrics introduced menswear at its newly opened Summerhill location and Winnipeg’s tailoring-focused Modern Ambition opened in Yorkville over the summer.

Harry Rosen’s new store is a clear example of how luxury retailers are thinking about physical space. The location features a bar and lounge, an outdoor patio and a private-client floor with its own bar, fitting rooms and space for wedding parties, trunk shows and brand events. The sales floor, meanwhile, will display fewer items displayed in more complete looks, with additional inventory kept out of sight.

For the brand’s president Ian Rosen, there’s a lot of confidence behind the investment. “When we put money into a store, it pays us back,” he said. “The client gets more excited, and new clients show up as well.”

Jonathan Elias, co-owner of Toronto menswear boutique Lost and Found, echoed that sentiment. Three years ago, the 15-year-old business moved to a new, larger location to handle increased sales. Along with the new space came higher-priced brands such as cult Japanese label Auralee (jeans, $905 ; button-up shirts, $735 ) and $1,200 heritage shoes from J.M. Weston and Alden.

“There’s been this natural progression of the store itself maturing and our taste maturing, and seeing a need in the market for higher-end products,” Elias said.

These openings coupled with high-profile closings suggest that retail’s difficulties aren’t being felt evenly. As the middle of the market gets squeezed, Canadian menswear appears to be splitting into affordable basics and expensive purchases worth seeking out, saving for and, crucially, leaving the house to experience. As Rosen put it, “I see our competition as, ‘I could do this sitting on the couch.’”

A recent report from global commercial real estate services firm JLL describes Canadian retail as an increasingly permanent barbell, with value and premium businesses gaining ground while the middle struggles. Dollar- and thrift-store openings more than doubled in 2025 while luxury investment continued to be concentrated in specific destinations such as Vancouver’s Oakridge Park and Robson-Alberni corridor.

The widening wealth gap helps explain the divide; the report states that the wealthiest 20 per cent of Canadian households now control nearly two-thirds of the country’s net worth, while the least wealthy 40 per cent hold just 3.1 per cent.

Lost and Found’s Elias sees that playing out on the ground, with customers bypassing mid-tier products. “People are really conscious of how they spend their money, and I don’t think that they’re going to accept mediocrity any more,” he said.

He also noted that he’s seen a “hyper-education” over the last six to eight years with customers learning more deeply about fabrics and construction. “For a lot of people now, it is their passion, and they enjoy it, and they want to save up to get something aspirational.”

Rosen has witnessed a similar trend with Harry Rosen’s custom suit business. “It’s on fire,” he said. “People want one-of-one pieces. They want to design it themselves. When they’re paying in the premium price points, they want to feel like, ‘This is for me.’”

Louis Cheslaw, a menswear writer and contributing editor at GQ, offered another explanation for the shift: The cheap stuff isn’t actually that cheap any more. When a pair of relatively ordinary jeans costs three figures, he said, consumers might decide they “May as well get something really great.” Cheslaw argued that high prices also encourage the kind of hyper-education Elias described.

“When it costs that much, you need to understand why,” he said. “You don’t want to feel like you’re making a reckless decision, so you want to understand what you’re paying for. I think learning about the fabric and construction can sometimes be as much about justification as interest.”

The increasingly knowledgeable menswear customer isn’t confined to Canada. A number of Canadian boutiques have achieved international recognition as tastemakers, building customer bases around specific buys that shoppers May not be able to find locally.

Last month, Absolutely Fabrics was included in the Business of Fashion’s Best Fashion Stores in the World . The owners of curated Vancouver shop Neighbour, Saager Dilawri and Karyna Schultz, made the Business of Fashion 500 , the publication’s annual list of people shaping the global fashion industry. Fashion media brand HighSnobiety called it “ menswear’s most important store .”

That online reach hasn’t lessened the need for brick-and-mortar investment. In March, Neighbour opened a new 3,000-square-foot space in Vancouver’s Gastown next to its womenswear store. Edmonton’s Henry Singer moved into an elaborate new ICE District flagship in 2024, complete with a barbershop and an Italian-style cocktail bar. Malls including Oakridge Park in Vancouver, Royalmount in Montreal and Yorkdale in Toronto continue to attract luxury brands such as Rolex, Tom Ford and Saint Laurent. And high-end streetwear brand Bape opened on Vancouver’s Alberni Street earlier this year.

Even stores with popular online shops see the IRL experience as the most important part of the equation. “There’s no way that you can mimic the in-store experience online,” said Elias. “You can’t go in, you can’t meet our staff, you can’t hang out with us, you can’t see the space, you can’t touch the clothes. We want it to be somewhere where you can kind of get lost and find things that you would never see before.”

Harry Rosen is applying the same logic nationwide. “Every time that you leave the home and go to a store, it has to be a value-add experience,” Rosen said. “It has to be exciting and it has to be interesting. [The new flagship] definitely accomplishes that.”

These experiences can turn an expensive purchase into more than a transaction. Menswear writer Cheslaw thinks that for some consumers, the appeal of building a lasting wardrobe May also reflect a general feeling of stalled adulthood.

“Maybe you can’t buy a house. Maybe you can’t afford to have kids yet,” he said. “But you can at least start building a collection of clothing that you won’t have to repurchase because it lasts a long time. There’s something grounding about that.”

Dollar- and thrift-store openings more than doubled in 2025 while luxury investment continued to be concentrated in specific destinations such as Vancouver’s Oakridge Park and Robson-Alberni corridor.

The widening wealth gap helps explain the divide; the report states that the wealthiest 20 per cent of Canadian households now control nearly two-thirds of the country’s net worth, while the least wealthy 40 per cent hold just 3.1 per cent.

Lost and Found’s Elias sees that playing out on the ground, with customers bypassing mid-tier products. “People are really conscious of how they spend their money, and I don’t think that they’re going to accept mediocrity any more,” he said.

He also noted that he’s seen a “hyper-education” over the last six to eight years with customers learning more deeply about fabrics and construction. “For a lot of people now, it is their passion, and they enjoy it, and they want to save up to get something aspirational.”

Rosen has witnessed a similar trend with Harry Rosen’s custom suit business. “It’s on fire,” he said. “People want one-of-one pieces. They want to design it themselves. When they’re paying in the premium price points, they want to feel like, ‘This is for me.’”

Louis Cheslaw, a menswear writer and contributing editor at GQ, offered another explanation for the shift: The cheap stuff isn’t actually that cheap any more. When a pair of relatively ordinary jeans costs three figures, he said, consumers might decide they “May as well get something really great.” Cheslaw argued that high prices also encourage the kind of hyper-education Elias described.

“When it costs that much, you need to understand why,” he said. “You don’t want to feel like you’re making a reckless decision, so you want to understand what you’re paying for. I think learning about the fabric and construction can sometimes be as much about justification as interest.”

The increasingly knowledgeable menswear customer isn’t confined to Canada. A number of Canadian boutiques have achieved international recognition as tastemakers, building customer bases around specific buys that shoppers May not be able to find locally.

Last month, Absolutely Fabrics was included in the Business of Fashion’s Best Fashion Stores in the World . The owners of curated Vancouver shop Neighbour, Saager Dilawri and Karyna Schultz, made the Business of Fashion 500 , the publication’s annual list of people shaping the global fashion industry. Fashion media brand HighSnobiety called it “ menswear’s most important store .”

That online reach hasn’t lessened the need for brick-and-mortar investment. In March, Neighbour opened a new 3,000-square-foot space in Vancouver’s Gastown next to its womenswear store. Edmonton’s Henry Singer moved into an elaborate new ICE District flagship in 2024, complete with a barbershop and an Italian-style cocktail bar. Malls including Oakridge Park in Vancouver, Royalmount in Montreal and Yorkdale in Toronto continue to attract luxury brands such as Rolex, Tom Ford and Saint Laurent. And high-end streetwear brand Bape opened on Vancouver’s Alberni Street earlier this year.

Even stores with popular online shops see the IRL experience as the most important part of the equation. “There’s no way that you can mimic the in-store experience online,” said Elias. “You can’t go in, you can’t meet our staff, you can’t hang out with us, you can’t see the space, you can’t touch the clothes. We want it to be somewhere where you can kind of get lost and find things that you would never see before.”

Harry Rosen is applying the same logic nationwide. “Every time that you leave the home and go to a store, it has to be a value-add experience,” Rosen said. “It has to be exciting and it has to be interesting. [The new flagship] definitely accomplishes that.”

These experiences can turn an expensive purchase into more than a transaction. Menswear writer Cheslaw thinks that for some consumers, the appeal of building a lasting wardrobe May also reflect a general feeling of stalled adulthood.

“Maybe you can’t buy a house. Maybe you can’t afford to have kids yet,” he said. “But you can at least start building a collection of clothing that you won’t have to repurchase because it lasts a long time. There’s something grounding about that.”

content_blocks.text: Canadian retail has seen better days. After nine years in business, Nordstrom left the country in 2023, and the collapse of the 355-year-old Hudson’s Bay two years later left a giant hole in the nation’s retail landscape. But amid the headline-making closures, an unlikely market is attracting new investment: premium and luxury menswear.

Harry Rosen just opened an ambitious new 38,000-square-foot, three-storey Yorkville flagship 200 metres away from its longstanding Bloor Street location in Toronto, after renovating a handful of other stores across the country. Holt Renfrew expanded its Bloor Street menswear space, Queen Street fashion boutique Absolutely Fabrics introduced menswear at its newly opened Summerhill location and Winnipeg’s tailoring-focused Modern Ambition opened in Yorkville over the summer.

Harry Rosen’s new store is a clear example of how luxury retailers are thinking about physical space. The location features a bar and lounge, an outdoor patio and a private-client floor with its own bar, fitting rooms and space for wedding parties, trunk shows and brand events. The sales floor, meanwhile, will display fewer items displayed in more complete looks, with additional inventory kept out of sight.

stories.title: After a stalled start, a lasting match
stories.summary: Paulina Munroe and Arjun Chelliah married in a Hindu-Western ceremony at Toronto’s Liberty Grand
stories.author: Andrea Yu
stories.content:
In our new Weddings series, Canadian couples tell us how they went from first dates to walking down the aisle

Paulina Munroe and Arjun Chelliah’s relationship began with a false start. They matched on Hinge in September, 2023, but the conversation fizzled out shortly after.

“People might use the term ‘ghosted,’” said Munroe, admitting that she didn’t respond to Chelliah’s follow-up message. They unmatched, only to rematch a few weeks later. “This time, I decided to skip the back-and-forth,” said Chelliah. He asked Munroe, 36, out on a date to Astoria, a bar on Toronto’s Queen Street West.

There, the couple learned about each other’s families – Munroe’s back in Nova Scotia, and Chelliah’s Hindu Sri Lankan culture. “In person, I felt very comfortable with him,” Munroe said. “I was definitely looking forward to a second date.”

They bonded over their shared values: A close connection to family, a love of entertaining and entrepreneurial spirits: Munroe is a lawyer and life coach, and Chelliah, 39, is an accountant and real estate investor. Early on, the couple shared their mutual desire for marriage and kids one day. “It wasn’t meant to be a heavy conversation,” said Chelliah. “It was more about making sure we were on the same page about our relationship goals right from the start.”

Munroe loved how Chelliah would plan thoughtful dates at his house. He would cook her elaborate meals, setting the table with candles. “He’s an amazing cook and cocktail maker, and at those dinners, we just got to get to know each other deeply,” she said.

Six months later, in March, 2024, Chelliah and Munroe made their relationship official. Things progressed swiftly after that. They met each other’s parents and siblings, then spent Christmas together. “I could immediately see that our families shared many of the same values,” Chelliah said. “It made it easy to imagine our lives becoming intertwined.” Over the holidays, he was scrolling on his phone when an engagement-related post popped up. He asked Munroe what kind of ring she wanted.

“I felt certain that he was the one for me after our lives fit so perfectly with each other,” she said. “Our favourite time together was always just the two of us before bed or having coffee in the mornings.”

Chelliah purchased a ring – an oval solitaire diamond on a thin gold band – and proposed in February, 2025, at the Toronto Reference Library. “It’s where Paulina used to study for her bar exams, and I used to walk around there at lunchtime when I worked in the area,” Chelliah said. He sourced a book safe with a combination lock, planted it on a shelf and asked a friend to guard it. When Chelliah returned with Munroe, he unlocked it, revealing the ring. “I was so surprised because he was cool as a cucumber,” Munroe said. “It was just so special, and it was private and intimate.”

Before the proposal, Chelilah had already done some research on wedding venues, and he compiled a spreadsheet comparing prices and dates. “It’s kind of funny because it’s the opposite of what happens,” he said, referring to gendered expectations around wedding planning. They chose the Liberty Grand Entertainment Complex, which they loved for its lakeside location, and lucked out with a September date that year.

Munroe and Chelliah settled on a guest list of 135 and a two-part ceremony: First, a Hindu ceremony honouring the groom’s roots, followed by a traditional Western ceremony. “Arjun’s dad’s side is Hindu, and I did my yoga teacher training in India,” said Munroe. “Yoga shares a lot of the same foundations of Hinduism.”

Both events would take place in the Liberty Grand’s private courtyard, separated by a 30-minute Champagne intermission and followed by cocktail hour in the venue’s foyer and dinner in the ballroom. The couple DIYed some of their decorations, sourcing lilies from Costco, buying candles and making name tags and a seating chart on a decorative mirror. In the midst of planning, Munroe moved into Chelliah’s semi in Toronto’s Junction neighbourhood.

With many of their guests flying in for the celebration, the couple hosted a welcome dinner at the CN Tower the evening before. “It was a Blue Jays playoff game, so we got to see a home run from up there,” Munroe said.

The morning of the celebration, Chelliah delivered decorations to the venue while Munroe got ready at the couple’s home. For the Hindu ceremony, she dressed in a deep pink sari and bridal jewellery, which Chelliah’s sister helped source from India and Sri Lanka. Chelliah dressed in a Champagne-hued sherwani – a traditional South Asian coat – with matching trousers from RSM Silks.

The Hindu ceremony consisted of 10 rituals. The bride’s mother fed the groom yogurt and honey to symbolize love and care for him, the bride and groom placed garlands on each other to signify their mutual acceptance in marriage, and the groom placed two rings on the bride’s toes for fertility.

For the Western ceremony, the bride changed into a ball gown-style dress from the Brides’ Project, an organization that sells donated wedding dresses to support cancer charities. The groom wore an ivory jacket and black pants from Tip Top. Justice Gloria Epstein, a judge who paved the way for same-sex marital rights in Canada, officiated the ceremony. The couple wrote their own vows. “There were a lot of tears,” said Chelliah. “Pretty much everyone was crying, including us.”

Cocktail hour featured oysters and lobster rolls – a nod to Munroe’s East Coast upbringing. A classic dinner followed: Caesar salad, parmesan tortellini, shrimp and steak and a chocolate hazelnut cake for dessert. Then the dance party kicked off, complete with glowsticks and a handheld carbon dioxide blaster to create atmospheric fog. “We wanted it to feel like a club,” Chelliah said.

Three days later, the newlyweds embarked on a three-week honeymoon to the south of France and the Dolomites in Italy. Since then, they’ve been relishing the simplicity of married life. “We’re so lucky to be best friends and that we love doing everything together,” Munroe said. “We’ll sit in the garden and go for walks in our neighbourhood.”

Their lives are set to change again soon, as they’re welcoming a child due in March, 2027. “The baby’s room is ready,” said Munroe. “Everything is happening with a lot of ease and excitement.”

Date: Sept. 27, 2026

Photography: Blue Dream Weddings

Venue and food: Liberty Grand Entertainment Complex

Officiants: Justice Gloria Epstein, Acharya Guruji

Florals: Costco, Leavenworth Floral, Babu Florist

Cake: Kay’s Cakes

DJ: House Party

Munroe’s dress: the Brides’ Project

Munroe’s hair and makeup: Robson Oliveira

Chelliah’s sherwani: RSM Silks

Chelliah’s suit: Tip Top

stories.title: B.C. Conservative turned New Democrat, Boultbee, won't run for re-election
stories.summary: A high-profile legislator who says she was “threatened, spat at, disowned, and abused” for crossing the floor to the British Columbia NDP this summer won’t be running again in the provincial election.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria — A high-profile legislator who says she was “threatened, spat at, disowned, and abused” for crossing the floor to the British Columbia NDP this summer won’t be running again in the provincial election.

Amelia Boultbee, who was first elected as a B.C. Conservative, says in a statement she can’t marshal the necessary resources to give the B.C. New Democrats a “fair shot” in her Penticton-Summerland riding.

Boultbee says she’s stepping aside “to make way for a more winnable candidate” in the Oct. 24 election.

The legislator from B.C.’s southern interior was first elected in October 2024 as a Conservative, only to leave that party a year later over ideological disagreements to sit as an Independent, before joining the New Democrats in July.

Boultbee’s move boosted the NDP caucus to 48 members, increasing Premier David Eby’s parliamentary majority to two seats, but it also drew criticism from her constituents.

She says in her statement that crossing the floor was incredibly difficult and carried considerable consequences, personally, professionally and politically.

“I have been threatened, spat at, disowned and abused in ways both public and private,” she said.

She says her primary reason for crossing the floor was to “join a credible and stable party,” something the B.C. Conservative Party lacked.

“I’m confident that I did the right thing for the right reasons when I made that decision,” she says.

“Not only that, but I was able to marshal the better resources for my community during the Bald Range wildfire, because I was able to access the deep bench of seasoned staff available to me through the (B.C. New Democrats).”

Thousands of people were forced to evacuate from Summerland and surrounding communities in August as the fast-moving fire raced through the area.

She is the sixth member of the governing NDP caucus to announce that she won’t run in the election, following announcements by Lana Popham, Ravi Kahlon, Kelly Greene, Brenda Bailey and George Chow.

Boultbee says she would have liked to continue as legislator, but “politics is hard and it’s not always fair” in framing her decision as a necessary move in the current political climate.

She says her decision to step down is about “ensuring this community and province are protected from the kind of right-wing, Trump-style populism and grave dysfunction on full display” among the Conservatives.

“My full confidence continues to rest with Premier Eby and his caucus,” she says.

“While the economic policies need work, this is being done and can be done. It’s fixable.

“The problems with the B.C. Conservatives are not fixable, maybe not ever and certainly not on the timeline British Columbia needs.”

B.C. Conservative leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay quit just days before David Eby called an election after more than a dozen of her caucus members left, citing her leadership.

Lorne Doerkson took over the job as interim leader of the party.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

Wolfgang Depner, The Canadian Press
