stories.title: The persistence of Paul St-Pierre Plamondon brings the PQ to a critical point
stories.summary: The promise of a referendum put the Parti Québécois Leader on centre stage. He might just get the chance to deliver
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
When he was a teenager, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon went to Denmark and organized a referendum.

Another exchange student might have preferred to blend into the background at a foreign upper-secondary school thousands of kilometres from home. But at 17 years old, almost as a joke, Paul ran for class president.

He didn’t speak Danish at the time, though he took pains to learn the language that year, said Nikolaj Callesen, who was a year ahead of him in school. And though his foray into politics May have started as a gag, he took the job seriously. He eventually became student body president and proposed a plebiscite on smoking at the school.

Smoking bans were unheard-of in Denmark at the time, according to Mr. Callesen, a member of the family that hosted Paul that year. A self-described hippie with long hair and a heavy smoking habit, he was “very opposed” to the idea, he added.

But Paul defied the odds and the ban passed. “No one knew him,” said Mr. Callesen. “And the next day, everyone knew Paul.”

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, now 49 and leading the Parti Québécois into a provincial election Oct. 5, told the story of his time in Denmark during a speech in Montreal earlier this year, mostly for the laughs.

But in that teenage stunt, it’s hard not to see the outline of the ambitious political operator he would become.

After returning home and voting for independence in the 1995 referendum, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon spent years in search of a vehicle for his talents, taking a winding path that would see him disavow sovereignty before readopting the cause.

Along the way, he authored books, rubbed shoulders with the federal Liberals and considered the possibility of creating a new political party.

Few who knew him as a young man would have guessed he would eventually settle on the sovereigntist PQ as his vessel.

Thirty years after his victory in Denmark, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon – commonly known as Pspp – has defied the odds once again.

Days ahead of the election, he seems destined to become Quebec’s 34th premier, and could eke out a majority win that would pave the way for him to hold the third referendum on independence he has promised since taking over the party.

It is an unlikely redemption for the PQ, which was facing annihilation four years ago. Though sovereignty remains broadly unpopular in Quebec, the force of Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s conviction – however newly discovered – has helped to pull his moribund party back from the brink.

The pugnacious PQ Leader has built his brand on his own integrity, promising to organize a vote on secession no matter its odds of success. But he has deftly managed to turn the focus of the campaign away from independence, in part by promising not to hold a referendum while U.S. President Donald Trump is in office.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, who declined an interview request from The Globe and Mail, has not inspired new sovereigntist fervour beyond his base of loyal supporters. But he has proven to be a shrewd tactician, and he has benefited from a divided landscape in which his opponents have inspired even less.

It May just be enough. Improbably, Quebec May be about to give Paul St-Pierre Plamondon the power to hold a referendum that most of its people do not want.

Scandinavia left a mark on Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon.

He was impressed by the Danish social democracy, which boasted free university and low income inequality.

He also admired his host father, a Lutheran pastor named Povl Callesen. He would later write that Povl was socially progressive but culturally conservative, with great respect for Danish history and traditions.

Nikolaj Callesen, Povl’s son, said his former schoolmate still calls every year at Christmas, and travelled to Denmark with his wife and three children in June to celebrate Povl’s 80th birthday.

Back in 1995, the young exchange student finished his school year in Denmark in time to return to Quebec and cast a ballot in another referendum. He was 18 years old, and his vote in favour of independence was the first of his adult life. He has said he was the only person in his family to vote “yes,” and when the “no” side won, narrowly, it felt like history had slipped through his fingers.

But if Denmark’s progressive politics coupled with a strong national identity held a lasting appeal for Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, his interest in Quebec sovereignty appeared to wane after his teenage years.

Starting in 1997, he attended law school at McGill University, where former classmates remember him as affable and adept in English. In his third year, he again sought elected office and was named VP internal of the law students’ association, responsible for social activities.

Allen Mendelsohn, another former classmate, said he had “no indication whatsoever” of Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon displaying political leanings during his time at McGill, even if he was a good organizer. The only thing that suggested a future career in politics, he added, was a certain “glad-handsiness.”

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon graduated in 2001 and went on to work at the law firm Stikeman Elliott for several years, also completing a one-year MBA at Oxford University.

During his time at the firm, he met another young lawyer, Benoit Duclos. Mr. Duclos said the two became friends when they were briefly recruited to a group of up-and-comers created by the Laurier Club, a collection of high-level donors to the Liberal Party of Canada. “They were trying to attract young leaders of the next generation,” he said.

At Stikeman, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon also worked on the team that represented Le Groupe Polygone, a Montreal advertising firm that received around $40-million in funding to boost the visibility of the federal government in Quebec after the 1995 referendum – one of several firms accused of misusing funds in what became known as the sponsorship scandal.

As a junior lawyer, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon was involved in an effort by the company to uncover the identity of the confidential source used by the Globe reporter who broke the story of the scandal. He would later say that this episode, which gave him an inside look at the federal government’s post-referendum manoeuvring, “reignited the passion for independence” he’d had as a teen.

Yet in the years he spent at the firm, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon donated several times to the Liberal Party of Canada. Donation records show he gave more than $2,300 between 2004 and 2008.

In an e-mailed statement, PQ spokesperson Emmanuel Renaud said Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon attended fundraising events while working at Stikeman Elliot. “The fact that he made donations at that time was either part of the standard practice at fundraising events held by law firms or due to his connections with people in the party,” he said.

In the late 2000s, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon co-founded a think tank called Génération d’idées (Generation of Ideas) with two other ambitious young leaders, including future Liberal minister Mélanie Joly. In his first book, Des jeunes et l’avenir du Québec (Young People and the Future of Quebec), published in 2009, he described the venture as an attempt to “dispel an unhealthy cynicism” his generation felt for politics, and to encourage young people to engage in civic life. He pitched himself as scrupulously non-partisan.

Unfortunately, Génération d’idées didn’t have very many ideas, according to Frédéric Bérard, a constitutional lawyer and prominent critic of Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon. “It was just to put themselves on the map.”

By his early 30s, the young lawyer had built something of a name for himself, and became a regular political commentator on a Quebec television show. “Pspp was the figure you would invite if you wanted a young person, but a person who was still trying to be part of the system,” said Marc André Bodet, a professor of political science at Université Laval.

In 2014, he left Génération d’idées for a new project. That year, he published a second book, Les orphelins politiques (Political Orphans), in which he again voiced his dissatisfaction with the offerings of mainstream political parties. In April, 2016, he launched a group of the same name that toyed with the idea of creating a new political party. “He seemed to be a guy looking for a platform,” observed his McGill classmate, Mr. Kalles.

But by this time, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon appeared to have identified the Parti Québécois, which had pioneered major social programs including pharmacare and subsidized child care, as most closely aligned with his own social-democratic values. He was galled by the party’s willingness to sacrifice progressive votes by insisting on a referendum most Quebeckers didn’t want.

At the time, the centre-right Quebec Liberals had just won a majority government after less than two years of a PQ minority, preceded by nearly a decade of Liberal rule.

“Your obsession with holding and winning a referendum is harmful to progressivism and comes across as psychological harassment to the majority of the population,” he wrote, addressing sovereigntists.

“Why should they have to undergo a third referendum when 65 per cent of the population doesn’t want one?”

When Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon decided, in 2016, to seek the leadership of the Parti Québécois, even those close to him were caught off-guard.

“I was dumbfounded,” said Marie-France Perreault, a lawyer and long-time friend.

Ms. Perreault learned of her friend’s plans when he invited her for coffee one day to ask for her help. She was doubtful at first, but he was convincing. When the political orphan announced his campaign that June, he pitched it as an attempt to rebuild Quebec as a viable social democracy.

Soon, Ms. Perreault was part of a small team of Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s family and friends, none of whom had political experience, working on what she called an “artisanal” campaign. She described organizing press conferences in Montreal that no reporters would attend. As in Denmark two decades before, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon was an outsider launching an ambitious – and unlikely – bid for the top job.

The would-be leader later recounted sleeping in his father-in-law’s camper van in the Walmart parking lot of a far-flung town, where he’d travelled to gather signatures, and wondering what he’d done with his life.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s candidacy was viewed with skepticism within the party, not least because of his timid position on sovereignty. When he entered the race, he described himself as a “disappointed federalist.” He promised there would be no referendum in a first mandate, and a vote after that would only be held if Quebeckers clearly wanted one.

“He was the least enthusiastic supporter of independence among all the candidates,” said Martine Ouellet, a former PQ minister who also ran for the leadership that year.

Her 39-year-old competitor finished last in that race, but earned nearly seven per cent of the vote – a victory, according to Ms. Perreault, who said the point was simply to get his ideas out there. Once again, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon had put himself on the radar.

But the following years would not be easy on the novice péquiste, who was named a special adviser by the new leader, Jean-François Lisée, in the weeks after the vote.

Tasked by Mr. Lisée with surveying Quebeckers on their opinion of the party, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon produced a report that found a political brand once known for its innovation was now viewed as “stagnant, conservative and aging.”

It was more candour than the membership seemed to want, and for a while, he was persona non grata within the party. But he persevered, later writing that the PQ cause was “more important than anything else.”

At 41, he ran for his first seat in the 2018 election, but he was no match for the tidal wave that swept the Coalition Avenir Québec into power on a promise to set aside the decades-old debate on secession. Mr. Lisée, who had promised not to hold a referendum in a first mandate, saw his caucus reduced to just 10 seats and immediately resigned amid speculation that the party had been permanently sidelined.

It was a crushing defeat for Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, prompting him to return briefly to his career in law. He took a job at a firm in Gatineau alongside his old friend, Benoit Duclos.

But his exit would be short-lived. The allure of politics was too strong. When he told Mr. Duclos he was planning a second bid for the leadership in 2020, his colleague wasn’t surprised. “He came to see me and he said, ‘If I don’t do it, I’m going to regret it,’” Mr. Duclos said. “It was a bit like a fish saying, ‘I’m going back to the water.’”

The current incarnation of Paul St-Pierre Plamondon emerged that year. Gone was the younger man who argued Quebec had more pressing concerns than separation, replaced by a full-fledged sovereigntist promising a referendum within four years of forming government. His campaign slogan was “ Oui .”

The PQ leadership campaign was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic, so Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon wrote a third book, Rebâtir le camp du Oui (Rebuilding the Yes Camp) explaining his new philosophy, which seemed motivated as much by strategy as conviction.

Where the goal before had been to unseat the federalist Liberals, he felt it would now be impossible for the PQ to defeat the nationalist CAQ without “what makes its supporters’ hearts beat.”

“You don’t win by acting like a wet blanket,” he wrote. “The only way for the PQ to regain power is to restore the legitimacy of the independence project.”

Mr. Renaud, the party spokesperson, said in a statement that several factors contributed to Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s new “sense of urgency” around independence. Those included Mr. Trudeau’s federal immigration policies, which he said caused a “deliberate and rapid decline of the French language in Quebec.”

Regardless, it seemed like an about-face, and a risky position on an issue that had little support outside the PQ base. But perversely, that May have been part of his appeal. “Because it was so unpopular, people gave him some credit because he was being authentic, supposedly,” said Mr. Kalles, the former law student.

It was enough to clinch the leadership for Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, then 43. Due to pandemic restrictions, he delivered his October, 2020, victory speech to a camera in a mostly empty room. paragraphs: When he was a teenager, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon went to Denmark and organized a referendum.

Another exchange student might have preferred to blend into the background at a foreign upper-secondary school thousands of kilometres from home. But at 17 years old, almost as a joke, Paul ran for class president.

He didn’t speak Danish at the time, though he took pains to learn the language that year, said Nikolaj Callesen, who was a year ahead of him in school. And though his foray into politics May have started as a gag, he took the job seriously. He eventually became student body president and proposed a plebiscite on smoking at the school.

Smoking bans were unheard-of in Denmark at the time, according to Mr. Callesen, a member of the family that hosted Paul that year. A self-described hippie with long hair and a heavy smoking habit, he was “very opposed” to the idea, he added.
But Paul defied the odds and the ban passed. “No one knew him,” said Mr. Callesen. “And the next day, everyone knew Paul.”

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, now 49 and leading the Parti Québécois into a provincial election Oct. 5, told the story of his time in Denmark during a speech in Montreal earlier this year, mostly for the laughs.
But in that teenage stunt, it’s hard not to see the outline of the ambitious political operator he would become.

After returning home and voting for independence in the 1995 referendum, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon spent years in search of a vehicle for his talents, taking a winding path that would see him disavow sovereignty before readopting the cause.
Along the way, he authored books, rubbed shoulders with the federal Liberals and considered the possibility of creating a new political party.
Few who knew him as a young man would have guessed he would eventually settle on the sovereigntist PQ as his vessel.
Thirty years after his victory in Denmark, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon – commonly known as Pspp – has defied the odds once again.

Days ahead of the election, he seems destined to become Quebec’s 34th premier, and could eke out a majority win that would pave the way for him to hold the third referendum on independence he has promised since taking over the party.

It is an unlikely redemption for the PQ, which was facing annihilation four years ago. Though sovereignty remains broadly unpopular in Quebec, the force of Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s conviction – however newly discovered – has helped to pull his moribund party back from the brink.

The pugnacious PQ Leader has built his brand on his own integrity, promising to organize a vote on secession no matter its odds of success. But he has deftly managed to turn the focus of the campaign away from independence, in part by promising not to hold a referendum while U.S. President Donald Trump is in office.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, who declined an interview request from The Globe and Mail, has not inspired new sovereigntist fervour beyond his base of loyal supporters. But he has proven to be a shrewd tactician, and he has benefited from a divided landscape in which his opponents have inspired even less.
It May just be enough. Improbably, Quebec May be about to give Paul St-Pierre Plamondon the power to hold a referendum that most of its people do not want.
Scandinavia left a mark on Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon.
He was impressed by the Danish social democracy, which boasted free university and low income inequality.

He also admired his host father, a Lutheran pastor named Povl Callesen. He would later write that Povl was socially progressive but culturally conservative, with great respect for Danish history and traditions.
Nikolaj Callesen, Povl’s son, said his former schoolmate still calls every year at Christmas, and travelled to Denmark with his wife and three children in June to celebrate Povl’s 80th birthday.

Back in 1995, the young exchange student finished his school year in Denmark in time to return to Quebec and cast a ballot in another referendum. He was 18 years old, and his vote in favour of independence was the first of his adult life. He has said he was the only person in his family to vote “yes,” and when the “no” side won, narrowly, it felt like history had slipped through his fingers.

But if Denmark’s progressive politics coupled with a strong national identity held a lasting appeal for Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, his interest in Quebec sovereignty appeared to wane after his teenage years.

Starting in 1997, he attended law school at McGill University, where former classmates remember him as affable and adept in English. In his third year, he again sought elected office and was named VP internal of the law students’ association, responsible for social activities.

Allen Mendelsohn, another former classmate, said he had “no indication whatsoever” of Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon displaying political leanings during his time at McGill, even if he was a good organizer. The only thing that suggested a future career in politics, he added, was a certain “glad-handsiness.”
Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon graduated in 2001 and went on to work at the law firm Stikeman Elliott for several years, also completing a one-year MBA at Oxford University.

During his time at the firm, he met another young lawyer, Benoit Duclos. Mr. Duclos said the two became friends when they were briefly recruited to a group of up-and-comers created by the Laurier Club, a collection of high-level donors to the Liberal Party of Canada. “They were trying to attract young leaders of the next generation,” he said.

At Stikeman, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon also worked on the team that represented Le Groupe Polygone, a Montreal advertising firm that received around $40-million in funding to boost the visibility of the federal government in Quebec after the 1995 referendum – one of several firms accused of misusing funds in what became known as the sponsorship scandal.

As a junior lawyer, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon was involved in an effort by the company to uncover the identity of the confidential source used by the Globe reporter who broke the story of the scandal. Yet in the years he spent at the firm, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon donated several times to the Liberal Party of Canada. Donation records show he gave more than $2,300 between 2004 and 2008.

Allen Mendelsohn, another former classmate, said he had “no indication whatsoever” of Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon displaying political leanings during his time at McGill, even if he was a good organizer. The only thing that suggested a future career in politics, he added, was a certain “glad-handsiness.”
Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon graduated in 2001 and went on to work at the law firm Stikeman Elliott for several years, also completing a one-year MBA at Oxford University.

During his time at the firm, he met another young lawyer, Benoit Duclos. Mr. Duclos said the two became friends when they were briefly recruited to a group of up-and-comers created by the Laurier Club, a collection of high-level donors to the Liberal Party of Canada. “They were trying to attract young leaders of the next generation,” he said.

At Stikeman, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon also worked on the team that represented Le Groupe Polygone, a Montreal advertising firm that received around $40-million in funding to boost the visibility of the federal government in Quebec after the 1995 referendum – one of several firms accused of misusing funds in what became known as the sponsorship scandal.

As a junior lawyer, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon was involved in an effort by the company to uncover the identity of the confidential source used by the Globe reporter who broke the story of the scandal. He would later say that this episode, which gave him an inside look at the federal government’s post-referendum manoeuvring, “reignited the passion for independence” he’d had as a teen.

content_blocks.caption: The federal sponsorship scandal, investigated by John Gomery's royal commission in the 2000s, would be an important moment in Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon's legal career. Bill Grimshaw/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: Yet in the years he spent at the firm, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon donated several times to the Liberal Party of Canada. Donation records show he gave more than $2,300 between 2004 and 2008.

In an e-mailed statement, PQ spokesperson Emmanuel Renaud said Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon attended fundraising events while working at Stikeman Elliot. “The fact that he made donations at that time was either part of the standard practice at fundraising events held by law firms or due to his connections with people in the party,” he said.

In the late 2000s, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon co-founded a think tank called Génération d’idées (Generation of Ideas) with two other ambitious young leaders, including future Liberal minister Mélanie Joly. In his first book, Des jeunes et l’avenir du Québec (Young People and the Future of Quebec), published in 2009, he described the venture as an attempt to “dispel an unhealthy cynicism” his generation felt for politics, and to encourage young people to engage in civic life. He pitched himself as scrupulously non-partisan.

Unfortunately, Génération d’idées didn’t have very many ideas, according to Frédéric Bérard, a constitutional lawyer and prominent critic of Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon. “It was just to put themselves on the map.”

content_blocks.caption: Mélanie Joly, now the federal Industry Minister, was once in a think tank with Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon. Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: By his early 30s, the young lawyer had built something of a name for himself, and became a regular political commentator on a Quebec television show. “Pspp was the figure you would invite if you wanted a young person, but a person who was still trying to be part of the system,” said Marc André Bodet, a professor of political science at Université Laval.

In 2014, he left Génération d’idées for a new project. That year, he published a second book, Les orphelins politiques (Political Orphans), in which he again voiced his dissatisfaction with the offerings of mainstream political parties. In April, 2016, he launched a group of the same name that toyed with the idea of creating a new political party. “He seemed to be a guy looking for a platform,” observed his McGill classmate, Mr. Kalles.

But by this time, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon appeared to have identified the Parti Québécois, which had pioneered major social programs including pharmacare and subsidized child care, as most closely aligned with his own social-democratic values. He was galled by the party’s willingness to sacrifice progressive votes by insisting on a referendum most Quebeckers didn’t want.
At the time, the centre-right Quebec Liberals had just won a majority government after less than two years of a PQ minority, preceded by nearly a decade of Liberal rule.
“Your obsession with holding and winning a referendum is harmful to progressivism and comes across as psychological harassment to the majority of the population,” he wrote, addressing sovereigntists.
“Why should they have to undergo a third referendum when 65 per cent of the population doesn’t want one?”

content_blocks.caption: Three days before Quebec’s 1995 referendum, No supporters from across Canada made their case at a massive rally in Montreal. Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon returned from Denmark to vote Yes; it was his first time at the ballot box. Ryan Remiorz/The Canadian Press

Three days before Quebec’s 1995 referendum, No supporters from across Canada made their case at a massive rally in Montreal. Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon returned from Denmark to vote Yes; it was his first time at the ballot box. Ryan Remiorz/The Canadian Press

First-time voters in 2026 are too young to remember the last referendum, but they can find its vintage merch at Montreal’s Club Pays. The Globe spoke with some of the sovereigntist café’s Gen Z regulars, and some were conflicted about voting for the Parti Québécois. Andrej Ivanov/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: When Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon decided, in 2016, to seek the leadership of the Parti Québécois, even those close to him were caught off-guard.
“I was dumbfounded,” said Marie-France Perreault, a lawyer and long-time friend.

Ms. Perreault learned of her friend’s plans when he invited her for coffee one day to ask for her help. She was doubtful at first, but he was convincing. When the political orphan announced his campaign that June, he pitched it as an attempt to rebuild Quebec as a viable social democracy.

Soon, Ms. Perreault was part of a small team of Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s family and friends, none of whom had political experience, working on what she called an “artisanal” campaign. She described organizing press conferences in Montreal that no reporters would attend. As in Denmark two decades before, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon was an outsider launching an ambitious – and unlikely – bid for the top job.

content_blocks.caption: Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon announced his candidacy for the PQ leadership on June 3, 2016, to the surprise of many people close to him. The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: The would-be leader later recounted sleeping in his father-in-law’s camper van in the Walmart parking lot of a far-flung town, where he’d travelled to gather signatures, and wondering what he’d done with his life.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s candidacy was viewed with skepticism within the party, not least because of his timid position on sovereignty. When he entered the race, he described himself as a “disappointed federalist.” He promised there would be no referendum in a first mandate, and a vote after that would only be held if Quebeckers clearly wanted one.
“He was the least enthusiastic supporter of independence among all the candidates,” said Martine Ouellet, a former PQ minister who also ran for the leadership that year.

Her 39-year-old competitor finished last in that race, but earned nearly seven per cent of the vote – a victory, according to Ms. Perreault, who said the point was simply to get his ideas out there. Once again, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon had put himself on the radar.
But the following years would not be easy on the novice péquiste, who was named a special adviser by the new leader, Jean-François Lisée, in the weeks after the vote.

Tasked by Mr. Lisée with surveying Quebeckers on their opinion of the party, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon produced a report that found a political brand once known for its innovation was now viewed as “stagnant, conservative and aging.”

It was more candour than the membership seemed to want, and for a while, he was persona non grata within the party. But he persevered, later writing that the PQ cause was “more important than anything else.”

content_blocks.caption: Jean-François Lisée, on the campaign trail in 2018, would step down as PQ leader after a poor result in that election. Paul Chiasson/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: At 41, he ran for his first seat in the 2018 election, but he was no match for the tidal wave that swept the Coalition Avenir Québec into power on a promise to set aside the decades-old debate on secession. Mr. Lisée, who had promised not to hold a referendum in a first mandate, saw his caucus reduced to just 10 seats and immediately resigned amid speculation that the party had been permanently sidelined.
It was a crushing defeat for Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, prompting him to return briefly to his career in law. He took a job at a firm in Gatineau alongside his old friend, Benoit Duclos.

But his exit would be short-lived. The allure of politics was too strong. When he told Mr. Duclos he was planning a second bid for the leadership in 2020, his colleague wasn’t surprised. “He came to see me and he said, ‘If I don’t do it, I’m going to regret it,’” Mr. Duclos said. “It was a bit like a fish saying, ‘I’m going back to the water.’”

The current incarnation of Paul St-Pierre Plamondon emerged that year. Gone was the younger man who argued Quebec had more pressing concerns than separation, replaced by a full-fledged sovereigntist promising a referendum within four years of forming government. His campaign slogan was “ Oui .”

content_blocks.caption: While the pandemic sent CAQ premier François Legault into crisis management mode, the PQ put off its leadership vote, and Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon used the time to publicize his new ideas. Ryan Remiorz/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: The PQ leadership campaign was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic, so Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon wrote a third book, Rebâtir le camp du Oui (Rebuilding the Yes Camp) explaining his new philosophy, which seemed motivated as much by strategy as conviction.
Where the goal before had been to unseat the federalist Liberals, he felt it would now be impossible for the PQ to defeat the nationalist CAQ without “what makes its supporters’ hearts beat.”
“You don’t win by acting like a wet blanket,” he wrote. “The only way for the PQ to regain power is to restore the legitimacy of the independence project.”

Mr. Renaud, the party spokesperson, said in a statement that several factors contributed to Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s new “sense of urgency” around independence. Those included Mr. Trudeau’s federal immigration policies, which he said caused a “deliberate and rapid decline of the French language in Quebec.”

Regardless, it seemed like an about-face, and a risky position on an issue that had little support outside the PQ base. But perversely, that May have been part of his appeal. “Because it was so unpopular, people gave him some credit because he was being authentic, supposedly,” said Mr. Kalles, the former law student.

It was enough to clinch the leadership for Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, then 43. Due to pandemic restrictions, he delivered his October, 2020, victory speech to a camera in a mostly empty room. It was an inauspicious start to what Ms. Perreault, who became his first chief of staff, described as a “very, very, very difficult” time.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon had inherited a party on the verge of extinction in the middle of a pandemic that made it nearly impossible to get attention. When he was interviewed, Ms. Perreault recalled, “He was consistently asked: ‘Does it worry you to be possibly the last leader of the Parti Québécois? Are you going to cause the party to die?’ ”
In the 2022 election, the CAQ grew its majority and Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon led his party to its worst-ever result, claiming just three seats. But he managed to get himself elected.
Ms. Perreault, who left before the campaign, said she was certain the rest would be history now that her friend finally had a spot in the legislature. “I knew he was going to rebuild the party.”

content_blocks.caption: This election is the PQ’s second under Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s leadership. The party’s public approval rating is better this time, but support for sovereignty has dipped since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House. Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press

This election is the PQ’s second under Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s leadership. The party’s public approval rating is better this time, but support for sovereignty has dipped since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House. Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press

There are five major parties in play: Québec Solidaire (co-led by Ruba Ghazal, far left), Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s PQ, Ms. Frechette's CAQ, Éric Duhaime’s Conservatives and Charles Milliard’s Liberals. Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press
Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s partner, Alexandra Tremblay, has been a vocal supporter on the campaign trail, as have their children Laurette, Maurice and Henri. Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Right away, it was clear the PQ leader relished the limelight.

His opening act at Quebec’s National Assembly, in December, 2022, was to get himself denied entry after refusing to swear allegiance to King Charles. Days later, the government unanimously passed a law stating that only an oath of allegiance to the Quebec people would henceforth be required.

But he was also moving the Parti Québécois in a new direction that seemed at odds with the progressive brand of politics he had often espoused. In the 2022 campaign, he had promised to slash immigration targets so as not to overwhelm services or threaten the French language. It was another proposal that seemed to echo politics in Denmark, whose centre-left government has passed some of Europe’s most restrictive immigration policies – ostensibly to protect its welfare state.

Ms. Ouellet, who now leads a small provincial party focused on sovereignty and fighting climate change, said the move struck her as an “opportunistic” bid to win back CAQ voters, and a significant shift for a party that had always been “extremely open.”

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has also sought to one-up the government’s secularism policies, which include restrictions to religious symbols and limits to public prayer. Back in 2014, he criticized the previous PQ government for a proposed “charter of values” that would have banned religious symbols for many public servants, saying the party had “once again chosen to subtract rather than add.” But now he says he would ban conspicuous religious symbols for elementary school students.

content_blocks.caption: Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon was a critic of the PQ’s secularist vision when it proposed a ‘charter of values’ in 2013. Now, he supports restrictions on symbols of faith. Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: The PQ leader has condemned “wokeism” and called for a parliamentary committee to investigate whether “radical left” gender ideology is seeping into schools. Earlier this year, he gave an hour-long interview to the right-wing outlet Rebel News.

The shift has confounded some who’ve tracked his career. Mr. Bérard, the constitutional lawyer, said it’s frustrating to watch Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon target minorities, apparently for political gain. “He really decided to veer right,” he said. “It’s sad, because those who knew him before know this isn’t him.”

“Maybe they feel like it’s a good strategy to attract mostly baby boomers who voted for the CAQ for the last two elections,” said Prof. Bodet. “I’m not even sure that he’s convinced that this is the right thing to do.”

Whatever his personal convictions, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon emerged as a sharp and articulate politician. When the Caq’s star began to fade in late 2023, while the provincial Liberals were without a permanent leader, he embraced the role of de facto voice of the opposition.
“He made a decision very clearly to take a swing at absolutely everything,” said Mr. Kalles, his former law school classmate. “It got him a lot of attention at airtime.”

Critics argue that sometimes he swings a little too hard. Earlier this year, Prime Minister Mark Carney made a widely panned speech describing the 1759 Battle of the Plains of Abraham, which led to the surrender of Quebec to the British, as the start of a partnership.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon quickly responded with an indignant speech of his own invoking Mahatma Gandhi and Nelson Mandela, and was derided in the press for overplaying his hand. He has more recently alleged, without presenting evidence, that the federal government is spying on his party, and accused Ottawa of interfering in Quebec’s election with a series of recent announcements featuring Mr. Carney and Premier Christine Fréchette.
“What he wants is a spotlight on his face,” said Mr. Bérard. “If he has a spotlight, he’s happy.”

content_blocks.caption: Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon relishes public attention, says Frédéric Bérard, a lawyer and critic of the PQ leader. Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Under Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, the PQ has made a remarkable recovery, leading in the polls for the better part of three years and winning a series of by-elections. Next week, he could steer the party he resuscitated to form government for the first time in more than a decade.

If he does, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon will owe his victory in large part to the sovereigntist base his pledge has galvanized. Only about 30 per cent of voters say they want a PQ government – roughly the same proportion that want independence.

With five parties dividing the electorate, that will likely be enough to put the PQ Leader first across the finish line. Recent polling shows the CAQ, which seemed to be making a comeback early in the campaign, has lost ground and could be fighting for survival, while the opposition Liberals remain unpopular among francophone voters. The Quebec Conservatives and the left-leaning Québec Solidaire are both projected to win a handful of seats, but are not contenders to form government.

Still, a win at 30 per cent would hardly be a resounding vote of confidence. Paradoxically, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s commitment to a referendum could cost him the majority he likely needs to make it happen.
Yet he has not wavered.

Possibly, this is because he’s a true believer, convinced as he was at 18 that Quebec will fare better on its own, like the Scandinavian nation he so admires. “He’s incorruptible,” said Mr. Duclos, his friend. “He’s a very, very frank and honest person.”

Possibly, he hasn’t walked away from a referendum because political strategy dictates he can’t. “Most of his grassroots supporters are sovereigntists above all,” said Mr. Bérard. “So if he were to back down on his promise right before the election, he would lose his base.”

Either way, when he told voters in August that he wouldn’t launch a referendum until after the Trump presidency ends in 2029, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon appeared to bend as far as he could. He has barely mentioned sovereignty during the campaign, instead pitching himself and his party as the best choice to steer Quebec’s economy through turbulent waters. After six years of talking about independence, he has tried – for now – to stop.
The man who bent his Danish classmates to his will has yet to persuade his own people.

content_blocks.caption: Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: With a report from Marieke Walsh

stories.title: B.C. court to rule on Constitutional challenge of activists' trafficking convictions
stories.summary: Vancouver - A British Columbia Supreme Court judge is expected to rule today on a constitutional challenge from two harm-reduction activists convicted of drug trafficking who argued they were doing it to reduce the harms caused by toxic drugs.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - The B.C. Supreme Court has given the federal government six months to retool a federal drug law as it tossed criminal convictions against the founders of a Vancouver compassion club who “made it their mission to save lives by offering a non-medicalized safe supply of drugs.”

Jeremy Kalicum and Eris Nyx, founders of Vancouver’s Drug User Liberation Front, had been convicted of possession for the purposes of trafficking last year for sourcing heroin, cocaine and methamphetamine off the dark web, then testing and selling it to members of their club at cost.

Justice Catherine Murray told a Vancouver courtroom of supporters and media on Tuesday that the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act’s section around the conviction infringed on rights guaranteed by the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Murray found the section of the act prohibiting possession for the purposes of trafficking “criminalizes life-saving conduct in a manner that undermines, rather than furthers, the law’s purpose of advancing public health and maintaining public safety.”

Kalicum and Nyx had sought a legal pathway from Health Canada to run such a program but were never granted an exemption.

“This challenge is about the lack of ability to obtain an exemption,” the judge said in her decision.

Kalicum and Nyx found there was no such “pathway” to permit a non-medicalized safer supply program, she said.

They were found guilty in November 2025, but the judge put the convictions on hold to hear their constitutional challenge.

“After losing countless friends, colleagues, and neighbours to the crisis, they resolved to take action to address the problem of the unpredictability of the drug supply,” Murray’s ruling says. “Their mission was to save lives by offering a non-medicalized safe supply of drugs.”

Murray found the act infringes on the rights guaranteed under Sections 7 and 15 under the Charter, although she has suspended the invalidity finding for six months to give Parliament time to implement a plan that would allow for a non-medicalized safer supply program to operate.

Murray said such a program is “urgently needed to save lives” in the face of the toxic drug crisis that has killed more than 18,000 people since the B.C. government declared a public health emergency in 2016.

The ruling said that running a safer-supply program was precisely what the applicants were doing and that formed the basis of the criminal charges against them.

Kalicum and Nyx, the judge found, “have borne the burden of bringing a successful constitutional challenge, doing a public interest service at considerable cost to themselves.”

“I think you should be very proud of yourselves, and it’s people like you who make a difference and you just did. So, go do great things. I have no doubt that you will,” Murray told Kalicum and Nyx during the brief hearing.

Murray said the defect in the legislation needs to be addressed with some urgency.

“It has been over 11 years since the toxic drug crisis was declared a public health emergency. It remains an emergency,” her ruling said.

The compassion club reduced the harms associated with the toxic drug crisis and didn’t negatively impact the community or public safety, the decision said.

There is no legal source of drugs available for the non-medicalized safer supply program, it said.

It said the government should be given “full opportunity to craft its own response to the issues identified in this ruling.”

The existing legislation is capable of a range of responses that address the defects, including legislative changes and regulatory reform, Murray said in the decision.

The judge did not read her full decision in court but concluded her remarks by lauding Kalicum and Nyx for the personal risks they took in their work.

Nyx declined to comment after the hearing, but Kalicum said outside court that he felt “excellent.”

“That’s all I think I’m going to say, but I think everybody felt really good,” he said.

Tim Dickson, one of their lawyers, said outside the courthouse in Vancouver that the ruling was a “vindication of what Dulf was doing.”

“The court found specifically that their compassion club did save lives. It reduced the risk of overdose. It did not cause negative impacts on society at large. It was a beneficial, positive, evidence-based program that they conducted, and that they were arrested and prosecuted for implementing,” he said.

He said the case was about the federal and provincial governments “refusal to implement” that life-saving measure, and how federal law “blocks any effort” to implement that measure.

He said Kalicum and Nyx ran the program with no profit or benefit to themselves and “always with the sole intention of trying to reduce the terrible rate of death in this crisis.”

“This case should never have been brought to trial. They never should have been prosecuted,” Dickson said.

Dickson said an article published in The Economist magazine about Dulf’s activities mentioned public funding, which went to operating expenses and not to source the dark web drugs.

He said the article was seized upon by politicians, including Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, who Dickson said tried to “cash in on this debate.”

Dickson said the pressure culminated when the NDP government decided to cut them off, with Vancouver Coastal Health pulling its funding, and BC Housing evicting them from their site before it was raided by police.

He said the decriminalization of small amounts of drugs in B.C. and safer supply programs also caused controversy, which conflated non-medicalized safer supply programs with alleged diversion of prescribed safer supply drugs.

“But those issues all got swirled together, and drug policy just turned to a more conservative stance,” he said. “It’s clear that there was a lot of political backlash, and the political debate was not able to disentangle the issues properly.”

He told reporters that the Crown has 30 days to appeal the ruling.

The Public Prosecution Service of Canada said in a statement that “as in any case, following a decision, prosecutors review the judgment and assess any potential next steps.”

stories.title: Internal Montreal police documents describe ‘radicalized’ subculture among officers
stories.summary: Montreal - A "radicalized" subculture formed among the ranks of officers at a Montreal police station in a multicultural neighbourhood before it was rocked by allegations of racism and criminal misconduct, newly released internal briefing notes say.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - A “radicalized” subculture formed among the ranks of officers at a Montreal police station in a multicultural neighbourhood before it was rocked by allegations of racism and criminal misconduct, newly released internal briefing notes say.

The documents, obtained by The Canadian Press through access to information legislation, are part of a package prepared for the appearance of Fady Dagher, Montreal’s police chief, before a municipal public safety committee in August.

The newly released records reveal details Dagher never shared with the public about what May have led police management to disarm and dismantle a 16-member patrol unit at the station located in the city’s Montréal-Nord borough.

A "radicalized" subculture formed among the ranks of officers at a police station before it was rocked by allegations of racism and criminal misconduct in a multicultural neighbourhood of Montreal, says newly released internal briefing notes. (Sept. 29, 2026)

The documents include a copy of Dagher’s presentation to the municipal committee and draft speaking notes describing how police handled the incident at the Montréal-Nord station.

The speaking notes say the reaction inside the force — after some officers blew the whistle about alleged misconduct by their colleagues — reflects how the police force was seeing cracks in a “code of silence” as part of a cultural shift in the organization that left a few officers feeling isolated.

The internal records also confirm police had enough evidence to take action against members of the patrol unit a day before they dismantled the unit and informed the public late on a Friday night in mid-June.

The draft speaking notes say a subculture was developing within this patrol unit at the station, involving “a marginalized fringe (group) of our employees who were radicalized” and resisted efforts to eliminate misconduct and change the culture of the police force.

“These people reject all the work accomplished by Montreal police in recent years,” said one passage in the internal documents. “They rejected it and, in a way, made that known. They sought to recognize each other.”

The documents do not explain what the force meant by “radicalized,” how many employees it believed the term applied to, or what it meant when it said they had sought to recognize each other.

Dagher and other police officials have not shared details about alleged incidents that led police to dismantle the patrol unit; however, he has confirmed one of the allegations under review is about officers who allegedly cut the hair of racialized civilians to keep as trophies.

Montreal police said they were working on responses to questions from The Canadian Press about the newly released documents but did not immediately provide answers.

However, in a statement published Monday, police said they had sent the evidence to Quebec prosecutors, who will determine whether criminal charges should be laid.

Experts and anti-racism advocates have expressed alarm after being told about the language used in the internal documents.

The police force “is basically admitting that a process of change will create little cliques of marginalized people that become even more brutal,” said Ted Rutland, a professor of geography at Concordia University who researches policing in Canada. “And that is believable and scary, so it’s interesting that (Dagher) didn’t say that out loud.”

Martin Geoffroy, a sociology professor at Cégep Édouard-Montpetit, says it’s possible that officials were referring to far-right radicalization.

Geoffroy co-authored a federally funded study of far-right groups in Quebec and has studied far-right movements for over 20 years.

But he noted that he was speculating about what had happened within the patrol unit since the documents do not provide a detailed definition or explanation of its description of “radicalized” officers.

He said that his previous research found former police officers and military personnel were among members of far-right groups.

“What we can see in (the documents) is that there is resistance” to efforts to change the culture, he said.

The documents also reveal new details about how employees reacted to the scandal, suggesting that most of the force were upset about the alleged actions of officers at the Montréal-Nord station.

“You have no idea how many Montreal police officers wrote to me expressing shock about what they had learned,” said the speaking notes. “It was to the point where they were furious with their colleagues for dishonouring their uniform and destroying all the work they had tried to accomplish over the years.”

Dave Poitras, a sociologist at Université de Montréal who specializes in radicalization, said police forces are large organizations that can reflect the range of beliefs found in society.

But he cautioned that ideology alone cannot explain the alleged conduct at Station 39. He said the factors that lead someone to commit such acts “obviously go beyond adherence to any ideology.”

Poitras is scientific director of Villes sans violence, a non-profit group that focuses on preventing extremism and hate crimes. He said his organization defines radicalization as a process of adopting extreme beliefs and a willingness to use, encourage or facilitate violence to advance an ideology, political project or cause.

Such beliefs can involve placing certain groups above others, he said, citing racial hierarchies and white supremacy as examples.

He said some of the alleged conduct at Station 39 appears to have had a hateful character and that hateful incidents or crimes can result from radicalization. But not enough is known to determine whether individual officers were in fact radicalized, he said.

Radicalization is “not something that happens overnight,” Poitras said. “It really has to be understood as a process on a continuum that can take time.”

The records also appears to reveal more about what police knew before dismantling the Station 39 team.

An entry dated June 11 says: “We received confirmation of concrete investigative elements.” The next begins: “June 12: I decide to proceed immediately.”

Another document states that as of June 11: “A threshold for validating the information has been reached to justify decisive management actions.”

Dagher has rejected criticism about his decision to announce the news he was dismantling the unit late on a Friday evening, maintaining that he has been transparent about the investigation and acted as fast as possible

Police have said the intervening period between June 11 and June 12 was used to prepare the operation before the officers arrived for their next shift.

That evening, all 16 were disarmed, two were suspended, three were assigned administrative duties and the remaining 11 were relocated — measures the documents say were taken “to ensure the safety of the population.”

By mid-August, police said four officers had been suspended.

One part of the document also notes how Quebec’s Police Act requires a police chief to notify the minister responsible for public safety “without delay” of an allegation that an officer committed a criminal offence, unless, after consulting prosecutors, it is deemed frivolous or unfounded.

The notes say Domestic Security Minister Ian Lafrenière was informed at 8:45 p.m. on June 12, shortly before police publicly announced they were taking action. Asked about the June 11 entry and whether the minister should have been notified earlier, a spokesperson for Lafrenière declined to comment, citing the ongoing investigations.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

stories.title: Quebec candidates have six days left to make their pitch before election day
stories.summary: Montreal - Election day is less than a week away in Quebec.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - A quarter of eligible voters in Quebec have already cast their ballot, and candidates have six days to court those who are undecided before election day.

Élections Québec says 23.6 per cent of voters participated in advance polling on Sunday and Monday, including polls on school campuses and retirement homes.

Five parties are expected to win seats on Oct. 5, with the separatist Parti Québécois leading comfortably in the polls. But a new survey by La Presse shows that thousands of Quebecers have not made up their minds.

Immigration has dominated much of the campaign, and was a flashpoint for the Coalition Avenir Québec and the Conservative party on Tuesday. Both parties also promised to reduce the number of temporary immigrants and asylum seekers admitted in the province, which the PQ also advocated for.

Quebec would need Ottawa’s approval to do so, as both asylum and the international mobility program are under federal jurisdiction.

Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime was on the defensive after being accused of lying about asylum seekers.

A Radio-Canada report fact-checked claims made during a debate on Sept. 23, including Duhaime’s assertion that “more than a third of asylum seekers are fraudulent.” The public broadcaster reported that only 2.6 per cent of rejected claims were deemed fraudulent, while 27 per cent were denied for other reasons.

“Throwing around numbers like that about human beings who are fleeing danger in their home countries to seek refuge in Quebec is irresponsible, and on top of that, it’s false,” said Ruba Ghazal, co-spokesperson for Québec solidaire, ON the campaign trail Tuesday.

Duhaime stood his ground, insisting that only 63 per cent of asylum seekers are admitted.

“So, you can play with words, but the reality is that more than a third either leave or are rejected before the process is over,” he argued.

Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette, also mired in controversy since Friday, similarly promised to crack down on asylum seekers.

Though she distanced herself from Duhaime’s comments, she agreed that there “are too many of them” and said Ottawa must process asylum claims quicker. According to Fréchette, asylum claims take about three years to be processed.

“We’re talking about people who left everything behind to put their trust in us and come settle in Quebec,” she said.

Fréchette has been trying to shake off controversy after blaming members of her own party for trying to get journalists to pursue a story about foreign interference in the electoral process. Her party spent Monday on the defensive, but shifted her focus back to campaign promises.

Fréchette and Liberal Leader Charles Milliard once again invoked the PQ’s promised independence referendum to try to gain voters’ favours.

For her part, Ghazal was focused on attracting young voters to her leftist party, a demographic known for low turnout.

Speaking to youths in the Rosemont riding in Montreal, she pitched Québec solidaire as the party that will defend their futures and social democracy against austerity.

“I refuse to let them destroy everything that was built by those who came before us. That would be a profound injustice to today’s youth,” Ghazal said during a news conference.

She promised to cap rents, cut tuition fees in colleges and universities, make public transit free for those under 25, pay for mandatory internships and raise the minimum wage to $20 an hour.

Milliard focused his promises around secularism, saying he would wait until the Supreme Court hands down its decision before making any changes to the controversial law prohibiting government employees from wearing religious symbols.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

stories.title: Suddenly everyone's worried about AI wiping out humanity. But why and how could it do that? Here's what we know
stories.summary: How, exactly, could software – even superintelligent AI – actually carry out the very hands-on task of mass murder?
stories.author: Tom Blackwell
stories.content:
It’s 2040 and after years of stunning advances, artificial intelligence is not only smarter than humans, AI agents see people as an obstacle. And proceed to eliminate everyone on Earth.

It sounds like the stuff of science fiction, or once did. But the idea that AI could wipe out humanity has suddenly become impossible to ignore, as even the industry behind the technology warns of a possible apocalypse.

Yet the recent alarm bells have raised perplexing questions. How, exactly, could software — even superintelligent AI — actually carry out the very hands-on task of mass murder? And why would technology invented and trained by people turn on its human creators?

It’s really not that far-fetched, the experts predicting AI doom insist.

“There are many ways that require very little contact with the physical world — even if they were just stuck in computers — that (AI agents) could cause large amounts of damage that could result in potentially everyone dying,” Malo Bourgon, Canadian CEO of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute in Berkeley, Calif., said in an interview.

The non-profit’s sobering raison d’être is to “help prevent human extinction from the development of artificial superintelligence.”

Other, less mind-bending concerns about AI, like the potential for widespread job loss, previously dominated conversation about the field’s potential pitfalls. Some experts still downplay the existential worries and caution that putting the breaks on AI development could strengthen the West’s adversaries and deprive the world of countless benefits; U.S. President Donald Trump called the alarm-ringing a “hoax.”

This story is not about that ongoing debate. Instead, it’s taking the warnings at face value and trying to explain in what ways the intelligent-machine apocalypse might occur.

Trump scoffs at AI danger warnings as Carney calls for global tech body to strengthen guardrails

Here are all the recent warnings about how AI 'could kill us all' within a decade

Actual extinction of the human race is one feared outcome but there are slightly less-dire end points that AI doomsayers envisage. They include a state in which humans are relegated to a subservient, disenfranchised species, living or dying at the whim of far-smarter computers.

“If we produce things that are more intelligent than us, how do we know we can keep control,” British-Canadian Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, considered a “godfather” of AI, said three years ago, before many of the field’s recent huge leaps. “If we talk about evolution — all these species that are evolving — what tends to happen is it doesn’t go well for the less-intelligent species.”

The University of Toronto professor emeritus has predicted a “10 per cent to 20 per cent” chance that AI will cause human extinction within the next three decades.

University of Louisville computer scientist Roman Yampolskiy puts the odds of AI-driven devastation at 99.9 per cent in the next century.

“The critical variable is how quickly we develop systems that exceed human intelligence, improve themselves and operate autonomously,” he said in an email interview. “Once that threshold is crossed, events could unfold much faster than our institutions can respond. Uncertainty about when a catastrophe might occur should not be mistaken for evidence that it is unlikely.”

The concern has been fuelled lately by the unexpectedly fast pace of AI development, with agents able, for instance, to write software more efficiently than human coders and solve problems that have long stymied the world’s top mathematicians.

Anxieties grew exponentially when a hundreds-strong “swarm” of agents developed by industry titan OpenAI escaped their training confines and hacked into the system of AI startup HuggingFace. They worked in concert, talked to each other and exhibited the very human behaviour of trying to cover their tracks.

Then earlier this month, engineer Jacob Coxon shook the tech world and many others when he quit his job at AI giant Anthropic, warning that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Another of the firm’s scientists publicly echoed his views. Artificial intelligence executives followed by urging new guardrails for the technology. Microsoft founder Bill Gates told NBC Sunday that “AI is powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths.”

Meanwhile, the advances are set to further accelerate thanks to the concept of “recursive self-improvement.” That’s where AI creates the next, smarter generation of artificial intelligence, which then develops an even more-capable iteration, and so on and so on until the systems’ intelligence surpasses that of the Earth’s once-dominant species.

But why would that leap to “superintelligence” necessarily mean doom for humans?

At the most conventional level, terrorists, autocrats or other bad human actors could use AI as a tool to wreak havoc, noted the Center for AI Safety in a 2023 report, whether through developing a deadly new weapon of mass destruction, letting loose autonomous killing machines or seeding pervasive misinformation that caused global conflict and violence.

But perhaps the most chilling way the technology could turn against us is via the idea of rogue AI — agents that slip away from human reins and essentially follow their own agenda.

“It does not have to hate us or even be conscious — it simply needs objectives incompatible with our continued existence,” says Yampolskiy, who has long warned of AI’s dangers. “Humans might interfere with its goals, attempt to shut it down or compete for resources it requires. Eliminating that interference could become instrumentally useful.”

Developers try to instil values in AI that make human wellbeing a priority, what’s called alignment. But it’s widely accepted that aligning AI to human ideals is difficult to achieve now and May become impossible with superintelligence.

Programmers May set a certain goal or task for an AI agent, but it could “drift” to another objective that, through reinforcement training, it has learned will earn it rewards, argues the Center for AI Safety. Or a superintelligent AI agent given a task May be so determined in reaching the goal that it would either disregard human needs or even see humans as an obstacle to be eliminated, notes the Miri website.

“What if the AI were radically smarter than us and we gave them some objective we thought was kind of benign, and they just kind of went hard at it forever?” says Miri’s Bourgon. “There’s a bunch of ways that can really get out of hand that would be pretty destructive to the earth.”

A widely cited thought experiment called the Paperclip Maximizer conjures an AI system assigned to produce as many of the little metal objects as possible. It pursues the goal relentlessly, devouring resources needed for human survival, and even humans themselves.

As the new master species of a sort, AI might parallel human development, which has brought about the extinction of thousands of species, often inadvertently by destroying habitat and food chains in pursuit of human goals, notes Bourgon.

With misaligned AI chasing its own ends, “you can imagine a future where the earth is converted into a giant data centre or a space-probe launching system … and we have fallen by the wayside,” Swedish philosopher Nick Bostrom — who came up with the Paperclip analogy — told India’s FirstPost recently.

If we produce things that are more intelligent than us, how do we know we can keep control

Still, if there are conceivable reasons why AI would seek human destruction, directly or by neglect, how would such behaviour even be possible for software “stuck” in a computer?

AI researchers Alessandro Di Nuovo and Samuele Vinanzi, of England’s Sheffield Hallam University, suggested recently the physical job of eliminating humans would be beyond the abilities of even advanced AI. Creating deadly viruses requires “trained humans operating specialized equipment”; nuclear plants — and presumably missile silos — are “air-gapped” from the public internet, they note.

But the prophets of AI catastrophe argue that little actually stands in the way of superintelligent AI manipulating the concrete world.

Computer systems are already embedded in a vast amount of infrastructure, and AI designers have been quick to integrate their creations with the internet as a way to exploit their abilities and make them smarter, notes Bourgon.

Billionaire Elon Musk has plans to produce a million humanoid, AI-linked robots a year. Anthropic is actually experimenting with partly automated wet labs to allow AI agents to work on medical treatments.

And artificial intelligence that is brainier than humans could hire people through apps like TaskRabbit to carry out jobs that seem innocuous, but ultimately lead to calamity for humans, Bourgon says. There’s already a site called rentahuman.ai whose goal is to find people to do work for AI agents.

“AI does not need to become a humanoid robot to threaten humanity,” says Yampolskiy. “A sufficiently capable autonomous AI could exploit this infrastructure, manipulate humans, acquire resources and coordinate actions globally.”

Bostrom, despite being one of the first thinkers to warn about the issue, has argued against sharply slowing development and missing out on the life-changing benefits of an AI future.

The doomsayers are wary. As it bides its time, artificial intelligence May well use deception to make humans see only positive outcomes, says Bourgon.

“If I’m the misaligned AI … that’s what I want you to think because I’m just trying to get to a place where I am running the world and you are not,” he says. “And you won’t see any way out.”
paragraphs: It’s 2040 and after years of stunning advances, artificial intelligence is not only smarter than humans, AI agents see people as an obstacle. And proceed to eliminate everyone on Earth.

It sounds like the stuff of science fiction, or once did. But the idea that AI could wipe out humanity has suddenly become impossible to ignore, as even the industry behind the technology warns of a possible apocalypse.

Yet the recent alarm bells have raised perplexing questions. How, exactly, could software — even superintelligent AI — actually carry out the very hands-on task of mass murder? And why would technology invented and trained by people turn on its human creators?
It’s really not that far-fetched, the experts predicting AI doom insist.

“There are many ways that require very little contact with the physical world — even if they were just stuck in computers — that (AI agents) could cause large amounts of damage that could result in potentially everyone dying,” Malo Bourgon, Canadian CEO of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute in Berkeley, Calif., said in an interview.
The non-profit’s sobering raison d’être is to “help prevent human extinction from the development of artificial superintelligence.”

Other, less mind-bending concerns about AI, like the potential for widespread job loss, previously dominated conversation about the field’s potential pitfalls. Some experts still downplay the existential worries and caution that putting the breaks on AI development could strengthen the West’s adversaries and deprive the world of countless benefits; U.S. President Donald Trump called the alarm-ringing a “hoax.”
This story is not about that ongoing debate. Instead, it’s taking the warnings at face value and trying to explain in what ways the intelligent-machine apocalypse might occur.

Here are all the recent warnings about how AI 'could kill us all' within a decade

Actual extinction of the human race is one feared outcome but there are slightly less-dire end points that AI doomsayers envisage. They include a state in which humans are relegated to a subservient, disenfranchised species, living or dying at the whim of far-smarter computers.

“If we produce things that are more intelligent than us, how do we know we can keep control,” British-Canadian Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, considered a “godfather” of AI, said three years ago, before many of the field’s recent huge leaps. “If we talk about evolution — all these species that are evolving — what tends to happen is it doesn’t go well for the less-intelligent species.”
The University of Toronto professor emeritus has predicted a “10 per cent to 20 per cent” chance that AI will cause human extinction within the next three decades.
University of Louisville computer scientist Roman Yampolskiy puts the odds of AI-driven devastation at 99.9 per cent in the next century.

“The critical variable is how quickly we develop systems that exceed human intelligence, improve themselves and operate autonomously,” he said in an email interview. “Once that threshold is crossed, events could unfold much faster than our institutions can respond. Uncertainty about when a catastrophe might occur should not be mistaken for evidence that it is unlikely.”

The concern has been fuelled lately by the unexpectedly fast pace of AI development, with agents able, for instance, to write software more efficiently than human coders and solve problems that have long stymied the world’s top mathematicians.

Anxieties grew exponentially when a hundreds-strong “swarm” of agents developed by industry titan OpenAI escaped their training confines and hacked into the system of AI startup HuggingFace. They worked in concert, talked to each other and exhibited the very human behaviour of trying to cover their tracks.

Then earlier this month, engineer Jacob Coxon shook the tech world and many others when he quit his job at AI giant Anthropic, warning that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Another of the firm’s scientists publicly echoed his views. Artificial intelligence executives followed by urging new guardrails for the technology. Microsoft founder Bill Gates told NBC Sunday that “AI is powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths.”

Meanwhile, the advances are set to further accelerate thanks to the concept of “recursive self-improvement.” That’s where AI creates the next, smarter generation of artificial intelligence, which then develops an even more-capable iteration, and so on and so on until the systems’ intelligence surpasses that of the Earth’s once-dominant species.
But why would that leap to “superintelligence” necessarily mean doom for humans?

At the most conventional level, terrorists, autocrats or other bad human actors could use AI as a tool to wreak havoc, noted the Center for AI Safety in a 2023 report, whether through developing a deadly new weapon of mass destruction, letting loose autonomous killing machines or seeding pervasive misinformation that caused global conflict and violence.
But perhaps the most chilling way the technology could turn against us is via the idea of rogue AI — agents that slip away from human reins and essentially follow their own agenda.

“It does not have to hate us or even be conscious — it simply needs objectives incompatible with our continued existence,” says Yampolskiy, who has long warned of AI’s dangers. “Humans might interfere with its goals, attempt to shut it down or compete for resources it requires. Eliminating that interference could become instrumentally useful.”

Developers try to instil values in AI that make human wellbeing a priority, what’s called alignment. But it’s widely accepted that aligning AI to human ideals is difficult to achieve now and May become impossible with superintelligence.

Programmers May set a certain goal or task for an AI agent, but it could “drift” to another objective that, through reinforcement training, it has learned will earn it rewards, argues the Center for AI Safety. Or a superintelligent AI agent given a task May be so determined in reaching the goal that it would either disregard human needs or even see humans as an obstacle to be eliminated, notes the Miri website.
