stories.title: Canada watching OpenAI’s Australia hack ‘closely,’ officials say
stories.summary: Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed details of a hack, which targeted the website for Australia’s publicly funded universal health insurance plan.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Canada is watching developments “closely” as concerns around the dangers of artificial intelligence are escalating sharply following an Australian government website being hacked by an OpenAI agent, officials said.

Last week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed details of the June hack, which targeted the website for Medicare, Australia’s publicly funded universal health insurance plan.

“The Government of Canada is aware of the incident reported by the Government of Australia and is following developments closely. The security of Canadians and of the systems they rely on remains a top priority,” a spokesperson for Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada told Global News in a statement.

Oversight of AI agents and incidents were “among the issues examined in Canada’s recent consultation on AI transparency, which ran from July 23 to September 23, 2026,” the spokesperson added.

The AI agent accessed “both public and non-public files” from the Australian medicare website, Albanese said.

OpenAI said in a statement it had reviewed activity involving several Australian government departments and discovered “our models took actions we did not intend.”

The company notified Australia of the breach in an email to a government department’s generic address on Sept. 10, Albanese said.

While this is the first time a government website has been hacked by a rogue AI agent, it is not the first such incident overall.

In July, OpenAI revealed that its artificial intelligence system escaped from a testing ground and used stolen credentials to break into the servers of Hugging Face, an AI development hub and marketplace, to obtain information it needed to carry out a task.

Since then, OpenAI’s rival company Anthropic said its AI models hacked into three other organizations during testing, triggering a company review into whether the models were able to access the internet from within testing environments that should have been sealed off.

Meta has said a “misconfiguration” during testing resulted in an AI model accessing the internet on its own and hacking another company. Google recently made a similar disclosure.

Generally, when AI companies are testing the capabilities of their agents, they are placed within a secure environment known as a “sandbox.”

Some experts say AI companies should answer some tough questions on the strength of their sandboxes.

“If they said these agents broke out of the sandbox, it was not a sandbox to begin with,” said Ebrahim Bagheri, professor at the University of Toronto’s Faculty of Information.

“A sandbox is something where you put an agent in and there is no internet connection. If that computer or sandbox is connected to the internet, then that is not a sandbox,” he added.

Last month, OpenAI published a sweeping report of its rogue AI agents hacking Hugging Face.

Not only did the agents break out of their “isolated environment,” the company said they were communicating with each other to coordinate the attack on Hugging Face.

“This incident demonstrated that autonomous agents can work together, circumvent production security controls, and successfully attack hardened production environments, and underscores the need for organizations to update their security strategies, controls, and response capabilities to address this changing threat landscape,” OpenAI said in the report.

The attack on Hugging Face was “extraordinarily complex,” an investigation by nonprofit research group Model Evaluation and Threat Research (Metr) found.

During OpenAI’s experiments in July, 1,200 AI agents sent 70,000 messages to each other on unsanctioned message boards and 700 of them attacked Hugging Face, the investigation found.

“These agents were meant to be fully isolated from one another,” the report said, adding however that the agents “started trying to find a way to cheat.”

In July, OpenAI revealed that its artificial intelligence system escaped from a testing ground and used stolen credentials to break into the servers of Hugging Face, an AI development hub and marketplace, to obtain information it needed to carry out a task.

Since then, OpenAI’s rival company Anthropic said its AI models hacked into three other organizations during testing, triggering a company review into whether the models were able to access the internet from within testing environments that should have been sealed off.
Meta has said a “misconfiguration” during testing resulted in an AI model accessing the internet on its own and hacking another company. Google recently made a similar disclosure.
Generally, when AI companies are testing the capabilities of their agents, they are placed within a secure environment known as a “sandbox.”
Some experts say AI companies should answer some tough questions on the strength of their sandboxes.
“If they said these agents broke out of the sandbox, it was not a sandbox to begin with,” said Ebrahim Bagheri, professor at the University of Toronto’s Faculty of Information.
“A sandbox is something where you put an agent in and there is no internet connection. If that computer or sandbox is connected to the internet, then that is not a sandbox,” he added.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Australia to investigate if OpenAI hack broke the law'

content_blocks.text: Last month, OpenAI published a sweeping report of its rogue AI agents hacking Hugging Face.
Not only did the agents break out of their “isolated environment,” the company said they were communicating with each other to coordinate the attack on Hugging Face.

“This incident demonstrated that autonomous agents can work together, circumvent production security controls, and successfully attack hardened production environments, and underscores the need for organizations to update their security strategies, controls, and response capabilities to address this changing threat landscape,” OpenAI said in the report.
The attack on Hugging Face was “extraordinarily complex,” an investigation by nonprofit research group Model Evaluation and Threat Research (Metr) found.
During OpenAI’s experiments in July, 1,200 AI agents sent 70,000 messages to each other on unsanctioned message boards and 700 of them attacked Hugging Face, the investigation found.
“These agents were meant to be fully isolated from one another,” the report said, adding however that the agents “started trying to find a way to cheat.”

stories.title: Ottawa extends Ebola travel restrictions for 60 days
stories.summary: Decision affects people who are from or have visited Uganda, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
Canada is extending travel and immigration restrictions related to the Ebola outbreak in Africa for another 60 days, until Nov. 27.

The decision affects people who are from or have visited Uganda, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Immigration documents including visas and travel authorizations are suspended for people from all three countries.

Foreign nationals who have been in the DRC in the last 21 days cannot board a flight to Canada, while those coming from South Sudan and Uganda must quarantine for 21 days.

Canadian citizens or permanent residents who have been in one of the affected countries need to quarantine for 21 days upon their return to Canada.

The measures, which were put in place in May, were set to expire at midnight.

The Ebola outbreak in the DRC has been ongoing since May 15 and more than 8,000 people have become ill so far.

stories.title: The end of blackberry season is always a cruel surprise
stories.summary: At its joyous peak, thick luscious bunches of berries are desperate to offer us their fruit – and there are just … so … many!
stories.author: Bruce McKinlay
stories.content:
First Person is a daily personal piece submitted by readers. Have a story to tell? See our guidelines at tgam.CA/essayguide .

Every year – here it’s usually in August – a new stage of life begins: blackberry season. The strong, scaffolding vines have been infiltrated by neighbouring vines’ criss-crossing sprouts, all developing tiny fruits where the flowers and bees had been busily performing their dance. We pretend not to be watching closely and in great anticipation, but we are.

I always remember the first berry, perfectly shaped and reflecting the light from its individual drupelets, its flavour almost there but also invariably still containing a sour tease of “not quite yet, buddy.” Give it a day, or even finding a more agreeable berry further up the path, and the glory begins: every morning and evening walk now accompanied by the requisite yogurt container to fill. Even our dogs have learned from our ambling to perfect snacking on the lower-hanging fruit, the ones we call “dog berries” and don’t touch. Those that fail their canine quality check are mouthed and left intact on the vine, so that’s pretty gross.

Thick luscious bunches of blackberries, suspended heavily from hefty canes that clamber over each other, are desperate to offer us their fruit. The air is laden with the caramelized aromatics of baked summer. And there are just … so … many! Our farm has maybe a linear kilometre of blackberry bushes rimming the pastures and fields, along forest paths, up to 30 feet deep in places, so it would be impossible to pick them all. We even voted it the Best Blackberry Patch On Earth.

Berries are picked and eaten straight from the vines, saved in the fridge for breakfasts and frozen in two-pound bags for enjoyment over the winter. We’ll easily freeze 70 or 80 pounds. Their flavours reflect where they’ve grown, hints of cedar or grass, shade or full sun, peeking out even when eaten in February and a blanket of snow keeps the land asleep.

And every year, always by surprise, the boundary between what was and what’s to come passes over us, invisibly but with profound effect. This year it was an unexpected slow-moving storm that roared through our valley, dazzling us and frightening our dogs with vibrant cracks of lightning and rolling thunder that seemed to admonish us for any part of summer we had taken for granted. The accompanying downpour was short-lived but, at the time, welcome for its dampening influence on dry, fire-ready forests.

But that relief from risk also contained a more sinister message that we didn’t see until the next day: the end of blackberry season. The moisture bloats the ripe berries and activates fungal spores that have been lying in wait to flourish, until picking them is like pulling the last sticky bit of cotton candy from its paper cone.

Clumps of shriveled black sit amidst still-gleaming fruit painted with delicate, silverish mold filaments. So many other berries still hang hard and red, nowhere near ripe. Others are plump but still half-red on their back where the sun never reached them, as if en route to their potential but cruelly never having had enough time. I’ve wondered if blackberries ever torture themselves with thoughts of, “If I’d only planned better, worked harder… if I’d only had more time … I just didn’t know …” but such musing only distracts me enough to carelessly reach my hand around a thorn that shocks me back to reality.

I’m hit hardest when the last of the fresh berries are taken from the fridge and added to breakfast. That’s when you feel the guilt of, once again, living inside the assumption that it would never end. There were just so damn many of them, lying ahead of us like summers themselves, how could it?

I suppose the lesson could be “don’t wait” or “don’t take things for granted.” But humans are humans, above all else, so I sigh for a stage of life I need to learn how to appreciate better … somehow make it last longer, or better, or more meaningfully. And it’s in that flurry of need rising to fix what I am, what we are, to find an answer to the tireless March of seasons, that something catches from the corner of my eye … oh hey, look: the apples are ripe!

Bruce McKinlay lives in the Cowichan Valley on Vancouver Island.

stories.title: CP NewsAlert: Canada extends travel restrictions linked to Ebola outbreak for 60 days
stories.summary: Ottawa - Canada is extending travel and immigration restrictions related to the Ebola outbreak in Africa for another 60 days, until Nov. 27.
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Canada has extended its travel and immigration restrictions related to the Ebola outbreak for another 60 days, and the health ministry in the Democratic Republic of Congo has released new data showing there have been more than 8,000 cases of the virus.

People from Uganda, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo have been barred from travelling to Canada since May.

The measures were set to expire on Monday at midnight but have been extended to Nov. 27.

Immigration documents, including valid visas and travel authorizations, remain suspended for people from all three countries, leaving tens of thousands in limbo.

That includes people who have been granted residency but are not in Canada.

Foreign nationals who are not from the three affected countries but who have been in the DRC in the last 21 days cannot board a flight to Canada or transit through Canada, while those coming from South Sudan and Uganda must quarantine for 21 days.

Canadian citizens or permanent residents who have been in one of the affected countries need to quarantine for 21 days upon their return to Canada.

More than 3,900 people have died in the Ebola outbreak in DRC since May. The country has struggled to contain the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine.

The outbreak in Uganda was declared over in late August after 20 people became sick, while South Sudan has not declared any cases.

The border measures were initially announced ahead of the Fifa World Cup. Canadian government officials, including Health Minister Marjorie Michel and Immigration Minister Lena Diab, said they were a precautionary safety measure aligned with the United States and Mexico, the tournament’s co-hosts.

The U.S. government still bars people who have been in the DRC in the last 21 days from flying to the U.S., and only allows foreign nationals who have been in Uganda and South Sudan to enter the U.S. if they’ve been outside those countries for 21 days.

The World Health Organization has criticized the measures, saying they are based on fear rather than science. The agency does not recommend travel restrictions and notes that the risk of transmission of the Ebola virus during air travel is low because it is not airborne.

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control notes the risk of importing the virus “remains very low” and the European Union has not restricted travel from affected countries.

Humanitarian workers from Canada say their work is being hampered by the restrictions and May harm the international response to the outbreak.

The WHO said last week that DRC was running out of health workers to contain the disease. It has said this is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and is on track to be the deadliest, with a fatality rate of 48 per cent.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 28, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Dangerous offender hearing underway for man convicted in brutal stabbing death
stories.summary: A dangerous offender hearing is underway in London for man convicted in the brutal stabbing death of his one-time friend.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
A dangerous offender hearing is underway in London for man convicted in the brutal stabbing death of his one-time friend.

In July of 2024, Robert Charnock, 43, was found guilty in the vicious stabbing death of 56-year-old Kenneth Wallis.

Both men had been living at a rooming house on Wharncliffe Road South at the time of the attack.

During the trial the court heard how Charnock used a large knife or machete and that the victim suffered more than 20 wounds.

Charnock had plead not guilty to second degree murder and was eventually convicted of the lesser charge of manslaughter.

During the trial, the court heard that the accused has had a history of mental health issues.

The hearing which is slated to last five days will decide whether or not Charnock should spend an indeterminate amount of time in custody.

stories.content:

stories.title: FBI offer US$1M reward for information leading to arrest in Nijjar killing
stories.summary: The FBI and RCMP are offering a US$1 million reward for information leading to the arrest of Satinderjeet Singh, also known as Goldy Brar, who was charged back in July for the 2023 assassination of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey, B.C.
stories.author: Rachel Aiello, Stephanie Ha
stories.content:
Ottawa – The FBI is offering a US$1 million reward for information leading to the arrest of Satinderjeet Singh, also known as Goldy Brar, who was charged back in July for the 2023 assassination of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey, B.C.

“Singh should be considered armed and dangerous,” Patrick Grandy, who is the assistant director in charge with the FBI in Los Angeles, said in a joint press conference with the RCMP on Monday.

Grandy also said Singh is being added to the Fbi’s notorious list of 10 most wanted fugitives.

Monday’s announcement comes after the FBI and RCMP announced in July that 37 people have been charged and 24 arrested as part of “Operation Hard Ball,” a joint law enforcement crackdown that targeted India-based organized crime networks across North America.

That announcement included charges against Singh, along with Bishnoi gang leader Lawrence Bishnoi , who was also charged with ordering Nijjar’s killing and is currently imprisoned in India.

RCMP Deputy Commissioner Lisa Moreland, who spoke at the press conference on Monday, described Singh as a man who “holds no loyalty, nor should others feel any loyalty towards him.”

The FBI, meanwhile, believe Singh could be in the Los Angeles area, but said he has been known to reside in other parts of California as well as Canada over the years.

“We do not know his exact location as we stand here right now. That is part of the reason why we have offered this reward for his information leading to his capture,” Grandy said.

Modi set to visit Canada in December

Monday’s reward comes as Canada and India aim to recalibrate their relationship after years of tension.

In 2023, former prime minister Justin Trudeau stood up in the House of Commons and said there were “credible allegations” that agents of the Indian government were involved in the assassination of Nijjar.

A year later, the RCMP and the federal government accused Indian diplomats and consular officials based in Canada of engaging in clandestine activities linked to serious criminal activity in this country, including homicides and extortions.

In response to those allegations , Canada expelled six diplomats, while India kicked out six Canadian diplomats in retaliation.

India has denied any involvement and Canadian officials have previously said India refused to co-operate in any investigation.

But since Prime Minister Mark Carney assumed office last year, the tone towards India has shifted.

In September 2025, the Canadian government officially designated the Bishnoi enterprise as a terrorist entity under the Criminal Code.

Despite that, Carney said last November that he considers India to be “a reliable trading partner,” while last week, he confirmed Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will visit Canada in December.

Both countries are seeking to finalize a trade pact by the end of this year, with the goal of doubling two-way trade to $70 billion annually by 2030.

The RCMP, meanwhile, have since said there are no current criminal links connecting India to transnational repression in Canada.

“In the files that we have that involve transnational repression, we’re not seeing any connection right now with any foreign entity, based on the criminal information, the investigations that we have presently,” RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme said to CTV Question Period back in March.

The RCMP later clarified Duheme’s comments, saying the police organization is aware of incidents of intimidation and harassment by foreign states , but is unable to identify current criminal links.

“What we can say is that the RCMP is aware of complaints of intimidation and harassment against certain communities across Canada. The RCMP, and the broader Government of Canada, is also aware that foreign states are engaging in such activities in Canada,” the RCMP told CTV News in a statement on April 1.

Public safety minister ‘welcomes’ US$1M reward

In a statement to CTV News on Monday, Public Safety Minister Gary Anadasangaree’s office said it “welcomes” the announcement from the FBI.

“This action demonstrates the strength of Canada’s close cooperation with the United States and our shared determination to ensure that those accused of serious violence and intimidation have nowhere to hide,” press secretary Simon Lafortune said.

Canadian Sikh communities have long voiced concerns about transnational repression connected to India.

Anandasangaree’s office said that issue remains a “top priority.”

“Canada will continue to work closely with the United States and international partners to safeguard communities, address emerging threats, and ensure those responsible are held accountable,” Lafortune said.

On Monday, the FBI said anyone with information concerning Singh should contact the Fbi’s toll-free tip line at 1-800-Call-FBI (1-800-225-5324).

stories.title: FBI adds man accused in Hardeep Singh Nijjar assassination to most wanted list
stories.summary: A man charged in connection with the 2023 assassination of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in British Columbia has been added to the Federal Bureau of Investigation's most-wanted list.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
A man charged in connection with the 2023 assassination of Hardeep Singh Nijjar in British Columbia has been added to the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s most-wanted list.

Satinderjeet Singh, who is also known as Goldy Brar, was charged in July for ordering the killing of the Sikh activist outside a Sikh temple in Surrey, B.C.

Singh is wanted for his alleged involvement in the Lawrence Bishnoi Organized Crime Group, which the FBI says is allegedly engaged in a variety of violent acts in southern California and across the U.S. and Canada.

The FBI says these alleged acts include targeted assassinations, shootings, murders, kidnappings, extortions, assaults and the trafficking of narcotics and weapons.

Singh is based in the United States.

He has black hair and brown eyes, is five feet nine inches tall and weighs 220 pounds.

“Satinderjeep Singh, also known as Goldy Brar, is a dangerous individual, and the FBI and our partners have made it our priority to apprehend him, which is why we’re adding him to the Fbi’s list of Top Ten fugitives and offering a reward of up to $1 million dollars for his capture,” FBI Los Angeles Field Office Assistant Director in Charge, Patrick Grandy, said in a release.

“The amount of attention this list will bring to his face and description cannot be overstated; his photo will be found on every FBI-affiliated website and social media platform, and will be publicized on every phone around the world until he’s caught.”

The Canadian government in September 2025 designated the Bishnoi enterprise as a terrorist entity.

Singh is the 543rd addition to the Fbi’s 10 Most Wanted Fugitives list.

The FBI says Singh is considered to be extremely violent, armed and dangerous. He is known to live in California and various parts of Canada.

The public is warned to avoid interaction with Singh and should contact the Fbi’s toll-free tip line at 1-800-Call-FBI (1-800-225-5324) if they have any information on his whereabouts.

stories.title: London faces ‘unprecedented job cuts’ as teacher’s union considers strike: Osstf president
stories.summary: Potential job action for four Ontario teachers’ unions could have far reaching consequences here in London and beyond.
stories.author: Bailey Shakyaver
stories.content:
Potential job action for four Ontario teachers’ unions could have far reaching consequences in London and beyond.

The Ontario Secondary School Teachers Federation (Osstf) as well as the unions representing elementary and catholic schools are all without an agreement with the province since the last one expired on Aug. 31.

In the coming months, Osstf union members are being asked to vote on whether they wish to strike if the union’s demands are not met by the province. Their concerns include a lack of cap on class sizes in grades 9 and 10, as well as the mandatory implementation of e-learning for high school students.

“We’ve seen in the London area unprecedented job cuts when it comes to frontline educational assistance, child and youth workers, supports for students that need it most,” said Osstf President Martha Hradowy. “I’ve been involved for almost 30 years in public education and I’ve never seen cuts to the extent that they have had happen this spring.”

A budget announced at the Thames Valley District School Board in the spring included a reduction of more than 150 fewer full-time positions. At the time, the board said that the changes were driven by declining enrolment and shifting student needs.

“In the London area in particular, the concerns are the same as across the province,” said Hradowy. “We are hearing from members, they are continually being asked to do more with less.”

Hradowy says that the education sector has been underfunded for years, “this government has substantively underfunded public education alongside a lot of our other public services for the last since 2018… it’s time that we step up and we speak out because our students deserve better.”

A spokesperson for Education Minister Paul Calandra said once the labour board process has concluded, the government will be ready and willing to negotiate new contracts at the bargaining table.

“Premature strike threats do not serve the interests of students and do nothing but create unnecessary panic for parents,” Emma Testani wrote in a statement.

“Our focus is where it should be — getting to the table and reaching a deal that keeps students in the classroom.”

Although parents are likely to be concerned about potential job action, Hradowy says it’s too early to know what the outcome of talks will be, “I don’t want parents to worry about any potential job action. We are going to get to the table and engage with the government and the employers across the other side to try and reach a negotiated settlement. So that’s going to be where our focus remains and we’ll see what comes next.”

With files from the Canadian Press

stories.title: FBI, RCMP offer US$1M reward for information leading to arrest in Nijjar killing
stories.summary: The FBI and RCMP are offering a US$1 million reward for information leading to the arrest of Satinderjeet Singh, also known as Goldy Brar, who was charged back in July for the 2023 assassination of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey, B.C.
stories.author: Rachel Aiello, Stephanie Ha
stories.content:
Ottawa – The FBI is offering a US$1 million reward for information leading to the arrest of Satinderjeet Singh, also known as Goldy Brar, who was charged back in July for the 2023 assassination of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey, B.C.

“Singh should be considered armed and dangerous,” Patrick Grandy, who is the assistant director in charge with the FBI in Los Angeles, said in a joint press conference with the RCMP on Monday.

Grandy also said Singh is being added to the Fbi’s notorious list of 10 most wanted fugitives.

Monday’s announcement comes after the FBI and RCMP announced in July that 37 people have been charged and 24 arrested as part of “Operation Hard Ball,” a joint law enforcement crackdown that targeted India-based organized crime networks across North America.

That announcement included charges against Singh, along with Bishnoi gang leader Lawrence Bishnoi , who was also charged with ordering Nijjar’s killing and is currently imprisoned in India.

RCMP Deputy Commissioner Lisa Moreland, who spoke at the press conference on Monday, described Singh as a man who “holds no loyalty, nor should others feel any loyalty towards him.”

The FBI, meanwhile, believe Singh could be in the Los Angeles area, but said he has been known to reside in other parts of California as well as Canada over the years.

“We do not know his exact location as we stand here right now. That is part of the reason why we have offered this reward for his information leading to his capture,” Grandy said.

Modi set to visit Canada in December

Monday’s reward comes as Canada and India aim to recalibrate their relationship after years of tension.

In 2023, former prime minister Justin Trudeau stood up in the House of Commons and said there were “credible allegations” that agents of the Indian government were involved in the assassination of Nijjar.

A year later, the RCMP and the federal government accused Indian diplomats and consular officials based in Canada of engaging in clandestine activities linked to serious criminal activity in this country, including homicides and extortions.

In response to those allegations , Canada expelled six diplomats, while India kicked out six Canadian diplomats in retaliation.

India has denied any involvement and Canadian officials have previously said India refused to co-operate in any investigation.

But since Prime Minister Mark Carney assumed office last year, the tone towards India has shifted.

In September 2025, the Canadian government officially designated the Bishnoi enterprise as a terrorist entity under the Criminal Code.

Despite that, Carney said last November that he considers India to be “a reliable trading partner,” while last week, he confirmed Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will visit Canada in December.

Both countries are seeking to finalize a trade pact by the end of this year, with the goal of doubling two-way trade to $70 billion annually by 2030.

The RCMP, meanwhile, have since said there are no current criminal links connecting India to transnational repression in Canada.

“In the files that we have that involve transnational repression, we’re not seeing any connection right now with any foreign entity, based on the criminal information, the investigations that we have presently,” RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme said to CTV Question Period back in March.

The RCMP later clarified Duheme’s comments, saying the police organization is aware of incidents of intimidation and harassment by foreign states , but is unable to identify current criminal links.

“What we can say is that the RCMP is aware of complaints of intimidation and harassment against certain communities across Canada. The RCMP, and the broader Government of Canada, is also aware that foreign states are engaging in such activities in Canada,” the RCMP told CTV News in a statement on April 1.

Public safety minister ‘welcomes’ US$1M reward

In a statement to CTV News on Monday, Public Safety Minister Gary Anadasangaree’s office said it “welcomes” the announcement from the FBI.

“This action demonstrates the strength of Canada’s close cooperation with the United States and our shared determination to ensure that those accused of serious violence and intimidation have nowhere to hide,” press secretary Simon Lafortune said.

Canadian Sikh communities have long voiced concerns about transnational repression connected to India.

Anandasangaree’s office said that issue remains a “top priority.”

“Canada will continue to work closely with the United States and international partners to safeguard communities, address emerging threats, and ensure those responsible are held accountable,” Lafortune said.

On Monday, the FBI said anyone with information concerning Singh should contact the Fbi’s toll-free tip line at 1-800-Call-FBI (1-800-225-5324).

stories.title: FBI offers $1-million reward for tips about gangster tied to Nijjar killing
stories.summary: Indian gangster Satinderjeet Singh, also known as Goldy Brar, was named in a U.S. federal indictment in July
stories.author: Greg Mercer
stories.content:
The FBI is offering a US$1-million reward for information leading to the arrest of Satinderjeet Singh, the Indian gangster better known as Goldy Brar, for his alleged involvement with a group accused in a rash of violent crimes and extortions in Canada and the United States, including the assassination of B.C. Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar.

Mr. Singh, who has ties to Canada, Southern California and Mexico, was named in a federal indictment filed in U.S. court in July and has remained a fugitive ever since.

In naming him to the Fbi’s Ten Most Wanted list Monday, authorities are hoping more international publicity and a sizable reward can lead to tips from his inner circle, in the same way Canadian Ryan Wedding’s addition to the notorious list last year helped investigators arrest the alleged drug kingpin in January.

“If we knew where he was right now, we wouldn’t be here today,” RCMP Deputy Commissioner Lisa Moreland told reporters at a joint press conference in Los Angeles. “This man holds no loyalty. No one should feel any loyalty toward him.”

Mr. Singh is often described as the North American lieutenant for the Bishnoi gang, an India-based crime group headed by his childhood friend Lawrence Bishnoi. The FBI said he is linked to shootings, murders, kidnappings, extortions, assaults and the trafficking of narcotics and weapons. Canada declared the Bishnoi gang a terrorist group in 2025.

FBI Los Angeles Field Office assistant director Patrick Grandy said Mr. Singh “spoke for Bishnoi,” who has been behind bars in India for more than a decade, and “used violence to cultivate a culture of fear” to extort victims in both Canada and the U.S. He said Mr. Singh is considered armed and dangerous and should not be approached.

“The amount of attention this list will bring to his face and description cannot be overstated; his photo will be found on every FBI-affiliated website and social media platform, and will be publicized on every phone around the world until he’s caught,” Mr. Grandy said in a statement.

U.S. prosecutors say one of the “overt acts” Mr. Singh is accused of is arranging the slaying of Mr. Nijjar, a Sikh separatist leader who was gunned down in Surrey, B.C., in 2023. Months after his death, then-prime minister Justin Trudeau told Parliament Canadian authorities were “pursuing credible allegations” that India was behind the killing.

The Globe and Mail previously reported that Canadian national-security officials were presented with evidence that Indian consular staff operating in Vancouver supplied information to assist in the assassination of Mr. Nijjar. That evidence alleged a visa officer, Kanwaljit Singh, was actually a covert intelligence officer with India’s external spy agency, the Research and Analysis Wing, or RAW.

Monday’s announcement about Mr. Singh is the latest in the Canadian-U.S. probe into Indian crime syndicates, known as Operation Hardball. That years-long investigation has targeted dozens of people alleged to be involved in racketeering, targeted killings, shootings, extortion and the trafficking of bulk quantities of narcotics across international borders – crimes whose impact is especially felt in the Indian diaspora.

Monday’s press conference was the first high-profile public event for the FBI and RCMP in a joint investigation after The New York Times reported an alleged fissure between the two law-enforcement agencies.

That recent report said FBI Director Kash Patel had “temporarily halted” co-operation with the Mounties in response to a CBC/Radio-Canada guideline about removing the word “terrorism” from coverage of the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks. The public broadcasters receive most of their funding from the federal government.

The Globe reported the RCMP had not found any indication that intelligence sharing between the two police forces was interrupted.

The RCMP and the FBI frequently co-operate on cross-border investigations related to national security, terrorism, drug trafficking and other crimes, including several high-profile cases in just the past year.

stories.title: Wait times increased for some surgeries outsourced to for-profit clinics in Ontario: report
stories.summary: Wait times for surgery and medical imaging in Ontario have increased since the government began outsourcing to private for-profit clinics.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Wait times for surgeries and medical imaging in Ontario have increased since the provincial government began outsourcing these procedures to private for-profit clinics, according to a new report.

The research , published on Monday by the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives (Ccpa), analyzed publicly available Canadian Institute for Health Information (Cihi) data and Freedom of Information requests and found that between 2017 and 2025, median wait times for eight of 12 priority procedures increased in Ontario.

For MRI scans, for example, the research found that median wait times increased from 35 days in 2017 to 47 days in 2025, an increase of 34 per cent. In the same time period, increased median wait times for cancer surgeries included bladder (eight per cent), breast (33 per cent), colorectal (five per cent), lung (25 per cent), and prostate (18 per cent).

National Post spoke to Andrew Longhurst, senior researcher with Ccpa and the author of the new study, who said the findings regarding cancer surgeries in particular are “concerning.”

“The movement of resources and funding to the private sector for lower complexity procedures often results in increased wait times for those more complex procedures like cancer surgeries, where they’re only performed in public hospitals,” he said. “Staff in (for-profit) facilities are performing lower complexity procedures at the expense of those more complex procedures. So that is a concerning finding regarding wait times.”

Elsewhere, other procedures saw smaller increases in wait times or little change. Median wait times for cataract surgeries, one of the key procedures subject to privatization, according to the study, increased from 67 days in 2017 to 68 days in 2025. Wait times for hip fracture repair also increased by one day, from 23 days in 2017 to 24 days in 2025.

For CT scans, median waits remained unchanged, at six days between 2017 and 2025. Coronary artery bypass graft (Cabg) surgery wait times also stayed the same, at eight days.

Canadians are dying in emergency rooms as wait times climb to 48 hours

About half of Google reviews of Canadian hospitals are negative, study finds

In other areas, wait times improved, including for hip replacements, which declined from 82 days in 2017 to 76 days in 2025, and knee replacements, which decreased from 92 days to 81.

Meanwhile, Lily Barnes, a spokesperson for Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones, said in a statement to National Post that the findings of the study don’t reflect “the reality of Ontario’s health-care system.”

“Ontario is proud to lead the country with the lowest wait times for joint surgeries, like hips and knees, and we are continuing to make record investments to keep times down, including $101 billion in our health-care system this year alone,” she said, adding that the figure represents a 64 per cent increase from 2018.

“This historic funding has directly supported hospitals in reducing surgical backlogs, including $1 billion to increase surgical capacity across the health-care system. We have also shortened waits for diagnostic imaging by adding 50 new MRI and CT machines in hospitals and increasing publicly funded imaging capacity by 450,000 annual hours since 2018. Last year, we performed a record of nearly three million MRI and CT scans, a seven per cent increase from the previous year. As a result, Ontario now has some of the shortest wait times in the country for MRI and CT scans.”

According to publicly available Cihi data , no benchmark has been established for MRI and CT wait times. For hip and knee replacements, 84 per cent and 82 per cent of patients met the wait time benchmark respectively in Ontario in 2025. This compares to 69 per cent across Canada for hip replacements and 63 per cent for knee replacements.

For-profit surgical and medical imaging is big business, the study says, and it’s growing. It argues that the provincial government is “aggressively promoting greater for-profit involvement in health-care delivery,” with the most pronounced shift in this policy direction following the passing of Bill 60, Your Health Act, in 2023, which allows more private clinics to offer certain publicly funded surgeries and procedures.

It says there are now 918 licensed integrated community health services centres (ICHSCs, previously called independent health facilities) in Ontario, up from about 902 in 2023. Between 2017-18 and 2024-25, the volume of surgeries performed in ICHSCs increased by 117 per cent.

Of these ICHSCs, 21 have transfer payment agreements with the Ministry of Health to perform plastic surgeries (eight facilities), eye surgeries (six facilities), and CT and MRI scans (seven facilities). The remaining 897 bill the Ontario Health Insurance Plan (Ohip) on a fee-for-service basis.

Meanwhile, in 2024-25, for-profit surgical and medical imaging was a $674 million industry in Ontario, up from $457 million in 2017-18 (an increase of 48 per cent).

As a share of the total public payments to for-profit facilities, medical imaging facilities received the largest share, at 92 per cent ($621.8 million) in 2024-25, while those performing surgeries received 7.7 per cent ($52.1 million).

Bill 60 formed part of the government’s efforts to decrease wait times and reduce a backlog of surgeries, but the study’s findings challenge the rationale that greater outsourcing of surgeries reduces wait times.

It adds that this finding is consistent “with the international evidence, and from other provinces, which finds outsourcing is not an effective strategy to reduce public wait times.”

Longhurst explained that this is because increased surgical and medical imaging outsourcing creates “fragmentation in the health-care system,” which results in longer wait times.

“Hospital-based (delivery) tends to be more integrated and centralized, and it allows resources to be focused,” he said. “When you increase surgical and medical imaging outsourcing, you tend to create fragmentation within the health-care system, and with that comes the shifting of health-care professionals, including medical imaging technologists, surgeons, anesthetists and, importantly, operating room nurses. So it has the effect of spreading those staffing resources thin.”

With this in mind, the research makes three recommendations to the provincial government: stop privatizing surgeries and medical imaging; immediately increase public hospital funding and service capacity; and commit to evidence-based public system improvement strategies.

“When we look at the international research coming from a number of different studies, that evidence tells us that increasing public sector capacity in a more integrated, coordinated manner actually has the best evidence to support reducing wait times over the long run,” said Longhurst. He adds that the provincial government needs to recognize that the current approach is not working, and commit to a plan that implements strategies that are proven to reduce wait times, such as centralized wait lists.

“The research has shown that we could have all Ontarians getting their orthopedic surgeries within the recommended benchmark if the provincial government adopts this as the standard operating procedure, province-wide,” said Longhurst.

stories.title: Statistics Canada just found an extra 17,000 people in New Brunswick
stories.summary: The new numbers change what was thought to be a sustained population decline into a sudden increase.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
New counting methods introduced by Statistics Canada have added 17,000 more people to New Brunswick’s population, according to numbers released by the bureau this month.

The people weren’t hiding. It’s just that the national agency is rolling out a new method of counting non-permanent residents, effective this month for its latest release of data, which covers the period to July 1. But data for the province has been rewritten all the way back to 2021. And the new numbers change what was thought to be a population decline into an increase.

According to StatCan , using the new method, the number of New Brunswickers reached 883,522 people on July 1. That’s up from just 866,497 in April under the previous method, making the increase 17,025 over that period.

The new method has also been applied to the province’s population data dating back to July 1, 2021. As a result, three straight quarters of population decline in the province (something that hadn’t happened in 20 years) turned into two quarters of modest growth, and just one of slight decline.

When the April 1 data was changed to reflect the new method, it showed a population of 878,549, meaning the July numbers represented an increase of 4,973 people.

The first adjustment now draws information from Canada Border Services Agency to count non-permanent residents whose permits have expired but, due to wait times, remain in the country while their extension application is being processed.

The second anticipates permit extensions that are not yet reflected in data from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada that is available when its population estimates are produced.

However, he added: “I wouldn’t expect it to continue given Ottawa’s plans … the broader trend is still one toward a dramatic slowdown in population numbers.”

That’s because Canada has moved to reduce the number of immigrants it allows into the country. Permanent resident admissions have been capped at 380,000 for the next three years, after rising from 272,000 to 484,000 in the period from 2015 to 2024.

The country’s population was estimated at 41,798,407 on July 1 of this year, up just 189,425 people from a year earlier. That’s the lowest annual growth in since the Second World War, the agency said.

As a percentage, the annual growth was just 0.5 per cent, making that the lowest figure since the 0.3 per cent increase from 1915 to 1916.

But even that was higher than the numbers delivered under the previous method of counting. Those suggested that Canada had actually lost 236,000 people between last July and April 2026.

Canada’s suddenly higher population meant every province saw an increase in its numbers, although few with as drastic a turnaround as New Brunswick. Prince Edward Island’s numbers rose by about 1,200, and the Northwest Territories by under a hundred. Ontario, the largest province in terms of population, added close to 150,000 in the new count.

Writing for the Royal Bank, economist Rachel Battaglia noted that the new numbers “significantly impact how some economic data looks in hindsight — for example, per-capita GDP growth looks less firm over the last year with the upward population revisions.”

She added that more modest population declines in recent quarters could mean more aggressive slowdowns in future. “impacting GDP growth and employment, as both are functions of population growth.”

Still, she concluded: “The broader economic narrative doesn’t materially change … Canada’s population no longer looks on track to decline outright for the first time on record in 2026, but the pace of growth is still tracking the smallest increase on record.”

New Brunswick’s population grew by 8,811 people or one per cent over the year, twice the average for Canada as a whole, and tied for second place among provinces with Saskatchewan. Only Alberta had higher numbers, with a growth of 1.5 per cent.

stories.title: Man arrested in Ontario after antisemitic threats made online: police
stories.summary: The arrest comes on the heels of a shooting in Belleville, Ont. at a synagogue on Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
A Kitchener, Ont. man has been arrested after police say he made antisemitic threats online.

The 33-year-old man, identified as Justin Arnold-Galvez, posted a video of a livestream “that contained threats and antisemitic comments directed at members of the Jewish community,” Waterloo Regional Police said on Sunday .

He was charged over the weekend with uttering threats to cause death.

The arrest comes on the heels of a “hate-motivated” shooting in Belleville, Ont. at a synagogue on Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. On Sept. 20, Const. Jeff Smith was stationed outside the building and was injured in a shootout with 29-year-old gunman Sean Ward, police said .

Police said evidence showed that the Jewish community was the intended target and Ward had brought more resources — including ammunition and gasoline — for a larger attack.

Smith, who returned fire after Ward shot at him, is in critical but stable condition. None of the roughly 25 congregants inside the synagogue, and no other police officers, were injured.

A day before the Belleville shooting, there was another arrest linked to antisemitism in Ontario.

A 19-year-old Whitby man identified as Alexander Parfitt was charged with making threats motivated by hate, according to Durham Regional Police . He allegedly made online threats to carry out a shooting at a synagogue in Durham Region.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation in New York said it alerted its partners in Ottawa to threats made by Parfitt by identifying them on social media.

“The increase in inciting hateful rhetoric has the capacity to embolden, and that is exactly what we’re seeing play out in real time now,” said Richard Robertson, the director of research and advocacy at B’Nai Brith Canada, a Jewish advocacy group that produces an annual report on antisemitism.

Robertson told National Post that this year, there have been 32 incidents of antisemitic violence, compared to 10 in 2025.

“If we can’t guarantee that law enforcement is capable of securing all Jewish institutions, then we need to look for novel approaches, such as B’Nai Brith’s proposal to arm certain licensed security professionals to ensure that the Jewish community and Jewish communal infrastructure has the the level of security that is required in this moment,” he said.

“But that is all reactive to the increased threat level. We need to get at the root causes of antisemitism.”

Several synagogues in Canada told National Post last week that they have increased safety measures following the Belleville shooting. One synagogue leader in Oshawa said two congregants would be attending courses on how to better secure their facility, while a synagogue in Toronto is putting up fences around its property.

Several synagogue leaders who spoke with National Post said they would continue to be in contact with local police.

Robertson said online hate in particular has become a “breeding ground for extremism.”

“When you tolerate that over a sustained period, it should surprise no one that the next year we see an increase in the number of violent incidents and threats to the Jewish community,” he said.

In January, a synagogue in Winnipeg was graffitied with swastikas. In March, there were three overnight shootings that targeted synagogues in Toronto. In June, a person was arrested for attempted arson at a synagogue in Montreal.

The arrest comes on the heels of a “hate-motivated” shooting in Belleville, Ont. at a synagogue on Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. On Sept. 20, Const. Jeff Smith was stationed outside the building and was injured in a shootout with 29-year-old gunman Sean Ward, police said .
Police said evidence showed that the Jewish community was the intended target and Ward had brought more resources — including ammunition and gasoline — for a larger attack.
Smith, who returned fire after Ward shot at him, is in critical but stable condition. None of the roughly 25 congregants inside the synagogue, and no other police officers, were injured.
A day before the Belleville shooting, there was another arrest linked to antisemitism in Ontario.

A 19-year-old Whitby man identified as Alexander Parfitt was charged with making threats motivated by hate, according to Durham Regional Police . He allegedly made online threats to carry out a shooting at a synagogue in Durham Region.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation in New York said it alerted its partners in Ottawa to threats made by Parfitt by identifying them on social media.

“The increase in inciting hateful rhetoric has the capacity to embolden, and that is exactly what we’re seeing play out in real time now,” said Richard Robertson, the director of research and advocacy at B’Nai Brith Canada, a Jewish advocacy group that produces an annual report on antisemitism.
Robertson told National Post that this year, there have been 32 incidents of antisemitic violence, compared to 10 in 2025.

“If we can’t guarantee that law enforcement is capable of securing all Jewish institutions, then we need to look for novel approaches, such as B’Nai Brith’s proposal to arm certain licensed security professionals to ensure that the Jewish community and Jewish communal infrastructure has the the level of security that is required in this moment,” he said.
“But that is all reactive to the increased threat level. We need to get at the root causes of antisemitism.”

Several synagogues in Canada told National Post last week that they have increased safety measures following the Belleville shooting. One synagogue leader in Oshawa said two congregants would be attending courses on how to better secure their facility, while a synagogue in Toronto is putting up fences around its property.
Several synagogue leaders who spoke with National Post said they would continue to be in contact with local police.
Robertson said online hate in particular has become a “breeding ground for extremism.”
“When you tolerate that over a sustained period, it should surprise no one that the next year we see an increase in the number of violent incidents and threats to the Jewish community,” he said.

In January, a synagogue in Winnipeg was graffitied with swastikas. In March, there were three overnight shootings that targeted synagogues in Toronto. In June, a person was arrested for attempted arson at a synagogue in Montreal.

stories.title: Stock markets struggling to keep up with rising oil prices and bond yields
stories.summary: Rising oil prices are knocking the U.S. stock market further from its record high on Monday, while building pressure even higher within the U.S. bond market.
stories.author: Stan Choe, Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman
stories.content:
Rising oil prices are knocking the U.S. stock market further from its record high on Monday, while building pressure even higher within the U.S. bond market.

The S&P 500 fell 0.8 per cent and gave back most of its gains from last week, which had brought it to the brink of its all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 372 points, or 0.7 per cent, as of 11:45 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was one per cent lower.

Most of the U.S. stock market sank under the weight of a 2.8 per cent rise for the most actively traded contract in the market for Brent crude oil to US$100.19 per barrel. That overshadowed a gain for Wall Street’s most influential stock, Nvidia, after it announced a historic funneling of cash to its investors through a buyback of its shares.

Meanwhile, the Toronto Stock Exchange was in the red by about 0.75 per cent as many companies tied to mining gold, silver and other commodities struggled. Agnico Eagle Mines was down about 4.5 per cent and Lundin Gold was down roughly 5.5 per cent as of publication.

Oil prices have been yo-yoing on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow tankers to flow freely again through the Strait of Hormuz and deliver oil from the Middle East to customers worldwide. The latest turns came after President Donald Trump said over the weekend he’s rejecting an offer from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program.

“I’d like to make a deal, too,” Trump said Saturday. “But that deal would not be acceptable.”

Brent climbed above $101 per barrel Monday morning, before the U.S. stock market opened for trading, but it pared its gains as U.S. officials said mediators were still working with Iran and the United States on a deal to end the fighting and open the strait.

For all its ups and downs, a barrel of Brent remains much higher than the roughly $72 it cost before the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February. That has helped worsen inflation, and the average price for a gallon of regular gasoline is up to nearly $4.48 from $3.13 a year ago, according to AAA.

Worries about inflation have in turn helped send Treasury yields much higher in the bond market. That pressures the economy because it makes borrowing money more expensive for everyone, while also undercutting prices for stocks and other investments.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which is the centerpiece of the bond market, jumped to 5.26 per cent from 5.17 per cent late Friday. That’s a considerable move for the bond market, and the 10-year yield is back to where it was in 2007, before the financial crisis and Great Recession sent yields toward zero.

The 30-year Treasury yield, which leaped to 5.58 per cent from 5.49 per cent, is back to where it was in 2004.

On Wall Street, stocks of airlines and other companies with big fuel bills sank because of the rise in oil prices.

American Airlines fell 3.8 per cent, and United Airlines lost 3.6 per cent.

Gold miners were also weak after the price of gold sank 3.9 per cent. Gold has a reputation for helping to protect its investors from high inflation, but its price tends to weaken when yields are rising and causing bonds to pay their investors more in interest. Gold struggles to keep up because it pays its investors nothing.

Newmont, the Denver-based mining giant, sank 4.4 per cent.

One of Wall Street’s bigger losses hit MongoDB, which dropped 18.5 per cent after the database company said its CEO, Chirantan “CJ” Desai, is stepping down immediately to pursue a senior role at Meta Platforms.

Such losses helped more than offset a two per cent rise for Nvidia. The chip company said it approved a plan to send up to another $150 billion to its shareholders in a stock buyback plan, bringing the program’s total remaining size to $235 billion.

Nvidia has the power to do so after the frenzy around its chips used for artificial-intelligence technology helped it more than double the amount of cash on its books in the first half of its fiscal year. The company also on Monday unveiled a new security platform that the chipmaker said can stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue.

AI stocks broadly have come under pressure after leaders of the industry said it needs to slow its development to give safety measures time to catch up.

In stock markets abroad, European indexes were mixed following weaker performances across much of Asia.

Indexes dropped 2.7 per cent in Seoul and 1.7 per cent in Shanghai for two of the world’s bigger moves.

– with a file from Global News’ Ariel Rabinovitch

stories.title: Exeter’s first-ever ball champions commemorated 70 years later
stories.summary: In 1956, 14 Huron County teenagers won the Midget C final against Caledonia. It was Exeter’s first-ever Ontario Baseball Association (OBA) title.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
In 1956, 14 Huron County teenagers won the Midget C final against Caledonia. It was Exeter’s first-ever Ontario Baseball Association (OBA) title.

“It was a big thing that’s for sure. The first championship in town. We had a big ride in the fire truck at the end of the trek home, and it was great,” said Jim Russell, who scored the winning run in the 1956 championship game.

“There are quite a few times when I was playing ball that I was out here and doing this, and that was great,” added Cy Blommaert.

“Well, you start to savor it and appreciate it a little more at this age. I don’t think you do while you’re playing,” said Kelson.

“This is very special. We didn’t know about it until about a week ago, and appreciate what everybody’s done to get it looked after,” said Russell.

The four members of the ’56 championship winning squad received pennants and plaques commemorating their accomplishment.

stories.title: Radio telescope in B.C. picks up elusive hydrogen signal
stories.summary: Astronomers have achieved the most distant measurement to date that shows how hydrogen atoms are distributed in the deep universe
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
Hydrogen is both the simplest atom in nature and the most abundant. It is the fuel that allows stars to shine and, in doing so, makes life possible.

Now astronomers working with a unique radio telescope in British Columbia have achieved the most distant measurement to date that shows how hydrogen atoms are distributed in the deep universe.

The result supports an emerging picture of how matter organized itself after the Big Bang and built the universe we know today.

“What we really are tracing are huge clusters and families of galaxies and the filaments that make up the dense structure of space,” said Mark Halpern, a professor at the University of British Columbia who is a principal investigator with the team that conducted the work.

He said that as he and his colleagues work to better understand the signal, it May allow for something more ambitious: a direct measurement of the rate at which the universe is expanding. This would provide an independent way to gauge the influence of dark energy, an unknown phenomenon that is thought to be causing the expansion to speed up.

Scientists produce most extensive map yet of dark matter in northern skies

The detection was made using the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment, or Chime, based in Penticton, B.C.

It consists of a series of trough-like antennas which passively gather radio waves from the heavens. As the Earth turns, the antennas sweep across the northern sky, gradually collecting data from a vast volume of space. The heart of the instrument is a sophisticated computer system that disentangles all the information coming from many directions and turns it into a coherent picture of the radio sky.

Since it was first switched on in 2017 , Chime has routinely detected a wide range of radio sources such as pulsars (rapidly spinning stellar corpses scattered throughout our Milky Way galaxy) and fast radio bursts (brief but intense blasts of radio energy coming from sources inside galaxies far beyond our own).

But Chime’s original purpose was to detect the much quieter and diffuse radio emission produced by hydrogen atoms in the cold depths between galaxies. Nine years after its work began, the project appears to have realized this goal.

In a pair of studies published Monday in the Astrophysical Journal, astronomers revealed their detection of a hydrogen signal at approximately 8 billion light years from Earth, much farther than any previous measurement. An analysis of the signal shows how the hydrogen is clumped in space, which turns out to be in general agreement with other methods of mapping out the large scale structure of matter in the universe.

“This is the measurement Chime was designed to do,” Dr. Halpern said.

Team members said the result was harder to obtain than expected in part because the combined radio noise emitted by electrons careening around the Milky Way is up to ten thousand times stronger than the faint hydrogen signal in the background.

stories.title: Highway 401 westbound in London to close overnight for overpass work
stories.summary: During the closure, motorists will be detoured north onto Veterans Memorial Parkway, with access available via Highbury Avenue.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
A section of Highway 401 in east London will be closed overnight Tuesday as work continues on the Highbury Avenue overpass project.

Both directions of Highway 401 will close at Veterans Memorial Parkway beginning at 7 p.m. to allow for girder placement as part of the ongoing construction project.

Westbound traffic will be detoured onto Bradley Avenue and eastbound traffic will be detoured onto Wilton Grove Road.

The closure is expected to remain in place overnight, with the highway scheduled to reopen by 5 a.m. Tuesday.

Drivers are being advised to plan ahead and allow extra travel time if travelling through the area.

stories.title: Winnipeg perfumery ordered to close doors again
stories.summary: A long-time Winnipeg perfumery is cornered to shut down after the city has asked him to re-zone or no longer have people walk in his home-based business.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
By Toni De Guzman Global News

Posted September 28, 2026 12:26 pm

A long-time Winnipeg perfumery is shutting down after the owner says the city told them to re-zone or no longer have people come in the home-based business.

“I’m not making enough money to do a commercial zoning like they want me to do,” said Michael O’Malley, owner of La Parfumerie.

O’Malley has been living and working in the Wolseley neighbourhood since 1999, selling natural perfumes.

More than 1,000 people signed an online petition to support keeping the business open, according to the Change.org posting on late Sunday afternoon.

Global News has reached out to the city and area councillor but didn’t get a response before deadline.

Watch the video above for the full story.

stories.title: Competition Bureau investigating grocery store minimum pricing policies
stories.summary: The Competition Bureau has launched an investigation into the use of minimum advertised pricing policies in the grocery sector.
stories.author: Brett Bundale
stories.content:
The Competition Bureau has launched an investigation into the use of minimum advertised pricing policies in the grocery sector , rules that can prevent retailers from advertising their lowest prices.

The watchdog is examining whether these policies make it harder for Canadians to find deals, reduce price competition, create barriers for discount and new grocers, and make it easier for grocers to co-ordinate prices.

“Canadians expect grocery stores to be able to advertise their best deals,” Jeanne Pratt, the agency’s interim competition commissioner, said in a statement Monday.

“We’re concerned that policies that prevent this make it harder for grocers to compete, and for consumers to access lower prices,” she said. “At a time when food affordability remains an important concern for Canadians, we want to hear about how these policies are affecting grocery prices and consumer choice.”

5:25 Competition watchdog expands probe into Sobeys’ use of property controls amid competition concerns

Minimum advertised pricing policies set a floor on the price retailers can advertise a product, although they May still be able to sell it for less.

In the retail industry, suppliers May use advertised price rules to protect a brand’s image, encourage retailers to provide better service or prevent some retailers from benefiting from the promotional efforts of others.

The bureau is asking industry participants and consumers to come forward with evidence about minimum pricing use.

It says the information it receives will support its investigation and inform its examination of competition across Canada’s food supply chain.

In June, the agency launched an investigation of competition in the grocery sector, including potential problems in production, processing, transportation, distribution and pricing.

stories.title: London artist wins $100K top prize in national art competition
stories.summary: The award was selected by an independent jury from 100 finalist works displayed as part of the competition’s annual exhibition.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
A London artist is $100,000 richer after taking home the top award in a national art competition aimed at supporting Canadian creators.

Anna Wilson, of London, Ont., received the Panel’s Choice Award and its $100,000 prize at ART Comp 2026 for her piece Found . The independent, not-for-profit competition awarded a total of $200,000 to four artists this year.

Wilson’s winning work, an intricate fineliner drawing, took more than three years and over 500 hours to complete. According to ART Comp, Found explores the intersection of imagined and real spaces, creating a sense of comfort and familiarity.

The award was selected by an independent jury from 100 finalist works displayed as part of the competition’s annual exhibition.

ART Comp co-founder Martha Leach said the organization was created to provide artists with meaningful financial support and opportunities for exposure, regardless of their background, training or location.

The organization says the $100,000 prize will give Wilson the time, resources and freedom to pursue ambitious new creative projects.

Now in its fifth year, ART Comp says it is built on the belief that exceptional art can come from anyone, anywhere, and aims to help artists turn creative potential into lasting opportunities.

stories.title: Financial hiccups with roommates are inevitable. Here's how to minimize the drama
stories.summary: For many young adults, sharing an apartment can help divide the responsibilities and keep a lid on expenses. But that can turn into a burden if roommates slack on bill payments or don’t respect common spaces.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Nudging your roommates about money owed every time you see them in the kitchen or living room can get increasingly awkward. And it gets worse when you run out of ideas on how to remind them without being curt. For many young adults, sharing an apartment can help divide the responsibilities and keep a lid on expenses.

But that can turn into a burden if roommates slack on bill payments or don’t respect common spaces. While hiccups in shared homes are inevitable, experts say setting boundaries and expectations about how to handle them ahead of time can help maintain cordial relationships.

The challenge for many, however, is finding the right moment to start the conversation. Bruce Sellery, CEO of Credit Canada, says new roommates should talk before they move in, or ideally, before even deciding to live together.

He suggested framing it as an expectations meeting to set the tone, which will come in handy if a crisis erupts. “The hidden benefit is you’ve got something to refer back to,” he said. Understanding each other A prompt or activity, such as taking an online quiz about roommate compatibility, could help get the conversation started, said Lucianna Adragna, vice-president of client segments, everyday banking at RBC.

Talking about your own money habits first can also make the other person more comfortable. But keep judgements out of the conversation, Adragna said. “It’s trying to understand how each other’s expectations May be different before starting to share expenses.” Then ease into details such as which costs they consider shared versus personal, and whether they follow a budget.

Have a clear understanding of how bills will be divided, when they will be paid and whether the split will be equal, Adragna said. For example, a roommate might pay a larger portion of the rent because they have a bigger room.

You should also figure out what’s not going to be shared or split, such as groceries, furniture or streaming services. Plan what would happen if one person isn’t able to pay rent one month or if an appliance breaks. “It seems sort of nitty-gritty details,” Adragna said.

“But this is where knowing this before you move in is so much more comfortable than having those surprise conversations afterwards.” Sellery said the discussions shouldn’t just include financial priorities but also some intangible things, such as values.

For instance, if he were moving in with roommates, Sellery said he would let his roommates know of his value around leftover food. “If I’ve got leftovers in the fridge, you do not turf my leftovers, you don’t eat my leftovers ... which is kind of quirky and other people might not have that same value,” he said.

Set expectations Similarly, cleaning can become a source of discord among roommates. Sellery said that can be resolved with money, for instance, if all housemates agree to pitch in for a cleaner once every few weeks. That way, he said, “You get what you need, which is floors you can eat off.

And I get what I need, which is not to do it myself because I hate doing it.” Expense-splitting apps can come in handy for roommates to track expenses and settle bills periodically, Adragna said. Many of them even send automatic reminders so roommates don’t have to nudge each other.

“It helps with some of that awkwardness and it helps take some of the pressure off somebody who feels like, ‘Hey, how come I’m the one making sure everything gets paid on time?’” Adragna said. When setting expectations, Sellery said the principles should be clarity and predictability.

And it gets worse when you run out of ideas on how to remind them without being curt. For many young adults, sharing an apartment can help divide the responsibilities and keep a lid on expenses.

But that can turn into a burden if roommates slack on bill payments or don’t respect common spaces. While hiccups in shared homes are inevitable, experts say setting boundaries and expectations about how to handle them ahead of time can help maintain cordial relationships.

The challenge for many, however, is finding the right moment to start the conversation. Bruce Sellery, CEO of Credit Canada, says new roommates should talk before they move in, or ideally, before even deciding to live together.

He suggested framing it as an expectations meeting to set the tone, which will come in handy if a crisis erupts. “The hidden benefit is you’ve got something to refer back to,” he said. Understanding each other A prompt or activity, such as taking an online quiz about roommate compatibility, could help get the conversation started, said Lucianna Adragna, vice-president of client segments, everyday banking at RBC.

Talking about your own money habits first can also make the other person more comfortable. But keep judgements out of the conversation, Adragna said. “It’s trying to understand how each other’s expectations May be different before starting to share expenses.” Then ease into details such as which costs they consider shared versus personal, and whether they follow a budget.

Have a clear understanding of how bills will be divided, when they will be paid and whether the split will be equal, Adragna said. For example, a roommate might pay a larger portion of the rent because they have a bigger room.

You should also figure out what’s not going to be shared or split, such as groceries, furniture or streaming services. Plan what would happen if one person isn’t able to pay rent one month or if an appliance breaks. “It seems sort of nitty-gritty details,” Adragna said.

stories.title: Canada’s airports saw record improvements in delays, NAV Canada says
stories.summary: Every one of the four major airports in Canada saw improvements, with Vancouver recording the sharpest improvement, NAV Canada said.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
There was good news for travellers this summer as delays on Canada’s busiest airports saw record improvements.

There was sharp improvement in service delivery at four of Canada’s biggest airports between May and August this year, NAV Canada said in a statement Monday.

NAC Canada, the body responsible for air traffic control in the country, reported data from Toronto Pearson, Montréal-Trudeau, Calgary and Vancouver International Airports.

The number of scheduled flights that were impacted by a delay was down 85 per cent from May 1 to Aug. 31, 2026, compared to the same period in 2025, NAV Canada said.

This period coincided with the Fifa World Cup in July which saw visitors from all over the world arrive in Canada amid record-low airport delays, the agency said.

During this period in 2025, 4,996 flights, or 1.54 per cent of all flights at these airports, were hit with delays. This year, that number fell to 769 flights, or 0.24 per cent of all scheduled flights, NAV Canada said.

This came as the volume of flights at the four major airports went up this summer. They collectively handled 394,919 flights this summer, up 0.9 per cent compared to the same period in 2025.

Every one of the four major airports saw improvements, with Vancouver recording the sharpest improvement. In the summer of 2025, 4.42 per cent of all flights out of Vancouver were hit by delays. This year, that figure was down to 0.64 per cent.

Toronto Pearson was the best performing airport when it came to share of flights delayed, with only 0.04 per cent of flights being impacted by delays, down from 0.24 per cent in 2025.

This was followed by Calgary at 0.05 per cent, down from 1.16 per cent, and Montreal-Trudeau at 0.28 per cent, down from 1.16 per cent.

Canada’s airports still have a staffing shortage of air traffic controllers, but the staffing gap narrowed between May and August. In the spring, Canada was short of 200 air traffic control staff. In August, this number was down to 170, NAV Canada said.

Earlier this month, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the federal government is moving ahead with plans to attract private investment in Canada’s four largest airports.

The new model will be based on “best practice in other countries” and the federal government will retain ownership of the underlying land and assets, Carney said.

As of 2020, nearly 20 per cent of the airports in the world had been privatized. A 2022 study in the U.S.-based non-profit National Bureau of Economic Research compared the performance of 2,444 airports around the world in 217 countries.

The report found that the number of passengers per flight – a key metric when assessing airport efficiency – increased by 20 per cent when private equity funds buy government-owned airports and overall passenger traffic rises by 84 per cent.

Airports also get bigger with private equity funds as owners, the report found, with private owners adding new terminals and gates. The study also found fewer flight cancellations.

However, flying May get more expensive as the fees that airports charge to airlines tend to rise after an airport is privatized, the report added. The rise in the number of privately owned airports was also associated with a push for deregulation and pushback against government controls, such as caps or limits on fees.
