stories.title: At first, case stumped doctors who determined Ontario woman had fatal case of rat bite fever
stories.summary: Rat bite fever has an estimated death rate of up to 13 per cent if left untreated. The disease destroyed large parts of the woman's heart.
stories.author: Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
Rat bite fever has an estimated death rate of up to 13 per cent if left untreated. The disease destroyed large parts of the woman's heart

For days and days on end, doctors didn’t know exactly what kind of organism they were up against. The infection spreading through the 48-year-old Ontario woman was so aggressive, large parts of her heart were destroyed. But all the usual blood work, all the cultures for typical bacterial infections came back negative. Doctors couldn’t fully understand what was feeding the infection. Until her sister wondered, could it be the rats? The woman’s death last year, published in a new case report , is being described as the first reported fatal case of rat bite fever that defeated even the most advanced “Hail Mary” form of out-of-body heart and lung bypass. The case “was a bit of a conundrum,” said cardiologist and intensivist Dr. Craig Ainsworth, chief of critical care at Hamilton Health Sciences, and co-author of the report in Jacc, the Journal of the American College of Cardiology. “Normally, when we have people with that degree of heart and heart valve infection, we usually get something in the blood work,” he said, typically one of the aggressive bugs “that do this sort of thing.” In this case, everything was negative until weeks later, when valve tissue taken during the woman’s emergency heart surgery was sent for specialized DNA testing, which ultimately identified streptobacillus moniliformis, a bacterium found in the oral, nasal and respiratory tract secretions of rats. The bug can be transmitted to people via broken skin, bites or scratches, but also from close contact, without a bite or scratch, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control. It can also be spread through exposure to contaminated food or water. Diagnosis can be challenging: the organism is “fastidious, difficult to grow and has limited diagnostic tests available for early detection,” Ainsworth and colleagues wrote in the Sept. 12 edition of Jacc Case Reports. The woman ultimately died, despite being treated with the proper antibiotics. “We just guessed and happened to guess properly,” Ainsworth said, however, the infection was too far gone by the time she was transferred to his ICU. “It wasn’t obvious to us for days and days what we were actually treating.” Rat bite fever is a rare infection with an estimated mortality rate of up to 13 per cent if left untreated. The disease often starts with vague symptoms such as fever, rash and generally just feeling unwell, which can delay people seeking medical attention. The woman was a bit of a “homebody” who kept to herself, Ainsworth said. She had some medical problems, including asthma and inflammatory bowel disease, and was a smoker. “She wasn’t a perfectly healthy 48-year-old, but she was totally functional and ambulatory.” After six to eight weeks of fatigue, lower back pain, facial flushing and peripheral numbness, the woman went to her local hospital’s emergency department, about 100 kilometres outside Hamilton. She described worsening diarrhea and fainting spells — spells owing to, in retrospect, “the infection eating into the electrical system of her heart,” Ainsworth said. Doctors suspected sepsis and started antibiotics, but while in emergency the woman suffered a cardiac arrest. The upper chambers of her heart were no longer communicating with the lower chambers, causing a dangerously slow heart rate. A temporary pacemaker was inserted. Three days later, a special echocardiogram that involves guiding a thin tube down the throat to examine the heart from inside the esophagus revealed extensive infection of various parts of the heart and valves. She was referred to a second hospital for urgent, complicated and prolonged heart surgery. Because of low oxygen levels, doctors couldn’t take the woman off the machine used to take over the function of her heart and lungs during surgery. She was placed on Ecmo, or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, an advanced form of life support. Her heart muscle continued to deteriorate, and the woman was transferred to Hamilton General Hospital, “still without a specific diagnosis or a bug,” Ainsworth said. “By the time we received the call, she was at best a Hail Mary; she was very unwell,” he said. But because she was 48 and otherwise fairly healthy, they tried every measure they could. “She just didn’t get any better,” Ainsworth said. At one point her sister, from whom she was semi-estranged, remarked to Ainsworth, “You know, I just wonder if it’s related to the rats she has in her house.” “As a non-infectious disease doctor, I didn’t put two and two together,” he said. “I thought it was like a guinea pig or a hamster, just a little more unusual. “But when we ultimately got this bug back from the DNA testing, it became clear that almost certainly this was related to her pet rats.” After several weeks in hospital, the woman succumbed to the infection. Life support was withdrawn “given the unfortunate futility of what we were doing and her worsening, despite all the heroic interventions,” Ainsworth said. It’s not clear if the rats were purchased or had infested her home. The sister said the rats seemed more like pets. “I don’t think they were just innocent bystanders,” Ainsworth said. The bacterium S. moniliformis is ubiquitous in all rodents, said infectious disease specialist Dr. Omar Mourad, a co-author of the case report. “It lives in their mouth, in their oral flora. Any rodent — though certainly rats are the famous ones — will have it. “It’s not harmful to the rats, similar to how we have a number of bacteria in our mouth and on our skin,” he said. But it can cause trouble when it gets into humans. Despite its name, more often than not rat bite fever is transmitted merely by handling rats, Mourad said. “Some people like to kiss the rat on the mouth, which I would not recommend,” he said. Or they don’t wash their hands properly after handling the rodents and get the bacteria into their mouth. “Once it gets in, occasionally it will make its way into the bloodstream and cause more trouble,” Mourad said. Classic symptoms of infection — rash, joint pain, vomiting and other GI symptoms — typically start three to 10 days after exposure. Most people who get infected get better on their own after feeling flu-like for a couple of days. “But you have to get it before it does anything like this,” Mourad said. Left untreated, severe cases can cause not only endocarditis, as it did in the 48-year-old woman, but also meningitis — infection of the brain and spinal cord. Although uncommon in Canada, rat bite fever is increasing because of “changing patterns of urban living (more dense urban housing) and pet-keeping practices,” other researchers have warned . As of 2106, the-then-largest single episode in Canada found 11 cases of reported rat bite fever on Vancouver Island between 2010 and 2016. Seven cases required hospitalization, but there were no deaths “or significant morbidity.” From the intensive care physician’s perspective, “It comes back to, if something is weird and a bit of a unicorn (exceptionally rare) case, I think it behooves us to dig deeper and start asking questions of loved ones and family members,” Ainsworth said. “Just by having a conversation with the sister and asking about habits and unusual things, the rats came out, which was helpful information.” It was the second case of a pet rat infection Mourad saw last year. The other involved a different bacteria called leptospirosis, spread through the urine of infected rats. The man, who got infected from handling his pet rats, spent a few weeks in hospital “until we figured it out,” Mourad said. “Fortunately, it ended much better, and the patient did very well,” he said “As far as I know, he did give away the rats.” National Post

The case “was a bit of a conundrum,” said cardiologist and intensivist Dr. Craig Ainsworth, chief of critical care at Hamilton Health Sciences, and co-author of the report in Jacc, the Journal of the American College of Cardiology.

“Normally, when we have people with that degree of heart and heart valve infection, we usually get something in the blood work,” he said, typically one of the aggressive bugs “that do this sort of thing.”

In this case, everything was negative until weeks later, when valve tissue taken during the woman’s emergency heart surgery was sent for specialized DNA testing, which ultimately identified streptobacillus moniliformis, a bacterium found in the oral, nasal and respiratory tract secretions of rats.

The bug can be transmitted to people via broken skin, bites or scratches, but also from close contact, without a bite or scratch, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control. It can also be spread through exposure to contaminated food or water.

Diagnosis can be challenging: the organism is “fastidious, difficult to grow and has limited diagnostic tests available for early detection,” Ainsworth and colleagues wrote in the Sept. 12 edition of Jacc Case Reports.

The woman ultimately died, despite being treated with the proper antibiotics. “We just guessed and happened to guess properly,” Ainsworth said, however, the infection was too far gone by the time she was transferred to his ICU.

“It wasn’t obvious to us for days and days what we were actually treating.”

Rat bite fever is a rare infection with an estimated mortality rate of up to 13 per cent if left untreated. The disease often starts with vague symptoms such as fever, rash and generally just feeling unwell, which can delay people seeking medical attention.

The woman was a bit of a “homebody” who kept to herself, Ainsworth said. She had some medical problems, including asthma and inflammatory bowel disease, and was a smoker. “She wasn’t a perfectly healthy 48-year-old, but she was totally functional and ambulatory.”

After six to eight weeks of fatigue, lower back pain, facial flushing and peripheral numbness, the woman went to her local hospital’s emergency department, about 100 kilometres outside Hamilton.

She described worsening diarrhea and fainting spells — spells owing to, in retrospect, “the infection eating into the electrical system of her heart,” Ainsworth said.

Doctors suspected sepsis and started antibiotics, but while in emergency the woman suffered a cardiac arrest. The upper chambers of her heart were no longer communicating with the lower chambers, causing a dangerously slow heart rate.

A temporary pacemaker was inserted. Three days later, a special echocardiogram that involves guiding a thin tube down the throat to examine the heart from inside the esophagus revealed extensive infection of various parts of the heart and valves.

She was referred to a second hospital for urgent, complicated and prolonged heart surgery.

Because of low oxygen levels, doctors couldn’t take the woman off the machine used to take over the function of her heart and lungs during surgery. She was placed on Ecmo, or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, an advanced form of life support.

Her heart muscle continued to deteriorate, and the woman was transferred to Hamilton General Hospital, “still without a specific diagnosis or a bug,” Ainsworth said.

“By the time we received the call, she was at best a Hail Mary; she was very unwell,” he said. But because she was 48 and otherwise fairly healthy, they tried every measure they could.

“She just didn’t get any better,” Ainsworth said.

At one point her sister, from whom she was semi-estranged, remarked to Ainsworth, “You know, I just wonder if it’s related to the rats she has in her house.”

It’s not clear if the rats were purchased or had infested her home. The sister said the rats seemed more like pets. “I don’t think they were just innocent bystanders,” Ainsworth said.

The bacterium S. moniliformis is ubiquitous in all rodents, said infectious disease specialist Dr. Omar Mourad, a co-author of the case report. “It lives in their mouth, in their oral flora. Any rodent — though certainly rats are the famous ones — will have it.

“It’s not harmful to the rats, similar to how we have a number of bacteria in our mouth and on our skin,” he said. But it can cause trouble when it gets into humans.

Despite its name, more often than not rat bite fever is transmitted merely by handling rats, Mourad said.

“Some people like to kiss the rat on the mouth, which I would not recommend,” he said. Or they don’t wash their hands properly after handling the rodents and get the bacteria into their mouth.

“Once it gets in, occasionally it will make its way into the bloodstream and cause more trouble,” Mourad said.

Classic symptoms of infection — rash, joint pain, vomiting and other GI symptoms — typically start three to 10 days after exposure.

Most people who get infected get better on their own after feeling flu-like for a couple of days.

“But you have to get it before it does anything like this,” Mourad said.

Left untreated, severe cases can cause not only endocarditis, as it did in the 48-year-old woman, but also meningitis — infection of the brain and spinal cord.

Although uncommon in Canada, rat bite fever is increasing because of “changing patterns of urban living (more dense urban housing) and pet-keeping practices,” other researchers have warned .

As of 2106, the-then-largest single episode in Canada found 11 cases of reported rat bite fever on Vancouver Island between 2010 and 2016. Seven cases required hospitalization, but there were no deaths “or significant morbidity.”

From the intensive care physician’s perspective, “It comes back to, if something is weird and a bit of a unicorn (exceptionally rare) case, I think it behooves us to dig deeper and start asking questions of loved ones and family members,” Ainsworth said.

“Just by having a conversation with the sister and asking about habits and unusual things, the rats came out, which was helpful information.”

It was the second case of a pet rat infection Mourad saw last year. The other involved a different bacteria called leptospirosis, spread through the urine of infected rats.

The man, who got infected from handling his pet rats, spent a few weeks in hospital “until we figured it out,” Mourad said.

“Fortunately, it ended much better, and the patient did very well,” he said

“As far as I know, he did give away the rats.”

The bacterium S. moniliformis is ubiquitous in all rodents, said infectious disease specialist Dr. Omar Mourad, a co-author of the case report. “It lives in their mouth, in their oral flora. Any rodent — though certainly rats are the famous ones — will have it.
“It’s not harmful to the rats, similar to how we have a number of bacteria in our mouth and on our skin,” he said. But it can cause trouble when it gets into humans.
Despite its name, more often than not rat bite fever is transmitted merely by handling rats, Mourad said.
“Some people like to kiss the rat on the mouth, which I would not recommend,” he said. Or they don’t wash their hands properly after handling the rodents and get the bacteria into their mouth.
“Once it gets in, occasionally it will make its way into the bloodstream and cause more trouble,” Mourad said.
Classic symptoms of infection — rash, joint pain, vomiting and other GI symptoms — typically start three to 10 days after exposure.
Most people who get infected get better on their own after feeling flu-like for a couple of days.
“But you have to get it before it does anything like this,” Mourad said.
Left untreated, severe cases can cause not only endocarditis, as it did in the 48-year-old woman, but also meningitis — infection of the brain and spinal cord.
Although uncommon in Canada, rat bite fever is increasing because of “changing patterns of urban living (more dense urban housing) and pet-keeping practices,” other researchers have warned .

As of 2106, the-then-largest single episode in Canada found 11 cases of reported rat bite fever on Vancouver Island between 2010 and 2016. Seven cases required hospitalization, but there were no deaths “or significant morbidity.”

From the intensive care physician’s perspective, “It comes back to, if something is weird and a bit of a unicorn (exceptionally rare) case, I think it behooves us to dig deeper and start asking questions of loved ones and family members,” Ainsworth said.
“Just by having a conversation with the sister and asking about habits and unusual things, the rats came out, which was helpful information.”
It was the second case of a pet rat infection Mourad saw last year. The other involved a different bacteria called leptospirosis, spread through the urine of infected rats.
The man, who got infected from handling his pet rats, spent a few weeks in hospital “until we figured it out,” Mourad said.
“Fortunately, it ended much better, and the patient did very well,” he said
“As far as I know, he did give away the rats.”

stories.title: AI agents booking doctor’s appointments: Inside PocketHealth’s drive to improve patient care
stories.summary: PocketHealth’s second act is a response to health care organizations grappling with disconnected record systems and demanding administrative work that takes time away from patient care
stories.author: Leah Golob
stories.content:
It’s a critical time for Canada’s economy and its business community. The country needs innovation and growth more than ever, yet businesses across a wide range of industries are facing trade disruptions, rising costs and technological change, among other challenges. This series profiles forward-thinking Canadian companies that are growing their markets by re-examining their business practices and trying new things.

When Harsh Nayyar injured his ankle playing tennis while living in California’s Bay Area in 2014, he received his MRI images on a CD.

For Harsh and his brother Rishi, both technologists, the experience seemed shockingly outdated. Tech platforms such as YouTube and Netflix offered instant online streaming, yet medical images still needed to be burned onto physical discs.

The brothers decided to tackle the problem together, launching the Toronto-based software development company PocketHealth in early 2016 to help patients access, share and understand their medical imaging records and reports – all online, from any device. Rishi is chief executive officer and his brother Harsh is chief technology officer.

Ten years in, PocketHealth’s platform has reached more than three million patients across Canada and the United States and operates at more than 900 sites across more than 250 health care organizations, such as UHN, Sinai Health, Trillium Health Partners, Mackenzie Health, William Osler Health System and Niagara Health. Its annual revenue, the company says, is in the $10-million to $50-million range, growing more than 25 per cent year over year.

Rishi says PocketHealth’s medical image sharing services help patients discover the results of a biopsy or MRI quickly and efficiently, plus patients can more easily share findings from an emergency department visit with their family physicians.

The company also has examples of patients who spotted items missing in their report that they were then able to get corrected, he says. “It changed the path of their care.”

Now, the company is pursuing its second act, expanding beyond medical-image access into agentic artificial intelligence that can automate administrative tasks in hospitals and clinics, such as processing referrals and scheduling appointments.

This innovation is a response to health care organizations grappling with disconnected record systems and demanding administrative work that takes time away from patient care, Rishi says.

“We are in a heavily overburdened health care system.”

Dr. Andrew Pinto, a physician and director of Upstream Lab, a non-profit research lab based at MAP Centre for Urban Health Solutions, St. Michael’s Hospital in Toronto, says that one of the big problems with Canada’s health care system is that it is enormously fragmented. Individual hospitals, clinics, primary care organizations and public health have their own record systems, meaning there isn’t a single electronic health record for the country.

As a result, each of these systems has a different way of defining data, Dr. Pinto says, and data can’t flow easily from one system to another. While PocketHealth came up with a solution that solved this fragmentation, ideally the fragmentation wouldn’t exist, he adds.

“They are bringing a new perspective to a very old problem and they are showing us what technology can do,” Dr. Pinto says, adding that Canada needs legislation that would mandate interoperability.

PocketHealth’s agentic AI platform, PocketHealth Conductor, launched in late 2025. Rishi explains that Conductor has a coordinated network of AI agents that can complete non-clinical tasks autonomously.

For example, when a physician sends a referral, Conductor processes it, calls the patient and immediately books an appointment live over the phone. It’s also able to read faxed and uploaded documents.

The aim is to automate the health care industry’s time-consuming administrative workflows so providers can spend more time on patient care. And PocketHealth says Conductor is live in production today at “dozens” of hospitals and imaging providers in Canada and the U.S.

But adoption isn’t without its challenges, Rishi says.

“No matter how incredible [AI] is, every health care system, every clinic we deploy in has its own unique way of performing tasks,” he explains. In other words, a company can’t install an AI system without adapting it. Also, there’s a lot of ongoing effort to make agentic AI systems feel human and improve – rather than impede – the care journey.

“The obstacles are that it still requires a lot of configuration work, a lot of testing, which means you have to test very carefully, you have to roll out slowly, and I think we have very, very ambitious plans,” he says.

From Dr. Pinto’s perspective, AI has great potential. But he points out that the health care industry needs to address equity concerns around the technology, such as whether it’s lifting everybody up, whether it’s accurate and whether it works well for groups of people that May not have the digital literacy or devices to use it.

Investors are interested in what PocketHealth is doing. The company raised $45-million in Series B financing in March 2024, bringing their total equity funding to $75-million. The Series B financing was led by Round 13 Capital, with Deloitte Ventures and Samsung Next joining as new investors and additional investment from Questa Capital and Radical Ventures.

Rishi says that at least for now, PocketHealth plans to concentrate on Canada and the U.S. as it expands its AI offerings, rather than enter new international markets.

He hopes the technology will enable patients to reach out and schedule their own exams, and better understand the preparation needed for procedures instead of just receiving a phone call or a letter in the mail.

“I want it to be that they can call in and they’re never on hold and they get their questions answered,” he adds. As well, agentic AI can help new immigrants get the same quality and access of care in their first language as English speakers do.

“Agentic AI is still in its infancy,” Rishi says. “It needs more case studies, more deployment stories. We’re not even in inning one.”

stories.title: Mild weather expected before cooler air arrives Friday
stories.summary: Expect a stretch of mild fall weather this week as forecast calls for several days of above-average temperatures for late September before a cooler air mass arrives to end the work week.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Expect a stretch of mild fall weather this week as forecast calls for several days of above-average temperatures for late September before a cooler air mass arrives to end the work week.

According to Environment Canada, increasing cloudiness is expected Monday morning, while areas of fog will dissipate as the day progresses. Winds are forecast to shift to the north near noon at 20 km/h, with a daytime high of 22 C. The UV index is expected to reach five, considered moderate.

Partly cloudy conditions are forecast Monday night, with fog patches developing overnight and a low of 9 C.

Tuesday is expected to bring a mix of sun and cloud after morning fog patches clear. The high will climb to 23 C, while the UV index is forecast at six, or high. Cloudy periods are expected overnight Tuesday, with a low of 13 C.

Cloud cover is forecast to continue Wednesday, with a daytime high of 22 C. Wednesday night will remain cloudy, with a 30 per cent chance of showers and a low of 14 C.

The chance of rain increases slightly Thursday, as Environment Canada is calling for cloudy skies and a 40 per cent chance of showers. The daytime high is expected to reach 23 C. Similar conditions are forecast Thursday night, with a low of 13 C.

Temperatures are expected to cool somewhat heading into Friday, when a mix of sun and cloud is forecast along with a high of 17 C.

stories.title: Biossil raises $153-million in OpenAI-led funding to bring resuscitated drugs to market
stories.summary: Toronto startup uses AI to save once-promising drug candidates from pharmaceutical discard pile
stories.author: Sean Silcoff
stories.content:
OpenAI has led a US$153-million venture capital financing of Biossil Inc., a Toronto startup that uses artificial intelligence to give failed drug candidates a second chance at becoming approved therapies.

The AI giant, best known for ChatGPT, provided the majority of the round through its OpenAI Startup Fund.

This latest financing values Biossil at US$1-billion. OpenAI co-led Biossil’s last venture capital financing a year ago with Silicon Valley billionaire Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund, when the Toronto company raised US$43-million.

Founders Fund, which led a previous US$22-million financing of Biossil in 2024, participated in the new deal, alongside existing investors Quiet Capital, Modern Capital, Golden Ventures and Panache Ventures, plus Duke University’s endowment fund and sovereign wealth fund Abu Dhabi Investment Council. Janet Bannister’s Staircase Ventures led Biossil’s $3.7-million seed financing in 2023.

Opinion: AI robots tempt the caregivers of loved ones with dementia to step aside

The latest deal was not announced, but details were shared by a source familiar with the matter. The Globe and Mail is not identifying the source as they are not authorized to discuss the information.

Biossil plans to use the financing to expand its capacity for clinical development and selectively buy more drug candidates, the source said. It is an all-equity deal, with a small portion being paid to early employees.

The company also disclosed in an August filing with Corporations Canada that it had created a new class of 5.37 million preferred shares, each valued at US$28.69 – triple the value of shares issued in last year’s financing.

Anthony Mouchantaf, chief executive officer of Biossil, declined to comment.

The funding is happening as OpenAI and rival Anthropic expand beyond offering broadly used AI models to delivering sector-specific tools . One such sector is health care , where some believe AI purveyors could make the strongest case that their technology can benefit humanity by discovering life-saving therapies, countering mounting concerns their algorithms could threaten civilization.

Both AI giants have launched specialized models and programs to help speed up life-sciences research. Earlier this month, Anthropic said it had set up a wet laboratory in the San Francisco Bay Area staffed by a life-sciences research group using its Claude AI assistant. It said Claude had already “discovered a novel enzyme system with properties reminiscent of Crispr,” a genetic modification technology used by medical researchers.

Andrew Coyne: The question isn’t whether we should slow down AI development. It’s whether we still can

Mr. Mouchantaf, a lawyer turned tech entrepreneur who previously headed Royal Bank of Canada’s venture capital investment strategy, co-founded Biossil in 2023 with Alexander Mosa, who had earned both a doctor of medicine degree as well as a PhD in virology and trained at the University Health Network.

Several companies have designed drug candidates using AI and taken them into trials; none have yet made it to market.

Biossil has taken a different approach. It built a software platform using OpenAI’s large language models to uncover promising molecules from the pharmaceutical discard pile. The Toronto company’s algorithms scavenge through the expanse of drug candidates that failed trials at advanced stages, detecting ways to give them a second chance. For example, some drugs failed because they only worked in certain patients with particular attributes. In some cases, trials were poorly designed or pursued the wrong outcomes.

The founders figured that if they could bring the molecules back into trials in a modified fashion, they could forgo years of studies and hundreds of millions of dollars in costs and advance toward regulatory approval. Their approach quickly won over investors and researchers .

Biossil has bought or licensed 12 molecules, including a July deal where it paid US$500,000 up front for a precision antibiotic from Summit Therapeutics Inc., with more money to follow if the drug clears regulatory and commercial milestones and gets to market. The drug faltered in a late-stage efficacy trial five years ago as a treatment for patients suffering from C. difficile infections.

The Toronto company has partnered with universities and research hospitals in Canada, the United States and Europe, including Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids), Harvard University and the Mayo Clinic. It recently signed trial collaboration agreements with SickKids, Toronto’s University Health Network and Stanford University’s Skin Innovation and Interventional Research Group.

From doomsday warnings to economic upheaval, one AI expert tries to cut through the noise

Two Biossil molecules target sickle cell disease, a debilitating genetic condition that predominantly affects people of African or Indian descent. Johnson & Johnson JNJ-N and Pfizer Inc. PFE-N each attempted to develop the drugs with biotechnology startups but abandoned those programs after they failed late-stage efficacy trials.

In both cases, Biossil’s AI uncovered reasons to revisit the drug candidates. For example, the J&J drug, called senicapoc, failed to show significant improvement over placebos in relieving pain, the study’s main goal. But the data showed it was better at preventing the breakdown of red blood cells, which would cause anemia and other serious complications.

Biossil is now sponsoring a sickle cell disease trial with J&J’s abandoned molecule, with recruiting under way at SickKids, Centre hospitalier de l’Université de Montréal and McGill University. It’s also launching a trial in Germany using the same molecule to treat glioblastoma, an aggressive cancerous brain tumour, in partnership with Heidelberg University Hospital and the German Cancer Research Center, and a separate trial for the same indication in Denmark with Aarhus University.

Editor’s note: This article was updated to add details about Alexander Mosa's educational background.

The founders figured that if they could bring the molecules back into trials in a modified fashion, they could forgo years of studies and hundreds of millions of dollars in costs and advance toward regulatory approval. Their approach quickly won over investors and researchers .

Biossil has bought or licensed 12 molecules, including a July deal where it paid US$500,000 up front for a precision antibiotic from Summit Therapeutics Inc., with more money to follow if the drug clears regulatory and commercial milestones and gets to market. The drug faltered in a late-stage efficacy trial five years ago as a treatment for patients suffering from C. difficile infections.

The Toronto company has partnered with universities and research hospitals in Canada, the United States and Europe, including Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids), Harvard University and the Mayo Clinic. It recently signed trial collaboration agreements with SickKids, Toronto’s University Health Network and Stanford University’s Skin Innovation and Interventional Research Group.
From doomsday warnings to economic upheaval, one AI expert tries to cut through the noise

Two Biossil molecules target sickle cell disease, a debilitating genetic condition that predominantly affects people of African or Indian descent. Johnson & Johnson JNJ-N and Pfizer Inc. PFE-N each attempted to develop the drugs with biotechnology startups but abandoned those programs after they failed late-stage efficacy trials.

In both cases, Biossil’s AI uncovered reasons to revisit the drug candidates. For example, the J&J drug, called senicapoc, failed to show significant improvement over placebos in relieving pain, the study’s main goal. But the data showed it was better at preventing the breakdown of red blood cells, which would cause anemia and other serious complications.

stories.title: Popular Night Owls philosophy series builds new nest with first event at U of T
stories.summary: In a Stem-focused postsecondary landscape, evening with celebrity philosopher promotes talking about ideas purely for their own sake
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
In his brief remarks welcoming University of Toronto students to the first Canadian instalment of the after-dark philosophy series “Night Owls,” Randy Boyagoda commended the audience for coming to an event that wouldn’t juice their résumés or help them score a job.

“This is not going to get you into law school,” Prof. Boyagoda, the new director of U of T’s Jackman Humanities Institute, said with a wink. “No one’s going to write you a rec. letter for being here. I will sign no co-curricular transcripts because you are here.

“Why are you here? You are here because you have made the decision to live as if ideas matter.”

For the nearly three hours that followed last Thursday night, about 100 rapt students sat – or stood if they had trickled in late to the packed, fluorescent-lit lecture room – as celebrity philosopher Agnes Callard of the University of Chicago and Joe Heath, a political and economic philosopher at U of T, debated the ethics of capitalism.

The Night Owls event gave students a chance to hear ideas bandied about for their own sake, something that isn’t exactly in vogue in Canada’s job-obsessed postsecondary education sector, where funding is increasingly directed to Stem, trades and professional fields.

The freewheeling discussion roamed from a comparison of co-operative and competitive capitalism, to talk of whether modern dentistry could be seen as a triumph of pricing and markets, to the differences between true socialism and what Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders advocates for. (“That’s just Canada,” Prof. Heath said to laughs.)

“I thought it was great,” Tiara Maleki Yazdi, a first-year student who plans to major in philosophy and English, said over pizza and cans of Bubly sparkling water at the break.

She and her friends still weren’t sure how some of the philosophical concepts Prof. Callard and Prof. Heath tossed around would apply in real life, but said “it was a real privilege to listen to it and get exposed to a new perspective.”

Opinion: Capitalism has always been deeply political

The Ontario government is spending $1.7-billion over four years to fund 70,000 new seats at colleges and universities for programs in Stem, health care, teaching and skilled trades. Forty-thousand of those spaces were allocated only after schools consulted local businesses to make certain their program expansions met labour-market demands, the provincial government announced Sept. 10 .

The following day, Alberta unveiled the next phase of its expanded enrolment plan , adding 8,000 seats at colleges and universities by 2028-29 in nursing, teaching, paramedicine, engineering, technology and trades.

The humanities haven’t benefited from the same government largesse or student demand.

Liberal arts programs are mostly contracting, although the specifics differ by school and discipline. About 70,000 fewer students were enrolled in humanities programs at universities and colleges across Canada in 2023-24 compared with a decade earlier, according to the most recent data from Statistics Canada.

And that was before Ottawa’s curbing of international student visas, which deprived postsecondary institutions of a major funding source. The policy change led some schools to cut or freeze their offerings, notably in the humanities.

Prof. Boyagoda is a novelist, critic and longtime English professor, who in July became director of the Jackman Humanities Institute, which hosted the Night Owls event. He said he is sympathetic to students who want to major in the Stem or professional fields that seem likeliest to land them a job.

“I acknowledge fully the importance of providing students with the practical skills needed to succeed in the professions,” he said. “But at the same time, we shouldn’t mistake universities for technical institutes − for trade schools with better architecture.”

Many undergraduate students pursuing professional degrees are eager to study subjects such as history, art, literature, and – especially – philosophy as second majors, minors or electives at a time when artificial intelligence makes the human mind feel more valuable, he added.

Opinion: What’s university even for? Schools are broke, and degrees are worth less and less

The number of registrations in undergraduate philosophy courses has held steady or ticked up slightly since 2018-19 at U of T’s three campuses, the school’s data show.

“Philosophy is teaching you how to actually think,” said Julia Nefsky, chair of the philosophy department at U of T Scarborough. “So it’s like a power combo with a technical field.”

Prof. Nefsky and her colleagues Daniel Silver, a professor of sociology at U of T Scarborough, and Gurpreet Rattan, chair of philosophy at U of T Mississauga, proposed the Night Owls event to Prof. Boyagoda.

They were inspired by the late-night philosophy rap sessions of the same name that Prof. Callard has emceed at the University of Chicago for nearly a decade.

Topics have ranged from “How do we judge the dead?” and “The ethics of artificial intelligence,” to “Is love worth the pain?” and the “Philosophy of divorce.”

Prof. Callard hosted the latter event with her ex-husband, fellow University of Chicago philosopher Ben Callard. The former couple later philosophized to The New Yorker about living together with Agnes’s new husband.

The University of Chicago, historically a giant of humanities education, stunned postsecondary observers when its Arts and Humanities Division decided to pause admissions to most PhD programs for the 2026-27 academic year to help the indebted school get back on its financial feet.

Opinion: We mustn’t lose sight of Canada’s education reputation on the world stage

Only the philosophy department and one program in music escaped the freeze.

After the Toronto Night Owls event wrapped up around 10:45 p.m., Prof. Callard said in an interview that enrolment in philosophy courses at the University of Chicago has bucked the downward trend of the humanities overall, just like at U of T.

Philosophy endures as a popular second choice for students majoring in hard-edged subjects such as economics, physics and math, she added.

“A lot of the humanities might seem kind of inaccessible or you’re not really sure what their concerns are,” she said. “I think philosophy wears its heart on its sleeve.”

stories.title: Woman convicted of manslaughter in shaken-baby case hopes to clear her name
stories.summary: Jennifer Gaskin’s appeal is the latest in an effort to undo the damage caused by the now widely contested forensic theory of ‘shaken baby syndrome’
stories.author: Molly Hayes
stories.content:
More than 20 years after she was convicted in the death of her baby boy, and more than a decade after the science of “shaken baby syndrome” was called into question, Jennifer Gaskin is hoping to finally clear her name.

The 51-year-old, convicted of manslaughter in 2002, is preparing to appear before the Ontario Court of Appeal. In advance of the Sept. 29 hearing, Ms. Gaskin’s lawyers and the Crown have come together, jointly submitting to the court that her conviction be quashed.

“In light of the overwhelming weight of the current expert opinion, the appellant’s conviction cannot and should not stand,” Crown lawyer Elise Nakelsky said in written arguments, filed in court. “This Court ought to set aside her conviction for manslaughter and enter an acquittal.”

For Ms. Gaskin, who spent 18 months in prison, it is a chance to lift the stigma she has long carried and an opportunity to prove to her surviving children, who were taken from her after Joeseph’s death, that she is innocent.

“For 27 years, my other two children have thought I killed their brother Joeseph,” she said in a statement to The Globe and Mail. “If my appeal goes well, I pray they will realize I did not kill their brother, and accept me as their loving mother.”

The appeal is the latest in a decades-long effort to undo the damage caused by the now widely contested forensic theory of shaken baby syndrome (SBS).

The term was first coined in the early 1970s and became a go-to diagnosis for pathologists probing baby deaths in cases where infants had a combination of brain swelling, retinal bleeding and tissue damage to the brain lining.

But it came under scrutiny in the early 2000s, when some experts began to dispute the validity of the diagnosis and raise concerns that it had led to wrongful convictions.

In Ontario, an inquiry into errors by Charles Smith, a former forensic pathologist at Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children, uncovered more than a dozen child-death cases that were tainted by flawed analyses, often involving marginalized families, including those involved with child welfare agencies.

A committee was established in 2008 to specifically probe so-called shaken-baby deaths in the province dating back to the 1980s. It reviewed 129 cases, ultimately narrowing in on 13 cases in which people were convicted.

Ms. Gaskin’s case was one of them.

The fresh evidence submitted by Ms. Gaskin’s legal team in her appeal includes the findings of that committee, along with new reports by a forensic neuropathologist, a biomechanical engineer and a forensic pathologist, who concluded that while it would be difficult to rule out an inflicted injury, natural causes could also have been to blame.

They pointed out that much more substantial testing and analysis would be done after a death like this today than was done (or even possible) at the time.

“As of today, the original expert evidence supporting the conviction of the appellant at trial has been wholly undermined and placed in grave doubt,” Ms. Nakelsky summarized in the Crown’s written arguments.

Baby Joeseph Gaskin was nine-and-a-half weeks premature when he was born via cesarean section on April 13, 1999.

He was intubated and ventilated for two days, according to the documents filed by Ms. Gaskin’s counsel, veteran wrongful convictions lawyer James Lockyer. He was kept on oxygen for five days, and was treated for moderate respiratory distress syndrome, hypoglycemia and an elevated white blood cell count usually associated with infection. He was given a 10-day drug regimen to fight bacterial infections.

As he gained weight, the monitoring was scaled back, and he was finally able to go home on June 11.

On June 30, Ms. Gaskin – who was 23 and also had a 13-month-old baby at the time – took Joeseph to the clinic, concerned that he’d been throwing up his formula feedings. According to the defence’s court filings, a nurse looked Joeseph over and said he was “fine as long as he kept peeing and pooping, and his skin didn’t get dried up.”

He’d gained half a pound from five days earlier. He was smiling and appeared healthy and hydrated. She took a swab of his right eye, which was crusty, but otherwise instructed not to overfeed him and to return if the vomiting continued.

The next day was Canada Day, so the clinic was closed. Ms. Gaskin remained concerned about Joeseph, who was still spitting up on and off, according to the defence’s court filings, but took solace in the nurse’s reassurances from the day before.

When a friend visited that evening, Ms. Gaskin told her she was having trouble coping, according to the defence’s court filings. She did not have a large support system in Ignace, Ont., where she was living with her boyfriend, Dale Jones, raising two kids under the age of 2.

After being diagnosed with severe pre-eclampsia during her pregnancy with Joeseph, she had asked the Children’s Aid Society to take care of her older baby on a temporary care arrangement.

A worker with CAS – who assisted the family after both babies came home – also visited on July 1. She said the baby seemed fine, according to the defence’s court filings, but noticed his eyes “had a type of glaze or a haze that wasn’t normal looking.”

Throughout the night and into the next morning, Joeseph continued to spit up, ON and off.

On the morning of July 2, Ms. Gaskin and Mr. Jones took the children to the health unit for their weekly weigh-in. A clerk recalled that the toddler seemed normal, but Joeseph was “cranky” and “pale looking,” according to her court filings.

Afterward, the couple ran into a friend and headed to a local restaurant for lunch.

Mr. Jones took the babies home around 11:30 a.m., after Joeseph started to whine for a bottle, and Ms. Gaskin stayed with her friend.

When he got home and changed Joeseph’s diaper, Mr. Jones noticed the baby turning bright red, according to the defence’s court filings. He tried CPR and then sought help from neighbours before an ambulance was called. By then the baby was grayish-blue, unresponsive and not breathing.

Mr. Jones called her at the restaurant.

“I hung up, ran and grabbed my things and ran to the clinic,” Ms. Gaskin later told police. “I got there before the ambulance.”

Joeseph was intubated and given oxygen, epinephrine and atropine. He was pronounced dead early that afternoon.

An autopsy was conducted by David Welbourne, a surgical pathologist at Thunder Bay Hospital. He described Joeseph as a normal-looking premature baby with no external injury or bruising and no fractures to his limbs or scalp.

But he identified bleeding and bruising on the baby’s brain, as well as epidural bleeding throughout Joeseph’s spinal column, retinal bleeding and bleeding in the optic nerve sheaths.

Dr. Welbourne concluded Joeseph had incurred multiple injuries at different times from shaking and that “head injury” was his cause of death.

William Halliday, a neuropathologist at the Hospital for Sick Children, who, according to Ms. Gaskin’s court filings, was qualified by the court as a “shaken baby syndrome” expert, provided a second opinion.

Dr. Halliday, too, concluded that the injuries were caused by shaking, and that the baby had been in a traumatic environment for about two weeks.

(A spokesperson for the Thunder Bay Hospital, where Dr. Welbourne works, directed The Globe to the provincial coroner’s office, where a spokesperson declined to comment. SickKids and Dr. Halliday did not respond to e-mails from The Globe.)

In interviews with police, Ms. Gaskin “vehemently and consistently” denied that she or her boyfriend had ever hit or shaken either of the children.

She told the officer that if she ever felt herself getting stressed out or overwhelmed, she would simply put the baby down and go for a cigarette.

“I’ve never shaken that baby,” she said, according to the court filings. “I could kill myself before I do anything to hurt my kids.”

Eight months after Joeseph died, Ms. Gaskin was arrested and charged with second-degree murder.

At trial, the Crown’s position was that the baby died from injuries inflicted by at least three incidents of shaking, and that as the primary caregiver, Ms. Gaskin was the only one who could have shaken him three times.

Her defence lawyer at the time argued that the Crown had not proven that Ms. Gaskin had injured the baby, either intentionally or unintentionally – and that many questions about his injuries remained unanswered by the evidence at trial. But the jury found her guilty of manslaughter. She was sentenced to two years less a day in prison.

In 2010 – as part of the Shaken Baby Death Review Committee’s process – Ms. Gaskin consented to having her case reviewed by an International Medical Panel (IMP).

The panel, according to the court filings, was unable to determine Joeseph’s cause of death, and “could not say whether death occurred ‘with’ or ‘of’ a head injury.”

In the Shaken Baby Death Review Committee’s report on Ms. Gaskin’s case, excerpted in both the Crown and defence’s court filings, they wrote that “the fact that the IMP could not determine the cause of death, or whether the baby died of a head injury at all, raises concerns about the evidence relied on to support Ms. Gaskin’s conviction.”

In addition to Ms. Gaskin’s case, the committee flagged concerns with three other cases involving convictions based on now discredited shaken-baby syndrome testimony.

One of them was that of Bernard Doyle, who was acquitted in 2023 of manslaughter charges in the 1996 death of his partner’s 17-month-old son. Mr. Doyle – who was convicted in 1997 and, like Ms. Gaskin, was represented on appeal by Mr. Lockyer – had maintained that he was dancing with the boy when he accidentally tripped and fell.

In the United States, too, the justice system continues to reckon with the fallout of the shaken-baby debate.

Robert Roberson, a death row inmate in Texas, narrowly escaped execution for the third time last fall, days before he was slated to become the first person in the U.S. to be put to death for a shaken-baby-syndrome murder conviction. Mr. Roberson and his lawyers assert that his 23-month-old daughter Nikki died not of abuse, but of complications from pneumonia.

The day after Joeseph’s funeral, in July, 1999, Ms. Gaskin’s 14-month-old daughter was apprehended by Children’s Aid and then adopted by a family in Dryden. While on bail awaiting her trial, Ms. Gaskin gave birth to a third child, a son. He too was apprehended.

Ms. Gaskin – who lives in Eastern Ontario today, where she works as a restaurant hostess – has not seen her surviving children since then, she wrote in an affidavit earlier this year, and has never been able to grieve Joeseph properly.

“I have never felt able to breathe freely because I feel everyone sees me to be a monster,” she wrote.

Editor’s note: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that Texan Robert Roberson’s daughter Nikki was 13 months old when she died. She was 23 months old.
paragraphs: More than 20 years after she was convicted in the death of her baby boy, and more than a decade after the science of “shaken baby syndrome” was called into question, Jennifer Gaskin is hoping to finally clear her name.

The 51-year-old, convicted of manslaughter in 2002, is preparing to appear before the Ontario Court of Appeal. In advance of the Sept. 29 hearing, Ms. Gaskin’s lawyers and the Crown have come together, jointly submitting to the court that her conviction be quashed.

“In light of the overwhelming weight of the current expert opinion, the appellant’s conviction cannot and should not stand,” Crown lawyer Elise Nakelsky said in written arguments, filed in court. “This Court ought to set aside her conviction for manslaughter and enter an acquittal.”

For Ms. Gaskin, who spent 18 months in prison, it is a chance to lift the stigma she has long carried and an opportunity to prove to her surviving children, who were taken from her after Joeseph’s death, that she is innocent.

“For 27 years, my other two children have thought I killed their brother Joeseph,” she said in a statement to The Globe and Mail. “If my appeal goes well, I pray they will realize I did not kill their brother, and accept me as their loving mother.”
The appeal is the latest in a decades-long effort to undo the damage caused by the now widely contested forensic theory of shaken baby syndrome (SBS).

The term was first coined in the early 1970s and became a go-to diagnosis for pathologists probing baby deaths in cases where infants had a combination of brain swelling, retinal bleeding and tissue damage to the brain lining.
But it came under scrutiny in the early 2000s, when some experts began to dispute the validity of the diagnosis and raise concerns that it had led to wrongful convictions.

In Ontario, an inquiry into errors by Charles Smith, a former forensic pathologist at Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children, uncovered more than a dozen child-death cases that were tainted by flawed analyses, often involving marginalized families, including those involved with child welfare agencies.

A committee was established in 2008 to specifically probe so-called shaken-baby deaths in the province dating back to the 1980s. It reviewed 129 cases, ultimately narrowing in on 13 cases in which people were convicted.
Ms. Gaskin’s case was one of them.

The fresh evidence submitted by Ms. Gaskin’s legal team in her appeal includes the findings of that committee, along with new reports by a forensic neuropathologist, a biomechanical engineer and a forensic pathologist, who concluded that while it would be difficult to rule out an inflicted injury, natural causes could also have been to blame.
They pointed out that much more substantial testing and analysis would be done after a death like this today than was done (or even possible) at the time.

“As of today, the original expert evidence supporting the conviction of the appellant at trial has been wholly undermined and placed in grave doubt,” Ms. Nakelsky summarized in the Crown’s written arguments.
Baby Joeseph Gaskin was nine-and-a-half weeks premature when he was born via cesarean section on April 13, 1999.

He was intubated and ventilated for two days, according to the documents filed by Ms. Gaskin’s counsel, veteran wrongful convictions lawyer James Lockyer. He was kept on oxygen for five days, and was treated for moderate respiratory distress syndrome, hypoglycemia and an elevated white blood cell count usually associated with infection. He was given a 10-day drug regimen to fight bacterial infections.
As he gained weight, the monitoring was scaled back, and he was finally able to go home on June 11.

On June 30, Ms. Gaskin – who was 23 and also had a 13-month-old baby at the time – took Joeseph to the clinic, concerned that he’d been throwing up his formula feedings. According to the defence’s court filings, a nurse looked Joeseph over and said he was “fine as long as he kept peeing and pooping, and his skin didn’t get dried up.”

He’d gained half a pound from five days earlier. He was smiling and appeared healthy and hydrated. She took a swab of his right eye, which was crusty, but otherwise instructed not to overfeed him and to return if the vomiting continued.

The next day was Canada Day, so the clinic was closed. Ms. Gaskin remained concerned about Joeseph, who was still spitting up on and off, according to the defence’s court filings, but took solace in the nurse’s reassurances from the day before.

When a friend visited that evening, Ms. Gaskin told her she was having trouble coping, according to the defence’s court filings. She did not have a large support system in Ignace, Ont., where she was living with her boyfriend, Dale Jones, raising two kids under the age of 2.
After being diagnosed with severe pre-eclampsia during her pregnancy with Joeseph, she had asked the Children’s Aid Society to take care of her older baby on a temporary care arrangement.

A worker with CAS – who assisted the family after both babies came home – also visited on July 1. She said the baby seemed fine, according to the defence’s court filings, but noticed his eyes “had a type of glaze or a haze that wasn’t normal looking.”
Throughout the night and into the next morning, Joeseph continued to spit up, ON and off.

On the morning of July 2, Ms. Gaskin and Mr. Jones took the children to the health unit for their weekly weigh-in. A clerk recalled that the toddler seemed normal, but Joeseph was “cranky” and “pale looking,” according to her court filings.
Afterward, the couple ran into a friend and headed to a local restaurant for lunch.
Mr. Jones took the babies home around 11:30 a.m., after Joeseph started to whine for a bottle, and Ms. Gaskin stayed with her friend.

When he got home and changed Joeseph’s diaper, Mr. Jones noticed the baby turning bright red, according to the defence’s court filings. He tried CPR and then sought help from neighbours before an ambulance was called. By then the baby was grayish-blue, unresponsive and not breathing.
Mr. Jones called her at the restaurant.
“I hung up, ran and grabbed my things and ran to the clinic,” Ms. Gaskin later told police. “I got there before the ambulance.”

stories.title: Anand hosting conference today on returning Ukrainian children from Russian abduction
stories.summary: Toronto — Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand is co-hosting a global meeting in Toronto today aimed at advancing work to return Ukrainian children abducted by Russian officials.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — Ukrainians who survived Russian captivity are thanking Canada for its advocacy and for funding programs to help children heal from trauma.

Dariia Tomashova, 18, told a Toronto conference Monday that she escaped Crimea four months ago, after a year of trying to flee the Ukrainian region Russia seized in 2014.

“Children were turned into Russians, into zombies,” she said through an interpreter.

Any mentions of Crimea being part of Ukraine were stripped from classroom instruction, as was any mention of the Soviet repression of the island’s Indigenous Peoples, Tomashova said. Children were made to write letters of support to Russian troops.

“We didn’t understand at that time that we were being prepared for a real war, that all of these events — when girls from being 10 years old, learning tactical medical support, boys being taught how to handle weapons — we were being trained to be Russian soldiers,” she said, pausing to hold back tears.

Tomashova was addressing a two-day conference aimed at advancing work to return Ukrainian children from captivity in Russia and the Ukrainian territories it occupies.

In 2024, the Trudeau government co-launched with Ukraine an international coalition of nations committed to finding and returning Ukrainian children abducted by Russia after Moscow invaded Ukraine in 2014 and launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.

Ukrainian authorities cite what they say are more than 20,651 records of possible unlawful deportations or forcible transfers of Ukrainian children to Russia or Russian-occupied territories of eastern Ukraine.

Officials in Ukraine say 2,573 of those children have been returned.

Bring Kids Back, a coalition launched by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has reported that abducted children returned to Ukraine have reported being subjected to physical and sexual violence.

One of the coalition members, Save Ukraine, has used Canadian funds to support Ukrainians who have been sexually abused while held by the Russian state or in foster homes.

“Their rescue only begins when they’re coming back from (the) Russian trap, because with that trauma they have, we have to provide constant 24-7 support for months, sometimes for years,” Save Ukraine co-founder Mykola Kuleba said in an interview.

“We are so grateful for Canada leading and supporting our rescue missions,” he said.

Kuleba called for more pressure and sanctions on Russia, saying this would lead to more children being returned home.

On Monday, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand announced $863,000 in new funding for civil society groups in Ukraine that help returned children and families. That sum brings Canada’s total funding for those efforts to $7 million.

Anand said Canada has used artificial intelligence technology to trace the whereabouts of Ukrainian children and prisoners of war. She noted that Russian officials have changed children’s names, making it harder to verify who is in an “indoctrination camp.”

“This is not an accident, this is not a side-effect of war. This is a systematic effort to separate Ukrainian children from Ukraine,” she said at a news conference.

“They must stop obstructing their return, provide information about where these children are (and) stop altering their identities.”

Ukraine’s allies have expanded their reunification efforts to include adult civilians and prisoners of war taken from parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia.

Margaryta Shabanova described her husband being taken by Russian officials in 2022 during his work with an independent monitoring mission in the occupied region of Luhansk.

She said she only learned he was alive when video surfaced of her emaciated husband facing espionage charges for his work with the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, a group of which both Canada and Russia are members.

“Thinking too much about this — where he is, and what he May be enduring there — is something you learn to manage. Not because the fear goes away, but because you cannot function, if you let it consume (you) entirely,” Shabanova said.

Tomashova and Shabanova were among four Ukrainians describing their experiences at this week’s conference. Dozens of countries sent representatives to the conference, including all G7 countries, most European states and other nations such as Qatar and Honduras.

But the flags of several major G20 countries were absent, including those of Brazil, China, India, Indonesia and Saudi Arabia. Global Affairs Canada did not immediately respond when asked for a list of conference attendees.

Anand said complex diplomacy has been required to get children out of Russia and the occupied Ukrainian territories. She said India’s direct talks with Russia have helped inform Canada’s work on understanding various Russian actions in the war.

“I have had numerous discussions with foreign ministers around the world about what more we can do to engage indirectly, and in some cases directly, with Russia,” she said.

“We’re very much relying on a full set of countries to assist with this process.”

This week’s talks are taking place in Toronto, where the CN Tower was set to project the blue and yellow colours of the Ukrainian flag Monday evening.

Since March 2023, Russian President Vladimir Putin and a senior Russian official have been subject to International Criminal Court arrest warrants on charges of unlawful deportation and transfer of children.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 28, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: B.C. election campaigns enter second week with candidate, policy announcements
stories.summary: Vancouver - The campaigns for the upcoming British Columbia election enter their second week, with major parties gearing up policy announcements and candidate nominations.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - Resource development and making British Columbia an “energy superpower” to grow the economy would allow for a new provincial government to pay down the record deficit, both the NDP and Conservative party leaders said on the campaign trail Monday.

Interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson promised to double liquefied natural gas production by 2032, if elected, while NDP Leader David Eby announced his government would double the export of critical minerals within five years.

Doerkson said there’s a global energy crisis and “our allies in Asia and Europe desperately need Canadian LNG.”

While Eby picked up on the same theme, saying B.C. has an abundance of critical minerals that other countries need.

“Getting them to world markets means less dependence on the U.S., while creating family-supporting jobs and the prosperity needed to strengthen health care and public services,” said Eby, who was in Prince Rupert on Monday.

He also said an NDP government would expand the Prince Rupert port to be the second-largest facility of its kind in Canada by 2030.

Eby said that unlike the B.C. Liberals, Doerkson’s former party, the B.C. New Democrats delivered on LNG.

“There are five LNG facilities reaching final investment decision or under construction right now in the province of B.C.,” Eby said.

Doerkson said if the New Democrats would have been interested in LNG six or seven years ago, the province would be in a different situation.

“It’s shocking to me that (NDP) interest in LNG has shown up 20 days before an election,” Doerkson said. “We need to get going on this right now.”

When questioned about the $13.8-billion deficit that Eby’s NDP government accumulated while in power, both party leaders said their plans to grow the economy would help trim the shortfall.

British Columbians demand that the deficit be reduced, Doerkson said at an event in Vancouver.

“We can’t be dealing with a $14-billion deficit in British Columbia,” he said. “How do we manage anything, knowing that we are faced with these deficits year after year?”

Doerkson did not offer details about how a future Conservative government would balance the budget.

“The reality is that we’re not sure how bad the books are,” he said.

The interim leader, who replaced Kerry-Lynne Findlay about a week ago following her resignation, pointed to an accounting error by the provincial government admitted to this year that overstated forecast revenues from natural gas by nearly $1.5 billion.

“It’s going to be almost impossible to commit to how quickly we will be able to arrive at balanced budgets,” he said. “But the reality is, we have to get back to that.”

Doerkson’s promised on Sunday that his government would not raise existing taxes or introduce new ones.

Eby said the promise of a tax freeze shows the Conservatives are not transparent about their plans.

“The math doesn’t work for the Conservatives,” he said. “It’s very clear that their agenda, when you do the math, is to dramatically cut health care and education.”

Eby pointed to comments from Conservative candidate Tony Luck, who is running for re-election in Fraser-Nicola.

Luck said in February 2024 that if education and health care are the two biggest budget items, then they will take “the brunt” of cuts.

Eby said there is no difference between the major parties when it comes fiscal sustainability.

The real question is how to get there, he said.

“We’ve got to end wasteful spending,” he said. “We’ve got to grow the economy with announcements like today’s.”

David Williams, vice-president of economics with the Business Council of B.C., said provincial spending has been out of control since 2021.

“Your fiscal situation is not the result of Donald Trump or external pressures or anything like that,” Williams said. “This is because of domestic policy choices around the rate of spending growth.”

Whoever forms government needs to get that spending under control, he said.

Bryan Yu, chief economist with Central 1 Credit Union, said there are many questions around how to boost the B.C. economy, which hasn’t grown much this year.

“It’s been a little bit troubling in terms … of business investment or business growth, like the number of business counts are very flat when it comes to Alberta and some of our other peer provinces,” he said.

B.C.’s public sector is quite large relative to the population and could be adjusted, Yu said.

“We really need to find a way to get more jobs, more private sector investment in the economy.”

paragraphs: Victoria - Resource development and making British Columbia an “energy superpower” to grow the economy would allow for a new provincial government to pay down the record deficit, both the NDP and Conservative party leaders said on the campaign trail Monday.

Interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson promised to double liquefied natural gas production by 2032, if elected, while NDP Leader David Eby announced his government would double the export of critical minerals within five years.
Doerkson said there’s a global energy crisis and “our allies in Asia and Europe desperately need Canadian LNG.”
While Eby picked up on the same theme, saying B.C. has an abundance of critical minerals that other countries need.

“Getting them to world markets means less dependence on the U.S., while creating family-supporting jobs and the prosperity needed to strengthen health care and public services,” said Eby, who was in Prince Rupert on Monday.
He also said an NDP government would expand the Prince Rupert port to be the second-largest facility of its kind in Canada by 2030.
Eby said that unlike the B.C. Liberals, Doerkson’s former party, the B.C. New Democrats delivered on LNG.
“There are five LNG facilities reaching final investment decision or under construction right now in the province of B.C.,” Eby said.
Doerkson said if the New Democrats would have been interested in LNG six or seven years ago, the province would be in a different situation.
“It’s shocking to me that (NDP) interest in LNG has shown up 20 days before an election,” Doerkson said. “We need to get going on this right now.”
When questioned about the $13.8-billion deficit that Eby’s NDP government accumulated while in power, both party leaders said their plans to grow the economy would help trim the shortfall.
British Columbians demand that the deficit be reduced, Doerkson said at an event in Vancouver.
“We can’t be dealing with a $14-billion deficit in British Columbia,” he said. “How do we manage anything, knowing that we are faced with these deficits year after year?”
Doerkson did not offer details about how a future Conservative government would balance the budget.
“The reality is that we’re not sure how bad the books are,” he said.

The interim leader, who replaced Kerry-Lynne Findlay about a week ago following her resignation, pointed to an accounting error by the provincial government admitted to this year that overstated forecast revenues from natural gas by nearly $1.5 billion.
“It’s going to be almost impossible to commit to how quickly we will be able to arrive at balanced budgets,” he said. “But the reality is, we have to get back to that.”
Doerkson’s promised on Sunday that his government would not raise existing taxes or introduce new ones.
Eby said the promise of a tax freeze shows the Conservatives are not transparent about their plans.
“The math doesn’t work for the Conservatives,” he said. “It’s very clear that their agenda, when you do the math, is to dramatically cut health care and education.”
Eby pointed to comments from Conservative candidate Tony Luck, who is running for re-election in Fraser-Nicola.
Luck said in February 2024 that if education and health care are the two biggest budget items, then they will take “the brunt” of cuts.
Eby said there is no difference between the major parties when it comes fiscal sustainability.
The real question is how to get there, he said.
“We’ve got to end wasteful spending,” he said. “We’ve got to grow the economy with announcements like today’s.”
David Williams, vice-president of economics with the Business Council of B.C., said provincial spending has been out of control since 2021.
“Your fiscal situation is not the result of Donald Trump or external pressures or anything like that,” Williams said. “This is because of domestic policy choices around the rate of spending growth.”
Whoever forms government needs to get that spending under control, he said.
Bryan Yu, chief economist with Central 1 Credit Union, said there are many questions around how to boost the B.C. economy, which hasn’t grown much this year.

“It’s been a little bit troubling in terms … of business investment or business growth, like the number of business counts are very flat when it comes to Alberta and some of our other peer provinces,” he said.
B.C.’s public sector is quite large relative to the population and could be adjusted, Yu said.
“We really need to find a way to get more jobs, more private sector investment in the economy.”
Both leaders were also asked about a gathering of alleged white nationalists on a B.C. First Nation reserve on Sunday, just days away from National Truth and Reconciliation Day.

Roseanne Casimir, chief of Tk’emlups te Secwepemc nation, said a group of masked people dropped a banner from an overpass in Kamloops on Sunday questioning reports of human burials at the former sites of residential schools.
Eby called the display “disgusting,” while Doerkson denounced the group.

In Victoria on Monday, Green Leader Emily Lowan said her party would lift the freeze on the NDP government’s $10-a-day childcare spaces, with a goal to achieve universal free children care space by 2031.
“Lack of access, lack of qualified educators, and unaffordable fees send a clear message to young people and families: the government is not investing in you,” Lowan said in a statement.
The current childcare model in B.C. is expensive and complicated, and it’s been exacerbated by the former NDP government’s funding pause in the last provincial budget, Lowan said.

stories.title: Alberta, Ontario premiers set to share stage in Calgary to talk energy policy
stories.summary: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Ontario Premier Doug Ford are set to share the stage in Calgary today to talk energy.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Calgary — Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Ontario Premier Doug Ford are set to share the stage in Calgary today to talk energy.

The leaders will be in the city’s downtown to talk about how to best get Canada’s natural resources to market in a world of fluctuating politics and conflicts.

Smith has placed energy at the centre of her government’s agenda, particularly the need to get more oil to the British Columbia coast and from there to markets in Asia.

It also comes as Canada navigates an ongoing tariff war with the United States.

Smith has rejected using oil as leverage in the tariff battle with U.S. President Donald Trump.

Ford, however, has publicly stated he does not agree oil should be off the table, but says both he and Smith agree more oil needs to flow within Canada.

stories.title: What Florida’s property tax vote means for Canadian snowbirds
stories.summary: A Florida ballot measure would sharply increase property tax exemptions for many permanent residents while keeping non-homesteaded properties in the tax base. Gov. Ron DeSantis has explicitly said snowbirds, including Canadians, could continue paying property taxes as Florida homeowners receive relief.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Florida voters will decide Nov. 3 whether to approve Amendment 3 , a constitutional measure that would substantially increase the homestead property-tax exemption for qualifying homeowners.

For Canadian snowbirds, who own property in Florida, the proposed tax overhaul comes with a twist: the biggest break would go to permanent Florida residents, while seasonal homeowners, including Canadians, could remain part of the tax base.

The proposal in May grew out of Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ campaign to reduce, and eventually eliminate, property taxes on homesteaded homes. He said that Florida could afford the change because “Property tax revenue collected by local governments has nearly doubled in the past seven years.”

He also made clear who would remain outside the main relief.

“We are focusing on homestead. Obviously they tax property that are non-homestead: Residential, Airbnb, Canadian snowbirds, commercial,” DeSantis said in an interview with Fox News in June.

In 2025 , while arguing against a sales-tax cut, he said he wanted “Canadian tourists and Brazilian tourists” to help subsidize Florida while residents received tax relief.

That is significant for Canadians, who make up a large share of Florida’s seasonal property owners.

The amendment , approved by Florida lawmakers, would increase the non-school homestead exemption from the current US$50,000 to US$150,000 in 2027 and US$250,000 in 2028. It would also reduce the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homesteaded properties from 10 per cent to five per cent.

In other words, the measure does not create a tax specifically targeting Canadians. Rather, Canadians who own properties that do not qualify for the permanent-resident homestead exemption would not receive the main tax break.

If approved by at least 60 per cent of Florida voters, Amendment 3 would take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Property taxes are local, not state. So we’d need to do a constitutional amendment (requires 60% of voters to approve) to eliminate them (which I would support) or even to reform/lower them… We should put the boldest amendment on the ballot that has a chance of getting that… https://t.co/WpOQmjNl0X — Ron DeSantis (@GovRonDeSantis) February 13, 2025

For Canadians, who own a winter home in Florida, the issue is therefore less about a new Canadian-specific tax than about who qualifies for the largest property tax relief and who remains responsible for local property taxes as Florida reshapes its tax base.

stories.title: Debris from missing Ontario-based air ambulance located: U.S. Coast Guard
stories.summary: Debris associated with an Ontario-based air ambulance that was carrying six people, including four Canadians, has been located hours after it went missing as it was flying from Bermuda to Boston.
stories.author: Bryann Aguilar, Joshua McGinnis
stories.content:
Debris associated with an Ontario-based air ambulance that was carrying six people, including four Canadians, has been located hours after it went missing as it was flying from Bermuda to Boston.

The U.S. Coast Guard said in a news release on Saturday night that crews discovered the debris field off the coast of Nantucket, Mass., where they had been conducting a search all day.

“Crews are continuing to search for the six people who were aboard the aircraft and the Coast Guard cutter William Sparling will continue search efforts throughout the night,” the release read, noting that 1,644 square miles have been searched over approximately 27 hours.

The U.S. Coast Guard added that next of kin have been notified.

The Coast Guard said the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration notified them around 2 a.m. that it lost contact with the aircraft, a Gulfstream G100 with the tail number C-Grjp and owned by Hamilton, Ont.-based Latitude Air Ambulance.
