Updates will be provided here as info becomes available.… — USCGNortheast (@USCGNortheast) October 3, 2026

Clarence Togeretz, the air ambulance company’s operations manager, told The Canadian Press on Saturday morning that the aircraft was transporting a patient and family member, who were Bermuda nationals.

He said the two pilots and two medical staff aboard were Canadians.

Togeretz also shared that his company had been tracking the flight and lost contact with it around 1:30 a.m. as it was approaching Boston. Togeretz said Latitude reached out to the U.S. Coast Guard when the aircraft failed to reach the tarmac.

“We’re praying for a safe outcome,” he said.

Togeretz noted that this is the first time Latitude Air Ambulance has lost contact with one of its planes.

The aircraft bound for Boston Logan International Airport departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport at 12:41 a.m. The air ambulance arrived in Bermuda from Hamilton the previous night.

Air traffic control audio captured by LiveATC.net indicates that the flight declared an emergency before it went missing.

“Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot, who cannot be heard in the audio.

The controller then asked the pilot if they were declaring an emergency.

“You’re coming in a little weak. I didn’t hear your response was if you were declaring an emergency or not,” the controller heard telling the pilot.

A short time later, the controller got a confirmation from the pilot that they were indeed declaring an emergency.

According to flight tracking website FlightAware, data shows that one hour and 23 minutes into the flight, the aircraft dropped from an altitude of 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet in two minutes and then levelled off before it vanished.

The search for the jet included crews in the air and on the water, the U.S. Coast Guard said, noting that it was using two planes, a search and rescue lifeboat, a helicopter, and a cutter.

The Coast Guard noted that crews

#Update Uscg assets responding include: - HC-144 Ocean Sentry airplane crew from AirSta Cape Cod - HC-130 Hercules crew from AirSta Elizabeth City - MH-60 Jayhawk helicopter crew from AirSta Cape Cod - 47-foot MLB crew from Station Brant Point - FRC William Sparling (WPC-1154)… — USCGNortheast (@USCGNortheast) October 3, 2026

Latitude Air Ambulance’s website says that it currently has four G100 jets in its fleet, each with a range of 5,000 km.

In a statement posted to X , Ontario’s air ambulance service provider Ornge said that “Our thoughts are with our colleagues at Latitude Air Ambulance at this time.”

“All of us at Ornge are hopeful the aircraft and all passengers are located safely and quickly.”

Ornge noted that the flight was not related to its operations.

Canadian government ‘closely monitoring the situation’

Canada’s Transportation Minister, Steven MacKinnon, said his department is aware of the situation and that they “are closing monitoring” in a post to X.

“My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones, and colleagues during this incredibly difficult time.”

“We are closely monitoring the situation and are working with the relevant authorities as search and rescue efforts continue. I want to thank all first responders involved for their ongoing efforts.”

I am aware of reports of a Canadian-registered air ambulance aircraft that went missing while travelling from Bermuda to Boston. Four Canadians are among the six people on board. My thoughts are with everyone on board, as well as their families, loved ones and colleagues during… — Steven MacKinnon (@stevenmackinnon) October 3, 2026

Global Affairs Canada said it was aware of reports of Canadians on board the missing Latitude Air Ambulance.

“Consular officials stand ready to provide consular assistance and are in contact with local authorities. Due to privacy considerations, no further information can be disclosed,” Global Affairs said in a statement to CTV News.

Bermuda government releases statement

A spokesperson on behalf of the Bermuda government confirmed the air ambulance’s departure from Bermuda to Boston this morning in a post to X.

Officials said they’ve been in contact with the families of those on board as well as the U.S. Coast Guard conducting the search.

In a statement, Bermuda’s Premier David Burt said that “his thoughts are with everyone on board and their families during this deeply worrying time.”

“We are praying that all six people will be found safe, and we thank the search and rescue crews for their continuing efforts.”

stories.title: New remote testimony room aims to make court less traumatic for London-area children
stories.summary: New remote testimony room aims to make court less traumatic for London-area children CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: October 4, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: 5 hours ago
London Family Court Clinic says new suite gives young witnesses a safe, trauma-informed alternative to court
For children involved in the justice system, testifying in court can be intimidating.
The London Family Court Clinic has developed a new remote testimony suite that lets young people give evidence from a safe, trauma-informed environment without having to enter a courtroom.

The suite uses CCTV technology to connect children with court proceedings. Joelene Bamford, the clinic's executive director, said the goal is to reduce some of the anxiety associated with the justice system.
"They don't have to go to the courthouse, they don't have to go into courtrooms," Bamford said. "They're able to provide that testimony from a safe place that's trauma-informed."
Bamford said research shows children can provide better evidence when they feel safer and less stressed.
"The literature certainly shows that when children feel safer, they're better able to speak in their own words," she said. "They're better able to provide a full and candid account of the evidence."

reviewed by the Department of Justice Canada has found that testimonial aids such as closed-circuit television can reduce stress for child witnesses, while studies have found children's accuracy is either improved or not significantly different compared with in-person testimony.
The clinic is also home to Beacon House, its Child and Youth Advocacy Centre, where young people can meet with police in a child-friendly environment.
Bamford said having a space away from a police station or courthouse can reduce stress and retraumatization.
"That safety reduces the amount of stress, reduces the amount of retraumatization," she said.
The clinic also has a specially trained facility dog, NSD Virgil, who can accompany children during court preparation, attend court with them and be present when they meet with police.
"He's definitely the star of the show," Bamford said.

The clinic also supports young people who are navigating the youth justice system themselves, including through counselling and assessments. Bamford said the court system can be overwhelming regardless of a young person's role.
"The court system can be extremely intimidating whether you're a victim, whether you're a witness, or whether you're an accused person," she said.
The London Family Court Clinic is a non-profit that has been serving children, youth and families involved in the justice system for more than 50 years.
The clinic is holding its second annual fundraiser,
Stronger Together: LFCC at the Met , on Wednesday, Nov. 25, at Metropolitan United Church, from 7 to 9 p.m.
Organizers say proceeds will directly support the clinic's clinical services for children and youth.

stories.title: Memorial ride planned for motorcyclist killed in city's northwest end
stories.summary: Memorial ride planned for motorcyclist killed in city's northwest end CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: October 2, 2026 8:19 PM | Last Updated: October 2
A London motorcycle club will hold a group ride Saturday in honour of one of their members killed in a collision in late September.
Steven Steinsland, 36, died Sept. 21 when his motorcycle and another vehicle collided at the intersection of
Sarnia Road and Castlegrove Boulevard in northwest London.
Steinsland was a member of

London Free Riders group. On Saturday about a hundred riders are expected to gather at noon at the Tim Hortons on Admiral Drive at Veterans Memorial Parkway. From there they will ride together to a memorial set up in
Steinsland's honour at Sarnia and Castlegrove.
His mother Kim Davies told CBC News Steinsland's death has been a huge blow to the wide group of people who knew him.
"He was larger than life, helped everybody, loved his friends and his family," she said. "It's overwhelming how many people knew him and loved him."
His father Mark Steinsland said Steven had an extended group of friends, including many who worked with him at Labatt brewery.
"It's an amazing group of people, they liked to have fun and help people," he said.

Davies said Steven "would be blown away" by the idea of a group ride. Riders are asked to gather in the Tim Hortons parking lot starting at noon with kickstands up at 1 p.m. The ride will be pushed to Sunday in the event of rain.
According to a memorial notice posted online , a celebration of life for Steve will be held at a later date.

| CBC News | Posted: October 2, 2026 8:19 PM | Last Updated: October 2

A London motorcycle club will hold a group ride Saturday in honour of one of their members killed in a collision in late September.

Steven Steinsland, 36, died Sept. 21 when his motorcycle and another vehicle collided at the intersection of

Sarnia Road and Castlegrove Boulevard in northwest London.

Steinsland was a member of

London Free Riders group. On Saturday about a hundred riders are expected to gather at noon at the Tim Hortons on Admiral Drive at Veterans Memorial Parkway. From there they will ride together to a memorial set up in

Steinsland's honour at Sarnia and Castlegrove.

His mother Kim Davies told CBC News Steinsland's death has been a huge blow to the wide group of people who knew him.

"He was larger than life, helped everybody, loved his friends and his family," she said. "It's overwhelming how many people knew him and loved him."

His father Mark Steinsland said Steven had an extended group of friends, including many who worked with him at Labatt brewery.

"It's an amazing group of people, they liked to have fun and help people," he said.

Davies said Steven "would be blown away" by the idea of a group ride. Riders are asked to gather in the Tim Hortons parking lot starting at noon with kickstands up at 1 p.m. The ride will be pushed to Sunday in the event of rain.

According to a memorial notice posted online , a celebration of life for Steve will be held at a later date.

stories.title: Canada Rocket Company breaks ground at $30M test facility in London, Ont.
stories.summary: Canada Rocket Company breaks ground at $30M test facility in London, Ont. CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: October 1, 2026 9:20 PM | Last Updated: October 1
Canada Rocket Company is building its new Jeremy Hansen Test Facility near the London airport
London, Ont., will be home to Canada's first large-scale rocket engine test facility as the country looks towards establishing Canadian launch capabilities.

On Thursday, Canada Rocket Company (CRC), founded in 2025, officially broke ground at the project site east of London International Airport, where the $30 million Jeremy Hansen Test Facility — named after the Canadian astronaut from London — is expected to be fully operational by 2028.

As part of Canada's 2026 Defence Industrial Strategy, space, including domestic launch capabilities, was identified as a high-value sector, and CRC's co-founder Hugh Kolias said that was the "trigger point" to start the company.
"Without that signaling from the federal government, none of this would have been possible," he said. "It's a key reason why we're standing here today"

With the help of $8.3 million in funding from the Department of National Defence, CRC will be using its new London facility to help develop and test a reusable, medium lift rocket that can carry up to 12,500 kilograms into orbit powered by its own methalox engine, the E-1.

The London facility, built on land leased from the Greater London Airport Authority on Nissouri Road, will not be used to launch rockets. The engine testing will be static, with up to three vertical and horizontal test stands capable of holding engines with more than one meganewton in thrust — a level of force similar to the Merlin 1D engines used on SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets.
The site will include a 12,000 square-foot office and shop building, housing a fabrication area for engineering, assembly and test preparation.

In total, CRC is expected to create about 40 full-time jobs in London, including engineers, technicians and co-ops, according to Kolias, and will help support CRC's broader rocket program, which the company projects will create
1,000 jobs across the country and more than $1 billion in new investment over the next decade.
The rocket testing facility is a "catalyst" according to London Mayor Josh Morgan, that builds on the vision of London as a bold and innovative partner in the future of the country.

"We are here to be a part of this," he said. "We're here to create jobs in our city, we're here to create innovation, and we're here to be part of Canada's future, especially as we move toward our own space independence and independent launch capacity"
"This is a very exciting day for London, Ontario and Canada."

Speaking to CRC's decision to make London the home of its new facility, Kolias pointed to the city's manufacturing history, talent and ambition, with more than 40 defence and aerospace companies already operating in the area.
A rocket test site is something that has never existed in Canada, he said, and many communities would turn down the opportunity because it "just seems a little too difficult."
Kolias said it was clear the London community was on board from CRC's first interaction with the city.

"Everyone was so excited at the opportunity and everyone really understood how important it was, not just for the community from an economic development perspective, but also for the country," he said.

stories.title: Ed Seaward's London Gothic turns familiar city landmarks into a dark mystery
stories.summary: London-born author Ed Seaward has turned his hometown and surrounding area into the setting for London Gothic, a dark mystery about a teenage girl trying to uncover the truth about her mother's disappearance. The novel moves between the 1970s and 1984, exploring family secrets, violence, abuse and incest against a backdrop of familiar London locations.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London-born author Ed Seaward has turned his hometown and surrounding area into the setting for London Gothic, a dark mystery about a teenage girl trying to uncover the truth about her mother's disappearance. The novel moves between the 1970s and 1984, exploring family secrets, violence, abuse and incest against a backdrop of familiar London locations.
· Posted: Oct 04, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 40 minutes ago
A London-born author is putting his hometown at the centre of a dark new gothic novel.

Ed Seaward’s London Gothic was released Friday and follows 17-year-old Bethany Caine, who has escaped her abusive father. Bethany's mother disappeared nine years earlier, and she begins pressing her older brother to reveal what really happened.

Seaward, who grew up in London and now lives in Georgetown, Ont., also wrote the 2020 novel Fair, which won a Silver Medal in Urban Fiction at the 2021 Independent Book Awards. London Gothic is published by DarkWinter Press.
The story moves between the 1970s and 1980s, gradually revealing the secrets surrounding the Caine family.
Seaward said the idea for the novel began with an image that came to him while he was out for a walk.
“This image of a father and son bearing a body popped into my head, as it will when you're out for a walk and you're a writer. I started to play with that and follow it through.”

Seaward said the concept of Southern Ontario Gothic, a literary tradition associated with dark themes and unsettling stories set in familiar Ontario communities, appealed to him because of his connection to London.
“That was coined by the late novelist Timothy Findley. When I came across that, I thought, ‘I like that idea,’ having been born and raised in London, Ontario.”
London Gothic by Ed Seaward was released on Oct. 2, 2026. (DarkWinter Press)
While the story is fictional, Seaward said the London setting is not.
“For people who read the book, all of the settings are real places," he said. "The story is fictionalized. Neither my father nor I buried a body."
"But all of the places are London, and my own experience growing up, like anyone's, you observe some darker things. So you pull on some of that, and then fictionalize it.”

That includes Victoria Park, which plays a role in the story. Seaward says using recognizable London locations also allowed him to play with the gothic tradition, which has roots in Victorian England.
“I had a lot of fun playing with some of these familiar tropes and things that are unfamiliar to some people, and teasing all that out.”
At the centre of the story is Bethany's search for answers about her mother. Her father and brother maintain that the woman abandoned the family, but Bethany isn't convinced.
Seaward said the novel's alternating timelines help readers understand how the family's secrets developed.
The novel explores violence, abuse and other disturbing family secrets. But Seaward said the Gothic elements ultimately explore what can haunt people long after events have happened.
“It's a story about the monsters in our life who are the real people in our life, and it's about the ghosts that are the memories that haunt us.”
Seaward will celebrate the release of London Gothic with a special book launch on Sunday, Oct. 4, from 4:30 to 6 p.m. at The Space, 23 Heather Cres.

stories.title: Here's what prompted London students to cast their municipal election ballots early
stories.summary: Advance polls continue until Oct. 10
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Advance polls continue until Oct. 10
Young Londoners had the chance to make their voices heard during the first day of advance voting for the 2026 municipal election.
Polls were open at both Western University and Fanshawe College's campuses on Oct. 1, allowing students to vote for candidates in both London and their home cities.
"It's just easier when it's here to get it over and done with," said Western student Alistair Sullivan, who cast his vote at the University Community Centre on Thursday.

Western's University Students Council (USC) ramped up to advance voting day with a "Get Out the Vote" campaign, which included meet and greets with candidates, election-based trivia games and social media posts about voting.
Media Video |
"Students work, study and contribute to London," said Stephen Titizian, the USC's vice president of external affairs, who helped organize the campaign.
"The city and city hall affects them, so it's important to have their voices heard," he added
Titizian estimates that about 100 politically engaged students attended a Pints and Politics event on campus, where more than 40 mayoral and ward candidates networked with the community.
However, he said a wider range of students have engaged with the USC's trivia games and giveaways on campus, including some who did not know about the election beforehand.

"We're spending a lot of time informing students on when and where to vote, and the eligibility requirements," Titizian said. "Those are the things that are really stressing students out or maybe stopping them from actually hitting the polling stations."
During early voting, Londoners can vote at any advance voting location that's open on the date they choose, regardless of which ward they live in.
People can bring their voter notification card if they received one.
Otherwise, they will need acceptable identification showing their name and London address, which can include student residence.
Advance voting continues until Oct. 10.
Voting Day is Monday, Oct. 26, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.
Some students said they plan to wait until election day to cast their votes.
"I want to wait a little bit longer because I'm not too familiar with all the candidates," Huron University College student Nicholas Yetming said.
"It's definitely great for us [students] to familiarize ourselves with all the candidates and their policies, rather than just voting based on a part or a name you've heard before," he added.
Medical sciences students Tatyana Wong and Renee Ramcharan said they hadn't engaged in the election until seeing the USC's campaign.
"We were just getting coffee and were like 'Wow, look at this stuff,' and now we're drawn in," Wong said.
"I wasn't [planning to vote] before, but I'm definitely considering now," she added.
Titizian said he wants students who did not vote early to use the next three weeks to research candidates and ensure they understand how to vote on election day.
"This is your home for the next four years .... and you deserve to have a voice in your home," he said.
Western sociology student John Heras cast his ballot during early voting on campus, saying he voted for a mayoral candidate who he believes will tackle his top election issue.

"One of the big things was sanitary stuff, especially the garbage pickup," Heras said. "That was something I really thought was important because if you walk down Richmond, there's always garbage all over the street."
Other Western students told CBC News their top election issues include public transit, construction, housing costs and community safety.

"Every single year, there's a whole rush of students who come in for the school year and I think it's really important they feel safe walking around the downtown London area," Wong said, adding that she sometimes feels unsafe walking downtown.
"I don't feel the most protected. It's not the most welcoming environment."
Sullivan said his early vote went to a mayoral candidate who made promises about improving the downtown core for businesses.

"I've lived in London my whole life and when I go downtown, I just see it slowly decline. It's filled with more homeless people and vacant lots," he said. "I like the stuff that [the candidate] is doing about hopefully bringing more business and people back downtown."

stories.content:
Advance polls continue until Oct. 10

Young Londoners had the chance to make their voices heard during the first day of advance voting for the 2026 municipal election.

Polls were open at both Western University and Fanshawe College's campuses on Oct. 1, allowing students to vote for candidates in both London and their home cities.

"It's just easier when it's here to get it over and done with," said Western student Alistair Sullivan, who cast his vote at the University Community Centre on Thursday.

Western's University Students Council (USC) ramped up to advance voting day with a "Get Out the Vote" campaign, which included meet and greets with candidates, election-based trivia games and social media posts about voting.

Media Video |

"Students work, study and contribute to London," said Stephen Titizian, the USC's vice president of external affairs, who helped organize the campaign.

"The city and city hall affects them, so it's important to have their voices heard," he added

Titizian estimates that about 100 politically engaged students attended a Pints and Politics event on campus, where more than 40 mayoral and ward candidates networked with the community.

However, he said a wider range of students have engaged with the USC's trivia games and giveaways on campus, including some who did not know about the election beforehand.

"We're spending a lot of time informing students on when and where to vote, and the eligibility requirements," Titizian said. "Those are the things that are really stressing students out or maybe stopping them from actually hitting the polling stations."

During early voting, Londoners can vote at any advance voting location that's open on the date they choose, regardless of which ward they live in.

People can bring their voter notification card if they received one.

Otherwise, they will need acceptable identification showing their name and London address, which can include student residence.

Advance voting continues until Oct. 10.

Voting Day is Monday, Oct. 26, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Some students said they plan to wait until election day to cast their votes.

"I want to wait a little bit longer because I'm not too familiar with all the candidates," Huron University College student Nicholas Yetming said.

"It's definitely great for us [students] to familiarize ourselves with all the candidates and their policies, rather than just voting based on a part or a name you've heard before," he added.

Medical sciences students Tatyana Wong and Renee Ramcharan said they hadn't engaged in the election until seeing the USC's campaign.

"We were just getting coffee and were like 'Wow, look at this stuff,' and now we're drawn in," Wong said.

"I wasn't [planning to vote] before, but I'm definitely considering now," she added.

Titizian said he wants students who did not vote early to use the next three weeks to research candidates and ensure they understand how to vote on election day.

"This is your home for the next four years .... and you deserve to have a voice in your home," he said.

Western sociology student John Heras cast his ballot during early voting on campus, saying he voted for a mayoral candidate who he believes will tackle his top election issue.

"One of the big things was sanitary stuff, especially the garbage pickup," Heras said. "That was something I really thought was important because if you walk down Richmond, there's always garbage all over the street."

Other Western students told CBC News their top election issues include public transit, construction, housing costs and community safety.

"Every single year, there's a whole rush of students who come in for the school year and I think it's really important they feel safe walking around the downtown London area," Wong said, adding that she sometimes feels unsafe walking downtown.

"I don't feel the most protected. It's not the most welcoming environment."

Sullivan said his early vote went to a mayoral candidate who made promises about improving the downtown core for businesses.

"I've lived in London my whole life and when I go downtown, I just see it slowly decline. It's filled with more homeless people and vacant lots," he said. "I like the stuff that [the candidate] is doing about hopefully bringing more business and people back downtown."

stories.title: London Police officer charged with assault for pepper spray use during arrest
stories.summary: A London police officer has been charged with assault and placed on administrative duties following a use-of-force investigation involving the officer's use of pepper spray during an arrest.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London·Breaking
A London police officer has been charged with assault and placed on administrative duties following a use-of-force investigation involving the officer's use of pepper spray during an arrest.
· Posted: Oct 02, 2026 8:46 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
London Police Const. Brandon Mihalides has been charged with one count of assault with a weapon and has been reassigned to non-operational administrative duties.(London Police Service)
A London police officer has been charged with assault and placed on administrative duties following a use-of-force investigation involving the use of pepper spray during an arrest.
Const. Brandon Mihalides, 29, of London has been charged with one count of assault with a weapon and reassigned to what police say are "non-operational administrative duties."
The charges stem from an incident at 2 a.m. on April 29 of this year when a 33-year-old woman was placed under arrest by London police officers.
Following her arrest, oleoresin capsicum spray, also known as pepper spray, was deployed.
A police news release says the use of pepper spray in Ontario is subject to mandatory use-of-force reporting requirements and a review process.
"During that review, concerns were identified regarding the circumstances surrounding the use of force," said a police news release.
The incident was referred to London police's major crimes section "to investigate possible criminal conduct arising from the use of the OC spray. "
Police say they won't be releasing any more information as the charges are now before the courts.
Const. Mihalides is scheduled to be in court on Dec. 30.

stories.title: London man dies after Old East Village stabbing, suspect charged with second-degree murder
stories.summary: The 34-year-old man stabbed at Dundas and Adelaide streets on Monday has died, with police announcing a second-degree murder charge in connection with his death.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London·Breaking
The 34-year-old man stabbed at Dundas and Adelaide streets on Monday has died, with police announcing a second-degree murder charge in connection with his death.
· Posted: Oct 01, 2026 4:08 PM EDT | Last Updated: 40 minutes ago
The 34-year-old man stabbed in London's Old East Village on Monday has died, police say.
Police were called to the area of Dundas Street and Adelaide Street at about 6:15 p.m. Monday after reports of a stabbing.
Officers found a man suffering from life-threatening injuries. He was taken to hospital by paramedics.
Charles Alexander Raymond George died in hospital after suffering life-threatening injuries in the stabbing, according to London police.

Police say members of the London Police Service's Major Crime Section identified the suspect, who was arrested Wednesday night in the downtown core by members of the Patrol Operations Investigative Branch.
A 26-year-old London man has been charged with second-degree murder and failing to comply with a release order in connection with George's death.
Police say the accused and George knew each other.
The accused remains in custody and is scheduled to appear in a London court Thursday.
George's death is the sixth homicide in London this year, and fourth in the last month.

On Jan 12, police responded to a multiple calls about a stabbing in the 700-block of Dundas Street. They found an unresponsive man in the hallway of an apartment building. Brandon Christopher Jamieson Nichols, 45, was identified as the man who died. Robert Mitchell Cornelius, 38 , was charged with second degree murder.

On Jan. 25, police were called to the same block of Dundas Street after reports of multiple gunshots. They found two men and took both to hospital. One of the men found, Ramone Thomas, 26, of Toronto, died of his injuries. Londoner Matthew Yousufy, 26, was charged with second-degree murder and a number of drug and firearm offences.

On Aug. 22, an elderly woman was woken up by a loud noise and found a man in her home on Raywood Avenue, near Wellington and Baseline roads. The 73-year-old was assaulted and stabbed and died of her injuries days later. Property records show the home was owned by Lillian Anne Leonard. Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, was charged with second degree murder.
On Sep. 15, a woman was killed, allegedly by her intimate partner in what police call an instance of femicide. Police have charged Mandeep Singh, 41, of London, with second-degree murder.

On Sep. 29, Just one day after the fatal stabbing, a man was shot and killed in downtown London. Mohamed Abdel Aziz Soumahoro, 21, of Laval, Que., has been charged with second-degree murder, among other offences.
Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area of Dundas and Adelaide around the time of the stabbing, or who had dashcam or surveillance video, to contact police.
Anyone with information about the incident is asked to contact London police at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477.

stories.title: Cornell's alleged frat house gang-rape case 'eerily similar' to Hockey Canada trial, says advocate
stories.summary: The head of a London, Ont., support centre for survivors of sexual assault says they see parallels between last year's Hockey Canada trial and a recently filed civil lawsuit alleging gang-rape at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: The head of a London, Ont., support centre for survivors of sexual assault says they see parallels between last year's Hockey Canada trial and a recently filed civil lawsuit alleging gang-rape at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y.
· Posted: Oct 01, 2026 1:06 PM EDT | Last Updated: 23 minutes ago
Jessie Rodger is executive director of Anova. The organization helps people impacted by gender-based violence in the London area.(CBC News)

The victim, known in court documents as Jane Doe, alleges the private Ivy League university protected the seven men, now dubbed "the Cornell 7," after she came forward saying they drugged and assaulted her over several hours at a frat house in October 2024.
The case has spurred boycotts, with alumni threatening to pull funding and celebrities speaking out.

"It's eerily similar to the Hockey Canada case, which was also reopened after a civil lawsuit was opened by the victim in that case," said Jessie Rodger, executive director of Anova. "So there's a sense of frustration of this playing out over again."
What to know about Cornell's alleged frat house gang-rape case and the 'Cornell 7'
Hockey Canada suspensions remain for four players on 2018 junior team
Five players from Canada's 2018 world junior team were acquitted last year in a London courtroom on sexual assault charges stemming from an encounter with a woman known as "E.M."
'Cornell 7' lawsuit: What we know
September 29|

Alumni are threatening to pull funding, celebrities are lashing out and people are boycotting institutions associated with Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., after an alleged gang rape ignited the internet. The case came into the spotlight after the victim, known in court documents as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16, alleging the private Ivy League university protected the seven men, now dubbed 'the Cornell 7.' She alleges they drugged and assaulted her over several hours at a frat house in October 2024. WARNING: This video may affect those who have experienced sexual violence or know someone affected by it. It also contains vulgar language.

She first came forward to London police in 2018 claiming the men sexually assaulted her at the London Armouries Hotel following a Hockey Canada gala, where the players were honoured for their victory at the world junior hockey championship.

The initial police investigation ended without charges in 2019. It was reopened in 2022 by then police Chief Steve Williams, in response to public outrage following a lawsuit that Hockey Canada settled for $3.5 million.

Michael McLeod, Dillon Dube, Cal Foote, Alex Formenton and Carter Hart were all later charged in 2024. At the time, current police Chief Thai Truong apologized that it took six years to lay out the charges.

"It's the same way that the Hockey Canada case came to fruition," Rodger said of the Cornell case. "It doesn't seem to matter what country you live in. We are all ill equipped to deal with sexual violence in the current system we have."
A timeline of the Hockey Canada sexual assault trial and key moments

Doe's lawsuit, filed in New York Supreme Court, alleges her assault happened on campus at a fraternity house, and that one of the frat brothers sent a Snapchat message inviting other members to join them for "free pussy."

It further says the accused only faced temporary suspensions and "were afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays" to the university - an allegation Cornell denies. None of the fraternity members have been criminally charged.

"It really appears to be terrible police work was done in this case," said Rodger. "I think it just reinforces the message that we try to share with survivors and victims of sexual assault that if you choose to go see the police and talk to them about your assault, you need to talk to a lawyer first."
LISTEN | London women’s advocate weighs in on the Cornell 7 case:
London Morning 8:15 London women’s advocate weighs in on the Cornell 7 case

As the Cornell 7 story unfolds, many are drawing links to the Hockey Canada case from London. CBC London Morning asked Anova executive director Jessie Rodger for their reaction to the unfolding of the case.
The unfolding Cornell case will likely retraumatize people who have had their own experiences of sexual violence as it unfolds, said Rodger.
They said they hope the case opens up a conversation about what needs to change in the legal system to bring more justice to survivors.
"I'm going to be watching to see if any lessons have been learned from the previous Hockey Canada experience," they said. "I don't know if I have much hope, but I am thinking about that."

stories.title: Cyclist dies after being struck by vehicle in Thames Centre
stories.summary: A 34-year-old Thames Centre resident has died after being struck by a vehicle on Richmond Street, east of London, provincial police say.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: A 34-year-old Thames Centre resident has died after being struck by a vehicle on Richmond Street, east of London, provincial police say.
· Posted: Oct 01, 2026 7:18 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) in Middlesex County say a cyclist has died after being hit by a vehicle in Thames Centre.(Ontario Provincial Police)
A 34-year-old cyclist has died after being struck by a vehicle in Thames Centre, east of London, according to provincial police.
Emergency crews were called to Richmond Street, between Gore Road and Marion Street, at about 12:22 p.m. Wednesday.
The cyclist, a Thames Centre resident, was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries and later died, police said.
The driver of the vehicle was not injured.
Middlesex County OPP Const. Jeff Hare said in a video posted to social media that police, paramedics and Thames Centre firefighters responded to the crash.
“Our thoughts go out to the families and everybody else involved in today's events,” Hare said.
Richmond Street in the area was closed while emergency crews responded but has since reopened.
Police are asking anyone who witnessed the crash or has information about what happened to contact Middlesex County OPP.

stories.title: Advance voting opens in London: Here's when and where you can vote
stories.summary: Advance voting for London's 2026 municipal election begins Thursday, giving voters several opportunities to cast their ballots before election day.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Advance voting for London's 2026 municipal election begins Thursday, giving voters several opportunities to cast their ballots before election day.
· Posted: Oct 01, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 41 minutes ago
Advance voting begins in London, Ont., on Thursday, Oct. 1.(Paula Duhatschek)
Advance voting for London's municipal election begins Thursday, giving voters several opportunities to cast their ballots before Voting Day on Oct. 26.
There are advance voting locations across the city between Oct. 1 and Oct. 10, with all locations open from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.
Unlike on Voting Day, Londoners can vote at any advance voting location that's open on the date they choose, regardless of which ward they live in.
Here are the dates and locations:
Two locations will be open:
Fanshawe College, Alumni Lounge (SC2013), 1001 Fanshawe College Blvd.
Western University, UCC 269C, 1151 Richmond St.
These seven locations will be open:
Beacock Library, 1280 Huron St.
Cherryhill Library, 301 Oxford St. W.
East Lions Community Centre, 1731 Churchill Ave.
Masonville Library, 30 North Centre Rd.
Sherwood Library, 1225 Wonderland Rd. N.
South London Community Centre, 1119 Jalna Blvd.
StarTech.com Community Centre, 501 Southdale Rd. W.
City Hall, second floor, Committee Room 5, 300 Dufferin Ave.
City Hall, second floor, Committee Room 5, at 300 Dufferin Ave., will be open for advance voting on:
Saturday, Oct. 3
Monday, Oct. 5, through Saturday, Oct. 10
The city is encouraging voters to check the Voters' List before heading to the polls.
Voters can use the city's online election tool to check or update their information, add themselves to the Voters' List, find their ward and find out where they will vote.
If you are registering online, you'll need identification showing your name, date of birth and London address.
You can also be added to the Voters' List when you go to vote, but checking your information ahead of time can make the process quicker.
Bring your voter notification card if you've received one. The card identifies your assigned Voting Day location.
You can still vote without the card, but you will need acceptable identification showing your name and address.
London's ward boundaries have changed for the 2026 election, so you may now be in a different ward than you were during the last municipal election.
The city has an online ward map where voters can check their ward before voting.
Slide the vertical bar to see changes to ward boundaries for the 2026 election:
Voting Day is Monday, Oct. 26, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Unlike advance voting, voters must go to their assigned voting location on Oct. 26. That location will be listed on their voter notification card or available through the city's online voter information tool.

stories.title: 5 candidates are running in London's Ward 5. here's what they say they're focused on
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: October 1, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: October 1
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: October 1, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: October 1
London's Ward 5 has new boundaries stretching from Wonderland Road N. to Adelaide Street N.
With five candidates vying for a seat on London City Council, the race for Ward 5 is largely focused on concerns over affordability and property taxes, public safety and construction.
The candidates are Corrine Rahman, Charles Spina, Abid Raza, Simon Sabeesh Karikkassery and Mary Blake Rose. One councillor will be elected.
Voting Day is October 26, with advanced voting begining on Thursday, Oct. 1.
This will be the first election with Ward 5's new boundaries. It saw significant changes following the 2024 review of ward boundaries, now shifting westward from Wonderland Road to Adelaide Street.
The boundary changes also mean current Ward 7 Coun. Corrine Rahman is running for re-election in Ward 5.
Rahman said the changes have required candidates to explain the new boundaries to residents while door-knocking.

“It's really been candidates in the election that have had to push the message of why the boundaries have changed and inform the residents of the change,” she said. “So that's definitely been part of the script when you're door knocking.”
Rahman said residents she's spoken with are looking for what she described as an "effective" city government.
If elected, she said she would focus on fiscal responsibility, more local police presence and support for vulnerable communities, including addressing upcoming funding pressures for services.
She also wants to see continued investment in infrastructure, including parks, facilities and trail connections, as well as a new community centre in northwest London.
Rahman said her experience on council is an asset.

“I'm able to really point to the fact that I've been a very active member of council,” she said. “I have a record for being somebody that is approachable, somebody that you can reach and talk with and engage with, but also that provides communication and feedback.”
Charles Spina is also looking to show residents that City Hall can work efficiently.

Spina comes from a corporate and consulting background, having held executive-level roles in multiple companies. He also spent 18 years on the Board of Directors at L'Arche and 11 years on the investment committee for the Catholic Diocese of London.
In his consulting work, he said he has gained a strong understanding of the operational workings of municipalities. If elected, he said will oppose any tax increases in the first year.
"I understand our financial statements," he said. "We have resources, we don't need money next year."
"I can tell you right now we probably wouldn't have to cut anything."
His campaign slogan is: "the good, the better, and less." Spina said it refers to appreciating the good things London has to offer, pushing for improvements, and reducing inefficiencies.
Abid Raza has lived in London for 10 years and has a background in logistics and supply chain management, he said.
He believes Londoners are paying too much property tax, while not getting enough services in return.

One issue he wants to tackle is construction, he said, pointing to multiple closures impacting residents in the ward, including projects on Sunningdale Road and one of Fanshawe Park Road, which he believes are impeding both residents and emergency services.
Raza wants to see construction projects completed faster, with crews avoiding work during rush hours and continuing work later into the day.
"Taxpayers are paying for these workers, so we should get it done, " he said.

Simon Sabeesh Karikkassery also indentified construction is a major issue in Ward 5.Karikkassery moved to London from the Greater Toronto Area in 2018 and has a background in supply chain management. He currently works as a personal support worker, he said.
He said construction projects should be planned and scheduled in a way that gets roads reopened more quickly.
"I see only one shift is happening for road construction," he said. "I know it will increase some expenditures, but it has to be two shifts, at least, so that it can be done fast."
Karikkassery also wants to change the city's garbage collection schedule, proposing weekly garbage pickup while collecting recycling every two weeks.

"Those who have small kids and elderly people at home, they're not happy," he said. "So instead of collecting (recycling) every week, you can do it every two weeks and you can collect the garbage every week."
Mary Blake Rose is making the environment front and centre in her campaign.
After moving to London in 2012 to pursue a degree in music, Rose went on to work for the national office of Citizens' Climate Lobby, a non-profit environmental advocacy organization.
"We need to protect things that we can't just rebuild, and I think that the planet is the most flagrant example of that," she said.
She said she wants a city that is "fairer, greener and undaunted."

She said that includes improving transportation, including expanding the network of protected cycling infrastructure. She also sees transportation policy as a way for London to work toward the targets in its Climate Emergency Action Plan.
Rose said she believes London has sometimes taken a cautious approach to major projects.
She pointed to the city's Bus Rapid Transit system as an example, saying she believes it could have been expanded further with additional funding from other levels of government.
Advance voting begins Thursday, with additional advance voting opportunities on Oct. 3 and from Oct. 5 through Oct. 10.
Voting Day is Monday, Oct. 26, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.
Because ward boundaries have changed, voters can use the City of London's online election tool to check which ward they live in and find their assigned Voting Day location.

| CBC News | Posted: October 1, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: October 1

London's Ward 5 has new boundaries stretching from Wonderland Road N. to Adelaide Street N.

With five candidates vying for a seat on London City Council, the race for Ward 5 is largely focused on concerns over affordability and property taxes, public safety and construction.

The candidates are Corrine Rahman, Charles Spina, Abid Raza, Simon Sabeesh Karikkassery and Mary Blake Rose. One councillor will be elected.

Voting Day is October 26, with advanced voting begining on Thursday, Oct. 1.

This will be the first election with Ward 5's new boundaries. It saw significant changes following the 2024 review of ward boundaries, now shifting westward from Wonderland Road to Adelaide Street.

The boundary changes also mean current Ward 7 Coun. Corrine Rahman is running for re-election in Ward 5.

Rahman said the changes have required candidates to explain the new boundaries to residents while door-knocking.

“It's really been candidates in the election that have had to push the message of why the boundaries have changed and inform the residents of the change,” she said. “So that's definitely been part of the script when you're door knocking.”

Rahman said residents she's spoken with are looking for what she described as an "effective" city government.

If elected, she said she would focus on fiscal responsibility, more local police presence and support for vulnerable communities, including addressing upcoming funding pressures for services.

She also wants to see continued investment in infrastructure, including parks, facilities and trail connections, as well as a new community centre in northwest London.

Rahman said her experience on council is an asset.

“I'm able to really point to the fact that I've been a very active member of council,” she said. “I have a record for being somebody that is approachable, somebody that you can reach and talk with and engage with, but also that provides communication and feedback.”

Charles Spina is also looking to show residents that City Hall can work efficiently.

Spina comes from a corporate and consulting background, having held executive-level roles in multiple companies. He also spent 18 years on the Board of Directors at L'Arche and 11 years on the investment committee for the Catholic Diocese of London.

In his consulting work, he said he has gained a strong understanding of the operational workings of municipalities. If elected, he said will oppose any tax increases in the first year.

"I understand our financial statements," he said. "We have resources, we don't need money next year."

"I can tell you right now we probably wouldn't have to cut anything."

His campaign slogan is: "the good, the better, and less." Spina said it refers to appreciating the good things London has to offer, pushing for improvements, and reducing inefficiencies.

Abid Raza has lived in London for 10 years and has a background in logistics and supply chain management, he said.

He believes Londoners are paying too much property tax, while not getting enough services in return.

One issue he wants to tackle is construction, he said, pointing to multiple closures impacting residents in the ward, including projects on Sunningdale Road and one of Fanshawe Park Road, which he believes are impeding both residents and emergency services.

Raza wants to see construction projects completed faster, with crews avoiding work during rush hours and continuing work later into the day.

"Taxpayers are paying for these workers, so we should get it done, " he said.

Simon Sabeesh Karikkassery also indentified construction is a major issue in Ward 5.Karikkassery moved to London from the Greater Toronto Area in 2018 and has a background in supply chain management. He currently works as a personal support worker, he said.

He said construction projects should be planned and scheduled in a way that gets roads reopened more quickly.

"I see only one shift is happening for road construction," he said. "I know it will increase some expenditures, but it has to be two shifts, at least, so that it can be done fast."

Karikkassery also wants to change the city's garbage collection schedule, proposing weekly garbage pickup while collecting recycling every two weeks.

"Those who have small kids and elderly people at home, they're not happy," he said. "So instead of collecting (recycling) every week, you can do it every two weeks and you can collect the garbage every week."

Mary Blake Rose is making the environment front and centre in her campaign.

After moving to London in 2012 to pursue a degree in music, Rose went on to work for the national office of Citizens' Climate Lobby, a non-profit environmental advocacy organization.

"We need to protect things that we can't just rebuild, and I think that the planet is the most flagrant example of that," she said.

She said she wants a city that is "fairer, greener and undaunted."

She said that includes improving transportation, including expanding the network of protected cycling infrastructure. She also sees transportation policy as a way for London to work toward the targets in its Climate Emergency Action Plan.

Rose said she believes London has sometimes taken a cautious approach to major projects.

She pointed to the city's Bus Rapid Transit system as an example, saying she believes it could have been expanded further with additional funding from other levels of government.

Advance voting begins Thursday, with additional advance voting opportunities on Oct. 3 and from Oct. 5 through Oct. 10.

Voting Day is Monday, Oct. 26, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

stories.title: Margaret Atwood donates $1M to Western for migratory bird research
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: October 1, 2026 1:31 AM | Last Updated: October 1
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: October 1, 2026 1:31 AM | Last Updated: October 1
Gift will create a research chair in honour of Atwood's late partner, author Graeme Gibson
Canadian literary icon Margaret Atwood has donated $1 million to Western University to support research into migratory birds.
The gift will create the Graeme Gibson Chair for Avian Biology, named after Atwood's late partner, who shared her passion for birds and co-founded the Pelee Island Bird Observatory.
Gibson, who died in 2019, also wrote The Bedside Book of Birds, which was published in 2005.
Speaking on The Current in 2021, Atwood recalled how Gibson was a "late-life convert" to bird watching.

"He had one of those light bulb experiences in one of the Don Valley ravines when he saw a large bird, and he didn't know what it was," she said. "So he found out it was a red-tailed hawk, and from that moment on, he was a bird-er, as we say."
The new chair will support research into how birds move, behave and adapt to changes in their environment, according to Western.

Chris Guglielmo, a biology professor and director of Western's Centre for Animals on the Move, said he was asked to sit down before being told about the donation during an emotional phone call this summer.
e're very, very excited and grateful for this gift," he said.
o get a gift like this is just such a boost for all of us. It tells us we're on the right track, and great people are interested in what we're doing."
Guglielmo said there are numerous unanswered questions about migratory birds and he's excited about what the new chair could bring to the university.

Western is already a leader in avian migration studies, housing not only the Centre for Animals on the Move, but also the Advanced Facility for Avian Research, which houses the world’s only hypobaric climatic wind tunnel designed for bird flight.
The faculty also had a longstanding connection to Atwood and Gibson throug h the Pelee Island Bird Observatory on Lake Erie, which the couple founded in 2003.
Southwestern Ontario is a major hub for migratory birds, according to Guglielmo, adding that the huge boreal forests to the north are "the nursery for hundreds of millions of birds."

When it's time to move, he said they tend to avoid the Great Lakes. and the birds are then funneled through the relatively small area of land and tend to especially pile up along the coasts of Lake Ontario and Lake Erie.
laces like Point Pelee, Pelee Island, Long Point, and Rondeau Park become havens for these birds, and people come from all over the world to birdwatch," he said.
Guglielmo said he does a lot of his own research around Long Point during the peak of migration, adding that it's "an amazing thing to witness."
t's like walking through this jeweled forest in the spring where the woods can be so full of these small warblers that are all different colors," he said.
"They can be down near eye level, so you're walking along, and it's just everywhere you look, it's a different species."

stories.title: Man banned from future London Comic Cons after vendor reports unwanted behaviour
stories.summary: A man was removed from London Comic Con last weekend after event staff received reports that he was allegedly acting inappropriately toward a woman. The organizer says he is now banned from future events, while London police say they have not received a report about the incident.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: A man was removed from London Comic Con last weekend after event staff received reports that he was allegedly acting inappropriately toward a woman. The organizer says he is now banned from future events, while London police say they have not received a report about the incident.
· Posted: Sep 30, 2026 8:17 PM EDT | Last Updated: 4 hours ago
A man has been banned from future London Comic Con events after staff received reports that he was allegedly acting inappropriately toward a woman at the event.
The organizer confirmed the attendee was asked to leave the event, which took place at the Western Fair District J-AAR Expo Centre on Sept. 26 and 27.

“Following a review of the circumstances, London Comic Con has determined that the individual will not be permitted to attend future London Comic Con events,” the organizer said in an email to CBC News.
“This decision is consistent with the event’s policies and is intended to help maintain a safe, respectful, and comfortable environment for attendees, guests, exhibitors, and cosplayers.”
The man allegedly tried to look up a cosplayer's skirt and ignored requests to stop their behaviour.
Neither event security nor the organizer contacted police about the incident.
London police said Tuesday they had not received a report related to the alleged incident.

“Under section 162 of the Criminal Code of Canada, it is an offence to secretly observe or record a person in circumstances where they have a reasonable expectation of privacy, including situations involving nudity, sexual activity, or where the observation or recording is made for a sexual purpose,” according to a statement from London police.
Police are encouraging anyone who May have been affected, witnessed the alleged behaviour or has information about the incident to contact them.
Jennifer Dunn, executive director at the London Abused Women's Centre, said people should be able to attend public events without having to worry about this type of behaviour.
“Safety is not just the absence of physical violence,” Dunn said. “Women have to be able to go to an event, or anywhere we want to go without having to worry about somebody else's behaviour.”
She was told 'upskirting' was not a crime in England and Wales — so she made it one
Dunn said preventing violence against women requires education and action from the broader community.
“There are a lot of people that definitely think that this is a woman's issue when really we need men standing up and saying this is not how we treat people,” she said.
Anyone who needs support can contact the London Abused Women's Centre at 519-432-2204.
Anyone with information about the alleged incident can contact the London Police Service at 519-661-5670 or submit an anonymous tip through Crime Stoppers.
A previous version of this story included alleged upskirt photos. A witness later told CBC News they could not confirm if the man was also taking photos.

stories.summary: London police say one man is dead and another in custody after a shooting in the area of Central Avenue and Richmond Street Tuesday afternoon.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London police say one man is dead and another in custody after a shooting in the area of Central Avenue and Richmond Street Tuesday afternoon.
· Posted: Sep 30, 2026 7:13 AM EDT | Last Updated: 11 hours ago
London police say one man is dead and another is in custody after a shooting in the area of Central Avenue and Richmond Street Tuesday afternoon.

stories.title: Council committee votes down proposal for 2 towers at Wellington and High street
stories.summary: Council's planning committee has voted down a proposal to build two large apartment towers on Wellington Road just south of the Thames River following concerns flagged by city staff and neighbours.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Council's planning committee has voted down a proposal to build two large apartment towers on Wellington Road just south of the Thames River following concerns flagged by city staff and neighbours.
· Posted: Sep 29, 2026 4:58 PM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
A rendering of two apartment towers proposed for 60-68 High St. and 57-75 Wellington Rd. in London.(Goodplace Design)
Ascity staff and neighbours flag concerns, council's planning committee has voted down a proposal to build two large apartment towers on Wellington Road just south of the Thames River.

An investment group called Foundation Development Fund submitted planning applications for properties at 60-68 High St. and 57-75 Wellington Rd. Together, the projects would include 1,000 apartments beside the city's rapid transit corridor currently under construction.
The High Street proposal included a 32-storey apartment building with 540 units, while the Wellington Road building proposal included a 22-storey high building with 440 units.
2-tower proposal would bring more than 1,000 apartments to London's Wellington Gateway

City staff recommended both proposals be refused, saying it would result in over-intensification of the site and would require setback amendments that would crowd the Wellington Road corridor. Staff also flagged concerns about the request to reduce required bicycle storage.

The building plans also had no underground parking, which is allowed in proposals along transit corridors. However, some neighbours who spoke at Tuesday's meeting expressed concern that parking and traffic from the two large buildings would spillover into the neighbourhood.
"We feel that the proposed towers are stark and out-of-character with the surrounding Old South neighbourhood," said Old South resident Patrick Clancy.
Renee Borg, who lives on nearby Grand Avenue, called the two towers "Lego-like developments."
"It is the design and size and height of these buildings that everybody is against," she said.

Michael Nemanic, representing the developer of the Wellington Road proposal, said the building will deliver much-needed affordable housing — with some of the units set at 80 per cent average market rent. Nemanic said rents in 98 of the units across both properties would be $850 for a studio unit and $1,100 for a one-bedroom unit.

Nemanic said the building's design elements — including the elimination of some balconies, the lack of underground parking and planned use of concrete poured off-site — are all aimed at keeping the building cost and rents low.
"We don't expect many of our tenants will own vehicles," said Nemanic. "That's not our target market."

Renderings submitted by the developer show the two tower proposals from High Street. Planning committee voted to follow a city staff recommendation that the proposed towers be voted down. (Foundation Development Fund)

Coun. Skylar Franke, who represents the area, said there was a strong community response against the proposal. She said most were not opposed to added density, but instead want something that's a better fit with the area.

"They accept there will be infill here, they understand it will probably be substantial, but they want something that adds to the neighbourhood and not feel like it's taking away from it," she said. "We're talking about two very large towers on a very constrained site."
The staff recommendation against both buildings was voted down by a 3-0 vote. It will next go to the Oct. 14 council meeting for consideration.

stories.title: London mom questions school response after children injured in violent altercation
stories.summary: CBC News | Posted: September 29, 2026 8:28 PM | Last Updated: September 29
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: A London, Ont., mom says she and her children were let down by school officials after a schoolyard fight, she says, resulted in both of her children being hurt and her son suffering a concussion.
· Posted: Sep 29, 2026 4:28 PM EDT | Last Updated: September 29
London police and the Thames Valley District School Board are investigating after a video of a fight at CC Carrothers Public School was shared on social media on Sept. 24.(Google Maps)

A London, Ont., mother says she and her children were let down by school officials after a schoolyard fight she says left both children injured, including her son, who was diagnosed with a concussion.
Samantha Riley shared a video of a fight involving her daughter and son at C.C. Carrothers Public School in southeast London that happened on Sept. 24.
Riley said both children were struck multiple times while on the ground and were later suspended for one day.

"My kids should be able to feel safe going to school. Any child should. It's not even my own," said Riley. "I'm speaking for all these kids that get bullied at this point now, because that's not fair to those kids. "
The video reviewed by CBC News shows Riley’s daughter being held by another student while the two exchange punches. Riley’s son then appears to intervene.
A separate video posted to social media shows Riley’s daughter sitting on the ground surrounded by several students. One student appears to stomp on her leg while another kicks her.

The video also shows a student bringing Riley’s son to the ground and punching him before dragging him toward a nearby wall. The student is then seen punching the boy several times and kicking him in the face.
Riley said she was appalled by what she saw.
"It feels like the teachers just stood there and did nothing about it," she said. "I'm upset. I'm sad that this happened."
Following the incident and a visit to the hospital, Riley's son was diagnosed with a mild concussion.
LISTEN | Concerns around violence in Ontario schools :
Ontario Morning 8:23 Concerns around violence in Ontario schools

While starting a new school year brings excitement, it can also bring considerable stress. Data from the Ontario Secondary School Teachers' Federation reveals a sharp surge in school violence across Ontario, with reported incidents climbing 77% between 2018 and 2025. Simcoe County school trustee Mike Foley is bringing his concerns directly to Premier Doug Ford and the Ministry of Education. He joins us to discuss why he felt compelled to take urgent action and shares the outcomes of these discussions.
London police told CBC News they are aware of the altercation and have been investigating since Sept. 24.
"At this time, we can confirm that all individuals involved are youths," police said in a statement.
Riley said she was shocked when she saw the videos of the fight, but she wasn't surprised that her children were involved in an incident at the school.
“Over the past three years, I have asked the school to help me transfer my children out because they do not feel safe,” Riley said.
She said the school board denied her requests to move her children to different schools. She now plans to try to move them into the Catholic school system.
The Thames Valley District School Board told CBC News an investigation into the incident is underway.
"The school board takes incidents like these very seriously, and there is no place for violence inside or outside of TVDSB classrooms," board officials said.
Riley said school officials suspended all of the students involved for one day, including her children.
“Everybody knows that my children were just trying to defend themselves from an attack,” Riley said.
After videos of the incident began circulating on social media, Riley said the response has been mixed. Some people have blamed her children, she said, while others have offered overwhelming support.
Riley said the divide in public reaction highlights the need for parents to take responsibility for their children's behaviour.
“Parents need to take accountability for their children's actions, stop defending abusive behaviour, and work together to teach children not to bully,” she said.

stories.title: Man fighting for life, suspect still at large after OEV stabbing
stories.summary: London police say a man is in hospital with life-threatening injuries after a stabbing Monday evening in the city's Old East Village neighbourhood, as officers continue to search for the suspect.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London police say a man is in hospital with life-threatening injuries after a stabbing Monday evening in the city's Old East Village neighbourhood, as officers continue to search for the suspect.
· Posted: Sep 29, 2026 11:19 AM EDT | Last Updated: 36 minutes ago
London police say a man is in hospital with life-threatening injuries after a stabbing Monday evening in London's Old East Village neighbourhood.
Police were called to the north side of Dundas Street, just east of Adelaide Street, at around 6:15 p.m.
The injured man was found at the scene and taken to hospital by paramedics, where he remained Tuesday morning, police said.

stories.title: London police officer suspended after video shows alcohol, firearm inside police vehicle
stories.summary: A police officer in London, Ont., has been suspended with pay and Toronto police are investigating after a video surfaced showing members of the London Police Service entering an unmarked police vehicle with alcohol visible inside.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: A police officer in London, Ont., has been suspended with pay and Toronto police are investigating after a video surfaced showing members of the London Police Service entering an unmarked police vehicle with alcohol visible inside.
· Posted: Sep 29, 2026 6:28 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago

A police officer in London, Ont., has been suspended after a video showed members entering an unmarked police vehicle with alcohol visible inside and a service-issued firearm stored in what the force's chief called concerning circumstances.

In a statement issued Monday night, London police Chief Thai Truong said the matter has been reported to the Toronto Police Service for a criminal investigation into the handling and storage of the firearm.

He said the incident happened June 24 in Toronto as officers left a restaurant following a police funeral. Truong said he was made aware of the video late Monday afternoon and personally viewed it before taking action.
"The video shows those members leaving a restaurant and entering an unmarked police vehicle, with alcohol visible inside," Truong said in a statement.
Truong said the video also shows a service-issued firearm stored in "circumstances that raise concerns."
He said he directed that the matter be reported to Toronto police, which will investigate the circumstances surrounding the handling and storage of the firearm.
The funeral was for Toronto police Const. Marc Pinizzotto, who was fatally shot while investigating multiple shootings, including an incident at the U.S. Consulate.
One senior London police officer has been suspended with pay pending further investigation. The identity of the officer was not released.
Truong said the decision to suspend the officer with pay reflects the legal requirements governing police suspensions.
"At this stage of the investigation, the statutory criteria under the Community Safety and Policing Act that would permit me to suspend the officer without pay have not been met," he said.
He emphasized that the suspension is not a finding of criminal or professional misconduct.
Once the criminal investigation is complete, Truong said LPS will investigate the overall conduct of the members involved under the Community Safety and Policing Act.
He said police officers are expected to conduct themselves in a way that maintains public confidence, particularly those in leadership positions.
"Those expectations apply to every member of our Service and are especially important for those entrusted with leadership responsibilities," Truong said.
Truong declined to provide further details about the video or the firearm, saying he did not want to compromise the investigations.
He said London police will provide additional information when appropriate.
With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Mission Services welcomes $1.1M in donations, challenges London to match it
stories.summary: Mission Services of London has received $1.1 million from two donors to strengthen its addiction recovery aftercare program, and is challenging Londoners to match the contribution.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 29, 2026 12:13 AM | Last Updated: 10 hours ago
The RBJ Schlegel Family Foundation gave $500K, while another $600K came from an anonymous donor
Mission Services of London has received $1.1 million from two donors to strengthen its addiction recovery aftercare program and is challenging Londoners to match the contribution.
The RBJ Schlegel Family Foundation donated $500,000, while an anonymous donor contributed another $600,000.

Rob Schlegel, whose grandfather Wilfred helped establish Mission Services 75 years ago, was at Quintin Warner House on Monday to unveil a sign for the newly renamed Wilfred Schlegel Aftercare Program.
Schlegel said the donation is a way to continue his grandfather's legacy of helping people in the community.

"It's something that we've been trying to do in terms of creating and strengthening community," he said. "This is a key part of that, and we've tried to continue my grandfather's legacy and this is just another way of celebrating that."
He said he hopes the second donation will inspire others to contribute.
"We hope the community will step forward with dollars and really get the whole program onto a roll to take it to the next level."

The aftercare program operates out of Quintin Warner House and other locations across London. It provides an abstinence-based environment for men who have completed addiction treatment and are transitioning back into the community.
Participants receive help with life skills such as budgeting, nutrition and job searching, along with case management, individual treatment plans and crisis and relapse supports.
Executive director Ericka Ayala Ronson said the program also gives participants a network of people supporting them through recovery.
"Because recovery is a choice that a person makes every moment of every day," she said. "It is not a process that is ever truly done."
Before the donations, Mission Services had closed some beds in the aftercare program because of funding gaps, Ayala Ronson said.
The new funding will allow the organization to reopen those beds, bringing the program back to its full complement of 17.
The money will also allow Mission Services to provide additional staff support outside regular business hours, she said.
While the program receives funding from Ontario's Ministry of Health, Mission Services also relies on donations to support its work.
Mission Services and the two donors are now asking Londoners to match the $1.1-million contribution.
Ayala Ronson said the goal is to build on the momentum created by the donations and ensure the program can continue supporting people through the often-challenging transition after treatment.

"That's what Londoners do," Ayala Ronson said. "This is a caring community and I have no doubt that once this becomes known, folks will want to help neighbours in need and men who are taking the courageous steps to to live in a different way and have a fresh start."

stories.title: City of London to remove non-compliant election signs after 'significant volume of complaints'
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: September 28, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: September 28
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 28, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: September 28
Municipal compliance officers will be doing a sweep of the city this week
The City of London is cracking down on election signs that violate the rules. As a result, some candidates may see their signs removed in the coming week.
Bylaws outline where a candidate may place a sign, as well as size limits, when they can go up and when a candidate needs to remove it after the election.

In a communication sent to candidates, the city said it has received "a significant volume of complaints" about election sign violations, and that municipal compliance staff would conduct a sweep this week.
Some candidates welcomed the announcement.
"As someone who plays by the rules, it's hard to watch other people play without them," said Ward 14 candidate Sarah Lehman. "I'm kind of excited to see what this coming week is going to bring."
Lehman ran in 2022, so her team was familiar with the rules and has made sure to follow them, she said. Candidates are given a "
pretty great booklet " at the start of the campaign that explains the rules clearly, she added.
Still, Lehman said she has seen a lot of signs outside the ward boundary that the candidate is running in, which is prohibited.

She has also seen other rules being ignored as well, including placing signs within 100 metres of each other, putting up signs on boulevards, city property, parks and buildings that will be used as polling stations.
"I've seen signs on fire hall properties, hospital property ... so it seems like people maybe have not opened that little booklet that we all received when we signed up to run," she said.

Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis, who is seeking re-election as the councillor for Ward 2, said he has seen many violations in his own ward, from signs littering the boulevards to signs posted on polling stations.
He said he's glad to see the city taking action against it, adding, "we all have a responsibility to follow the rules, and they're just not being followed."
Lewis pointed out that sometimes it's just an honest mistake.
His own volunteers had involuntarily broken the rules by placing signs in the wrong place, Lewis said. He clarified the rules to them and moved the signs so they complied with the bylaws, he added.
But when mistakes continue to happen "hundreds of times", it becomes an issue, he said.

"We have to follow all kinds of rules as members of council," he said. "If you're not gonna respect something as basic as where the signs are allowed to be, then I do think it kind of undermines your credibility as a legitimate candidate."

While he said the majority of sign violations he sees around London are from first-time candidates, he also sees experienced candidates with "a number of signs" that don't belong where they have been placed.

Any signs the city removes in its sweep will be taken to the A.J. Tyler Operations Centre on Bathurst Street, according to the memo sent to candidates, where they will be kept for 30 days should any candidates wish to retrieve them.
