stories.title: Defendant says sorry to former UBC professor days before defamation trial to start
stories.summary: Vancouver - One of several accusers of former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway has issued a lengthy apology just days before a defamation trial in the case is expected to begin.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - One of several accusers of former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway says she now understands her conduct toward him was “serious and harmful” as she apologized just days before a defamation trial in the case is expected to begin.

Chelsea Rooney’s statement said she communicated serious and unproven allegations against Galloway and that she was involved in collecting complaints in an attempt to build a case against him.

“I recognize that statements and communications about allegations of this nature can cause profound harm to a person’s reputation, work, personal life, and family, and did in fact do so to Mr. Galloway. I deeply regret my role in contributing to the harm Mr. Galloway has suffered in this regard,” her statement said.

Much of Rooney’s apology appeared in the National Post newspaper on Saturday and the entire statement is posted on the website gallowayapologies.com , along with eight other apologies from those who say they regret communications or actions that accused Galloway of sexual assault.

Rooney, who is a defendant in the B.C. Supreme Court case due to start Monday, said she recognizes the communications she circulated about Galloway caused others to believe they were true, and she’s aware he firmly denies that he sexually assaulted a student only know as A.B.

The apology is the latest occurrence in what began as an accusation against Galloway in November 2015. He sued numerous people in 2018, alleging he was defamed with false sexual assault allegations by fellow professors, a former student and others who repeated the statements on social media and elsewhere.

The Supreme Court of Canada in 2024 dismissed an appeal by his accusers, clearing the way for the defamation trial.

Galloway is the author of novels including “The Cellist of Sarajevo” and “The Confabulist” and was a tenured professor and the chair of the creative writing program at UBC.

He was never charged, though he was fired from his job.

A report commission by the University of B.C. by retired B.C. Supreme Court judge Mary Ellen Boyd concluded the claims against Galloway were unsubstantiated.

Galloway’s lawyer, Dan Burnett, could not be immediately reached for comment on Saturday, although he said in an interview after the High Court’s ruling that his client’s “reputation and life were devastated by the criminal allegations.”

Rooney is among the defendants who fought the defamation case all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada, claiming the accusations of sexual assault must be protected speech, true or not, and “regardless of the circumstances in which the statement was published.”

B.C. Supreme Court Justice Elaine Adair said in her ruling on the case in 2021 that if the defendants arguments were true, “there would be no legal consequences of any kind” to publicly calling someone a rapist.

“It is difficult to see how something so extreme and potentially reckless would be in the public interest,” her decision said.

Rooney said in her statement that because she didn’t know the allegations were true, she should not have communicated them or posted them publicly on social media.

She said she has reflected on Galloway’s steadfast efforts over the years and she has come to better understand the basis for his position and his commitment to clearing his name and reputation.

“I should not have listened only to one side, or allowed that one-sided understanding to shape my communications, my tweets, or my participation in the process.”

Rooney said Galloway considered her a friend before A.B. made the allegations, and on multiple occasions went out of his way to help her, with nothing asked in return, she said.

“In my 2014 book, I thanked him as someone ‘who encouraged me to commit to writing at a very important time in my life.’ That was a true statement,” her apology said.

“I know that nothing I say now can undo the harm or give back the years affected by these events, but I am genuinely sorry for the part I played in causing that harm.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 3, 2026.

stories.title: 'Disturbing': Belleville, Ont., synagogue receives antisemitic flyers after shooting
stories.summary: The president of a Belleville, Ont., synagogue targeted in a shooting last month says he woke up Thursday morning to find antisemitic flyers had been distributed to the synagogue and the surrounding neighbourhoods.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Antisemitic flyers were distributed this week to a Belleville, Ont., synagogue targeted in a shooting last month as well as the surrounding neighbourhoods, the synagogue’s president said Friday.

Norman Weddum said he woke up Thursday morning to find four different flyers blaming Jewish people “for everything under the sun” had been distributed overnight to the Sons of Jacob synagogue and throughout the city’s east end.

“The number of flyers that were distributed and posted, it couldn’t have been done by one person,” he said.

Police said they’re aware of the flyers and are “actively investigating.”

Sons of Jacob congregants returned to the building for the first time since bullets pierced its stained-glass window.

Weddum said the incident is particularly “disturbing” in the wake of the Sept. 20 attack police have described as a thwarted mass killing of Jewish worshippers at the start of Yom Kippur, the holiest day on the Jewish calendar.

Police have said the shooter, 29-year-old Sean Ward, had multiple guns, large amounts of ammunition, gasoline and the motive to carry out an extended attack when he opened fire on an officer stationed outside the synagogue.

Const. Jeff Smith suffered multiple gunshot wounds but “stayed engaged” with the shooter and soon after, a second officer arrived and joined the shootout, they said.

No one inside the synagogue was hurt but Smith is expected to undergo multiple surgeries. Ward was fatally injured and died in hospital the next day.

The Canadian Armed Forces have since said that Ward was a former soldier who served for about five years before he was released from the military at the rank of corporal in 2022.

The shooting was widely condemned by politicians and prompted synagogues and Jewish institutions elsewhere to review their security measures.

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs and United Jewish Appeal Federation of Greater Toronto expressed gratitude Friday for the police’s quick response to the “troubling development” of the flyers.

“This is more than hateful rhetoric,” they said in a statement.

“Canada’s security services have sounded the alarm of the current situation in which acts of antisemitism become so prevalent and frequent that they create an environment that influence extremists toward more violent pathways.”

Weddum said Sons of Jacob has held some services since the attack and will hold another Friday evening.

“We’re trying to get people back into the building, and I think it’s helping,” he said in a phone interview Friday.

“They were traumatized, and it’s going to be a long healing process. But we are working on it, and we are not going to be stopped by it.”
